The student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿Ḥā Mīm. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing. The Forgiver of sin, the Acceptor of repentance, the Severe in punishment, the Possessor of bounty. There is no god but Him; to Him is the final return. None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve, so do not let their movement throughout the land deceive you.﴾ [Ghafir 1–4].

The Shaykh: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family, his companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾ The basmalah (the phrase "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful") is a verse of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, standing on its own. It is not part of the surah before it nor of the surah after it. It is recited at the beginning of every surah except one, which is Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). No report has come from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he placed a basmalah in it. For this reason the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, left it without a basmalah, since this was not established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

As for what has been said, that it was left without a basmalah because it was revealed with the sword, this is a false statement. That is not the reason. The sword, when it is used against the disbelievers, is a mercy and a means of gain, and it is well known that the sword used against the disbelievers is a mercy, intended to raise the word of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Then, as you can see, the basmalah is a sentence that contains no verb and no active participle. Rather, it consists of a prepositional phrase (jar wa majrur), an annexed noun and what it is annexed to (mudaf and mudaf ilayhi), and an adjective and what it describes (sifah and mawsuf). The jar is the bāʾ (ب), the majrur is the noun, the mudaf is the noun, the mudaf ilayhi is the word Allah, the mawsuf is Allah, and the sifah are al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm. Where, then, is the mutaʿallaq (the word the prepositional phrase depends on)? Every prepositional phrase or adverbial expression must have a mutaʿallaq, as the author of the poem on sentence structure (al-Jumal) said:

There must be an attachment for the prepositional particle
To a verb or to what carries its meaning, such as "murtaq" (climbing).
Exclude every redundant particle that has no governing effect,
Like the bāʾ, min, and the kāf, and also laʿalla.

So where is the mutaʿallaq of the basmalah, ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾? The best thing to say is that its mutaʿallaq is a verb placed after it, one that suits the act for which the basmalah was begun. So when we want to recite, we say the implied sense is: "In the name of Allah I recite." When we want to perform ablution, we say the implied sense is: "In the name of Allah I perform ablution." When we want to slaughter, we say the implied sense is: "In the name of Allah I slaughter." We estimated it as a verb rather than an active participle because the basic principle in governing is the verb. We estimated it as coming later for two reasons:

The first reason: to seek blessing by beginning with the name of Allah.

The second: to indicate restriction (ḥaṣr). When you place the governing word later and bring forward the governed element, this is evidence of restriction, since the known rule in rhetoric is that placing first what should come later indicates restriction.

We estimated it as suited to what the act begins with, because it points more clearly to the intended meaning. For example, if you said, "The implied sense is: In the name of Allah I begin," that would be correct. But begin with what? When we say we estimate it as a specific verb suited to what the act begins with, it becomes more clearly indicative of the intended meaning, and it is well known that what indicates the intended meaning more clearly is clearer in its meaning. This is the grammatical analysis (iʿrab) of this basmalah.

As for its meaning: the word "ism" (name) is a singular noun in annexation (mufrad mudaf), and every singular noun in annexation is general in meaning. Have you not seen the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you should count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [al-Nahl 18]. The word niʿmah (favour) is a singular in annexation, but it does not refer to one single favour, since a single favour could be counted. Rather, it refers to many favours, so it includes everything that Allah has bestowed upon the servant.

If a singular noun in annexation conveys generality, what is the meaning of our saying "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"? The meaning is: "By every name of Allah I do such and such," so you are now seeking help through every name of Allah for this act for which you have said the basmalah.

As for "ism," it has been said that it derives from "sumuw," which means elevation, because a name raises the named thing and makes it clear. It has also been said that it derives from "simah," which means a mark. Allah says: ﴿Their mark is on their faces﴾ [al-Fath 29], meaning their sign is on their faces. Whichever is the case, a name identifies what it names and distinguishes it from others.

The names of Allah, the Exalted, as we have passed over in the study of Tawhid, are not limited to a fixed number, as has come in the authentic hadith: "I ask You by every name that is Yours, which You have named Yourself with, or revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen that is with You."[[Recorded by Ahmad (4318) from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

As for "Allah," it is a proper name for the sacred and exalted Essence, which is Allah, the Exalted. The grammarians said: it is the most definite of the definite nouns (aʿraf al-maʿārif). As you know, they arranged definite nouns so that the most definite is the pronoun, then proper names. But this proper name (Allah) is the most definite of them, since it does not admit sharing in its reference, whereas other definite nouns may be shared.

As for His saying ﴿al-Raḥmān﴾, it is one of the names of Allah indicating vast mercy. "al-Raḥīm" is another name of Allah indicating the mercy that actually takes effect. So al-Raḥmān relates to description, and al-Raḥīm relates to action. That is, He is merciful in a comprehensive way and He shows mercy. Through this, the benefit of combining the two becomes clear. The benefit of combining them is to show that Allah's mercy is vast, which is conveyed by "al-Raḥmān," because the pattern faʿlān indicates fullness and breadth, as you say "shabʿān" (full, sated) and "rayyān" (fully watered) and the like. As for "al-Raḥīm," it is considered with regard to action, that is, delivering mercy to whomever Allah has decreed to show mercy to.

The basmalah has rulings. Among them: sometimes it is a condition for permissibility, as with saying the name of Allah over the slaughtered animal. Saying the name over the slaughtered animal is a condition for its permissibility, so that if one leaves out the name, even by forgetfulness, the animal is not lawful. Sometimes it is obligatory but not a condition, as with ablution according to some scholars. Saying the name in ablution is obligatory, but it is not a condition for validity, since if one leaves it out by forgetfulness, the ablution is still valid. Sometimes it is recommended in every matter of importance, as has come in the hadith: "Every important matter that is not begun with the name of Allah is cut off (abtar)," or in another version: "Every matter of importance (dhū bāl)."[[Recorded by al-Khatib in al-Jamiʿ (1210) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] That is, a matter of significance that is not begun with the name of Allah is abtar, meaning stripped of blessing. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) would begin his letters to kings and others with it, and so did the prophets before him, as Allah says in the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it reads: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Do not be haughty toward me, but come to me in submission﴾ [al-Naml 30–31].

Then Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ [Ghafir 1]. This is a word composed of two unconnected letters of the alphabet, the ḥāʾ and the mīm. For this reason we pronounce them by their letter names, not by their sounds. We do not say "Ḥam," but we say "ḥāʾ mīm" by their names. These are therefore two unconnected alphabetic letters from which human speech is composed. Does a meaning exist for these two letters?

The author says: "Allah knows best what He intends by it." That is, we do not know what He intended. Did He intend to establish a meaning, or did He not intend to establish a meaning? And did He intend a specific meaning or something else? The main point is that we entrust its knowledge to Allah. Our position on this is like our position on the other alphabetic letters with which some surahs begin.

However, the requirement that the Qur'an is in the Arabic language is that we say these are two unconnected alphabetic letters with no meaning. That is, we affirm definitively that they have no meaning, because the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, and the Arabic language does not assign meaning to individual alphabetic letters. This is narrated from Mujahid, the imam of the exegetes of his time, the era of the Successors (tabiʿun), and it is the truth. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shuʿaraʾ 193–195].

If someone says: an objection to this view is that there is something in the Qur'an that has no meaning and no benefit, being only disconnected letters without purpose.

We answer: the response to this objection is that Allah, the Exalted, spoke this way for a purpose and not for a meaning. That is, for a profound wisdom: this Qur'an which has defeated you, O eloquent Arabs, did not come with any new letters. Rather, it came with the same letters from which you compose your speech, and yet it defeated you. You were unable to arrange these letters to produce something like the Qur'an. If you were unable to do that, then your inability to grasp the meaning of these words is all the more so. This is what al-Zamakhshari mentioned in his tafsir and what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, approved, and what others also mentioned, either originally or by following others. The main point is that this is the correct view among the scholars who verify matters. It is that Allah sent them down to complete the challenge to these eloquent people who were unable to produce the like of the Qur'an, or even a part of it. They supported this view by noting that Allah never began a surah with alphabetic letters without mentioning the Qur'an after them, except rarely.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾ [Ghafir 2], meaning the Qur'an. The word "al-Kitāb" here refers to the Qur'an, although "kitāb" is a generic noun that could carry the definite article to indicate the whole category, thereby including every book. But the apparent meaning is what the author stated, because the purpose here is to establish that this Qur'an, which was revealed to those who deny it, comes from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for the author's saying "subject" (mubtada'), he means "tanzil" (revelation). It is the subject, and the subject needs a predicate. The predicate is His saying ﴿from Allah﴾. For this reason the commentator said: "﴿from Allah﴾ is its predicate." The revelation of the Book is from Allah, not from anyone else.

﴿al-ʿAzīz﴾: the author said: "in His dominion." ﴿al-ʿAlīm﴾: "in His creation." Al-ʿAzīz means the one possessing might. It has already been mentioned that the might of Allah is divided into how many categories? Three: the might of rank (ʿizzat al-qadr), the might of subjugation (ʿizzat al-qahr), and the might of invulnerability (ʿizzat al-imtinaʿ). This is so in every place in which al-ʿAzīz appears; that is its meaning, meaning He is possessor of might. Might is of three categories: the might of rank, meaning He possesses nobility and sovereignty; the might of subjugation, meaning He possesses dominance and authority; and the might of invulnerability, meaning He is beyond every deficiency and defect. The evidence for these three meanings and an explanation of their derivation has already been given. Therefore the author's statement "al-ʿAzīz in His dominion" is deficient, because he limited it to the meaning of dominance only. The correct view is what we have mentioned to you.

As for al-ʿAlīm, the author said "in His creation." Al-ʿAlīm means the one possessing knowledge. The knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, is not limited, neither in beginning, nor in end, nor in quantity. The knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, is vast and encompasses everything. The knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, is eternal (azali), meaning no ignorance has preceded it. The knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, is everlasting (abadi), meaning no forgetfulness reaches it. So the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, becomes vast and comprehensive in time and in manner. In time, meaning in the future and in the past; and in manner, meaning it encompasses everything that can be known.

﴿Forgiver of sin﴾ [Ghafir 3] for the believers, ﴿Acceptor of repentance﴾ for them, ﴿Severe in punishment﴾ for the disbelievers. The phrase ﴿Forgiver of sin﴾: al-Ghafr is concealment together with protection. From it comes al-Mighfar, which is what is put on the head during war to protect against arrows. As you see, the mighfar is a covering, so it combines concealment and protection. Sin (dhanb) is disobedience. It is said: "adhnaba al-rajul" when he disobeyed. The meaning of "Forgiver of sin" is that He conceals it and overlooks it. The author's statement "for the believers" has a clear problem, because the forgiveness of sin includes both believers and non-believers. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, they will be forgiven what has already passed﴾ [al-Anfal 38]. So He is the Forgiver of sin for everyone who turns in repentance to Allah and asks for forgiveness.

﴿Acceptor of repentance﴾: its meaning is that whoever repents to Allah, Allah accepts his repentance. Al-Tawb means returning to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His disobedience to His obedience. The author said "for them." For whom? "For the believers." This is also not correct, since repentance is accepted from both believers and disbelievers. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said about the polytheists: ﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, then they are your brothers in religion﴾ [al-Tawbah 11]. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after. Those - Allah will accept their repentance; and ever is Allah Knowing and Wise. And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Nisa' 17–18]. He said "while they are disbelievers." So if they repented before that, it would have been accepted. Thus it becomes clear that the view of the author, may Allah have mercy on him, which restricts this to believers, is a deficiency.

He said: "a verbal noun" (maṣdar). Which one is it, qabil or al-tawb? Qabil is an active participle, so the verbal noun is al-tawb.

﴿Severe in punishment﴾ for the disbelievers. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, seems to restrict the Forgiver and the Acceptor to the believers, because of His saying ﴿Severe in punishment﴾, since severity of punishment is only for the disbelievers. However, there is something to consider in this, because the intention here is to mention the attribute of Allah, the Exalted, that He combines grace and justice: grace in being Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance, and justice in being Severe in punishment. Severe punishment from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for whoever deserves it, is justice, since Allah has informed us and made clear that whoever does such and such, He will punish with severe punishment. So when a person does what he was threatened with severe punishment for, he is the one who chose it for himself, and Allah's treatment of him with it is justice.

His saying: "meaning making it severe" (ay mushaddidihi). Pay attention to this explanation, "meaning making it severe." Why did he turn away from the apparent meaning of the verse, which indicates that He Himself is severe in punishment? Yes: because they deny the attributes, the Ashʿarites, and "making severe" (tashdid) is an act separate from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Now let us look: according to the author's statement, "shadid" would mean "mushaddid" (one who makes severe). We may demand and say: does the pattern fʿīl come with the meaning of mufʿil?

The answer: yes, the pattern faʿīl comes with the meaning of mufʿil, as in the statement of the poet:

Is it from Rayhanah, the summoner, the hearer,
That keeps me sleepless while my companions are asleep?

Here "al-samīʿ" means "al-musmiʿ" (the one who makes hear). The summoner who makes me hear keeps me awake, while my companions lie sleeping. So regarding the wording, there is no objection to the author's taking faʿīl to mean mufʿil, because that is attested in the Arabic language. But regarding the meaning, there is a problem, because the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Severe in punishment﴾ is that His own punishment is severe, and that is indeed so. If the punishment is severe, then the pain of the one punished must also be severe.

The word ʿiqāb (punishment) is derived from al-muʿāqabah, which is recompense. Recompense is called ʿiqāb because it follows (taʿqub) the deed. But it is generally mentioned in what is bad, not in what is good.

﴿Severe in punishment, Possessor of bounty; there is no god but Him; to Him is the final return﴾. The word dhī (possessor) means "owner," and it is in the genitive by the yāʾ, standing in for the kasrah, because it is one of the five nouns. As for ﴿al-Ṭawl﴾, the author says: "meaning wide bestowal." This ṭawl is what Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford (ṭawlan) to marry free believing women﴾ [al-Nisa' 25], and so on. So ṭawl means wide wealth. Part of complete wealth is that one is a bestower, and Allah, the Exalted, is the bestower of vast wealth, ﴿Possessor of bounty﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verses 1–3 (part 2 of 4):

He said: "He is described constantly by each of these attributes, so the idafah (genitive construction) of the derived noun to the definite is like the last one." Here there are several attributes: ﴿the Forgiver of sin, the Acceptor of repentance, the Severe in punishment, the Possessor of bounty﴾. How many are these? These are four. The last one is not a derived noun, since ﴿dhi﴾ (possessor of) is not derived, but it is interpreted as a derived noun. As for what comes before it, "severe in punishment," "acceptor of repentance," and "forgiver of sin," these are derived nouns. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, held that these attributes are not meant to establish the meaning from which they are derived, but are only for definition. The complete deficiency of this statement is evident. How can we make a derived noun merely a means of definition? How can we say "forgiver of sin" and mean by it only a definition of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and not that He forgives, nor that He accepts, nor that He is severe in punishment? This is extremely deficient, and it is not valid to interpret the words of Allah, the Exalted, in this way. Rather, we say: "Forgiver" is derived from forgiveness (ghafr), and it is an intended attribute, not meant for definition. The same applies to "acceptor of repentance" and "severe in punishment."

The author's words, "described constantly by each of these attributes," were said to avoid affirming the attributes of action (sifat al-af'al, attributes relating to Allah's acts), because if you say "forgiver" meaning "He forgives," it becomes an attribute of action connected to His will.

According to the Ash'arites (al-Ash'ariyyah) and others among the mutakallimun (scholastic theologians), it is impossible to describe Allah, the Exalted, with an attribute that is an action. It is not possible. Why? They said: because an action indicates occurrence (huduth), and occurrence cannot be in the Eternal (al-qadim); occurrence can only be by something that occurs. We have already explained the falsity of this view. So the correct position is that "forgiver" and "acceptor" are two attributes of action. As for "severe in punishment," it is also an attribute of action, because the meaning is "His punishment is severe," so it is an example of attributing an attribute to what it qualifies (idafat al-sifah ila al-mawsuf), meaning that His punishment is severe. Therefore it is, as explained earlier, an attribute of action.

As for "Possessor of bounty," if we say its meaning is "possessor of vast wealth," then it is an attribute of the Essence (sifat al-dhat). If we say it means "vast bestowal," then it is an attribute of action.

﴿To Him is the final return﴾, that is, the destination (al-marji'). The sentence is a declarative sentence consisting of a subject and a predicate. Is the predicate in it placed first or last? It is placed first. When the predicate is placed first, it conveys restriction and limitation (al-takhsis wa al-hasr).

﴿To Him﴾, that is, to Allah alone, ﴿is the final return﴾, the destination. Does His saying ﴿To Him is the final return﴾ mean the destination in every matter, or the destination after death? The answer is that the destination is to Him in every matter. So the return is to Him in judging between people, the return is to Him in managing affairs, the return is to Him after death, the return is to Him in everything. ﴿He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, and He is Knowing of all things﴾ (al-Hadid 3).

Student: We mentioned that "shadid" (severe) is an attribute of action.

Shaykh: How is it an attribute of action?

Student: Because the author fled from (...).

Shaykh: No. It is an attribute of His act, not an attribute of action in the sense you said. It is an attribute of Allah's act: the punishment itself is severe. He made "severe" (mushaddid) something separate from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Can we not say that these disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) at the beginning of the surahs fall under what Ibn 'Abbas said: that the Qur'an has four categories, and the fourth is what no one knows except Allah?

Shaykh: No. That applies according to the author's view. As for the view we preferred, it is known that they have no meaning, meaning that they are among what lies within our knowledge as having no meaning.

Student: The author's words "mushaddid" (...).

Shaykh: No, because "mushaddid" means "one who makes it severe." It is like "qadir" (capable). The attribute reverts, according to the Ash'arite school, to power (qudrah), and according to the Maturidi school (al-Maturidiyyah) to creation (al-khalq), because the Maturidiyyah affirm creation and bringing into being (al-takwin), unlike the Ash'arites.

Student: Regarding His saying ﴿the Acceptor of repentance﴾ (...).

Shaykh: No, these are descriptions. ﴿Forgiver of sin﴾ is a description, and that is why it comes in the form of the active participle. The name "al-Ghafur" (the Most Forgiving), which is one of His names, comes in the intensive form (sighat al-mubalaghah).

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Did you all hear the question? He asks: how do we reconcile the statement that the names of Allah cannot be counted with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever counts them enters Paradise"?[1]

The answer to that: the answer... is it "al-jawab 'an dhalik" or "al-jawab 'ala dhalik"? If the questioner is inquiring, say "al-jawab 'ala dhalik" (the answer to that). If he is raising an objection, meaning contradicting, say "al-jawab 'an dhalik" (the answer to that, in refutation). Therefore the answer "an dhalik" comes in response to someone who objects to you, while "ala dhalik" is in response to someone who seeks guidance. Now, regarding the brother's question, should we say "al-jawab 'ala dhalik" or "an dhalik"? "Ala dhalik," out of charitable assumption. Otherwise, if someone came intending to object, we would say "al-jawab 'an dhalik." But now we say: the answer to that is that the words of the Prophet ﷺ, like the words of Allah, never contradict. Since it is established from him that he said: "...or You have kept it with You in the knowledge of the unseen," we know that among the names of Allah there are some that cannot be reached and cannot be comprehended, because what Allah has kept to Himself cannot be known by us. Then it is necessary to say that the meaning of the saying "Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever counts them enters Paradise" is: among His names are ninety-nine, whoever counts them enters Paradise. So the clause "whoever counts them" is a description of the word "names" and not an independent new sentence. The meaning of "Allah has ninety-nine names" is described as: whoever counts them enters Paradise. He has other names, but choose from them ninety-nine; if you count them, you enter Paradise. What does counting them mean? Does it mean reciting them verbally? No. Counting them means knowing them verbally and in meaning, and worshipping Allah according to what they require, that is, knowing their wording and meaning and worshipping Allah, the Exalted, according to their requirements.

Student: Shaykh, the punishment of Allah is the Fire, and it seems that it is the Fire that is described as severe. How then do we describe Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, with it?

Shaykh: He Himself is severe in punishment. For example, if I say "so-and-so is strong in striking," that means his striking that occurs from him is strong. The punishment that occurs from him is severe.

Student: (...) the described thing is the punishment?

Shaykh: What is described is the severity of His punishment, which is His own. As for what He punishes with, that is something else. There is the punishment, the thing with which one is punished, and the one punished upon whom the punishment falls. If you punish a person by striking him, the striking is the thing by which he is punished, but the striker's striking is his attribute, which is his punishment.

* * *

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾. ﴿Ha Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing. Forgiver of sin, Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment, Possessor of bounty. There is no god but Him; to Him is the final return. None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve, so let not their movement throughout the land deceive you. The people of Noah denied before them, and the factions after them, and every nation plotted against their messenger to seize him, and they argued with falsehood to refute the truth thereby, so I seized them, and how was My punishment! Thus the word of your Lord was fulfilled against those who disbelieve, that they are the companions of the Fire﴾ (Ghafir 1–6).

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, ﴿Ha Mim﴾, and so on. The basmalah is a prepositional phrase with a genitive, and an idafah and its genitive, and an attribute and its qualified noun. Where is its complement (muta'alliq), that is, what is it connected to?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, from the standpoint of i'rab (grammatical inflection)?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: It is connected to a deleted verb placed later, suitable to the context. Good. Now, if I want to recite, how do you estimate this deleted word?

Student: "Bismillah aqra'" (In the name of Allah I read).

Shaykh: "Bismillah aqra'," well done. In the Noble Qur'an: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ (al-'Alaq 1). He used "iqra'" (read). Those who estimated "abtadi'" (I begin), is their estimate correct or weaker?

Student: No.

Shaykh: Why?

Student: Because the estimated verb must be suitable to the context.

Shaykh: It is not "must," that is not what this is.

Student: So that it is more appropriate.

Shaykh: More appropriate, meaning suitable to the context.

Student: Their estimate is correct, but it is better that their estimate be more indicative (adall).

Shaykh: Exactly. Their estimate is correct, but that the verb be suitable indicates the intended meaning more clearly, because if you say "abtadi'" (I begin), begin with what? But if you estimate it as "aqra'" (I read), "atawadda'" (I perform ablution), "aghtasil" (I bathe), and similar, it indicates the intended meaning better.

There is also another point that has become clear to us: if you say "Bismillah abtadi'," the basmalah applies only to the beginning. If you say "Bismillah aqra'," the basmalah applies to the whole action. This benefit is far greater than the benefit of suitability for specification. If you say "Bismillah abtadi'," the basmalah applies only to the beginning. If you say "Bismillah aqra'," the basmalah applies to the whole act. Likewise, if you say "Bismillah atawadda'," the basmalah applies to the entire act from beginning to end, unlike when you say "Bismillah abtadi'," where the basmalah applies only to the beginning.

Is the surah of Ghafir Meccan or Medinan?

Student: Meccan. We infer that from the context of the surah itself (...).

Shaykh: It is Meccan. Every surah that begins with the letters of the alphabet is Meccan except al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran.

So what is the Meccan and the Medinan?

Student: The Meccan is what was revealed in Mecca.

Shaykh: Then ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ (al-Ma'idah 3) is Meccan, since it was revealed on the Day of 'Arafah?

Student: (...) it was revealed before the Hijrah.

Shaykh: What was revealed before the Hijrah is Meccan, and what was revealed after it is Medinan. This is the most preferred of the opinions: that what was revealed before the Hijrah is Meccan, and what was revealed after it is Medinan, even if it was revealed in Mecca.

What is the preferred opinion regarding the alphabetic letters with which surahs begin? "Ha Mim." What is the preferred opinion about them?

Student: The author said: "Allah knows best what He means by them."

Yes, the author said: "Allah knows best what He means by them." But did we not say that it is preferred?

Student: The implication of the language is that they are two alphabetic letters.

Shaykh: And they have no meaning in themselves.

What is the basis for our preferring this view? The Qur'an is Arabic, revealed in the Arabic language. Does the implication of Arabic speech indicate that these letters, in this context, have no semantic meaning? Since the Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and the language of the Arabs implies that these letters have no meaning? But we mentioned that they have a purpose. What is it?

Student: It is the challenge to the Arabs: the Qur'an was revealed and composed with the very letters you speak, yet they were unable to produce its like, which shows that it is from Allah, the Exalted.

Shaykh: Correct. That is why we find that every surah that begins with these letters is followed by a mention of the Qur'an. Correct.

What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ (Ghafir 2)?

Student: This Book, the Qur'an, was sent down from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Shaykh: Yes, its revelation is from Allah, not from anyone else.

What about the choice of the words ﴿the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾, or the choice of these two names over others in this surah? In Fussilat He said: ﴿A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ (Fussilat 2). Here He said: ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: And Fussilat is Meccan.

Student: Because this fits the variation between might at times and mercy at times.

Shaykh: We will put that among the benefits, better.

What is the meaning of: ﴿Possessor of bounty﴾?

Student: "Dhi" means possessor of, of vast wealth.

Shaykh: Vast wealth, and from it follows generosity and kindness.

His saying: ﴿To Him is the final return﴾, the return of what?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: The return of everything. Good. Is there evidence that the return here is the return of everything?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No.

Student: That Allah, the Exalted...

Shaykh: No, I do not want a reason. I want evidence from the verse that the return of everything is to Allah.

Student: "And to Him all affairs are returned."

Shaykh: The same thing.

Student: ﴿And to Him the whole matter is returned﴾ (Hud 123).

Shaykh: ﴿And to Him the whole matter is returned﴾ (Hud 123), and ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾ (al-Baqarah 210).

Now let us return to the benefits of these two verses. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Ha Mim﴾ (Ghafir 1).

* Among its benefits: the Qur'an consists of letters through which Allah spoke, so there is a refutation of the Ash'arites and those who follow their path, who say that the speech of Allah is the meaning that subsists in the self, and that Allah does not speak with letters and sound, but creates letters and sounds that are heard as an expression of what is in His self. The reality of this view is the denial of speech, because what is in the self of ordered knowledge is not speech, but knowledge. It is knowledge, not speech. Understood?

The refutation of them is known from the books of creed. Among them: when speech is mentioned without qualification, it means speech of the tongue. When the speech of the self is intended, it is specified, as in: ﴿And they say to themselves, "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?"﴾ (al-Mujadilah 8), and as in: "Allah has overlooked for my community what they whisper to themselves" (agreed upon).[2]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the exaltedness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is derived from His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah﴾ (Ghafir 2), because descent (nuzul) only occurs from above.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Qur'an is the speech of Allah and not the speech of anyone else, because of His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah﴾ (Ghafir 2). That is because what Allah says He sent down falls into two categories: either it is substances that subsist by themselves, and these are created, or it is attributes that subsist only through something else, and these are not created. Do you understand? An example of what Allah attributed sending down to Himself, and which is a substance subsisting by itself, is His saying: ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might﴾ (al-Hadid 25). Is iron created or not created? Good. ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ (al-Zumar 6), substances subsisting by themselves, created. ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing﴾ (al-A'raf 26), created. So whatever Allah attributes its sending down to Himself, if it is a substance subsisting by itself, it is created; otherwise it is not created. Is the Qur'an a substance subsisting by itself, or speech that subsists only through something else? The second. Therefore it is not created.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the description of the Noble Qur'an as "the Book." Why was it described as a Book?

We say: first, because it is written, and it is written in the copies in our hands.

Second: it is in scrolls in the hands of the angels: ﴿So whoever wills, remembers it, in honored scrolls﴾ (Abasa 12–13).

Third: it is written in the Preserved Tablet: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet﴾ (al-Buruj 21–22). Accordingly, "kitab" means "maktub" (written). Then we ask: does the pattern fa'al come in the sense of maf'ul (passive)? We say often: such as "ghirас" meaning "maghrus" (planted), "bina'" meaning "mabni" (built), "firash" meaning "mafrush" (spread), and similar.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming three names of Allah: Allah, al-'Aziz (the Mighty), and al-'Alim (the All-Knowing): ﴿from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ (Ghafir 2). And affirming the attributes indicated by these names: "Allah" indicates divinity (uluhiyyah), "al-'Aziz" indicates might ('izzah), and "al-'Alim" indicates knowledge ('ilm).

Know that each of Allah's names includes an attribute, but not every attribute yields a derived name. That is why we say that the attributes are broader than the names.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verses 1–3 (part 3 of 4):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the mention of names suited to the context. That is, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, mentions from His names those that fit the context. This surah speaks of those who denied the messengers and of the destruction and retribution that befell them. Which names fit this? The "Mighty" (al-'Aziz), which implies dominance and seizing. Therefore "the Mighty" is mentioned here, and "the All-Knowing" (al-'Alim) comes to indicate that, in His might, He seized these deniers, and in His knowledge He sent down the Books and knew how to seize these deniers.

* Among the benefits of the verse that follows, the second verse: Allah, Majestic and Exalted, forgives all sins. This is based on His saying ﴿the Forgiver of sin﴾ [Ghafir 3]. "Sin" here is singular with the definite article (al-), so it is general, because a singular noun with the definite article is general, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr 2], meaning every human being.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the encouragement to do what brings forgiveness. The reason is that Allah did not inform us that He is the Forgiver of sin merely so that we would know that He forgives, but so that we would place ourselves in the way of His forgiveness. So what are the means by which forgiveness is obtained?

The means are many. Among them is seeking forgiveness, saying "O Allah, forgive me." Among them are righteous deeds by which Allah expiates sins. Among them is kindness to creation. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, forgave a prostitute because she gave water to a thirsty dog. So the means of forgiveness are many. He also forgave a man who found a tree on the road harming people and removed it, and Allah forgave him. The main point is that we should place ourselves in the way of the means of forgiveness, because that is what His saying ﴿the Forgiver of sin﴾ requires.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse is that He accepts the repentance (tawbah, turning back to Allah) of His servants. However, nothing is accepted unless it conforms to the requirements of the Shari'ah, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our matter, it is rejected." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari, in a similar wording (2697), and Muslim, with this wording (1718/18), from the hadith of 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her.] So what is repentance that conforms to the requirements of the Shari'ah?

Repentance that conforms to the requirements of the Shari'ah is that which combines five matters, known as the conditions of repentance:

The first: sincerity to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, meaning that what moves a person to repent is his sincerity to Allah, the desire to draw near to Him and to flee from His punishment. Thus, he is not moved to repent by seeking the approval of people or by attaining status and leadership. Rather, sincerity to Allah moves him.

The second: regret for committing the sin. A person must feel the emotion of remorse and anguish over what he has done. Remorse is necessary, because the remorse by which the reality of a person's return to Allah becomes evident is that the sin has affected his soul, so he regrets what he did. It may be said: remorse is an emotion, and emotions come involuntarily, like anger, for example, or sorrow over an event. The answer is that what is meant by remorse here is the heart's anguish. It is an emotion that arises in a person, unlike an emotion whose cause comes from outside. This is something a person may not be able to change after it has occurred.

The third condition: abandoning the sin and separating oneself from it. If someone repents while still persisting in it, his repentance resembles mockery. How can one who eats pork say, "I ask Allah's forgiveness, and I ask Allah to make my food pure"?! What is this?! Is this acceptable or not? He is eating, chewing the meat well, and saying, "I ask Allah's forgiveness for eating pork, and I ask Allah to make my food pure." This is very much like one who mocks.

If a man forbids you from something and finds you doing that very thing, while you say, "I hope you will excuse me," or something similar, and yet you are eating and he tells you, "Do not eat," and you keep eating, the one who addressed you will say, "You are mocking me and ridiculing me." So there is no repentance with persistence. The sin must be abandoned.

If the sin was against Allah, abandoning it is easy. But if the sin was against someone other than Allah, meaning you wronged someone else, how does one renounce it?

We say: if it was wealth, then renouncing it means returning it to its owner by whatever means possible. If the owner has died, then return it to his heirs. If you do not know them, then give it to the public treasury (bayt al-mal). Or if the public treasury is not well-managed, or it is feared that it will be wasted, then give it in charity on behalf of its owner. How many stages are there now? Four: to its owner, to his heirs, to the public treasury if you do not know them, or give it in charity. Which is preferable, the public treasury or charity? Generally, charity is preferable, especially in our time, when the public treasury may not be managed by the ruler in a way that pleases.

If it was an aggression against a person's body, not wealth, then repentance from it is to enable the one who was wronged to exact retaliation (qisas) from you. For example, if you attacked someone and beat him, go to him and say, "I attacked you and beat you; beat me as I beat you." This is what the Prophet (ﷺ) did with the man whom the Prophet (ﷺ) struck when he saw him ahead of the row. The man said, "Let me take retaliation, O Messenger of Allah." So the Prophet (ﷺ) uncovered his stomach so that he could be retaliated against. [Al-Bayhaqi (16020) narrated from Sawad ibn 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while I was perfumed with saffron. When he saw me, he said to me: "O Sawad ibn 'Amr, saffron and safflower? Did I not forbid saffron?" And he poked me in my stomach with a stick in his hand, and it hurt me. I said: "O Messenger of Allah, retaliation!" He said: "Retaliation." So he uncovered his stomach for me, and I began to kiss it. Then I said: "O Messenger of Allah! Let me leave it as an intercession for me on the Day of Resurrection."] So what did the man do? He kissed it. Here is the Prophet (ﷺ), the most noble of creation and the most beloved of people to his followers, enabling him to take retaliation against him. These are two: wealth and the body.

If it was an attack on someone's honour, meaning you slandered someone by backbiting him or insulting him. The difference between backbiting (ghibah) and insult (sabb) is that insult is face-to-face, while backbiting is in his absence. So if you mention your brother with what he dislikes while he is absent, it is backbiting; if he is present, it is insult. The repentance from this is that you seek his pardon (istihlal). So if you say, "Insult me as I insulted you," is that valid or not? It is not valid, because this is an additional wrong against yourself. Rather, seek his pardon. This applies if it was an insult, since he knows about it. If it was backbiting, must you seek his pardon by going to him and saying, "I backbit you, so excuse me, forgive me"?

The answer: some scholars said: yes, you must go to him and say, "I backbit you, so excuse me, pardon me." Other scholars said: it is not required to seek his pardon; it is sufficient to ask Allah's forgiveness for him, as is mentioned in a hadith, although it is weak: "The expiation of one whom you have backbitten is that you ask forgiveness for him." [Al-Bayhaqi in al-Da'awat (575) from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the expiation for backbiting is that you ask forgiveness for the one you backbit; you say: O Allah, forgive us and him." Al-Bayhaqi said: there is weakness in this chain, and Allah knows best.] Ask forgiveness for him and praise him with what he deserves in the places where you backbit him, so that good deeds erase bad deeds. This opinion is more correct, because it involves freedom from the wrong and avoids confusion. If you go to him and say, "I backbit you, so pardon me," he may not be convinced by whatever wording of backbiting you use. If you say, "I said about you that you are stingy," he may say, "You said he is stingy and cowardly, didn't you?" Perhaps Satan says this to him, and he refuses to pardon you. So if he did not hear it, praise Allah for that, ask forgiveness for him, and praise him with what he deserves in the places where you backbit him. In this way you are safe from sin. This is the manner of renouncing a sin when it concerns the rights of someone other than Allah.

Here is a question: some people owe a financial right to a person, either because they stole it or denied it or something similar. Then this wrongdoer repents and goes to the rightful owner and says, "Take your right," but the owner refuses to take it. What should he do? This happens often: the owner has harboured resentment toward this wrongdoer who wronged him and refuses to accept. So what should be done? Do we say that his right has then lapsed, the wrongdoer's repentance is valid, and if the owner later asks for his right he will be given it, and if he does not ask, the wrongdoer is clear?

We say: this situation is judged according to the Shari'ah principles. The Shari'ah principles require that this person who owes the right is cleared, because Allah says ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 286], and this is within his capacity. He presented the right to its owner and said, "Take it." He said, "No, I will not take it; you wronged me at first, and I will not accept from you." The one who refused to accept is the one who erred and committed a wrong, because when a person's brother apologizes to him, he should accept his apology. But it is this one who has now committed the wrong. So we say to this man: your obligation is now cleared. Leave the dirhams with you; if a day comes when he asks, give them to him. If he dies, must the wrongdoer give them to his heirs?

The answer: there is consideration in this. The man who was wronged did not accept this money, and it did not enter into his ownership. If he did not accept it and it did not enter his ownership, how would it pass to his heirs? Inheritance requires that property transfer from the deceased. Did this deceased person accept this money?

It may be said: the principle is that it is his property, so it must be returned to his heirs. This latter view is more cautious, but its obligation is debatable, because the one who wronged and wanted to return it says, "I gave the man, and he refused to take possession of it, so how would it pass to the heirs?" Nevertheless, we say: the more cautious and preferable course is that he return it to the heirs in order to be free of it. But if it is assumed that he has no heirs, or his heirs are unknown, then this repentant man has fulfilled his obligation. These are three conditions.

The fourth condition: that he resolves not to return to the sin, or not to return to the sin. The first or the second? The first: that he resolves not to return to the sin. Or is the condition "not to return to the sin"?

The first? What is the difference between them? The difference is that if we say the condition is "not to return," and then he returns, the first repentance is void. But if we say the condition is "resolving not to return," and he resolved not to return, and then he returned, the first repentance remains valid, and he must repent again for the new sin. In any case, the condition is the resolve not to return in the future. If he returns, he must repent again: he repents, returns, repents, returns, repents.

If someone says: is it not established in the authentic collection that the Prophet (ﷺ) reported "that a man committed a sin and repented, then committed a sin and repented, then committed a sin and repented, then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: My servant knows that he has a Lord who forgives sin and seizes for it. I have forgiven My servant, so let him do what he wishes"? [Al-Bukhari (7507) and Muslim, with this wording (2758/29), both with their chains from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), relating from his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, who said: "A servant committed a sin and said: O Allah, forgive my sin. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: My servant committed a sin and knew that He has a Lord who forgives sin and seizes for sin. Then he returned and sinned, and said: O Lord, forgive my sin. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: My servant committed a sin and knew that He has a Lord who forgives sin and seizes for sin. Then he returned and sinned, and said: O Lord, forgive my sin. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: My servant committed a sin, and knew that He has a Lord who forgives sin and seizes for sin. Do what you wish, for I have forgiven you."] Does this mean that if a person repeatedly commits sin while seeking forgiveness, he will be forgiven?

The answer: yes, however many times he sins and then seeks forgiveness, he will be forgiven.

But if someone says: the apparent meaning of the hadith "let him do what he wishes" means "let him disobey Allah," we say: this does not stand, because it contradicts the many texts indicating that every sin requires repentance, except for one group from this Ummah, namely the people of Badr, who do not need repentance from sin. Allah looked upon them and said: "Do what you wish, for I have forgiven you." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4890) and Muslim (2494/161), from the hadith of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.]

The fifth condition: that the repentance be made at the time when repentance is accepted, which is before the sun rises from the west and before the appointed time of death arrives. The first applies to everyone: there is no repentance for anyone once the sun rises from the west, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Migration does not cease until repentance ceases, and repentance does not cease until the sun rises from its west." [Abu Dawud (2479), from the hadith of Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, and his wording is: "Migration will not cease until repentance ceases, and repentance will not cease until the sun rises from the west."] This is supported by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before, or had not earned good through its faith﴾ [al-An'am 158]. What is meant by "some of the signs" is the sun rising from the west.

The second: that repentance be before the appointed time of death arrives. If the appointed time arrives, repentance does not benefit, based on the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now"﴾ [al-Nisa' 18]. Those have no repentance. A practical example of this is that when Pharaoh was overtaken by drowning, he said: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims﴾ [Yunus 90]. He was told: ﴿Now?﴾ [you believe] ﴿and you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters. So today We will save you in your body﴾ [Yunus 91–92], not out of mercy toward you, but ﴿so that you may be a sign for those who come after you﴾. As for your soul, there is no salvation for it. Allah saved only his body, because he had terrified the Children of Israel, and they could hardly believe he had perished until they saw him, and then they would be reassured. Therefore Allah saved him in his body so that they could see him.

Is it a condition that a person not be persisting in another sin? That is, suppose he repented from drinking alcohol but still persists in fornication, may Allah protect us. Is his repentance from drinking alcohol valid?

On this there is disagreement. Some scholars say: repentance from one sin is not valid while persisting in another sin.

Others say: rather, it is valid, because each sin has its own gravity. Others say: if the sin he persists in is of the same kind as the one he repented from, then the repentance is not valid. For example, a man who repents from fornication but lets his gaze roam over what is forbidden to see: his repentance from fornication is not valid. Or a man who repents from looking at what is forbidden but has not repented from forbidden touching: his repentance is also not accepted.

Some scholars say: it is accepted absolutely. If one repents from a sin, Allah accepts his repentance from that sin, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is the Just Judge, and His mercy precedes His wrath. This man has multiple wrongs, and he repented from one of them, so let him be a repentant one. This is the more correct view. However, the absolute description of "one who repents" is not applied to this repentant person, because his repentance is restricted; that is, he does not deserve the description of the repentant in an unqualified sense. So he is not included in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 222], because this man cannot be described as repentant in an unqualified way. Rather, he is repentant from one sin while committing another. This view is the one in which the evidences converge: it is said that the absolute description is not deserved by one who repents from one sin while persisting in another, but describing him as repentant in a restricted sense is correct.

* Student: (...) like fornication.
* Shaykh: No, fornication does not fall under this. Say: like theft.
* Student: And his hand was cut off (...).
* Shaykh: If his hand is cut off, the property must still be returned to its owner. We say: as regards the right of Allah, the prescribed punishment (hadd) has been carried out on him, but the property must still reach its owner.
* Student: Alright, O Shaykh, fornication is not something shared...
* Shaykh: In fact, fornication is shared between the doer and the one to whom it is done. Even the one to whom it is done derives pleasure and feels desire. Yes, if we say it was under compulsion, then this is valid, it is aggression, and seeking his pardon is necessary.
* Student: (...) the right of Allah?
* Shaykh: The right of Allah: we establish the prescribed punishment upon him. The right of the servants, which is compulsion and aggression against them: seeking their pardon is necessary.

**Student:** The rule you mentioned, that what is sent down from entities (*a'yan*) is... from non-entities... Is the tranquility (*sakinah*) itself an entity?

**Shaykh:** It is a description in something else: ﴿He it is who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers﴾ [al-Fath 4]. It is a description in something else: the tranquility is in their hearts.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** He asks, saying: A man stole money from a person, then returned it to him and said, "This is a gift." Is he cleared of it?

No, he is not cleared. If his returning it was as a gift, and the other person received it as a gift, and the giver has a favor over him and needs a reward, then it is a difference.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** If he placed a riyal and said, "This is a gift"?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** That would be deceptive. [If someone owes you] a thousand riyals, he puts a riyal with it and says, "This is a gift," so that it counts as one out of a thousand? No, no, it must be [returned in full]. But thank God, he says, "By God, I was in a state of foolishness." This happens often in childhood. Otherwise, many a person is not a thief, God willing. But a child who steals from a shop, or from a friend of his, takes a pen or takes a watch, he must return it to him and say, "This is your right over me." But if he says, for example, "This is from a person who repented, and he had stolen it from you," and he does not say, "I" or "someone else," is that valid or not? This is valid, and apparently it is based on the permissibility of [returning property to] an unknown owner (*istihlal al-majhul*).

**Student:** In the last lesson, the author, may God Most High have mercy on him, [said that] Allah, with the emphatic *shaddah*, means he evades affirming the active attributes (*al-sifat al-fi'liyyah*)... He said here: (﴿Possessor of abundance﴾: the vast bestowal, and He is continually described by each of these attributes). So he affirmed the attributes here?

**Shaykh:** Yes, but as essential attributes (*sifat dhatiyyah*). Then also, the author, notice something else from the standpoint of grammar: (*ghafir al-dhanb*, forgiver of sin), (*qabil al-tawb*, accepter of repentance), and (*shadid al-iqab*, severe in punishment) are annexed attributes (*sifat mudafah*), and their annexation is not pure (*mahdah*); their annexation is a verbal annexation (*idafah lafziyyah*), and verbal annexation does not entail definiteness. Do you understand?

**Student:** But he called them attributes.

**Shaykh:** Yes, there is no contradiction: they are attributes. But what is his intent? Look at the author's expression: (and He is continually described by each of these attributes). If He is continually described by them, what are they? Essential attributes. Then he says: (So the annexation of the derived noun of them is for definiteness, like the last one). The derived nouns *ghafir*, *qabil*, *shadid*. He says: (for definiteness), meaning their annexation conveys definiteness, (like the last one). What is the last one? (*dhi al-tawl*). This annexation certainly conveys definiteness, because it is the annexation of a fixed noun (*ism jamid*) to a definite noun, so it becomes definite.

Pay attention: the active participle, the passive participle, and the adjective of quality (*sifah mushabbahah*), when annexed, do not convey definiteness. Their annexation does not convey definiteness. They call this annexation verbal, not semantic (*ma'nawiyyah*). Some say "pure" and "not pure." The author brought up this matter because a question is raised against him: *Allah al-'Aziz al-'Alim*, are these definite or not definite? Definite.

If we say *ghafir* is an attribute of Allah, and we say its annexation is verbal, a problem arises: verbal annexation does not entail definiteness, so the attribute would be indefinite while it describes a definite noun. Describing a definite noun with an indefinite is not permissible, is it? It is not permissible to say, "Zayd *fadil* came." It is not permissible; you must say, "Zayd *al-fadil* came." So if the annexation in *ghafir*, *qabil*, and *shadid* does not convey definiteness, and we parse them as attributes, a problem arises: we would be describing a definite noun with an indefinite, and this is not permissible. The author wanted to correct the matter, so he said: these attributes are not meant to indicate occurrence (*huduth*), but are attributes held continually. When the attributes are continual, they leave the resemblance to the verb, and the annexation becomes for definiteness, so that it is valid to describe the name of majesty, or the expression of majesty, with these attributes, since their annexation is pure and semantic.

But the grammarians (*al-mu'rabin*) have another view, indeed a third view. The other view says: *ghafir*, *qabil*, and *shadid* are an apposition (*badal*) of Allah, and apposition does not require agreement with what it replaces. But the claim that they are an apposition is not correct, because the sign of an apposition is that it can take the place of the word it replaces, and this is not valid here; this is an attribute added to the described noun.

There is a third opinion from our Kufan brethren, the easy and facilitating ones. They say: it is permissible to describe a definite noun with such a construction, even if the annexation is verbal and not pure. That is, they say: what is annexed to a definite noun, even if the annexation is not pure, may be an attribute of the definite noun, by consideration of the wording, because the expression *ghafir al-dhanb* is definite, or indefinite? Definite, because it is annexed to a definite noun, even though in their view the annexation is not real but only verbal. So the grammarians say: it does not matter, verbal or semantic; as long as the apparent wording of the attribute agrees with the described noun, that suffices. The principle we follow when a disagreement occurs among the grammarians is to follow the easier view, emulating the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, who, whenever he was given a choice between two matters, chose the easier of them, so long as it was not sinful.

*[Recorded by al-Bukhari (6786), and Muslim, with his wording (2327), from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was never given a choice between two matters, one of which was easier than the other, except that he chose the easier of them, so long as it was not sinful. If it was sinful, he was the furthest of people from it."]* And we do not incur sin if we follow the Kufans in their view, because these are not matters of Sharia ruling.

Alright, in any case, according to the view of the Kufans, there is no need for the author's statement. We say: the annexation is verbal, but its form is that of a semantic annexation, because it is annexed to a definite noun, so it is valid that the definite noun is described by it.

In any case, a person does not fully grasp this topic unless he knows that annexation is of two kinds: pure and semantic, and verbal and not pure.
