This is the means. ﴿Our Lord, so forgive us our sins, expiate from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous﴾. This is seeking a means to God through what? Through belief in Him.

The fifth category: seeking a means to God through righteous deeds, because righteous deeds are a cause for reward, and among the reward is the attainment of what you have asked for. Its evidence is the story of the people of the cave, which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) related to us. Three people sought shelter from a night's rain and entered a cave. A great boulder rolled down from the mountain and blocked the entrance of the cave, and they could not move it, and there was no one to help them except God; there was no human being around them. So what did they do? They sought a means to God through their righteous deeds. One of them sought a means to God through his kindness to his parents, the second through complete chastity, and the third through complete trustworthiness. Do you know the story? So there is no need for detail.

Kindness to parents is a righteous deed, chastity is a righteous deed, and trustworthiness and fulfilling a trust is a righteous deed. When the first of them sought a means, the rock opened a little, but they could not come out. The second sought a means, the rock opened a little, but they could not come out. The third sought a means, and the rock opened once more, and they came out walking.[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2215) and Muslim (2743/100), both through their chains from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Three men from among those before you set out until they took shelter for the night in a cave. They entered it, and a rock came down from the mountain and sealed the cave's entrance. They said: Nothing will save you from this rock except that you call upon God by your best deeds. One of them said: O Allah, I had two elderly parents, and I would not give anyone, family or property, precedence over them in giving the evening milk. One day I went far in search of something, and I did not return to them until they had slept. I milked for them their evening milk, and found them asleep, and I disliked to give the evening milk to anyone, family or property, before them. So I remained with the vessel in my hand, waiting for them to wake, until dawn broke. They woke and drank their evening milk. O Allah, if I did that seeking Your face, then relieve us of what we are in from this rock. So it opened a little, but they could not come out." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The second said: O Allah, I had a cousin on my father's side who was the dearest of people to me. I desired her, but she refused me, until a year of hardship struck her, and she came to me, and I gave her one hundred and twenty dinars on condition that she let me have her. She agreed, and when I had power over her, she said: It is not lawful for you to break the seal except by its right. So I shrank from having intercourse with her, and I left her, though she was the dearest of people to me, and I left the gold I had given her. O Allah, if I did that seeking Your face, then relieve us of what we are in. So the rock opened, but they still could not come out." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The third said: O Allah, I hired workers and gave them their wages, except one man who left his wage and went away. I invested his wage until it grew into great wealth. After a time he came to me and said: O servant of God, give me my wage. I said: All that you see of your wage, the camels, cattle, sheep and slaves. He said: O servant of God, do not mock me. I said: I am not mocking you. So he took it all and drove it off, leaving nothing behind. O Allah, if I did that seeking Your face, then relieve us of what we are in. So the rock opened, and they came out walking."]] This is seeking a means to God through what? Through righteous deeds.

The sixth: seeking a means to God through the state of the person. You seek a means to God by mentioning your state: that you are poor, in need of God, ill, and the like. Among it is the saying of Musa (peace be upon him), whose evidence, or rather whose example, is: ﴿My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾ [al-Qasas 24]. When he had watered the flock for the two women, he turned to the shade to shelter in it, and said: ﴿My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need.﴾ He did not say "give me" and nothing more, but he sought a means to God through his state, because the words of one who says "I am poor, I am in need, harm has touched me" and the like imply: so give me, cure me. Ayyub (peace be upon him) combined mention of his state with seeking a means through the names, saying: ﴿Indeed, harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾. The first, ﴿harm has touched me﴾, is mention of his state; the second, through the names.

The seventh of the permissible kinds of tawassul: seeking a means to God through the supplication of one whose supplication is hoped to be answered. Among it is the tawassul of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he should supplicate to God for them, such as in seeking rain and in other matters, and there is much of this. Among it is the tawassul of people generally on the Day of Resurrection through the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ) to God that He judge between them. These are seven.

Our saying "seeking a means to God through one whose supplication is hoped to be answered" indicates that seeking a means to God through one whose supplication is not hoped to be answered is not permissible, because this is mockery of God. If you were to bring a person who practises usury, who consumes wealth by wrongdoing, deceit and lying, and say: "Supplicate to God for me," this is not permissible, because you have sought a means to God through one whose answer is far off. The Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned a man who travels far, dishevelled and dusty, who raises his hands to the sky, saying "O Lord, O Lord," while his clothing is unlawful, his food is unlawful, and he is nourished with the unlawful. He said: "How could that be answered?"[[Narrated by Muslim (1015/65) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).]] And this is mockery. If you were to bring a person, and to God belongs the highest likeness, to intercede for you with a king who hated this person and kept him away, what would that be? Mockery of the king and contempt for him; everyone knows this. So it is not permissible to seek a means to God, Exalted, through the supplication of one whose supplication is not hoped for, because this is a form of mockery of God, Mighty and Majestic. These are seven categories of permissible tawassul.

As for impermissible tawassul, such as seeking a means to God through what is not a means, like the tawassul of the polytheists through their idols, when they say: ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us near to God in position﴾ [al-Zumar 3]. This is of no benefit.

Among it is seeking a means to God through the status (jah) of the Messenger (ﷺ). This is not permissible, because it is seeking a means through what is not a means. What benefit do you gain from the status of the Messenger with God? None, because the status of the Messenger with God benefits whom? It benefits the Messenger alone; I have no connection with it. Therefore seeking a means through the status of the Messenger (ﷺ) is forbidden and unlawful: first, because it has not been reported; second, because it is not a means, since a means is doing what leads to the intended goal, and what connection is there between the Messenger's status with God and your request?

So the impermissible tawassul becomes two things. The first is shirkī tawassul, the tawassul of the polytheists through their deities to bring them near to God. There is no doubt that this is an incorrect and false means. Our calling it a means is only in order to address those who do not worship idols; as for those who worship idols, they are polytheists and have not sought a means to God at all.

The second is seeking a means to God through the status of the Messenger.

If someone says: Is it permissible for me to seek a means through my love for the Messenger, saying: "O Allah, by my love for Your Messenger"? Is it permissible? What benefit is there for you in your love for the Messenger?

* Students: A righteous deed.

* Shaykh: Yes, because love for the Messenger is undoubtedly a righteous deed, indeed among the best deeds is love for the Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. Indeed, a person does not believe until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is dearer to him than himself, his child, his parent and all people.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the explanation of the formula the angels use in seeking forgiveness for the believers, that they first seek a means and then ask: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent﴾ [Ghafir 7].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the vastness of God's mercy, as shown by His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed everything in mercy﴾.

If someone says: How is that valid, when most of the children of Adam are disbelievers? Where is the mercy? We say: they are shown mercy by the general mercy. Who brings forth plants for them? Who sends down rain for them? Who keeps them healthy? Who grants them hearing and sight? None but God. This is mercy, and the mercy of God encompasses everything.

* Among its benefits: the vastness of God's knowledge, as shown by His saying: ﴿and knowledge﴾. These two benefits imply that whenever a person knows this, he exposes himself to God's mercy, perhaps he will be among those who enter it; and when he believes in the vastness of God's knowledge, he is ashamed before God to be found lacking where God has commanded him, or to be found where God has forbidden him. Is that not so?

Now, if your father said to you: "My son, do not do such and such." If he is absent and you have a desire for it, will you do it or not? You will do it, without doubt, because he does not see you. If he is watching you, you will not do it. God, Mighty and Majestic, is never absent from you. Therefore do not do what God has forbidden, neither in secret nor in public; and do not abandon what He has commanded. This is why we say: may God not find you absent where He has commanded you, nor find you present where He has forbidden you.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of repentance, since the angels linked seeking forgiveness to it, saying: ﴿for those who repent﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the realisation of repentance is following the way of God, as shown by His saying: ﴿and follow Your way﴾. This is why we find that God always pairs mention of repentance with mention of righteous deeds: ﴿except for those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Furqan 70].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of Islam. How so? Because it is attributed to God, Mighty and Majestic.

* Among its benefits: the perfection of Islam through its attribution to God. There is virtue in its attribution to God as that which leads to Him, and there is perfection in its attribution to God as its Lawgiver: that He is the one who legislated it, and He is perfect, and the Perfect does not legislate except perfectly.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the angels emphasized the forgiveness by mentioning its effect, which is their saying: ﴿and protect them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾. This is because repentance is not complete unless it brings protection from Hellfire. But they stated this explicitly because of the great severity of the punishment of Hellfire, so they specified it for this reason. Otherwise, in reality, repentance and forgiveness necessarily bring protection from the punishment of Hellfire, but stating it explicitly adds to what the general meaning already includes.

Can this verse be used to refute the Jabriyyah (determinists)?

* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: From where? From His saying: ﴿and follow Your way﴾. He attributed the following to them. If they were compelled to it, it would not be correct to attribute the action to them. This is why, if a person is forced into disbelief, he does not become a disbeliever, because the act is not truly attributed to him; he is coerced into it. And Allah knows best.

* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Some scholars mentioned that it is part of good manners with Allah the Mighty and Majestic, with His Messenger (ﷺ), with his Companions, and with the scholars, that when Allah is mentioned one says "Mighty and Majestic," and when the Prophet is mentioned one sends blessings upon him, and the scholars are invoked for mercy, and the Companions are invoked with "may Allah be pleased with them" (...). Is this absolute? And he said that whoever neglects it has missed a great good.
* The Shaykh: As for sending blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ), there is no doubt that when he is mentioned, a person is commanded to send blessings upon him, either obligatorily or recommendedly. Some scholars held it obligatory for you, when the name of the Messenger is mentioned in your presence, to send blessings upon him, based on the hadith: "Disgraced is the man in whose presence you are mentioned and he does not send blessings upon you. Say: Amen. So I said: Amen."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad (646) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] As for Allah the Mighty and Majestic, praising Him is not a condition at (...). This is why the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) always says a statement attributed to Allah and does not always mention a description of might, majesty, exaltation, or blessing. Sometimes he says it, and sometimes he does not. So your sometimes saying it and sometimes not is better. Likewise, invoking "may Allah be pleased with" the Companions, or invoking mercy upon those after them, all of this is not to be made a fixed regular Sunnah. Rather, if it is mentioned sometimes, it is good; but making it a fixed regular Sunnah requires evidence.

* A student: What is the criterion distinguishing the shirki means from the innovated (bid'ah) means?
* The Shaykh: The innovated means is what has not been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) or from his Companions. The shirki means is what includes associating others with Allah. However, innovation is called shirk in a general sense, because the innovator legislates something Allah did not legislate, and Allah called that shirk when He said: ﴿Or do they have partners who have ordained for them in religion that which Allah has not permitted?﴾ [ash-Shura 21]. But whatever its appearance is that of shirk, it is characterized by the name shirk; and whatever its appearance is other than that, it is named by the name specific to it. This is why some scholars said: all sins are shirk, because a person has associated his desire with Allah in them, as the Most High said: ﴿Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiyah 23].
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The means do not have intermediaries except the seventh, which is seeking a means to Allah through the supplication of one whose answer is hoped for.
* A student: Is the shirki (means) the same thing?
* The Shaykh: We say: the permissible [one is permissible]. The shirki [one] is shirki.
* The student: Regarding seeking a means to Allah through righteous deeds, why did the scholars exclude it from seeking a means to Allah through faith?
* The Shaykh: Yes, because faith is in the heart and righteous deeds are by the limbs.
* A student: Does that not fall under faith?
* The Shaykh: No, ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [ash-Shu'ara 227]. So faith is in the heart and righteous deeds are by the limbs, but righteous deeds are part of faith.
* A student: Seeking a means to Allah through love of the righteous and the scholars?
* The Shaykh: What do you say? Is it permissible to seek a means to Allah through love of the righteous and the scholars? Is love of the righteous and the scholars an act of worship that brings one closer to Allah, or not?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Then it is a righteous deed, and it falls under seeking a means to Allah through righteous deeds.
* The student: Specifying a particular scholar by name?
* The Shaykh: No, it is better not to specify, because a particular scholar, (we ask Allah the Most High to protect us and you, and to make our outward states like our inward states, or our inward states better than our outward ones), you do not truly know; you may be deceived by a person, and he may not be as you think. Rather, generalize: "O Allah, by my love for the scholars of the Sharia, gather me with them; by my love for the righteous, make me among them," and similar invocations.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. "Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden which You promised them, and whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants. Indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise. (8) And protect them from evil deeds. And whoever You protect from evil deeds that Day, You will have had mercy on him. And that is the great triumph. (9) Indeed, those who disbelieve will be called: 'Surely the hatred of Allah toward you is greater than your hatred toward yourselves, when you were being called to faith but you disbelieved.'" [Ghafir 8–10].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: "Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden which You promised them." This is part of the supplication of those who carry the Throne and those around it, who say: "Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden." "Our Lord" means: O our Lord. They repeated the address by the title of Lordship (rubbubiyyah) because at first they were asking Allah for forgiveness for them and protection from the punishment of Hellfire, and this is from the category of takhliyah (clearing away), i.e., safety from what harms. As for the second part, it is from the category of tahliyah (adornment), i.e., the attainment of what is sought: "Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden which You promised them." So you see that the first part of the supplication contains deliverance from what is feared, and the second contains the attainment of what is desired. For this reason they repeated their words "Our Lord": "Our Lord" and "Our Lord, and admit them." They made this clause conjoined (ma'tufah) to what preceded it, not independent (mustanifah). That is, they did not say "Our Lord, admit them," but said "and admit them," to affirm what came before it, because conjunction (al-'atf) requires the establishment of the thing conjoined to and its being fundamental. It is as if they said: "Our Lord, and gather for them, along with what has been mentioned, that You admit them to the Gardens of Eden."

His saying "Jannat" (Gardens) is the plural of "jannah," and "jannah" in the Qur'an appears both in the plural and in the singular. Considered as a genus, it is one jannah; considered by its types, it is jannat. Allah, exalted, mentioned four types in one place: "And for one who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens" [al-Rahman 46], "and besides them two gardens" [al-Rahman 62]. So it is pluralized when considering types and singularized when considering the genus. Linguistically, "jannah" originally means an orchard with many trees; it is so called because it covers (yujinn) whoever is in it, i.e., shields him by the abundance of its trees. Legally, it means the abode of bliss which Allah has prepared for His friends, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived, and its ceiling is the Throne of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; so they are the closest people to Allah.

His saying "Jannat 'Adn" (Gardens of Eden): "Adn" means residence (al-iqamah). It is said: "'adana bi-makan," meaning he resided in a place. From it comes "al-ma'din" (the mine), for the minerals of the earth, because the mine is settled, firm and fixed in the earth. So "jannat 'adn" means gardens of residence. They are described thus because their inhabitants do not desire any removal from them, and because they are everlasting, forever and ever.

His saying "allati wa'adtahum" (which You promised them) is an adjective of "jannat." They only said this in acknowledgment of Allah's favour, first and last, and as a means of seeking nearness to Him through the fulfilment of what they asked for, because when Allah promises something He completes it, for He does not break His promise. Thus the mention of "allati wa'adtahum" has two benefits:

The first: acknowledgment of His favour, glorified and exalted, in that He promised them these gardens.

The second: seeking a means (tawassul) to Allah through the answering of the supplication, as if they are saying: "Admit them to this, because You promised them it," so it is from the category of seeking a means through His promise to the realisation of what was promised.

His saying "wa man salaha min aba'ihim wa azwajihim wa dhurriyyatihim" ("and whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants"): "man salaha" — he says: (it is a conjunction upon "hum" in "adkhilhum" or in "wa'adtahum"). So the "waw" is a conjunctive particle, and "man" is a relative pronoun, indeclinable with sukun, in a position of accusative by conjunction upon "adkhilhum" or upon "wa'adtahum." The better view is that it is a conjunction upon "adkhilhum," so that the supplication for entry includes them and whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants.

"And whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants; indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise." This is a fine precaution, for they said "man salaha" (whoever was righteous) and did not say "wa aba'ahum wa azwajahum wa dhurriyyatahum" (all their fathers, spouses and descendants). They said "whoever was righteous," because if they had supplicated in generality, there would have been a kind of transgression in supplication. Transgression in supplication is for a person to supplicate for what is impossible either legally or sensorily. Whoever supplicates to Allah for what is impossible legally or sensorily is a transgressor in supplication, and if we add "or customarily," it is also transgression. So if one asked Allah to bring forth a child from the wall of his house, this would be transgression in supplication; and if one asked Allah to make him a prophet, this would be transgression in supplication, because that is impossible legally. And if one asked Allah to place the heavens and the earth in his hand, this would be transgression in supplication because it is impossible rationally. So what is impossible legally, rationally, customarily, or sensorily is not to be asked of Allah, because that is transgression in supplication.

Here Allah, glorified and exalted, says: "whoever was righteous among their fathers." If they had said "and their fathers," there would have been a kind of transgression, since the fathers of these people may be polytheists and disbelievers who do not deserve to enter the Garden. So He says: "whoever was righteous among their fathers and their spouses" — "azwaj" is the plural of "zawj" — "and their descendants" — "dhurriyyah" is the plural of "dhurriyyah." They mentioned the roots, the branches, and the relations by marriage: roots and branches are fathers and descendants, and relations by marriage are spouses.

"Indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise": this is an independent clause (jumlah isti'nafiyyah) by which is intended seeking a means to Allah through His might and wisdom, that He realise this supplication or this thing asked for.

* In this verse there are benefits:

* First: the affirmation that the angels are servants who are under Lordship; from their saying: "Our Lord, and admit them..." to the end.

* Among its benefits: that a thing is not completed except by the removal of what harms and the attainment of what is sought. The reason is that when they finished supplicating Allah for the removal of what harms, they asked Allah for the attainment of what is sought, which is admission into the Gardens.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Gardens are of various kinds; we derive this from the plural form.

* Among its benefits: that the Gardens are an abode of residence, whose dweller does not desire any removal from them and to which no annihilation reaches; this is from His saying: "Gardens of Eden."

* Among the benefits of this verse: seeking a means to Allah through His action or His word; from His saying: "which You promised them," for His promise is a word, and these angels sought a means to Allah through this word.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of the favour of Allah, mighty and majestic, upon the people of Paradise, first and last; first, in that He promised them Paradise, because the promise of Paradise implies working for it; and second, in admitting them into it.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that completeness of bliss is that Allah gathers a person with his relatives and his spouses; from His saying: "admit them to the Gardens of Eden which You promised them, and whoever was righteous among their fathers..." to the end.

If someone says: Does it necessarily follow from this that they will all be at one rank? We say: It does not necessarily follow, but spouses must be at the rank of their spouses, and as for descendants, Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned in Surat al-Tur that they are also at the rank of their fathers. Allah says: "And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith — We will join them with their descendants and We will not deprive them of anything of their deeds. Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned" [al-Tur 21]. This indicates that descendants who had not reached the stations of their fathers are raised until they are in their fathers' stations, and that this does not entail a diminishing of the fathers' stations. That is to say: we do not say that the matter is a midpoint, raising these somewhat and lowering those somewhat. For this reason He said: "and We will not deprive them of anything of their deeds," lest one suppose that when the descendants are raised, they are raised a little and the fathers are lowered by the amount that these were raised, so that they meet at a midpoint. This is not so, for if the fathers were lowered a little, it would follow that they were diminished. Rather Allah says: "and We will not deprive them" — i.e., We did not diminish the fathers — "of anything of their deeds. Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned."

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: caution in supplication against generalisation; from their saying: "and whoever was righteous among their fathers and their spouses" [Ghafir 8]. From this is the saying of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: "And provide its people" [al-Baqarah 126], i.e., the people of the Sacred Mosque, "with fruits, those of them who believe in Allah and the Last Day" [al-Baqarah 126]. "Its people" was then specified by his saying: "those of them who believe in Allah and the Last Day," so he took precaution. But Allah, exalted, said: "And whoever disbelieves" — meaning: I provide for those in this land even if they are disbelievers — "but I will grant him enjoyment for a little, then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination" [al-Baqarah 126]. The point is that a person should, in supplication, take care to avoid generalisation which may include one who does not deserve the supplication, so that there would be a kind of transgression in his supplication.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of these two names, al-'Aziz and al-Hakim, as names of Allah, and the affirmation of what they contain of attributes or qualities: al-'Aziz includes 'izzah (might), and al-Hakim includes hikmah (wisdom) and hukm (judgment).

* Among the benefits of the verse: seeking a means to Allah in supplication through His names.

If someone says: You have mentioned in several places that seeking a means through the names should correspond to the request or to the one requested. What is the correspondence of "the Mighty" and "the Wise" to the supplication for these people's admission into Paradise?

The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that the correspondence lies in their having asked that Allah admit those who were righteous among their fathers, spouses and descendants, and this is a matter requiring might, complete authority, judgment and wisdom. Therefore they concluded this supplication with their saying: "Indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise," rather than saying: "Indeed You are the Lord of Great Bounty."

* Among the benefits of this verse: the natural order (al-tartib al-wujudi) in things. In what? "Their fathers, their spouses and their descendants," for this is the order: a father, then marriage, then offspring. This is a natural order, and there is no doubt that this is among the embellishments of expression.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And protect them from evil deeds﴾ [Ghafir 9]. This is conjoined to what came before, His saying: ﴿and admit them﴾. That is: protect them from the evil deeds. The sentence is an imperative verb, with a subject and two objects. The sentence contains a verb, a subject and two objects: the verb is qi (قِ), the subject is a concealed pronoun obligatorily, the first object is the hā' (الهاء), and the second object is "the evil deeds" (السيئات). Qi (قِ) here is an imperative verb, but it is formed from a single letter after two letters have been deleted from it, the first and the third. Likewise, every defective mithal verb (مثال ناقص), when it is triliteral, its imperative is on one letter. This is the rule: every defective mithal, its imperative when triliteral is on one letter. Do you understand? What is the mithal? It is the verb whose first radical is a weak letter (حرف علة), and the defective is the one whose last radical is a weak letter.

Good. This rule therefore covers many examples, and al-Khudari gathered them in his gloss on Ibn 'Aqil's commentary on the Alfiyya of Ibn Malik, gathering them in verses. Among them are qi (قِ), fi (فِ), and ʿi (عِ), meaning "count" (عَدَّدَ). I do not recall now everything he enumerated, but the governing principle is this: every triliteral verb that is a defective mithal has its imperative on a single letter.

﴿And protect them from evil deeds﴾. The commentator said: (that is, its punishment). This is when we take "evil deeds" to mean the evil actions. Then it is necessary to interpret it as the punishment of the evil deeds. Why? Because the time for performing evil deeds has now ended, and what remains is the recompense, so it is then interpreted as punishment. But if we interpret "evil deeds" as whatever distresses (يسوء), without the deed performed by the servant, then there is no need to say "its punishment". Why? Because punishment is among what distresses, so it is as if they said: protect them from what distresses them of punishment. The rule in interpretation and in explaining hadiths is that when there is a matter between the possibility of supplying an implied element and not supplying one, the preferable course is not to supply it. Accordingly, we say: "evil deeds" here does not mean the evil deeds which are the servant's action, definitely, because that has ended. Rather, "evil deeds" is intended to mean what distresses, of deeds, of punishments, of chastisements, and of other things.

(﴿And whoever You protect from evil deeds that Day﴾ — the Day of Resurrection — ﴿You have indeed granted him mercy﴾). (مَن) is conditional. The clause ﴿You have indeed granted him mercy﴾ is the answer of the condition. The answer of the condition is joined with the fa' (الفاء) because it begins with qad (قد). When the answer of the condition begins with qad, it must be joined with the fa'. There are similar cases that require the fa'. Shall we recite the verse containing it? In any case, the answer of the condition must be linked with fa' when it falls into one of seven categories, gathered in the statement of the versifier:

Nominal, imperative, and with a rigid (non-derived) word, and with mā, and with qad, and with lan, and with the tanfis.

The tanfis includes sawfa and the sin. Which of the seven types is this verse? His saying: (qad) — ﴿fa-qad rahimtahu﴾.

﴿And whoever You protect from evil deeds that Day, You have indeed granted him mercy. And that﴾ — the referent being the protection from evil deeds and the mercy — ﴿is the great triumph﴾. ﴿Huwa﴾ may be a subject with "the triumph" as its predicate, and the second subject with its predicate is the predicate of the first subject. It may also be that ﴿huwa﴾ is a pronoun of separation (ضمير الفصل) with no place in the grammatical analysis, and the meaning would be "and that the great triumph". This is supported by its appearing in this form in some places: ﴿And that is the great triumph﴾ [an-Nisa' 13].

The pronoun of separation, grammatically, has no place in the analysis, but semantically it has three benefits. The first benefit is restriction (الحصر), the second is emphasis (التوكيد), and the third is distinguishing between the adjective and the predicate (التمييز بين الصفة والخبر). These are three benefits of the pronoun of separation. The first benefit?

* Student: Restriction.

* Shaykh: That is one. The second?

* Student: Emphasis.

* Shaykh: Emphasis or affirmation (التأكيد)?

* Student: Emphasis.

* Shaykh: Tawkid is more eloquent: ﴿and do not break oaths after their confirmation (tawkid)﴾ [an-Nahl 91]. He did not say ta'kidiha, though the hamza is permissible. The third benefit?

* Student: Distinguishing between the predicate and the adjective.

* Shaykh: Distinguishing between the predicate and the adjective. This appears in the example: if you say "Zayd al-fadil" and you want al-fadil to be the predicate of the subject, it may be that al-fadil is an adjective and the predicate has not yet come; it may be that the intended meaning is "Zayd, the virtuous, is understanding," and it may be that al-fadil is the predicate of the subject. When you say "Zayd is the virtuous one," the ambiguity is removed and it is fixed that al-fadil is the predicate of the subject. As for emphasis and restriction, they are evident: when you say "Zayd is the virtuous one," you have emphasized that he is virtuous and restricted virtue to him.

His saying: ﴿the great triumph﴾. Al-fawz (الفوز) is the attainment of what is sought and deliverance from what is feared. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has indeed triumphed﴾ [Al 'Imran 185]. What is the deliverance from what is feared in the verse? ﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire﴾. The attainment of what is sought? ﴿and admitted to Paradise﴾. There is no clearer or more explicit interpretation than the interpretation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so al-fawz is deliverance from what is feared and attainment of what is sought, and the evidence is what you have heard.

His saying: ﴿the great (al-'azim)﴾ is a description of it as great, because there is no triumph greater than this. There is no triumph greater than that Allah bestows upon you residence in this abode — may Allah make us and you among its residents — in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and nothing has occurred to the heart of a human being. All people in this world, the believers, strive to reach this abode. For this reason, when a Bedouin said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Messenger of Allah, I do not excel at your dandana (murmuring) nor at Mu'adh's dandana, but I ask Allah for Paradise and seek refuge in Him from the Fire," he said: «Around them we murmur» [Abu Dawud (792) from some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ibn Majah (3847) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (رضي الله عنه)]. We want nothing but this. This hadith, although its authenticity is debated, the reality is this: all believers work to reach this abode, and working for it is easy, but for those whom Allah makes it easy. When does Allah make that easy for you? Listen to the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿As for he who gives and fears Allah, and believes in the best [reward], We will ease him toward ease﴾ [al-Layl 5–7]. You act, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «Act, for each is made easy for that for which he was created» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4949) and Muslim (2647/6) from the hadith of 'Ali (رضي الله عنه)].

He says: ﴿And that is the great triumph﴾. Let us take the benefits of this verse:

* Among the benefits of this verse: the angels who carry the Throne and those around it ask Allah, the Exalted, to protect those who believed from evil deeds, that is, from their punishment, until what they seek is complete for them.

If someone says: Is this not already included in what preceded: ﴿and protect them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾ and ﴿and admit them to gardens of perpetual residence﴾?

We say: Yes, but the station of supplication calls for expansion, for several reasons:

The first reason: supplication is an act of worship, so the more you expand in it, the more you increase in devotion to Allah and increase in reward.

Second: expansion includes detail, and detail is better than summary, because in summary a person may forget important things that do not come to his mind, but when he details, the matter becomes clear.

Third: detail in supplication is an intimacy with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because the supplicant is conversing with his Lord. It is known that conversing with the Beloved is recommended to be lengthy, or we may say in other words: it is known that the lover loves that the conversation between him and his beloved be prolonged. This is something observed: if someone you love sits with you, you wish the conversation to last and the sitting to be long, so that time passes quickly. If a burdensome person sits with you, and whenever he addresses you with a word, even if it is praise of you, it is as if he slapped your face, because it is as though he is sitting on your heart. But when the beloved sits with you, you do not wish to part from him and you do not tire of his talk. Yet who are the best companions?

We have companions whose talk we never tire of, / they are faithful, trustworthy, whether absent or present.

That is, books.

The most precious place in this world is the saddle of a swift steed, / and the best companion in this age is a book.

These are the companions who never tire and who benefit and do not harm.

In any case, we say: supplication should be expanded for three reasons:

The first: it is worship, so the more you expand in it, the more you increase in devotion and nearness to Allah.

The second: it is detail, and detail is better than summary, because in detail there may be what is absent from you in summary.

The third: it is intimacy with Allah, who is the most beloved thing to you, and there is no doubt that everyone loves that conversation with the Beloved be prolonged. Consider the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): «O Allah, forgive me all my sin, small and great, first and last, open and secret» [Muslim (483/216) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (رضي الله عنه)]. It suffices in all this to say: "O Allah, forgive me my sin," but expansion has an effect on the heart.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whoever is protected from evil deeds on the Day of Resurrection has entered into the mercy of Allah, by His saying: ﴿And whoever You protect from evil deeds that Day, You have indeed granted him mercy﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse: mercy, just as it is in bringing what is loved, it is also in warding off what is disliked, by His saying: ﴿And whoever You protect from evil deeds that Day, You have indeed granted him mercy﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: this is the greatest triumph, by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that is the great triumph﴾. Its aspect is that He indicated it with the demonstrative of the distant, to show the loftiness of this triumph, and described it as great, so it combines the loftiness of rank and the loftiness of its essence, that it is great.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: What benefit is there in bodies that have no movement?

* Student: It is enough, Shaykh, that they (...).

* Shaykh: No, it is not enough that they were protected from the Fire, because if that sufficed we would not need Paradise at all. We would say: it is enough for you that you were saved from the Fire, and there is no need for Paradise.

* Student: If the description in the supplication requested differs, is it transgression? For example, some people, if you say: "O Allah, guide (...) the guided," or "humiliate shirk and the polytheists," you say: "By Your mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful," and he says: this is transgression in supplication.

* Shaykh: No, that is a mistake. Have you not heard: ﴿And whoever You protect from evil deeds that Day, You have indeed granted him mercy﴾? This is the removal of something disliked, and the humiliation of shirk is without doubt a blessing and a mercy.

* Student: In the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has indeed triumphed﴾ [Al 'Imran 185], and in Paradise we affirmed the seeing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Does this enter into this verse?

* Shaykh: Yes indeed.

* Student: From what aspect?

* Shaykh: Because entering Paradise and what is in it is triumph, and the greatest bliss in Paradise is looking at the Face of Allah. For this reason we mentioned to you, brothers, that the statement of al-Zamakhshari, "what triumph is greater than this," we said: this is a true statement, and it is not objected to except because we know that the man does not affirm the seeing of Allah's Face. Otherwise we would say: once you enter Paradise, you have entered Paradise with all the bliss in it.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Did they repeat the supplication or repeat the one for whom it is made?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No. "O Allah, forgive us, our parents, our offspring, our brothers, our grandmothers and grandfathers, our maternal aunts and uncles, our paternal aunts and uncles, the ascendants, the descendants, and the relatives." This is not a repetition of the supplication; it is a repetition of those for whom it is made. And you see that the angels here only prayed for three categories: the ascendants, the descendants, and the in-laws (the spouses). But in any case, we do not say there is anything wrong with it, and we do not object to it. But if it lengthens over people with such things, it may be a burden and a harm to them.

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.

Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved will be called, "Allah's detestation [of you] is greater than your detestation of yourselves"﴾ [Ghafir 10]. ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved will be called﴾. Al-nida' (calling) is speech from a distance, and al-munajat (intimate speech) is speech from close by. Allah did not specify who will call out to them, but the commentator said: (from the angels), and that is at the time they enter the Fire. At that time they will detest themselves with the greatest detestation, and al-maqt (detestation) is the most intense hatred. So at the time they enter the Fire, they hate themselves with intense hatred, because they could not reach salvation from it. Then they are called and told: ﴿Allah's detestation [of you] is greater than your detestation of yourselves﴾. The lam here is lam al-ibtida' (the lam of inception), which enters upon the subject for emphasis.

As for his saying: (﴿Allah's detestation﴾ of you), this is one of the two interpretations of the verse. On this view, maqt is in the genitive construction with its agent, not its object; meaning, Allah's hatred of you is greater than your hatred of yourselves. It has also been said that it is in the genitive construction with its object, not its agent. On this view the meaning is: Allah's detestation of you when you were called to faith is greater than your detestation of yourselves today; that is, they disliked what they were called to in the world, namely the love of Allah, and replaced it with the most intense hatred. This meaning is closer than the one the commentator followed, may Allah have mercy on him, (Allah's detestation of you). According to what we have preferred, the meaning is Allah's detestation of you, so it is in the genitive construction with its object. When did they detest Allah? ﴿When you were called to faith﴾. On this view, his saying ﴿when you were called﴾ is linked to ﴿Allah's detestation﴾; that is, when you were called to faith, you disliked it and were not convinced by it, but rather hated it with the most intense hatred.

As for his saying: ﴿greater than your detestation of yourselves﴾, when did they detest themselves? When it was said to them: "Enter the fire of Hell," and they hated themselves.

As for his saying: ﴿your detestation of yourselves﴾, (maqt) here is a verbal noun in a genitive construction with what? ﴿your detestation of yourselves﴾: is (maqt) here in a genitive construction with its agent or its object?

* Student: With its agent.

* The Shaykh: With its agent. No, it is not according to the author's view; the author's view concerns ﴿Allah's detestation﴾. But ﴿your detestation of yourselves﴾ is a verbal noun in a genitive construction with its agent; meaning, they themselves detested their souls, and (anfus, souls) is the object of (maqt).

As for his saying: ﴿when you are called to faith and you disbelieve﴾, you are called in the world to faith, and the caller is left unspecified, because the call to faith comes from the messengers, and from the heirs of the messengers, who are the scholars. So the one calling them to faith in the world is not one person; rather, the messengers call them, and the heirs of the messengers, who are the scholars, also call them.

﴿When you are called to faith and you disbelieve﴾. Faith in what? That is, in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree, both its good and its evil. This is faith, as the Prophet ﷺ explained it when Jibril asked him. He said: "Tell me about faith." He said: "That you believe in Allah..." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. It is also in Muslim (8/1) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the wording is his.] ...and so on to the end.

﴿When you are called to faith and you disbelieve﴾. The meaning of faith here, as I mentioned to you, is faith in the six pillars, as well as the submission that necessarily follows from faith in these six pillars. For this reason they were called to the faith that is in the hearts, and they were also called to submission, which consists of the actions of the limbs, and they disbelieved in all of that: ﴿when you are called to faith and you disbelieve﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it shows that the disbelievers will be rebuked on the Day of Resurrection with a rebuke that adds pain to their pain, from His saying: ﴿Allah's detestation [of you] is greater than your detestation of yourselves﴾. Among the benefits of this is that the misguidance and disbelief they were upon becomes clear to them when they see the punishment. Its basis is that they detested themselves at that time when they saw the torment, and this indicates that misguidance became clear to them on that day.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse, according to what the author followed: the affirmation of detestation for Allah; that is, Allah detests, meaning He hates. This is according to the author's view that maqt is in a genitive construction with the agent. If we adopt the preferred view, the verse contains no evidence that Allah detests, but the proof that Allah detests and has detestation comes from other texts, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is greatly detestable in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff 3]. Maqt is the most intense hatred, and hatred is one of the attributes of action that are connected to His will and His determination.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a person may hate himself. And when is that? When he sees in his own conduct something that displeases him, he hates himself and says: "This is from the soul that commands to evil."

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the proof has been established against these deniers who are punished; from His saying: ﴿when you are called to faith and you disbelieve﴾. Is the call a call with understanding, or a call by mere delivery?

The first: it is a call with understanding, from the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, to make [the message] clear to them﴾ [Ibrahim 4]. So the proof must be understood. But when the message reaches a person, it is obligatory for him to seek understanding; if he does not do so, he is negligent.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: these people disbelieved out of obstinacy. From where is this derived? Because they were called and they disbelieved, and this is the disbelief of obstinacy, and we seek refuge in Allah.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, You have caused us to die twice and You have given us life twice, so we acknowledge our sins. Is there any way out?"﴾ [Ghafir 11]

﴿They will say: "Our Lord, You have caused us to die twice"﴾ The death here refers to what came before life and what came after life. What came before life is when they were embryos in their mothers' wombs. What came after it is the death that occurs after existence in this world. These are two deaths.

﴿and You have given us life twice﴾: the first life is when they were embryos in their mothers' wombs, and the second life is after resurrection on the Day of Resurrection, or at the moment of resurrection on the Day of Resurrection.

This is like the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then He will give you life again﴾ [al-Baqarah 28]. These are four: two deaths and two lives. So they say: (﴿Our Lord, You have caused us to die twice﴾, two deaths, ﴿and You have given us life twice﴾, two lives, because we were drops of semen, dead, then we were given life, then we were caused to die, then we were given life for resurrection). This is the explanation of ﴿You have caused us to die twice and You have given us life twice﴾. The first death is not a death after life, but a loss of life, so it is correct to call it death. Their purpose in this acknowledgment is that the matter is true: just as we realize that these four stages have passed over us, death, then life, then death, then life, we are certain that we had been wrong. For this reason they said: ﴿so we acknowledge our sins﴾, meaning: we have acknowledged our sins.

"Dhunub" is the plural of "dhanb" (sin), which is disobedience, and what is meant here is disbelief, as the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (because of our disbelief in resurrection). ﴿Is there any way out?﴾ from the Fire. The word (hal) here is used to express a wish, meaning that we wish to get out of the Fire, but this will not happen for them.

(﴿Is there any way out?﴾ from the Fire, and a return to the world so that we may obey our Lord, ﴿any way?﴾ a path? Their answer is: No.) This is from the author, based on the view that the interrogative retains its original meaning, that they ask: is there any path for us so that we may come out? But according to what we have said, that it expresses a wish, it does not require an answer, as in His words: ﴿Do we have any intercessors who will intercede for us, or could we be sent back so that we might act differently from what we used to do?﴾ [al-A'raf 53].

* In this verse there is affirmation that these deniers acknowledged that they disbelieved in Allah and that they deserve this punishment.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the disbelievers' admission of what they used to deny before, namely resurrection, and this is the meaning of His words: ﴿so we acknowledge our sins﴾.

* Among its benefits: that on that Day the truth and the soundness of the analogy become clear to them, because they said: ﴿You have caused us to die twice and You have given us life twice﴾. The first death, before the breath was blown into them, they had already acknowledged, and the life of this world they had already acknowledged. When did they acknowledge it? They acknowledged it in this world while they were alive, but they denied resurrection after death. Now, however, they say: yes, resurrection after death is like the breathing of the spirit into the fetus; meaning, we are now certain that what Allah the Mighty and Majestic mentioned, the analogy of re-creation to initial creation, is a real matter, and that we were given life twice and caused to die twice.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the intensity of these people's regret for what they did, and their wish to get out of the punishment they have fallen into, by their words: ﴿Is there any way out?﴾

In this verse there is a difficult point of i'rab (grammatical analysis). The phrase ﴿fa-hal ila khurujin min sabil﴾ is a clause lacking one of its two pillars, the subject (mubtada'), because what is before us now is a prepositional phrase in the predicate position, and the place where the subject would be is empty.

* Student: The subject is ﴿min sabil﴾.

* Shaykh: Can the subject be in the genitive case?

* Student: No, and "min" here is a superfluous particle.

* Shaykh: So the subject is "sabil", on which the superfluous particle "min" has entered grammatically. Therefore, in its i'rab we say: "min" is a superfluous preposition (harf jarr za'id), and "sabil" is a subject in the nominative case, marked by an assumed damma at its end, its appearance prevented by the place being occupied by the movement of the superfluous preposition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 12 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is because, when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when partners were associated with Him, you believed. So judgement belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Most Great.﴾ [Ghafir 12] ﴿That﴾ The mufassir says: (i.e., the punishment you are in). So the one pointed to exists; that is, the punishment you are in is due to such-and-such. Here He said ﴿dhalikum﴾, and sometimes it comes as (dhalika), sometimes as (dhalikunna), and sometimes as (dhalikuma). So what is the reason for the change in address in these demonstratives?

It is said: the demonstrative noun follows the one pointed to, and the second-person particle (kaf) that follows it follows the one addressed. So if you point to one person while addressing two, say: dhalikuma, as Yusuf said to his two companions in prison: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾ [Yusuf 37].

And if you point to two while addressing one person, what do you say?
* Student: dhankum.
* Shaykh: Dhankum? You pointed to two while addressing one?
* Student: dhanka.
* Shaykh: Dhanka, as in the Most High's saying: ﴿So those two are two proofs from your Lord﴾ [al-Qasas 32].

And if you point to one person while addressing a group of males?
* Student: dhakum.
* Shaykh: Dhakum? Say it with the lam, better.
* Student: dhalikum.
* Shaykh: Dhalikum. From it is the Most High's saying: ﴿And that is your assumption which you assumed about your Lord﴾ [Fussilat 23]. Good.

And if you point to one person while addressing a group of females?
* Student: dhalikunna.
* Shaykh: Dhalikunna. She said: ﴿That is the one about whom you blamed me﴾ [Yusuf 32]. Good.

And if you point to two while addressing two?
* Student: dhalikuma.
* Shaykh: Dhanikuma. Good.

And if you point to two while addressing a group of males?
* Student: dhankum.
* Shaykh: Dhankum, correct.

And if you point to two while addressing a group of females?
* Student: dhankunna.
* Shaykh: Dhankunna, good.

And if you point to a group while addressing a group of males?
And if you point to two while addressing a group of females?
* Student: dhankunna.
* Shaykh: Dhankunna, good.

And if you point to a group while addressing a group of males?
* Student: ulaikum.
* Shaykh: Ulaikum, correct? This is when we point to a group while addressing a group of males.
To a group while addressing a group of females?
* Student: ulaikunna.
* Shaykh: Ulaikunna, good.
You pointed to a group while addressing two?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: ulaikuma.
* Shaykh: Ulaikuma. In any case, the demonstrative noun follows the one pointed to, and the kaf follows the one addressed. If it is singular masculine, the kaf is singular masculine; if it is singular feminine, likewise; dual and plural likewise. This is the most eloquent usage.

Sometimes the kaf is fixed with a fatha for a masculine addressee in general, whether one, two, or a group, and with a kasra for a feminine addressee in general, whether one, two, or a group.

Sometimes the kaf is fixed with a fatha in the singular for every addressee, so you say dhalika when addressing a man, a woman, two, or a group. These are three dialects regarding the kaf of address attached to the demonstrative: the most eloquent is that it agrees with the addressee, then fixed with a fatha for the masculine and kasra for the feminine, and then fixed with a fatha in every case in the singular masculine form.

Here the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿dhalikum bi-annahu﴾. The one pointed to is singular and the addressees are a group of males, so dhalikum. The addressees are a group of males (i.e., the punishment you are in), ﴿bi-annahu﴾, i.e., because of the fact that in the world ﴿when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved﴾, and associated partners, and said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ [Sad 5].
(﴿you disbelieved﴾ in His Oneness, ﴿but when partners were associated with Him﴾ a partner was made for Him, ﴿you believed﴾ you affirmed the association.) And this is the reality: when Allah is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter recoil, and when those other than Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice. Thus they affirm with their hearts and rejoice with their tongues. This belief, in reality, we may say is genuine belief, and we may say it is a claimed belief; that is, it is a claim, and in the depths of their souls they believe in Allah. Consider Pharaoh, the most disbelieving of the people of the earth: how he denied the Creator and claimed lordship and said to his people: ﴿I know of no god for you other than myself﴾ [al-Qasas 38]. Yet in the depths of his soul he was a believer. Moses said to him in debate: ﴿You have certainly known that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence﴾ [al-Isra 102]. I say to you: this verse shows that Pharaoh believed in the lordship of Allah. How so?
* Student: Because he did not say: "I did not know" (...).
* Shaykh: No, because when Moses said to him: ﴿You have certainly known that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, he did not say: "I did not know," and he was in a position where he saw himself as higher than Moses; that is, he could deny Moses' claim if he were denying it, but he acknowledged that Allah sent the Torah to Moses. This is indicated by the Most High's saying: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml 14]. Therefore it is impossible for any intelligent person—by intelligent I mean anyone other than a madman—to deny that this world has a Creator. Every intelligent person who reflects even slightly on this universe knows that it has a Lord who manages it, and this cannot be denied.

So His saying here: ﴿When Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved, but when partners were associated with Him, you believed﴾: is it a claimed belief or a genuine belief? What appears to us is that it is a claimed belief; that is, they say: "We believe that this is a partner with Allah," they say it with their tongues, but in the depths of their hearts we do not think anyone denies that Allah, glorified and exalted, is One.

It may be said that what is meant by His saying: ﴿When Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved, but when partners were associated with Him, you believed﴾ is the Oneness of worship: they disbelieve in the Oneness of worship and believe in association in worship, because they believe that these deities bring them near to Allah in closeness. So they believe in Allah as Lord and believe that the idols are intercessors.

(﴿But when partners were associated with Him, you believed. So judgement﴾ regarding your punishment ﴿belongs to Allah, the Most High﴾ over His creation, ﴿the Most Great﴾, the Mighty.) That is: based on the fact that in this state of yours the judgement is to Allah, the fa' here may be either for resumption or for consequence of what came before; that is, on that basis the judgement in your affair is to Allah, the judgement regarding your punishment belongs to Allah alone. The lam may sometimes mean "towards," as you say: (wa-lillahi turja'u al-umur), meaning "to Allah," and here (al-hukmu lillah) means: to Allah, that is, your judgement ends with Allah. It may also be that the meaning is: judgement belongs to Allah, that is, it is due to Him, and none shares it with Him.

﴿Al-'Aliyy﴾: the author says: (over His creation). It is elevation of essence and elevation of attribute. Allah, glorified and exalted, is elevated over His creation in His essence, above everything, and He is elevated over His creation in His attributes. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And His is the highest description in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Rum 27]; "al-mathal" means the highest description in the heavens and the earth.

The elevation of Allah, glorified and exalted, in the sense of elevation of attribute is a matter agreed upon; none of the people of the religion disputed it, even the deniers (mu'attilah) who deny the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. They denied them only on the basis of their glorifying Allah above resembling created beings, although they erred in the path. But they say: "We say this in order to exalt Allah." For this reason they call those who affirm the attributes "anthropomorphists" (mushabbihah), "corporealists" (mujassimah), and "literalists" (hashwiyyah) and the like, and they consider themselves the people of Oneness. My point is: no one among the people of the religion denies the elevation of attribute; even the people of innovation affirm it.

As for elevation of essence, it is the point of contention between Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah and the Mu'attilah. Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah believe that Allah, the Most High, is elevated over His creation by His very self. The Mu'attilah deny this, and then they divided into two groups. One group said: He is in every place; Allah is in every place, in the heavens and on the earth, in the markets, in the mosques, in the houses, in every place.

Another group said: He cannot be described as being in a place. So it is not said that He is above the world, nor in the world, nor beneath it, nor to its right, nor its left, nor connected to the world, nor touching it. This is pure ta'til (denial of attributes), for if we wanted to describe non-existence we would find no more eloquent description than this.

So two groups opposed the elevation of essence. The first group?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: They are all mu'attilah, all Jahmiyyah.
* Student: The first group said: Allah is in every place.
* Shaykh: Allah is in every place.
* Student: The second group denied it and said: Allah cannot be described as being in a place.
* Shaykh: Well said.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Right. So two groups opposed: the first group said Allah is in every place by His essence. This—my brothers—is a real position; it is a statement that has been made. Do not think it is imagined. There are people now who believe that Allah is in every place: if you come to the market you find Him in the market; and when they speak of compulsion (jabr), they say: in the market He buys and sells, because the act of the servant is attributed to Allah; so if He is in the market, and the servant's act is His act, He buys and sells. We seek Allah's protection. This is a necessary consequence of their statement. If you come to the mosque, He is in the mosque; whether He prays or sits, we do not know. Wherever you come, you find Him there. We separate this from the issue of compulsion so that we do not reach a very bad conclusion. They say: Allah is in every place. Ahl al-Sunnah asked them: how can you say He is in places of filth and harm? They said: when you enter a place, Allah is with you; wherever you enter, Allah is with you.

The second opinion is the opposite of these: they said it is not correct to describe Allah as being in any place, neither above nor below, nor to the right of the world, nor to its left, nor connected to the world, nor separated from the world. Mahmud ibn Sabuktakin said to Muhammad ibn Fawrak while debating him on this issue: "If you say this, then establish for us your Lord. If He is neither above, nor below, nor to the right, nor to the left, nor connected, nor separated, nor distinct, nor adjacent, where is He? He is not anywhere; this is complete non-existence."

In sum, the elevation mentioned in the author's words, may Allah have mercy on him: ("'Aliyy over His creation"), we say: elevation is of two kinds, elevation of attribute and elevation of essence. As for elevation of attribute, no one among the people of the qibla, not even the innovators, has denied it for Allah; they all affirm for Allah elevation of attribute. But the mu'attilah see their denial as a form of glorifying Allah and exalting Him, and the mumaththilah (anthropomorphists) likewise see their affirmation as exalting Allah and establishing His reality. As for elevation of essence, this is the matter on which people divided into the three categories you have heard.

﴿Al-Kabir﴾: he said: (the Great). This is an approximate explanation; if he had said: the Great, possessor of greatness (dhu al-kibriya'), it would have been closer. He, the Mighty and Majestic, is Great and possessor of greatness. He is Great in His essence; nothing of His creation encompasses Him. The seven heavens and the seven earths in His hand are like a mustard seed in the hand of one of us.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you, we said that the call (da'wah) (...), and when it reaches a person it is obligatory on him to seek (knowledge). Should we tell people that it is obligatory on them to seek, and how do we say this to them when they are in fact lazy and do not seek, meaning ignorant, not...?
* Shaykh: We are not speaking of the Arabs; the Arabs understand the call as soon as it reaches them. We are speaking of people who do not understand the meaning; it is obligatory on them to seek. As for the common people now, the call has reached them and they have understood it; that is why they know the meaning of "There is no god but Allah" and the meaning of "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," and similar things.
* Student: (...) If someone asks about the words of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿They made us die twice﴾ [Ghafir 11]: is it meant that there are two deaths: the death in this world during sleep, and the other death on the Day of Resurrection?
* Shaykh: This is not correct, because the death of this world during sleep is not two, three, four, or a hundred. How many times does a person sleep in a month? At least thirty times. ﴿And He it is who takes you in death by night and knows what you have earned by day; then He resurrects you therein﴾ [al-An'am 60]. When we are raised from the sleep of last night, the second night comes, and we die again, and so on; and the one who sleeps after the Fajr prayer, and the one who sleeps at midday rest, and the one who sleeps after 'Asr: four deaths in one day.
* Student: (...) on the right or the left (...) he described himself (...)?
* Shaykh: No, (...) He is not on the right or the left, but He described Himself with what is better than this, because if He had said: "No right and no left," the description would have been negative. But when He says: ﴿And He is the Most High﴾ [al-Baqarah 255], the right and left are negated by an affirmative attribute, not a negative one, and an affirmative attribute is more complete than a negative one, because the indication of a negative attribute upon affirmation is an implication (dalalat al-iltizam), which a denier may deny and not accept.
* Student: (...) non-existence; he says: Allah is neither above nor below nor to the right nor left. What is his evidence?
* Shaykh: He says: because if you establish that He is in a direction, you have made Him a body (jism); if He is above, this means He is a body; right and left likewise. All of this is to flee from tajsim (corporealism). The reality is that Satan played with them. Otherwise we say to them: what is the tajsim you want to deny of Allah? If you want to say that Allah is not a thing, we do not agree with you. If you want to say that Allah is a body described with perfect attributes, then He is indeed described with perfect attributes; but we never apply the word "body" (jism) to Allah. It has been reported in a hadith what indicates that He is described as a "shakhs" (person), yet we still do not say that He is a person like the persons of created beings, never: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura 11].
* Student: Those who (...) in any place cite the verse: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 115].
* Shaykh: Does this contradict elevation, so that it could serve as evidence for its absence? Is it not possible for a thing to be above you while also in front of you? It is possible. If this is possible for a created thing, how about the Creator who encompasses everything? Then how can we bring a verse that admits of possibilities against clear, decisive verses that do not admit of them, namely elevation? Be careful, my brothers, about this, because the people of falsehood bring the ambiguous (mutashabih) to override the decisive (muhkam), and do not interpret the ambiguous in light of the decisive. They bring the ambiguous against the decisive in order to contradict it, and they do not interpret the ambiguous in light of the decisive so that it becomes decisive. This is the trial. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous of it, those are the ones Allah has named; so beware of them." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4547), and Muslim (2665/1), from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.] She related it thus from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Pay attention. This is a matter I want to draw your attention to: when conflicting verses and conflicting hadiths appear, do not bring them to yourselves as being in conflict. Bring them to yourselves on the basis that you are seeking to reconcile them, so that you may be granted success in reconciling them. If you bring them as being in conflict, they remain a source of doubt. I always forbid you from this. I say: do not bring the ambiguous verses whose apparent meaning is conflict, or the hadiths likewise, as being in conflict. Bring them on the basis that you want to reconcile them, not that some of them oppose others, so that you may be guided to the straight path. For there is a difference between presenting (the ambiguous) and returning (it). Presenting the ambiguous (mutashabih) against the clear (muhkam) means that one seeks conflict. But returning the ambiguous to the clear means that one attempts reconciliation without presupposing conflict. This matter occurs in matters of knowledge, and it also occurs in matters of practice. Sometimes descriptions of one act of worship are reported from the Prophet ﷺ, and the one who thinks about it supposes that this is a contradiction. But we say: do not recite them or bring them to yourself as contradictory. No; bring them on the basis that you reconcile them, so you understand this one in one way and that one in another way. Most doubt for the student arises when he brings verses whose apparent meaning is conflict, or hadiths whose apparent meaning is conflict, as being contradictory. But if he brings them on the basis that he returns some to others and joins some to others, he will find a way out and an explanation of what he had thought. This is something they have tested, and by God's permission you will benefit from it.

As for those who said: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west; wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 115], it indicates the absence of height, and so it contradicts the evidences for height. We say: Who said this? Who said that it indicates the absence of height? And if a thing is opposite you, must it be directly facing you? Not at all, it is not necessary. You may say: this is on my right, and it is the lowest thing, yet it is in the right direction; and this is on my left, and it is the lowest thing, and it is in the left direction. As in the hadith of the Ascension: "On the right of Adam are black figures, and on his left are black figures; when he looks to the left he weeps." [Related by al-Bukhari (3342) and Muslim (163/263) with their chains from the hadith of Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The roof of my house was opened while I was in Makkah, and Jibril descended and opened my chest, then washed it with Zamzam water, then brought a golden basin full of wisdom and faith, and poured it into my chest, then closed it, then took my hand and ascended with me to the heaven. When he came to the lowest heaven, Jibril said to the keeper of the heaven: Open. He said: Who is this? He said: This is Jibril. He said: Is there anyone with you? He said: With me is Muhammad. He said: Has he been sent for? He said: Yes. So open. When we ascended to the lowest heaven, behold, a man, on his right are black figures, and on his left are black figures; when he looks to his right he laughs, and when he looks to his left he weeps..." The hadith.] The left is the offspring of the disbelieving sons of Adam, in the Fire, and this is below. So it does not follow that what is on your right must be directly facing you, nor that what is above you must be directly facing you, nor that what is below you must be directly facing you. This is not necessary. But those in whose hearts is deviation follow what is ambiguous in it, seeking to create doubt.

* * *

* The student: ﴿Raised in degrees, Owner of the Throne, He casts the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants, that He may warn of the Day of Meeting (15). The Day they will come forth; nothing of them will be hidden from Allah. "Whose is the dominion today?" "For Allah, the One, the Subduer" (16). Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned. No injustice today. Indeed Allah is swift in account﴾ [Ghafir 15-17].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. The Blessed and Exalted Allah said: ﴿It is He who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the sky﴾ [Ghafir 13].
﴿That is because﴾ [Ghafir 12]... and so on to the end.
* In this verse there are benefits. First: the affirmation of causes, by His saying: ﴿That is because﴾. The "bi" (because of) indicates causation. It has passed with us many times that the People of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah affirm causes for their effects, but not as if they act by themselves; rather by the effective powers that Allah has placed in them. This is derived from His saying: ﴿That is because﴾, since the "ba" indicates causation.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: clarifying the state of these disbelievers, that when Allah alone is invoked they disbelieve, and when partners are associated with Him they accept that association. This is from His saying: ﴿Because when Allah alone was called upon, you disbelieved, and when partners were associated with Him, you believed﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that judgment belongs to Allah, by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So judgment belongs to Allah﴾, and not to other than Him. The judgment of Allah the Exalted is divided into two types: cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i). The cosmic is what He has decreed over His servants as a fact and as a measure; the legislative is what He has decreed over His servants as law and regulation. Both judgments are present in the Qur'an. From the decreed judgment is the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah judges for me﴾ [Yusuf 80]. From the legislative judgment is His saying: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges among you, and Allah is Knowing, Wise﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 10]. The difference between them is that the legislative judgment is what Allah the Mighty and Majestic is pleased with, whereas the cosmic judgment concerns what He is pleased with and what He is not pleased with. The second difference is that the legislative judgment may or may not occur from the one upon whom it is imposed, whereas the cosmic judgment must occur. If Allah decrees for a person death, illness, poverty, a defect, or other than that, it occurs without fail. If Allah decrees for a person that he believe and do righteous deeds, it may occur or may not occur.
And His saying: ﴿So the judgment﴾ here includes both matters together. From this it is derived that it is not permissible to judge by laws that contradict the Sharia; by His saying: ﴿So judgment belongs to Allah﴾, and this sentence conveys restriction, i.e., judgment belongs to Allah and not to other than Him. Judging by laws that contradict the Sharia may be disbelief, may be wrongdoing, and may be sinfulness, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic mentioned these three aspects in Surat al-Ma'idah, which is among the last revealed. If one establishes a man-made legal judgment as binding in place of the Sharia, this is disbelief, because it entails abolishing the legislative judgment and substituting another in its place. This is disbelief in what Allah has sent down, and it nullifies deeds, because one cannot abolish the legislative judgment except after hating it, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿That is because they disliked what Allah sent down, so He nullified their deeds﴾ [Muhammad 9]. On this basis, those who govern their peoples by laws contrary to the Sharia are regarded as disbelievers, and they must repent to Allah and judge by the Sharia of Allah, or else they die as disbelievers, and we seek refuge in Allah. We do not pass this judgment on each one individually, since some of them may be deceived, misled, or may have heard from someone they trust who misguided them. The one who enacted the law may have been deceived by someone who says that the legislative judgment applies only between a person and his Lord in worship, personal status and inheritance, while the affairs of this world belong to the people of this world.
