This is compared to his saying ﷺ: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world" [Related by Muslim (2363/141) with his chain from the hadith of Aisha and Anas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the Prophet ﷺ passed by people pollinating palms, and said: "If you did not do it, it would be good." He said: so it came out as shrivelled dates. He passed by them and said: "What is wrong with your palms?" They said: We said such and such. He said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world."].
Then this poor judge comes, who knows nothing of the matter and who has been deceived by the outward show of this world and its adornments, and thinks this is the truth, and enacts a law contrary to the Sharia. We do not judge such a person as a disbeliever, because he has been deceived and is a misinterpreter. But if it is made clear to him and he persists, then he is judged a disbeliever.
As for the second: judging by other than what Allah has sent down, which is wrongdoing, is when the motive is love of transgressing against others, not hatred of the Sharia nor judging by other than what Allah has sent down; rather, out of enmity toward another he judges against that other by other than what Allah has sent down, out of injustice and aggression. This one has the ruling of wrongdoers, not the ruling of disbelievers, because he has not disbelieved. He says: I know that what the Sharia brought is the truth, but I want to avenge myself on this man and attack him. So this one has the ruling of the wrongdoer: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down, those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45].
As for the third type: one who judges by other than what Allah has sent down out of a desire within himself, not from hatred of the truth nor from substituting something else for it, but he wants something in himself and so judges by other than what Allah has sent down, such as desiring to own this land or this car or the like, and judges in its favour for a purpose. His intent is not to wrong the one judged against, but his aim is to follow desire. So he judges, and by this he is among the defiantly disobedient.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that judgment belongs to Allah the Mighty and Majestic in this world and the Hereafter. For this reason some scholars divided judgment into three types: cosmic, legislative, and retributive. The retributive judgment is what occurs in the Hereafter, but the correct view is that the retributive judgment is not outside being a cosmic judgment, since it is the act of Allah; and then there is no need for many divisions, since whenever a division can be shortened, it is preferable. For this reason, and Allah knows best, the Messenger ﷺ would sometimes say: "Three whom Allah will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor look at, nor purify, and for them is a painful punishment" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2672) and Muslim (108/173) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)].
Although there are others whom Allah will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor look at, nor purify, and for whom is a painful punishment, nonetheless, dividing a thing into parts and reducing its types is closer to understanding. For this reason a distinction is made between giving water to a thirsty person all at once or giving it to him in sips. The second is more wholesome, more refreshing, and more pleasant, as in the hadith [Muslim in his Sahih (2028/123) with his chain from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ would breathe three times while drinking, and say: "It is more quenching, more wholesome, and more pleasant."] that it is appropriate for a person when drinking to breathe three times. For example, if you are thirsty, do not drink the cup all at once; breathe into it three times: drink, then take the cup away from your mouth, then return it, then take it away again and return it, so that this is more wholesome, more pleasant, and more refreshing.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's highness (uluww) the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿the Most High﴾. It is highness in His essence and highness in His attributes; His attributes are exalted, and He Himself, glorified and exalted is He, is above everything.
The evidences for Allah's essential highness are five kinds: the Book, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma'), reason, and innate nature (fitrah). As for the Book, it is full of this, meaning of its indication that Allah is above everything in various ways: at times it explicitly states that He is in the heaven, at times it explicitly states that He has risen over the Throne, at times it explicitly states that things descend from Him, and at times it explicitly states that things are raised up to Him, ascend to Him, and ascend to Him. All of this indicates Allah's highness in His essence.
The Sunnah likewise came in its three aspects: speech, action, and tacit approval. As for speech, the Messenger ﷺ used to say: "Our Lord is Allah, who is in the heaven, Your name is sanctified, Your command is in the heaven and the earth" [Related by al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (10809) from the hadith of Abu al-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him)], and he used to say in his prostration: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High" [Related by Muslim (772/203) from the hadith of Hudhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him)].
As for action, his gesture toward the sky when he said: "O Allah, bear witness" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1741) and Muslim (1679/31) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah (may Allah be pleased with him)].
As for tacit approval, his approval of the slave girl when she said that Allah is in the heaven, when he asked her: "Where is Allah?" [Related by Muslim (537/33) from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami (may Allah be pleased with him)].
As for consensus, the salaf agreed that Allah the Exalted is high in His essence above everything. The evidence of this consensus is that not a single letter has come from them contradicting what the Book and Sunnah indicate about Allah's highness. This shows that they held this view. This is among the methods we mentioned to you earlier: if someone said: "Bring us one letter from the salaf saying that Allah is high in His essence," we would say: there is no need to bring you that, because its appearance in the Book and Sunnah, without anything from them opposing it, shows that they held it, and they are unanimous on this.
Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned words in which he said: "And Allah knows that after thorough research and my review of what I could of the speech of the salaf, I did not find any one of them who stated explicitly that Allah is not in the heaven or that things do not ascend to Him." And he mentioned something similar. On this basis we say: the highness of Allah in His essence has been agreed upon by the salaf. Whoever says otherwise has opposed the Messenger and followed other than the way of the believers. But Allah has made a condition, saying: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him﴾ [al-Nisa' 115].
As for reason, its indication of Allah's highness is clear, because we ask: which is more perfect, the high or the low? By the agreement of rational people, the high is more perfect. And if it is established that highness is perfection, it must be affirmed for Allah the Mighty and Majestic, since Allah the Exalted is described by attributes of perfection.
As for innate nature, ask about it the old women of the Muslims; do not ask the students of knowledge. Ask the old woman: "Where is Allah?" and she will say to you: "In the heaven." Ask every supplicant, when he supplicates, where his heart soars: to the heaven. This innate nature is what silenced Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni when Abu al-'Ala' al-Hamadhani said to him: "O Shaykh, leave aside mention of the Throne." When Abu al-Ma'ali said: "Allah was and nothing was" — meaning: there was no Throne and nothing other than the Throne, and He is now as He was. What does he want? He wants to negate the istiwa'. If He was when there was no Throne, and He is now as He is, it follows that He is not established over the Throne. So he (al-Hamadhani) said to him: "O Shaykh, leave aside mention of the Throne — because the evidence of His istiwa' over the Throne is an evidence from revelation — but tell us about this innate nature that we find in our souls. No knower has ever said 'O Allah' without finding in his heart a necessary inclination to seek highness." So Abu al-Ma'ali struck his head and said: "Al-Hamadhani has bewildered me." He was bewildered because this is a matter of innate nature that cannot be denied at all. If a person denies it, he has denied what innate nature indicates.
So the conclusion is that Allah's highness in His essence is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, reason, and innate nature, and, praise be to Allah, it needs no dispute. Had it not been that the people of innovation and denial (ta'til) forced the People of the Sunnah to speak about it, there would be no need for a person to speak of it, because it is an innate matter that requires no great effort. But these innovating, denying, distorting, and deviant speculative theologians are the ones who compelled the People of the Sunnah to say such things and to try to establish these matters with whatever evidences they could.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of greatness (kibriya') to Allah, and of bigness (kibr); by His saying: ﴿the Great﴾. Allah the Exalted combines kibriya', kibr, and kibar in more than one verse. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿the Great, the Most High﴾ [al-Ra'd 9], and here He says: ﴿the Most High, the Great﴾, because through this the absolute perfection is attained: highness, greatness, and bigness, and in it is the perfection of perfection.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It is He who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the sky. Yet none remembers except one who turns back (to Him)﴾ [Ghafir 13]. ﴿It is He who shows you﴾, i.e., He manifests His signs to you so that you see them. The pronoun refers to Allah. He is the One who holds judgment, the Most High, the Great. Yet despite this, He has not left His servants neglected; rather, He has shown them His signs so that they may believe.

So His words ﴿It is He who shows you His signs﴾ mean that He makes them manifest to you so that you see them with your own eyes. The "signs" (ayat) here are the indications that point to what they signify, and they are more eloquent than miracles and the like.

The signs of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, are of two kinds: cosmic signs (ayat kawniyyah) and legislative signs (ayat shar'iyyah). The cosmic signs are the creatures of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The legislative signs are the revelation that the messengers brought. All creatures are signs from the signs of Allah: ﴿And on the earth are signs for those who are certain, and within yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 20-21]; ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves that you may find tranquility in them﴾ [ar-Rum 21]; ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has dispersed within them of living creatures﴾ [ash-Shura 29]. The examples of this are many, all of which point to their Creator, Mighty and Majestic, and to His sole creation, His wisdom, His mercy, His might, and other meanings of lordship (rububiyyah) indicated by these signs. A single sign may point to several signs and several attributes. As I told you, these cosmic signs encompass all creatures, and on this someone has said:

How strange that the Deity is disobeyed,
or how the one who denies Him can deny Him!
And in everything there is a sign for Him
that points to the fact that He is One.

Consider everything, and you will find the complete proof that it has a Creator who manages it, is wise, and is all-knowing, along with other meanings of lordship.

As for the legislative signs, they are what the messengers brought. Allah, exalted be He, has shown us them, and He gave the messengers, peace be upon them, signs of the kind by which mankind can be made to believe. The messengers did not come simply saying to people, "We are messengers to you." Rather, they came with signs that point to what they were sent with and to the One who sent them.

﴿It is He who shows you His signs﴾: so the signs include both the cosmic and the legislative. Lightning is a cosmic sign: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope﴾ [ar-Ra'd 12].

﴿And sends down for you provision from the sky﴾: sending down (tanzil) is from what is above, and here He says ﴿from the sky﴾, which denotes height. The "sky" here does not mean the protected roof (as-sama' al-mahfuzah al-saqf al-marfu'), but rather height. This is shown by His words: ﴿and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 164]. The rain does not descend from the protected roof of the sky; rather it descends from height, from the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth. This is an observed matter.

His words ﴿provision (rizq)﴾ mean water through which provision is obtained. What descends is water through which provision comes, so the water itself is provision: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? Is it you who brought it down from the clouds, or are We the sender?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 68-69]. And through it provision comes: ﴿So We brought forth by it fruits of every kind﴾ [al-A'raf 57]. The fruits are provisions, and water is provision to be drunk; so it is provision in every case.

In placing the signs before the sending down of provision from the sky, there is evidence that the religious blessing is more important and greater than the worldly blessing.

﴿And none remembers except one who turns back (to Him)﴾. The author (al-Mufassir) said: (﴿It is He who shows you His signs﴾: the proofs of His oneness), meaning the signs that indicate His oneness and other meanings of lordship that they indicate.

(﴿And sends down for you provision from the sky﴾: by rain). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that provision is what comes out by rain, meaning plants and the like. But what we have mentioned is more correct: that the rain itself is provision, because Allah said: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? Is it you who brought it down from the clouds﴾. And sometimes the body's need for water is greater than its need for food.

(﴿And none remembers﴾: takes heed ﴿except one who turns back﴾: returns from polytheism). As for his words ﴿except one who turns back﴾, he said: (returns from polytheism). This is undoubtedly correct but incomplete. The correct meaning is: ﴿one who turns back﴾ means one who returns to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from polytheism and from other sins and transgressions. This is more general than what the author said.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, since He shows us the signs.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: that the signs which Allah shows us are a binding proof, so that no one may say, "No signs came to us by which we might take heed."

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: that creatures and legislated matters all point to the Creator, the Legislator, glorified and exalted be He.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the favour of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in sending down rain from the sky, and that it is provision for us.

* And from its benefits: the wisdom in rain descending from the sky. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is able to make rivers for the earth that flow over its surface and water whatever Allah wills to water. But rain is more beneficial and better, because when rain descends from above it reaches the peaks of mountains, covering the plain and the rugged, the low and the high. This is among the wisdoms of rain descending from above so that it encompasses the whole earth.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: what the spirit is nourished by is more important than what the body is nourished by, since He placed the showing of the signs before the provision that descends from the sky. This indicates that it is more important, and so it is. This is the reality, because the loss of bodily nourishment only brings about what is unavoidable, namely death, which is unavoidable even if a person is in the greatest bodily comfort and luxury. But the nourishment of the spirit is what needs striving and treatment, and by losing it comes ruin in this world and the Hereafter: ﴿Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [az-Zumar 15]; ﴿Say: Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in deeds? Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think they are doing well in work. Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in meeting Him﴾ [al-Kahf 103-105]; ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except those who believe and do righteous deeds and advise each other to truth and advise each other to patience﴾ [al-'Asr 1-3].

So the loss of the body, without the loss of the spirit, is far less; the loss of the world, without the loss of religion, is far less. For this reason Allah placed His blessing of showing the signs before His blessing of sending down rain.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the signs, the provision, and the bounty are not benefited from except by one who turns back to Allah. As for one who does not turn back to Allah, Allah says: ﴿And signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus 101].

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the more a person turns back to Allah, the stronger his faith in the signs will be, because a ruling attached to an attribute grows with its strength and weakens with its weakness. If remembrance is for one who turns back, then the more a person turns back, the stronger his remembrance.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: whoever does not have turning back will be deprived of benefiting from the signs, because Allah says: ﴿And none remembers except one who turns back﴾.

* And from its benefits: turning back to Allah is a cause of abundant provision. This is shown by His words: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out, and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [at-Talaq 2-3]. And Allah knows best.

* Student: If someone said, regarding the words of Allah, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45], and ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then those are the defiant﴾ [al-Ma'idah 47]: the intended meaning is disbelief. How (...)?

* The Shaykh: We answer that this is an error. How can one meaning be intended while Allah repeats it in different wordings? The principle is that a difference in wording indicates a difference in meaning. But some scholars said: describing the ruler as a disbeliever does not prevent describing him as defiant, because Allah, exalted be He, described the disbelievers as defiant, saying: ﴿And as for those who committed defiance, their refuge is the Fire. Whenever they wish to leave it, they will be returned to it﴾ [as-Sajdah 20], and He described the disbelievers as wrongdoers, saying: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 254]. So He attributed these three descriptions to one subject. There is no obstacle to a person being described by several attributes. The disbeliever is undoubtedly a wrongdoer, and undoubtedly a defiant one who has left obedience. Indeed, his defiance is absolute defiance, while the defiance of a believing sinner is restricted defiance. But if we take the difference in these wordings as referring to different circumstances, it is more eloquent, because we say: disbelief includes wrongdoing and defiance, so its indication of them is by implication. Thus, merely describing him as a disbeliever is describing him as a wrongdoer and defiant. Then we gain a new benefit from the ruling of judging by other than what Allah has revealed, where it is pure wrongdoing and not disbelief, or defiance and not disbelief.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, I am saying that treating a difference in wording as a difference in meaning is better, because that is the principle. The scholars said on this issue: interpreting speech as establishing a new meaning (ta'sis) is preferable to interpreting it as emphasis (tawkid).

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, we did not say that. He says we said that what descends from the sky is substances and attributes.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, absolutely we did not say this. Did we say: what descends from the sky, or what is attributed to Allah as sent down? Yes, there is a difference between the two. According to your statement, sheep would descend from the sky, and cattle would descend from the sky. We said: what is attributed to Allah as sending down is either substances or attributes. If it is attributes, then it is an attribute of Allah; and if it is substances, then they are substances subsisting in themselves.

* Student: We said: the spirit (...) attributes (...).

* The Shaykh: It is not attributes. The correct view is that the spirit is a body, but a body unlike the known dense bodies. We said that what Allah, exalted be He, sent down is divided into two categories, and Allah, exalted be He, did not mention that He sent down the spirit.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you well, regarding His words: ﴿That is because when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when others were associated with Him, you believed﴾ [Ghafir 12]. Some scholars said: there is an omitted element that is dispensed with because the apparent meaning indicates it, and its figurative sense is: "There is no way out, wherever you wish."

* The Shaykh: This is what he intended when they said: ﴿Is there any way to get out?﴾ It is as if he said: there is no way out, because you have put forward for yourselves what makes leaving impossible, namely that when Allah alone is invoked you disbelieve, and when others are associated with Him you believe.

* Student: The scholars say: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44]: if he considers it lawful. But if he does not consider it lawful, then he is not a disbeliever.

* The Shaykh: In any case, the one who sets up a law in place of the heavenly law: did he consider it lawful or not?

* Student: He says: the Sharia is better.

* The Shaykh: My question: did he consider it lawful or not? I say: he considered it lawful, indeed he saw it as better, so he is a disbeliever. Even so, whoever considers judging by other than what Allah has revealed to be lawful is a disbeliever, even if he does not actually judge by it. Whoever says it is permissible for us to judge by other than what Allah has revealed is a disbeliever, even if he does not judge.

This is a problem. Some people often resort to considering it lawful or to denial. For example, someone says: whoever abandons prayer out of denial has disbelieved. This is distorting words from their places. I tell you that those who are fanatical toward their own opinion resort to this matter, trying to twist the texts to fit what they say. For example, "Whoever abandons prayer has disbelieved"[[Narrated by Ibn Hibban (1463) from the hadith of Buraydah al-Aslami, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. Those who said that he does not disbelieve, what did they do? They said: whoever abandons it while denying its obligation has disbelieved. We say: Glory be to Allah! If you do that, you have wronged the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ twice. The first time, you made his words other than their apparent meaning. The second time, you asserted something the Messenger, peace be upon him, did not say. The Messenger said: "Whoever abandons it," and did not say: "whoever denies it." Was there any impediment on his tongue that prevented him from saying "whoever denies it"? Then we tell you: denial is disbelief even if one prays, while the Messenger said: "Whoever abandons prayer." If a person said: prayer is not obligatory, but he is persistent in it and is the first to come to the mosque and the last to leave, will he disbelieve or not? He disbelieves. How do you discard the description of abandonment and bring in a new description on which you hang the ruling? This is a problem.

When Imam Ahmad was asked about His words: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein; and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment﴾ [an-Nisa' 93], they said to him: "So-and-so says this is about one who considers killing a believer lawful." Imam Ahmad laughed and said: "Glory be to Allah! Whoever considers killing a believer lawful is a disbeliever, whether he kills him or not." This distortion is undoubtedly laughable. Likewise, whoever considers judging by other than what Allah has revealed lawful is a disbeliever, whether he judges or does not judge. The verse attached the ruling to the act of judging: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed﴾. Do you understand now?

Beware of this matter. Beware of distorting words from their places for the sake of a belief you hold. Make your belief and your judgment about a thing follow the texts; do not make the texts follow your belief. If you make the text follow what you believe, this is pure following of desire. Place yourself before the texts like the corpse before the washer: the texts turn you over, and you do not turn them over. This is the believer. Yet sometimes some texts qualify others or specify others, or understanding the Sharia requires restricting the absolute or specifying the general, and similar matters. This does not take us outside of following the texts.

Student: ﴿Exalted in degrees, Lord of the Throne. He casts the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants, that he may warn of the Day of Meeting (15). The Day when they will come forth, nothing of them being hidden from Allah. "To whom belongs the dominion this Day? To Allah, the One, the Subduer" (16). "This Day every soul will be recompensed for what it earned. No injustice this Day. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning" [Ghafir 15–17].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion, although the disbelievers dislike it﴾ [Ghafir 14]. When Allah, glorified and exalted, made clear that He had shown us His cosmic and legislative signs, He commanded us to call upon Him alone, sincere to Him in religion. His words ﴿So call upon Allah﴾: the mufassir said, "(So worship Him)." This is one of the two meanings of du'a' (supplication/invocation), and the second meaning is du'a' al-mas'alah (request), i.e., ask Him. The correct view is that it encompasses both matters: du'a' al-mas'alah and du'a' al-'ibadah (worship). Worship is called du'a', as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord said, "Call upon Me; I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated"﴾ [Ghafir 60]. He said ﴿Call upon Me﴾, then said ﴿those who are too proud to worship Me﴾. As for du'a' al-'ibadah, every person who calls upon Allah, glorified and exalted, does not call upon Him except while believing that He is All-Knowing of everything and All-Powerful over everything; therefore he calls upon Him, and thereby he becomes one who worships Him.

He said: ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾. "Sincere" (mukhlisin) is a state (hal) of the waw in His saying ﴿call upon Allah﴾. Ikhlas (sincerity) is purification; the purification of a thing is called ikhlas. The meaning: purify your religion from shirk.

As for His saying ﴿in religion﴾, what is meant by religion here is action, whether it is worship or supplication. The word "din" is applied to action and also applied to the recompense for action. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun 6] is an instance of applying din to action. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Master of the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Fatihah 4] is an instance of applying din to recompense. It is said: "As you do, so you will be repaid" (kama tadin tadan), i.e., as you act, so you will be recompensed. So din here means action.

(﴿Sincere to Him in religion﴾ from shirk), as the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: that we call upon Allah sincerely directing the supplication to Him, and that we worship Him sincerely directing the worship to Him, free from shirk, so that we do not associate anything with Him, neither in our supplication nor in our worship.

(﴿Although the disbelievers dislike it﴾ your sincerity): meaning, call upon Allah sincerely in every state, whether the disbelievers are pleased or angry. It is well known that they will be angry, but it does not matter that they are angry with us when we make our religion sincere to Allah. The author's words "(﴿although the disbelievers dislike it﴾ your sincerity)" should rather be phrased: "although they dislike your sincere action," because ikhlas is the intention of the heart, whereas the disbeliever only dislikes what appears of a person's action. So the meaning: although the disbelievers dislike your action by which you are sincere to Allah, in spite of their noses (i.e., in defiance of them).

Then he said: (﴿Exalted in degrees﴾ [Ghafir 15] i.e., Allah is great in attributes, or raising the degrees of the believers in Paradise).

His words ﴿Exalted﴾ (rafi') come from rif'ah, which is height. The author, may Allah have mercy on him and pardon him, explained it by one of two meanings: that rif'ah means greatness and "degrees" means attributes, i.e., Allah, exalted is He, is great in attributes. The second meaning: "exalted in degrees," i.e., raising the degrees of others, namely the believers in Paradise. Both meanings are a distortion of the words from their places (tahrif al-kalim 'an mawadi'ihi), because rafi' is an active participle or an attributive adjective whose subject refers to Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned in His saying ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾. Based on this, it is not valid to interpret it as meaning "raising the degrees of the believers," because by that interpretation the degrees would be the degrees of another, the degrees of the believers. Nor is it valid to interpret "exalted in degrees" as "great in attributes," because of the great difference between them. But the author, may Allah pardon him, explained it this way in order to flee from affirming intrinsic elevation (al-'uluww al-dhati), since he is among those who do not hold that He is high in His essence. Therefore he distorted the Qur'an to one of these two meanings, and both are false. The correct view is that He, glorified is He, is Exalted in degrees. What supports and specifies this is His saying ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾, i.e., Possessor of the Throne. The Throne is the highest of created things, so it is as if He said: "Exalted in degrees above the Throne," and this is the definite meaning.

The author's words "(the Creator of it)" also contain an indication of denying istiwa' (settling/being established); because the meaning of "Lord of the Throne" is its possessor, the one who is established upon it. This is the meaning. For this reason one does not say "Lord of the earth," "Lord of the heavens," "Lord of the mountains," or "Lord of the clouds," even though He is their Creator. So interpreting "Lord of the Throne" as "its Creator" is undoubtedly a distortion of the words from their places, fleeing from affirming istiwa' upon the Throne.

The definite interpretation of the verse is that we say: He is Exalted in degrees, i.e., He Himself, glorified and exalted, is elevated; rather, "Exalted in degrees" comes with the adjective pattern (sifah mushabbahah) indicating permanence and continuity. "Degrees" is from the well-known degrees, i.e., what is some above others until it reaches the ultimate. As for "Lord of the Throne," its meaning is the Possessor of the Throne, specifically by being established upon it. This is the definite meaning of the verse.

(﴿He casts the Spirit﴾: revelation; ﴿by His command﴾, i.e., His word; ﴿upon whom He wills of His servants﴾), to the end. ﴿He casts the Spirit﴾: the Spirit is revelation, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a Spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura 52]. Allah, exalted is He, called revelation a spirit because by it the hearts live.

As for His saying (﴿by His command﴾, i.e., His word), this is a good interpretation: meaning that revelation is from the speech of Allah, glorified and exalted; He speaks, Jibril hears, and then he descends with it to whom Allah, glorified and exalted, wills.

As for His saying ﴿upon whom He wills of His servants﴾, He did not specify who these are, but we know they are the prophets, because they are the ones to whom revelation is cast, whether they are messengers or non-messengers.

Furthermore, His saying ﴿upon whom He wills﴾: the unrestricted mention of will in every place in the Qur'an is qualified by wisdom. Whenever you see Allah saying "wills," it is a will accompanied by wisdom, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for whoever among you wills to go straight. And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Takwir 28–29], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30].

Who are these whom Allah wills to cast the Spirit upon? Allah explained them in His saying: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 124].

As for His saying ﴿of His servants﴾, what is meant by "servants" here is the special servitude, namely those who believed in Allah, glorified and exalted; rather, it is even more specific: they are the messengers.

﴿That he may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾. He said: (﴿that he may warn﴾ — frighten). The lam here indicates purpose (ta'lil), and warning (indhar) is notification accompanied by fear; for this reason the author said "to frighten," explaining it by its necessary implication, since warning is notification accompanied by intimidation.

As for his words "(the one upon whom it is cast is the people)", the mufassir, may Allah have mercy on him, informed us that the subject of ﴿yun动dhir﴾ (he warns) is the one upon whom it is cast, namely the Messenger. There is no doubt he is the direct warner. It is possible that the subject refers back to the subject of ﴿casts the Spirit﴾, namely Allah, glorified and exalted; i.e., so that Allah may warn. The wisdom in not mentioning the subject, and Allah knows best, is to make the verb suitable for both: that the warning may refer back to Allah, and may refer back to the Messenger. If it refers to Allah, it is because He is the origin; if it refers to the Messenger, it is because he is the direct conveyor of the warning.

His words "(the people)" are an estimate of the first object of ﴿yundhira﴾, because "yundhira" takes two objects that are not originally subject and predicate: either the first object or the second object may be omitted. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And warn them of the imminent Day﴾ [Ghafir 18], which contains both objects; ﴿And warn mankind of the Day when there will come to them﴾ [Ibrahim 44], likewise both objects. One of them may be omitted, either the first or the second, when the context indicates it.

(﴿Day of Meeting﴾ with the yā' deleted and affirmed): meaning there are two readings: al-Talaqi with the yā', and al-Talaq with the yā' deleted. Affirming the yā' is the original form; deleting the yā' is for lightness, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Great, the Exalted﴾ [al-Ra'd 9], whose original form is al-Muta'ali, but the yā' was deleted for lightness. Likewise here, al-talaq's original form is al-talaqi, and the yā' was deleted for lightness.

The Day of Meeting (yawm al-talaq) is the Day of Resurrection, and the mufassir gave the reason with his words: (for the meeting of the people of the heavens and the earth, the worshipper and the worshipped, and the oppressor and the oppressed on it), i.e., on that day. If we took a more general meaning, "for the meeting of all creatures on that day," because everything meets the other, even the beasts: ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾ [al-Takwir 5]. It is called the Day of Meeting because creation meets on it: Allah, glorified and exalted, gathers all creatures on that day, and they meet one another.

* Among the benefits of these verses and those before them: the obligation of sincerity to Allah in supplication, due to His saying: ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere﴾. Calling upon other than Allah in matters the one called upon cannot do is considered shirk; then it may be major shirk or minor shirk depending on the situation. Whoever calls upon a grave, this is major shirk; whoever calls upon another to carry his belongings and the like, while the other cannot carry them, this is not major shirk, rather it is either futility or minor shirk. Whoever calls upon an absent one to rescue him from hardship, this is major shirk, because this is called secret shirk (shirk al-sirr): one cannot call upon an absent one except while believing he has some control over the universe, acting from afar. This is unlike one who calls upon a nearby person, saying, "O so-and-so, carry this with me, help me with that," for this calls upon him to do something perceptible.

* Also among its benefits: the obligation of sincerity in worship to Allah. Since we interpreted du'a' as both du'a' al-mas'alah and du'a' al-'ibadah, the obligation of sincere worship to Allah follows. Whoever worships other than Allah independently has directed some kind of worship to other than Allah, and thereby becomes a major polytheist (mushrik shirkan akbar); that is, whoever prays to a person is a major polytheist, or whoever slaughters for a person, seeking nearness to him and venerating him, is a major polytheist, expelled from the religion.

As for one who performs worship for Allah but shows off in it or seeks to be heard, this is not major shirk, but minor shirk, and his worship is rejected, due to the Prophet's ﷺ saying, related from his Lord: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in need of partners. Whoever does an action in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his association." (Narrated by Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.)

Know also that when showing off (riya') occurs to the heart: if it occurs before entering into the act of worship, it nullifies it from its root, because he entered it upon shirk. If it occurs in the course of the worship: if the latter part is built upon the first part, the worship is nullified; if the latter part is not built upon the first, such that the first can be distinguished from the second, then what contains the showing off is invalid, and what preceded the showing off is valid.

Example of the first: if showing off enters during prayer, in the second rak'ah, the whole prayer is nullified, because if the second rak'ah is nullified, the first rak'ah is nullified too, since prayer is not divisible.

Example of the second: a man prepared a hundred ṣā' for charity and gave fifty ṣā' sincerely, then showing off entered regarding the remaining ṣā'. Here the remaining ṣā' are nullified, but the first ones are valid, because this act of worship—namely charity—is divisible, and its last part is not built upon its first. Even if it were something specified by the law, such as feeding sixty poor people in expiation, for example: he fed thirty poor people sincerely, then showing off entered afterward, the portion preceding the last thirty is accepted. This applies if he yielded to showing off and continued in it. But if showing off occurred to him and he resisted it and continued striving against it, it does not harm him at all, due to the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Indeed, Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper, as long as they do not act upon it or speak of it." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5269) and Muslim (127/201), from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.) He did not act upon it nor speak; indeed perhaps he did not even whisper it to himself, but showing off assailed him.

So now: whoever performs worship for other than Allah—meaning he worships other than Allah—is his ruling major or minor shirk? Major. And whoever performs worship for Allah but showing off enters into it—

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Shirk? Is there no detail, or...?
* Student: If it was before (...) the worship, it is nullified; and if it comes...
* The Shaykh: Just so, state the detail for us (...).
* The Student: As for if it is in the course of it, then there is detail.
* The Shaykh: And what is it?
* Student: If (...) the worship (...).
* The Shaykh: Or the reverse; if the end of the worship is built upon its beginning, even if it preceded—how is it built upon it? If its end is built upon its beginning, meaning it is not divisible.
* The Student: (...) not divisible, it is nullified; and if its end is not built upon its beginning..
* The Shaykh: That is, if it is divisible.
* The Student: It is nullified in (...) the showing off.
* The Shaykh: And what preceded it is valid. Is his statement correct?
* Students: Correct.
* The Shaykh: Good. With what did we qualify this detail?
* Student: If he yielded..
* The Shaykh: If he yielded to showing off and the show-off persisted. Good. And if he resisted it?
* The Student: Then there is nothing upon him.
* The Shaykh: Then there is nothing upon him, and it does not harm him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: opposing the disbelievers in sincerity to Allah in the act and in the deed, due to His saying: ﴿although the disbelievers dislike it﴾. From this follows that a person must perform what is obligatory even if others dislike it, and not show favor to anyone in this. For example, if the father of a young man dislikes that his son pray in congregation—as is common now—should he flatter his father in this? No; he prays in congregation even in defiance of his father's nose, even if he dislikes it.

If a young man maintains kinship ties with his paternal uncle, maternal uncle, and the like, while there is personal enmity between him and his father, such that the father dislikes his son keeping ties with relatives whom the father dislikes—should he maintain them even though he dislikes it, or not? Yes, he maintains them even though he dislikes it, but in this situation he should be discreet with his father, meaning he conceals from him that he maintains them, so that the benefit is achieved without harm. There is a difference between mudara (tactful accommodation) and mudahanah (flattery): mudara is that a person does what he is obliged to do while concealing it from the other person who dislikes it; that is why it is called mudara, from al-dar' which is repelling. As for mudahanah, it is agreeing with him in abandoning what is obligatory, out of flattery, from al-duhn (oil), because it softens.

In any case, we say: from this benefit it follows that a person does what is incumbent upon him even if others dislike it, even if the one who dislikes it is the closest person to him.

Then he said: ﴿Exalted in degrees﴾ [Ghafir 15]... to the end.

* Among the benefits of this verse: affirmation of Allah's elevation, glorified and exalted, contrary to the mufassir author; due to His saying: ﴿Exalted in degrees﴾, and by elevation we mean elevation of essence. As for elevation of attribute, the author acknowledged it when he said: (i.e., great in attributes). So in this verse is affirmation of the elevation of the essence of Allah, glorified and exalted, due to His saying: ﴿Exalted in degrees﴾.

This has passed us many times, and we explained that the five categories of evidence all indicate Allah's elevation: the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus of the Salaf, reason, and innate nature (fitrah).

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the excellence of the Throne, due to His saying: ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾, for the Throne's being specifically attributed to Allah, glorified and exalted, is undoubtedly a great excellence.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of the Throne, due to His saying: ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾.

* Among its benefits: affirmation of Allah's greatness, because the Throne is specific to dominion and sovereignty. One does not say of a man sitting on a chair that he is "on a throne," but one says of a king or ruler sitting on a grand, magnificent chair that he is "possessor of a throne."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verses 14–15 (part 2 of 2):**

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the affirmation of Allah's favour, glorified and exalted be He, upon whomever He wills through revelation, based on His saying: ﴿He casts the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾.
* Among its benefits: revelation is a spirit by which hearts come to life, based on His saying: ﴿He casts the Spirit by His command﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of speech, based on His saying: ﴿by His command﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, speaks and talks whenever He wills, with whatever He wills, however He wills. We do not restrict our Lord, glorified and exalted be He, in speech, neither in time nor in manner. Rather, He may speak with whatever He wills, whenever He wills, however He wills.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of will, based on His saying: ﴿upon whomever He wills﴾.
* Among its benefits: the rank of prophethood is not attained through acquisition (kasb) and chivalry (futuwwah), as al-Saffarini said in his creed (al-'Aqidah), but it is a bounty from Allah, glorified and exalted be He, upon whomever He wills of His servants.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the scholars have a share and portion of the Spirit that Allah, exalted be He, casts upon the messengers, because they are the heirs of the prophets. So they have a share and portion of this Spirit that Allah casts upon whomever He wills. However, they have a share of this guidance, the guidance of direction and clarification (hidayat al-dalalah wa al-bayan). Then they may or may not have a share of the guidance of success (hidayat al-tawfiq). For the scholar may act upon his knowledge, and then he has a share of both guidances: the guidance of instruction (hidayat al-irshad) and the guidance of success (hidayat al-tawfiq). Or he may not act upon his knowledge, and then he has a share of the guidance of knowledge and instruction, but it becomes a burden upon him, since he opposed the truth while knowing it. This is worse than one who opposes it without knowledge of the truth.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom behind the revelation that Allah, mighty and majestic, sends down upon whomever He sends down among His servants is to warn people of the Day of Judgment: ﴿that he may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾.

Because the scholar may act upon his knowledge and thus have a share of both guidances, the guidance of instruction and the guidance of success, or he may not act upon his knowledge and thus have a share of the guidance of knowledge and instruction, but it becomes a burden upon him, since he opposed the truth while knowing it. This is worse than one who opposes it without knowledge of the truth.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom behind the revelation that Allah, mighty and majestic, sends down upon whomever He sends down among His servants is to warn people of the Day of Resurrection, ﴿that he may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾ [Ghafir 15].
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's wisdom, and that His actions are accompanied by wisdom, based on His saying: ﴿that he may warn﴾. The particle of purpose (lam al-ta'lil) and "min" of causation (min al-ta'liliyyah) occur very often in the Qur'an and likewise in the Sunnah, and all of them indicate the affirmation of wisdom for Allah.
Some scholars have mentioned that wisdom is indicated by a thousand proofs from the Book and the Sunnah. The proofs affirming the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, in what He does cannot be counted. This is contrary to those who say that He does it merely by will, not for any wisdom. This amounts to negating one of the greatest attributes of Allah, because it entails that His action would be purposeless, without any praiseworthy end.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever Allah has given knowledge should be a warner, meaning he should combine knowledge and understanding of religion with warning. For if he limits himself to mere teaching of jurisprudence, for example, or to monotheism without stirring hearts, people will not benefit much from him. There must be warning in order to stir hearts. When the Prophet (ﷺ) delivered a sermon, his eyes would turn red, his voice would rise, and his anger would intensify, until he seemed like one warning of an army, saying: "Your enemy will attack you at dawn or in the evening."[1]
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: warning against the disgrace of the Day of Resurrection, since it is the Day of Meeting. There is no doubt that punishment witnessed by few is lighter than punishment witnessed by many. So how about when all of creation witnesses it? It will be far more severe and greater.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's power, in that Allah gathers all of creation on one plain after death, and Allah, glorified and exalted be He, is over all things Competent.

Then He, exalted be He, said: ﴿The Day they come forth, nothing of them will be hidden from Allah. "Whose is the dominion today?" "It is Allah's, the One, the Subduer." Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned; there is no injustice today. Indeed, Allah is swift in account. And warn them of the Imminent Day, when hearts will be at the throats, choking. The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend, nor any intercessor who is obeyed. He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal. And Allah judges with truth, while those they invoke besides Him judge nothing. Indeed, Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [Ghafir 16–20].

* Shaykh: This is the opposite of "the she-camel of Allah." In "the she-camel of Allah," the created thing is attributed to the Creator. Here, the Creator is attributed to the created thing.

[2] Mentioned by al-'Ajluni in Kashf al-Khafa' (1367) with the wording: "May Allah have mercy on a person who cuts off backbiting from himself," and he did not mention an origin for this report.

Student: ﴿Exalted in degrees, Lord of the Throne. He casts the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants, that he may warn of the Day of Meeting (15). The Day when they will come forth, nothing of them being hidden from Allah. "To whom belongs the dominion this Day? To Allah, the One, the Subduer" (16). "This Day every soul will be recompensed for what it earned. No injustice this Day. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning" [Ghafir 15–17].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion, although the disbelievers dislike it﴾ [Ghafir 14]. When Allah, glorified and exalted, made clear that He had shown us His cosmic and legislative signs, He commanded us to call upon Him alone, sincere to Him in religion. His words ﴿So call upon Allah﴾: the mufassir said, "(So worship Him)." This is one of the two meanings of du'a' (supplication/invocation), and the second meaning is du'a' al-mas'alah (request), i.e., ask Him. The correct view is that it encompasses both matters: du'a' al-mas'alah and du'a' al-'ibadah (worship). Worship is called du'a', as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord said, "Call upon Me; I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated"﴾ [Ghafir 60]. He said ﴿Call upon Me﴾, then said ﴿those who are too proud to worship Me﴾. As for du'a' al-'ibadah, every person who calls upon Allah, glorified and exalted, does not call upon Him except while believing that He is All-Knowing of everything and All-Powerful over everything; therefore he calls upon Him, and thereby he becomes one who worships Him.

He said: ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾. "Sincere" (mukhlisin) is a state (hal) of the waw in His saying ﴿call upon Allah﴾. Ikhlas (sincerity) is purification; the purification of a thing is called ikhlas. The meaning: purify your religion from shirk.

As for His saying ﴿in religion﴾, what is meant by religion here is action, whether it is worship or supplication. The word "din" is applied to action and also applied to the recompense for action. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun 6] is an instance of applying din to action. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Master of the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Fatihah 4] is an instance of applying din to recompense. It is said: "As you do, so you will be repaid" (kama tadin tadan), i.e., as you act, so you will be recompensed. So din here means action.

(﴿Sincere to Him in religion﴾ from shirk), as the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: that we call upon Allah sincerely directing the supplication to Him, and that we worship Him sincerely directing the worship to Him, free from shirk, so that we do not associate anything with Him, neither in our supplication nor in our worship.

(﴿Although the disbelievers dislike it﴾ your sincerity): meaning, call upon Allah sincerely in every state, whether the disbelievers are pleased or angry. It is well known that they will be angry, but it does not matter that they are angry with us when we make our religion sincere to Allah. The author's words "(﴿although the disbelievers dislike it﴾ your sincerity)" should rather be phrased: "although they dislike your sincere action," because ikhlas is the intention of the heart, whereas the disbeliever only dislikes what appears of a person's action. So the meaning: although the disbelievers dislike your action by which you are sincere to Allah, in spite of their noses (i.e., in defiance of them).

Then he said: (﴿Exalted in degrees﴾ [Ghafir 15] i.e., Allah is great in attributes, or raising the degrees of the believers in Paradise).

His words ﴿Exalted﴾ (rafi') come from rif'ah, which is height. The author, may Allah have mercy on him and pardon him, explained it by one of two meanings: that rif'ah means greatness and "degrees" means attributes, i.e., Allah, exalted is He, is great in attributes. The second meaning: "exalted in degrees," i.e., raising the degrees of others, namely the believers in Paradise. Both meanings are a distortion of the words from their places (tahrif al-kalim 'an mawadi'ihi), because rafi' is an active participle or an attributive adjective whose subject refers to Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned in His saying ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾. Based on this, it is not valid to interpret it as meaning "raising the degrees of the believers," because by that interpretation the degrees would be the degrees of another, the degrees of the believers. Nor is it valid to interpret "exalted in degrees" as "great in attributes," because of the great difference between them. But the author, may Allah pardon him, explained it this way in order to flee from affirming intrinsic elevation (al-'uluww al-dhati), since he is among those who do not hold that He is high in His essence. Therefore he distorted the Qur'an to one of these two meanings, and both are false. The correct view is that He, glorified is He, is Exalted in degrees. What supports and specifies this is His saying ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾, i.e., Possessor of the Throne. The Throne is the highest of created things, so it is as if He said: "Exalted in degrees above the Throne," and this is the definite meaning.

The author's words "(the Creator of it)" also contain an indication of denying istiwa' (settling/being established); because the meaning of "Lord of the Throne" is its possessor, the one who is established upon it. This is the meaning. For this reason one does not say "Lord of the earth," "Lord of the heavens," "Lord of the mountains," or "Lord of the clouds," even though He is their Creator. So interpreting "Lord of the Throne" as "its Creator" is undoubtedly a distortion of the words from their places, fleeing from affirming istiwa' upon the Throne.

The definite interpretation of the verse is that we say: He is Exalted in degrees, i.e., He Himself, glorified and exalted, is elevated; rather, "Exalted in degrees" comes with the adjective pattern (sifah mushabbahah) indicating permanence and continuity. "Degrees" is from the well-known degrees, i.e., what is some above others until it reaches the ultimate. As for "Lord of the Throne," its meaning is the Possessor of the Throne, specifically by being established upon it. This is the definite meaning of the verse.

(﴿He casts the Spirit﴾: revelation; ﴿by His command﴾, i.e., His word; ﴿upon whom He wills of His servants﴾), to the end. ﴿He casts the Spirit﴾: the Spirit is revelation, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a Spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura 52]. Allah, exalted is He, called revelation a spirit because by it the hearts live.

As for His saying (﴿by His command﴾, i.e., His word), this is a good interpretation: meaning that revelation is from the speech of Allah, glorified and exalted; He speaks, Jibril hears, and then he descends with it to whom Allah, glorified and exalted, wills.

As for His saying ﴿upon whom He wills of His servants﴾, He did not specify who these are, but we know they are the prophets, because they are the ones to whom revelation is cast, whether they are messengers or non-messengers.

Furthermore, His saying ﴿upon whom He wills﴾: the unrestricted mention of will in every place in the Qur'an is qualified by wisdom. Whenever you see Allah saying "wills," it is a will accompanied by wisdom, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for whoever among you wills to go straight. And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Takwir 28–29], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30].

Who are these whom Allah wills to cast the Spirit upon? Allah explained them in His saying: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 124].

As for His saying ﴿of His servants﴾, what is meant by "servants" here is the special servitude, namely those who believed in Allah, glorified and exalted; rather, it is even more specific: they are the messengers.

﴿That he may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾. He said: (﴿that he may warn﴾ — frighten). The lam here indicates purpose (ta'lil), and warning (indhar) is notification accompanied by fear; for this reason the author said "to frighten," explaining it by its necessary implication, since warning is notification accompanied by intimidation.

As for his words "(the one upon whom it is cast is the people)", the mufassir, may Allah have mercy on him, informed us that the subject of ﴿yun动dhir﴾ (he warns) is the one upon whom it is cast, namely the Messenger. There is no doubt he is the direct warner. It is possible that the subject refers back to the subject of ﴿casts the Spirit﴾, namely Allah, glorified and exalted; i.e., so that Allah may warn. The wisdom in not mentioning the subject, and Allah knows best, is to make the verb suitable for both: that the warning may refer back to Allah, and may refer back to the Messenger. If it refers to Allah, it is because He is the origin; if it refers to the Messenger, it is because he is the direct conveyor of the warning.

His words "(the people)" are an estimate of the first object of ﴿yundhira﴾, because "yundhira" takes two objects that are not originally subject and predicate: either the first object or the second object may be omitted. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And warn them of the imminent Day﴾ [Ghafir 18], which contains both objects; ﴿And warn mankind of the Day when there will come to them﴾ [Ibrahim 44], likewise both objects. One of them may be omitted, either the first or the second, when the context indicates it.

(﴿Day of Meeting﴾ with the yā' deleted and affirmed): meaning there are two readings: al-Talaqi with the yā', and al-Talaq with the yā' deleted. Affirming the yā' is the original form; deleting the yā' is for lightness, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Great, the Exalted﴾ [al-Ra'd 9], whose original form is al-Muta'ali, but the yā' was deleted for lightness. Likewise here, al-talaq's original form is al-talaqi, and the yā' was deleted for lightness.

The Day of Meeting (yawm al-talaq) is the Day of Resurrection, and the mufassir gave the reason with his words: (for the meeting of the people of the heavens and the earth, the worshipper and the worshipped, and the oppressor and the oppressed on it), i.e., on that day. If we took a more general meaning, "for the meeting of all creatures on that day," because everything meets the other, even the beasts: ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾ [al-Takwir 5]. It is called the Day of Meeting because creation meets on it: Allah, glorified and exalted, gathers all creatures on that day, and they meet one another.

* Among the benefits of these verses and those before them: the obligation of sincerity to Allah in supplication, due to His saying: ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere﴾. Calling upon other than Allah in matters the one called upon cannot do is considered shirk; then it may be major shirk or minor shirk depending on the situation. Whoever calls upon a grave, this is major shirk; whoever calls upon another to carry his belongings and the like, while the other cannot carry them, this is not major shirk, rather it is either futility or minor shirk. Whoever calls upon an absent one to rescue him from hardship, this is major shirk, because this is called secret shirk (shirk al-sirr): one cannot call upon an absent one except while believing he has some control over the universe, acting from afar. This is unlike one who calls upon a nearby person, saying, "O so-and-so, carry this with me, help me with that," for this calls upon him to do something perceptible.

* Also among its benefits: the obligation of sincerity in worship to Allah. Since we interpreted du'a' as both du'a' al-mas'alah and du'a' al-'ibadah, the obligation of sincere worship to Allah follows. Whoever worships other than Allah independently has directed some kind of worship to other than Allah, and thereby becomes a major polytheist (mushrik shirkan akbar); that is, whoever prays to a person is a major polytheist, or whoever slaughters for a person, seeking nearness to him and venerating him, is a major polytheist, expelled from the religion.

As for one who performs worship for Allah but shows off in it or seeks to be heard, this is not major shirk, but minor shirk, and his worship is rejected, due to the Prophet's ﷺ saying, related from his Lord: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in need of partners. Whoever does an action in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his association." (Narrated by Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.)

Know also that when showing off (riya') occurs to the heart: if it occurs before entering into the act of worship, it nullifies it from its root, because he entered it upon shirk. If it occurs in the course of the worship: if the latter part is built upon the first part, the worship is nullified; if the latter part is not built upon the first, such that the first can be distinguished from the second, then what contains the showing off is invalid, and what preceded the showing off is valid.

Example of the first: if showing off enters during prayer, in the second rak'ah, the whole prayer is nullified, because if the second rak'ah is nullified, the first rak'ah is nullified too, since prayer is not divisible.

Example of the second: a man prepared a hundred ṣā' for charity and gave fifty ṣā' sincerely, then showing off entered regarding the remaining ṣā'. Here the remaining ṣā' are nullified, but the first ones are valid, because this act of worship—namely charity—is divisible, and its last part is not built upon its first. Even if it were something specified by the law, such as feeding sixty poor people in expiation, for example: he fed thirty poor people sincerely, then showing off entered afterward, the portion preceding the last thirty is accepted. This applies if he yielded to showing off and continued in it. But if showing off occurred to him and he resisted it and continued striving against it, it does not harm him at all, due to the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Indeed, Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper, as long as they do not act upon it or speak of it." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5269) and Muslim (127/201), from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.) He did not act upon it nor speak; indeed perhaps he did not even whisper it to himself, but showing off assailed him.

So now: whoever performs worship for other than Allah—meaning he worships other than Allah—is his ruling major or minor shirk? Major. And whoever performs worship for Allah but showing off enters into it—

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: opposing the disbelievers in sincerity to Allah in the act and in the deed, due to His saying: ﴿although the disbelievers dislike it﴾. From this follows that a person must perform what is obligatory even if others dislike it, and not show favor to anyone in this. For example, if the father of a young man dislikes that his son pray in congregation—as is common now—should he flatter his father in this? No; he prays in congregation even in defiance of his father's nose, even if he dislikes it.

If a young man maintains kinship ties with his paternal uncle, maternal uncle, and the like, while there is personal enmity between him and his father, such that the father dislikes his son keeping ties with relatives whom the father dislikes—should he maintain them even though he dislikes it, or not? Yes, he maintains them even though he dislikes it, but in this situation he should be discreet with his father, meaning he conceals from him that he maintains them, so that the benefit is achieved without harm. There is a difference between mudara (tactful accommodation) and mudahanah (flattery): mudara is that a person does what he is obliged to do while concealing it from the other person who dislikes it; that is why it is called mudara, from al-dar' which is repelling. As for mudahanah, it is agreeing with him in abandoning what is obligatory, out of flattery, from al-duhn (oil), because it softens.

In any case, we say: from this benefit it follows that a person does what is incumbent upon him even if others dislike it, even if the one who dislikes it is the closest person to him.

Then he said: ﴿Exalted in degrees﴾ [Ghafir 15]... to the end.

* Among the benefits of this verse: affirmation of Allah's elevation, glorified and exalted, contrary to the mufassir author; due to His saying: ﴿Exalted in degrees﴾, and by elevation we mean elevation of essence. As for elevation of attribute, the author acknowledged it when he said: (i.e., great in attributes). So in this verse is affirmation of the elevation of the essence of Allah, glorified and exalted, due to His saying: ﴿Exalted in degrees﴾.

This has passed us many times, and we explained that the five categories of evidence all indicate Allah's elevation: the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus of the Salaf, reason, and innate nature (fitrah).

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the excellence of the Throne, due to His saying: ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾, for the Throne's being specifically attributed to Allah, glorified and exalted, is undoubtedly a great excellence.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of the Throne, due to His saying: ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾.

* Among its benefits: affirmation of Allah's greatness, because the Throne is specific to dominion and sovereignty. One does not say of a man sitting on a chair that he is "on a throne," but one says of a king or ruler sitting on a grand, magnificent chair that he is "possessor of a throne."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verses 14–15 (part 2 of 2):**

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the affirmation of Allah's favour, glorified and exalted be He, upon whomever He wills through revelation, based on His saying: ﴿He casts the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾.
* Among its benefits: revelation is a spirit by which hearts come to life, based on His saying: ﴿He casts the Spirit by His command﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of speech, based on His saying: ﴿by His command﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, speaks and talks whenever He wills, with whatever He wills, however He wills. We do not restrict our Lord, glorified and exalted be He, in speech, neither in time nor in manner. Rather, He may speak with whatever He wills, whenever He wills, however He wills.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of will, based on His saying: ﴿upon whomever He wills﴾.
* Among its benefits: the rank of prophethood is not attained through acquisition (kasb) and chivalry (futuwwah), as al-Saffarini said in his creed (al-'Aqidah), but it is a bounty from Allah, glorified and exalted be He, upon whomever He wills of His servants.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the scholars have a share and portion of the Spirit that Allah, exalted be He, casts upon the messengers, because they are the heirs of the prophets. So they have a share and portion of this Spirit that Allah casts upon whomever He wills. However, they have a share of this guidance, the guidance of direction and clarification (hidayat al-dalalah wa al-bayan). Then they may or may not have a share of the guidance of success (hidayat al-tawfiq). For the scholar may act upon his knowledge, and then he has a share of both guidances: the guidance of instruction (hidayat al-irshad) and the guidance of success (hidayat al-tawfiq). Or he may not act upon his knowledge, and then he has a share of the guidance of knowledge and instruction, but it becomes a burden upon him, since he opposed the truth while knowing it. This is worse than one who opposes it without knowledge of the truth.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom behind the revelation that Allah, mighty and majestic, sends down upon whomever He sends down among His servants is to warn people of the Day of Judgment: ﴿that he may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾.

Because the scholar may act upon his knowledge and thus have a share of both guidances, the guidance of instruction and the guidance of success, or he may not act upon his knowledge and thus have a share of the guidance of knowledge and instruction, but it becomes a burden upon him, since he opposed the truth while knowing it. This is worse than one who opposes it without knowledge of the truth.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom behind the revelation that Allah, mighty and majestic, sends down upon whomever He sends down among His servants is to warn people of the Day of Resurrection, ﴿that he may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾ [Ghafir 15].
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's wisdom, and that His actions are accompanied by wisdom, based on His saying: ﴿that he may warn﴾. The particle of purpose (lam al-ta'lil) and "min" of causation (min al-ta'liliyyah) occur very often in the Qur'an and likewise in the Sunnah, and all of them indicate the affirmation of wisdom for Allah.
Some scholars have mentioned that wisdom is indicated by a thousand proofs from the Book and the Sunnah. The proofs affirming the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, in what He does cannot be counted. This is contrary to those who say that He does it merely by will, not for any wisdom. This amounts to negating one of the greatest attributes of Allah, because it entails that His action would be purposeless, without any praiseworthy end.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever Allah has given knowledge should be a warner, meaning he should combine knowledge and understanding of religion with warning. For if he limits himself to mere teaching of jurisprudence, for example, or to monotheism without stirring hearts, people will not benefit much from him. There must be warning in order to stir hearts. When the Prophet (ﷺ) delivered a sermon, his eyes would turn red, his voice would rise, and his anger would intensify, until he seemed like one warning of an army, saying: "Your enemy will attack you at dawn or in the evening."[1]
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: warning against the disgrace of the Day of Resurrection, since it is the Day of Meeting. There is no doubt that punishment witnessed by few is lighter than punishment witnessed by many. So how about when all of creation witnesses it? It will be far more severe and greater.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's power, in that Allah gathers all of creation on one plain after death, and Allah, glorified and exalted be He, is over all things Competent.

Then He, exalted be He, said: ﴿The Day they come forth, nothing of them will be hidden from Allah. "Whose is the dominion today?" "It is Allah's, the One, the Subduer." Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned; there is no injustice today. Indeed, Allah is swift in account. And warn them of the Imminent Day, when hearts will be at the throats, choking. The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend, nor any intercessor who is obeyed. He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal. And Allah judges with truth, while those they invoke besides Him judge nothing. Indeed, Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [Ghafir 16–20].

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: If worship is nullified, it is not (...) valid. That is, someone asks: a man entered prayer sincerely, then a person came and saw him, then the person left, and he returned to sincerity.
We say: his worship is nullified, because his concern for being watched by others is stronger than his concern for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He was not mindful of Allah except once the watching of people had ended. So his worship is invalid without doubt. Perhaps if someone else comes, showing off (riya') will arise again, and when that person leaves, the showing off ceases. If another comes...
* Student: If a person begins prayer showing off, then struggles against the showing off, is it valid?
* Shaykh: Was he content with showing off at the start or not?
* Student: He began showing off.
* Shaykh: Yes, I am asking you: when he began, was he content with showing off, or did showing off come upon him while he was still resisting it?
* Student: He was content with it.
* Shaykh: Then his worship is not valid, his worship is not valid.
But here is an issue: if a man made his worship good in order to teach people, not intending that they praise him for his worship or that he draw closer to them through worship, but so that people might take him as an example, does this count as showing off? No. This falls under teaching, and he is rewarded for it. But there is a difference between this and another person who wants people to praise him for his prayer.
* Student: May Allah bless you. Does it count as showing off if a person displays some of what he has, so as not to be blamed, or...
* Shaykh: You mean warding off blame?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: There is a hadith: "May Allah have mercy on a person who keeps backbiting away from himself,"[2] and also: when the Messenger (ﷺ) went out at night with Safiyyah to escort her home, two men of the Ansar passed by him and hastened. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Slow down, both of you, she is Safiyyah."[3] This was to ward off blame from himself. He was sincere to Allah, but he wanted, along with that, to ward off blame from himself, lest it be said that he was stingy, for example, or that he did not pray in congregation, and similar things. The origin of intention is for Allah, but warding off blame is not for praise. So there is a difference between one who intends praise and one who intends to ward off blame.
* Student: Some people say regarding the phrase "Dhu al-'Arsh" (Lord of the Throne) that it is merely an idafah (attributive construction) of honour, not of exaltation. How do we respond to them? Like their saying "the she-camel of Allah" and...
* Shaykh: This is the opposite of "the she-camel of Allah." In "the she-camel of Allah," the created thing is attributed to the Creator. Here, the Creator is attributed to the created thing.
* Student: We said: an idafah of honour.
* Shaykh: What (...) is like "the she-camel of Allah"? If he said "the Throne of Allah," it would be like that. But this is the reverse.
* Student: What is meant by "al-darajat" (the degrees)?
* Shaykh: You have heard what I said about it: its meaning is that by which a person ascends stage by stage to the utmost height.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) its meaning is the elevator in which a person rises, meaning that he is lofty. This is its meaning, that He is lofty. So if you say "so-and-so is lofty in degrees," you might say "lofty in degrees" even if it were on an airplane, where there are no stairs.
* Student: Is the negation of attributes disbelief?
* Shaykh: No. The negation of attributes (nafy al-sifat) is divided into two types: negation of denial (nafy juhud), and this is disbelief; and negation through interpretation (nafy ta'wil), of which some is disbelief and some is less than that.
So if someone says: Allah did not settle (istawa) upon the Throne, what is this?
* Students: Disbelief.
* Shaykh: Why? Because it is a disbelief of denial (juhud), the rejection of the report.
And if he says: Allah settled upon the Throne, but the meaning of "istawa" is "istawla" (seized control), this is disbelief of interpretation (ta'wil). Disbelief through interpretation may be disbelief that removes one from the religion, or it may be less than that, according to what the legal principles require.
* Student: O Shaykh, does wishing (tamanni) fall under showing off?
* Shaykh: Wishing for what?

* Shaykh: Why?

* Shaykh: It does no harm. This does no harm. Rather, this is among the early glad tidings of the believer, that a person finds the reward of his deed in advance, while the reward of the Hereafter is in the Hereafter.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, it is a ta'wil (interpretation), because they say: if He did it for a wisdom, He would have done it for a purpose, and only one who is in need of a purpose does things for a purpose. What a comparison!
It is said: is this wisdom for a matter that returns to Himself or one that returns to His servants? Then if it returns to Himself, He is deserving of praise. If wisdom is an attribute of perfection in Himself, then He, Mighty and Majestic, is deserving of praise. And which is more perfect: one who does things without wisdom, or one who does things with wisdom? Without doubt, the second is more perfect.
