[1] Recorded by Muslim (867/43) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.
[2] Mentioned by al-'Ajluni in Kashf al-Khafa' (1367) with the wording: "May Allah have mercy on a person who cuts off backbiting from himself," and he did not mention an origin for this report.
[3] Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3281) and Muslim (2175/24) from the hadith of Safiyyah bint Huyayy.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿On the Day they will come forth, nothing of them will be hidden from Allah.﴾ [Ghafir 16]

﴿Yawm﴾ ("the Day") here is a substitute (badal) for the first "yawm" (day).

﴿Yawma al-talaq﴾ [Ghafir 15] ("the Day of Meeting") ... ﴿Yawma hum barizun﴾ [Ghafir 15, 16].

His saying ﴿hum barizun﴾ ("they are exposed") is a subject and predicate, and the clause is in the position of a genitive, being the object of the annexation of "yawm" (day) to it.

As for ﴿barizun﴾, the exegete said: (coming out of their graves). But the meaning is more specific than what he said. Rather, the meaning is: the Day when they are exposed, i.e., visible, with no shade to shelter them, neither from a tree nor a rock, nor a house or anything else, because the one who is "barz" is the apparent one that nothing screens from view. They will be exposed on that Day, and the sun will draw near to them the distance of a mile. People will sweat on that Day according to their deeds: some of them the sweat will reach their ankles, some will reach their knees, some will reach their waists, and some will be bridled by the sweat, bridled according to their deeds.

As for ﴿nothing of them will be hidden from Allah﴾ [Ghafir 16], meaning: nothing of them will be concealed from Allah, and nothing of them will be absent from His knowledge. Rather, He encompasses them with complete encompassing, just as nothing is hidden from Him on earth or in heaven, before that as well, because Allah the Exalted encompasses all things in knowledge.

But He said here: ﴿nothing of them will be hidden from Allah﴾ [Ghafir 16] for the sake of complete warning.

﴿To whom belongs the dominion this Day? To Allah, the One, the Subduer.﴾ [Ghafir 16]

﴿Li-man al-mulk﴾ ("To whom belongs the dominion") is the quoted speech of an omitted verb of saying; the estimate is: it is said: "To whom belongs the dominion today?"

The one speaking is Allah, Mighty and Majestic; He, the Exalted, will fold the heavens with His right hand and the earth with His other hand and shake them, and He says: "I am the King; where are the kings of the world?" He also says: "To whom belongs the dominion today?" Then He answers Himself: "To Allah, the One, the Subduer."

He said: (He, the Exalted, says it and answers Himself) ﴿To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ghafir 16] (i.e., to His creation).

So His saying ﴿To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject; the estimate is: the dominion belongs to Allah, the One, the Subduer.

"Al-Wahid" means the one who has no second, neither in His essence, nor in His actions, nor in His rulings, nor in His attributes, glory be to Him and exalted.

His saying ﴿al-Qahhar﴾ is an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah) from "qahr", which is subjugation, so He is Subduer of everything.

The exegete said: (i.e., to His creation).

* Among the benefits of this verse: first, that people will be exposed on the Day of Resurrection; no tree, clod, building, mountain or anything else will shade them, due to His saying: ﴿On the Day they will come forth﴾ [Ghafir 16].

* Among its benefits: that on that Day nothing of them will be hidden from Allah, because He encompasses them in knowledge, power and authority.

If someone says: Is any exception made from His saying ﴿On the Day they will come forth﴾?

We say: Yes, an exception is made for those whom Allah shades in His shade on a Day when there is no shade but His shade. They are seven, and indeed they are more; they reach twenty-one men, but the Prophet ﷺ gathered seven in one context.

Good. An exception is made from that: those whom Allah shades in His shade on a Day when there is no shade but His shade. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, gathered seven of them in one well-known hadith: «Seven will be shaded by Allah in His shade on a Day when there is no shade but His shade: a just ruler...»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (660) and Muslim (1031/91) from Abu Hurayrah.]] to the end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that dominion, indeed all possessions, will vanish on that Day, so there is no distinction then between owner and owned, master and servant, free and slave, male and female. No one has any dominion on that Day, and for this He said: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion this Day?﴾ and He answers: ﴿To Allah﴾ [Ghafir 16].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the names of Allah is "al-Wahid" (the One), and al-Wahid is the Singular who has no second. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do not take two gods; He is only one God﴾ [al-Nahl 51].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the names of Allah is al-Qahhar, due to His saying: ﴿al-Qahhar﴾ [Ghafir 16].

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of two attributes of Allah, indicated by His saying ﴿al-Wahid al-Qahhar﴾ [Ghafir 16]: the attribute of oneness (wahdah) in "al-Wahid," and the attribute of subjugation (qahr) in "al-Qahhar."

From this follows, on the practical side, that when a person believes that Allah, glory be to Him, is One, he does not turn to anyone other than Him; and when he believes that Allah is Subduer, he fears His subjugation and seeks help through His subjugation against His enemy. Thus he benefits from this belief by fearing Allah's subjugation and by seeking help through Allah's subjugation against the enemy of Allah and his own enemy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 17:

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it has earned.﴾ [Ghafir 17]

﴿Today⁠﴾ (al-yawm) is an adverbial of time (zarf). What does it depend on? It depends on ﴿will be recompensed⁠﴾ (tujza). An adverbial of time, or a prepositional phrase, must have something it depends on, because it occurs only as a complement or as a place where something happens. For that reason it needs a governing verb to attach to.

He said: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it has earned⁠﴾. ﴿Will be recompensed⁠﴾ means "will be repaid" (tukafa'), because jaza' means mukafa'ah (requital). One says "jazaytuhu 'ala 'amalihi" (I repaid him for his deed), meaning I rewarded him for it. So the meaning of "tujza" is that every soul will be repaid for what it has earned, good or evil. However, this recompense in the Hereafter differs from the recompense of this world, by which people repay one another.

So the recompense there is ﴿There will be no injustice today. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning⁠﴾ [Ghafir 17].

﴿No injustice⁠﴾ (la zulm): the "la" is the negation of the genus (la nafy li-l-jins), and "zulm" is its ism (noun).

The grammarians said: the negation of the genus negates this genus absolutely, that is, its little and its much, its single instance and its multiple instances.

They have another "la" which they call the negation of unity (la nafy al-wahdah). The negation of unity does not function like "inna"; it functions like "laysa" (is not). You say "la rajul fi al-dar", meaning "there is not a single man in the house", but there may be three men, for example. If you want the genus, say "la rajul fi al-dar" meaning "there is not one and not many."

The genus-negation is explicit in generality (nass fi al-'umum), meaning it indicates generality by its explicit wording. So ﴿no injustice today⁠﴾ means: no injustice from Allah, and no injustice by creatures against one another. Rather, every creature flees from the other, ﴿no injustice today⁠﴾.

﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning⁠﴾ [Ghafir 17] means He is swift in calling creatures to account for their deeds.

The scholar, may Allah have mercy on him, explained this swiftness, saying: "He will call all creatures to account within about half a day of the days of this world, based on a hadith reported about it." He will reckon all creatures in the measure of half a day. But is it half a day of the days of this world? This requires verification, because the Day of Resurrection has a length of fifty thousand years. Allah, the Exalted, will finish reckoning the creatures in half of that day. This is why Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The companions of Paradise on that Day will be better in their resting place and finest in their place of rest at midday⁠﴾ [al-Furqan 24]. It is well known that the qaylulah (midday rest) takes place at midday. This indicates that midday arrives only after Allah, the Exalted, has finished reckoning the creatures, and each one has gone to his destination. But is it like a day of this world, or is it the Day of Resurrection whose length is fifty thousand years?

* In this noble verse: the affirmation of recompense, based on His saying: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed⁠﴾ [Ghafir 17].

* And in it: the full recompense occurs on that Day. Recompense may occur in this world. Allah may repay a person in this world, giving him many good deeds for one good deed and holding the wrongdoer accountable for his wrong. This happens frequently. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whatever disaster strikes you is for what your hands have earned, and He pardons much⁠﴾ [al-Shura 30]. This indicates that a person may be repaid in this world for his deeds, but the complete and perfect recompense will be on the Day of Resurrection.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the soul is recompensed only for what it has earned. And how is earning done? Earning is done either by speech or by action. Mere intention is not earning, and mere inner talk (hadith al-nafs) is not earning. Earning is speech or action. As for mere inner talk, it is not earning, because the person has not inclined to it. The evidence for this is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper, as long as they do not act on it or speak it." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5269) and Muslim (127/201), from Abu Hurayrah.]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse, according to the view of some scholars that gifting the reward of acts of worship (ihda' al-qurab) is not valid: that is, if you perform a righteous deed and give its reward to someone else, it is not valid, because the other person did not earn it, except what the Sunnah has indicated. This is an exception. Many scholars held that only what the Sunnah has brought may be gifted as reward.

Others held that it is permissible to gift all acts of worship. They said: what the Sunnah has reported are individual cases (qadaya a'yan). If a ruling is established in them, it is established for their counterparts, because the Shari'ah does not distinguish between like things. The Sunnah has reported the validity of financial acts of worship, physical acts of worship, and acts combining wealth and body.

As for financial acts of worship: in the story of the man who said, "O Messenger of Allah, my mother died suddenly (iftutat nafsuha, meaning she was taken unexpectedly), and if she had been able to speak she would have given charity. Shall I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1388) and Muslim (1004/12), from 'A'ishah.]

Likewise, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, may Allah be pleased with him, had a mikhraf (an orchard whose fruit is harvested), and he gave it in charity on behalf of his mother, with the permission of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. This is a financial act of worship.

As for physical acts of worship: the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever dies owing fasting, his guardian shall fast on his behalf." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1952) and Muslim (1147/153), from 'A'ishah.] This is a purely physical act of worship.

As for those that combine both: Hajj. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to the woman who asked him about her mother, who had died (...) without performing Hajj: "Perform Hajj on her behalf." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1852) and Muslim (1334/407), and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from Ibn 'Abbas.]

This is the view of Imam Ahmad, namely that gifting acts of worship to another is permissible on condition that the recipient is a Muslim. If he is a disbeliever, then even if it is gifted to him, it is not accepted, because a disbeliever's deeds are not accepted, neither for himself nor for others.

This view is closer to the truth than the view of prohibition.

However, we do not favor a person giving anything to his dead as a regular practice, because this was not the custom of the early generations (al-salaf), especially excessive doing of it, as some people do today. You find some people in Ramadan completing the Quran several times, each completion dedicated to one of their relatives: this one to his mother, this one to his father, this one to his brother, this one to his paternal uncle, and so on. In reality this contradicts the custom of the early generations.

We say: if you want to benefit your deceased with a certain benefit, act upon what the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, guided to, when he said: "When a person dies, his deeds end except for three: a continuing charity, knowledge from which benefit is gained, or a righteous child who prays for him." [Reported by Muslim (1631/14), from Abu Hurayrah.] This is what we favor. We say: increase your supplication for your dead. As for gifting acts of worship, keep them for yourself, because this is the Sunnah. And you, O living one, will need these righteous deeds, just as the dead also need an increase of righteous deeds, as in the hadith: "No dead person dies but that he regrets: if he was a doer of good, he regrets not having increased it, and if he was a doer of evil, he regrets not having sought to make amends." [Reported by al-Tirmidhi (2403), from Abu Hurayrah.]

So we say: regarding ﴿for what it has earned⁠﴾ [Ghafir 17], some scholars used it as evidence for what? For the view that whoever is gifted something of acts of worship does not benefit from it, because it is not his earning, except what the Sunnah has brought. But the correct view is that he does benefit from it.

If you say this is the correct view, how do you answer the verse?

The answer is that the verse indicates that the soul is recompensed for what it has earned, but it does not indicate that it does not benefit from the deeds of others. What is entirely guaranteed is what it has earned. As for what others gift to it, that is something else, and it has other evidence.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the absence of injustice on that Day, based on His saying: ﴿There will be no injustice today⁠﴾ [Ghafir 17]. Yet a person is recompensed according to his deeds. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer will fear neither injustice nor diminution⁠﴾ [Ta-Ha 112]. The exegetes said: "injustice" means an increase in his sins, and "diminution" means a reduction in his good deeds.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of reckoning, that Allah reckons the creatures. This is indicated by the texts, and it is also required by wisdom. It is not wise that people be commanded and forbidden, and then this command and prohibition go to waste without the servant being held accountable for them. If that were so, it would be pointless, and Allah, the Exalted, is far above that, as He said: ﴿Did you then think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?⁠﴾ [al-Mu'minun 115], and He said: ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?⁠﴾ [al-Qiyamah 36]. Therefore there must be recompense and there must be reckoning, so that what is for a person and what is against him becomes clear.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the perfection of Allah's power and might, derived from His saying: ﴿Swift in reckoning⁠﴾ [Ghafir 17], because swiftness indicates power and might. How can He reckon these creatures, whom none can count but Him, the Mighty and Majestic, in half a day? This is evidence of complete power and complete might.

If someone asks: how does the reckoning happen?

We say: the reckoning differs according to the one being reckoned. As for the believer, Allah, the Exalted, places His kanaf upon him (meaning His covering and concealment), brings him aside, and makes him acknowledge his sins, saying: "You did such-and-such on such-and-such a day," until he confesses. When he confesses and acknowledges, Allah, the Exalted, says: "I concealed them for you in the world, and today I forgive them for you." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52), from Ibn 'Umar.] Then he goes off free.

As for the disbelievers, they are not reckoned in the manner of one whose good and evil deeds are weighed, because they have no good deeds. Rather, their deeds are counted, and they are made to stand before them and are made to acknowledge them, and they are humiliated and rebuked for them. ﴿Did there not come to you a warner? They will say: Yes, indeed a warner came to us, but we denied and said, "Allah has not sent down anything. You are not but in great error"⁠﴾ [al-Mulk 8-9]. They are rebuked, increasing their regret, and we seek refuge with Allah. This also demonstrates that they were not wronged. So the reckoning differs.

* From the ethical standpoint, this verse teaches: warning a person against opposition and urging him toward compliance. From where do you derive this?

* Student: From His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning⁠﴾ [Ghafir 17].

* Shaykh: No. Warning against opposition and urging toward compliance?

* Student: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿will be recompensed⁠﴾ [Ghafir 17].

* Shaykh: Just "will be recompensed"?

* Student: ﴿Today will be recompensed⁠﴾ [Ghafir 17].

* Shaykh: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it has earned⁠﴾ [Ghafir 17]. This obliges a person, if he believes it, to be keen to comply with the command and to obey Allah, because he is earning.

I ask you, as I ask myself: when we pray, do we believe, or rather, is there in our souls a feeling that we will receive a reward for this prayer, or is the prevailing feeling that we have only fulfilled what is obligatory upon us? The latter. This is why, if we had the first feeling, that we would be rewarded for this prayer, and in proportion to how well we perform it, we would perform it well, because we know that recompense is of the same kind as the deed. Spend many dirhams and a good commodity will come to you; but spend little and an inferior commodity will come to you.

Therefore it is incumbent upon us, and we ask Allah to help us and protect us from heedlessness, that when we do a righteous deed we feel that we will be rewarded for it, so that this sharpens our resolve to perfect the deed, because when a person knows that his deed is his recompense, he will perfect it and will do it in the way that pleases Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 18 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Approaching (al-Azifa)﴾ [Ghafir 18]: the Day of Resurrection. (Azif al-rahil: qarib, meaning "the departure has drawn near.")

﴿Warn them﴾: the pronoun, as the subject of the verb, refers to whom? To the Messenger, and the object is the people. That is, warn the people of this Day. This verb takes two objects: the ha' (them) is the first object, and "the Day of the Approaching" is the second object.

As for His saying ﴿the Day of the Approaching﴾, it means "the approaching Day," and it is of the type of an adjective being annexed to its noun, i.e., "warn them of the near Day."

If you wish, you may say: "al-Azifa" is an adjective of an elided noun, and the implied phrase is "the Day of Resurrection, the Approaching." Al-Azifa means al-qarība (the near one). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Approaching has drawn near (azifat al-azifa). None besides God can remove it﴾ [al-Najm 57-58].

And the poet said:
"The departure has drawn near, though our mounts
have not yet moved with our baggage, as if it had already come."

That is, as if it had already departed.

The summary is that azf means qurb (nearness), so al-azifa means the near one, and it refers to the Day of Resurrection. God, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura 17]. It is near however long time passes; even if the world remains millions upon millions upon millions of years, it is near. If you want this made clear to you, look at what you are facing now. If you want to know this, look at the future: you look at it as one looks at something far away, yet it comes quickly, like a flash of lightning. Thus the future of the whole world is near. If you reach it, you reach it; and if you do not, your own resurrection will have come before it. Your resurrection is near, and even if you remain until the Greater Resurrection, it too is near.

So every coming thing is near, and every past thing is far. The past, even if it was an hour before your time, is far, because it cannot return; while the future is near.

Thus the Resurrection was named "the Approaching" for its nearness. The aspect of its nearness, though between us and it lies what only God knows of years, is that the future, however distant, is near.

﴿When hearts are at the throats, choking with grief. The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend, nor any intercessor who will be obeyed﴾ [Ghafir 18].

﴿When the hearts﴾: (idh) is a substitute for "the Day of the Approaching": "warn them of the Day of the Approaching, [warn them] when the hearts are at the throats." (Idh) is an adverb of past time, and it also comes as an adverb and as a cause, according to the meanings it carries in the Arabic language.

As for His saying ﴿the hearts﴾, the (al) here is for totality, i.e., all hearts.

As for His saying ﴿at﴾: he says it means (ʿinda), "near/with."

The commentator said: (﴿When the hearts﴾ rise in fear ﴿at﴾ near ﴿the throats, choking﴾).

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿When the eyes were dazed, and the hearts reached the throats﴾ [al-Ahzab 10], at the battle of the Confederates. This is something known and perceived: that when fear intensifies on a person, his heart rises, contracts, and his palpitations increase. So on the Day of Resurrection hearts will rise until they reach the throats. The throat (hanjara) is what lies between the two collarbones.

﴿Choking﴾ (filled with grief): a circumstantial clause of the hearts, treated with the plural suffix of the sound masculine (-ina) in accordance with the treatment of their possessors.

﴿When the hearts are at the throats﴾: the hearts, as you know, are inanimate; they themselves are inanimate, and the inanimate is not pluralized with the sound masculine ending (waw and nun), because only a rational being is pluralized that way, whether a proper noun or an adjective. It has been mentioned to you among the conditions for the sound masculine plural that it must be a proper noun or an adjective for a rational being. Here the hearts are not rational; the hearts are a part of the body and are not rational. So how is the circumstantial state that came in this plural form to be explained?

The author says: because by them is meant their possessors, "the hearts at the throats," and the one choking is their possessor. Is this clear? And this is correct: that "choking" is a circumstantial state of the hearts by considering their possessors.

And "choking" means filled with grief. Why are they filled with grief? Because of the severity of the terrors and the fear: hearts raised up, souls filled with grief.

﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend, nor any intercessor who will be obeyed﴾ [Ghafir 18].

﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend﴾: the wrongdoers (al-zalimin) here are the disbelievers, according to God's saying: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqara 254]. The intended meaning is not wrongdoing in general, but absolute wrongdoing, which is the wrongdoing of disbelief. So the wrongdoers on that Day have no intimate friend.

The intimate friend (hamim) is the lover, as the author said, and it is said: the close relative, as God said: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any close friend (hamim)﴾ [al-Shu'ara 100-101], i.e., a relative. We do not say "a friend who loves," because every friend is one who loves, and were it not for love he would not be your friend. Accordingly, we say that it is better to interpret hamim as "close relative."

Generally, the one who defends you, protects you, and intercedes for you is a close relative; this is the usual case.

He says: ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend, nor any intercessor who will be obeyed﴾. Shafi' (intercessor) means shafi' (one who intercedes); it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il, like sami' meaning sami'.

Who is the intercessor? The intercessor is one who pairs with you, so that after being alone you become a pair. That is why it is said: the intercessor is one who mediates on your behalf to bring a benefit or ward off a harm; this is the intercessor. Intercession (shafa'a) is mediation for another to bring about good or repel harm. This is if you want to express it in rhymed prose, as it is more comfortable.

So on the Day of Resurrection they will have no intercessor; no one will intercede for them, because one of the conditions of intercession is that God be pleased with the intercessor and with the one for whom intercession is made.

He said: ﴿nor any intercessor who will be obeyed﴾. He said: (The adjective has no implicit contrary, since they have no intercessors at all, as God said: ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ [al-Shu'ara 100]; or it has an implicit contrary based on their claim that they have intercessors, meaning that even if they were to intercede, supposing it, they would not be obeyed.)

The noble verse: ﴿nor any intercessor who will be obeyed﴾: the phrase "yuta'" (will be obeyed) is a verbal clause in the position of a genitive-governed adjective, modifying "intercessor." If we convert it into an active participle, the sense would be "nor any intercessor who is obeyed." So is this adjective a restriction, meaning that they have an intercessor who is not obeyed, or is it a statement of fact, with the intended meaning being the negation of any intercessor?

The author mentioned two possibilities. The first: that the intended meaning is that they have no intercessor at all, and he cited in support God's saying about them: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any close friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara 100-101]. Or the meaning is: supposing they had intercessors, these intercessors would not be obeyed, based on their claim that those they worship besides God will be their intercessors. The verse allows what the author said.

If we take the first option, the negation of intercessors altogether, the matter is clear and has no difficulty.

As for the second, that intercessors are set up for them but their intercession is rejected, this is for the sake of humiliating them: that they be shamed when the intercessors they claimed would intercede for them are presented, and then their intercession is rejected. This is more powerful in their shame and in their rejection and in their failure to benefit from their gods. And God knows best.

* Shaykh: ﴿Indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Hajj 47], and He said: ﴿He directs the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a day whose extent is a thousand years﴾ [al-Sajda 5]. But for the Day of Resurrection only fifty thousand years is mentioned: ﴿in a day whose extent is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij 4]. And in the sound hadith about the one who withholds zakat: "in a day whose extent is fifty thousand years" [narrated by Muslim (987/24) from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him].

Accordingly, the day that is with our Lord as a thousand years, we do not know what that day is; it is an unknown day to us. As for ﴿He directs the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a day whose extent is a thousand years﴾ [al-Sajda 5], this is because the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years; so if the distance between them is five hundred years, the ascent of the command to God and its return takes a thousand years.

So the days are three: a day whose extent is fifty thousand years, which is the Day of Resurrection; a day with God whose extent we do not know, which is a thousand years; and a day whose extent is a thousand years in the directing of the command from heaven to earth and its ascent to Allah, mighty and majestic.

They were greater than them in strength and in traces upon the earth, but Allah seized them for their sins, and they had no protector from Allah. That is because their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they disbelieved, so Allah seized them. Indeed He is Strong, severe in punishment﴾ [Ghafir 19-22].

* Shaykh: Now let us return to deriving benefits from the verse. God, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Approaching﴾ [Ghafir 18].
Several benefits are drawn from this verse:
* Among them: the obligation of warning upon the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, because of His saying: ﴿and warn them﴾; and the default in a command is obligation, especially since the Messenger ﷺ is charged with this.
* Among its benefits: that it is fitting for the caller to be sometimes one who frightens and sometimes one who gives glad tidings.
As for glad tidings at times, there are many verses: ﴿And give glad tidings to the believers﴾ [al-Baqara 223], ﴿And give glad tidings to those who believed﴾ [al-Baqara 25], and what is similar to that.
As for warning, likewise in verses like this one; so the caller should be a warner and a bringer of glad tidings, in order to move hearts.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that in warning it is fitting to mention to people the states of the Day of Resurrection and its terrors; because of His saying: ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Approaching, when the hearts﴾ [Ghafir 18].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the verse is near; because of His saying: ﴿the Day of the Approaching﴾ [Ghafir 18], and nearness here means that time passes quickly, so that a person perceives nothing until the Resurrection has come, whether his own resurrection, called the Lesser Resurrection, or the general Resurrection.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the clarification of this great depiction of the state of people on that day: ﴿when the hearts are at the throats﴾ [Ghafir 18].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that this state is general for believers and disbelievers; the evidence is the generality of His saying: ﴿when the hearts﴾ [Ghafir 18], then His saying: ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend﴾ [Ghafir 18]; this shows the verse is general. But will harm from that Day reach the believers? No; because God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So God protected them from the evil of that Day﴾ [al-Insan 11]; and mere grief and distress do not necessarily entail evil or harm.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that hearts, at the time of intense fear, rise up until they reach the throats (al-hanajir), and this is attested by experience. Allah, blessed and exalted, said in Surat al-Ahzab: ﴿When the eyes shall swerve and the hearts reach the throats﴾ [al-Ahzab 10]. A person also senses within himself that when he fears greatly, it is as if his heart has become lodged in his throat.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that people on that day, along with intense fear, are filled with grief (ghamm), due to His saying: ﴿restraining [their rage]﴾ [Ghafir 18]. Ghamm is sorrow or anticipation of what is to come; so ghamm concerns the future, while hamm and huzn concern the past.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that means are severed for the wrongdoers, so they will have no close friend (hamim) and no intercessor (shafi') who is obeyed, due to His saying: ﴿There will be no close friend for the wrongdoers, nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ [Ghafir 18]. The "wrongdoers" here refers to what has preceded, namely the disbelievers.

If someone says: Injustice (zulm) is more general than disbelief (kufr), so how have you explained injustice here as disbelief?

We say: Because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 254]. And because sins below the level of disbelief are amenable to intercession, for intercession is established for the people of major sins from this community.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning to these disbelievers about that day, for in this world they find someone to support them, befriend them, assist them and aid them, but in the Hereafter they will find none of that at all.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir 19].

"Yaʿlamu" (He knows): the subject is Allah, mighty and majestic.

"Khaʾinat al-aʿyun" (the treachery of the eyes): this is an idafa of an attribute to its qualified noun, meaning "the treacherous eyes." The treachery of the eye is its stealing a glance at what is forbidden. That is, a person may look at something forbidden while his companion sits beside him without noticing, because he steals the glance, as if he watches for an opportunity when his companion is heedless, so that he may look at what Allah, mighty and majestic, has forbidden. This is the first point.

Second: a person may look without stealing, but openly, and his companion does not perceive that he is looking in a forbidden way. Therefore Allah, mighty and majestic, warned against this state, saying: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾. The author of the tafsir said: (by their stealing a glance at what is forbidden), ﴿and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir 19]: the hearts. The author explained "the breasts" as "the hearts" because they are within the breasts, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts﴾ [al-Hajj 46]. Thus Allah, mighty and majestic, shows here the precision and subtlety of His knowledge, that He knows even this state which people who witness it do not know: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir 19].

﴿And Allah judges with truth, while those they invoke besides Him do not judge anything. Indeed, Allah is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾ [Ghafir 20]. ﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾: the clause is conjoined to His saying ﴿He knows﴾.

﴿Yaqḍī bil-ḥaqq﴾ (judges with truth), meaning He rules by it, legally and decreed. This is because judgment, that is, the judgment of Allah mighty and majestic, is of two kinds:

A cosmic (kawnī) judgment, as in His saying: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture that you will cause corruption in the land twice and become arrogant with great arrogance﴾ [al-Isra' 4].

And a legal (sharʿī) judgment, as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isra' 23]. "Qaḍā" here means legal judgment, and its meaning is: "your Lord has enjoined that you worship none but Him." So here Allah says "yaqḍī bil-ḥaqq."

Is the intended meaning the cosmic judgment or the legal judgment? Both are intended. That is, He decrees cosmically with truth, so there is in His cosmic decree no vanity or play: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhan 38-39].

Likewise He decrees legally with truth, so all of His legal decree, glorified and exalted is He, is true, because it is good, so He commands it; or evil, so He forbids it, and this is the truth.

Thus Allah judges with truth in both kinds, the cosmic judgment and the legal judgment.

﴿And those they invoke besides Him﴾ [Ghafir 20]: the conjunction "wa" here is coordinating, and it may also be resumptive.

﴿And those they invoke besides Him﴾: he said (they worship, i.e. the disbelievers of Makkah, with the yāʾ and the tāʾ). Here is an explanation of the word ﴿yadʿūna﴾, an explanation of the pronoun in the "wāw", and a reading.

As for the reading, the author mentioned that there are two readings: the first reading is ﴿yadʿūna﴾ with the yāʾ, and the second reading is ﴿tadʿūna﴾ with the tāʾ in direct address, and both are canonical (sabʿiyya) readings.

As for ﴿yadʿūna﴾, he explained it with the word "yaʿbudūn" (they worship).

The correct view is that what is meant by it is that they worship and supplicate, because they worship the idols and ask them to bring benefits and repel harms, and they also worship them by bowing, prostrating, vows, and other things.

As for the "wāw", the author explained it as the disbelievers of Makkah, making the pronoun refer to the disbelievers of Makkah. Here we ask: is there no one who worships idols and invokes idols except the disbelievers of Makkah? There are some of them and others besides them. If that is so, then restricting the general to the specific is a deficiency in the explanation. The explanation that corresponds to the "wāw" is that it is general to everyone who invokes besides Allah, whether the disbelievers of Makkah, the disbelievers of Madinah, the disbelievers of Ta'if, the disbelievers of Iraq, the disbelievers of Sham, the disbelievers of this nation, or the disbelievers of those before it: everyone who invokes besides Allah invokes one who does not judge anything.

And His saying ﴿min dūnihi﴾ [Ghafir 20] means "besides Allah." The word "dūn" here means "other than," that is, other than Allah mighty and majestic, and they are the idols. Here the author said: (and they are the idols). Arabic grammar would require him to say: "and they are the idols" (wa hiya al-aṣnām), because the plural of non-rational things does not take a pronoun for rational beings: "hum" is for rational beings, not for non-rational ones. But the author departed from the original and said "wa hum al-aṣnām" (and they are the idols), in observance of His saying ﴿those who invoke﴾, as you know, which is for the rational. This is because Allah the Exalted gave these objects of worship the status of rational beings, and despite being given that status, they do not judge anything.

﴿And those they invoke besides Him do not judge anything﴾. He did not match this clause with the preceding clause but made it more general. In the first clause He said ﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾, and here He said ﴿do not judge anything﴾, and He did not say "do not judge with truth," indicating that they judge neither with truth nor with falsehood, so they are not worthy to be worshipped besides Allah mighty and majestic.

﴿Do not judge anything﴾ at all: neither legal nor cosmic, neither truth nor falsehood. How then could they be partners with Allah? This is the point of the negation: if these idols do not judge anything, how can they be made partners to Allah? This is a rebuke to those who worship these idols besides Allah.

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾: "al-Samīʿ" (the Hearing) of their words, "al-Baṣīr" (the Seeing) of their deeds.

In His saying ﴿huwa al-Samīʿ﴾, "huwa" may be a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and it may be a subject (mubtada'), with the clause being the predicate of "inna." But the pronoun of separation is better than the subject.

Allah mighty and majestic says: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir 19].

* In this verse there are benefits. Among them: the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge, mighty and majestic, of everything, even hidden things, which He knows.
* Among them, that is, among the benefits: the subtlety of Allah's knowledge and its precision, and that it reaches things that the knowledge of others does not reach, namely the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal. Indeed, this is known only to Allah; even the one beside you does not know it.
* Among them: a warning against opposing the command of Allah. Its direction: He knows, so beware, beware of opposing Allah mighty and majestic, whether in your secret or in your open conduct.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that the hearts are in the breasts, by His saying ﴿and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir 19]; concealment and secrecy occur in the heart, therefore He said ﴿and what the breasts conceal﴾.

Then He said: ﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾ to the end.

* From its benefits: the affirmation that all of Allah the Exalted's judgment is truth, by His saying ﴿judges with truth﴾, whether the judgment is cosmic or legal.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: praise of Allah mighty and majestic with this perfect attribute, namely the judgment of truth, and that He does nothing in vain or idly, but everything He decrees is truth.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the denunciation of idol-worshippers, since they worshipped with Allah one who is nothing in relation to Allah mighty and majestic, by His saying ﴿those they invoke besides Him do not judge anything﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that these idols do not benefit their worshippers at all, by His saying ﴿do not judge anything﴾, and "shay'" (anything) is indefinite in a negative context, so it encompasses everything.

If someone says: among the people who invoke a god besides Allah are those whom, when they call upon these idols, the idols answer them; when they call upon them to remove harm, the harm is removed from them; and among people are those who, when they oppose these idols, are afflicted with a trial. So what is the answer?

The answer is to say: what occurs, occurs from Allah mighty and majestic, not from these idols, as a trial and a test. And it is said regarding it: it happened at that time, not by it. That is, this judgment came from Allah mighty and majestic at the time of invoking these idols, not by the invocation of these idols.

If someone says: why do you turn away from the apparent cause to another cause that is not known?

We say: we turned to that because of the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿And those they invoke besides Him do not judge anything﴾, and by His saying: ﴿If you call upon them, they do not hear your call, and if they heard, they would not respond to you; and on the Day of Resurrection they will deny your association. And none can inform you like one who is all-aware﴾ [Fatir 14], and by His saying: ﴿And who is more astray than one who invokes other than Allah, one who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection, and they are unaware of their supplication? (5) And when the people are gathered, they will be enemies to them and will deny their worship﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5-6].

Otherwise, the common person may go to the owner of a grave and say: "O my master, O friend of Allah, O my lord, rescue me from this calamity, rescue me from this distress." Then he goes home and finds the matter has been relieved. In any case, he will attribute this relief to the apparent cause he performed, namely invoking this grave, until the distress was lifted from him.

We say: this is a trial, and we know with certainty that he, that is the owner of the grave, is not the one who removed the harm; rather, it was Allah mighty and majestic who removed it, but the removal occurred at the invocation of the owner of the grave, not by his invocation.

Pay attention to this, for the people of graves constantly raise this doubt against us. They say: "I invoked so-and-so, and he responded to me, and the distress was lifted." And one of us came from Makkah to Madinah a long time ago. When we approached Madinah, they began to invoke, and to invoke the Messenger. I said, "Fear Allah, O people," and at that time the person was still young and not yet grown: "Fear Allah, invoke Allah." They said: "No, this is our master, one of the people whose belly was split open and whose intestines hung out, and the earth became too narrow for him. They said: go to the Prophet of Allah." So he went, and when he approached Madinah he invoked Allah, and the intestines went back in and the belly closed.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, he invoked the Prophet. When he approached Madinah, he invoked the Prophet, saying: "O Messenger of Allah, rescue me," the belly was split and the intestines hanging out, so the intestines went back into the belly and the belly closed.

First, as to this story: whoever says it is true. Then, supposing it has become true, did this happen by the invocation of the Messenger? Never; this did not happen. The Messenger does not possess this at all. During his life, Allah may show them a sign of the Messenger's, and such a thing happens, as happened to the eye of Abu Qatada, which was injured and hung out until it lay on his cheek; the Prophet, peace be upon him, put it back in its place and it healed immediately [narrated by Abu Ya'la in al-Musnad (1549) and in al-Mafarid (61), al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (19/8) (12), and al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwa (1043, 1184), from the hadith of Qatada ibn al-Nu'man]. This is a sign of Allah, but it occurred during his life; after his death, no.

The point is that Allah the Exalted may make healing follow the invocation of the owner of a grave as a trial and a test, so a person believes by the senses and disbelieves the Shari'a. He believes by the senses, building this matter on the apparent thing, and disbelieves the Shari'a.

If someone says: are there parallels to this? We say: yes. Allah may test a person by facilitating the means of disobedience, as a trial to know who fears Him in the unseen, as He tested the Children of Israel with the fish. Allah forbade them to hunt fish on the Sabbath and tested them: on the Sabbath the fish would come upon the water in abundance, and on other days they did not come. A long time passed, and they said: "We must catch these fish, but the Sabbath is forbidden to us. What shall we do?" He said: there is a stratagem—and the Jews are people of stratagems: place a net on Friday, the fish will enter on Saturday, and take the fish on Sunday, and say to Allah: "We did not hunt on the Sabbath." So what were they treated with? ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: Be apes, despised﴾ [al-Baqarah 65]. Allah the Exalted turned them into something resembling a human but not a human, as they did something resembling lawfulness but not lawful—a recompense in kind.

This nation: Allah forbade hunting while in the state of ihram, and Allah tested them. The game began to come in abundance: flying game could be reached by the spear, and creeping game by the hand. ﴿O you who believe, Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your spears can reach, that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen﴾ [al-Ma'idah 94]. So the flying game came to be reached by a person with his spear, though flying game is ordinarily reached only with an arrow, and creeping game by the hand. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, avoided this: they did not catch with the hand, nor hunt with the spear.

So beware, O Muslim, lest you be deceived when the means of disobedience are made easy for you. Allah may test you. Perhaps Allah tests a person with a position in which he could steal from the public treasury, either by outright theft, taking dirhams, or indirect theft, such as arriving late to work or leaving early. For whoever does that is a thief. If we suppose he is late by a sixth, or leaves early by a sixth, how much has he stolen from his salary? He has stolen a sixth, because if he is late by a sixth he deserves only five-sixths of the salary, and the rest he takes without right. He is content, because no one is above him—he is the manager, for example—or he is content because his manager is also late, and it is known that when a manager is late and those under him are late, he says nothing to them, for if he said something to them he would expose himself.

So beware of being deceived when Allah makes the means of disobedience easy for you; for Allah knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal. Do not be deceived by this matter.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a sharp rebuke of the foolishness of those people who worship besides Allah—from where do they take this? In that they turned away from worshipping the One who judges with truth to worshipping one who judges nothing, and this is the utmost foolishness.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names: al-Samī' (the Hearing) and al-Baṣīr (the Seeing).

And the affirmation of what they indicate of attributes, and the affirmation of what they indicate of effect or of ruling.

This is because faith in Allah's names is not complete except by believing in three matters, if they are transitive: first, affirming the name; second, affirming the attribute it indicates; third, affirming the effect or ruling it indicates. This is if it is transitive.

But if it is intransitive, faith in it is complete only by two matters: affirming the name, and affirming the attribute it indicates.

Is al-Samī' intransitive or transitive?

* Students: Intransitive.

* Other students: Transitive.

* Shaykh: How intransitive, transitive? Then we move to the third category: neither intransitive nor transitive.

Is it intransitive or transitive?

* Students: Transitive.

* Shaykh: Transitive. ﴿Allah has certainly heard the saying of﴾ and ﴿Allah hears your mutual dialogue﴾ [al-Mujadila 1]: transitive. So you must believe in al-Samī' as a name of Allah.

And has anyone denied the names? Yes: among the Mu'attila who claim to belong to the Islamic community are those who deny Allah's names.

And you must believe in the attribute it indicates, which is hearing. Allah is not Hearing without hearing; rather, He is Hearing with hearing.

Has anyone affirmed the name without the attribute? Yes: the Mu'tazila. Their principle is to affirm the names and deny the attributes indicated by these names.

They say: Allah is Hearing without hearing, Seeing without sight. Glory be to Allah! How is He Seeing without sight? He says: Yes, Seeing without sight, because if you affirm sight, then sight is an attribute added to the essence, or not? The attribute is other than the qualified. If you say it is eternal, you affirm a plurality of eternals, and become more disbelieving than the Christians. How many did the Christians affirm? Three gods. You now want to affirm fifty gods or more, according to the number of names for which you affirm an attribute, and this is disbelief. If we declare the Christian disbeliever for three and say: he is a disbeliever, we say: you are a disbeliever, a disbeliever, a disbeliever; multiply three by... until you reach the names. You are more disbelieving than the Christians if you affirm an eternal attribute.

If I assert that it is created (ḥādith), then it follows that created events subsist in Allah. But created events cannot subsist except in something created, so you would be establishing that Allah is created and that He is originated.

What about when this statement is phrased in words more eloquent and more forceful than mine? Would the ignorant not be deceived by it? Undoubtedly they would be deceived by it.

But we say: Allah, exalted is He, is All-Hearing (samī') with a hearing (sam'), and it is not conceivable that a derived name (mushtaqq) exists without that from which it is derived, never. For it is not correct to say of the deaf that he is "All-Hearing," nor of the blind that he is "All-Seeing." It is impossible for a derived name in all the languages of the world to exist without its root from which it is derived preceding it.

As for your statement that the attribute is other than the one described, we say: Allah, exalted is He, has never ceased and will never cease to be with His attributes, and there is absolutely no existing essence without an attribute. Whoever claims that there exists an essence without an attribute has claimed the impossible. Nothing that exists is without an attribute. Even if the only attributes it has were the attribute of existence, of self-subsistence, and the like, still everything described has an attribute. However, the one described by his attributes is not something separate from him. Therefore we do not say, "The attributes of Allah are Allah," nor do we say, "They are other than Allah." Rather we say, "Allah with His attributes." Because if you say, "The attributes are Allah," the meaning becomes that He has no attribute. And if you say, "They are other than Him," you have separated the attribute from the one described, and this is impossible.

So, belief in a name requires that you believe in what it contains of an attribute. Its containing of the attribute may be by inclusion (taḍammun), and it may be by necessary implication (iltizām). So do we believe in the attribute that the name indicates by inclusion only, or by inclusion and necessary implication? Do you not know what the meaning is? By inclusion and by necessary implication.

For example: "the Creator" (al-Khāliq) is a name that indicates the attribute of creating by inclusion. Its indication of knowledge is by necessary implication, because there is no creating except with knowledge. Its indication of power is also by necessary implication, because there is no creating except with power.

So you believe in what the name indicates of an attribute, whether that is by inclusion or by necessary implication.

The third condition: if the name is transitive (muta'addiyan), the third matter is the effect or the judgment (ḥukm). For example, "the All-Hearing" is one possessing hearing which hears. You must believe in a hearing that extends to others, so that He hears every speech. "The All-Seeing" is likewise transitive. We believe in "the All-Seeing" as a name, in "sight" as an attribute, and that He sees, as a judgment or an effect.

But if the name is intransitive (lāzim), then one believes in two matters: the first is the name, and the second is the attribute.

Is "the Living" (al-Ḥayy) intransitive or transitive?
* Student: Intransitive.
* Shaykh: How? Is not Allah giving life (yuḥyī)?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: "Yuḥyī" is not from "al-Ḥayy"; it is from "al-Muḥyī." "Al-Ḥayy" is an intransitive description, or "life" is an intransitive attribute that does not extend to anyone other than Allah.

So "al-Ḥayy" is therefore one of the intransitive names. You believe in "al-Ḥayy" as one of Allah's names, and you believe in the attribute indicated by "al-Ḥayy," which is life.

... Because there is no creating except with power. Good. So you believe in what the name indicates of an attribute, whether by inclusion or by necessary implication.

The third matter: if the name is transitive, the effect or the judgment. For example, the All-Hearing, who possesses hearing that hears, you must believe in a hearing that extends to others, so that He hears every speech. The All-Seeing, likewise transitive: we believe in "the All-Seeing" as a name, in "sight" as an attribute, and that He sees as a judgment or an effect.

But if the name is intransitive, one believes in two matters: the first, the name, and the second, the attribute. Is "al-Ḥayy" intransitive or transitive?
* Students: Intransitive.
* Shaykh: How? Is it not Allah who gives life?
* Students: Yuḥyī.
* Shaykh: "Yuḥyī" is not from "al-Ḥayy"; it is from "al-Muḥyī." "Al-Ḥayy" is an intransitive description, or "life" is an intransitive attribute that does not extend to anyone other than Allah. So "al-Ḥayy" is one of the intransitive names. You believe in "al-Ḥayy" as one of Allah's names, and you believe in the attribute indicated by "al-Ḥayy," which is life.

Thus, if we hold to this, we oppose all the people of ta'ṭīl (the denial of Allah's names and attributes). We oppose those who do not name Allah with any name nor describe Him with any attribute, and these are the extreme Jahmiyyah (followers of Jahm ibn Ṣafwān). We oppose those who believe that Allah has names but has no attributes, like the Mu'tazilah. And we oppose those who say: He has names and attributes, but they have no judgment, they do not extend, because if they extended to others, it would necessitate the subsistence of created events in Him. For what is heard is created, or is it eternal? It is created. So when hearing is connected to a created thing, the hearing becomes created in the same way as the thing heard, and so created events would subsist in Him. Therefore say: He is All-Hearing, He has hearing, but He does not hear by it, lest created events subsist in Him. So when we come to these three conditions: (1) belief in the name; (2) what it includes of an attribute; (3) the effect or judgment, our belief in the names is sound.

As for "the All-Hearing" and "the All-Seeing," we have already explained their meanings, and we mentioned that "the All-Hearing" indicates hearing, and that the hearing of Allah, exalted is He, is of two kinds: hearing in the sense of responding, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is All-Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrāhīm 39]. Does hearing come in the sense of responding in the Arabic language?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The evidence?
* Student: He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And if they had heard, they would not have responded to you﴾ [Fāṭir 14].
* Shaykh: ﴿And if they had heard, they would not have responded to you.﴾ But is there any evidence in that?
* Student: ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾.
Yes, ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfāl 21], meaning: they do not respond. And from it is the saying of the one praying, and you, every day, pray at least seventeen rak'ahs and say: "Allah hears whoever praises Him" (sami'a Allāhu liman ḥamidah). What does it mean? It means "He responds." It does not mean merely hearing the one who praises, because that would not benefit anything. Rather its meaning is "He responded." This is hearing in the sense of responding.

The second kind: hearing in the sense of perceiving what is heard (idrāk al-masmū'). This divides into three categories. The first is what is meant as a threat (tahdīd). The second is what is meant as support (ta'yīd). The third is what is meant to show the comprehensiveness of Allah's hearing, that is, the hearing of encompassing knowledge (samā' al-iḥāṭah).

An example of the first, which is meant as a threat: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private conversation? Yes, and Our messengers with them are recording﴾ [al-Zukhruf 80]. This is for a threat; that is why He said: ﴿Yes, and Our messengers with them are recording﴾ [al-Zukhruf 80].

An example of hearing meant as support is His saying to Mūsā and Hārūn: ﴿Do not fear; indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 46].

An example of what is meant to show encompassing hearing is His saying: ﴿Allah has already heard the statement of she who argues with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah, and Allah hears your mutual dialogue﴾ [al-Mujādilah 1]. So hearing is first divided into two: hearing of response and hearing of perception. Perception is three categories, or if you wish, say: three kinds, so that the categories do not overlap: hearing that entails a threat, hearing that entails support, and hearing that shows encompassment. All of this is established for Allah, mighty and majestic.

If a questioner says: What determines that this hearing is for support, or for threat, or for encompassment?

We say: the context of the speech and the indications of the circumstances. Therefore it can be said of Allah's saying to Mūsā and Hārūn: ﴿Do not fear; indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 46], that this hearing is for support and for threat, support of whom?
* Students: Mūsā.
* Shaykh: And a threat to Pharaoh. But what prevents saying that it is a threat to Pharaoh is that Pharaoh was not hearing these words from Allah. So how is one threatened who does not hear the threat? Therefore the scholars said: the hearing in this verse is for support. I have not seen them say that it is for threat, nor for the threat to Pharaoh. The reason is that Pharaoh now is not hearing what Allah, mighty and majestic, says. So how is one threatened who does not hear the threat?!

As for "the All-Seeing" (al-Baṣīr), it means the one possessing piercing sight, from whose gaze nothing is absent, mighty and majestic. Whatever movement or whatever action, Allah, exalted is He, sees it. Good. If He sees everything, what is our position regarding His saying (ﷺ): "Three whom Allah will not speak to, nor look at, nor purify" — and He said, "nor look at them," so He negated looking at them?

We say: the affirmed look is not the negated look. The negated is the look of mercy, and the affirmed is the look of encompassment. Allah, exalted is He, looks at everything with a look of encompassment; even those upon whom is wrath are seen before Allah, mighty and majestic, but with a look of encompassment. As for what is negated, it is the look of mercy: "He will not look at them." By this the evidences harmonize, and it becomes clear that there is no contradiction between them. There is "al-Baṣīr" in the sense of knowledge, but what comes to mind from it is sight, as has already been explained.

* Student: What happens to the worshippers of graves of trial and testing? If we tell them that Allah, mighty and majestic, says such and such, they are not convinced. The believer in the Qur'an who accepts it is convinced by the verses, but these are not convinced by the Qur'an.
* Shaykh: May Allah bless you. Most of the people of graves are Muslims; that is, they see themselves as being upon Islam and believe in the Qur'an.
* Student: Is there a stronger proof, O Shaykh, (...)? The auditory (sam'iyyah) proof is a theoretical argument for debating them. Is there not another proof?
* Shaykh: It is possible, by way of challenge, that a person challenges them with something that would anger their gods, which he does, and nothing happens. This may be part of the challenge.
* Student: Regarding "the All-Hearing": is it an attribute of essence or an attribute of action?
* Shaykh: "The All-Hearing" is an attribute of essence. But what makes the thing heard exist is an attribute of action. As for hearing, Allah has never ceased and will never cease to be All-Hearing; it is not connected to His will. If you want to know the difference: if it were possible for Allah to be free of this attribute, it would be an attribute of action; if it is not possible, it is an attribute of essence. And it is known that it is impossible for Allah, mighty and majestic, to be free of the attribute of hearing so that He would be deaf, for Allah is exalted above that. But what occurs is the thing heard.
* Student: Is the look of mercy the same as the mercy of Allah, mighty and majestic? I mean, what is meant by ...?
* Shaykh: What is meant is that Allah looks at him with a look by which He shows him mercy. It is not the same as mercy itself. This is why you now distinguish between looking at your child who pleases you and looking at your child who angers you. When you look at the child who pleases you, you look at him with a cool look, while he feels that your eye has been delighted by him. "Delighted" (qarrat) comes from "qarr," which is coolness, and therefore "Allah cool your eye" (aqarra Allāhu 'aynak) means He made it cool. What is the meaning of "qarrahā"? He calmed it so that it does not move. Good. The child with whom you are angry: when you look at him, how is your eye? Hot and red, with sparks coming from it, almost blinding the child. Is that not so?
* Student: May Allah be good to you. In His saying: ﴿And those who call upon other than Him﴾ [Ghāfir 20], the author applied it to (...), and it has also passed us that the polytheists, the author always applies it to the people of Makkah, perhaps because the surah was revealed in Makkah, so perhaps the author applied it to this. What do you say about this?
* Shaykh: No, this is not correct. What matters is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause (sabab). He has a view, and a stronger view than this is His saying after this verse: ﴿Have they not traveled in the land and seen?﴾ [Ghāfir 21]. But we say: what matters is the generality of the wording, and the cause does not specify the general, and if a ruling is mentioned that relates to some individuals of the general, that does not require restricting it either, as is the established principle.
* Student: The expression, for example, if we say: "This deed is closer to the look of Allah's mercy"?
* Shaykh: It is not correct to say "closer to the look of Allah's mercy." Mercy is not looked at. Say "closer to the mercy of Allah."
* Student: Interpreting "those called upon" as idols excludes the rabbis and monks and others. Is there not a deficiency in this?
* Shaykh: What do you say about this question? Yes, there is no doubt that worship of rabbis and monks in the sense that the Messenger (ﷺ) explained is not like the worship of idols, because the worship of idols is worship of approach and submission, while the worship of rabbis and monks is worship of following. And there is no doubt that it is worship, as came in the hadith: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and the Messiah, son of Mary; and they were not commanded except to worship one God﴾ [al-Tawbah 31]. So if the worship of rabbis and monks is like the worship of the Messiah son of Mary, it follows that they worship them with the worship of approach. But the Messenger (ﷺ) said to 'Adī ibn Ḥātim: "Do they not make lawful what Allah has made unlawful, and you make it lawful, and make unlawful what Allah has made lawful, and you make it unlawful?" He said: Yes. He said: "That is their worship." This is worship of following, while most of the worship of the polytheists is worship of approach and exaltation.

[Footnote: Al-Ṭabarānī in al-Kabīr (218) and al-Bayhaqī in al-Kubrā (20350) with their chains from 'Adī ibn Ḥātim (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a golden cross around my neck. He said: "O 'Adī, throw this idol away from your neck." So I threw it away, and I came to him while he was reciting Sūrat Barā'ah. He recited this verse: ﴿They took their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah 31] until he finished it. I said: We do not worship them. He said: "Do they not forbid what Allah has permitted and you forbid it, and permit what Allah has forbidden and you permit it?" I said: Yes. He said: "That is their worship."]

* Student: Does His saying: ﴿Indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ not include the hearing of encompassment (...)?
* Shaykh: The hearing here is hearing of encompassment, but what is intended by it is victory and support, because mere encompassment, even Pharaoh is heard by Allah, mighty and majestic.
* Student: What are the best books (...) on the names and attributes?
* Shaykh: By Allah, the books are many and differ in method. For example, for mere affirmation, establishing the creed, the best is al-'Aqīdah al-Wāsiṭiyyah, because it is all built on verses and hadiths. For the aspect of debate and argument, the best I have seen is al-Ṣawā'iq al-Mursalah by Ibn al-Qayyim, and its abridgment. This is among the best for the student of knowledge in debate. Al-Ṣawā'iq al-Mursalah 'alā al-Jahmiyyah wa al-Mu'aṭṭilah (The Dispatched Thunderbolts Against the Jahmiyyah and the Denialists), and its abridgment is also beneficial, because he, may Allah have mercy on him, mentions the principal issues in which there is disagreement, then debates these people or argues with the more correct view. It is not a mere discussion; he argues with them until the truth becomes clear.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: By Allah, I have forgotten the one it belongs to.
* Student: al-Mawṣilī.
* Shaykh: Al-Mawṣilī, what is his name?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Just al-Mawṣilī? In any case, the abridgment is known by this name: Mukhtaṣar al-Ṣawā'iq al-Mursalah.
* Student: Is it permissible to classify shirk, for example the verse: ﴿They took their rabbis and monks as lords﴾? Meaning this is the shirk of obedience and the shirk of following?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is the shirk of following and the shirk of obedience, but that is shirk of worship. This is why among the best definitions of ṭāghūt is what Ibn al-Qayyim said: whatever a servant transgresses his limit with, of a deity worshipped, or a leader followed, or an authority obeyed. The worshipped are idols, the followed are scholars, and the obeyed are rulers. This is the best that is said in defining ṭāghūt. But this is considering the transgressor. As for considering the worshipped, the followed, or the obeyed, these are not ṭawāghīt in terms of their own essences, because the scholar may not be pleased with this matter, and the ruler likewise, and the worshipped likewise. But in terms of the actor, they are ṭawāghīt, because he has transgressed concerning them; they are the place of his transgression, and they are not themselves transgressing. So 'Īsā ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, is worshipped. Do we say he is a ṭāghūt? No, but he is the place of transgression of those who worshipped him. Pay attention to this point, because some people raised an objection to Ibn al-Qayyim's words and said: How does he say this? So is 'Īsā a ṭāghūt because he is worshipped? It is said: his intention, may Allah have mercy on him, is that the place of transgression is in the worshipped, the followed, and the obeyed.
* Student: What is the difference between a transitive verb and an intransitive verb?
* Shaykh: The intransitive is what does not govern a direct object, and the transitive is what governs a direct object. Does "sami'a" (to hear) govern a direct object or not? Living? Great (ʿaẓuma)? Can you make "ʿaẓuma" act on something? "ʿAẓuma" is itself; but "ʿaẓẓama" (to magnify) is correctly transitive, while "ʿaẓuma" is undoubtedly intransitive. "Jalla"? Intransitive. So "al-ʿAẓīm" (the Mighty) is one of Allah's intransitive names, "al-ʿAlī" (the Most High) is one of Allah's intransitive names, and "al-Ajall" or "al-Jalīl" (the Majestic) is one of Allah's intransitive names.
* Student: (...) ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾. How (...) our master Jesus and other righteous people?
* Shaykh: Do you memorize the Qur'an?
* Student: I have not memorized it.

The Shaykh: Good. "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell; you will be its certain entrants. Had these been gods, they would not have entered it, and all will abide therein forever. For them therein is a roaring, and they therein will not hear. Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us, they will be kept far from it" [al-Anbiya 98–101] [al-Anbiya: ]. And 'Isa is among those for whom the best reward has preceded, do you understand? For this reason the disbelievers cited 'Isa as an example, and when the verse "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell" was revealed, they said: "Then 'Isa is in the Fire as well, by way of dispute." So Allah the Exalted revealed: "Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us, they will be kept far from it." It is like His saying: "Are our gods better, or he?" Allah the Exalted said: "They did not cite it to you except for argument; rather, they are a contentious people" [al-Zukhruf 58]. And the most hated of men to Allah is the most quarrelsome adversary.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir 19].

"Yaʿlamu" (He knows): the subject is Allah, mighty and majestic.

"Khaʾinat al-aʿyun" (the treachery of the eyes): this is an idafa of an attribute to its qualified noun, meaning "the treacherous eyes." The treachery of the eye is its stealing a glance at what is forbidden. That is, a person may look at something forbidden while his companion sits beside him without noticing, because he steals the glance, as if he watches for an opportunity when his companion is heedless, so that he may look at what Allah, mighty and majestic, has forbidden. This is the first point.

Second: a person may look without stealing, but openly, and his companion does not perceive that he is looking in a forbidden way. Therefore Allah, mighty and majestic, warned against this state, saying: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾. The author of the tafsir said: (by their stealing a glance at what is forbidden), ﴿and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir 19]: the hearts. The author explained "the breasts" as "the hearts" because they are within the breasts, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts﴾ [al-Hajj 46]. Thus Allah, mighty and majestic, shows here the precision and subtlety of His knowledge, that He knows even this state which people who witness it do not know: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir 19].

﴿And Allah judges with truth, while those they invoke besides Him do not judge anything. Indeed, Allah is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾ [Ghafir 20]. ﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾: the clause is conjoined to His saying ﴿He knows﴾.

﴿Yaqḍī bil-ḥaqq﴾ (judges with truth), meaning He rules by it, legally and decreed. This is because judgment, that is, the judgment of Allah mighty and majestic, is of two kinds:

A cosmic (kawnī) judgment, as in His saying: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture that you will cause corruption in the land twice and become arrogant with great arrogance﴾ [al-Isra' 4].

And a legal (sharʿī) judgment, as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isra' 23]. "Qaḍā" here means legal judgment, and its meaning is: "your Lord has enjoined that you worship none but Him." So here Allah says "yaqḍī bil-ḥaqq."

Is the intended meaning the cosmic judgment or the legal judgment? Both are intended. That is, He decrees cosmically with truth, so there is in His cosmic decree no vanity or play: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhan 38-39].

Likewise He decrees legally with truth, so all of His legal decree, glorified and exalted is He, is true, because it is good, so He commands it; or evil, so He forbids it, and this is the truth.

Thus Allah judges with truth in both kinds, the cosmic judgment and the legal judgment.

﴿And those they invoke besides Him﴾ [Ghafir 20]: the conjunction "wa" here is coordinating, and it may also be resumptive.

﴿And those they invoke besides Him﴾: he said (they worship, i.e. the disbelievers of Makkah, with the yāʾ and the tāʾ). Here is an explanation of the word ﴿yadʿūna﴾, an explanation of the pronoun in the "wāw", and a reading.

As for the reading, the author mentioned that there are two readings: the first reading is ﴿yadʿūna﴾ with the yāʾ, and the second reading is ﴿tadʿūna﴾ with the tāʾ in direct address, and both are canonical (sabʿiyya) readings.

As for ﴿yadʿūna﴾, he explained it with the word "yaʿbudūn" (they worship).

The correct view is that what is meant by it is that they worship and supplicate, because they worship the idols and ask them to bring benefits and repel harms, and they also worship them by bowing, prostrating, vows, and other things.

As for the "wāw", the author explained it as the disbelievers of Makkah, making the pronoun refer to the disbelievers of Makkah. Here we ask: is there no one who worships idols and invokes idols except the disbelievers of Makkah? There are some of them and others besides them. If that is so, then restricting the general to the specific is a deficiency in the explanation. The explanation that corresponds to the "wāw" is that it is general to everyone who invokes besides Allah, whether the disbelievers of Makkah, the disbelievers of Madinah, the disbelievers of Ta'if, the disbelievers of Iraq, the disbelievers of Sham, the disbelievers of this nation, or the disbelievers of those before it: everyone who invokes besides Allah invokes one who does not judge anything.

And His saying ﴿min dūnihi﴾ [Ghafir 20] means "besides Allah." The word "dūn" here means "other than," that is, other than Allah mighty and majestic, and they are the idols. Here the author said: (and they are the idols). Arabic grammar would require him to say: "and they are the idols" (wa hiya al-aṣnām), because the plural of non-rational things does not take a pronoun for rational beings: "hum" is for rational beings, not for non-rational ones. But the author departed from the original and said "wa hum al-aṣnām" (and they are the idols), in observance of His saying ﴿those who invoke﴾, as you know, which is for the rational. This is because Allah the Exalted gave these objects of worship the status of rational beings, and despite being given that status, they do not judge anything.

﴿And those they invoke besides Him do not judge anything﴾. He did not match this clause with the preceding clause but made it more general. In the first clause He said ﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾, and here He said ﴿do not judge anything﴾, and He did not say "do not judge with truth," indicating that they judge neither with truth nor with falsehood, so they are not worthy to be worshipped besides Allah mighty and majestic.

﴿Do not judge anything﴾ at all: neither legal nor cosmic, neither truth nor falsehood. How then could they be partners with Allah? This is the point of the negation: if these idols do not judge anything, how can they be made partners to Allah? This is a rebuke to those who worship these idols besides Allah.

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾: "al-Samīʿ" (the Hearing) of their words, "al-Baṣīr" (the Seeing) of their deeds.

In His saying ﴿huwa al-Samīʿ﴾, "huwa" may be a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and it may be a subject (mubtada'), with the clause being the predicate of "inna." But the pronoun of separation is better than the subject.

Allah mighty and majestic says: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir 19].

* In this verse there are benefits. Among them: the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge, mighty and majestic, of everything, even hidden things, which He knows.
* Among them, that is, among the benefits: the subtlety of Allah's knowledge and its precision, and that it reaches things that the knowledge of others does not reach, namely the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal. Indeed, this is known only to Allah; even the one beside you does not know it.
* Among them: a warning against opposing the command of Allah. Its direction: He knows, so beware, beware of opposing Allah mighty and majestic, whether in your secret or in your open conduct.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that the hearts are in the breasts, by His saying ﴿and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir 19]; concealment and secrecy occur in the heart, therefore He said ﴿and what the breasts conceal﴾.

Then He said: ﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾ to the end.

* From its benefits: the affirmation that all of Allah the Exalted's judgment is truth, by His saying ﴿judges with truth﴾, whether the judgment is cosmic or legal.
