It is as if he were saying: "The people are holding me back from killing Moses, and were it not for them restraining me, I would have killed him." So he says, "Leave me to him, leave me to kill him," even though no one could turn him away from his purpose, because he tells them, "I am your Lord, the Most High." Yet he deceives them, saying, "Leave me to kill Moses." And ﴿aqtul﴾ ("I kill") is in the jussive mood as the answer to the imperative ﴿Leave me, I will kill Moses﴾, and the answer to an imperative is in the jussive mood. Is it jussive by the imperative itself, or by a conditional that is implied? There are two opinions:

The first opinion: it is jussive by the imperative itself.

The second: it is jussive by an implied conditional, the implied meaning being: "If you leave me, I will kill Moses."

The rule we follow in tafsir and in hadith is that when a statement can be read either with an implied element or without it, the default is that nothing is implied. On this basis we say: ﴿aqtul﴾ is a present-tense verb in the jussive mood as the answer to the imperative, and the sign of its jussive is the sukun.

Regarding ﴿Moses, I will kill him﴾, he said: (because they were restraining him from killing him). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, based this statement on the apparent wording: that they were restraining him, and he says, "Leave me, I will kill him." But what we see is that he is a liar; no one restrained him from killing him, and no one can ever restrain him from killing him. Rather, he wanted to deceive, because he could not actually kill Moses, so he pretended that he was being restrained from killing him, and he says: ﴿Leave me to kill Moses﴾.

He said: ﴿and let him call upon his Lord﴾: this is a challenge, and we seek refuge in Allah. The ﴿wa﴾ is a conjunction particle, the ﴿li﴾ is the imperative lam, and ﴿walyadʿu rabbahu﴾: ﴿yadʿu﴾ is a present-tense verb in the jussive mood by the imperative lam, and the sign of its jussive is the deletion of the ﴿wāw﴾ and the ḍamma preceding it, which indicates it. The original form of ﴿yadʿu﴾ is ﴿yadʿū﴾.

His saying (I will kill him, and let him call upon [his Lord]) is an open challenge to Moses and to the One who sent him, may He be glorified and exalted. That is, if he is truthful, let him call upon this Lord who sent him to protect him from me.

As for his saying ﴿and let him call upon his Lord﴾, we have told you that the lam is the imperative lam. Is the imperative lam unvowelled (sakin) or vowelled with a kasra? We say: it is sakin, but after the ﴿wa﴾, the ﴿fa﴾, and ﴿thumma﴾ it is sakin. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿let him extend a rope to the sky, then let him cut it off﴾ [al-Hajj 15], and He said: ﴿then let them complete their rites and fulfil their vows﴾ [al-Hajj 29], and here He said: ﴿and let him call upon his Lord﴾.

As for his saying ﴿his Lord﴾ and not "our Lord": that is because he does not openly acknowledge the lordship of Allah, and he attributed the lordship to Moses only for the purpose of mockery (tankīt). That is, it is as if he were saying: "This is your Lord whom you claim. If you are truthful, let Him protect you from me."

﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion, or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land.﴾ I have in my copy: ﴿and that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾. Wait, the author will mention the readings. ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾: is this fear real or not? Yes, it is real. He fears that Moses, with those who follow him, will change the religion of these people, because their religion is worship of Pharaoh, while Moses says: "Worship Allah." So if he brings the signs and the people follow him, he changes the religion: instead of turning to Pharaoh and worshipping him, the people turn to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason he said: (﴿that he will change your religion﴾ from your worship of me, so that you follow him). So their religion is their worship of Pharaoh; when Moses calls them to worship Allah, they turn to Allah, the religion changes, and they follow Moses.

﴿and that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾: corruption, according to his claim, is turning people away from worshipping him to worshipping Allah. This is one aspect. Another aspect is the division of the people: instead of being united in their allegiance, some fearful and some desiring, they would differ, some following Moses and some following Pharaoh, and the division of a community is undoubtedly corruption. So the corruption he claims to appear has two aspects: the first, changing the religion; the second, dividing the community.

(﴿and that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, such as killing and other things.) Killing is usually a consequence of disagreement: the consequence of disagreement among a community is that the dispute reaches fighting, or other things, and from it comes the change of people's worship from the worship of Pharaoh to the worship of Allah.

He said: (And in another reading: ﴿aw﴾ [or].) Now, does the commentator explain the reading with ﴿wa﴾ or with ﴿aw﴾? With ﴿wa﴾, because he said: (And in a reading: ﴿aw﴾).

Now, is this reading canonical (sabʿiyyah) or irregular (shādhdhah)? It is canonical, according to the convention we mentioned to you: when he says "and in a reading" or mentions a vowel variant such as a ḍamma or a fatḥa, it is canonical; when he says "it was read" (quriʾa), it is irregular.

(And in another: with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and the hāʾ and a ḍamma on the dāl.) And ﴿wa-an yaẓhara fī al-arḍi al-fasādu﴾ (with a ḍamma on the dāl) indicates that corruption is the subject of ﴿yaẓhara﴾. Now, do these readings differ in meaning? Yes, they differ in apparent meaning, but their import is one: if Moses causes corruption to appear in the land, corruption appears, so the difference in readings has a benefit.

First, the benefit of ﴿aw﴾ and ﴿wa﴾: with ﴿aw﴾, he fears one of two things: that he will change the religion or that he will cause corruption to appear. With ﴿wa﴾ ("and"), he fears the combination of both: the changing of the religion and the appearance of corruption, and one of the two must happen, either he changes the religion or corruption appears. If he does not change the religion, there will still be killing and dispute. And there must also be another aspect in which both are combined: the changing of the religion and the appearance of corruption.

As for ﴿yaẓhara﴾ and ﴿yuẓhira﴾: if he intends to cause corruption to appear, it may appear or may not appear. When it is ﴿wa-an yaẓhara fī al-arḍi al-fasādu﴾, the attainment of what he wanted, the appearance of corruption, is realised.

So the readings have one import. ﴿and that he will cause corruption to appear in the land (26)﴾, and [then] ﴿Moses said﴾, and so on.

* We take the benefits:

* Among the benefits of this noble verse, ﴿And Pharaoh said, "Leave me..."﴾ and so on: Pharaoh's deception, and that he was a cunning, deceitful man who displays the opposite of reality, as in his saying: ﴿Leave me to kill Moses.﴾

* Among its benefits: the intensity of Pharaoh's rage against Moses, to the point that he wanted to kill him.

* Among its benefits: the intensity of Pharaoh's challenge, when he said: "Let me kill him, and let him call upon his Lord," meaning that he challenges him: if he calls upon his Lord, will it benefit him or not?

* Among its benefits: the disbelievers' fear of the believers' weapon of supplication, as shown in his saying ﴿and let him call upon his Lord﴾. Even though the purpose is challenge, there is no doubt that he understood that supplication was a weapon for Moses, peace be upon him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the fanaticism of the disbelievers for their religion, as shown in his saying ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion.﴾

* Among its benefits: that the people of Pharaoh owed him worship, meaning they regarded their submission to him as worship, as shown in his saying ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion.﴾

* Among its benefits: that the disbelievers regard faith as corruption in the land, as shown in his saying ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land.﴾ If they regard it so, they must stand between the people and it, so that the land is not corrupted in their view.

* Among its benefits: that the disbelievers claim what is false in order to keep themselves in what they are upon, namely his claim that if the people submit to Allah, corruption will appear in the land, so that the people will remain in their submission to Pharaoh. And Allah knows best.

* Student: What is your opinion of the one who says that Moses and other messengers who were denied, and who were called a sorcerer and a liar, suffered more than Joseph, peace be upon him, who was accused of adultery (...), is more severe than slander?

* Shaykh: He says: some scholars said that what befell the messengers of denial and torment is more severe than what befell Joseph from being accused of what he was accused of?

It is said: everything has its ruling. Joseph, peace be upon him, was accused of what he was accused of, was punished for it, and was imprisoned despite his innocence, and his innocence became evident in the end. These deniers received more punishment than Joseph received, and some of them were even killed. So everything has its aspect, and no comparison can be made between this and that.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. We know that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, destroyed Pharaoh, Haman, and Qarun. Did they all perish at the same time, or each one separately?

* Shaykh: As for Qarun, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, made clear that the earth swallowed him and his home, so he was not among those who perished by drowning. As for Haman, the apparent view is that he perished along with Pharaoh.

* Student: Was the cause of Qarun a woman who (...) brought a prostitute who said that Moses committed adultery with her? Is this a sound report?

* Shaykh: Not at all. His boasting of his wealth is what caused the earth to swallow him.

* Student: Shaykh, there is a saying that Pharaoh was originally an Arab, and his name was Musʿab ibn al-Rayyan?

* Shaykh: They say his name was Musʿab ibn al-Rayyan. We say: who said this?! Pharaoh was a wicked Copt, and he is innocent of being an Arab, and the Arabs are innocent of him. But the Jews may say so, because the Jews are from the Children of Israel and Pharaoh was their enemy, and the Arabs are now their enemies. They said: let us attach Pharaoh to them, so that he walks with them.

* Student: His saying ﴿Indeed, Qarun was from the people of Moses﴾ [al-Qasas 76]. It is said that Qarun was the paternal uncle of Moses, so he was from the Children of Israel?

* Shaykh: Allah knows best.

* Student: The imperative lam is sakin when preceded by wa, fa, and thumma. That is, if it is not preceded by these three it is vowelled with a kasra. Shaykh, what about His saying ﴿so that you may settle upon their backs﴾ [al-Zukhruf 13] (...), is it not vowelled with a kasra?

* Shaykh: First, it is not the imperative lam, and it is also vowelled with a kasra. Even if it were the imperative lam it would be vowelled with a kasra. But the lam in His saying ﴿li-tastawū﴾ is not imperative; its meaning is causal (lam al-taʿlīl, the lam of purpose). ﴿And He made for you of the ships and the cattle what you ride, so that you may settle upon their backs﴾ [al-Zukhruf 12-13]. Do you understand?

* Student: The rule?

* Shaykh: The rule is context. ﴿Let the one of wealth spend from his wealth﴾ [al-Talaq 7]: this is an imperative lam. ﴿Indeed, We sent you as a witness, a bearer of good news, and a warner, so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Fath 8-9]. This lam may be causal, and it may be imperative, but the causal reading is more evident.

* Student: May Allah reward you. What about the lam in His saying ﴿and so that they may be pleased with it, and so that they may commit what they commit﴾ [al-An'am 113]?

* Shaykh: ﴿And so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it, and so that they may be pleased with it, and so that they may commit﴾: this is not the imperative lam; it is the causal lam. For this reason the causal lam is never sakin, even after the three letters; it is always vowelled with a kasra: ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them, and so that they may enjoy themselves﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut 66]. You would not say: "walyatamattaʿū."

* Student: (...) I did not state my question correctly, I did not make my question clear. I am the one who narrates this hadith to people, meaning I narrate this report to people.

* Shaykh: I told you that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, destroyed Qarun by what destroyed him, because he boasted of his wealth: ﴿He said, "I was only given it on account of knowledge I have"﴾ [al-Qasas 78]. And the matter of the woman whom he claimed Moses committed adultery with is not sound.

* Student: So this report, that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, spoke to him and said: "By My might and My majesty..."

* Shaykh: I say: it is not sound. Do you know it is not sound or not?

* Student: So I should not narrate it?

* Shaykh: No.

* * *
* Student: ﴿And Moses said, "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning." And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said: "Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' when he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? And if he is a liar, upon him is his lie; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar. O my people, to you belongs the kingdom today, dominant in the land, but who will help us against the might of Allah if it comes to us?" Pharaoh said, "I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct."﴾ [Ghafir 27-29].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said in the story of Moses with Pharaoh that he, that is Pharaoh, said: ﴿Leave me to kill Moses.﴾ Is this on its apparent meaning, or is it deception?

* Student: Deception.

* Shaykh: Deception. How so?

* Student: He said: ﴿Leave me, I will kill Moses,﴾ while he was able to do that.

* Shaykh: That is, (...) would prevent him, but he deceived the people that he was prevented from killing him, so that they would say: why did he not kill him?

Now, His saying ﴿and let him call upon his Lord﴾: what does this sentence convey?

* Student: (...) that Moses (...) and their weapon was supplication.

* Shaykh: Yes, but what does this statement from Pharaoh convey?

* Student: It conveys a challenge.

* Shaykh: It conveys a challenge: that is, if (...) he is a lord who answers him, then let him call upon him.

His saying ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾: change it to what?

* Student: Moving them from Pharaoh's religion to another religion, all of them, or that they scatter into factions (...).

* Shaykh: No, that he will change your religion only; he does not want (...).

* Student: He will change their religion to another religion, or move them to (...).

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: He will move them from the worship of Pharaoh to the worship of Allah.

* Shaykh: To the worship of Allah. Correct. His saying ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾: there is a reading ﴿and that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿yaẓhara﴾ and ﴿yuẓhira﴾. Now, how is (al-fasād) in the two readings?

* Student: Al-fasād (...) is the subject.

* Shaykh: So it is in the nominative. And with ﴿yuẓhira﴾, ﴿an yuẓhira fī al-arḍi al-fasād﴾, is it with a fatḥa or a ḍamma?

* Student: With a fatḥa.

* Shaykh: On what basis?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Now, is there a second reading for ﴿aw﴾?

* Student: With wa.

* Shaykh: With wa: ﴿wa-an yuẓhira﴾, ﴿aw an yuẓhira﴾.

Now, what is the corruption that Pharaoh spoke of?

* Student: Corruption has two meanings. The first meaning is turning people away from the worship of Pharaoh to the worship of Allah, Exalted is He, and the second meaning...

* Shaykh: And he considers that to be corruption, as shown in his saying: ﴿that he will change your religion.﴾ And the second?

* Student: That (...) the people; so some of them become partisans of Pharaoh and some of them partisans of Moses, peace be upon him.

* Shaykh: And that leads to chaos and fighting.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verses 27–28 (part 1 of 2):**

Allah, blessed and exalted, says: (﴿And Musa said﴾ to his people, when he had heard that, ﴿"I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord"﴾), and so on to the end. As for His words, (﴿And Musa said﴾ to his people, ﴿"I have sought refuge"﴾), directing the speech to the people of Musa is not correct. Rather, Musa said to Fir'awn, ﴿"I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord"﴾. This is if Fir'awn had said it to him face to face, meaning he said, ﴿"Leave me to kill Musa"﴾ to his face, and Musa then said, "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from you," but he said "from every arrogant one." However, if Fir'awn was speaking with his people and Musa heard that, then according to what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said, Musa, when he heard this, said, "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord." But the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that the first meaning is more correct: that he said it to Fir'awn when he said, ﴿"Leave me to kill Musa"﴾.

He says: ﴿"I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord"﴾. ﴿"ʿUdtu"﴾ (I have sought refuge) means "I have held fast to Allah," because seeking refuge in a thing is holding fast to it. The scholars said: it is said ʿiyadh and liyadh. The scholars said: the difference between ʿiyadh (seeking refuge) and liyadh (clinging for protection) is that liyadh is for what is hoped for, while ʿiyadh is for what is feared. They cited the verse of the poet on this:

*O You to whom I cling for what I hope from Him,*
*and from whom I seek refuge from what I fear—*
*No bone of people is mended, if You are the one who breaks it,*
*and they cannot break a bone that You have mended.*

So the meaning of ﴿"ʿudtu"﴾ is "I have held fast." ﴿"In my Lord and your Lord"﴾: this is the Lordship both general and specific. ﴿"My Lord"﴾ is a specific lordship, and ﴿"your Lord"﴾ is Allah's lordship over Fir'awn and his people, which is of the general lordship.

﴿"From every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning"﴾. This description applies entirely to Fir'awn: he was arrogant, tyrannical, transgressing, and haughty. The arrogant one is the one who elevates himself in pride above the truth and over the creation, because arrogance is either toward the truth or toward the people. This is due to the saying of the Prophet, ṣallā Allāh ʿalayhi wa-ālihi wa-sallam: "Arrogance is rejecting the truth (baṭr al-ḥaqq) and looking down on people (ghamṭ al-nās)." [Narrated by Muslim (91/147) from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him.] "Baṭr al-ḥaqq" means despising it and belittling it, and this is arrogance toward the truth. "Ghamṭ al-nās" means belittling people, and this is arrogance toward the creation. When a person's heart combines arrogance toward the creation and arrogance toward the truth, he is the one who is ruined, and we seek refuge in Allah.

As for His words, ﴿"who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning"﴾, it means the Day of Resurrection. He turned away from saying "the Day of Resurrection" to "the Day of Reckoning," because reckoning is more frightening than the Resurrection. When a person is told, "You will be called to account for what you did of good and evil," he will fear, be anxious, and go straight. The word "reckoning" was mentioned instead of "resurrection" because it is more intimidating, for when a person knows that he will be held accountable for his deeds, he will refrain from sins and carry out the commands.

﴿"And a believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who concealed his faith, said: 'Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?'"﴾ [Ghafir 28], and so on to the end.

When this believing man heard Fir'awn's threat to Musa with killing, he said that. Consider the context of the verse: ﴿"a believing man"﴾. He did not specify him by name, but said "a man" in concealment, because the aim is not to know the name; the aim is to know the matter. Specifying names is among the surplus of knowledge, meaning that if it is attained, that is good, and if it is not attained, it is of no importance.

﴿"A believing man from the family of Fir'awn"﴾. Believing in whom? In Allah. And perhaps we can also say he believed in Musa. ﴿"From the family of Fir'awn"﴾ may mean from his relatives, since the family of a person is his kin, and it may mean from his followers, since "family" (āl) is also used for followers. In either case, the man was not of the Children of Israel, but was from the people of Fir'awn, whether he was from his relatives or from his people who belonged to him.

As for the author's words, "It was said: he was his cousin," this is an opinion whose weakness the author indicated with the word "it was said." ﴿"Who concealed his faith"﴾ means he hid it and kept it secret out of fear for himself.

In His words, ﴿"a believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who concealed his faith"﴾, there are three descriptions: a believer, from the family of Fir'awn, and one who conceals his faith.

The grammarians have said: when an indefinite noun is described the first time, what follows it may be either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a descriptive adjective (ṣifah). On this basis, ﴿"from the family of Fir'awn"﴾ may be a circumstantial clause, and ﴿"who concealed his faith"﴾ a circumstantial clause. It may also be that ﴿"from the family of Fir'awn"﴾ is a second description and ﴿"who concealed his faith"﴾ is a circumstantial clause, or that ﴿"from the family of Fir'awn"﴾ is a second description and ﴿"who concealed his faith"﴾ is a third description. ﴿"Who concealed his faith"﴾ means he hid it from Fir'awn and his people.

﴿"Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'?"﴾ The interrogation here is for denunciation, meaning: how can you kill a man who has done nothing except say, ﴿"My Lord is Allah"﴾?! This is like His saying: ﴿"And they resented them only because they believed in Allah, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy"﴾ [al-Buruj 8].

As for His words, ﴿"because he says"﴾, the particle ﴿"an"﴾ here is verbal (maṣdariyyah) with the implied lām (of causation); this is why the commentator estimated it by saying: "i.e., because he says." On this basis, the ﴿"an"﴾ is stripped of the causative lām; that is, "because of his saying, 'My Lord is Allah,'" meaning "My Lord is Allah, not Fir'awn," while they regarded their lord to be Fir'awn.

﴿"And he has certainly brought you clear proofs from your Lord"﴾ (meaning: with manifest miracles). In ﴿"he has brought you with clear proofs"﴾, the bāʾ indicates accompaniment, and ﴿"clear proofs"﴾ is a description of an omitted noun. Its estimate, contrary to the author, is "ayāt" (signs): i.e., he brought you with clear signs, that is, manifest ones that indicate with decisive indication that he is a prophet.

﴿"And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; and if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you"﴾. This is called by the logicians *al-sabr wa al-taqsīm* (the method of elimination and division), because Musa is now either truthful or a liar. There is no level between truthfulness and falsehood, since he says he is the Messenger of Allah; so either he is truthful in this, or he is a liar. In any case, your believing him does not harm you. This is why he said, ﴿"And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie"﴾, meaning: upon him is the harm of his lie, and Allah will bring disgrace and shame upon him if he lied about Allah. Allah says: ﴿"Who is more unjust than one who lies against Allah and denies the truth when it comes to him?"﴾ [al-Zumar 32]. There are many verses with this meaning, and Allah, the Exalted, exposes his secret and shows his lie, so that the lie falls upon him.

﴿"And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you"﴾: ﴿"if he is truthful"﴾ in that he is a messenger, and you deny him, then some of what he promises you of punishment will strike you in this world hastily; likewise it will strike you in the Hereafter later. So now the danger falls on whom? The danger falls on him if he is a liar, and you will be safe. The danger falls on you if he is truthful, and he will be saved. There is no doubt that this is part of his sincere advice. This man, who descended with the family of Fir'awn to this lowering of speech, did not say that he was truthful, although he believed in him; but this is from the method of condescension (tanazzul). Here he said, ﴿"Will you kill a man"﴾, and did not say, "Will you kill Musa," in order to remove suspicion from himself, lest anyone think he knew Musa and was defending him out of acquaintance. Rather, he used the indefinite ﴿"a man"﴾ to make the matter ambiguous and to strongly conceal it.

﴿"Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar"﴾. ﴿"Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor"﴾, meaning one who exceeds the limit. ﴿"A liar"﴾, meaning one characterized by lying. Does this causal sentence refer to Musa or to Fir'awn? We say it is suitable for both: whoever is a transgressor and a liar, Allah does not guide him. This description applies to Fir'awn, does it not? He is a transgressor who exceeds the limit, a liar who claims what is not his; he said, ﴿"I am your most high lord"﴾, and he lied in that. So he is a transgressor and a liar. Likewise, in the context of argument and condescension, it also applies to Musa if he were a liar, for then he would be a transgressor exceeding the limit in claiming prophethood while lying, and also a liar, because he claimed what he was not truthful about. In any case, the sentence here is suitable to apply to Fir'awn, and it applies in reality, or to Musa by way of condescension toward the opponent.

* In this verse and the one before it there are benefits. Among them: the strength and frankness of Musa, peace be upon him, in that he declared before those who threatened him with death that he had sought refuge in Allah, his Lord and theirs, as in His words: ﴿"I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord"﴾.

* Among them: the strength of his reliance (tawakkul), peace be upon him, in that he depended on Allah before this tyrant who could easily carry out what he threatened.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the description of Fir'awn with these two blameworthy traits: arrogance, and that he does not believe in the Day of Reckoning.

* Among its benefits: the turn to generality rather than specificity, because he did not say, "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from Fir'awn," but said, "from every arrogant one," so that it includes Fir'awn and others besides him.

* Among its benefits as well: when it comes in the form of generality and by description, it applies to Fir'awn and shows that he is characterized by arrogance, and likewise disbelief in the Day of Reckoning.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the Day of Reckoning, which is the Day of Resurrection. And reckoning is not the scrutinizing of a person for his deeds, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever is scrutinized in reckoning will be punished." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6536) and Muslim (2876/79) from the hadith of ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her.] This is because if Allah were to scrutinize you, one of His blessings would cover all the good deeds you have done. Indeed, the good deeds you have done are a blessing from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which require thanks. Then, if you are enabled to thank for them, you need another thanks for being enabled to thank, and so on indefinitely. This is why the poet said:

*If my thanks is a blessing from Allah,*
*upon me, for it, thanks is obligatory in turn.*
*How can thanks be fulfilled except by His favor,*
*even if the days are prolonged and life continues?*

This is true. Reckoning means that Allah, the Exalted, meets His servant, the believer, alone and makes him acknowledge his sins, saying: "You did such and such; you did such and such." When he acknowledges, He says: "I concealed them for you in the world, and I forgive them for you today." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52) from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both.] As for the disbelievers, they are not reckoned in the manner of one whose good and bad deeds are weighed, because they have no good deeds. Rather, their deeds are counted, they are made to stand before them, and they are disgraced by them, meaning they are humiliated by them. It is said: ﴿"These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers"﴾ [Hud 18]. This is the reckoning of the disbelievers, and that is the reckoning of the believers.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿"And a believing man"﴾ [Ghafir 28], and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that attention should be paid to the content of the story rather than to the identity of the person it concerns, as shown by His words: ﴿"a believing man"﴾. Otherwise, we know that Allah knows who this man is, knows his name and lineage and everything related to him. But Allah mentioned him indefinitely, indicating that what matters is the content of the story, not the identity of the person it happened to, unless there is a benefit in specifying him, in which case the benefit is to mention and specify him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the most hostile enemies there may be one who is among the friends of Allah, as His words here show: ﴿"from the family of Fir'awn"﴾. Whether we say he was from his relatives or from his followers in his religion, it indicates that Allah is powerful over all things, and that He may facilitate or prepare faith for one who is among a people immersed in disbelief.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of concealing faith when a person fears for himself, as shown by His words: ﴿"who concealed his faith"﴾. But if a person cannot live as a believer except by concealment, is emigration (hijrah) obligatory upon him?

The answer: yes. In the religion of Islam, whoever cannot live openly practicing his religion is obligated to emigrate, but on the condition that he is able to do so. If he is incapable, Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿"Except the oppressed among men, women, and children who are not able to devise a plan nor are they guided to a way. For those, it is expected that Allah will pardon them, and Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving"﴾ [al-Nisa 98–99].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the severity of this believer's denunciation of Fir'awn, who threatened to kill, as shown by His words: ﴿"Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'?"﴾

* Among its benefits: denunciation of one who does an action without a cause that calls for it. From where is this taken? From ﴿"Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'?"﴾ This is not a cause for killing. At the very least, he should be left alone. As for being killed for this reason, this is objectionable and it is not permissible to approve of it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: avoiding specifying a name out of fear of accusation, or, if you wish, say: the use of ambiguous speech (maʿārīḍ), as shown by His words: ﴿"Will you kill a man"﴾, and he did not say, "Will you kill Musa." Because if he had named him, people would have accused him of having a connection to him, and what he intended would have been ruined. But he left him unspecified and said: ﴿"Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'?"﴾ and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Musa, peace be upon him, brought clear signs of the kind by which people believe, as shown by His words: ﴿"And he has certainly brought you clear proofs from your Lord"﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strength of this man's faith, in that he confronted these people by implicitly denying Fir'awn's lordship. From where? From His words: ﴿"from your Lord"﴾. He confronted them with the fact that they have a lord other than Fir'awn, and this shows the strength of this man. As for His words, ﴿"because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'"﴾, there is no proof in it, because the lordship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, over Musa contains nothing of denial. But ﴿"from your Lord"﴾ is clear that he is alluding that Fir'awn is not a lord, and that the Lord is Allah. This shows the perfect courage of this man.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the use of *al-sabr wa al-taqsīm*, meaning alternating between two states or several states beyond which the matter does not go, as shown by His words: ﴿"And if he is a liar"﴾ and ﴿"and if he is truthful"﴾.

* Among its benefits, that is, the benefits of the verse: consideration of the opponent in what one says and in bringing him closer, because he began with what they believed, which was that Musa was a liar, and began with the lie before beginning with the truth, for the sake of winning them over and showing that the man had no partisanship for Musa. This is why he did not begin with the truth, which is one of the two possibilities.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of equivocation (tawriyah), as shown by His words: ﴿"And if he is a liar"﴾ and His words: ﴿"And if he is truthful"﴾. For we know that this man believed that he was truthful, but he spoke this way as an equivocation that he did not believe in him, and this was for the sake of having his words accepted, because if they had perceived that he believed, they would have killed him. He believed in Musa while being one of their own family, but he used words indicating equivocation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the evil consequence of lying returns to the liar, and so it is, as shown by His words: ﴿"And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie"﴾. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has exposed those who lie and fabricate against Him in this world, and He will expose them in the Hereafter.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strength of this man's faith, in that he believed and was certain that some of what Musa, peace be upon him, promised them would strike them if he was truthful, and they had denied him, as shown by His words: ﴿"And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you"﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verses 27–28 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the one who is extravagant (musrif) and a habitual liar (kadhdhab), that is, one who exceeds the limits in his deeds and in his words (in his words because he is a liar, and in his deeds because he is extravagant), is far from guidance. This is because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾

Here we ask: does the meaning refer to guidance of tawfiq (divine enabling and granting of success) or guidance of bayan (explanation) and irshad (direction)? It is the guidance of tawfiq. Allah the Exalted has made clear the truth to the extravagant liar and to others, but He grants success to whom He wills of His servants and forsakes whom He wills. And Allah knows best.

* Student: His saying: ﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ (...).

* Shaykh: Because he said: ﴿some of what he promises you﴾, meaning in this world. For this reason the commentator specified it by saying: (the immediate punishment).

* Student: Regarding the believer: was he from the family of Pharaoh, or from the Children of Israel?

* Shaykh: Not from the family of Pharaoh, clearly. But is he a relative of his, or one who follows him in his religion?

* Student: (...) the ma'arid (allusive or indirect speech)?

* Shaykh: Ma'arid means that you speak in a way that conceals your meaning by using something contrary to the reality (tawriyah).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: That is, it is as if he is saying: when is ma'arid permissible?

Ma'arid is permissible when there is a benefit in it or when it averts a harm. The use of ma'arid takes three forms:

The first form: oppression (zulm).
The second: averting oppression.
The third: what involves neither of these.

Oppression is when a person uses ma'arid to avoid a right he owes. Averting oppression is when he uses ma'arid to repel injustice from himself. What is neither of these, such as using it in permissible matters.

An example of the first: Zayd and 'Amr dispute before a judge. 'Amr owes Zayd one hundred dirhams. The judge says to the claimant: "Do you have evidence?" He says: "No." The judge says: "Then you have the right to make the other party swear." So the defendant says: "By Allah, I have nothing of his." The apparent wording is a denial, but in his heart he intended affirmation, and he intended by "má" (what) the relative meaning "that which," so the sentence in his intention reads: "By Allah, that which he has is with me." This is true, he does have something of his with him, but he used tawriyah by making "má" a negation, meaning he has nothing. The judge will rule according to what? According to the apparent sense, that it is a negation. This ma'arid we say is haram, because he used it to bring about the loss of a right owed to another.

Likewise, in a claim: if his opponent says: "I am content with you swearing that you have something of mine," and he swears while using tawriyah, then it is haram for him.

As for averting oppression, it is like swearing to repel injustice from oneself or from another. An example: a thief or an oppressive soldier enters upon a man wanting to take his wealth, and says: "Open this chest for me." He says: "By Allah, there is nothing in this chest." The addressee will think the statement is a denial and be satisfied, while he intends affirmation. This tawriyah, there is no doubt about its permissibility. Indeed, if the property belongs to someone else, such as when a person comes and says: "So-and-so has such-and-such with you." I say: "By Allah, I have nothing of his," knowing that if I informed him, he would take it (...).

He says: the disaster (al-da'irah) belongs to Allah and His Messenger. These people were three hundred and some men, and they were the people of Badr. Allah looked upon them and rewarded them with a reward not granted to others. He looked upon them and said: "Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you." This great virtue erased all the misdeeds they might commit. This campaign benefited even whoever participated in it, including Hatib, may Allah be pleased with him, who wrote news of the Prophet (ﷺ) to the Quraysh shortly before the conquest of Mecca. When what he had done was discovered, 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "Let me strike his neck, for he has become a hypocrite." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was a man of the sword, courageous. He (ﷺ) said: "Do you not know that Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: 'Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you'?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4890) and Muslim (2494/161), from the hadith of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and its wording: "Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you."]] So this great misdeed fell among what is forgiven for the people of Badr. For this reason the people of Badr were superior to the people of the Pledge of Ridwan (bay'at al-Ridwan), superior because of the great support they gave the Prophet (ﷺ). For this reason the day of Badr is called the Day of the Criterion (yawm al-Furqan).

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. If someone says: what is meant by the angels fighting alongside the believers at Badr? It is known that the angels are enormous in form, so one of them suffices with a single strike (...) the polytheists?

* Shaykh: It is also known that if Allah had said to those disbelievers: "Be dead," they would have died. The matter is not one of inability or ability. The descent of the angels was to strengthen the hearts of the believers, and their participation was a form of support for the believers and the victory of truth. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is so. And had Allah willed, He would have defeated them, but [He sets them against one another] so that He may test some of you by means of others.﴾ [Muhammad 4]

* Student: What is the evidence for testifying that they are in Paradise?

* Shaykh: The evidence: if the Messenger testifies that someone is in Paradise, we testify for him.

* Student: (...) and you said: they, as individuals, are among the people of Paradise (...)?

* Shaykh: Generally, except for one whom the Messenger testified for, such as Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah. We say of him that he is forgiven. But there is no doubt that if Hatib is forgiven, then Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman are more deserving of that.

* Student: What is your opinion regarding what Shaykh al-Islam (...) held?

* Shaykh: By Allah, this is a strong opinion, without doubt. That is, what Shaykh al-Islam held is supported by the hadith: "You are the witnesses of Allah on earth."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1367) and Muslim (949/60), from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him.]] When the community, or most of the community, agrees on this, it is sufficient. Were it not for a problem: the people of deviant sects would come to us and say: "We are unanimous in testifying that so-and-so is [righteous], and he is the head of an innovation," and they claim that they are the people of truth. But this objection can be avoided by saying: their testimony is not accepted, because they are upon falsehood and misguidance, and what is meant is the testimony of the people of truth.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, in general, all of them are in Paradise. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those of you who spent and fought before the conquest are not equal [to those who did so later]. Those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. But to each Allah has promised the best.﴾ [al-Hadid 10]

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, we do not say that of the Successors (al-tabi'un) (...).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Do not say: "I think he is a martyr." Say: "Whoever is killed in the way of Allah is a martyr."[[Narrated by Muslim (1915/165), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] As 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said. 'Umar addressed the people and said: "You say: so-and-so was martyred, and so-and-so is a martyr, when perhaps he did such-and-such. But say: 'Whoever is killed or dies in the way of Allah is a martyr.'"

* Student: How do we reconcile the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab with (...)?

* Shaykh: What is the contradiction?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: It agrees with the ruling of Allah, because he is speaking about the ruling of Allah, mighty and majestic.

* Student: (...) the caravan of Quraysh: that everyone who takes your wealth by force and usurpation (...) that one should do what the Prophet (ﷺ) did, or is it a special case?

* Shaykh: No, it is not special, if they are at war with us.

* Student: And outside of war?

* Shaykh: No. Outside of war, do not betray the one who betrayed you. But if they are at war with us, it is permissible for us to take their wealth.

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿O my people, today the kingdom is yours, dominant in the land. But who will support us against the might of Allah should it come upon us?" Pharaoh said, "I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct." (29) And the one who believed said, "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions (30), like the custom of the people of Noah and 'Ad and Thamud and those after them. And Allah does not want injustice for His servants.﴾ [Ghafir 29–31]

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said, concerning the rest of the speech of the believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who delivered counsel to his people in His saying: ﴿And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾ [Ghafir 28]. Here we discuss what preceded:

His saying: ﴿And a man of believers from the family of Pharaoh who concealed his faith said﴾. How do you parse: ﴿who concealed his faith﴾?

* Student: It has two grammatical possibilities.

* Shaykh: Two possibilities are permitted. The first?

* Student: That it is a circumstantial clause (hal), or that it is a second attribute.

* Shaykh: A second attribute, or a third? A third.

How can it be a circumstantial clause when the word it describes is indefinite, and a circumstantial clause does not come from an indefinite noun?

* Student: We said: when an indefinite noun is described (...) the first with a description, whereas these descriptions (...) it is a circumstantial clause or an attribute.

* Shaykh: Well said, may Allah bless you.

Why did he conceal his faith, meaning he hid it?

* Student: Out of fear that they would kill him.

* Shaykh: Out of fear that they would kill him, because since they had threatened Musa with death, he feared for himself, so he concealed his faith.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there has come to you clear proofs from your Lord.﴾ What is meant by "clear proofs"?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: By the clear signs. Good. Signs of what?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Why did the signs come with Musa?

* Student: So that they would support him (...).

* Shaykh: Well said, correct.

Why did he say: ﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ and not say "all"?

* Student: Because the punishment in this world is not the whole punishment.

* Shaykh: What is meant is the punishment of this world, not the whole punishment.

Why did this alternation come in his saying "if he is" and "if he is," even though he believes that he is truthful?

* Student: First, as a matter of condescension toward the opponent. He believes in what he said, but as a matter of condescension and of distancing (...).

* Shaykh: Of silencing the opponent: that the situation does not leave it except in one of two states. Yes, good.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾ How did He negate guidance when He may guide such people?

* Student: The negated guidance is the guidance of tawfiq. As for the guidance of direction and instruction, it is for everyone.

* Shaykh: Good. Is there not among people one who is extravagant and a liar, whom Allah guided?

* Student: Yes, but this is not the usual case, because the arrogant one, Allah the Exalted may perhaps turn him toward guidance, since Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took revenge upon them﴾ [al-Zukhruf 55], and He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights away, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [al-An'am 110].

* Shaykh: That does not contradict it. Let us set this question aside. Pharaoh remained upon his disbelief until he perished. But others: a person may be an extravagant liar and then be guided.

* Student: That if Allah wants guidance for His servant, at the time of that guidance, extravagance and lying depart from him, and Allah guides him.

* Shaykh: That is: He does not guide one who is an extravagant liar as long as he remains in that state?

* Shaykh: This is the closest view: that what is meant is Pharaoh. Because we said earlier, yesterday, that the matter is either that he is an extravagant liar, so he cannot be guided, or that you are, so you cannot be guided. Another answer is that whoever Allah has decreed in eternity to be an extravagant liar will not be guided. We did not speak about this point yesterday. Therefore, you are excused for these many opinions you have put forward.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verses 27–28 (part 1 of 2):**

Allah, blessed and exalted, says: (﴿And Musa said﴾ to his people, when he had heard that, ﴿"I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord"﴾), and so on to the end. As for His words, (﴿And Musa said﴾ to his people, ﴿"I have sought refuge"﴾), directing the speech to the people of Musa is not correct. Rather, Musa said to Fir'awn, ﴿"I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord"﴾. This is if Fir'awn had said it to him face to face, meaning he said, ﴿"Leave me to kill Musa"﴾ to his face, and Musa then said, "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from you," but he said "from every arrogant one." However, if Fir'awn was speaking with his people and Musa heard that, then according to what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said, Musa, when he heard this, said, "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord." But the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that the first meaning is more correct: that he said it to Fir'awn when he said, ﴿"Leave me to kill Musa"﴾.

He says: ﴿"I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord"﴾. ﴿"ʿUdtu"﴾ (I have sought refuge) means "I have held fast to Allah," because seeking refuge in a thing is holding fast to it. The scholars said: it is said ʿiyadh and liyadh. The scholars said: the difference between ʿiyadh (seeking refuge) and liyadh (clinging for protection) is that liyadh is for what is hoped for, while ʿiyadh is for what is feared. They cited the verse of the poet on this:

*O You to whom I cling for what I hope from Him,*
*and from whom I seek refuge from what I fear—*
*No bone of people is mended, if You are the one who breaks it,*
*and they cannot break a bone that You have mended.*

So the meaning of ﴿"ʿudtu"﴾ is "I have held fast." ﴿"In my Lord and your Lord"﴾: this is the Lordship both general and specific. ﴿"My Lord"﴾ is a specific lordship, and ﴿"your Lord"﴾ is Allah's lordship over Fir'awn and his people, which is of the general lordship.

﴿"From every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning"﴾. This description applies entirely to Fir'awn: he was arrogant, tyrannical, transgressing, and haughty. The arrogant one is the one who elevates himself in pride above the truth and over the creation, because arrogance is either toward the truth or toward the people. This is due to the saying of the Prophet, ṣallā Allāh ʿalayhi wa-ālihi wa-sallam: "Arrogance is rejecting the truth (baṭr al-ḥaqq) and looking down on people (ghamṭ al-nās)." [Narrated by Muslim (91/147) from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him.] "Baṭr al-ḥaqq" means despising it and belittling it, and this is arrogance toward the truth. "Ghamṭ al-nās" means belittling people, and this is arrogance toward the creation. When a person's heart combines arrogance toward the creation and arrogance toward the truth, he is the one who is ruined, and we seek refuge in Allah.

As for His words, ﴿"who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning"﴾, it means the Day of Resurrection. He turned away from saying "the Day of Resurrection" to "the Day of Reckoning," because reckoning is more frightening than the Resurrection. When a person is told, "You will be called to account for what you did of good and evil," he will fear, be anxious, and go straight. The word "reckoning" was mentioned instead of "resurrection" because it is more intimidating, for when a person knows that he will be held accountable for his deeds, he will refrain from sins and carry out the commands.

﴿"And a believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who concealed his faith, said: 'Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?'"﴾ [Ghafir 28], and so on to the end.

When this believing man heard Fir'awn's threat to Musa with killing, he said that. Consider the context of the verse: ﴿"a believing man"﴾. He did not specify him by name, but said "a man" in concealment, because the aim is not to know the name; the aim is to know the matter. Specifying names is among the surplus of knowledge, meaning that if it is attained, that is good, and if it is not attained, it is of no importance.

﴿"A believing man from the family of Fir'awn"﴾. Believing in whom? In Allah. And perhaps we can also say he believed in Musa. ﴿"From the family of Fir'awn"﴾ may mean from his relatives, since the family of a person is his kin, and it may mean from his followers, since "family" (āl) is also used for followers. In either case, the man was not of the Children of Israel, but was from the people of Fir'awn, whether he was from his relatives or from his people who belonged to him.

As for the author's words, "It was said: he was his cousin," this is an opinion whose weakness the author indicated with the word "it was said." ﴿"Who concealed his faith"﴾ means he hid it and kept it secret out of fear for himself.

In His words, ﴿"a believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who concealed his faith"﴾, there are three descriptions: a believer, from the family of Fir'awn, and one who conceals his faith.

The grammarians have said: when an indefinite noun is described the first time, what follows it may be either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a descriptive adjective (ṣifah). On this basis, ﴿"from the family of Fir'awn"﴾ may be a circumstantial clause, and ﴿"who concealed his faith"﴾ a circumstantial clause. It may also be that ﴿"from the family of Fir'awn"﴾ is a second description and ﴿"who concealed his faith"﴾ is a circumstantial clause, or that ﴿"from the family of Fir'awn"﴾ is a second description and ﴿"who concealed his faith"﴾ is a third description. ﴿"Who concealed his faith"﴾ means he hid it from Fir'awn and his people.

﴿"Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'?"﴾ The interrogation here is for denunciation, meaning: how can you kill a man who has done nothing except say, ﴿"My Lord is Allah"﴾?! This is like His saying: ﴿"And they resented them only because they believed in Allah, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy"﴾ [al-Buruj 8].

As for His words, ﴿"because he says"﴾, the particle ﴿"an"﴾ here is verbal (maṣdariyyah) with the implied lām (of causation); this is why the commentator estimated it by saying: "i.e., because he says." On this basis, the ﴿"an"﴾ is stripped of the causative lām; that is, "because of his saying, 'My Lord is Allah,'" meaning "My Lord is Allah, not Fir'awn," while they regarded their lord to be Fir'awn.

﴿"And he has certainly brought you clear proofs from your Lord"﴾ (meaning: with manifest miracles). In ﴿"he has brought you with clear proofs"﴾, the bāʾ indicates accompaniment, and ﴿"clear proofs"﴾ is a description of an omitted noun. Its estimate, contrary to the author, is "ayāt" (signs): i.e., he brought you with clear signs, that is, manifest ones that indicate with decisive indication that he is a prophet.

﴿"And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; and if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you"﴾. This is called by the logicians *al-sabr wa al-taqsīm* (the method of elimination and division), because Musa is now either truthful or a liar. There is no level between truthfulness and falsehood, since he says he is the Messenger of Allah; so either he is truthful in this, or he is a liar. In any case, your believing him does not harm you. This is why he said, ﴿"And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie"﴾, meaning: upon him is the harm of his lie, and Allah will bring disgrace and shame upon him if he lied about Allah. Allah says: ﴿"Who is more unjust than one who lies against Allah and denies the truth when it comes to him?"﴾ [al-Zumar 32]. There are many verses with this meaning, and Allah, the Exalted, exposes his secret and shows his lie, so that the lie falls upon him.

﴿"And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you"﴾: ﴿"if he is truthful"﴾ in that he is a messenger, and you deny him, then some of what he promises you of punishment will strike you in this world hastily; likewise it will strike you in the Hereafter later. So now the danger falls on whom? The danger falls on him if he is a liar, and you will be safe. The danger falls on you if he is truthful, and he will be saved. There is no doubt that this is part of his sincere advice. This man, who descended with the family of Fir'awn to this lowering of speech, did not say that he was truthful, although he believed in him; but this is from the method of condescension (tanazzul). Here he said, ﴿"Will you kill a man"﴾, and did not say, "Will you kill Musa," in order to remove suspicion from himself, lest anyone think he knew Musa and was defending him out of acquaintance. Rather, he used the indefinite ﴿"a man"﴾ to make the matter ambiguous and to strongly conceal it.

﴿"Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar"﴾. ﴿"Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor"﴾, meaning one who exceeds the limit. ﴿"A liar"﴾, meaning one characterized by lying. Does this causal sentence refer to Musa or to Fir'awn? We say it is suitable for both: whoever is a transgressor and a liar, Allah does not guide him. This description applies to Fir'awn, does it not? He is a transgressor who exceeds the limit, a liar who claims what is not his; he said, ﴿"I am your most high lord"﴾, and he lied in that. So he is a transgressor and a liar. Likewise, in the context of argument and condescension, it also applies to Musa if he were a liar, for then he would be a transgressor exceeding the limit in claiming prophethood while lying, and also a liar, because he claimed what he was not truthful about. In any case, the sentence here is suitable to apply to Fir'awn, and it applies in reality, or to Musa by way of condescension toward the opponent.

* In this verse and the one before it there are benefits. Among them: the strength and frankness of Musa, peace be upon him, in that he declared before those who threatened him with death that he had sought refuge in Allah, his Lord and theirs, as in His words: ﴿"I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord"﴾.

* Among them: the strength of his reliance (tawakkul), peace be upon him, in that he depended on Allah before this tyrant who could easily carry out what he threatened.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the description of Fir'awn with these two blameworthy traits: arrogance, and that he does not believe in the Day of Reckoning.

* Among its benefits: the turn to generality rather than specificity, because he did not say, "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from Fir'awn," but said, "from every arrogant one," so that it includes Fir'awn and others besides him.

* Among its benefits as well: when it comes in the form of generality and by description, it applies to Fir'awn and shows that he is characterized by arrogance, and likewise disbelief in the Day of Reckoning.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the Day of Reckoning, which is the Day of Resurrection. And reckoning is not the scrutinizing of a person for his deeds, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever is scrutinized in reckoning will be punished." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6536) and Muslim (2876/79) from the hadith of ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her.] This is because if Allah were to scrutinize you, one of His blessings would cover all the good deeds you have done. Indeed, the good deeds you have done are a blessing from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which require thanks. Then, if you are enabled to thank for them, you need another thanks for being enabled to thank, and so on indefinitely. This is why the poet said:

*If my thanks is a blessing from Allah,*
*upon me, for it, thanks is obligatory in turn.*
*How can thanks be fulfilled except by His favor,*
*even if the days are prolonged and life continues?*

This is true. Reckoning means that Allah, the Exalted, meets His servant, the believer, alone and makes him acknowledge his sins, saying: "You did such and such; you did such and such." When he acknowledges, He says: "I concealed them for you in the world, and I forgive them for you today." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52) from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both.] As for the disbelievers, they are not reckoned in the manner of one whose good and bad deeds are weighed, because they have no good deeds. Rather, their deeds are counted, they are made to stand before them, and they are disgraced by them, meaning they are humiliated by them. It is said: ﴿"These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers"﴾ [Hud 18]. This is the reckoning of the disbelievers, and that is the reckoning of the believers.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿"And a believing man"﴾ [Ghafir 28], and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that attention should be paid to the content of the story rather than to the identity of the person it concerns, as shown by His words: ﴿"a believing man"﴾. Otherwise, we know that Allah knows who this man is, knows his name and lineage and everything related to him. But Allah mentioned him indefinitely, indicating that what matters is the content of the story, not the identity of the person it happened to, unless there is a benefit in specifying him, in which case the benefit is to mention and specify him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the most hostile enemies there may be one who is among the friends of Allah, as His words here show: ﴿"from the family of Fir'awn"﴾. Whether we say he was from his relatives or from his followers in his religion, it indicates that Allah is powerful over all things, and that He may facilitate or prepare faith for one who is among a people immersed in disbelief.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of concealing faith when a person fears for himself, as shown by His words: ﴿"who concealed his faith"﴾. But if a person cannot live as a believer except by concealment, is emigration (hijrah) obligatory upon him?

The answer: yes. In the religion of Islam, whoever cannot live openly practicing his religion is obligated to emigrate, but on the condition that he is able to do so. If he is incapable, Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿"Except the oppressed among men, women, and children who are not able to devise a plan nor are they guided to a way. For those, it is expected that Allah will pardon them, and Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving"﴾ [al-Nisa 98–99].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the severity of this believer's denunciation of Fir'awn, who threatened to kill, as shown by His words: ﴿"Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'?"﴾

* Among its benefits: denunciation of one who does an action without a cause that calls for it. From where is this taken? From ﴿"Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'?"﴾ This is not a cause for killing. At the very least, he should be left alone. As for being killed for this reason, this is objectionable and it is not permissible to approve of it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: avoiding specifying a name out of fear of accusation, or, if you wish, say: the use of ambiguous speech (maʿārīḍ), as shown by His words: ﴿"Will you kill a man"﴾, and he did not say, "Will you kill Musa." Because if he had named him, people would have accused him of having a connection to him, and what he intended would have been ruined. But he left him unspecified and said: ﴿"Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'?"﴾ and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Musa, peace be upon him, brought clear signs of the kind by which people believe, as shown by His words: ﴿"And he has certainly brought you clear proofs from your Lord"﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strength of this man's faith, in that he confronted these people by implicitly denying Fir'awn's lordship. From where? From His words: ﴿"from your Lord"﴾. He confronted them with the fact that they have a lord other than Fir'awn, and this shows the strength of this man. As for His words, ﴿"because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'"﴾, there is no proof in it, because the lordship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, over Musa contains nothing of denial. But ﴿"from your Lord"﴾ is clear that he is alluding that Fir'awn is not a lord, and that the Lord is Allah. This shows the perfect courage of this man.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the use of *al-sabr wa al-taqsīm*, meaning alternating between two states or several states beyond which the matter does not go, as shown by His words: ﴿"And if he is a liar"﴾ and ﴿"and if he is truthful"﴾.

* Among its benefits, that is, the benefits of the verse: consideration of the opponent in what one says and in bringing him closer, because he began with what they believed, which was that Musa was a liar, and began with the lie before beginning with the truth, for the sake of winning them over and showing that the man had no partisanship for Musa. This is why he did not begin with the truth, which is one of the two possibilities.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of equivocation (tawriyah), as shown by His words: ﴿"And if he is a liar"﴾ and His words: ﴿"And if he is truthful"﴾. For we know that this man believed that he was truthful, but he spoke this way as an equivocation that he did not believe in him, and this was for the sake of having his words accepted, because if they had perceived that he believed, they would have killed him. He believed in Musa while being one of their own family, but he used words indicating equivocation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the evil consequence of lying returns to the liar, and so it is, as shown by His words: ﴿"And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie"﴾. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has exposed those who lie and fabricate against Him in this world, and He will expose them in the Hereafter.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strength of this man's faith, in that he believed and was certain that some of what Musa, peace be upon him, promised them would strike them if he was truthful, and they had denied him, as shown by His words: ﴿"And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you"﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verses 27–28 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the one who is extravagant (musrif) and a habitual liar (kadhdhab), that is, one who exceeds the limits in his deeds and in his words (in his words because he is a liar, and in his deeds because he is extravagant), is far from guidance. This is because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾

Here we ask: does the meaning refer to guidance of tawfiq (divine enabling and granting of success) or guidance of bayan (explanation) and irshad (direction)? It is the guidance of tawfiq. Allah the Exalted has made clear the truth to the extravagant liar and to others, but He grants success to whom He wills of His servants and forsakes whom He wills. And Allah knows best.

* Student: His saying: ﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ (...).

* Shaykh: Because he said: ﴿some of what he promises you﴾, meaning in this world. For this reason the commentator specified it by saying: (the immediate punishment).

* Student: Regarding the believer: was he from the family of Pharaoh, or from the Children of Israel?

* Shaykh: Not from the family of Pharaoh, clearly. But is he a relative of his, or one who follows him in his religion?

* Student: (...) the ma'arid (allusive or indirect speech)?

* Shaykh: Ma'arid means that you speak in a way that conceals your meaning by using something contrary to the reality (tawriyah).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: That is, it is as if he is saying: when is ma'arid permissible?

Ma'arid is permissible when there is a benefit in it or when it averts a harm. The use of ma'arid takes three forms:

The first form: oppression (zulm).
The second: averting oppression.
The third: what involves neither of these.

Oppression is when a person uses ma'arid to avoid a right he owes. Averting oppression is when he uses ma'arid to repel injustice from himself. What is neither of these, such as using it in permissible matters.

An example of the first: Zayd and 'Amr dispute before a judge. 'Amr owes Zayd one hundred dirhams. The judge says to the claimant: "Do you have evidence?" He says: "No." The judge says: "Then you have the right to make the other party swear." So the defendant says: "By Allah, I have nothing of his." The apparent wording is a denial, but in his heart he intended affirmation, and he intended by "má" (what) the relative meaning "that which," so the sentence in his intention reads: "By Allah, that which he has is with me." This is true, he does have something of his with him, but he used tawriyah by making "má" a negation, meaning he has nothing. The judge will rule according to what? According to the apparent sense, that it is a negation. This ma'arid we say is haram, because he used it to bring about the loss of a right owed to another.

Likewise, in a claim: if his opponent says: "I am content with you swearing that you have something of mine," and he swears while using tawriyah, then it is haram for him.

As for averting oppression, it is like swearing to repel injustice from oneself or from another. An example: a thief or an oppressive soldier enters upon a man wanting to take his wealth, and says: "Open this chest for me." He says: "By Allah, there is nothing in this chest." The addressee will think the statement is a denial and be satisfied, while he intends affirmation. This tawriyah, there is no doubt about its permissibility. Indeed, if the property belongs to someone else, such as when a person comes and says: "So-and-so has such-and-such with you." I say: "By Allah, I have nothing of his," knowing that if I informed him, he would take it (...).

He says: the disaster (al-da'irah) belongs to Allah and His Messenger. These people were three hundred and some men, and they were the people of Badr. Allah looked upon them and rewarded them with a reward not granted to others. He looked upon them and said: "Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you." This great virtue erased all the misdeeds they might commit. This campaign benefited even whoever participated in it, including Hatib, may Allah be pleased with him, who wrote news of the Prophet (ﷺ) to the Quraysh shortly before the conquest of Mecca. When what he had done was discovered, 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "Let me strike his neck, for he has become a hypocrite." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was a man of the sword, courageous. He (ﷺ) said: "Do you not know that Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: 'Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you'?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4890) and Muslim (2494/161), from the hadith of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and its wording: "Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you."]] So this great misdeed fell among what is forgiven for the people of Badr. For this reason the people of Badr were superior to the people of the Pledge of Ridwan (bay'at al-Ridwan), superior because of the great support they gave the Prophet (ﷺ). For this reason the day of Badr is called the Day of the Criterion (yawm al-Furqan).

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. If someone says: what is meant by the angels fighting alongside the believers at Badr? It is known that the angels are enormous in form, so one of them suffices with a single strike (...) the polytheists?

* Shaykh: It is also known that if Allah had said to those disbelievers: "Be dead," they would have died. The matter is not one of inability or ability. The descent of the angels was to strengthen the hearts of the believers, and their participation was a form of support for the believers and the victory of truth. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is so. And had Allah willed, He would have defeated them, but [He sets them against one another] so that He may test some of you by means of others.﴾ [Muhammad 4]

* Student: What is the evidence for testifying that they are in Paradise?

* Shaykh: The evidence: if the Messenger testifies that someone is in Paradise, we testify for him.

* Student: (...) and you said: they, as individuals, are among the people of Paradise (...)?

* Shaykh: Generally, except for one whom the Messenger testified for, such as Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah. We say of him that he is forgiven. But there is no doubt that if Hatib is forgiven, then Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman are more deserving of that.

* Student: What is your opinion regarding what Shaykh al-Islam (...) held?

* Shaykh: By Allah, this is a strong opinion, without doubt. That is, what Shaykh al-Islam held is supported by the hadith: "You are the witnesses of Allah on earth."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1367) and Muslim (949/60), from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him.]] When the community, or most of the community, agrees on this, it is sufficient. Were it not for a problem: the people of deviant sects would come to us and say: "We are unanimous in testifying that so-and-so is [righteous], and he is the head of an innovation," and they claim that they are the people of truth. But this objection can be avoided by saying: their testimony is not accepted, because they are upon falsehood and misguidance, and what is meant is the testimony of the people of truth.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, in general, all of them are in Paradise. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those of you who spent and fought before the conquest are not equal [to those who did so later]. Those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. But to each Allah has promised the best.﴾ [al-Hadid 10]

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, we do not say that of the Successors (al-tabi'un) (...).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Do not say: "I think he is a martyr." Say: "Whoever is killed in the way of Allah is a martyr."[[Narrated by Muslim (1915/165), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] As 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said. 'Umar addressed the people and said: "You say: so-and-so was martyred, and so-and-so is a martyr, when perhaps he did such-and-such. But say: 'Whoever is killed or dies in the way of Allah is a martyr.'"

* Student: How do we reconcile the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab with (...)?

* Shaykh: What is the contradiction?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: It agrees with the ruling of Allah, because he is speaking about the ruling of Allah, mighty and majestic.

* Student: (...) the caravan of Quraysh: that everyone who takes your wealth by force and usurpation (...) that one should do what the Prophet (ﷺ) did, or is it a special case?

* Shaykh: No, it is not special, if they are at war with us.

* Student: And outside of war?

* Shaykh: No. Outside of war, do not betray the one who betrayed you. But if they are at war with us, it is permissible for us to take their wealth.

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿O my people, today the kingdom is yours, dominant in the land. But who will support us against the might of Allah should it come upon us?" Pharaoh said, "I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct." (29) And the one who believed said, "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions (30), like the custom of the people of Noah and 'Ad and Thamud and those after them. And Allah does not want injustice for His servants.﴾ [Ghafir 29–31]

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said, concerning the rest of the speech of the believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who delivered counsel to his people in His saying: ﴿And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾ [Ghafir 28]. Here we discuss what preceded:

His saying: ﴿And a man of believers from the family of Pharaoh who concealed his faith said﴾. How do you parse: ﴿who concealed his faith﴾?

* Student: It has two grammatical possibilities.

* Shaykh: Two possibilities are permitted. The first?

* Student: That it is a circumstantial clause (hal), or that it is a second attribute.

* Shaykh: A second attribute, or a third? A third.

How can it be a circumstantial clause when the word it describes is indefinite, and a circumstantial clause does not come from an indefinite noun?

* Student: We said: when an indefinite noun is described (...) the first with a description, whereas these descriptions (...) it is a circumstantial clause or an attribute.

* Shaykh: Well said, may Allah bless you.

Why did he conceal his faith, meaning he hid it?

* Student: Out of fear that they would kill him.

* Shaykh: Out of fear that they would kill him, because since they had threatened Musa with death, he feared for himself, so he concealed his faith.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there has come to you clear proofs from your Lord.﴾ What is meant by "clear proofs"?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: By the clear signs. Good. Signs of what?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Why did the signs come with Musa?

* Student: So that they would support him (...).

* Shaykh: Well said, correct.

Why did he say: ﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ and not say "all"?

* Student: Because the punishment in this world is not the whole punishment.

* Shaykh: What is meant is the punishment of this world, not the whole punishment.

Why did this alternation come in his saying "if he is" and "if he is," even though he believes that he is truthful?

* Student: First, as a matter of condescension toward the opponent. He believes in what he said, but as a matter of condescension and of distancing (...).

* Shaykh: Of silencing the opponent: that the situation does not leave it except in one of two states. Yes, good.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾ How did He negate guidance when He may guide such people?

* Student: The negated guidance is the guidance of tawfiq. As for the guidance of direction and instruction, it is for everyone.

* Shaykh: Good. Is there not among people one who is extravagant and a liar, whom Allah guided?

* Student: Yes, but this is not the usual case, because the arrogant one, Allah the Exalted may perhaps turn him toward guidance, since Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took revenge upon them﴾ [al-Zukhruf 55], and He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights away, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [al-An'am 110].

* Another student: Here the extravagance and the lying are unrestricted, so they are taken to mean the greatest extravagance, which is disbelief.
