* Shaykh: Yes, that does not contradict it. But Allah says: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide﴾, although Allah has guided peoples who were extravagant liars?

* Student: Yes, but it is in its general sense: if a person persists in it, meaning unrestricted extravagance or unrestricted lying, which is disbelief, then if he remains in his extravagance and his lying, he is deprived of guidance. But if he repents and returns, Allah the Exalted will guide him.

* Another student: (...) upon the negation of perfection (...).

* Another student: The point here in the verse is that this man either was condescending toward Pharaoh, thereby intending Musa, for if he was a liar, then Allah does not guide him. Or he intended the truth, and by this he intended Pharaoh, and that Pharaoh is the arrogant one (...).

* Shaykh: That does not contradict it. Let us set this question aside. Pharaoh remained upon his disbelief until he perished. But others: a person may be an extravagant liar and then be guided.

* Student: That if Allah wants guidance for His servant, at the time of that guidance, extravagance and lying depart from him, and Allah guides him.

* Shaykh: That is: He does not guide one who is an extravagant liar as long as he remains in that state?

* Student: This is a general statement intended in a specific sense, meaning Pharaoh.

* Shaykh: This is the closest view: that what is meant is Pharaoh. Because we said earlier, yesterday, that the matter is either that he is an extravagant liar, so he cannot be guided, or that you are, so you cannot be guided. Another answer is that whoever Allah has decreed in eternity to be an extravagant liar will not be guided. We did not speak about this point yesterday. Therefore, you are excused for these many opinions you have put forward.

We recite the new lesson: ﴿O my people, today the kingdom is yours, dominant in the land﴾ [Ghafir 29]. Consider the fine manner of this man's address. Earlier he had denounced them: ﴿Will you kill a man merely for saying, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ But when he wished to win their affection and to show them God's blessing upon them, he spoke to them gently, saying: ﴿O my people,﴾ as though he were one of them. This gentleness in addressing people in the matter of da'wah (calling to Islam) is among the things that God has commanded by sacred law (shar'an), and through which God guides whom He wills of His servants by divine decree (qadaran). God said to Moses and Aaron: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed. Then speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will be reminded or fear.﴾ [Ta-Ha 43-44].

Moreover, divine decree (qadar) confirms this. How many a person has softened because of gentle speech, and how many a person has been provoked into aggression because of harsh speech. For this reason you find that this man, in his wisdom, when they threatened to kill Moses, denounced them openly: ﴿Will you kill a man merely for saying, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ But when he wished to explain the blessings to them and call them to the truth, he said: ﴿O my people, today the kingdom is yours, dominant in the land,﴾ meaning: overpowering and exalted over its people. His words ﴿today the kingdom is yours﴾ mean: today you are the possessors. Consider also the fine caution in this address: ﴿today the kingdom is yours,﴾ meaning: the future is unknown; your kingship may cease. But today you are in blessing, dominant in the land and prevailing over its people, so you must thank God for this blessing.

As for His words ﴿in the land,﴾ the mufassir (commentator) said: "the land of Egypt." On this reading, the definite article in "al-ardi" (the land) is of mental reference (al-'ahd al-dhihni), meaning: the land known to you, your land.

(﴿Who then will help us against the might of Allah﴾, His punishment, ﴿if it comes upon us﴾.) ﴿Who will help us﴾: the word ﴿man﴾ here is interrogative in meaning of negation, that is: no one will help us. The word "naṣr" (help) here means "prevention," that is: who is it that will prevent us from the might of Allah? And "ba's" (might) means punishment.

His words ﴿if it comes upon us﴾ mean: if it descends upon us. Will anyone then help us? Even if we are today dominant in the land and are kings, when the might of Allah descends upon us, no one will prevent us.

As for the mufassir's statement: "if you kill His allies," it may be said that what the mufassir specified is indicated by the context, since he denounced them for wanting to kill Moses. It may also be said that what is meant is: if you remain upon disbelief and transgression, of which the killing of Moses is a part. This is more correct and more comprehensive. That is, what will help us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us, since we deserve this punishment for disbelief and for killing His allies.

Pharaoh said in reply to this man: ﴿I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct.﴾ This is the most lying statement on earth. ﴿I show you only what I see﴾ means: I reveal to you nothing except what I see to be the truth. This is a false claim, for he knows that the truth lies in following Moses, as Moses said to him: ﴿You know that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear proofs, and I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed.﴾ [al-Isra' 102]. And He, exalted, said: ﴿They denied them wrongfully and arrogantly, though their souls were convinced of them.﴾ [al-Naml 14]. So he says: ﴿I show you only what I see,﴾ that is: I see only what is right and true, and this claim is false.

If, however, he meant: "I show you only what I see to be in my own interest," then this is true but deceitful. In any case the sentence is blameworthy, for it is either a lie or deception: a lie if he means "I show you only what I see to be right," or deception if he sees the truth to be other than what he showed them, but for his own benefit he showed them what he did not see.

The mufassir said: its meaning is "I advise you only what I advise myself, namely the killing of Moses." This too is a restriction out of place, for Pharaoh was not concerned whether they said "Kill Moses" or "Do not kill him," since he was determined upon what he wanted. But the most important thing for him was that they not disbelieve in him, and that his religion not be changed. On this basis, the intended meaning of his words ﴿except what I see﴾ concerns your remaining upon your religion. This is the meaning of the verse, since the root of the denunciation of Moses and the threat to kill him was that he feared the religion would be changed.

He said: ﴿I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct,﴾ meaning: I direct you only to the path of right conduct. Right conduct (rushd) is the opposite of error (ghayy); for this reason it is said: rushd and ghayy. ﴿The right path has become clear from error﴾ [al-Baqarah 256], meaning the correct and sound. "Sabil" means "path" or "way." Is he truthful in this or lying? He is the most lying of liars, for he does not guide them to the path of right conduct, but rather guides them to the path of error, arrogance, stubbornness and disbelief. Thus he is lying in both sentences: ﴿I show you only what I see,﴾ if we say the meaning is "except what I see to be right," and ﴿I guide you only to the path of right conduct,﴾ which is also a lie, for without doubt he guides them to the path of error and corruption.

* In this verse: the fine address of this believing man when he was gentle in calling to God, the Mighty and Majestic, in his words ﴿O my people.﴾

* Among its benefits: the caller should remind those he calls of God's blessing upon them, so that they may submit and thank for this blessing, as in His words ﴿today the kingdom is yours, dominant in the land.﴾

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the fine caution of this believing man, as in His words ﴿today the kingdom is yours,﴾ meaning: as for the future, your kingship may cease, but be thankful for the present blessing.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the consideration in the present is based on what things are now, whereas the future may change. Yet we are addressed and commanded to look to the present state now.

From this matter there branches a social question: some people have a daughter proposed to by a man who is not upright, meaning not a disbeliever but a sinner, such as one who smokes tobacco, shaves his beard, deals in usury, or the like. Greed takes hold of them and they accept the proposal, then say: "Perhaps Allah will guide him," or "Perhaps this committed girl will strive for his guidance." It is said in reply: we do not look to the future; the future belongs to Allah. Indeed, perhaps this man will seduce the woman, since he is stronger than she in his position. So you are now commanded to look to the present state, while as for the future you are not commanded to look to it, and it is not permissible for you to look to it, since it is an unseen future. So know now the condition you are in and act according to what it is now. We take this from the words of this believing man: ﴿today.﴾

And know that when I say: "the fine address of this man," or "his cautions," or the like, I do not mean that I am telling you about a past story and a bygone history. No. I want you to take from it a lesson to follow, for as long as we praise this man for his address and his handling of affairs, it means that we urge following his way.

So know now the condition you are in, and act according to what it is now. We take this from the words of the believing man: "today." And know that when I say: "the fine address of this man," or "his cautions," or the like, I do not mean that I am telling you about a past story and a bygone history. No, I want you to take from it a lesson to follow, for as long as we praise this man for his address and his handling of affairs, it means that we urge following his way.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the family of Pharaoh had prevailed in Egypt and dominated it, with no rival, as in His words ﴿dominant in the land﴾ [Ghafir 29]. Hence Pharaoh became arrogant and did not submit to Moses, since Moses was from the Children of Israel, who were a small and humiliated people in Egypt, while the dominance belonged to the Copts.

* Among its benefits: dominance and victory may be a cause of insolence and exultation, except for one whom Allah has granted success. Some people, when Allah gives them a means of elevation, it only increases them in humility toward truth and toward people. Other people, when Allah gives them elevation, it becomes a cause of their exalting themselves over people and being arrogant toward truth. This is a trial in which a person must treat himself. Do not, when Allah gives you wealth, become proud, overbearing and arrogant, for He who gave you this wealth is able to destroy it for you. Nor should one who has been given knowledge by Allah say: "I am a scholar, and who am I?" and then exalt himself over truth and over people. Rather, a person must, each time Allah gives him knowledge, increase in humility.

This is what I say, and I hope that I and you will be characterized by it. A person must know this matter, that Allah may test a person with something that may be a cause of his exaltation and arrogance toward truth and toward people, so let him beware of this matter.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strength of this man's faith, and that nothing repels or prevents what Allah wills, as in His words ﴿Who then will help us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?﴾ [Ghafir 29]. This shows the perfection of his certainty, may Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him, in that he believed that when the might of Allah comes, there is no repelling it.

* Among its benefits also: gentleness in address so that the one addressed feels as though he is the first one meant by this matter or this address, as in His words ﴿Who then will help us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?﴾ He did not say: "Who will help you against the might of Allah if it comes upon you?" All of this is from the method of condescension with these people and making them feel that he is one of them. It may also be said that in this there is an indication that when punishment descends it encompasses the righteous and the corrupt, and his words ﴿Who then will help us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?﴾ may be meant literally, that is: he himself will be struck by what struck them. Its evidence is the saying of Allah, exalted: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike only those among you who have wronged in particular﴾ [al-Anfal 25]. This is not far-fetched.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that when the might of Allah descends, there is no repelling it. This is supported by the saying of Allah, exalted: ﴿So when they saw Our might they said, "We believe in Allah alone and disbelieve in what we had been associating with Him." But their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might.﴾ [Ghafir 84-85].

Is anyone excepted from this?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, the righteous is righteous.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No. I ask you: have you travelled?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: The point is that it must not be merely the distance for shortening the prayer.

* Student: The people of Yunus.

* Shaykh: Yes, the people of Yunus. ﴿Why was there not a city which believed, so that its faith benefited it?﴾ [Yunus 98], meaning when the punishment had descended upon it. ﴿Except the people of Yunus: when they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace﴾ [Yunus 98]. And why were the people of Yunus singled out? For a wisdom, since Allah, mighty and majestic, cannot single out anyone with something except for a wisdom. People are equal in His sight: ﴿Indeed the most honorable of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat 13].

The wisdom is that Yunus, peace be upon him, left his people in anger before he was given permission, as though he had not completed the da'wah, so the full proof had not been established against them. For this reason they were saved when they believed after seeing the punishment. Their deliverance became a wisdom, namely the departure of their prophet in anger before he was given permission. It is as though he had not completed establishing the proof against them, so there became in this a kind of excuse for them, and Allah, mighty and majestic, saved them.

A verse always raises a difficulty for me when I read it, and I say: how can this be? Nuh said to his people: ﴿He will forgive you of your sins and delay you until a specified term. Indeed the term of Allah, when it comes, is not delayed﴾ [Nuh 4]. How did he say that if they believe, He will forgive them of their sins and delay them until a specified term, then say: ﴿Indeed the term of Allah, when it comes, is not delayed﴾? Initially he said: ﴿and delay you until a term,﴾ and then he said: ﴿Indeed the term of Allah, when it comes, is not delayed.﴾

* Student: By supposition: if you disbelieve, then indeed the term of Allah is not delayed; if you deny...

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever wishes to have his provision expanded for him and his life extended..."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5986), and Muslim (2557/21), from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, and its wording: "Whoever loves to have his provision expanded and his life extended, let him keep the ties of kinship."]].

* Shaykh: Yes, that is not it.

* Student: (...) when it comes, the punishment is not delayed...

* Shaykh: Yes, correct. That is, I warn you of the punishment, for when it comes it is not delayed. But if you believe, He will delay you until a specified term. On this basis there is no contradiction in the verse. Yes.

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Pharaoh said﴾ and so on. In this sentence and what follows is evidence of Pharaoh's deception, his fraud, his lying and his misguidance, for he deceived his people with his words: ﴿I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾ [Ghafir 29]. He lied in his words ﴿and I guide you only to the path of right conduct,﴾ definitely, and he lied in his words ﴿I show you only what I see﴾ on one of the two possible meanings.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that people of falsehood may have ornamented speech that is deceptive, since such a leader, whose leadership has reached the point that they made him a lord, will without doubt deceive his people when he says: ﴿I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct.﴾ On this basis we must beware of the deception of some people. When they say: "We want such-and-such, and such-and-such reform," we must look at their actions. Do their actions testify to their words? If so, they are truthful and righteous. If it is the opposite, they are liars and deceivers, deceiving with ornamented speech.

For this reason, the person who has insight does not get deceived by the outward appearance of statements, but measures what is said, or judges what is said by what is done. If he sees that their actions contradict their words, he knows that they are liars and deceivers. If he sees that their actions confirm their words, they become truthful, and he becomes sincere, since their inner state agrees with their outward state.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that every person knows that right conduct is sought and error is hated. From where is this taken?

* Student: ﴿I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾: Pharaoh and his people.

* Shaykh: The second sentence or the first?

* Student: The second.

* Shaykh: The second. So they know that right conduct is something sought. Every person, even the disbeliever, sees that right conduct is sought. But what is true right conduct? Is it following desire or following guidance? The second: following guidance. But the deception is a problem.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 30–31 (part 1 of 5):

Then He said: ﴿And said a man of believers, from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, "Would you kill a man for saying, 'My Lord is Allah'..."﴾ [Ghafir 28]. Here He says: ﴿And said the one who believed﴾ [Ghafir 30]. Why was this description of this man repeated? Because of the length of the speech and the separation between them. As for the difference between the two clauses, the second one emphasizes the first: this man was steeped in faith and fulfilled faith.

﴿And said the one who believed, "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions"﴾ [Ghafir 30]. "O my people": he means Pharaoh and his people, and this is a form of gentleness in speech. ﴿Indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions﴾ means: the earlier groups. It is as if this inspired man had knowledge of the conditions of the earlier nations, and the discussion of the benefit of this clause will come, God willing.

﴿Like the day of the factions﴾ means a day of one faction after another. Then he substituted for it His words: ﴿like the custom of the people of Noah﴾ [Ghafir 31]. Da'b (دأب) means custom or habit. The people of Noah were mentioned because he was the first messenger sent to the inhabitants of the earth. ﴿And of 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Ghafir 31]. All of these are early peoples, distant in time, before Musa and before Pharaoh; they are among the first messengers.

﴿The people of Noah and 'Ad﴾: (ʿĀd) is coordinated with what?
* Students: With "people" (qawm).
* The Shaykh: With "people." It is not valid for it to be coordinated with "Noah," because if it were coordinated with "Noah" the meaning would be "like the people of 'Ad," and the sentence would not be sound. Rather it means "like 'Ad," who were the people of Hud, and Thamud were the people of Salih.

﴿And those after them﴾ [Ghafir 31]: from the nations. It will come that he pointed to Yusuf, peace be upon him, son of Ya'qub, son of Ibrahim.

He says: "(Like) is a substitute for the 'like' before it, meaning: like the requital of the custom of those who disbelieved before you, of their punishment in this world." So "like da'b" is what, "like their custom"? Unless it is intended to be a construct with the object, i.e., like the custom that Allah inflicted upon them. But it seems the author made it a construct with the subject and that it is in the sense of "like the requital of their custom," because the requital is from Allah, and the custom is from these peoples, the factions. The custom is the custom of the factions, and the punishment is the punishment of Allah. So either we say the speech is in the sense of "like the punishment of the custom of the people of Noah," and so on, or we say "like the custom of the people of Noah," i.e., like the custom that Allah did to them. The meaning is one. The intent is that he fears for them days like these, which are punishment for those who denied their messengers.

﴿And Allah does not intend injustice for the servants﴾ [Ghafir 31]. Ma (ما) is a negation that operates like laysa (ليس) because the conditions are complete, and the name of Allah is its subject, and "yurid" (يريد) is a clause that is its predicate. Had it been a noun, the sentence would be: "and not Allah intending..." Injustice (ظلم) encompasses two things: either an increase in sins or a decrease in good deeds. Both are impossible with respect to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It cannot occur from Him, and He cannot intend it, why? Because of His perfect justice.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the intensity of this man's fear of Allah's punishment, and this indicates the completeness of his faith, because no one fears something unless he believes in it.
* Among its benefits: this man had knowledge of the news of the earlier peoples, as shown by His words: ﴿like the day of the factions (30) like the custom of the people of Noah﴾ [Ghafir 30, 31] to the end.
* Among its benefits: a person should have knowledge of the conditions of the earlier nations so that he may take warning from those who passed concerning those who remain. Accordingly, the knowledge of history is an important science, but we must know that history has been subject to some fabrication (wad'), i.e., distortion, alteration, lies, addition, and omission, so a person must be careful in this, so that he does not transmit or narrate except what is sound.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud were the first factions, as shown by His words: ﴿And those after them﴾ [Ghafir 31].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the negation of the intention of injustice from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as shown by His words: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice﴾ [Ghafir 31]. When the intention is negated, the act is certainly negated, because Allah does what He wills; so if He does not intend injustice, injustice does not occur.

However, in other verses He negated injustice itself, saying: ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ [al-Kahf 49], and He said: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat 46], and He said: ﴿The word is not changed with Me, and I am not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Qaf 29]. Thus Allah negated injustice from Himself and negated the intention of injustice, and that is because of His perfect justice.

This attribute is among those that they call the negative attributes (al-sifat al-salbiyyah) or the negated attributes. We have a principle in the chapter on the names and attributes: pure negation (al-nafy al-mahd) is never found in the attributes of Allah. Every negation in the attributes of Allah includes two things: one, the negation of what is negated from Allah, and the second, the affirmation of the perfection of its opposite. So it is said: He does not wrong, because of His perfect justice. Or if you wish, say: because of His perfect justice, He does not wrong, since if his justice were not perfect he might wrong in some matters. As for the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, His justice is perfect; injustice cannot enter it in any way.

Is this injustice that is negated from Allah for the sake of perfect justice impossible in its essence, or is it permissible but impossible for Allah because of His perfection?
* Students: The second.
* The Shaykh: The second, in contrast to the Jahmiyyah, who said that injustice is impossible for Allah in the essence of injustice, because if it were impossible in its essence it would not be praise, since one is not praised for what is impossible for him. They say it is impossible in its essence because all creatures are His possession, and He acts in His possession as He wills, and one who acts in his own possession is not called unjust even if he gives priority to one thing over another or diminishes something from its due right. But we say: Allah, the Most High, has explicitly declared that He has forbidden injustice to Himself, and this indicates that injustice concerning Him is rationally possible, but He forbade it to Himself because of His perfect justice.

The conclusion: among the principles of the names and attributes is that pure negation is not found in the attributes of Allah; rather no negation is found in the attributes of Allah except for the perfection of its opposite: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qaf 38]. Why? Because of His perfect power, not because fatigue does not reach Him. Rather, because of His perfect power, fatigue cannot reach Him. The meaning is not that it is not among what could reach Him; no, it is impossible because of His perfect power.

The scholars said: We only say this because pure negation is pure nonexistence. Is that correct or not? Pure negation: if you negate something, it means it is not existent, and pure nonexistence is not a thing, let alone praise, because it is nonexistence, and nonexistence is not praised.

Or the negation includes an affirmation, and this affirmation may be a deficiency. For example, if we say: "So-and-so does not wrong," because he is unable to wrong, this does not mean we have praised him; rather this is a blame of him, like the poet's saying:

A tribe that does not betray a covenant, and does not wrong people even by a mustard seed.

When you first hear this speech you say: "Masha'Allah, these are faithful, just people." But in reality it is a blame. He says: none of them is able to betray, and none is able to wrong. And the second says:

"But my people, though they are many in number, are not in any evil, and if they are wronged, they respond with forgiveness; and if the people of evil wrong them, they respond with kindness."

He means that if a person wrongs them, they treat him well, and if someone harms them, they forgive him and overlook it. But is it because of their perfect kindness and perfect forgiveness, or because of their weakness? Because of their weakness. Hence he said:

"Would that I had in their place a people who, when they ride, launch raids as horsemen and as riders."

"Would that I had in their place": i.e., instead of them. This shows that he blamed them greatly.

The negation may also be because the attribute is not suitable for what is negated from them: a negation of a thing from a thing because it is not receptive or suitable to be described by it. As when you say: "The wall does not wrong." Is that praise of the wall?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: Why?
* The student: Because it is not suitable, nor...
* The Shaykh: Because it is neither receptive nor suitable for injustice or non-injustice. Thus it becomes clear that Allah, the Most High, negates from Himself nothing except for the perfection of the opposite of that negated thing, not because it is not receptive to it or not suitable in His case, or anything similar in the rational sense.

﴿And Allah does not intend injustice for the servants﴾ [Ghafir 31]. So from this we derive the negation of the intention of injustice from Allah because of His perfect justice.

(...)
* Student: Shaykh, how did we deduce from the verse that it refers to Yusuf?
* The Shaykh: It is mentioned in this: he will say: ﴿And Yusuf had already come to you before with clear proofs﴾ [Ghafir 34].
* Student: Does he take as evidence Musa's words to Pharaoh: ﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed﴾ [al-Isra 102], as evidence for harshness in calling to the faith?
* The Shaykh: Harshness in its place, yes, because he himself said to him a harsher word than this: ﴿Indeed, I think you, O Musa, are bewitched﴾ [al-Isra 101]. So should he speak harshly to him and remain silent?! And Musa, peace be upon him, is known for strength.
* Student: O Shaykh, out of gentleness, the caller says: "And I am the one most deficient among you," and the weak-minded ignorant ones hear and say: "Since this caller or this shaykh is very deficient, we are even more so," and then what befalls them befalls them.
* The Shaykh: In any case, a person should consider the benefit of this statement. Otherwise, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him, said it at the end of a sermon he gave: "Indeed I say this to you, and I know of no one who has more deficiency, or he said: more sins, than I do." In reality it may be encouraging and it may be discouraging. Someone may say: if this worshipping caller is deficient, how about us? So let us roll up our sleeves in earnest. And it may be as you said; it is a double-edged weapon. So a person should look to the benefit. A person sometimes says such a thing because he fears for himself from self-admiration.
* Student: Shaykh, you said before: one should not marry his daughter to a sinner and say: perhaps Allah will guide him. What if the reverse happens and a man wants to marry a woman who is not upright, and says: perhaps Allah will guide her through me, or else I will divorce her?
* The Shaykh: The same thing. No, it is not "or else I will divorce her." A person may have resolve in this at first, but if he marries her and desires her, she overpowers him. Attracting women to men is not easy.
* Student: What if he thinks she will accept the call?
* The Shaykh: The word "think" here does not hold in reality, and therefore you are only responsible for what is before you. Even if matters turn out differently later, you are a mujtahid and there is no blame or sin on you. But you bear sin for proceeding with something you know is not suitable now, hoping it will become suitable; this is a mistake.

A woman may sometimes overcome a man. If he loves her intensely, she may say to him: "Prostrate to me." He says: "No, Allah is greater; you are greater?" Have you not known that one of the scholars—I forgot who—mentioned that a muezzin, whose mother had cursed him, and he was a righteous man, when he climbed the minaret to call the adhan, saw a beautiful Christian woman on the roof of her house, and she captivated his heart. He sent to propose to her. She said: "That is impossible unless you become a Christian." He tried; she said: "Never." So he became a Christian, may Allah protect us, and apostatized from Islam. Then he renewed the proposal, and she said: "Now you are neither a Muslim nor a Christian, so I am not lawful to you." That is, this man—we ask Allah for well-being—left his religion for the sake of this woman, and this woman's cunning became greater than his. She told him: "You are neither Muslim nor Christian, and Christianity is not lawful except to a Muslim or a Christian. Go back where you came from." We ask Allah for well-being.
* Student: May Allah reward you well, Shaykh. You mentioned a principle and said pure negation is not found in the attributes of Allah, and every negation in the attributes of Allah includes two things...
* The Shaykh: The first thing: the negation of the attribute; the second: the affirmation of the perfection of its opposite.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the problem?
* The student: Their taking Pharaoh (...).
* The Shaykh: Not at all (...).
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, they say that they have a lord, but their lord is Pharaoh.
* The student: So they affirm lordship.
* The Shaykh: For Pharaoh.
* The student: Not for Allah.
* The Shaykh: Not for Allah.
* The student: They are considered monotheists in lordship?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is known: monotheists in the lordship of Pharaoh. Do they have the tawhid of Pharaoh or not?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: (...). What do you say, everyone?
* Students: No, they do not have tawhid.
* The Shaykh: They do not have tawhid. Tawhid is the tawhid of the Lord of the worlds; as for the tawhid of Pharaoh or others, no.
* The student: (...) the prophets and the righteous in the Qur'an, are they in its exact wording?
* The Shaykh: In the exact wording, no, they are not in its wording; they are in meaning. That is why you find the expressions differing, which indicates that Allah, the Most High, transmits them in meaning, and though He attributes them to them as speech, it is in meaning. Moreover, their language was not Arabic.
* The student: In some verses where Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, relates about a person, such as His words: ﴿I am less than you in wealth and children﴾ [al-Kahf 39], should a person say: "Allah the Most High said, relating about a man," or should he say: "Allah the Most High said: ﴿I am less than you in wealth and children﴾"?
* The Shaykh: No, he says: "relating," because it may give the impression that the pronoun refers to Allah.
* Student: If the husband is a disbeliever and the wife is a Muslim (...), like Pharaoh and his wife?
* The Shaykh: This objection is valid. The question is: is it permissible for a disbeliever to marry a believing woman? We say: no. So an objection is raised against us: the wife of Pharaoh was certainly a believer, and he was the greatest of disbelievers.
The answer: this is the law of those before us, but our law is not so. And you know the principle in legal theory: the law of those before us is law for us as long as our law does not state otherwise. That is one answer. Another answer: it may be said that Pharaoh compelled her to it, and that she did not love him; this is why she says: ﴿My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Tahrim 11]. But he was a wrongdoer and did not care.
* Student: Shaykh, you mentioned that it is not permissible for a Muslim to marry an unrighteous Muslim woman?
* The Shaykh: Did I say this? I seek refuge in Allah.
* Student: Not permissible, not recommended.
* The Shaykh: But there is a difference between "not permissible" and "not recommended." You are my students, and you know my speech and my manner. If you transmit from me that it is not permissible for a sinner to marry a Muslim woman, this is a calamity; it means we marry no one at all, because most people are sinners. Correct the wording.
* Student: It is not recommended for him to marry a woman who is not committed, because she may draw him back to her way.
* The Shaykh: That is correct. That is why the Prophet ﷺ said: "A woman is married for four things," and then said at the end: "So win the one with religion, may your hands be rubbed with dust."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5090), Muslim (1466/53), and al-Nasa'i, whose wording this is (5318), all from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the problem?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: "Indeed, if Allah punishes the people of His heavens and His earth, He would punish them while He is not unjust to them."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4699) from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, and Zayd ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with them.]]

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verses 30–31 (part 2 of 5):**

* **Student:** ﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Mutual Calling (al-Tanad), the Day you will turn back fleeing. You will have no protector from Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide. And Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs, yet you continued in doubt about what he brought you, until, when he died, you said, "Allah will never send after him a messenger." Thus does Allah leave astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter. Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without any authority having come to them. It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah and in the sight of those who believe. Thus does Allah seal the heart of every arrogant tyrant.﴾ [Ghafir 34, 35].

* **The Shaykh:** I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Mutual Calling﴾. Before beginning the tafsir, we present an introduction, asking Allah, glorified and exalted, to benefit us by it.

We say: Among the blessings Allah bestows upon a servant is that He makes knowledge beloved to him, because sound religious knowledge is the key to every good. This is due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whomever Allah wills good for, He grants him understanding in the religion."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (71) and Muslim (1037 / 100), from the hadith of Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] This is good news for everyone whom Allah grants understanding of His religion, and knowing that Allah has willed good for him.

Fiqh (understanding of the religion) is knowing the legal rulings from their evidences, and then applying those rulings that one has learned, because whoever does not apply them is not a faqih (jurist); rather, he is merely a reciter. For this reason, "'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, warned against the readers increasing while the jurists decrease."[[Malik narrated it (1037 / 100) with his chain from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that he said to a man: "You are in a time whose jurists are many and whose reciters are few. The limits of the Qur'an are preserved in it, and its letters are lost. Few ask, many give. They lengthen the prayer and shorten the sermon. They put their deeds ahead of their desires. A time will come upon the people when its jurists are few and its reciters are many. The letters of the Qur'an will be preserved in it, and its limits will be lost. Many ask, few give. They lengthen the sermon and shorten the prayer. They put their desires ahead of their deeds."]] So the faqih in the religion of Allah is the one who knows the Shari'ah of Allah and then applies it to himself and to others according to his ability.

The student of knowledge bears a great responsibility, because he is an intermediary between the creation and the Messenger (ﷺ), since he transmits the Shari'ah of the Messenger (ﷺ) to his nation. For this reason, he must be a good example in his worship, his manners, and his dealings. If he is a good example in these, then knowledge has borne its noble fruits in him. Moreover, if he is an example of the Prophet (ﷺ) in these matters, people will love him, become attached to him, follow him, and he will become an imam, even if not a great imam, but an imam according to his condition. The more a person increases in knowledge and in adherence to what he knows, the more people's respect for him increases, and their following of him, and they take him as an example.

Furthermore, the student of knowledge must be sincere to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in seeking it, because sincerity is the most important thing; through it the servant achieves what he intends. Concerning sincerity to Allah in seeking knowledge, Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed to something of it when he said: "Nothing equals knowledge for one whose intention is sound." They said: "And how is the intention made sound?" He said: "By intending to remove ignorance from himself and from others."

There is no doubt that this is part of making the intention sound, but it is not the whole of it. There are other things that must also be observed. One must intend, in seeking knowledge, to carry out the command of Allah, glorified and exalted, because Allah commanded knowledge and encouraged it, saying: ﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah, and seek forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Muhammad 19], and He, exalted, said: ﴿Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who were given knowledge by degrees﴾ [al-Mujadilah 11]. This is something observed. Show me a merchant, one of the greatest merchants in the era of the four Imams, who attained the elevation of mention that these four Imams attained. You will not find a way to that. The people of knowledge are elevated with Allah and elevated among the servants: elevated in their lifetimes and elevated after their deaths. Even if someone suffers torture, harassment, or the like, he increases in elevation with Allah and elevation among the servants.

So when you seek knowledge intending to carry out the command of Allah, every movement you make in this field becomes an act of worship. If you review the lesson, it is worship; if you memorize, it is worship; if you walk, it is worship. "It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that 'Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge therein, Allah will make easy for him a path to Paradise.'"[[Narrated by Muslim (2699 / 38), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] This is a matter that is often overlooked by us. We frequently review books to verify a matter, but we forget that we are, at that moment, in an act of worship by which we hope for the reward of Allah. However, when the student of knowledge keeps in mind that he is carrying out the command of Allah, glorified and exalted, by seeking knowledge, his seeking becomes worship.

Second: that he intends by seeking knowledge the preservation of the Shari'ah, because the Shari'ah is preserved by its men. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah does not take away knowledge by snatching it from the breasts of men, but He takes it away by the death of the scholars, until when no scholars remain, people will take ignorant leaders who will give verdicts without knowledge, so they will be misguided and will misguide others."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari, whose wording this is (7307), and Muslim (2673), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Indeed Allah does not remove knowledge after He has given it to you by snatching it away, but He removes it by taking the scholars with their knowledge. Ignorant people will remain, who are consulted and give verdicts according to their opinion, so they will go astray and lead others astray."]] So the preservation of the Shari'ah is through the scholars, through its men. Therefore, intend by your seeking of knowledge the preservation of the Shari'ah, and how excellent a man you are if you are a treasury of the Shari'ah of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Third: that he intends by this, that is, by his seeking of knowledge, the protection of the Shari'ah and defending it. The Shari'ah has enemies who openly declare their enmity, and enemies who hide from people but do not hide from Allah, Who is with them when they plot by night what He does not approve of in speech. So it has enemies. Therefore, intend by your seeking of knowledge the protection of the Shari'ah and its defense. When this is the aim of the student of knowledge, he will choose the front from which the enemies of the Muslims attack. Accordingly, he must be knowledgeable about what is happening in the arena of corrupt ideas and corrupt beliefs. Let us give an example from a time that passed when people did not know the doctrines of the people of ta'til (denial of Allah's attributes), nor the deviant and destructive ideas, because they had not left their lands and no one from outside had come to them. They were gathered around their scholars and knew only the truth. For these people, it was not important to occupy themselves with other matters such as the means of knowledge or the defense of the Shari'ah, because they were secure. But when the enemy comes, we must prepare for him, and our preparation must be with a weapon suited to his weapon. For it is known, for example, that whoever attacks you with cannons and missiles, it is not right or correct for you to defend yourself with what is called the white weapon, the daggers, swords, and the like, because the obligation is to prepare for every enemy with what suits his weapon.

Now there are corrupt and evil ideas in the arena. If they are not atheistic, they are closer to atheism than to moderation. There is no need to specify, because this is known to many of you.

We need to know these ideas and how to refute them. I say to you: refuting all deviant ideas is very easy, even if they magnify the matter and inflate it. They are like a sponge: squeeze it with your hand and all that is in it comes out. Do not be intimidated, for they have no knowledge that is heard, nor a reason that is fabricated. Certainly, when a person has intended by seeking knowledge the protection of the Shari'ah and its defense, he must know what is happening in the arena, so that he can defend. Every situation has its fitting speech, and every place has what suits it.

I say to you: the protection of the Shari'ah and its defense can only be done by its men. If you were in a library with a group of people, and an atheist entered, declaring atheism, and you had no knowledge, but the library was full of books that refute the atheists and show the falsehood of what they are upon, is it possible that a book would leap off the shelf to answer this atheist? It is not possible. Books, however many, do not benefit without men. There must be scholars. If in this place that I mentioned there is a scholar, he will speak in a way that refutes the words of this atheist, until he turns back on his heels.

These are three matters, all of which follow from sincerity of intention.

Fourth: what Imam Ahmad, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, pointed to: that he intends to remove ignorance from himself and from others. Whenever he intends this, he must strive in seeking, because whoever wants wealth must earn, must trade, and must enter all fields of commerce. So if he wants to remove ignorance from himself, it is neither possible nor reasonable for him to sit without learning. He must strive in seeking. And if he wants to remove ignorance from others, he must be extremely eager to spread his knowledge by suitable means, the strongest means in every field.

Knowledge can be spread through speaking in ordinary gatherings. If he sits in a gathering at a feast, or in any place, he can spread his knowledge. But how? By a graceful manner that is beloved to souls and does not cause boredom or weariness. He can raise a question among those present, saying: "What do you say about a man who did such and such, or said such and such?" Or he can pose a riddle to open minds. Then he enters into teaching the people. I am not saying to impose yourself on the gathering you are in, because that is difficult for souls. Rather, draw them to knowledge through beloved and suitable methods until the gathering occupies itself with knowledge: discussion, lecturing, or the like.

Likewise, he can spread his knowledge through audio recordings. The recordings, praise be to Allah, have benefited many people greatly, especially since many people, particularly the youth, receive these recordings with eagerness and longing. Hardly does one come out but people receive it and benefit from it. These recordings, praise be to Allah, contain great benefit and the spread of knowledge, and not only in your place, your town, or your region, but they extend beyond your country. We have heard that the recordings of the callers and scholars reach distant places. These are among the means of spreading knowledge.

Third: you can spread knowledge through writing: writing treatises, authoring books, printed publications, and the like, to the extent possible, so that you spread your knowledge and benefit and are benefited.

There is also a hidden way of spreading knowledge that is overlooked by the student of knowledge, or by many students of knowledge, namely spreading knowledge through acting upon it. People often observe this scholar and see what he does, and so they follow him. Some people said: "He used to pray," and some of those who witnessed him said: "You do such and such in your prayer." So look at how people observed the actions of the student of knowledge in order to follow him. This is one of the means of spreading knowledge. Indeed, this may be one of the most effective ways by which people are influenced, because people's being influenced by action may be stronger and more forceful than their being influenced by speech. For this reason we repeat what we have previously stated: the student of knowledge is not a faqih unless he acts upon his knowledge; otherwise he is a reciter and not a faqih.

On this occasion, I would like to urge you to noble manners: generosity, giving greetings, doing good, forbearance among yourselves, and meeting people with cheerfulness and an open face. Among the characteristics of the Prophet (ﷺ) was that he was always cheerful and often smiled, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him. He was always cheerful; you would not find him closed off or frowning, smiling much at the proper time. For us in him, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, there is a good example. Allah said about him: ﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character﴾ [al-Qalam 4].

Among what is fitting for the student of knowledge: that he preserve his time from being wasted. The wasting of time occurs through various causes or aspects:

The first aspect: that he abandons review and revision of what he has read.

The second aspect: that he sits with his friends and loved ones and talks with them about idle talk with no benefit.

The third aspect, and the most harmful to the student of knowledge: that he has no concern except following people's sayings, what has been said and what is being said, and what has happened and what is happening in matters that do not concern him. This is undoubtedly a weakness in Islam, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Part of the goodness of a person's Islam is his leaving what does not concern him."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2317), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Occupation with this gossip and excessive questioning is a waste of time. In reality, it is a sickness that, if it takes hold of a person, we ask Allah for well-being, becomes his greatest concern. Sometimes he may become hostile toward one who does not deserve hostility, or allied with one who does not deserve alliance, because of his preoccupation with these matters that distract him from seeking knowledge, under the pretext that he is defending the rightful party. This is not so. Rather, this is occupying the self with what does not concern the person.

As for when news comes to you without your pursuing it and without your seeking it, everyone receives news, but do not be preoccupied with it. Do not make it your greatest concern, for this distracts the student of knowledge and spoils his affair, and it opens among the nation the door of partisanship and loyalty and disavowal, so the nation becomes divided. We ask Allah, the Exalted, to grant us and you success in what is good and righteous, to unite hearts upon His obedience, and to provide us with beneficial knowledge, righteous action, and good, abundant provision by which He makes us independent of His creation.

* **Student:** (...).

* **The Shaykh:** In truth, people in all their affairs divide into three categories. All of people's affairs have two extremes and a middle. There is an extreme of neglect and an extreme of excess, and a middle. Among people are those who occupy themselves with what they call fiqh al-waqi' (understanding of the reality), and have no concern except to follow people, gossip, and ask excessively. This is undoubtedly a waste and a preoccupation with what is perhaps important, if it is important, instead of what is more important. This is an error. Among people are those who occupy themselves with Shari'ah fiqh and are eager for it, but they pay no attention whatsoever to people's conditions. Rather, some of them may deny from Shari'ah fiqh what they think the evidence does not indicate. This is also an erroneous extreme. Among people are those who try to combine this and that.

When we examine the biography of the Prophet (ﷺ), we find that he, peace and blessings be upon him, understood the reality and understood people, and distinguished the good from the wicked. But he (ﷺ) was concerned with the second matter, which is fiqh in the religion. For this reason he said: "Whomever Allah wills good for, He grants him understanding in the religion."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (71) and Muslim (1037 / 100), from the hadith of Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] He did not say "understanding in reality." Understanding reality is only a means to application. So the student of knowledge must have both this and that. Do not incline to the extreme of understanding reality, nor exaggerate in fiqh of the religion so that you turn away from everything else. The person must be moderate.

* **Student:** O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, (...) the protection of the Shari'ah. And as for us, when we look at our contemporary reality, the media now calls to disbelief, atheism, polytheism, and so on, while the people of truth are prevented from that. So how can the protection of the Shari'ah be done, may Allah be good to you?

* Shaykh: He—may Allah bless you—intend by that the protection of the Shariah. As for your applying it in society, that is not up to you; that is up to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, you guide not whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas 56]. You know what befell Imam Ahmad and other imams of trials in attempting to apply the Shariah among people, yet they were patient and sought reward until the truth prevailed, and praise be to Allah. So applying the Shariah does not mean that the student of knowledge, if he intends to apply and protect the Shariah, is able to do so; he may not be able to. But he intends this, and he makes his pursuit of knowledge centered on this intention, and Allah, glorified and exalted, makes the matter easy for him. Then if he is harmed for the sake of Allah, that is an elevation of his ranks and an elevation of his mention. If you reflect on those among the scholars who suffer the most harm, you will find that they are the great scholars: they are subjected to imprisonment, beating, and humiliation, and perhaps killing, and this is part of Allah's elevation of them.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, what are the sciences with which it is good for a student of knowledge to begin (...)?

* Shaykh: By Allah, we see that the most important of necessities is knowledge of this Noble Book, the Book of Allah, before everything else, because the Companions would not go beyond ten verses until they had learned them along with their knowledge and practice. Then attention to what is authentically established from the Sunnah. Then attention to what the scholars have written and derived from these two primary sources: the Book and the Sunnah.

When we say: be keen to know the words of Allah and the words of His Messenger, this does not mean that you turn away from everything else. We must benefit from the views of the scholars who devoted their efforts to serving knowledge; otherwise we would be lost. For this reason the scholars—may Allah have mercy on them—wrote on the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), the principles of hadith (usul al-hadith), the rules of jurisprudence (qawa'id al-fiqh), the rules of hadith transmission (qawa'id al-tahdith), and other works, for the sake of precision, so that people would be disciplined and walk upon known rules.

* Student: May Allah bless you. It is noticeable that memorizing the matn (core texts) is difficult. Some people say: I repeat the issues many times, I understand them, and that suffices me instead of memorizing the texts. Memorizing matns in fiqh, for example, they say: these are merely the words of men, and we can produce the like of them. What is your view?

* Shaykh: My view is that memorizing the matns is the foundation. I have not benefited from anything as much as from what I memorized of books, because memorizing issues evaporates, except for issues that recur for a person daily, which he does not forget due to practice. So memorizing the matns is knowledge in reality. That it is difficult for some people is true; some find it very hard to memorize. You find him repeating the matn many times, yet he does not memorize it. But be keen on this. As a person advances in age, his understanding grows strong and his memorization weakens; that is, his understanding strengthens and he is opened to insights he did not know before, but his memorization decreases. For this reason we advise the young man to memorize, and the first thing that must be memorized is the Book of Allah, which is the foundation of everything.

* Student: Should a student of knowledge be advised to specialize in one field, such as fiqh, or should he move between fields, from creed to fiqh?

* Shaykh: You know that the sciences are not equal; some are more important than others. So devote your efforts to the more important, and do not empty yourself of the other sciences that support the more important. For example, a man said: I love grammar (nahw); I want to devote my efforts to grammar and not engage with anything else. We say: that is a mistake. Devote your efforts to what your soul desires, lest time be wasted on you, because if a person tries to force himself to study something he does not choose, time will be lost to him. But do not forget the other sciences.

Likewise, do not overload yourself with sciences, because the multiplicity of sciences weakens a person in his resolve and in his understanding. Those who studied in the regular schools know this. You find, for example, in institutes or secondary schools, fifteen subjects that waste a person's time; if you wanted to discuss something deep with someone from the subjects he studied, you would find nothing with him.

So when a person focuses on the sciences and condenses them as much as he can, this is better for him and more beneficial. It is mentioned that some people say: whoever masters one of the sciences with excellent mastery is thereby independent of all other sciences. This is without doubt a mistake. If you have truly mastered grammar, would it suffice you from knowing fiqh?

What is reported about Abu Yusuf and al-Kisa'i, that they debated in the presence of al-Rashid, and al-Kisa'i said: whoever masters a science—whatever science he masters—is independent of others by it; and that Abu Yusuf objected to him with a man who forgets during the prostration of forgetfulness (sujud al-sahw), so al-Kisa'i said: he has no prostration upon him. He said: From where does this come in your knowledge? —because al-Kisa'i was an imam in grammar— He said: From the rules of my science: the diminutive does not take a diminutive. Is this valid as evidence for a legal ruling? Not at all. I think this story is fabricated and is not authentic.

However, in any case, a person should focus. In my view, the most important thing I focus on is the Noble Qur'an. The Qur'an contains great treasures; whenever you take a verse and begin to reflect on it, there is opened to you from its sciences what none knows except Allah. Then the Qur'an is a proof: it is not like the book of any scholar; it is a proof by which a person argues before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because it is the speech of Allah, glorified and exalted. Therefore I see that we should focus on the science of tafsir, and then on knowing what is authentically established from the Prophet ﷺ.

You know that what is attributed to the Messenger ﷺ requires effort before it can be evidence. The effort is to know its authenticity back to the Messenger, because many hadiths have been narrated by weak narrators, either due to their lack of trustworthiness or their poor memory or the like. Indeed, how many fabricated, forged hadiths have been attributed to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him! Because desires have multiplied, so whoever does not fear Allah fabricates whatever he wishes and attributes it to the Messenger ﷺ. The Sunnah requires great care in establishing its authenticity from the Messenger ﷺ.

As for the Qur'an, it does not require this, because it is established by mass-transmission (tawatur), which the younger generations transmit from the older ones. So attention to the Book and the Sunnah is the most important, but that does not mean turning away from what the scholars have written. It is necessary to seek help from the opinions of the scholars and from how they derived rulings from the Qur'an and Sunnah, and we will limit ourselves to this.

* * *

* Student: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them. And Allah does not wish injustice for the servants (31). And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out (32), the Day you will turn away retreating; you will have from Allah no protector. And whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ [Ghafir 31–33].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. We begin this morning's tafsir lesson, and it is necessary to become acquainted with some rules of tafsir. We say:

First: Tafsir is derived from fasr (explanation/clarification), as in "fasarat al-thamarah 'an qishrihā," i.e., the fruit became clear and manifest. It is an explanation of the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Tafsir may be meant in the lexical sense, i.e., explaining a word apart from its context, and it may be meant in the sense of meaning, i.e., explaining a word according to its context.

For example, the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of power﴾ [al-Anfal 60]. If we explain "power" (quwwah) lexically, its meaning becomes the opposite of weakness. But the Prophet ﷺ said: «Indeed, power is archery»[[Narrated by Muslim (1917/167) from the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. So we say the meaning of quwwah in terms of wording is the opposite of weakness; this is in terms of the wording, and the intended meaning is archery; this is in terms of the intended meaning.

Similarly: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more﴾ [Yunus 26]. Ziyadah (increase) means excess, the addition of something to something; this is from the standpoint of wording. But the intended meaning is looking at the Face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as the Prophet ﷺ explained. Thus the lexical tafsir is not the intended meaning; the intended meaning is determined by context, or explained by the Prophet ﷺ or the like. As for the wording, you explain the word according to its meaning in isolation, without regard to its context.

Is the Noble Qur'an interpreted by the first meaning or the second? By the second meaning, i.e., by what Allah intended by it.

Second: Does the intended meaning contradict the apparent meaning, or is it the apparent meaning unless there is evidence? The intended meaning is the apparent meaning; that is, Allah intends by His speech its apparent sense, necessarily, and we cannot depart from the apparent sense except by evidence. Whoever departs from the apparent sense to something else without evidence is among those who distort words from their places.

An example of this rule: Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days; then He istawa upon the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf 54]. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿then He istawa upon the Throne﴾ is that He rose above it in a manner befitting His majesty and greatness, an elevation specific to the Throne, and not the general elevation over all creation. If a person comes and says: istawa means istawla (took dominion), we do not accept this from him. Why? Because this contradicts the apparent sense without evidence, and if it contradicts the apparent sense without evidence, it is from the category of distorting words from their places. And even if its adherents call themselves ta'wil-ists (interpreters), they only call themselves that in order to make their statements acceptable and to make their error easier for people, because there is a difference between saying "this is an interpretation" and "this is a distortion," whereas in reality they are distorters.

For this reason you find Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, in al-'Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah, expressed it by saying: "without distortion" (min ghayr tahrif). He did not say "without interpretation" (min ghayr ta'wil), because tahrif is blameworthy in every case, whereas ta'wil includes both sound and corrupt forms.

If evidence indicates that the intended meaning differs from the apparent sense, we explain it by the intended meaning, such as the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 98]. The meaning of "recite" (qara'ta) is: when you intend to recite. It does not mean: when you have finished. If we explained the wording by its apparent sense, we would say: when you have recited, i.e., when you have finished reciting, then seek refuge in Allah. But this is not intended. What shows that this is not intended? The Prophet's ﷺ practice, for he would seek refuge before beginning the recitation. These are two rules.

Third rule: To whom does one refer in explaining the Qur'an? Does one refer to the language and its literal meaning, or to the legal meaning, or what?

We say first: one refers in tafsir to the explanation of the One who spoke it, namely Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So one first refers in tafsir to the words of Allah. If a word is general (mujmal) in one place of the Qur'an and detailed (mufassal) in another, one refers to what is detailed in the Qur'an itself. If it is ambiguous in one place but clarified in another, we refer to the other place. Thus the Qur'an is first explained by the Qur'an, because the One who spoke it knows it better than anyone else. In the saying of Allah: ﴿The Striking Calamity (1). What is the Striking Calamity? (2). And what can make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ [al-Qari'ah 1–3]: what is the Striking Calamity? Allah clarified it by His saying: ﴿The Day when people will be like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'ah 4]. And He said: ﴿And what can make you know what the Day of Recompense is? Then what can make you know what the Day of Recompense is?﴾ [al-Infitar 17–18], and explained it by His saying: ﴿The Day no soul will have power for another soul at all﴾ [al-Infitar 19]. Likewise His saying: ﴿We will surely seize him by the forelock﴾ [al-'Alaq 15]: which forelock? Is every forelock seized by Allah? No: ﴿a lying, sinning forelock﴾ [al-'Alaq 16]. Measure on this basis. So we first refer to the explanation of the One who spoke it, which is Allah, i.e., explaining the Qur'an by the Qur'an.

Then after this we refer to explaining the Qur'an by the Sunnah, because the one most knowledgeable of the speech of Allah is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So we refer to his explanation and do not accept the explanation of anyone else. For example, the saying of Allah: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more﴾ [Yunus 26]: the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, explained it as looking at the Face of Allah. If someone came and said: "and more" means an increase in beauty, we would say: we do not accept your statement, even though the word, lexically, may bear what you said. We would not accept it, why? Because the Prophet ﷺ explained it as looking at the Face of Allah, and he is the most knowledgeable of people about the intention of his Lord, so we do not accept your statement.

Third: We refer to the explanation of the Companions. That is, if we do not find it in the Qur'an, nor in the Sunnah, we refer to the explanation of the Companions, because the Companions are the most knowledgeable of people about the intention of Allah and His Messenger, since they lived in the era of revelation, witnessed the circumstances and the indicators that point to the intended meaning. There is no doubt that one who witnesses a thing is not like one who is absent from it. Now, I may speak with emotion and say: "Do you do such and such? And why such and such?" You find me agitated, while one who hears my words without having seen me takes them as ordinary speech and does not understand, because he does not have the indicator. Therefore we say: the Companions are the most knowledgeable of people about the explanation of the speech of Allah and His Messenger, because they witnessed the circumstances and knew the indicators, so one refers to their explanation.

An example: the saying of Allah: ﴿And if a man or woman leaves neither ascendants nor descendants as heir, but has a brother or a sister, then for each of them is a sixth﴾ [al-Nisa' 12]. Here Abu Bakr explained kalalah as one who has no child and no father: the deceased who dies leaving neither child nor father, i.e., no ascendants or descendants. Here we adopt the explanation of Abu Bakr, why? Because he is among the Companions, and the Companions are the most knowledgeable of people about the explanation of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. And the meaning of our saying is that if anyone from the later generations came and explained the Qur'an contrary to what the Companions explained, we would never refer to his opinion.

Fourth: If we do not find it in the Qur'an, nor in the Sunnah, nor in the words of the Companions, we refer to the statements of the Successors (tabi'un), especially those known for receiving from the Companions, such as Mujahid ibn Jabr, may Allah have mercy on him, who said: "I presented the mushaf to Ibn 'Abbas twice or more, stopping at each verse and asking him about its meaning." Such a person's statement is taken, because he received from the Companions, although some Successors may not attain this rank because they did not receive from the Companions. Nevertheless, the Successors are, in general, closer to the correct meaning than those who came after them, though, as you know, they are lower in rank than the Companions.

Fifth: We refer to the true meaning of the word, which is its linguistic meaning; that is, we refer to the meaning of the word in the Arabic language. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you might reason﴾ [al-Zukhruf 3], i.e., that you might understand the meaning. This is a referral by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to the Arabic language, and that understanding the Qur'an is according to the requirement of the Arabic language, and we have proof for this. If someone asks: what is your evidence that the meaning of this word is such-and-such? We say: this is its meaning in the language, and the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language. Allah indicated this in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you might reason﴾, and ﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue that they might remember﴾ [al-Dukhan 58], among other clear verses.

If the linguistic meaning and the legal (shar'i) meaning of a word differ, we return to the legal meaning. The linguistic and legal meanings certainly agree in many things. Heaven (samā') is heaven both linguistically and legally, earth is earth both linguistically and legally, camels are camels both linguistically and legally, and similar examples. But if the legal meaning conflicts with the linguistic meaning, we give precedence to the legal meaning, because there are words that the Shari'ah transferred from their original linguistic meaning to a legal meaning. An example is faith (īmān). Linguistically, faith is acknowledgment, recognition, or affirmation, though the scholars differ in their explanations. In the Shari'ah, however, it is other than that. Faith in the Shari'ah is broader than this. It includes the linguistic meaning and also more, such as statements, actions, deeds, and abstentions. All of these are part of faith in the legal sense. Likewise, salah (prayer). We find in the Qur'an: ﴿And establish prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah 43]. How do we understand salah? Do we take it in its linguistic meaning, which is supplication, or in its legal meaning? In its legal meaning, because the Shari'ah transferred some Arabic words to a new meaning that is not used in the Arabic language, so we adopt what the Shari'ah has established.

We have now taken five sources: we refer in tafsir to the Qur'an, the Sunnah, the Companions, the Successors, and the linguistic meaning. If the linguistic and the legal meanings conflict, we give precedence to the legal meaning. This, I think, is the third topic.

The fourth topic: Is it permissible for us to interpret the Qur'an without referring to the written or spoken words of the scholars?

This requires consideration. If a word has a linguistic meaning, and we do not know of a legal meaning that contradicts it, then we may interpret the Qur'an according to the requirements of the language, provided we do not know that the word has been transferred to a legal meaning. This is because the Qur'an, as we have said and demonstrated, was revealed in the Arabic language. So if you interpret it according to the requirements of Arabic, there is no harm. But on the condition that I have knowledge of the Arabic language. It is not the case that any layman comes along and interprets the Qur'an.

As for interpreting the Qur'an in a way that agrees with my own opinion while contradicting the previously mentioned principles, the hadiths have come with a warning about this: "Whoever speaks about the Qur'an according to his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2951) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Beware of narrating from me except what you know. Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire, and whoever speaks about the Qur'an according to his opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire."]] There are many examples of this in creed and jurisprudence. Many scholars interpreted the Qur'an according to their own opinions, that is, in accordance with their schools of thought. This is well known and recognized in matters of creed. For example, interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ [al-Fajr 22] as meaning "the command of your Lord came." Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the words of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah 6] as meaning "the created speech." Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then He rose over the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf 54] as meaning "He took control of it." Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That which I created with My hands﴾ [Sad 75] as meaning "with My power," and similar examples. This person is undoubtedly one who speaks about the Qur'an according to his own opinion, because he has interpreted it neither according to the requirements of the language nor according to the requirements of the Shari'ah, but only according to his opinion, which agrees with his school of thought or his method.

There are many examples of this in creed and jurisprudence. Many scholars interpreted the Qur'an according to their opinions, that is, in accordance with their schools of thought. This is well known and recognized in matters of creed:
- Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ [al-Fajr 22] as meaning "the command of your Lord came."
- Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the words of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah 6] as meaning "the created speech."
- Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then He rose over the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf 54] as meaning "He took control of it."
- Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That which I created with My hands﴾ [Sad 75] as meaning "with My power," and similar examples. This person has undoubtedly spoken about the Qur'an according to his own opinion, because he has interpreted it neither according to the requirements of the language nor according to the requirements of the Shari'ah, but only according to his opinion, which agrees with what? With his school of thought or his method.

Therefore, interpreting the Qur'an according to personal opinion (tafsir bil-ra'y) is forbidden and is one of the major sins. It falls under the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ [al-An'am 21]. This is because the interpreter says, "Allah intended this," so is he truthful or lying? He is lying, and so he is one who fabricates a lie against Allah by saying that Allah intended such-and-such. Then he is also one who transgresses against the right of Allah by saying that He did not intend such-and-such. Notice the danger here: when he says, ﴿And your Lord comes﴾, he claims that Allah meant "the command of your Lord came," and so he has lied about Allah, and he says that He did not mean that He Himself came. He has transgressed against the words of Allah and exceeded his limits. Who told you that Allah did not intend this, when this is the apparent meaning of His words? So this person is a transgressor who distorts the text, and we seek refuge in Allah.

Similarly, in matters of jurisprudence, for example: ﴿And wipe over your heads and your feet﴾ [al-Ma'idah 6]. The Rafidah said that it means Allah commanded us to wipe the feet instead of washing them. It is said to them: these people spoke according to their own opinions, because they neglected the recitation in the accusative ﴿wa-arjulakum﴾ and did not act upon it, then they contradicted the intended meaning with the recitation in the genitive. The intended meaning is that the feet are wiped in the manner explained by the Sunnah. And what has the Sunnah explained? That the feet are wiped when one is wearing leather socks, thick socks, or similar coverings. It is now clear that interpreting by personal opinion is one of the major sins, because it involves two great corruptions:
- First: distorting words from their proper places.
- Second: lying against Allah and transgressing against His rights, by claiming that He did not intend such-and-such and intended such-and-such.

The fifth topic: The importance of tafsir. Tafsir is among the most noble sciences and the highest in status, because a person seeks through it to understand the meaning of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Sciences are ennobled according to their subject matter, and there is no subject more noble than the interpretation of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Therefore tafsir is among the noblest sciences, if not the noblest and greatest in status, because it is an attention to the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
