That is, if we do not find it in the Qur'an, nor in the Sunnah, we refer to the explanation of the Companions, because the Companions are the most knowledgeable of people about the intention of Allah and His Messenger, since they lived in the era of revelation, witnessed the circumstances and the indicators that point to the intended meaning. There is no doubt that one who witnesses a thing is not like one who is absent from it. Now, I may speak with emotion and say: "Do you do such and such? And why such and such?" You find me agitated, while one who hears my words without having seen me takes them as ordinary speech and does not understand, because he does not have the indicator. Therefore we say: the Companions are the most knowledgeable of people about the explanation of the speech of Allah and His Messenger, because they witnessed the circumstances and knew the indicators, so one refers to their explanation.

An example: the saying of Allah: ﴿And if a man or woman leaves neither ascendants nor descendants as heir, but has a brother or a sister, then for each of them is a sixth﴾ [al-Nisa' 12]. Here Abu Bakr explained kalalah as one who has no child and no father: the deceased who dies leaving neither child nor father, i.e., no ascendants or descendants. Here we adopt the explanation of Abu Bakr, why? Because he is among the Companions, and the Companions are the most knowledgeable of people about the explanation of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. And the meaning of our saying is that if anyone from the later generations came and explained the Qur'an contrary to what the Companions explained, we would never refer to his opinion.

Fourth: If we do not find it in the Qur'an, nor in the Sunnah, nor in the words of the Companions, we refer to the statements of the Successors (tabi'un), especially those known for receiving from the Companions, such as Mujahid ibn Jabr, may Allah have mercy on him, who said: "I presented the mushaf to Ibn 'Abbas twice or more, stopping at each verse and asking him about its meaning." Such a person's statement is taken, because he received from the Companions, although some Successors may not attain this rank because they did not receive from the Companions. Nevertheless, the Successors are, in general, closer to the correct meaning than those who came after them, though, as you know, they are lower in rank than the Companions.

Fifth: We refer to the true meaning of the word, which is its linguistic meaning; that is, we refer to the meaning of the word in the Arabic language. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you might reason﴾ [al-Zukhruf 3], i.e., that you might understand the meaning. This is a referral by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to the Arabic language, and that understanding the Qur'an is according to the requirement of the Arabic language, and we have proof for this. If someone asks: what is your evidence that the meaning of this word is such-and-such? We say: this is its meaning in the language, and the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language. Allah indicated this in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you might reason﴾, and ﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue that they might remember﴾ [al-Dukhan 58], among other clear verses.

If the linguistic meaning and the legal (shar'i) meaning of a word differ, we return to the legal meaning. The linguistic and legal meanings certainly agree in many things. Heaven (samā') is heaven both linguistically and legally, earth is earth both linguistically and legally, camels are camels both linguistically and legally, and similar examples. But if the legal meaning conflicts with the linguistic meaning, we give precedence to the legal meaning, because there are words that the Shari'ah transferred from their original linguistic meaning to a legal meaning. An example is faith (īmān). Linguistically, faith is acknowledgment, recognition, or affirmation, though the scholars differ in their explanations. In the Shari'ah, however, it is other than that. Faith in the Shari'ah is broader than this. It includes the linguistic meaning and also more, such as statements, actions, deeds, and abstentions. All of these are part of faith in the legal sense. Likewise, salah (prayer). We find in the Qur'an: ﴿And establish prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah 43]. How do we understand salah? Do we take it in its linguistic meaning, which is supplication, or in its legal meaning? In its legal meaning, because the Shari'ah transferred some Arabic words to a new meaning that is not used in the Arabic language, so we adopt what the Shari'ah has established.

We have now taken five sources: we refer in tafsir to the Qur'an, the Sunnah, the Companions, the Successors, and the linguistic meaning. If the linguistic and the legal meanings conflict, we give precedence to the legal meaning. This, I think, is the third topic.

The fourth topic: Is it permissible for us to interpret the Qur'an without referring to the written or spoken words of the scholars?

This requires consideration. If a word has a linguistic meaning, and we do not know of a legal meaning that contradicts it, then we may interpret the Qur'an according to the requirements of the language, provided we do not know that the word has been transferred to a legal meaning. This is because the Qur'an, as we have said and demonstrated, was revealed in the Arabic language. So if you interpret it according to the requirements of Arabic, there is no harm. But on the condition that I have knowledge of the Arabic language. It is not the case that any layman comes along and interprets the Qur'an.

As for interpreting the Qur'an in a way that agrees with my own opinion while contradicting the previously mentioned principles, the hadiths have come with a warning about this: "Whoever speaks about the Qur'an according to his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2951) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Beware of narrating from me except what you know. Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire, and whoever speaks about the Qur'an according to his opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire."]] There are many examples of this in creed and jurisprudence. Many scholars interpreted the Qur'an according to their own opinions, that is, in accordance with their schools of thought. This is well known and recognized in matters of creed. For example, interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ [al-Fajr 22] as meaning "the command of your Lord came." Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the words of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah 6] as meaning "the created speech." Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then He rose over the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf 54] as meaning "He took control of it." Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That which I created with My hands﴾ [Sad 75] as meaning "with My power," and similar examples. This person is undoubtedly one who speaks about the Qur'an according to his own opinion, because he has interpreted it neither according to the requirements of the language nor according to the requirements of the Shari'ah, but only according to his opinion, which agrees with his school of thought or his method.

There are many examples of this in creed and jurisprudence. Many scholars interpreted the Qur'an according to their opinions, that is, in accordance with their schools of thought. This is well known and recognized in matters of creed:
- Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ [al-Fajr 22] as meaning "the command of your Lord came."
- Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the words of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah 6] as meaning "the created speech."
- Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then He rose over the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf 54] as meaning "He took control of it."
- Interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That which I created with My hands﴾ [Sad 75] as meaning "with My power," and similar examples. This person has undoubtedly spoken about the Qur'an according to his own opinion, because he has interpreted it neither according to the requirements of the language nor according to the requirements of the Shari'ah, but only according to his opinion, which agrees with what? With his school of thought or his method.

Therefore, interpreting the Qur'an according to personal opinion (tafsir bil-ra'y) is forbidden and is one of the major sins. It falls under the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ [al-An'am 21]. This is because the interpreter says, "Allah intended this," so is he truthful or lying? He is lying, and so he is one who fabricates a lie against Allah by saying that Allah intended such-and-such. Then he is also one who transgresses against the right of Allah by saying that He did not intend such-and-such. Notice the danger here: when he says, ﴿And your Lord comes﴾, he claims that Allah meant "the command of your Lord came," and so he has lied about Allah, and he says that He did not mean that He Himself came. He has transgressed against the words of Allah and exceeded his limits. Who told you that Allah did not intend this, when this is the apparent meaning of His words? So this person is a transgressor who distorts the text, and we seek refuge in Allah.

Similarly, in matters of jurisprudence, for example: ﴿And wipe over your heads and your feet﴾ [al-Ma'idah 6]. The Rafidah said that it means Allah commanded us to wipe the feet instead of washing them. It is said to them: these people spoke according to their own opinions, because they neglected the recitation in the accusative ﴿wa-arjulakum﴾ and did not act upon it, then they contradicted the intended meaning with the recitation in the genitive. The intended meaning is that the feet are wiped in the manner explained by the Sunnah. And what has the Sunnah explained? That the feet are wiped when one is wearing leather socks, thick socks, or similar coverings. It is now clear that interpreting by personal opinion is one of the major sins, because it involves two great corruptions:
- First: distorting words from their proper places.
- Second: lying against Allah and transgressing against His rights, by claiming that He did not intend such-and-such and intended such-and-such.

The fifth topic: The importance of tafsir. Tafsir is among the most noble sciences and the highest in status, because a person seeks through it to understand the meaning of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Sciences are ennobled according to their subject matter, and there is no subject more noble than the interpretation of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Therefore tafsir is among the noblest sciences, if not the noblest and greatest in status, because it is an attention to the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is also following the path of the early pious predecessors, who would not go beyond ten verses until they had learned them along with what they contain of knowledge and action. And when a person understands the speech of Allah, he tastes its sweetness, and he begins to recite it while finding the sweetness of its meaning and intimacy with it, more than an illiterate person who does not know the Book except as wishful recitation.

In the science of tafsir the heart is reassured, and through it a person recognizes the value of this great Qur'an, which Allah described with many great attributes: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated and the great Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr 87]. Most of us, may Allah pardon us, do not care for tafsir or give it attention. Perhaps one may look into a scholar's book, which may be right or wrong, and reflect on it through its explicit meaning, implicit meaning, allusions, indications, and other types of significance. But he does not care for the speech of Allah. If it were not for the blessing sought through its recitation for reward, he would not turn to it at all. This is an error.

Even among students of knowledge today, there are those who do not care for tafsir. You find them concerned with books of jurisprudence, books of hadith, and books on the narrators, while turning away from this, which is the foundation, the foundation of foundations that we must know and for which we will be held accountable. "The Qur'an is either a proof in your favor or against you." [[Narrated by Muslim (223) from the hadith of Abu Malik al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him).]] Stop one of the greatest students of knowledge and say, "I have a verse from the Qur'an. What is its meaning?" What does he say? Either he is bold and says, "Allah intended by this such-and-such," even though He did not intend it, or he is cautious and says, "I do not know." But if students of knowledge took the Qur'an from its beginning, reciting it, reflecting on it, and contemplating it, they would find much good, and doors of knowledge would open for them that they could not imagine.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says in the Noble Qur'an: ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar 17]. It is not difficult. When you truly turn to the Qur'an with a heart and a firm intention, it is easy, easier than all other books, because He says: ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar 17].

These are some notes I have spoken about, and I ask Allah, the Exalted, to benefit by them in the introduction to tafsir, because some of our brothers may not have attended such principles, which will benefit them, Allah willing. Now, to the lesson we are engaged in.

* Student: Some say that there are two things that have no chain of transmission: tafsir and history. What is the accuracy of this statement?
* Shaykh: Yes, this is reported from Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him). He said there are three: the campaigns (maghāzī), biographies (siyar), and tafsir. He meant by this that they have no chain of transmission, in that people pass them on without isnad. For example, one says, "Mujahid said such-and-such," or "Ibn 'Abbas said such-and-such," without an isnad for this meaning. Likewise histories: you find people speaking about, for example, the Battle of Uhud, but you do not find a man saying, "So-and-so narrated to me from so-and-so from so-and-so," until he reaches the battle. It is also said about biographies. This is what Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) meant. His purpose is that when you hear something like this, which is widely known and transmitted, you should verify it.
* Student: If a shaykh or teacher now presented to his students the interpretation of a verse and said, "What do you say about this verse?" while he himself is knowledgeable about it, and the students then say, "This says this, and that says that," do they fall under (...)?
* Shaykh: No, this does not fall under it, because the one who said, "The meaning of the verses is such-and-such," does not intend that this meaning is settled. Rather, he presents it to a shaykh more knowledgeable than himself. So when he says, "Allah intended such-and-such," it is as if he is saying through his state: "Did Allah intend such-and-such by this?" Therefore this is not considered interpretation of the Qur'an by opinion, nor is it forbidden.
* Student: Some people leave tafsir and follow the Sunnah, the reports of the early figures, and similar things. They argue that the people of innovation (bid'ah) use the general statements of the Qur'an as evidence, so we read the Sunnah to clarify these generalities (...) the Sunnah. What is your opinion on this?
* Shaykh: My opinion is correct that we should not neglect the Sunnah, nor knowledge of the narrators, nor knowledge of the terminology. But we see that there are priorities and more important matters before the most important matters. As for his claim that the Qur'an did not clarify the refutation of the people of innovation, and that only the Sunnah did, this is not correct. The Qur'an does not contain a single proof for any innovation at all. Indeed, Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his book Dar' Ta'arud al-'Aql wal-Naql: "Any proof that a person uses for an innovation, I make it a proof against him." He spoke the truth.

Let me give you an example: ﴿No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision﴾ [al-An'am 103]. Some who hold that Allah cannot be seen use this verse as evidence. Do you understand? In reality, it indicates that Allah can be seen. They used it as evidence, but it is evidence against them. This is because negating the more specific implies the existence of the more general. ﴿No vision can grasp Him﴾ means that He can be seen. If He could not be seen, He would have said, "No vision sees Him." But to express "cannot see Him" with ﴿cannot grasp Him﴾ is without doubt obscurity and riddle, and this cannot be in the speech of Allah, which He made "an explanation of all things." Do you understand?

They also used Musa's words: ﴿My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look at You. He said, "You will not see Me"﴾ [al-A'raf 143]. They said: this shows that Allah cannot be seen. We say: this is evidence against you. Did Musa ask for the vision in the Hereafter or in this world? In this world. How then do you transfer it to the Hereafter? That is why He said, ﴿You will not see Me﴾, meaning: right now you do not have the capacity to bear My seeing. The seeing of Allah, the Exalted, is impossible in this world, not because of something related to the act of seeing, but because of something related to the one who sees. The seer cannot bear it. This is why Allah gave Musa an example. He said: ﴿Look at the mountain. If it remains in its place, then you will see Me.﴾ So when His Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, what happened? ﴿He made it crumble to dust﴾ [al-A'raf 143]. This great mountain, which no bombs can crush, became dust merely because Allah manifested Himself to it. This is why Musa fell down unconscious. He was unable to bear the situation, let alone seeing his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic.

The main point is that the verse contains evidence against them, because Musa asked for the vision when? In this world, not in the Hereafter.

Furthermore, Musa asked for the vision, and you say that seeing Allah is impossible. Then you know more about Allah than Musa does. Either you know more about Allah than Musa, because Musa did not ask for something impossible, since he believed that Allah can be seen but humans cannot bear it; or else he was ignorant of the majesty of Allah while you know it; or else he transgressed against Allah by asking what was not lawful for him to ask.

So I say to you, my brothers: whoever says that innovations cannot be repelled except by the Sunnah, or that they cannot be repelled except by the Sunnah, has erred. This indicates a deficiency in his understanding of the Qur'an or a shortcoming in comprehending it. Otherwise, the Qur'an itself cannot contain any innovation without refuting it, never. Even if there were nothing in it except His saying: ﴿Have they associates who have instituted for them in religion that which Allah has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shura 21], this verse would be decisive against every innovation. Every innovation is invalidated by this verse, whether it is doctrinal, verbal, or practical.

* Student: You said that interpreting the Qur'an by the Qur'an, then by the Sunnah, then by the Companions. But if a person wanted to trace every verse through the sayings of the Companions, the Sunnah, and so on, he would waste his time. But (...) a tafsir book from the well-known imams (...) until he memorizes it.
* Shaykh: This would be taqlid (blind following). That is, my holding the tafsir of Ibn Kathir or another scholar is taqlid. But I want the tafsir of the mujtahid (independent scholar). As for one who finds nothing but carrion, he eats carrion out of necessity. Therefore Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "We should know that taqlid is like eating carrion. If you are compelled to it, then follow taqlid; otherwise, exert independent reasoning. Lower your bucket into the well as the people have lowered theirs." In reality, taqlid is not permissible except in cases of necessity and incapacity. Otherwise, whoever is able to take rulings or beliefs from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger should do so. This is because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And the Day He calls them and says, "What did you answer the messengers?"﴾ [al-Qasas 65]. This requires an answer. Were it not for the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun 16], we would say that every person must exert effort and take rulings from the Qur'an and the Sunnah. But praise be to Allah, He has made things easy for us: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 286], ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾. Otherwise, we would say that everyone must take from the Book and the Sunnah, because we will be asked about the Qur'an and the Sunnah.
* Student: Which tafsir books are the best that follow the principles you have mentioned, so that the student can understand them and train himself in them?
* Shaykh: In my view, the best of the tafsirs that focus on transmitted reports (bil-athar) is the tafsir of Ibn Kathir. The tafsir of Ibn Kathir is among the best books that rely on interpretation by transmitted reports. But you know that the Qur'an, glory be to Allah, is vast. If all people gathered to comprehend its meaning, they would not be able to. You find, for example, that one researches the Qur'an from a linguistic perspective, another from a doctrinal perspective, another from a jurisprudential perspective, and another from the perspective of eloquence. The Qur'an contains many diverse sciences. Ibn Kathir, for example, is without doubt good in reports, but in many matters of language he is deficient. Also, in deriving rulings, he rarely speaks about rulings. We find, for example, that al-Qurtubi is concerned with rulings and derives branches from the verse and similar things. In short, every scholar has a methodology in interpreting the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Student: (...) The Noble Qur'an is only interpreted through language. So do we conclude that linguistic interpretation is the correct one?

**The Shaykh:** That is, if we find a word that has not been explained by the Qur'an, the Sunnah, or the statements of the Companions, we return in any case to the language, because the Qur'an, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 195]. ﴿Indeed, We have made it﴾ [al-Zukhruf 3], meaning: We have made it ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾, meaning: in the Arabic language, ﴿that you may understand﴾ [al-Zukhruf 3]. Look at the following verses: ﴿And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs, and he had recited it to them, they would not have been believers in it﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 198–199]. Why? Because they would not understand its meaning.

**A student:** (...) So how do we reconcile this with the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "If a scholar exerts effort (ijtihad) and is correct, he has two rewards, and if he errs, he has one reward"?

**The Shaykh:** Yes, if he exerts effort. But the one who explains the Qur'an by his own opinion has not exerted effort. I have given you several examples of tafsir by opinion (al-tafsir bil-ra'y). Tafsir by opinion does not mean that you explain the Qur'an according to what the Arabic language requires. Tafsir by opinion means that you impose the meaning of the Qur'an upon your own view. And this occurs with whom? With those who are fanatical toward their schools of thought, who try to twist the necks of the texts to conform to what they were upon.

**A student:** The jurists say that a man who marries a woman during her waiting period ('idda) and consummates the marriage is forbidden to her permanently?

**The Shaykh:** Which jurists?

**The student:** The scholars say so, in the books of jurisprudence.

**The Shaykh:** Which books?

**The student:** The books of the school (al-kutub al-ma'rifiyya).

**The Shaykh:** This, may Allah bless you, according to the school of the Hanbalis, does not make her forbidden. However, it has been narrated from 'Umar a report that he made her forbidden to the man who married her as a punishment for him. It is a punishment for him, not a prohibition by lineage or by affinity, but a punishment. Perhaps the rule of Ibn Rajab has passed you by: "Whoever hastens something before its time, in a prohibited manner, is punished by being deprived of it." This is a beneficial rule for the seeker of knowledge.

**The student:** Does this come under this rule?

**The Shaykh:** Yes, indeed.

* * *

**A student:** I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, indeed I fear for you a like of the day of the confederates (al-Ahzab), a like of the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them. And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants. And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out, the day you will turn back fleeing; you will have no protector from Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide. And Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs, but you continued in doubt about what he brought you, until, when he died, you said: 'Allah will never send after him a messenger.' Thus does Allah leave astray whoever is a transgressor and doubter."﴾ [Ghafir 30–34].

**The Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, indeed I fear for you a like of the day of the confederates"﴾. ﴿And the one who believed said﴾: Allah left unspecified who it was who believed, since he was introduced at the beginning of the story: ﴿And a man of believers from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said﴾ [Ghafir 28]. Thus the reference to him remains in the form of indefiniteness, because there is no need to specify him by name, as naming him might carry some harm. The intended purpose is the meaning and what this story contains.

﴿Said the one who believed: "O my people, indeed I fear for you a like of the day of the confederates"﴾. ﴿O my people﴾: It is known that the vocative particle "yā" when it enters upon a determined indefinite noun is built on a ḍamma, as when it enters upon a definite noun. Here it was not built on a ḍamma, but its final letter is kasra. So it is said that its original form is "yā qawmī" ("O my people, with my pronoun"), but the yā (of the first person) was deleted for lightness. In his saying ﴿O my people﴾ there is gentleness in calling them, since otherwise they were hostile to him, because they were disbelievers and he was a believer. But out of gentleness in calling to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, he said to them: "O my people."

﴿Indeed I fear for you a like of the day of the confederates﴾: He emphasized the sentence, even though it was firmly established in his own mind, because the one addressed by it acts as one who denies it.

(﴿Indeed I fear for you a like of the day of the confederates﴾ — meaning: a day of one confederacy after another.) The commentator said "one confederacy after another" because these confederacies were not gathered at one time or in one place. Rather, we find the story of Noah alone, Hud alone, Salih alone, and so on. For this reason the author explained his saying ﴿the day of the confederates﴾ with his saying: "a day of one confederacy after another."

﴿A like of the custom of the people of Noah﴾: ﴿a like﴾ here is an apposition (badal) to the ﴿a like﴾ before it: ﴿a like of the day of the confederates, a like of the custom﴾. Apposition is one of the four well-known followers (tawabi'), or as Ibn Malik said:
"It follows in case the first nouns: an adjective, an emphasis, a conjunction, and an apposition."
The sign of an apposition is that it can take the place of the noun it replaces (mubdal minhu). That is, it is valid to delete the replaced noun and let the apposition take its place.

If someone says: What is the benefit of mentioning the replaced noun and then the apposition? Why did we not mention the apposition from the outset?

We say: There must be a benefit; either it is detail after generality, or clarification after vagueness, or something similar. The apposition must have a benefit.

﴿A like of the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud﴾ and so on: "a like of their custom" — he does not mean a like of their custom, he means a like of the requital of their custom, because there is a custom and there is a requital. The requital is from Allah, and the custom is from the peoples or the confederates. So: "a like of the requital of their custom." What then was their custom? Allah explained their custom by His saying: ﴿as the custom of the family of Pharaoh and those before them, who denied Our signs﴾ [Al 'Imran 11]. This is their custom.

﴿A like of the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud﴾: all of these, what was their custom? Denying the messengers and disbelieving in them.

﴿And those after them﴾: after whom? After the people of Noah, who were the first of the nations, and 'Ad and Thamud.

The exegete said: "(A like of) is an apposition of the ﴿a like﴾ before it; that is: a like of the requital of the custom of those who disbelieved." So the author, may Allah have mercy on him, informed us that there is an implied element in the speech; that is, something is omitted. What is it? "Requital." A like of the requital of their custom, because this is what is feared: that these people will receive a punishment as those received it.

If someone asks: How is the word "custom" applied to "requital"? We say: Because it is its cause. This occurs frequently in the Qur'an, that Allah applies the term "work" to requital, as in: ﴿Taste what you used to do﴾ [al-'Ankabut 55]. The meaning is: taste the requital. But the term "work" is used to express requital, because requital is of the same kind as work, and so that a person may beware of his deeds just as he beware of the punishment of his deeds.

He says: "(A like of the requital of the custom of those who disbelieved before you, of their punishment in this world.)"

He said: ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾. Is the particle "mā" (negative) Tamimi or Hijazi? Tamimi. Is the Qur'an Tamimi or Hijazi?

**A student:** The Qur'an is in Arabic, but sometimes some verses come in the dialect of Tamim and sometimes in the dialect of...

**The Shaykh:** Are you from Tamim?

**The student:** No.

**The Shaykh:** What do you say about this?

**A student:** Hijazi.

**The Shaykh:** Hijazi, because this Qur'an is in the Hijazi dialect. Look at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿This is not a human being﴾ [Yusuf 31], and He did not say "mā hādhā basharun" in the Tamimi manner. So we take everything of this kind as following it. Otherwise, it is true that in "mā Allahu yurīdu ẓulman lil-'ibād" we cannot determine whether it is Hijazi or Tamimi, because the predicate is a clause, not a single noun in which the accusative would appear. But what does not show its case-ending is interpreted by what does show it, which is His saying: ﴿mā hādhā basharan﴾. Furthermore, know that the Qur'an was only written in the dialect of Quraysh, as 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, said to those who copied the mushafs: "If you differ about something, then write it in the dialect of Quraysh." (Al-Bukhari (3506) narrated from Anas that 'Uthman summoned Zayd ibn Thabit, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn al-'As, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham, and they copied it into the mushafs, and 'Uthman said to the three Qurashi men: "If you and Zayd ibn Thabit differ about something in the Qur'an, write it in the language of Quraysh, for it was revealed in their language," and they did so.) That is, in their dialect.

﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾.

* From the benefits of this verse: the demonstration of the sincere advice of this believing man, since he warned his people of the punishment of Allah.
* And in it: evidence for gentleness in calling to Allah, and that a person should not use his emotion in calling to Allah, for if he uses his emotion, zeal takes hold of him and he does what does not lead to a good end. Rather, he should employ reason and look to the consequences and results. There is no harm if a person is humbled at the beginning of a matter if the outcome is good. I do not think it is hidden from you what happened to the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions at the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya, with its conditions which apparently were humiliating, yet their outcome was good, to the extent that Allah named it a conquest: ﴿Those of you who spent before the conquest and fought are not equal﴾ [al-Hadid 10]. So the conclusion is that when calling to Allah, a person should not let emotion rule, lest his foot slip, but should let reason rule and look to the consequences and results.
* And among the benefits of this verse: the demonstration that the mention of past nations spreads among later nations, either through the revealed books or through transmitted history. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed I fear for you a like of the day of the confederates﴾ [Ghafir 30], because he could not warn them of a matter they did not know. Had that been the case, they would have said: "What are these days?" or "What is this requital?"
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the warning to the later that what befell the earlier may befall him, from His saying: ﴿a like of the day of the confederates, a like of the custom of the people of Noah﴾. The reason is that the sunnah (way) of Allah, the Exalted, in His creation is one. He does not punish these people because He personally hates them; He punishes these people because He hates their deeds. So if their deeds are found in others, then the dislike is present. Recall the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Have they not traveled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers are similar things﴾ [Muhammad 10]. Shu'ayb also warned his people that what befell those before them might befall them. So the conclusion is that nations must have the later take warning from the earlier, based on the fact that Allah's sunnah is one.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the negation of Allah's willing injustice to His servants: ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾. It is known that when the will is negated, the act is negated. So the negation of the desire of injustice is a negation of injustice a fortiori, just as verses explicitly negating injustice from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, have also come.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation that Allah, the Exalted, is described by negation, meaning that Allah is described by negative attributes, which some scholars call negative attributes (al-sifat al-salbiyya), because negation is a privation.

But if someone says: Is there praise and commendation in negation, given that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾ [al-Nahl 60]? The attributes of Allah are all attributes of perfection, and negation is an absence, so is it praise and commendation?

The answer: As for other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, it does not indicate perfection or praise. As for Allah, it must indicate perfection, because of His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾. So every negation that Allah negated of Himself includes perfection. The evidence is this verse: ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾. Otherwise, bare negation does not indicate perfection at all, and sometimes it indicates deficiency. Consider the saying of a poet, for example:
"A tribe that does not betray a covenant, and does not wrong people even by a mustard seed."
He described them as not breaking covenants and not wronging. Apparently this is praise, but in reality it is a reproach: it reproaches them as cowardly and weak people, who do not betray because they lack the courage, and do not wrong because they lack the power. Likewise is the saying of another poet:
"But my people, though they are numerous, are in no way evil, even if they are humiliated."
That is, they are not evil at all, even if they are humbled.
"They repay the injustice of the unjust with forgiveness, and the evil of the evildoers with kindness."
Then he said:
"Would that I had among them a people who, when they ride, launch raids as horsemen and riders."
Here he reproaches them, although when wronged they forgive their wrongdoers, and when wronged they do good to those who wronged them. This is a trait that may appear desirable and praiseworthy, but if the reason for it is that they are weak, it becomes blameworthy.

The summary now is that it is impossible for there to be in the attributes of Allah a pure negation at all. The evidence is His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾, and pure negation is not part of the highest description in any way. But when Allah negates something of Himself, the intent is to affirm the perfection of its opposite; that is, because the perfection of its opposite is established, that thing is negated of Him.

So what is the opposite of injustice? Justice. Therefore, when we negate injustice from Allah, we affirm the perfection of His justice, and that He, the Majestic and Exalted, does not wrong because of His perfect justice, not because of incapacity. No, He is able to wrong, but He does not wrong because of the perfection of His justice. For this reason, in the authentic hadith qudsi: "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself," he did not say "O My servants, I am unable to wrong." He said: "I have forbidden injustice to Myself." This indicates that He is capable of wronging, but He does not wrong because of the perfection of His justice. And if He were incapable of wronging, the negation of injustice from Him would not be praise, because He would be powerless. But He is capable, and yet He does not wrong.

I say this because the Jahmiyya and others said: Allah is unable to wrong at all. To this Ibn al-Qayyim alluded in his Nuniyya when he said:
"Injustice, in their view, is impossible by its very nature..."
That is: it is impossible in its essence, not because of Allah's perfection, but in its essence; it is impossible for Him to wrong. Why? He said: Because injustice is for a person to dispose of the property of another, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, disposes of His own dominion, so if He wrongs He is not a wrongdoer, because it is His dominion. It is said to them: Woe to your corrupt minds! If the believer is promised something for a specific deed, and he performs that deed, and He does not give it to him, what would that be? It would be injustice without doubt. Yet you say: It is permissible that He reward the disobedient who disobeys Allah all his life, and punish the obedient who obeys Allah all his life, and that both are equal, because He does not wrong since He disposes of His own dominion. We say: This is without doubt foolishness in intellect and error in religion. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, promised the doer of righteous deeds reward, and the opponent punishment. How could it be permissible for Allah to break His promise?

In any case, this is a false view, and merely conceiving it shows a person that it is false.

So the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾: we say: The negation of the desire of injustice entails the perfection of His justice, and it also entails the negation of injustice, because whoever does not desire injustice cannot possibly commit injustice.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 32 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said: ﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out (yawm al-tanad)﴾ [Ghafir 32]. May Allah be pleased with this man. He first warned them of worldly punishment when he said: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you a day like the day of the factions﴾, then he warned them of the punishment of the Hereafter, saying: ﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out﴾. He said: (with the letter ya' omitted and affirmed). ﴿al-tanadi﴾ with the ya' affirmed, and ﴿al-tanad﴾ with it omitted. As for its affirmation, it is the original form; as for its omission, it is for lightness (of pronunciation). The ya' is always omitted for lightness, a recitation, yes indeed, and the ya' is always omitted, always, for lightness, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So do not hasten Me﴾ [al-Anbiya' 37]. What is its original form? (tasta'jiluni), and the nun here is not the nun of raising (nun al-raf') because it is kasra, so it is the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya), and the ya' was omitted for lightness.

Now, ﴿O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out﴾: the word ﴿yawm﴾ here, is it a temporal adverb in the accusative, with the meaning: "Indeed I fear for you the punishment on the Day of Calling Out"? Or is the verb applied to it so that it is a direct object? The second, because of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They fear a Day in which hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾ [al-Nur 37], where He made the fear govern a day, because yawm can be a temporal object, a direct object, a subject, or the predicate of a subject; it is inflected.

He says: (﴿Yawm al-tanad﴾ with the ya' omitted and affirmed, meaning: the Day of Resurrection). This is what is meant by it. In my speech I have pointed to the rules of tafsir: that there is a verbal (lafzi) explanation and a second, meaning-based (ma'nawi) explanation. The verbal explains the wording, and the meaning-based explains the intended sense. So here, the verbal explanation of ﴿yawm al-tanad﴾ is: the day when people call out to one another. Its intended meaning is the Day of Resurrection. So when we say ﴿yawm al-tanad﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, this is not a verbal explanation but a meaning-based explanation of what the verse intends.

He says: (﴿Yawm al-tanad﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, in which the calls of the people of Paradise to the people of the Fire, and the reverse, will abound, and the calling out for the happiness of its people and the wretchedness of its people, and other things). Calling out on the Day of Resurrection abounds: Allah calls the people, and the people call one another, the people of the Fire call the people of Paradise, and the people of Paradise call the people of the Fire. The calling out that occurs on the Day of Resurrection is not like the calling out that occurs in this world, because it is with disturbing and sorrowful voices when the people of the Fire call the people of Paradise and the like. This day is what this believer reminded his people of, so that they would beware of the punishment of the Day of Resurrection.

Then He clarified that by His saying: (﴿The day you will turn back, fleeing﴾ from the place of reckoning to the Fire, ﴿you will have no protector from Allah﴾, meaning: from His punishment, ﴿none to save you﴾ preventing it, ﴿and whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾). He described this day with attributes:
First: it is the Day of Calling Out, when people call to one another, and Allah also calls to them, and they call out with calls some of which may be unknown to us now.

The second attribute: ﴿the day you will turn back, fleeing﴾. ﴿Yawm﴾ here is either a substitute for ﴿yawm al-tanad﴾ or an explanatory apposition. ﴿Mudbirin﴾ here is a circumstantial clause (hal). Is it a confirming hal for its governing verb or for its subject? For its governing verb, because turning back is fleeing. On this basis it is a confirming hal for its governing verb; meaning: you turn back on the Day of Resurrection while you are fleeing. To what do they turn? To the Fire, and we seek Allah's refuge. ﴿The Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation, and drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ [Maryam 85-86]. So they, we seek Allah's refuge, turn back fleeing.

He said: ﴿You have no protector from Allah﴾. This sentence is a declarative sentence beginning with the negating (ma), and its subject is ﴿from a protector﴾, but the superfluous ﴿min﴾ has entered upon it for emphasis; the sense of the sentence is: "If not for min, what you have from Allah is a protector." Here we ask: is it the Tamimi or the Hijazi dialect? Both dialects agree on it, because it is not Hijazi except with the word order, as Ibn Malik said:
"... with the persistence of negation and order it is retained"
and here there is no order, because the predicate is fronted. On this basis we say: the ma here is one in which both the Tamimi and Hijazi dialects agree.

﴿You have no protector from Allah﴾, meaning: no preventer. ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾. This sentence may raise a difficulty: how did he conclude his call to Allah with it, since the situation would seem to call for him to say: "And I ask Allah to guide you"?
It is said: is the saying ﴿whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ from the words of the man or from the words of Allah? We must investigate before anything else: is it from the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to show that these people, despite the strength of the call, did not benefit; or is it from the words of the believer? If it is from the words of Allah, there is no difficulty, except that it intervened between the beginning and end of the speech, and this is not harmful, because parenthetical sentences come often. If it is from the words of the man, then this is the point of difficulty, and we defer the matter to you until tomorrow, God willing; let the answer come from you tomorrow, and Allah knows best.

* A student: (...) at the beginning of the call, pressure upon him or the like (...) and reason judges, how does a person know that the results will be good (...)?
* The Shaykh: There is no doubt that calling to Allah with gentleness is closer to good results than harshness, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «Indeed Allah is gentle and loves gentleness in all matters»[[Reported by al-Bukhari (6927) from the hadith of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her.]] and likewise he said: «Indeed Allah gives through gentleness what He does not give through harshness»[[Reported by Muslim (2593/77) from the hadith of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her.]]. This is clear; meaning: even if we only used what is better and what Allah the Mighty and Majestic loves, it would suffice, and we now observe that good results in calling come through gentleness.
There are many incidents. It is said that one of the shaykhs of the call from the family of the Shaykh, people came to him to complain about a worker, not a foreign worker: in the past people would water camels, cows and donkeys, and the one who drives the water-wheel is called a worker, and usually he has a long stick of good palm-frond stalk, because he wants to drive camels, cows or donkeys. Some of those who enjoin good and forbid evil came to him at sunset, when people were glorifying Allah and proclaiming His oneness, while this man was singing at the top of his voice, for what purpose? Because this causes the animals to become excited and hasten, the animal delights in singing, as the Messenger said: «Gently with the glass vessels»[[Reported by al-Bukhari (6149) and Muslim (2323/70) from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, and its wording: "Woe to you, O Anjasha, gently, drive the glass vessels."]]. So they spoke to him: people are glorifying and praising and proclaiming at this time, and you have raised the voice of Satan. He said: What do you say? They said: This is what we say. The driving-stick you call the driving-stick (...) he struck them, and said: I drive my camels to water my crops, and you say I raise Satan's voice. They left, because he was strong, large of body and energetic. They turned away from him and came to the Shaykh and said: O Shaykh, this man so-and-so did such-and-such. He said: What did you say to him? They said: (...) people are glorifying and proclaiming, and you are singing; so he rose against one of us with the stick. He said: Alright, apparently the error is on your part, but let us first try gentleness. The next day that scholarly shaykh went at sunset and found the man in the same state, singing and driving the camels. He placed his cloak on the stick on a palm tree there and performed ablution, and had called the adhan after finishing the ablution. He came to the man while he was singing. Apparently I do not know whether he responded to the muezzin or not. In any case, he said to him: O good man, shall I not direct you to something better than this? Now, if you go and pray and then return, Allah will send blessing upon you, and prayer is a cause of provision: ﴿Enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it; We do not ask you for provision, We provide for you﴾ [Ta-Ha 132]. In any case, he spoke to him calmly. He said: May Allah protect you, may Allah reward you with good. Yesterday some men came to me, I was doing the same as I do today, and they stood speaking against me, and said: this is the voice of Satan. By Allah, I was unable to control myself and struck one of them, but may Allah reward you with good on my behalf. The shaykh went to pray, and when he had prayed and finished, the man had caught up but missed one rak'ah. He left him and said nothing. On the next day he went to perform ablution at sunset and he said nothing to him at all; he found him on the next day praying and nothing had been missed. Glory be to Allah! In any case, gentleness is all good, and this is a tested matter. But sometimes a person, because of the zeal within him, is stirred and cannot control himself; we say: calm down, because you are like a doctor who wants to cut the wound, so it must be done calmly and in the manner by which the desired result is achieved.

* The student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out (32). The day you will turn back, fleeing; you will have no protector from Allah, and whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide (33). And Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you, until, when he died, you said: Allah will never send after him any messenger. Thus does Allah leave astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter﴾ [Ghafir 32-34].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾. Before we enter the explanation of the new part, let us ask about what has preceded:
The saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, about the believer of Pharaoh's family: ﴿like the custom of the people of Noah and 'Ad and Thamud﴾. What is the meaning of "mithl da'b"?
* The student: Like the recompense of the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud.
* The Shaykh: That is, like their recompense, not like their custom.
* The student: By supposing an omitted noun (...).
* The Shaykh: So it is an expression of the recompense by the deed.
Is this common in the Qur'an, to express the recompense by the deed?
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: What is the wisdom in it?
* The student: Because the intended thing is the recompense (...) so that it is more forceful in warning, where the deed is mentioned and the recompense is mentioned.
* Another student: The recompense is of the same kind as the deed.
* The Shaykh: To show that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed, whether in good or in evil.
The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾. Does the verse contain anything indicating the negation of injustice from Allah?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And how is that, when the verse does not say "Allah does not do injustice" but says: ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice﴾?
* A student: That Allah did not desire injustice (...).
* The Shaykh: I ask you now: is there evidence in it for negating injustice from Allah?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: How is that, when the verse says: ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice﴾?
* A student: That he mentioned it in a hadith..
* The Shaykh: Leave the hadith; we want from the verse itself?
* A student: Because the negation of the desire (...).
* The Shaykh: Correct; because negating the desire necessarily entails negating its occurrence all the more.
The negation of the desire of injustice is a negation of injustice. What do we benefit from the negation of injustice, which is a negative attribute, and negation is an absence?
* A student: Negation is an absence; this is in the attributes of created beings, but in the attributes of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, negation is intended to affirm the perfection of its opposite.
* The Shaykh: That is, pure negation does not exist..
* The student: In the attributes of Allah.
* The Shaykh: So what does negating the desire of injustice include here?
* The student: The perfection of justice for Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.
* The Shaykh: Well done, may Allah bless you. Now, the saying of Allah: ﴿The Day of Calling Out﴾?
* A student: The Day of Resurrection.
* The Shaykh: What is meant by it is the Day of Resurrection.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And what is the meaning of "tanad"?
* The student: The calling of the people of the Fire.
* The Shaykh: That is, the calling out among the people, and from it?
* The student: The calling of the people of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection..
* The Shaykh: To whom?
* The student: The people of Paradise.
* The Shaykh: Good. What is the difference between the first warning and the second? ﴿Like the day of the factions﴾, then he said: ﴿Indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out﴾?
* A student: He warned them of worldly punishment and of the punishment of the Hereafter.
* The Shaykh: Well done. The first is a worldly punishment, and the second is an otherworldly punishment.

We take the benefits, God willing:
From the benefits of the verse ﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out﴾ [Ghafir 32]:
* From the benefits of the verse: that this warner was a believer in the Last Day.
* And from its benefits: that what happens on the Last Day was known to people before the Qur'an was revealed, as shown by His saying ﴿the Day of Calling Out﴾; this is because it is a matter that cannot be avoided, that is, the servants must know what happens on the Last Day in order to be informed about their affair.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that the Day of Resurrection has states; Allah the Exalted said in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿And voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a murmur﴾ [Ta-Ha 108]. Here He mentions that it is a day of calling out, and calling is a loud voice; on this basis the combination of this verse with His saying ﴿And voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a murmur﴾ [Ta-Ha 108] is that the Day of Resurrection has states, because its duration is fifty thousand years, so the conditions of people must change.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: the counsel of this man to his people, in that he addresses them with this gentle call ﴿O my people﴾.
Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said, completing what this warner mentioned: ﴿The day you will turn back, fleeing; you will have no protector from Allah﴾ [Ghafir 33]. Its grammatical analysis is well known: it is a substitute for what preceded. In it: confirmation that the people of Pharaoh will turn back fleeing on the Day of Resurrection if they do not believe. Allah has explained in another verse that they are presented to the Fire morning and evening, and that on the Day of Resurrection it will be said: admit the people of Pharaoh to the severest punishment. So they, we seek Allah's refuge, will turn back fleeing, tormented in the Fire of Hell.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that no one can protect from the punishment of Allah; because of His saying ﴿You will have no protector from Allah﴾. This is like Noah's saying to his son when ﴿he said: I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾ [Hud 43], and he said: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah, except for whom He shows mercy.﴾ And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned﴾ [Hud 43].
* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ [Ghafir 33]. ("Man") here is conditional, the conditional verb is ("yudlil"), and it was given a kasra because two unvocalized letters met; the response of the condition is the clause ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ and it is joined with "fa'" because it is not suitable to be a verb of the condition; every response that is not suitable to be a verb of the condition must be joined with "fa'", as Ibn Malik said:
"Join with fa' absolutely a response if it is made the condition of 'in' or other than it, if it is not..."
They mentioned six rules for it, gathered in his saying:
"Nominal, imperative, and with a rigid word, and with ma, qad, and with lan, and with the future marker..."
So when these six sentence types occur as a response to the condition, it must be joined with "fa'". Here the sentence is? It begins with (ma), or if you wish, say it is a nominal sentence; there is no objection to two causes existing for one ruling.
And His saying ﴿min hadin﴾ originally was: "min hadi", with the ya' and the ya' was omitted for lightness.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: "Whoever Allah causes to go astray" — i.e., whoever Allah has decreed to lead astray, there is no one who can guide him, because the One who guides and leads astray is Allah alone; the affair is entirely in His hand. However, it should be known that He does not guide anyone except for a wisdom, and He does not lead anyone astray except for a wisdom. So whoever is deserving of guidance, He guides him, and whoever is deserving of being led astray, He leads him astray — and we seek refuge in Allah. Otherwise, Allah, glorified and exalted, does not withhold His bounty from one who desires it; rather, He withholds His bounty only from one who does not desire it. The evidence for this is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5]. Thus He made Allah's causing their hearts to deviate a consequence of their deviation. As for one who sincerely desires guidance, Allah, glorified and exalted, facilitates it for him: ﴿As for he who gives and fears Allah, and believes in the best [reward], We will ease him toward ease﴾ [al-Layl: 5–7]. So, His statement ﴿And whoever Allah leads astray, for him there is no guide﴾ is restricted by what? By one who has done what necessitates his being led astray, because Allah does not lead anyone astray except for a wisdom.

* Among the benefits of this verse: when a person wishes to ask for guidance, he must ask for it only from Allah, the One in whose hand is misguidance and guidance. So do not ask for guidance from other than Him; ask it from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Thus it is derived from it that the matter is to be entrusted to Allah, blessed and exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 34 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Joseph had already come to you before with the clear proofs, but you continued in doubt about what he had brought you.﴾ [Ghafir 34] Whose speech is this? It is the speech of the believing man who warned his people. He said: ﴿Laqad ja'akum (Indeed, he came to you)﴾. The sentence here is emphasized by three emphatics: the lam (the emphatic lam), qad, and the oath. Whenever you encounter a construction like this, it is emphasized by three emphatics: the lam, qad, and the oath, because the underlying sense of the sentence is: "By Allah, indeed he came to you."

His saying ﴿Yusuf (Joseph)﴾ refers to Joseph son of Jacob. If someone says: How does he address them by saying "he came to you" when Joseph son of Jacob was many ages before them?

It is said: What happened to the forefathers is attributed to their descendants. That is, what came to their forefathers is like what came to them. The evidence for this is that Allah addresses the Children of Israel in the time of the Prophet ﷺ with what happened to their forefathers in the time of Moses, and many generations lay between them: ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly," so the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on. Then We revived you after your death that you might be grateful. And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah 55-57]. It is well known that all of this did not happen to the Jews in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, but it happened to their forefathers. Whatever is true of the first of a nation is established for its last. So there is no difficulty in this verse, as long as we say that their forefathers came, and that what happened to their forefathers in the past is ascribed to all of them, so long as they do not depart from this course.

(﴿And Joseph had already come to you before with the clear proofs﴾, that is, before Moses, and he is Joseph son of Jacob) and so on to the end.

His saying ﴿min qabl (before)﴾: why is it put in the nominative with a damma, when it is well known that min is a preposition, and when it governs a noun it makes it genitive by kasra? You say: min Zaydin. Here he said min qablu?

A student: It is indeclinable (mabniyy).

The Shaykh: Indeclinable! La ilaha illa Allah. What is the reason for its being indeclinable?

The student: Sometimes it is inflected and sometimes it is indeclinable.

The Shaykh: Good, sometimes it is indeclinable and sometimes it is inflected. When is it indeclinable and when is it inflected?

The student: (...).

The Shaykh: That is, when it is not annexed (idafah), it is indeclinable. Good, and when it is annexed?

The student: It is inflected.

The Shaykh: Absolutely.

The student: The second term of the annexation has been omitted and its meaning is intended.

The Shaykh: Excellent. The second term of the annexation has been omitted and its meaning is intended. This is because either the first term of the annexation exists, or it is omitted while its meaning is intended, or it is omitted while its wording is intended, or it is omitted and neither its wording nor its meaning is intended. So there are four cases. It is indeclinable in one of them, and the rest are inflected. It is indeclinable when the second term is omitted and its meaning is intended.

If someone says: What is the evidence? We say: The evidence is that it is vowelled with a damma, because it is built on the damma. So when someone who knows Arabic speaks to us and vowels it with a damma, we know that he omitted the second term and intended its meaning.

He says: ﴿min qabl (before)﴾, that is, before the coming of Moses, peace be upon him. (And he is Joseph son of Jacob according to one opinion, who lived until the time of Moses; or Joseph son of Ibrahim son of Joseph son of Jacob according to another opinion.) That is, the author, may Allah have mercy on him, related two opinions about who is meant by Joseph. It was said that he is Joseph son of Jacob, and that he lived until the time of Moses. This is a false opinion with no difficulty about it; it is not correct but rather false, because if that were the case, he would have come to Moses and been connected with him, since both were messengers.

The second opinion is that he is Joseph and his grandfather Joseph son of Jacob, Joseph son of Ibrahim son of Joseph. This too has no evidence. The correct view is that the intended one is Joseph son of Jacob, and that he did not live until the time of Moses, but died in his own time. Yet what came to their forefathers came to them, because, as you know, Joseph, peace be upon him, was taken by the passing caravan that came by the well into which he had been thrown, and they took him to Egypt. The story is well known and is told in a full surah.

His saying ﴿bil-bayyinat (with the clear proofs)﴾: "al-bayyinat" comes from "bana yubinu," meaning it became manifest. It is well known that it is an adjective of an omitted noun. This is because it is permissible to omit the adjective and to omit the noun modified when a clue indicates it. So what is omitted here? The omitted noun is estimated as "al-ayat (the signs)," as the Quran often expresses it: "al-ayat al-bayyinat (the clear signs)," "ayat bayyinat (clear signs)," and similar expressions.

As for his saying "(bil-mu'jizat, with miracles)," this is a later expression that was not known in the time of the early generations (salaf), and it is an incomplete expression. This is because the word "mu'jizah (miracle)" includes what sorcerers and charlatans do of extraordinary things that defy custom, since it defeats those who are not of their kind. But when it is said "ayah (sign)" in the sense of an indication, it becomes clearer, more evident, and more fitting, because it agrees with the Quranic expression. Moreover, it is not possible for a sign to be given to a messenger unless people are unable to produce its like, and why is that? Because if they were able to bring its like, it would not be a sign for the Prophet, since each person would bring it.

Good, so the estimated sentence is: "bil-ayat al-bayyinat," but the noun modified has been omitted because the context indicates it. Among its examples is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Make full coats of mail and proportion well the links﴾ [Saba' 11], meaning: make full coats of mail. Good.

﴿bil-bayyinat, fa-ma ziltum fi shakkin mimma ja'akum bihi (but you continued in doubt about what he had brought you)﴾. That is, from the time of Joseph until the time of Moses and the family of Pharaoh. If you wish, you may express it as "the Copts": in doubt about what Joseph brought, so they did not believe in it with the obligatory faith that is free of doubt.

(﴿Until, when he died, you said﴾, without proof, ﴿"Allah will never send after him a messenger"﴾). That is, they were in doubt about what Joseph brought and did not believe him. When he died, their own souls said to them: Now you have rested. Allah will never send a messenger after him. You have been spared. The one who was sent has died, and you denied him, so be at ease: Allah will never send a messenger after him. They said this on the basis of a false wish, because they said: This messenger who came to us and threatened us if we opposed him has died, so no messenger will come after him, and then we will be rid of the messengers and their troubles, according to their claim.

(﴿You said, "Allah will never send after him a messenger"﴾, that is, you will continue disbelieving in Joseph and others), because when they settled in their souls that Allah would never send a messenger, they would deny every messenger who came after Joseph on the basis of this corrupt belief they had established.

Allah, the Exalted, said: (﴿Thus﴾, that is, like your misguidance, ﴿Allah misguides whoever is a transgressor﴾, an associator, ﴿a doubter﴾, one who is in doubt about what the clear proofs testified to.) ﴿Thus﴾: the mufassir said: "that is, like your misguidance, Allah misguides." On this basis, its grammatical analysis is: the kaf is a noun meaning "like," and it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) annexed to the demonstrative noun, and its governing verb is ﴿yudillu (misguides)﴾. Its governing element comes after it. This Quranic expression is frequent in the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and its grammar is as you have heard: you say, the kaf is a noun meaning "like," in the accusative as an absolute object, annexed to the demonstrative.

If it is said: Does the kaf come as a noun? We say: Yes, the Arabic language is wide. Otherwise, the basic status of kaf is a particle, but it can be a noun. Ibn Malik said:

"Liken with the kaf, and with it the causal (ta'lil) may be intended; it may be an extra one for emphasis, and it occurs. It is used as a noun, and likewise 'an and 'ala..."

"Used as a noun": that is, the kaf is used as a noun in the Arabic language.

﴿Thus﴾, that is, like that, ﴿Allah misguides whoever is a transgressor, a doubter﴾. Allah, the Exalted, does not misguide a believing man who is moderate and firmly certain, ever. Allah, may we seek refuge with Him, misguides whoever is a transgressor and a doubter.

He says: (﴿Transgressor﴾, an associator). There is no doubt that shirk is a form of transgression (israf), because israf means exceeding the limit, and whoever sets up a partner with Allah has undoubtedly exceeded the limit. But the meaning of the verse is more general than the associator. The transgressor is one who exceeds his limit, whether by excess or by deficiency, though usually it is by excess, because transgressing the limit is an increase. So the associator is undoubtedly a transgressor, and the arrogant one is a transgressor, and the denier is a transgressor, and so on. Thus ﴿man huwa musrif (whoever is a transgressor)﴾ should be explained as: whoever goes beyond his limit, like the associator.

As for his saying: (﴿Murtab (a doubter)﴾, that is, one in doubt), we ask Allah, the Exalted, to protect us and you from doubt. The doubter, may we seek refuge with Allah, is one who is at ease with doubting, and he is not guided; he remains in his misguidance, may we seek refuge with Allah. But if Satan casts doubt into your heart and you then try to pull it out of your heart, Allah helps you against it and guides you. The true calamity is that you incline toward this doubt and do not free yourself from it. The evidence for this is what the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about what occurred in their souls, until they said: "We would wish that one of us were a charred coal (hummah), that is, a burnt ember, rather than speak of it." The Prophet ﷺ informed them that this does not harm them. Why? Because they do not incline to what came into their hearts. For this reason you must be courageous. If Satan casts such matters into your heart, be courageous. Do not incline to them and do not give yourself over to them. Be courageous. Use against him the weapon given to you by the One who knows it best, and the one who knows how to strike the enemy, which is the Messenger ﷺ. This is done by two things only:

To seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed, and then stop, turn away. Seek refuge with Allah, then stop, and this calamity will leave you. But if you give yourself over to it, the matter is extremely dangerous, because it works within your soul and grows until it reaches the level of doubt and uncertainty, and then you are deprived of guidance. There is no doubt that this expression is part of the wisdom of the Quran, so that what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned does not befall your soul. Its remedy is these two matters. If the most intelligent scholar tried to find a remedy for this calamity, he would not find one in this concise and easy expression. He said: "Let him seek refuge with Allah, then let him stop." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3276) and Muslim (134/214), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] Turn away from it, busy yourself with your affairs, and say: "I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed." Your busying yourself with your affairs and turning away from it causes you to forget it, and this is something observed and tested.

- Among the benefits of the verse: the completeness of this man's advice when he reminded his people of what had passed.
- Among them: a person should have knowledge of what came before, for history contains lessons, both in this great matter and in smaller matters. Read history and it will become clear to you what Allah has decreed for His servants, and that Allah's way (sunnah) with those before will be His way with those after. So among the benefits of the verse: a person should have experience of what came before.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the greatest messenger sent to the family of Pharaoh after Moses was Joseph. For this reason, the mention of those after him was folded away. Apparently, and Allah knows best, Allah does not leave this nation, that is, the nation of Pharaoh, without a messenger after Moses, who had many ages, but they were not like Joseph, so He highlighted the mention of Joseph.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: messengers come with clear proofs indicating their truthfulness and prophethood, because this is part of Allah's wisdom. If Allah sent a messenger to people with no sign and he said, "I am the messenger of Allah to you; believe in me, or else you will have the Fire," would they obey him? Never. They would say, "This is a madman." A sign that proves his truthfulness is necessary. It is established from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: "There is no messenger whom Allah sent except that He gave him signs by which mankind believed in the like of him." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7274) and Muslim (152/239), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and the wording is: "Of the prophets, there is no prophet except that he was given signs by which mankind believed in the like of him, but what I was given is a revelation that Allah revealed to me, so I hope to be the most numerous of them in following on the Day of Resurrection."] This is necessary.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the signs brought by the messengers are clear and are hidden only from the blind. The evidence for this is His saying ﴿bil-bayyinat (with the clear proofs)﴾. Here He emphasized the attribute rather than the modified noun, because the attribute is more important: that these signs are clear and hidden from no one.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the family of Pharaoh remained in doubt even with Joseph present. They were in doubt because Allah had not decreed their guidance, so they remained bewildered and persisted in disbelief.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the clarification of the aversion of the peoples who denied the messengers to what the messengers brought, because they seized the opportunity when Joseph died and said: ﴿Allah will never send after him a messenger﴾. This shows that they were extremely constricted by the presence of Joseph, peace be upon him.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: belief in the existence of Allah is not sufficient for monotheism (tawhid) and for deliverance from the punishment of Allah. From where is this taken? From their saying: ﴿Allah will never send﴾. These people acknowledged Allah, yet their acknowledgment of Allah did not benefit them.

Likewise, those to whom the Messenger ﷺ was sent acknowledged Allah. ﴿Say, "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth, or who controls hearing and sight, and who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and who arranges the affair?" They will say, "Allah."﴾ [Yunus 31] They affirmed lordship completely, and that the Arranger is Allah. Yet the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, made their blood, wealth, women, offspring, and land lawful, because mere belief in Allah is not belief at all. Belief in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in its four known aspects, is necessary: belief in His existence, in His lordship, in His divinity, and in His names and attributes. This is required, and whoever does not believe in this way is not a believer in Allah.

- Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's misguidance occurs only in the case of one who deserves misguidance, as in His saying: ﴿Thus Allah misguides whoever is a transgressor, a doubter﴾ [Ghafir 34].
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever keeps to his limit and is certain of what must be believed with certainty is farthest from being misguided. Is this taken from the implication (mafhum) or from the explicit statement (manțuq)? From the implication. If Allah misguides whoever is a transgressor and a doubter, then He guides whoever keeps to his limit, is certain about his affair, and believes in that. ﴿Thus Allah misguides whoever is a transgressor, a doubter﴾. And Allah knows best.

A student: Shaykh, in the previous lesson there was a difficulty you asked us to tell you about, which is His saying: ﴿Whomever Allah misguides, there is for him no guide﴾. You said: why did he not say, after this advice, "I ask Allah to guide you," or something of this sort? (...).

The Shaykh: Good, read.

The student: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. It is stated in the tafsir Al-Tahrir wa-l-Tanwir: His saying ﴿Whomever Allah misguides, there is for him no guide﴾ is coordinated (ataf) with the clause ﴿Indeed, I fear for you﴾, because it includes the meaning: "I guide you to beware of the Day of Calling Out." There is an implicit brevity in the speech, indicated by the coordinated clause, and the estimated sense is: this is guidance for you. If Allah guides you, you will act upon it, and if you turn away from it, that is because Allah has misguided you, ﴿Whomever Allah misguides, there is for him no guide﴾. The clause contains the sense of a concluding generalization (tadhyil). He did not say to them, "Whomever Allah guides, there is for him no misguider," because he sensed their turning away and did not discern in them signs of benefiting from his advice and admonition.

His saying ﴿Whomever Allah misguides, there is for him no guide﴾ means: He guides him to the path of salvation in the first place. It is as if the man despaired of their accepting his advice, so he said that.

The Shaykh: This is the apparent meaning: that the man was in despair. This is like the saying of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant. Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not beget except a wicked disbeliever﴾ [Nuh 26-27].

The student: We said: (...) the verse, that israf is divided into two categories. Here he explained israf as associating partners, and another verse says: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be excessive﴾ [al-A'raf 31] (...). Is it divided into two categories?

Shaykh: Most things are divided into two or more categories. Extravagance (israf) has a greater and a lesser degree and a middle degree. So the one who is extravagant in associating partners with God is not like the one who is extravagant in a loaf of bread that he eats.

(...)

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 35 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Those who dispute﴾ [Ghafir 35]. Al-mujadalah (disputation) is contention and debate aimed at silencing the opponent. It is derived from jadl al-habl, meaning twisting a rope; when a rope is twisted it becomes firmer and stronger.
