Thus you will find the disputant becoming stubborn and hardening himself in order to overcome his opponent.

His saying: ﴿concerning the signs of Allah﴾. The author of the tafsir said: (His miracles). The correct formulation is to say: the signs of Allah, meaning the indications that point to what Allah, may He be exalted, deserves of lordship, divinity, names, attributes, rulings and other things. This is the intended meaning. We have already noted that one should not call the ayat "miracles," because that is an imprecise expression which does not define the meaning, and it may lead to confusion with the deeds of charlatans and magicians, since they too are (apparently) miraculous.

His saying: ﴿who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾. Do they dispute in order to establish the signs or to deny them? The latter, without doubt. For this reason He said: ﴿without any authority﴾, because if they were disputing in order to establish the signs and affirm them, they would have had authority.

His saying: ﴿without any authority having come to them﴾. The author said: (proof). That is, without any evidence. Al-sultan (authority) is everything by which authority is exercised, and its meaning varies according to context. The supreme ruler is called al-sultan because he possesses authority, and evidence is called sultan because the one who grasps it possesses authority. Accordingly, the meaning of ﴿without authority﴾ is: without evidence.

He said: ﴿without authority﴾, because if they were disputing in order to establish the signs and affirm them, they would have had authority.

His saying: ﴿without any authority having come to them﴾. The author said: (proof), that is, without evidence. Al-sultan is everything by which authority is exercised, and it varies according to context; the supreme ruler is called al-sultan because he possesses authority, and evidence is called sultan because the one who grasps it possesses authority. Accordingly, the meaning of ﴿without authority﴾ is: without evidence.

This qualification, or circumstantial clause, namely ﴿without authority﴾, is a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to the subject of ﴿yujadilun﴾. This description is a description that clarifies the actual state of affairs and is not a restrictive qualifier. The difference is that if we said it is a restrictive qualifier, it would mean that those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah in order to nullify them sometimes have authority and sometimes do not; whereas in reality they have no authority at all. A qualifier that clarifies the actual state carries no implied restriction (mafhum), and this occurs frequently in the Qur'an. Its purpose is argumentation, that is, it functions as a justification (ta'lil) for the thing described.

Consider the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof, then his account is only with his Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun 117]. His saying ﴿for which he has no proof﴾ describes the actual state and is not a restriction, because it is impossible for anyone to call upon another god besides Allah for which there is any proof.

Likewise His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾ [al-Anfal 24]. This does not mean that he may call us to what does not give us life; rather, he calls only to what gives us life. So it functions as a justification for the thing it qualifies, though it has become a qualifier in form.

Therefore, ﴿without any authority having come to them﴾ [Ghafir 35] we say: it is a description that clarifies the circumstance and reality, and that they have no authority for that. Thus it serves as a justification for what it describes. By "description" here I mean what includes both the circumstantial phrase and what is not circumstantial.

His saying: ﴿having come to them﴾ is a clause describing ﴿authority﴾. His saying: ﴿Great is their hatred﴾ is a clause that is the predicate of a subject. His saying: ﴿kabura﴾ means: became great. The letter "ba" is given a damma so that it takes the pattern fa'ula, because it is meant in the sense of wonder, that is: how great is their hatred in the sight of Allah!

He said: ﴿maqtan﴾ (hatred) is a specifier (tamyiz) of ﴿kabura﴾, because the greatness here refers to the disputation, meaning: their disputation is great in hatred. Thus it specifies the hidden subject.

The author's statement: (﴿kabura﴾ their disputation ﴿maqtan﴾) is more correctly expressed as: their hatred is great in hatred in the sight of Allah, because the specifier clarifies the hidden subject. His saying: ﴿maqtan﴾: al-maqt is the most intense hatred. His saying: ﴿'inda Allah﴾ is related to ﴿kabura﴾.

﴿Great is their hatred in the sight of Allah and in the sight of those who have believed﴾ [Ghafir 35]. That is: likewise the believers abhor these disputants concerning the signs of Allah without authority, who seek to refute the truth and promote falsehood. His saying: ﴿'inda alladhina amanu﴾: when "faith" (iman) is mentioned alone, it includes Islam, and when "Islam" is mentioned alone, it includes faith. So if you are asked whether Islam and faith are synonymous with one meaning, say: when mentioned separately they are synonymous; but when mentioned together, faith is explained as the deeds of the heart and Islam as the deeds of the limbs. An example is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿The bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts"﴾ [al-Hujurat 14]. Here He distinguished between faith and Islam, and clarified that faith had not yet entered their hearts, though it was close to entering, since "lamma" indicates proximity.

Thus, in the hadith of Jibril He distinguished between faith and Islam. Why?

* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And likewise when they are combined.

From the same: ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers. But We did not find therein except one house of the Muslims﴾ [al-Dhariyat 35-36]. He distinguished between this and that: those brought out were believers, and the house was Muslim, because in the house there was a disbelieving woman, the wife of Lut, who in outward appearance was a submitting Muslim, since she did not show that she was a disbeliever, as Allah said: ﴿but they betrayed them﴾ [al-Tahrim 10]. But when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, willed to save those who were to be saved from the people of Lut, He saved only the believers, while the woman remained with her people and perished.

He says: ﴿Thus does Allah seal every heart of arrogant tyrant﴾ [Ghafir 35]. We seek refuge in Allah. ﴿Thus﴾ has been discussed before, and we said that a construction like this parses as follows: the kaf is a noun meaning "like," and it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of the verb following it, the verb governing it being the verb that follows; and ﴿yatba'u﴾ is the governing verb. Accordingly we say: like this sealing, Allah seals.

As for the author's statement, may Allah have mercy on him, (like their misguidance), there is room for scrutiny, although sealing does imply misguidance. But it is better to explain it in a way that matches the governing verb, so it is said: like this sealing, Allah seals.

He said: (﴿yatba'u﴾ means: seals). Yes, tab' means sealing, as if Allah placed a covering over their hearts and then sealed it, just as documents are sealed. Allah alluded to this in His saying: ﴿And for their saying, "Our hearts are uncovered." Rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief﴾ [al-Nisa' 155].

(﴿Thus Allah seals﴾ with misguidance ﴿upon every heart of arrogant tyrant﴾): his saying "Allah seals with misguidance" is to be understood as previously stated, that the meaning is: Allah seals by sealing upon the hearts, upon every arrogant heart.

His saying: (﴿upon every heart of arrogant tyrant﴾ with tanwin on qalb and without it): ﴿'ala kulli qalbin mutakabbirin﴾ and ﴿'ala kulli qalbi mutakabbirin﴾. The difference is that on the reading with tanwin, arrogance is a description of the heart; on the reading with the construct (idafah), the sealing is upon the heart of the arrogant one, and the heart is not itself the arrogant one. The meaning is the same, because when the heart becomes arrogant the self becomes arrogant, according to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh: if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (52) and Muslim (1599), from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]

His saying: ﴿upon every heart that is arrogant﴾ or ﴿upon a arrogant heart﴾. Takabbur means self-elevation: a person raises himself up. It is of two kinds: arrogance toward creation and arrogance toward the truth. To this the saying of the Prophet ﷺ alludes: "Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down upon people."[[Narrated by Muslim (91/147) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Rejecting the truth means refusing it and not submitting to it; looking down upon people means despising them, so that one sees himself as above people. This is arrogance, and we seek refuge in Allah. It is well known that whoever rejects and disdains the truth will not act upon it, for how can one act upon something he regards as a deficiency? Likewise whoever looks down upon people will not be just with them, but will treat them with haughtiness, and we seek refuge in Allah. Thus sealing is fitting for such a heart. The Prophet ﷺ informed that "he who has in his heart an atom's weight of arrogance will not enter Paradise."

* Benefits of this verse:
* First: Allah's abhorrence of those who dispute concerning His signs in order to nullify them; from His saying: ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without authority having come to them—great is their hatred in the sight of Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: no one who disputes to refute the truth and promote falsehood has any authority; this is taken from His saying: ﴿without authority﴾.
* Among its benefits: strengthening the hearts of those who dispute for the truth. You know that disputation involves two sides. The disputant against Allah's signs, seeking to nullify them, has no argument; but does the opposing party have an argument or not? Thus, when one who seeks to establish the truth and nullify falsehood knows that his opponent has no authority, his heart will grow stronger and firmer. By implication, one learns that the disputant in defense of Allah's signs will have authority and strength.
* But does everyone who has an argument always manage to use it? No, he may not. He may know he is right, yet be unable to argue with it. For this reason a person should know the falsehood held by people in order to be able to refute them. As for one who does not read falsehood and says: whatever falsehood reaches me, I have the ability to defend against it, such a person may be left helpless in a place where he wishes to prevail. So a person must know falsehood in order to respond to it. This is why we see the research scholars reading the books of the logicians, the philosophers and others, and then refuting them. This applies to a man whose feet are firmly planted in knowledge. As for one who is just beginning as a student, we do not advise him to read the books of the people of misguidance, because he has no firm defense and it is feared he will be influenced by those books and go astray. But for one firmly grounded in knowledge we say: read, so that you know how to respond to them.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: one who disputes with truth is not blameworthy; this is shown by His saying: ﴿without authority﴾, for if they had authority they would be upon truth, but they have no authority.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of hatred (maqt) for Allah, Exalted is He, and that it varies in degree, so that His hatred toward one person or group may be greater than His hatred toward another. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿Great is their hatred in the sight of Allah﴾.

Is this hatred a true attribute, or is what is meant its consequence, which is punishment? The former. This is the position of the people of the Sunnah and the community, who say: whatever Allah has described Himself with is upon its reality, but we must know that it does not resemble the attributes of created beings, for Allah affirmed and negated: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾ [al-Shura 11]. Take this as a firm principle and proceed by it in everything Allah has described Himself with. Do not say: this is not meant in its apparent sense. Whatever Allah has described Himself with is meant in its apparent sense, yet exalted above resemblance to created beings. Thus Allah, Exalted is He, truly hates, detests, abhors and loves, in accordance with its reality, yet He does not resemble the attributes of created beings.

Those people of negation (ta'til) who judge Allah by their intellects rather than by His speech and the speech of His Messenger hold that such descriptions must necessarily be interpreted as their consequences. They say, for example: the hatred meant is vengeance and punishment, not detestation, dislike, or anything stronger. It is said to them: if you interpret it as punishment, you commit two errors:

The first error: removing the speech of Allah from its apparent meaning.
The second error: affirming a meaning that is not intended by the words.

Do you understand?

Likewise we say of every distorter that he has committed two errors: the first, removing speech from its apparent meaning, which is certainly a transgression, since it strips the word of its meaning; the second, affirming a meaning the word does not carry, which is also aggression. Thus every interpreter commits these two errors.

It is strange that they call themselves "the people of ta'wil" (interpretation), whereas the correct term is "the people of tahrif" (distortion). They adopted this name to soften what they hold of falsehood, since ta'wil may denote a sound meaning and may denote a false one: if we interpret speech according to what the speaker intended, that is sound; but otherwise it is false, and this is what they hold. Yet they shifted from the term tahrif to the term ta'wil.

Observe the precision of the expression of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, in al-'Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah, where he said: "without distortion (tahrif) and without negation (ta'til)." He did not say "without interpretation (ta'wil)," even though most of those who speak or write on creed say "without interpretation." What he said is correct, because every interpretation not indicated by evidence is distortion.

So we affirm for Allah that He truly hates, detests and abhors, in accordance with its reality. As for punishment, it is a necessary consequence of that. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, and others said: if you affirm that Allah punishes, then you have affirmed by implication that Allah hates, since He punishes only those He hates; it is impossible for one to punish someone he loves. Thus, in fleeing from affirming hatred or detestation, you have fallen into it from another direction. We say: punishment is only after hatred and detestation; this is a necessary matter, since no one who loves a person would stand up and strike him.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of "with Allah" (indah Allah). The "with" is of two kinds: "with" of attribute and "with" of nearness. The saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship﴾ [al-A'raf 206] is "with" of nearness. His saying here: ﴿Great is their hatred in the sight of Allah﴾ is "with" of attribute, because hatred is not something separate and detached from Allah such that it would be "with" of nearness. Rather, this is "with" of attribute, just as you say to someone: "You are dear to me," meaning it while he is far from you; the meaning is not that you are dear to me in the sense of being near; no, this is "with" of attribute, that is, your honour subsists in me.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the believers also abhor what Allah abhors, from His saying: ﴿and in the sight of those who have believed﴾. This is a sign of faith. Take it as a measure and a balance of justice: whenever you find in yourself that you hate what Allah hates and love what Allah loves, that is faith. This verse and other verses and hadiths indicate it, and reason indicates it too, for part of the perfection of love and faith is that you love what the one you love loves, and hate what he hates.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of faith, in that the believer revolves with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in loving what He loves and hating what He hates.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: warning against arrogance, and that it is a cause of the sealing of the heart, we seek refuge in Allah, in His saying: ﴿Thus does Allah seal every heart of arrogant tyrant﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: warning against tyranny (jabarut), which is exalting oneself over others, being harsh toward them, and the like, from His saying: ﴿every arrogant tyrant heart﴾. So the verse contains a warning against arrogance and tyranny.
* Among the benefits of the verse: a refutation of the one who says: "Perfection is to be characterised by the attributes of the Perfect." They mean Allah, and none is more perfect than Allah.

We say: this is among the best of principles, and a human being cannot compete with Allah in His attributes. So how about arrogance, tyranny, haughtiness and self-magnification with respect to Allah?

* Students: Perfection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 35 (part 2 of 2):

* The Shaykh: And as for us? It is a deficiency, a defect, and a cause of trials. With this, this principle that has no basis in soundness is nullified.
Indeed, some of them fabricated a hadith saying: "Take on the character of Allah" [[Al-Albani said in Silsilat al-Ahadith al-Da'ifa wa al-Mawdu'a (6/346): it has no basis. We say: but its meaning has come in some hadiths that have been spoken about, among them what al-Khatib narrated in his Tarikh (3/701) from Anas: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, what are the best deeds?" He said: "Prayer at its time." I said: "What is the best thing a person has been given?" He said: "Good character. Verily, good character is from the character of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." Al-Dhahabi, in his Mizan (1/524), accused some of its narrators of fabrication, and al-Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) refuted that in al-Lisan (2/257). Its meaning has also been reported from some of the salaf, such as Dhu al-Nun al-Misri and others, and from the statements of a group of scholars.]] I seek refuge in Allah. Do we name the attributes of Allah "characters"? Never, we do not name them so, because the word "akhlaq" (characters) may indicate an acquired character. Characters are of two kinds: innate (gharizi) and acquired (kasbi). There is no problem with this. For this reason, when the Messenger ﷺ said to the Ashajj of 'Abd al-Qays: "Verily, in you are two qualities that Allah loves: forbearance (al-hilm) and deliberation (al-anah)," he said: "O Messenger of Allah, are these two qualities that I acquired, or did Allah create me upon them?" He said: "Rather, Allah created you upon them" [[Ahmad (54) narrated with his chain from al-Wazza', may Allah be pleased with him: I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with al-Ashajj al-Mundhir ibn 'Amir, or 'Amir ibn al-Mundhir, and with them a man who was afflicted. They reached the Prophet ﷺ, and when they saw the Prophet ﷺ they leapt down from their mounts, came to the Prophet ﷺ, and kissed his hand. Then al-Ashajj dismounted, tied his mount, opened his saddlebag, took out two white garments from his clothes and wore them, then came to their mounts and tied them, and came to the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "O Ashajj, verily in you are two qualities that Allah and His Messenger love: forbearance and deliberation." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, are they qualities I acquired, or did Allah create me upon them?" He said: "Rather Allah created you upon them." He said: "Praise be to Allah who created me upon two qualities that Allah and His Messenger love." The hadith... Muslim (17/25) narrated it in abridged form from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] He said: "Praise be to Allah who created me upon what He loves," or words to that effect.
So character is both acquired and innate, and we cannot call the attributes of Allah Most High "characters" of His. Rather, we say: attributes, qualities, and the like. Moreover, some scholars denied that one should say "Allah has a sifah (attribute)," such as Ibn Hazm. Ibn Hazm, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Beware of saying 'Allah has a sifah'; Allah has no sifah. Names are fine, but sifah, no." However, he is refuted by the words of the man who used to recite "Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad" and said: "It is the attribute of the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7375) and Muslim (813/263) from the hadith of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, and the wording is that the Prophet ﷺ sent a man at the head of a detachment, and he used to lead his companions in prayer and would end with "Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad." When they returned they mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "Ask him why he does that." They asked him, and he said: "Because it is the attribute of the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Tell him that Allah loves him."]].
In any case, we say that this verse clearly indicates the falsehood of this principle that some people have laid down. We say to every believer: take on the character of the Prophet ﷺ, for our Prophet ﷺ is an excellent example for us.
* * *
Then we return to the words of the commentator, who says: (With the tanwin on ﴿قَلْبٍ﴾ and without it; whenever the heart is arrogant, its owner is arrogant, and vice versa.)
His words "and vice versa" are open to question, because they imply that the owner of the heart becomes arrogant before the heart does; for if you reverse the statement: whenever the heart is arrogant, its owner is arrogant; whenever the owner of the heart is arrogant, the heart is arrogant. Is this correct? No. But his intention, may Allah have mercy on him, is that the arrogance of the heart and the arrogance of the self are mutually connected: if the heart is arrogant, the self becomes arrogant, and if the self is arrogant, that is evidence that the heart is arrogant.
(And both readings, due to the generality of the sealing, cover the whole heart, not the generality of hearts.)
* Student: (Due to the generality of the sealing, cover all hearts, not the generality of hearts.)
* The Shaykh: Fine, it does not contradict. Perhaps "the hearts" is more correct. Do you not have the marginal notes of al-Jamal? What does it say? Apparently "the hearts" is more correct.
* The Student: His words: (due to the generality of the sealing, all of the heart), meaning all its parts, so there remains in it no place that accepts guidance; and his words: (not due to the generality of hearts), meaning: not due to the generality of the removal of hearts. This usage is a removal of it from its proper function: when it enters an indefinite noun absolutely, or a definite plural noun, it denotes the generality of individuals; and when it enters a singular definite noun, it denotes the generality of parts. Here it has entered an indefinite noun, so its proper function should be the generality of individuals, not the generality of parts, as the commentator took it. So let it be considered. The end, our shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Did he mention "hearts" here?
* The Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: (not due to the generality of hearts).
* The Student: Yes, (not due to the generality of hearts).
The author's words now say that the totality here returns to the individual, not to the individuals: ﴿عَلَى كُلِّ قَلْبِ﴾, meaning: upon the whole heart, not upon part of it, and not due to the generality of hearts, meaning not due to the generality of each heart individually. But what he went to is not correct. Rather we say: upon all hearts, and the generality is derived from the phrase "He seals upon the heart," not upon part of it. So if we say it is for the generality of hearts, it includes the generality of the heart, but not the reverse. Then, the apparent context: ﴿عَلَى كُلِّ قَلْبٍ مُتَكَبِّرٍ﴾ or ﴿عَلَى كُلِّ قَلْبِ مُتَكَبِّرٍ﴾; when we consider the context, what do we understand? Do we understand that all arrogant hearts are sealed, or that one heart is sealed in its entirety and not in part? The first, without doubt; this is the apparent context. And just as it is the apparent context, it is also more comprehensive in meaning, because if it is said: "Thus Allah seals upon every arrogant, tyrannical heart," sealing upon the heart includes sealing upon all of it, unless there is evidence that the intended meaning is sealing upon part of it. In that case the correct view is the reverse of what the author said.
The correct view is that this is for the generality of hearts, not the generality of the heart. But do you understand the difference?
If we say it is for the generality of the heart, the meaning of the verse becomes: Allah seals the whole heart, not all hearts, so some hearts are excluded; He seals the whole heart, but for example upon the heart of so-and-so among people.
If we say it is for the generality of hearts, the meaning of the verse becomes: Allah seals all arrogant hearts, in any person. So if we say "generality of hearts," it becomes general to individual hearts; if we say "generality of the heart," it becomes general to a single heart, and other hearts are left unmentioned. This is the point of difference.
But we say: the correct meaning of His words ﴿عَلَى كُلِّ قَلْبٍ مُتَكَبِّرٍ﴾ is: from among all people. And when he says "sealed upon the heart," the meaning is upon all of the heart, unless it is stated that the intended meaning is part of the heart.
* Student: His words "upon all of the heart" mean that the heart is divided (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, but sealing is not divided. Sealing is a seal upon the heart, with no window through which it could exit.
* The Student: Then into how many parts is the heart divided?
* The Shaykh: Hearts, considered as individuals, are divided into types, but a single heart is not divided.
* The Student: Then why does he say "upon all of the heart"?
* The Shaykh: This means: not upon part of it. Therefore the author's words are open to question from several angles; the more you reflect, the more you find it to be wrong. And the annotator (al-Jamal) says "let him consider it"; we considered it and found it incorrect.
* Student: What is the wisdom in their wives remaining with them while they were disbelievers?
* The Shaykh: Who?
* Student: Noah, peace be upon him, and Lot. Did they not know that?
* The Shaykh: Since Allah says: ﴿فَخَانَتَاهُمَا﴾ [al-Tahrim 10], and He said to him: ﴿إِلَّا امْرَأَتَكَ﴾ [Hud 81].
* Student: They did not know.
* The Shaykh: They did not know. And this is for the sake of lesson-taking regarding the wives of the Messenger ﷺ. You know this whole surah was revealed in the manner of a reproach to the wives of the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿إِنْ تَتُوبَا إِلَى اللَّهِ فَقَدْ صَغَتْ قُلُوبُكُمَا وَإِنْ تَظَاهَرَا عَلَيْهِ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ مَوْلَاهُ وَجِبْرِيلُ وَصَالِحُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمَلَائِكَةُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ ظَهِيرٌ﴾ [al-Tahrim 4].
I heard one of the pseudo-intellectuals say: this verse proves the greatness of women's scheming: that Allah (...), He, Jibril, the righteous believers, and the angels against two wives of the Messenger! This is a grave error. The purpose is not to show the strength of the two women; the purpose is to show Allah's, Most High, care for His Messenger, and that if you two band together against him, he has protectors: ﴿فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ مَوْلَاهُ وَجِبْرِيلُ وَصَالِحُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمَلَائِكَةُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ ظَهِيرٌ﴾.
* Student: O Shaykh, regarding the commentator's words "the generality of hearts," should we not say it is the generality of the heart, and that this heart includes everyone described with defiance and tyranny (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, that is not his meaning. His meaning, for example, is the hearts of Zayd, 'Amr, Bakr, and Khalid; these are the hearts. But if we say "the generality of the heart," it means the heart of Zayd alone, and the sealing is general to it.
* Student: All of them are described with this quality of tyranny and arrogance (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, but we do not say "the generality of the heart"; we say "the generality of hearts." This is general to every arrogant heart. So distinguish between saying this totality refers to parts or to individuals. If we say it is the generality of parts, it means the generality of the heart; and if we say it is the generality of individuals, it means all hearts. Even if hundreds of millions are described with this, each is sealed. There is no doubt that the author's words, may Allah have mercy on him, have no valid basis at all, but Glory be to Allah.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. "Pharaoh said: O Haman, build for me a tower that perhaps I may reach the ways (36), the ways of the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses; and indeed, I think he is a liar. Thus was made attractive to Pharaoh the evil of his deed, and he was averted from the path. And the plot of Pharaoh was not but in ruin (37). And the one who believed said: O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct (38). O my people, this worldly life is but enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the home of settlement (39)." [Ghafir 36–39].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, said in the story of Moses with Pharaoh: "Pharaoh said: O Haman, build for me a tower that perhaps I may reach the ways." Pharaoh is the king of Egypt. It has been said that it is the name of a person, or a personal name (ʿalam shakhs), and it has been said that it is a generic name (ʿalam jins). If we say it is a personal name, it becomes the name of a specific individual; if we say it is a generic name, it becomes the name for every king of Egypt who was a disbeliever, and this is what most scholars hold. But the Pharaoh of Moses is both a personal name and a generic name.

"Pharaoh said: O Haman, build for me a tower." Haman was his vizier (wazir). His saying "build for me a tower" means: order whoever builds to build it for me, because it is known that the vizier would not personally undertake the construction. "A tower" (ṣarḥan): the commentator said: "a lofty building," meaning elevated.

"that perhaps I may reach the ways" — "la'alla" (perhaps) here expresses causation (ta'lil). It comes sometimes for causation, sometimes for apprehension (ishfaq), and sometimes for hope (tarajji).

Among its use for causation is this verse, and His saying, exalted is He: "Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand" [Yusuf 2]; this is for causation. And whenever "la'alla" occurs with reference to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, it is for causation, because the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, does not hope, since everything is easy for Him.

It comes for apprehension, like saying: "Perhaps the beloved is lost," meaning, I fear that he may be lost.

It comes for hope, like: "I attended the lesson, so perhaps I will understand." If you say "la'alli afham" (perhaps I understand) it may be taken as causation; when you say "fa-la'alli" (so perhaps I) it becomes hope.

It also comes for anticipation (tawaqquʿ), as when you say to someone you are addressing: "Perhaps you understand."

These meanings that come for particles, and even for nouns and verbs when they are multiple, are determined by the context and indications of the situation.

He said: "that perhaps I may reach the ways (36), the ways of the heavens." "Al-asbab" is the plural of "sabab," which is everything that leads to the intended goal. So the sabab is a means, and the musabbab is the end. What are the ways here? He clarified them by His saying: "the ways of the heavens." So "asbab al-samawat" (the ways of the heavens), in its position relative to what precedes it, is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan), clarifying the ambiguity present in "al-asbab."

If someone says: why was the speech not clear from the outset, so it would be said: "perhaps I may reach the ways of the heavens"?

We say: ambiguity first and then detail and clarification afterward has a stronger effect on the soul, because when a thing comes ambiguous and then is clarified, the clarification falls upon a soul that is eager to know this ambiguous matter. That is, if the speech had come clear from the beginning, it would have been easy on souls; but when it comes first ambiguous, the soul becomes eager to know what is ambiguous, then the clarification comes while the soul is prepared to accept it and yearning to reach it.

"the ways of the heavens": the commentator said: "its paths that lead to it." "fa-aṭṭali'a" (so that I may look) is read in the nominative (raf'), as coordinated (ʿatf) with "ablugh," and in the accusative (naṣb), as an answer (jawab) to "ibni." That is, there are two Sab'i (seven-mode) readings: "fa-aṭṭali'u" and "fa-aṭṭali'a." As for the reading in the nominative, it is coordinated with "ablugh": that is, "perhaps I reach the heavens, so that I may look." As for the reading in the accusative, it is an answer to "ibni," and "ibni" is an imperative verb; an imperative verb's answer, when preceded by "fa," is in the accusative, "fa-aṭṭali'a," so the "fa" here is causal (sababiyya).

Know that the two readings found in the Noble Qur'an are among the seven modes in which the Qur'an was revealed, for the Qur'an was sent down in seven ahruf (modes). When it was in the time of ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, he ordered that the Qur'an be made into one mode, the mode of Quraysh; that is, its dialect. So these readings that exist are not the seven modes, but they are upon one mode.

Second: know that both readings are authentically transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, because they were transmitted by tawatur (mass transmission).

Third: know that a person should not recite among the common people with a reading that differs from what is in their hands of the copies (mushafs), because that causes confusion, perplexity, and accusation against the reciter, and perhaps the greatness of the Qur'an may diminish in their souls because of this difference. As for between you and yourself, it is best that you recite with this one at times and with that one at times, on condition that you are knowledgeable and not confused. We say this is best because each of the two readings was recited by the Prophet ﷺ, so this is like acts of worship that come in various forms, such as the opening supplications, the tashahhud, and the like. But this is when? Between you and yourself, or in a situation of teaching when you are instructing students.

"perhaps I may reach the ways (36), the ways of the heavens, so that I may look upon the God of Moses." That is: I reach it and look to see whether this is true or not true. Then he corrected himself, fearing that one of his soldiers might say that it is true, so he said: "and indeed, I think him" — that is, Moses — "a liar" in that he has a god other than me. He said this as deception toward his companions and out of fear that something might enter their souls when he ordered his vizier to build him a tower. He said: "and indeed, I think him a liar," and Pharaoh in this statement is a liar; he does not think that Moses is a liar, rather he knows that he is truthful, due to the saying of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, about Moses, that he said to him, that is to Pharaoh: "You have certainly known that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence" [al-Isra' 102]. He said this speech: "You have certainly known" — he said this emphasizing it with an oath, the lam, and qad. And he addresses this man who was capable of denying what Moses said if it were false, and said to him: "You have certainly known that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence, and indeed I think you, O Pharaoh, are destroyed." Does Pharaoh have any barrier preventing him from saying: "I did not know"? No, he is capable, but he knows that he knows that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence.

And Allah, exalted, said: "And they denied them, while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance" [al-Naml 14]. This is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) for "jahadu," not for "istayqanat": they denied them out of wrongdoing. The point is that his saying: "and indeed I think him a liar" — is this sentence a lie or true? He is a liar; he says "I think him a liar" while he is a liar, for he knows that he is truthful, but he said that as deception to his people and out of fear that some doubt might enter their hearts.

Allah, exalted, said about Pharaoh: "And indeed I think him a liar." The commentator says: "Pharaoh said that as deception."

"Thus was made attractive to Pharaoh the evil of his deed, and he was averted from the path." "Thus" (wa-kadhalika): that is, like this act or like this adornment. Which of them is according to the rule? The second; because we said that "kadhalika" is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of the verb that follows it: that is, like this adornment that was made attractive to Pharaoh, and this deception and promotion to his people. The evil of his deed was made attractive to Pharaoh. And who made it attractive? Satan and the commanding soul to evil. It may also be said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic; because Allah misguides whom He wills, as He said, exalted: "Thus We made attractive to every nation their deeds" — so Allah made it attractive by decree, meaning He withheld guidance from him, then Satan and the commanding soul made attractive to him that he do this deed.

"the evil of his deed and he was averted from the path." "al-sabil" here has the "al" of the known reference (al-'ahd). Which of the three references: the mentioned (dhikri), the present (hudluri), or the mental (dhihni)? The mental. "from the path": the path of guidance. Therefore the author said: "the way of guidance, and there are two readings: 'suddа' with a fatha on the ṣad and with a ḍamma." "ṣuddа" with a ḍamma on the ṣad is in the passive voice (mabni li-ma lam yusamma fa'iluh), and "ṣadda" with a fatha on the ṣad is in the active voice (mabni li-ma summiya fa'iluh). But is it transitive or intransitive? Does its meaning mean that he averted himself or averted others? It includes both meanings, because it is a shared term suitable for both meanings together. The rule in exegesis is that every word that can have two meanings that do not contradict each other is to be applied to both together, unless one of them has something that favors it, in which case the favored meaning is acted upon.

"and he was averted from the path." Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: "And the plot of Pharaoh was not but in ruin." Kayd, makr, khida' (scheming, deceit, deception) and similar words are all close in meaning, and their meaning is that a person reaches his goal against his opponent by hidden means. Every person intends that his opponent be defeated, so he reaches this by hidden means that the opponent does not know of, to achieve it.

Pharaoh schemed a scheme in telling Haman: "Build for me a tower," so that he could ascend this tower; then when he reached its summit, he would look before the people, then descend and say: "I did not find the Lord of Moses." Is this deception or not deception? Deception, especially toward the common people, especially toward a common people like the family of Pharaoh whom this oppressive tyrant had dazzled, so everything becomes reality to them. But does this scheme benefit him? Allah, exalted, said: "And the plot of Pharaoh was not but in ruin," that is, except in loss.

"ma" here: is it Hijazi or Tamimi?

Student: Hijazi.

Shaykh: Yes, it is Hijazi and inactive (muhmalah), meaning it does not operate. What nullified its operation? The affirmation (ithbat). Ibn Malik says:
"Its operation, as with laysa, was given to 'ma' only when 'in' is not present, with the negation remaining..."
And the negation here has not remained, so we say: it is inactive due to the nullification of the negation and its cancellation by "illa."

In this verse there are benefits:

From the benefits of this verse: the haughtiness and self-exaltation of Pharaoh, shown by directing the command to his vizier to build him a tower. Consider His saying "ibni li" (build for me) and not "ibn" (build), because this is greater in self-exaltation and arrogance; for if he had said "ibn," it would apply to anyone who builds, which contains ambiguity, but when he says "li" (for me), this shows that he employed this man, the vizier, in a complete employment.

And from the benefits of this noble verse: that taking viziers was an ancient custom, whether a vizier in good or a vizier in evil. From the viziers of good is the saying of Moses, peace be upon him: "And appoint for me a vizier from my family, Harun, my brother" [Ta-Ha 29–30]. And the saying of ʿAli ibn al-Husayn ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, when the leaders of the Shi'a, who are the Rafidah, asked him about Abu Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and he asked Allah's mercy upon them and said in praising them: "They are the two viziers of my grandfather" — meaning the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family. They rejected him, because their evil deeds had been made attractive to them, that whoever loves Abu Bakr and ʿUmar has hated ʿAli. According to this, the Prophet ﷺ would be hating ʿAli, because he was asked: "Who among men is most beloved to you?" He said: "Abu Bakr." So by their principle the Messenger would be hating ʿAli. See how the consequence of this corrupt, false principle turned out.

From the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of attributing a thing to the one who commands it rather than to its doer. It is derived from His saying: "build for me a tower," while he did not want Haman to undertake the building himself, but commands, because he is a vizier.

And from the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's exaltation by His essence (al-ʿulw al-dhati) in the previous laws, derived from His saying: "Build for me a tower that perhaps I may reach the ways (36), the ways of the heavens" [Ghafir 36–37]. This indicates that Moses, peace be upon him and his family, had informed them that Allah is in the heaven.

This, I mean the essential exaltation of Allah, is a matter that cannot be denied, because all the proofs point to it: the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus (ijma'), reason, and the innate nature (fitrah). All of them indicate the essential exaltation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that He, glorified and exalted, is in the heaven, and that He cannot be in the earth. We emphasize this point because of its importance, for it concerns the creed.

As for the Qur'an, the varied proofs that indicate with decisive indication the essential exaltation of Allah are numerous.

Likewise the Sunnah indicates this by saying, action, and affirmation. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, affirmed Allah's essential exaltation by his saying, his action, and his affirmation:
As for his saying: he, peace be upon him, said in his prostration: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High."
As for his action: he pointed to Allah's exaltation at the standing at ʿArafat when he addressed the people and said: "O Allah, bear witness."
As for his affirmation: by his affirmation of the slave-girl who said, "In the heaven," when he asked her: "Where is Allah?"

As for consensus: the predecessors (salaf) agreed upon this. None of them said that Allah is not in the heaven, none of them said that Allah is in the earth, and none of them said that Allah is not described as high, nor low, nor facing, nor distant; that is, none of them said that Allah is not above, nor below, nor right, nor left, nor connected to creation, nor separated from it, as the negators (mu'attilah) said.

If someone says: we grant that no negation has come from them, so what is the proof of affirmation, that they affirmed it? We say: the proof of that is that every text in the Qur'an and Sunnah for which no contrary report came from the Companions, we know with certainty that they held it, because the Qur'an was revealed in their language and they understood it. When they were addressed with this and no opposite was reported from them, this indicates that they held it. This is an important point that benefits you in debate with opponents: if he says to you: where did the Companions say that Allah is above, for example? You say: the Companions said that, because every text that came affirming exaltation, and no opposite was reported from the Companions, they certainly held it, since it was revealed in their language, and they knew it and understood it as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended.

As for reason: if you asked any person, is exaltation an attribute of perfection or descent? He would say to you: exaltation. If you said: is exaltation more perfect, or being opposite? He would say to you: exaltation. So exaltation, reason indicates its establishment for Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

As for innate nature: do not ask. Ask an old woman among the old women who has not read the words of the speculative negator theologians (mutakallimin al-mu'attilah): what does she tell you? If you asked her: where is Allah? She would say: in the heaven, and she knows nothing but that. And it is remarkable that the very people who say the negation, when they call upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, raise their hands by compulsion toward the heaven, and this is an accepted matter.

As for their claim that they say: the heaven is the qibla of the one who supplicates, just as the Ka'bah is the qibla of the one who prays, we say: then you are calling upon the heaven, and you have fallen into shirk without knowing it. In any case, praise be to Allah, that the exaltation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is a matter of innate nature that needs no learning and no effort, and despite that all the proofs indicate it. Then there come people whom Allah, exalted, has blinded in their insight, and they say: Allah, exalted, is not in exaltation. So what do they say? Listen:

Among them is one who says: Allah is in every place. These are the incarnationist Jahmiyyah (hulūliyyat al-Jahmiyyah): Allah is in every place, in the mosques, in the markets, in the houses, in the air, in the heaven, and, may Allah protect us, in the latrines. In every place. This is false, just as the sun nullifies the darkness of the night, because it necessarily entails one of two things:
Either Allah is multiple, or Allah is divisible, part of Him here and part of Him there, or multiple, one here and one there. This is apart from the corrupt consequences that necessarily follow, which would require that Allah be in the filthiest and most putrid places.

The second opinion concerns those who deny Allah's essential elevation (ʿulūw dhātī). They say: "We do not say that Allah is above or below, nor to the right or left, nor that He is joined to the world or separate from it." And where is He then? Non-existence. That is to say, some scholars have said: if it were said, "Describe non-existence for us," we would not find a more comprehensive description than this. The reality of the matter is that they do not worship Allah, and that they have no god at all.

Returning to the commentary, we say: the verse contains evidence for Allah's essential elevation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is part of the eloquence of a speaker to take the closest routes to attracting the listener.

* Among them: ambiguity followed by clarification (al-ibhām thumma al-bayān, i.e., leaving something vague and then making it clear), as in His saying: ﴿Perhaps I may reach the means, (36) the means of the heavens﴾ [Ghafir 36–37]. This is common in the Qur'an and in human speech.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that "the heavens" is plural and countable, as in His saying: ﴿the heavens﴾. They are, as is well known, seven. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We built above you seven strong [heavens]﴾ [An-Naba' 12], and He the Exalted says: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 86]. This is agreed upon. Are these heavens tightly joined or are there gaps between them? The answer is the second: that they have gaps between them. The hadith of the Mi'raj gives decisive evidence for this, for the Prophet (ﷺ) would ascend from one heaven to another.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the leaders of misguidance and the imams of error call people to error by every means they can, and try to prevent them from reaching the truth; this is shown by His saying: ﴿And indeed I think him a liar﴾. We have explained in the commentary why he said this word. So do not be deceived by the leaders of misguidance and the imams of error, nor by what they say of deception and fraud. This is not restricted to the imams of authority who hold power; rather, it extends even to the imams of propagation who call people to their destructive ideas and base morals. You will find among them such deception and misleading that it becomes a trap into which whoever lacks insight falls.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah the Mighty and Majestic tests the servant by making the evil of his deeds appear attractive to him; this is shown by His saying: ﴿And thus the evil of his deeds was made attractive to Pharaoh﴾. The saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, supports this: ﴿Thus We made attractive to every nation their deeds﴾ [Al-An'am 108], and His saying the Exalted: ﴿Is he, for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive so that he sees it as good, [equal to one who is rightly guided]? For indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. So let not your soul expire in regret over them﴾ [Fatir 8]. So be careful to pay attention to this matter, for a person may find his evil deed made attractive to him. Attractiveness is of two kinds:
The first kind: that a person sees this evil as good. This is the greater of the two.
The second kind: that he does not see it as evil, so he inclines toward it through his desire and says: "This is easy and there is nothing wrong in it." This is in reality a form of making it attractive, for whoever does not see evil as evil will fall into it, either out of desire for it, because it has been made attractive to him, or out of a whim in his soul, because he does not see it as evil.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Pharaoh was barring people from the way of Allah. He was one of the imams of barring from the path of Allah the Exalted. Allah the Exalted has said in another verse: ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ [Al-Qasas 41]. So beware of these imams; let them not deceive you, for they plot a plot, and Allah plots a plot for His believing servant.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Pharaoh ordered the building of this lofty tower as a scheme, not in reality; otherwise it is known that he would lose great expenses on this high edifice, but for his purpose and his desire he does not concern himself with that.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the scheme of the misguiders, praise be to Allah, ends in loss. Every misguider's scheme ends in loss. For if the scheme of this tyrant ends in loss, then those below him are all the more so, without doubt. For this reason He restricted his scheme to loss: it is nothing but loss. Allah, blessed and exalted, has said: ﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot, (15) and I am plotting a plot﴾ [At-Tariq 15–16], i.e., a plot greater than their plot.
He the Exalted has said: ﴿Or do they intend a plot? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be plotted against﴾ [At-Tur 42]. This is among the greatest verses that gladden the believer: that the plot of the disbeliever makes him the one who is plotted against. The verse came with a nominal sentence, ﴿those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be plotted against﴾, and with the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), indicating the establishment of this against them and its confirmation. As to how it indicates establishment: by its being a nominal sentence, for the nominal sentence, as the scholars say, conveys firmness and stability. And it came with restriction through the pronoun of separation: ﴿those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be plotted against﴾.

These verses, praise be to Allah, gladden the believer. But note that this is the promise of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and He does not break His promise, yet it requires a cause: that the believer perform a corresponding action. When the believer performs the action opposed to the plotting of the disbelievers, he trusts in Allah's promise and says: this plot will fall upon them while they are at a loss from it.

As for saying that Allah plots against them while they are the ones plotted against, yet we sleep on our beds and leave the beasts to eat the sheep, this is not correct. Action is necessary: ﴿O you who believe, if you support Allah, He will support you﴾ [Muhammad 7], and ﴿And the plot of Pharaoh was not but in ruin﴾ [Ghafir 37].

* Student: Correct (...) some exegetes say that Haman did not build for Pharaoh only (...) confirms it (...).
* Shaykh: This does not appear, because his saying: ﴿Build for me a tower﴾ [Ghafir 36] and it not being built is far-fetched; for he would say it while people heard, either they were present or the news reached them, and the tower would be built.

* Student: Why do we say that Pharaoh learned that Allah the Exalted [is above] from Moses? Would this be by his nature (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, whether it was by his nature or by Moses' call. But if we say it was by Moses' call, nothing remains for us. As for his nature, it may have been deviated, as in the hadith: «Then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1358) and Muslim (2658/23), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. But the thing certain for us now is the statement of Moses and his affirmation that Allah is in the heaven.

* Student: Regarding the readings of Ibn Mas'ud, are they established, or is it an explanation by the Companion, considered Qur'an?
* Shaykh: Which ones?
* Student: The readings of Ibn Mas'ud, for example (...) Tafsir Ibn Kathir: "And Ibn Mas'ud read..." Is it an explanation of the Qur'an by the Companion?
* Shaykh: But give me an example.
* Student: Like his reading in the verses of expiation: "three days consecutive." Is it a reading of the seven [canonical readings], which is recited, or is it an explanation by the Companion?
* Shaykh: It is not one of the seven. But if the reading is sound in its chain of transmission, the correct view is that it is permissible to recite it, neither in prayer nor outside prayer. As for the saying of some that it is not permissible to recite except the seven, and that if one recites a reading other than the seven that is authentically transmitted from the Messenger (ﷺ), his prayer is invalidated, this is weak. Furthermore, the word "consecutive" (mutatābi'ah) is not an explanation but a qualification, and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, would not read a reading that serves as a qualifier of an absolute unless he had heard it from the Messenger (ﷺ).
* Student: Regarding a specific reading, must one know which of the reciters it belongs to, or is it enough that one knows and is fully certain that it is among the seven?
* Shaykh: No, it is not necessary; for what matters is the transmission. If someone tells you that there is a reading such-and-such, you must know that the transmitter is trustworthy. If you know he is trustworthy, there is no need to know which of the seven reciters it is, as that is not required.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. "Pharaoh said: O Haman, build for me a tower that perhaps I may reach the ways (36), the ways of the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses; and indeed, I think he is a liar. Thus was made attractive to Pharaoh the evil of his deed, and he was averted from the path. And the plot of Pharaoh was not but in ruin (37). And the one who believed said: O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct (38). O my people, this worldly life is but enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the home of settlement (39)." [Ghafir 36–39].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, said in the story of Moses with Pharaoh: "Pharaoh said: O Haman, build for me a tower that perhaps I may reach the ways." Pharaoh is the king of Egypt. It has been said that it is the name of a person, or a personal name (ʿalam shakhs), and it has been said that it is a generic name (ʿalam jins). If we say it is a personal name, it becomes the name of a specific individual; if we say it is a generic name, it becomes the name for every king of Egypt who was a disbeliever, and this is what most scholars hold. But the Pharaoh of Moses is both a personal name and a generic name.

"Pharaoh said: O Haman, build for me a tower." Haman was his vizier (wazir). His saying "build for me a tower" means: order whoever builds to build it for me, because it is known that the vizier would not personally undertake the construction. "A tower" (ṣarḥan): the commentator said: "a lofty building," meaning elevated.

"that perhaps I may reach the ways" — "la'alla" (perhaps) here expresses causation (ta'lil). It comes sometimes for causation, sometimes for apprehension (ishfaq), and sometimes for hope (tarajji).

Among its use for causation is this verse, and His saying, exalted is He: "Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand" [Yusuf 2]; this is for causation. And whenever "la'alla" occurs with reference to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, it is for causation, because the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, does not hope, since everything is easy for Him.

It comes for apprehension, like saying: "Perhaps the beloved is lost," meaning, I fear that he may be lost.

It comes for hope, like: "I attended the lesson, so perhaps I will understand." If you say "la'alli afham" (perhaps I understand) it may be taken as causation; when you say "fa-la'alli" (so perhaps I) it becomes hope.

It also comes for anticipation (tawaqquʿ), as when you say to someone you are addressing: "Perhaps you understand."

These meanings that come for particles, and even for nouns and verbs when they are multiple, are determined by the context and indications of the situation.

He said: "that perhaps I may reach the ways (36), the ways of the heavens." "Al-asbab" is the plural of "sabab," which is everything that leads to the intended goal. So the sabab is a means, and the musabbab is the end. What are the ways here? He clarified them by His saying: "the ways of the heavens." So "asbab al-samawat" (the ways of the heavens), in its position relative to what precedes it, is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan), clarifying the ambiguity present in "al-asbab."

If someone says: why was the speech not clear from the outset, so it would be said: "perhaps I may reach the ways of the heavens"?

We say: ambiguity first and then detail and clarification afterward has a stronger effect on the soul, because when a thing comes ambiguous and then is clarified, the clarification falls upon a soul that is eager to know this ambiguous matter. That is, if the speech had come clear from the beginning, it would have been easy on souls; but when it comes first ambiguous, the soul becomes eager to know what is ambiguous, then the clarification comes while the soul is prepared to accept it and yearning to reach it.

"the ways of the heavens": the commentator said: "its paths that lead to it." "fa-aṭṭali'a" (so that I may look) is read in the nominative (raf'), as coordinated (ʿatf) with "ablugh," and in the accusative (naṣb), as an answer (jawab) to "ibni." That is, there are two Sab'i (seven-mode) readings: "fa-aṭṭali'u" and "fa-aṭṭali'a." As for the reading in the nominative, it is coordinated with "ablugh": that is, "perhaps I reach the heavens, so that I may look." As for the reading in the accusative, it is an answer to "ibni," and "ibni" is an imperative verb; an imperative verb's answer, when preceded by "fa," is in the accusative, "fa-aṭṭali'a," so the "fa" here is causal (sababiyya).

Know that the two readings found in the Noble Qur'an are among the seven modes in which the Qur'an was revealed, for the Qur'an was sent down in seven ahruf (modes). When it was in the time of ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, he ordered that the Qur'an be made into one mode, the mode of Quraysh; that is, its dialect. So these readings that exist are not the seven modes, but they are upon one mode.

Second: know that both readings are authentically transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, because they were transmitted by tawatur (mass transmission).

Third: know that a person should not recite among the common people with a reading that differs from what is in their hands of the copies (mushafs), because that causes confusion, perplexity, and accusation against the reciter, and perhaps the greatness of the Qur'an may diminish in their souls because of this difference. As for between you and yourself, it is best that you recite with this one at times and with that one at times, on condition that you are knowledgeable and not confused. We say this is best because each of the two readings was recited by the Prophet ﷺ, so this is like acts of worship that come in various forms, such as the opening supplications, the tashahhud, and the like. But this is when? Between you and yourself, or in a situation of teaching when you are instructing students.

"perhaps I may reach the ways (36), the ways of the heavens, so that I may look upon the God of Moses." That is: I reach it and look to see whether this is true or not true. Then he corrected himself, fearing that one of his soldiers might say that it is true, so he said: "and indeed, I think him" — that is, Moses — "a liar" in that he has a god other than me. He said this as deception toward his companions and out of fear that something might enter their souls when he ordered his vizier to build him a tower. He said: "and indeed, I think him a liar," and Pharaoh in this statement is a liar; he does not think that Moses is a liar, rather he knows that he is truthful, due to the saying of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, about Moses, that he said to him, that is to Pharaoh: "You have certainly known that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence" [al-Isra' 102]. He said this speech: "You have certainly known" — he said this emphasizing it with an oath, the lam, and qad. And he addresses this man who was capable of denying what Moses said if it were false, and said to him: "You have certainly known that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence, and indeed I think you, O Pharaoh, are destroyed." Does Pharaoh have any barrier preventing him from saying: "I did not know"? No, he is capable, but he knows that he knows that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence.

And Allah, exalted, said: "And they denied them, while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance" [al-Naml 14]. This is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) for "jahadu," not for "istayqanat": they denied them out of wrongdoing. The point is that his saying: "and indeed I think him a liar" — is this sentence a lie or true? He is a liar; he says "I think him a liar" while he is a liar, for he knows that he is truthful, but he said that as deception to his people and out of fear that some doubt might enter their hearts.

Allah, exalted, said about Pharaoh: "And indeed I think him a liar." The commentator says: "Pharaoh said that as deception."

"Thus was made attractive to Pharaoh the evil of his deed, and he was averted from the path." "Thus" (wa-kadhalika): that is, like this act or like this adornment. Which of them is according to the rule? The second; because we said that "kadhalika" is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of the verb that follows it: that is, like this adornment that was made attractive to Pharaoh, and this deception and promotion to his people. The evil of his deed was made attractive to Pharaoh. And who made it attractive? Satan and the commanding soul to evil. It may also be said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic; because Allah misguides whom He wills, as He said, exalted: "Thus We made attractive to every nation their deeds" — so Allah made it attractive by decree, meaning He withheld guidance from him, then Satan and the commanding soul made attractive to him that he do this deed.

"the evil of his deed and he was averted from the path." "al-sabil" here has the "al" of the known reference (al-'ahd). Which of the three references: the mentioned (dhikri), the present (hudluri), or the mental (dhihni)? The mental. "from the path": the path of guidance. Therefore the author said: "the way of guidance, and there are two readings: 'suddа' with a fatha on the ṣad and with a ḍamma." "ṣuddа" with a ḍamma on the ṣad is in the passive voice (mabni li-ma lam yusamma fa'iluh), and "ṣadda" with a fatha on the ṣad is in the active voice (mabni li-ma summiya fa'iluh). But is it transitive or intransitive? Does its meaning mean that he averted himself or averted others? It includes both meanings, because it is a shared term suitable for both meanings together. The rule in exegesis is that every word that can have two meanings that do not contradict each other is to be applied to both together, unless one of them has something that favors it, in which case the favored meaning is acted upon.

"and he was averted from the path." Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: "And the plot of Pharaoh was not but in ruin." Kayd, makr, khida' (scheming, deceit, deception) and similar words are all close in meaning, and their meaning is that a person reaches his goal against his opponent by hidden means. Every person intends that his opponent be defeated, so he reaches this by hidden means that the opponent does not know of, to achieve it.

Pharaoh schemed a scheme in telling Haman: "Build for me a tower," so that he could ascend this tower; then when he reached its summit, he would look before the people, then descend and say: "I did not find the Lord of Moses." Is this deception or not deception? Deception, especially toward the common people, especially toward a common people like the family of Pharaoh whom this oppressive tyrant had dazzled, so everything becomes reality to them. But does this scheme benefit him? Allah, exalted, said: "And the plot of Pharaoh was not but in ruin," that is, except in loss.

"ma" here: is it Hijazi or Tamimi?

Student: Hijazi.

Shaykh: Yes, it is Hijazi and inactive (muhmalah), meaning it does not operate. What nullified its operation? The affirmation (ithbat). Ibn Malik says:
"Its operation, as with laysa, was given to 'ma' only when 'in' is not present, with the negation remaining..."
And the negation here has not remained, so we say: it is inactive due to the nullification of the negation and its cancellation by "illa."

In this verse there are benefits:

From the benefits of this verse: the haughtiness and self-exaltation of Pharaoh, shown by directing the command to his vizier to build him a tower. Consider His saying "ibni li" (build for me) and not "ibn" (build), because this is greater in self-exaltation and arrogance; for if he had said "ibn," it would apply to anyone who builds, which contains ambiguity, but when he says "li" (for me), this shows that he employed this man, the vizier, in a complete employment.

And from the benefits of this noble verse: that taking viziers was an ancient custom, whether a vizier in good or a vizier in evil. From the viziers of good is the saying of Moses, peace be upon him: "And appoint for me a vizier from my family, Harun, my brother" [Ta-Ha 29–30]. And the saying of ʿAli ibn al-Husayn ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, when the leaders of the Shi'a, who are the Rafidah, asked him about Abu Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and he asked Allah's mercy upon them and said in praising them: "They are the two viziers of my grandfather" — meaning the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family. They rejected him, because their evil deeds had been made attractive to them, that whoever loves Abu Bakr and ʿUmar has hated ʿAli. According to this, the Prophet ﷺ would be hating ʿAli, because he was asked: "Who among men is most beloved to you?" He said: "Abu Bakr." So by their principle the Messenger would be hating ʿAli. See how the consequence of this corrupt, false principle turned out.

From the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of attributing a thing to the one who commands it rather than to its doer. It is derived from His saying: "build for me a tower," while he did not want Haman to undertake the building himself, but commands, because he is a vizier.

And from the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's exaltation by His essence (al-ʿulw al-dhati) in the previous laws, derived from His saying: "Build for me a tower that perhaps I may reach the ways (36), the ways of the heavens" [Ghafir 36–37]. This indicates that Moses, peace be upon him and his family, had informed them that Allah is in the heaven.

This, I mean the essential exaltation of Allah, is a matter that cannot be denied, because all the proofs point to it: the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus (ijma'), reason, and the innate nature (fitrah). All of them indicate the essential exaltation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that He, glorified and exalted, is in the heaven, and that He cannot be in the earth. We emphasize this point because of its importance, for it concerns the creed.

As for the Qur'an, the varied proofs that indicate with decisive indication the essential exaltation of Allah are numerous.

Likewise the Sunnah indicates this by saying, action, and affirmation. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, affirmed Allah's essential exaltation by his saying, his action, and his affirmation:
As for his saying: he, peace be upon him, said in his prostration: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High."
As for his action: he pointed to Allah's exaltation at the standing at ʿArafat when he addressed the people and said: "O Allah, bear witness."
As for his affirmation: by his affirmation of the slave-girl who said, "In the heaven," when he asked her: "Where is Allah?"

As for consensus: the predecessors (salaf) agreed upon this. None of them said that Allah is not in the heaven, none of them said that Allah is in the earth, and none of them said that Allah is not described as high, nor low, nor facing, nor distant; that is, none of them said that Allah is not above, nor below, nor right, nor left, nor connected to creation, nor separated from it, as the negators (mu'attilah) said.

If someone says: we grant that no negation has come from them, so what is the proof of affirmation, that they affirmed it? We say: the proof of that is that every text in the Qur'an and Sunnah for which no contrary report came from the Companions, we know with certainty that they held it, because the Qur'an was revealed in their language and they understood it. When they were addressed with this and no opposite was reported from them, this indicates that they held it. This is an important point that benefits you in debate with opponents: if he says to you: where did the Companions say that Allah is above, for example? You say: the Companions said that, because every text that came affirming exaltation, and no opposite was reported from the Companions, they certainly held it, since it was revealed in their language, and they knew it and understood it as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended.

As for reason: if you asked any person, is exaltation an attribute of perfection or descent? He would say to you: exaltation. If you said: is exaltation more perfect, or being opposite? He would say to you: exaltation. So exaltation, reason indicates its establishment for Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

As for innate nature: do not ask. Ask an old woman among the old women who has not read the words of the speculative negator theologians (mutakallimin al-mu'attilah): what does she tell you? If you asked her: where is Allah? She would say: in the heaven, and she knows nothing but that. And it is remarkable that the very people who say the negation, when they call upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, raise their hands by compulsion toward the heaven, and this is an accepted matter.

As for their claim that they say: the heaven is the qibla of the one who supplicates, just as the Ka'bah is the qibla of the one who prays, we say: then you are calling upon the heaven, and you have fallen into shirk without knowing it. In any case, praise be to Allah, that the exaltation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is a matter of innate nature that needs no learning and no effort, and despite that all the proofs indicate it. Then there come people whom Allah, exalted, has blinded in their insight, and they say: Allah, exalted, is not in exaltation. So what do they say? Listen:

Among them is one who says: Allah is in every place. These are the incarnationist Jahmiyyah (hulūliyyat al-Jahmiyyah): Allah is in every place, in the mosques, in the markets, in the houses, in the air, in the heaven, and, may Allah protect us, in the latrines. In every place. This is false, just as the sun nullifies the darkness of the night, because it necessarily entails one of two things:
Either Allah is multiple, or Allah is divisible, part of Him here and part of Him there, or multiple, one here and one there. This is apart from the corrupt consequences that necessarily follow, which would require that Allah be in the filthiest and most putrid places.

The second opinion concerns those who deny Allah's essential elevation (ʿulūw dhātī). They say: "We do not say that Allah is above or below, nor to the right or left, nor that He is joined to the world or separate from it." And where is He then? Non-existence. That is to say, some scholars have said: if it were said, "Describe non-existence for us," we would not find a more comprehensive description than this. The reality of the matter is that they do not worship Allah, and that they have no god at all.

Returning to the commentary, we say: the verse contains evidence for Allah's essential elevation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is part of the eloquence of a speaker to take the closest routes to attracting the listener.

* Among them: ambiguity followed by clarification (al-ibhām thumma al-bayān, i.e., leaving something vague and then making it clear), as in His saying: ﴿Perhaps I may reach the means, (36) the means of the heavens﴾ [Ghafir 36–37]. This is common in the Qur'an and in human speech.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that "the heavens" is plural and countable, as in His saying: ﴿the heavens﴾. They are, as is well known, seven. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We built above you seven strong [heavens]﴾ [An-Naba' 12], and He the Exalted says: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 86]. This is agreed upon. Are these heavens tightly joined or are there gaps between them? The answer is the second: that they have gaps between them. The hadith of the Mi'raj gives decisive evidence for this, for the Prophet (ﷺ) would ascend from one heaven to another.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the leaders of misguidance and the imams of error call people to error by every means they can, and try to prevent them from reaching the truth; this is shown by His saying: ﴿And indeed I think him a liar﴾. We have explained in the commentary why he said this word. So do not be deceived by the leaders of misguidance and the imams of error, nor by what they say of deception and fraud. This is not restricted to the imams of authority who hold power; rather, it extends even to the imams of propagation who call people to their destructive ideas and base morals. You will find among them such deception and misleading that it becomes a trap into which whoever lacks insight falls.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah the Mighty and Majestic tests the servant by making the evil of his deeds appear attractive to him; this is shown by His saying: ﴿And thus the evil of his deeds was made attractive to Pharaoh﴾. The saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, supports this: ﴿Thus We made attractive to every nation their deeds﴾ [Al-An'am 108], and His saying the Exalted: ﴿Is he, for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive so that he sees it as good, [equal to one who is rightly guided]? For indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. So let not your soul expire in regret over them﴾ [Fatir 8]. So be careful to pay attention to this matter, for a person may find his evil deed made attractive to him. Attractiveness is of two kinds:
The first kind: that a person sees this evil as good. This is the greater of the two.
The second kind: that he does not see it as evil, so he inclines toward it through his desire and says: "This is easy and there is nothing wrong in it." This is in reality a form of making it attractive, for whoever does not see evil as evil will fall into it, either out of desire for it, because it has been made attractive to him, or out of a whim in his soul, because he does not see it as evil.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Pharaoh was barring people from the way of Allah. He was one of the imams of barring from the path of Allah the Exalted. Allah the Exalted has said in another verse: ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ [Al-Qasas 41]. So beware of these imams; let them not deceive you, for they plot a plot, and Allah plots a plot for His believing servant.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Pharaoh ordered the building of this lofty tower as a scheme, not in reality; otherwise it is known that he would lose great expenses on this high edifice, but for his purpose and his desire he does not concern himself with that.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the scheme of the misguiders, praise be to Allah, ends in loss. Every misguider's scheme ends in loss.
