For if the scheme of this tyrant ends in loss, then those below him are all the more so, without doubt. For this reason He restricted his scheme to loss: it is nothing but loss. Allah, blessed and exalted, has said: ﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot, (15) and I am plotting a plot﴾ [At-Tariq 15–16], i.e., a plot greater than their plot.
He the Exalted has said: ﴿Or do they intend a plot? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be plotted against﴾ [At-Tur 42]. This is among the greatest verses that gladden the believer: that the plot of the disbeliever makes him the one who is plotted against. The verse came with a nominal sentence, ﴿those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be plotted against﴾, and with the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), indicating the establishment of this against them and its confirmation. As to how it indicates establishment: by its being a nominal sentence, for the nominal sentence, as the scholars say, conveys firmness and stability. And it came with restriction through the pronoun of separation: ﴿those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be plotted against﴾.

These verses, praise be to Allah, gladden the believer. But note that this is the promise of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and He does not break His promise, yet it requires a cause: that the believer perform a corresponding action. When the believer performs the action opposed to the plotting of the disbelievers, he trusts in Allah's promise and says: this plot will fall upon them while they are at a loss from it.

As for saying that Allah plots against them while they are the ones plotted against, yet we sleep on our beds and leave the beasts to eat the sheep, this is not correct. Action is necessary: ﴿O you who believe, if you support Allah, He will support you﴾ [Muhammad 7], and ﴿And the plot of Pharaoh was not but in ruin﴾ [Ghafir 37].

* Student: Correct (...) some exegetes say that Haman did not build for Pharaoh only (...) confirms it (...).
* Shaykh: This does not appear, because his saying: ﴿Build for me a tower﴾ [Ghafir 36] and it not being built is far-fetched; for he would say it while people heard, either they were present or the news reached them, and the tower would be built.

* Student: Why do we say that Pharaoh learned that Allah the Exalted [is above] from Moses? Would this be by his nature (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, whether it was by his nature or by Moses' call. But if we say it was by Moses' call, nothing remains for us. As for his nature, it may have been deviated, as in the hadith: «Then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1358) and Muslim (2658/23), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. But the thing certain for us now is the statement of Moses and his affirmation that Allah is in the heaven.

* Student: Regarding the readings of Ibn Mas'ud, are they established, or is it an explanation by the Companion, considered Qur'an?
* Shaykh: Which ones?
* Student: The readings of Ibn Mas'ud, for example (...) Tafsir Ibn Kathir: "And Ibn Mas'ud read..." Is it an explanation of the Qur'an by the Companion?
* Shaykh: But give me an example.
* Student: Like his reading in the verses of expiation: "three days consecutive." Is it a reading of the seven [canonical readings], which is recited, or is it an explanation by the Companion?
* Shaykh: It is not one of the seven. But if the reading is sound in its chain of transmission, the correct view is that it is permissible to recite it, neither in prayer nor outside prayer. As for the saying of some that it is not permissible to recite except the seven, and that if one recites a reading other than the seven that is authentically transmitted from the Messenger (ﷺ), his prayer is invalidated, this is weak. Furthermore, the word "consecutive" (mutatābi'ah) is not an explanation but a qualification, and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, would not read a reading that serves as a qualifier of an absolute unless he had heard it from the Messenger (ﷺ).
* Student: Regarding a specific reading, must one know which of the reciters it belongs to, or is it enough that one knows and is fully certain that it is among the seven?
* Shaykh: No, it is not necessary; for what matters is the transmission. If someone tells you that there is a reading such-and-such, you must know that the transmitter is trustworthy. If you know he is trustworthy, there is no need to know which of the seven reciters it is, as that is not required.

**Student:** I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct. O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement. Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account. And O my people, what is with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire? You invite me to disbelieve in Allah and associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I invite you to the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving."﴾ [Ghafir 38–42].

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct."﴾ [Ghafir 38]. At the beginning of these verses Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh said﴾ [Ghafir 28]. Here and in what precedes it, He says: ﴿the one who believed﴾, confirming his faith and that he was truly a believer.

﴿The one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct."﴾ ﴿O my people﴾: its grammatical analysis (i'rab) has already been discussed, and we explained that it is a vocative in the accusative, with the accusative marked on the letter before the omitted first-person ya' (the ya' of the speaker), which was dropped for lightness; the case-ending could not be shown because the final letter is occupied by the vowel of harmony (kasrah).

As for His saying: ﴿O my people, follow me; I will guide you﴾, it is read both with the ya' and without it (ittabi'uni and ittabi'u, and aheedkum). This means that there are two readings: "ittabi'uni" and "ittabi'u". With the ya' the matter is clear, since it is the ya' of the speaker. Without it, it has been dropped for lightness.

His saying ﴿follow me﴾ is an imperative verb, and ﴿I will guide you﴾ is the answer to the imperative. For this reason it is in the jussive mood, with the ya' dropped and the kasrah before it as evidence of it. The original form of ahdikum is ahdeekum (ahdiyukum), but when the present-tense verb comes as an answer to an imperative it is jussive. It is said that it is jussive because of the imperative itself, and it is said that it is jussive because of an implied condition, the meaning being "if you follow me, I will guide you." The same is said of everything that comes in this construction.

﴿I will guide you to the path of right conduct﴾: that is, to its way. The guidance here is guidance of indication (hidayat al-dalalah), because it cannot mean guidance of divine enabling (hidayat al-tawfiq), which lies in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He said to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas 56], meaning you cannot give guidance of enabling. So His saying ﴿I will guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ means: I will show you the path of right conduct. The "path of right conduct" is the opposite of the "path of error" (ghayy). Rushd (right conduct) is good management of one's affairs, and ghayy is committing error deliberately.

﴿O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement.﴾ When he urged them to follow him, he made them renounce the world, because the root of the deviation of the children of Adam is greed for this world, and rivalry is only over it. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, I do not fear poverty for you; rather, I fear that the world will be opened to you so that you compete for it as those before you competed for it, and it destroys you as it destroyed them."[1]

So when he asked them to follow him, he explained to them the state of the world over which they compete, and by which they turned away from the way of Allah. He said: ﴿O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment.﴾ ﴿Only﴾ (innama) is a particle of restriction; ﴿this worldly life﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿a passing enjoyment﴾ is its predicate (khabar). That is, this world is nothing but an enjoyment which a person enjoys for a little while and then it vanishes. For this reason the author says in his commentary: ﴿enjoyment﴾ is a passing enjoyment.

﴿And indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement.﴾ ﴿The Hereafter﴾ is what comes after this world; ﴿is﴾ is a pronoun of separation (dhamir al-fasl), and ﴿the abode of settlement﴾ is the predicate of ﴿indeed (inna)﴾.

Know that the pronoun of separation is a pronoun that has no place in grammatical analysis: it is not parsed as subject, predicate, or anything else. It has no grammatical position.

Know also that it has three benefits:
The first benefit: emphasis.
The second benefit: restriction.
The third benefit: distinguishing the predicate from the adjective.

This appears in the example: if you say "Zayd huwa al-fadil" (Zayd is the excellent one), then "huwa" is a pronoun of separation, from which we derive three benefits.
First, emphasis: we have emphasized that Zayd is the excellent one, or rather, that Zayd is excellent.
Then, restriction: because you said "Zayd huwa," meaning, not someone else: Zayd is the excellent one.
The third benefit: distinguishing between adjective and predicate. If you say "Zayd al-fadil," it could be that "al-fadil" is an adjective of Zayd and the predicate has not yet come. But if you say "huwa al-fadil," it becomes certain that "al-fadil" is the predicate, and thereby the predicate is distinguished from the adjective.

We have mentioned that it has no place in grammatical analysis, and the evidence for this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians if they are the victors﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 40]. Here ﴿the victors﴾ came as the predicate of ﴿kana (were)﴾. If it had a place in grammatical analysis, it would have been "in kanu hum al-ghalibun" (if they were the victors, in the nominative), but it has no place in grammatical analysis.

So what is the abode of settlement? It is the Hereafter, and this has been emphasized by the use of the pronoun of separation.

﴿And indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾: that is, the abode of permanent residence. For this reason: "Death will be brought in the form of a ram, and it will be stopped between Paradise and the Fire, and it will be said: 'O people of the Fire!' And they will stretch their necks and look. Likewise it will be said to the people of Paradise: 'O people of Paradise!' And they will stretch their necks and look. Then it will be said to them: 'Do you recognize this?' They will say: 'Yes, this is death.' It will be slaughtered before them, and it will be said: 'O people of Paradise, there is eternity and no death; O people of the Fire, there is eternity and no death.'"[2]

So this is the settlement. Since there is no movement from this abode, it is the abode of settlement. Now, if it is the abode of settlement and the world is an enjoyment, what should a person work for? The Hereafter, because it is the abode of settlement. As for this world, it is an abode of passing through, an abode of enjoyment. "Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler passing through."[3]

Then he said: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account﴾ [Ghafir 40]. This is an explanation of the state of the Hereafter and how people are recompensed in it. He said: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like.﴾ ﴿Whoever (man)﴾ is conditional; ﴿does﴾ is the conditional verb; and the clause ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ is the answer to the condition.

His saying ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾: ﴿like (mithl)﴾ is the second object of ﴿yujza (is recompensed)﴾, and the first object is the implied subject (naib al-fa'il).

He says: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾. The evil deed (sayyi'ah) is what is bad in its state or in its outcome. What befalls a person of sickness, poverty, affliction or the like is evil in its present state. What befalls a person as punishment for his deeds is evil in its outcome. Sometimes a person is hastened with punishment in this world. So the evil deed is everything that is bad in its present state or in its outcome.

﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾: one evil deed is repaid with one, whatever it is, even if the person is in Makkah, or in Madinah, or in the mosque, or in any place, or at any time. Even if it is in the sacred months in which Allah has forbidden injustice, He said: ﴿Of them four are sacred; that is the correct religion, so do not wrong yourselves therein﴾ [al-Tawbah 36]. For the evil deed is not increased, but know that it may be more severe in its quality, not in its quantity. What is the quality? We see that one blow may be more severe on a person than ten blows because of its intensity and the effect of its impact. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said about the Sacred House in Makkah: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj 25].

By this explanation, which is indicated by the Book and the Sunnah, it becomes clear that what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), that he left Makkah and said: "I will not remain in a city where its evil and good deeds are equal," is not authentic from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him). Ibn 'Abbas was too learned and knowledgeable to be confused about this matter. Moreover, Allah said in Surat al-An'am, which is Makkan: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and they will not be wronged﴾ [al-An'am 160].

He said: ﴿And whoever does righteousness, male or female﴾ [Ghafir 40]. ﴿Whoever (man)﴾ here is conditional. ﴿Righteousness (salihan)﴾ may be parsed as an adjective of an omitted noun, the meaning being "a righteous deed," or it may be taken as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), since the adjective of an omitted verbal noun may be parsed as an absolute object or as an adjective of an omitted noun. The meaning would be "a righteous action."

So what is the righteous deed? The righteous deed is that which meets the conditions of acceptance, which is that it be sincerely for Allah and in accordance with the Law (shari'ah) from Him. That is, it combines two matters: sincerity to Allah, and following His messengers, peace be upon them. This is the righteous deed. So it is what meets the conditions of acceptance, which are sincerity to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and second, following the messengers of Allah, whether Muhammad or others. But it is well known that after the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) it is not valid to follow anyone else.

If sincerity is lacking, the deed is not righteous but is rejected for its doer, because of the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, in the sacred hadith: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in associating others with Me. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his association."[4]

If following is lacking, the deed is not righteous and is rejected, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever does a deed which is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected."[5]

His saying ﴿male or female﴾ is an explanation of ﴿whoever (man)﴾. The "min" here is explanatory (bayaniyyah). How do we say it explains ﴿man﴾? Because ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun is basically vague, so when an explanation follows it, that explanation makes its vagueness clear.

﴿male or female, while being a believer﴾: this is the condition. He must be a believer. If he is not a believer, his righteous deed does not benefit him, even if the deed is one whose benefit extends to others, because of the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah 54]. So the deed of a non-believer does not benefit him. If a disbelieving man repaired the roads, laid water pipes to give water to people, built mosques, printed books, clothed the naked, and fed the hungry, would this benefit him? No. For this reason the deeds of the hypocrites do not benefit them, because they are not believers. And by this we know that faith is the foundation: believe, then act.

He must be a believer. If he is not a believer, his righteous deed does not benefit him, even if the deed's benefit extends to others, because of the saying of Allah: ﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah 54]. So the deed of the non-believer does not benefit him. If a disbelieving man repaired the roads, laid water pipes to give water to people, built mosques, printed books, clothed the naked, and fed the hungry, would this benefit him? No. For this reason the deeds of the hypocrites do not benefit them, because they are not believers. And by this we know that faith is the foundation: believe, then act. As for action without faith, we ask Allah not to strip us and you of faith. Action without faith is dust: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan 23]. Faith must come first; then, when a person believes, he acts; and when he acts, he is sincere and follows.

﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾ [Ghafir 40]: the clause ﴿those﴾ is the answer to the condition, that is, the condition is ﴿and whoever does righteousness﴾ [Ghafir 40].

﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾: here He said ﴿those (ulaika)﴾, the demonstrative used for the distant, indicating the loftiness of their rank, as if you point to them while they are above.

﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾: he said (with the ya' pronounced with a dammah and the kha' with a fathah, "yudkhalun" and the reverse). What is the reverse? "Yadkhulun" is permitted: "yudkhalun" means that Allah causes them to enter; and "yadkhulun" means that they enter by themselves, but by the permission of Allah. It is well known that the people of Paradise do not enter Paradise except after intercession, after the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ) to open Paradise, because they arrive at it while its gate is closed, so they ask someone to intercede for them with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that the gate be opened for them. So the Prophet (ﷺ) alone intercedes that the gate be opened for them, and it is opened.

﴿Being provided therein without account﴾ [Ghafir 40]: ﴿provided (yurzaqun)﴾: provision here means giving, and from it is His saying: ﴿And when relatives, orphans and the needy are present at the division, provide them from it﴾ [al-Nisa' 8], meaning give them. So the meaning of ﴿yurzaqun﴾ is that they are given.

His saying: (﴿without account﴾ means without consequence). It means they will not be held to account for it, and they will not pay a price for it. In this world you do not own provision except for a price; but in the Hereafter you are given provision without price and without consequence, and you will not be held to account for it. Why? Because the price was paid in advance, as a salam (advance sale). Do you know salam? It is paying the price in advance and delaying the delivery of the goods. Here the price was paid in advance: the price was in this world, when they acted in obedience to Allah, and this was the exchange. So these people had entered into this transaction and paid its price in advance. For this reason He said: ﴿being provided therein without account﴾.

* In these three verses there are benefits.
* First: the gentleness (talattuf) of this caller, this believing man who calls to Allah, as shown by his saying ﴿O my people﴾. There is no doubt that this is one of the methods of gentleness.

---

[1] Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3158) and Muslim (2961/6), from the hadith of 'Amr ibn 'Awf al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him), and its wording: "...So rejoice and hope for what pleases you. By Allah, it is not poverty I fear for you, but I fear that the world will be spread out over you as it was spread out over those before you, so you compete for it as they competed for it, and it destroys you as it destroyed them," the hadith.

[2] Related by al-Bukhari (6548) and Muslim, with his wording (2850/43), with their chains from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), that his father told him, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, death will be brought until it is placed between Paradise and the Fire, then it will be slaughtered, then a caller will call: 'O people of Paradise, no death! O people of the Fire, no death!' So the people of Paradise will increase in joy over their joy, and the people of the Fire will increase in grief over their grief." Al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (11255) also related it with his chain from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) with the wording: "...He calls: 'O people of Paradise!' and they stretch their necks and look; and He calls: 'O people of the Fire!' and they stretch their necks and look. It is said: 'Do you know death?' They say: 'Yes.' Death is brought in the form of a white-spotted ram, and it is said: 'This is death,' and it is brought forward and slaughtered. He said: 'O people of Paradise, eternity and no death; and it is said: O people of the Fire, eternity and no death.'" He said: then he recited ﴿And warn them of the Day of regret, when the matter is decided﴾ [Maryam 39].

[3] Related by al-Bukhari (6416) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both).

[4] Related by Muslim (2985/46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).

[5] Agreed upon: al-Bukhari, in a similar wording (2697), and Muslim, with his wording (1718/18), from the hadith of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her).

* One of the benefits of this verse, the first verse, is the steadfastness of this believer, for he was one man saying to this group, "Follow me." This is, as we said in the commentary, an imperative verb.

* Another benefit of this verse is that when a caller invites people to something, he should explain what would encourage the one he invites, so that he becomes active and acts. This is based on His saying: ﴿I will guide you to the path of right guidance﴾ [Ghafir 38].

* Another benefit of this noble verse is the indication of Pharaoh's lie when he said to his people: ﴿I only show you what I see, and I only guide you to the path of right guidance﴾ [Ghafir 29]. So it distinguishes between Pharaoh's statement and the statement of this believer. Pharaoh's statement is a lie, and the statement of this man is undoubtedly true.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that paths differ: there are paths of misguidance, paths of error (ghayy), and paths of right guidance (rashad). The path that leads to Allah is the path of right guidance, and these scattered paths are paths of misguidance. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And that this is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow the [other] paths, for they will separate you from His way. That is what He has instructed you with, that you may become righteous﴾ [al-An'am 153].

* Another benefit of this noble verse is the explanation of the condition of this world: that it is an enjoyment (mata') that a person enjoys, and then it passes away, either by the passing of this enjoyment or by the passing of the one who enjoys it. For this reason, look at the places where worldly people have fallen. Has anyone in it been made eternal? Has anyone in it been granted eternity for what lies before him? None of that has ever happened. So the world is either passing, or it will be taken away from its people. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not grant to any human before you eternity. So if you die, would they be eternal?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 34].

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that the entire world is confined to this small word, "enjoyment." All of the world is enjoyment, and it cannot bear more than that.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is preparation for, and desire for, the Hereafter, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾ [Ghafir 39]. When this is combined with what came before it, it contains two benefits: abstention from the world (zuhd), and desire for the Hereafter.

Then He said: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾ [Ghafir 40], and so on to the end.

* Among its benefits: an evil deed does not increase in sin beyond the measure of the evil itself, based on His saying here: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with the like of it﴾ [Ghafir 40].

* Another benefit of the verse: in a context of warning, one should begin with what indicates warning before beginning with what indicates encouragement, because here He began with the evil deed and then followed it with the righteous. Look at the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, in a context of mentioning the legal rulings, when He said: ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 98].
When Allah, may He be exalted, wanted to speak about Himself and to clarify the perfection of His attributes, He said: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful. And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾ [al-Hijr 49–50]. So for every situation there is a suitable speech. A person should arrange his meanings according to what the situation requires, and not throw out his speech at random. "And the bounty of Allah is given to whom He wills" (Qur'an 57:21). A person may want something and wish to arrange his speech and build it on what the situation requires, but his expression fails him. However, if a person seeks help from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and relies upon Him, Allah makes the matter easy for him.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: a deed is not accepted unless it is righteous, and it does not benefit its doer unless it is righteous.
We have mentioned that the righteous deed is one in which the conditions of acceptance are combined, and they are two: sincerity (ikhlas) and conformity to the Sunnah (mutaba'ah). If sincerity is lacking, the person becomes a polytheist (mushrik); if conformity is lacking, the person becomes an innovator (mubtadi'). For this reason, no deed is accepted except that which is sincere and in accordance with the Shari'ah.
When sincerity is lacking, a person falls into shirk, and when conformity is lacking, a person falls into bid'ah (innovation). Which of them is worse? The first. The second may be worse depending on the degree of opposition, but shirk, as such, is greater than bid'ah. It has been said that bid'ah is more severe and greater, because Allah said: ﴿Say: "My Lord has only forbidden the shameful deeds, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, sin, unjust transgression, associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know"﴾ [al-A'raf 33]. The verse proceeds gradually from the lower to the higher. The people of bid'ah harm themselves and harm others, because such a person becomes a leader calling to opposition to the messengers. What appears is that shirk, as shirk, is greater, but the consequence of bid'ah may be more severe than the consequence of shirk.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: males and females are equal in reward and punishment. This means that Allah does not punish a female more than a male, nor a male more than a female, and likewise He does not reward a male more than a female, nor a female more than a male, based on His saying in this verse: ﴿whether male or female﴾.
A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿So their Lord responded to them: "Indeed, I will not allow to be lost the work of any worker among you, whether male or female"﴾ [Al 'Imran 195].

* Another benefit of this noble verse: a righteous deed does not benefit unless it is built upon faith, based on His saying: ﴿while he is a believer﴾. The clause, as you know, O grammarians (al-mu'ribun, those who study i'rab, grammatical parsing), is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject), meaning: while the state is that he is a believer.
Based on this, we ask: does the deed of a hypocrite benefit him? No, because of the absence of faith; he is not a believer.
Is faith that you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree, both its good and its bad, or is there a faith beyond all that? The second answer is correct. Among the faith upon which righteous deeds must be built is believing in the reward for the deed. For this reason, when a person does a righteous deed while hoping for this reward, there is no doubt that he will increase in desire for the deed and will increase in performing it well, because he knows that the goods are in proportion to the price. If you are working while feeling that you will be fully repaid for this deed, you will do the work well so that the reward and recompense will be good for you. This is an important matter that people often neglect, namely intending by it the reward that Allah has prepared for the one who does this deed.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: the provision of Paradise has no reckoning, meaning that nothing is demanded from the person in exchange, and no liability falls upon him, based on His saying: ﴿They will be provided therein without account﴾ [Ghafir 40].

Then this believing man said: ﴿And O my people, what is [wrong] with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir 41]. This is an interrogative of wonder and denial, as if he is saying: "How strange you are! I invite you to Paradise, and you invite me to the Fire." By Allah, this is truly a matter for wonder: that you invite a man to Paradise while he invites you to the Fire. For example, you come to a man and say: "O so-and-so, leave off drinking wine; drinking wine is forbidden and not permissible. Whoever drinks it in this world will not drink it in the Hereafter. It is the mother of wickedness, the key to every evil." He says to you: "O boy! Pleasure, delight, joy and happiness! Drink, for when you drink you will see yourself as the king of kings." Then he encourages him, and then he also gives him false hopes, saying: "Drink, and when you drink and attain pleasure and delight, then seek forgiveness from Allah; the door is open." Which of them has more right to be answered? The first, of course. This one says: ﴿What [wrong] with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?﴾ This, as I have told you, is an interrogative of wonder and denial, and it is a place for wonder and also a place for denial.

* Student: (...) Is the intention to disobey something for which a person is sinful?
* Shaykh: Intention, may Allah bless you, is of two kinds: an intention accompanied by resolve (hamm), and a mere passing thought (khatir). The second kind does not make a person sinful, neither in Makkah nor elsewhere. The first kind, an intention accompanied by resolve, is one for which a person is sinful.
* Student: In the verse: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation [in it] through injustice – We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj 25]?
* Shaykh: Yes, a painful punishment, because the Sacred Precinct is not like anywhere else. If the resolve to deviate, combined with injustice, brings a painful punishment, then what about the act itself? It will be more severe.
* Student: The saying of Allah in Surah Ibrahim: ﴿To the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy – Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 1–2]. What is the reason for the genitive case (jarr)?
* Shaykh: ﴿To the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy – Allah﴾. This is in the form of an explicative apposition ('atf al-bayan). Who is the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy? Allah. So He clarified it. The word ﴿Allah﴾ in the genitive is an explanation of ﴿the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy﴾.
* Student: Does anything follow from it if we say it is an adjective?
* Shaykh: The custom is that the word of majesty (lafz al-jalalah, "Allah") is the one that is described, because it is the proper name that specifies its referent without any ambiguity. For this reason the grammarians said that it is the most definite of definites, and that it is more definite even than the pronoun. When it is the most definite, it cannot be an adjective; it is a substitute (badal) or an explicative apposition ('atf al-bayan). Concerning explicative apposition, Ibn Malik says:
"And it is seen to be suitable for substitution, except in cases like 'O boy, may he live long' and like 'Bishr, follower of al-Bakri'; and it is not that it is replaced by al-Mardi."
Every explicative apposition is suitable to be a substitute, except in these two matters.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It is not in any case, because by "fighting" here it may be intended a deviation with injustice if he intends a major sin.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, it is the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl). Other separate pronouns, however, originally have a place in the grammatical structure.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. This, may Allah keep you safe, is after the people of Paradise have settled in Paradise, after everything has been finalized. That is, the people of Paradise will not leave it, and the people of the Fire will not leave it, meaning after everything has settled.

**Student:** I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct. O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement. Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account. And O my people, what is with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire? You invite me to disbelieve in Allah and associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I invite you to the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving."﴾ [Ghafir 38–42].

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct."﴾ [Ghafir 38]. At the beginning of these verses Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh said﴾ [Ghafir 28]. Here and in what precedes it, He says: ﴿the one who believed﴾, confirming his faith and that he was truly a believer.

﴿The one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct."﴾ ﴿O my people﴾: its grammatical analysis (i'rab) has already been discussed, and we explained that it is a vocative in the accusative, with the accusative marked on the letter before the omitted first-person ya' (the ya' of the speaker), which was dropped for lightness; the case-ending could not be shown because the final letter is occupied by the vowel of harmony (kasrah).

As for His saying: ﴿O my people, follow me; I will guide you﴾, it is read both with the ya' and without it (ittabi'uni and ittabi'u, and aheedkum). This means that there are two readings: "ittabi'uni" and "ittabi'u". With the ya' the matter is clear, since it is the ya' of the speaker. Without it, it has been dropped for lightness.

His saying ﴿follow me﴾ is an imperative verb, and ﴿I will guide you﴾ is the answer to the imperative. For this reason it is in the jussive mood, with the ya' dropped and the kasrah before it as evidence of it. The original form of ahdikum is ahdeekum (ahdiyukum), but when the present-tense verb comes as an answer to an imperative it is jussive. It is said that it is jussive because of the imperative itself, and it is said that it is jussive because of an implied condition, the meaning being "if you follow me, I will guide you." The same is said of everything that comes in this construction.

﴿I will guide you to the path of right conduct﴾: that is, to its way. The guidance here is guidance of indication (hidayat al-dalalah), because it cannot mean guidance of divine enabling (hidayat al-tawfiq), which lies in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He said to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas 56], meaning you cannot give guidance of enabling. So His saying ﴿I will guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ means: I will show you the path of right conduct. The "path of right conduct" is the opposite of the "path of error" (ghayy). Rushd (right conduct) is good management of one's affairs, and ghayy is committing error deliberately.

﴿O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement.﴾ When he urged them to follow him, he made them renounce the world, because the root of the deviation of the children of Adam is greed for this world, and rivalry is only over it. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, I do not fear poverty for you; rather, I fear that the world will be opened to you so that you compete for it as those before you competed for it, and it destroys you as it destroyed them."[1]

So when he asked them to follow him, he explained to them the state of the world over which they compete, and by which they turned away from the way of Allah. He said: ﴿O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment.﴾ ﴿Only﴾ (innama) is a particle of restriction; ﴿this worldly life﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿a passing enjoyment﴾ is its predicate (khabar). That is, this world is nothing but an enjoyment which a person enjoys for a little while and then it vanishes. For this reason the author says in his commentary: ﴿enjoyment﴾ is a passing enjoyment.

﴿And indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement.﴾ ﴿The Hereafter﴾ is what comes after this world; ﴿is﴾ is a pronoun of separation (dhamir al-fasl), and ﴿the abode of settlement﴾ is the predicate of ﴿indeed (inna)﴾.

Know that the pronoun of separation is a pronoun that has no place in grammatical analysis: it is not parsed as subject, predicate, or anything else. It has no grammatical position.

Know also that it has three benefits:
The first benefit: emphasis.
The second benefit: restriction.
The third benefit: distinguishing the predicate from the adjective.

This appears in the example: if you say "Zayd huwa al-fadil" (Zayd is the excellent one), then "huwa" is a pronoun of separation, from which we derive three benefits.
First, emphasis: we have emphasized that Zayd is the excellent one, or rather, that Zayd is excellent.
Then, restriction: because you said "Zayd huwa," meaning, not someone else: Zayd is the excellent one.
The third benefit: distinguishing between adjective and predicate. If you say "Zayd al-fadil," it could be that "al-fadil" is an adjective of Zayd and the predicate has not yet come. But if you say "huwa al-fadil," it becomes certain that "al-fadil" is the predicate, and thereby the predicate is distinguished from the adjective.

We have mentioned that it has no place in grammatical analysis, and the evidence for this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians if they are the victors﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 40]. Here ﴿the victors﴾ came as the predicate of ﴿kana (were)﴾. If it had a place in grammatical analysis, it would have been "in kanu hum al-ghalibun" (if they were the victors, in the nominative), but it has no place in grammatical analysis.

So what is the abode of settlement? It is the Hereafter, and this has been emphasized by the use of the pronoun of separation.

﴿And indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾: that is, the abode of permanent residence. For this reason: "Death will be brought in the form of a ram, and it will be stopped between Paradise and the Fire, and it will be said: 'O people of the Fire!' And they will stretch their necks and look. Likewise it will be said to the people of Paradise: 'O people of Paradise!' And they will stretch their necks and look. Then it will be said to them: 'Do you recognize this?' They will say: 'Yes, this is death.' It will be slaughtered before them, and it will be said: 'O people of Paradise, there is eternity and no death; O people of the Fire, there is eternity and no death.'"[2]

So this is the settlement. Since there is no movement from this abode, it is the abode of settlement. Now, if it is the abode of settlement and the world is an enjoyment, what should a person work for? The Hereafter, because it is the abode of settlement. As for this world, it is an abode of passing through, an abode of enjoyment. "Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler passing through."[3]

Then he said: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account﴾ [Ghafir 40]. This is an explanation of the state of the Hereafter and how people are recompensed in it. He said: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like.﴾ ﴿Whoever (man)﴾ is conditional; ﴿does﴾ is the conditional verb; and the clause ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ is the answer to the condition.

His saying ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾: ﴿like (mithl)﴾ is the second object of ﴿yujza (is recompensed)﴾, and the first object is the implied subject (naib al-fa'il).

He says: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾. The evil deed (sayyi'ah) is what is bad in its state or in its outcome. What befalls a person of sickness, poverty, affliction or the like is evil in its present state. What befalls a person as punishment for his deeds is evil in its outcome. Sometimes a person is hastened with punishment in this world. So the evil deed is everything that is bad in its present state or in its outcome.

﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾: one evil deed is repaid with one, whatever it is, even if the person is in Makkah, or in Madinah, or in the mosque, or in any place, or at any time. Even if it is in the sacred months in which Allah has forbidden injustice, He said: ﴿Of them four are sacred; that is the correct religion, so do not wrong yourselves therein﴾ [al-Tawbah 36]. For the evil deed is not increased, but know that it may be more severe in its quality, not in its quantity. What is the quality? We see that one blow may be more severe on a person than ten blows because of its intensity and the effect of its impact. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said about the Sacred House in Makkah: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj 25].

By this explanation, which is indicated by the Book and the Sunnah, it becomes clear that what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), that he left Makkah and said: "I will not remain in a city where its evil and good deeds are equal," is not authentic from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him). Ibn 'Abbas was too learned and knowledgeable to be confused about this matter. Moreover, Allah said in Surat al-An'am, which is Makkan: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and they will not be wronged﴾ [al-An'am 160].

He said: ﴿And whoever does righteousness, male or female﴾ [Ghafir 40]. ﴿Whoever (man)﴾ here is conditional. ﴿Righteousness (salihan)﴾ may be parsed as an adjective of an omitted noun, the meaning being "a righteous deed," or it may be taken as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), since the adjective of an omitted verbal noun may be parsed as an absolute object or as an adjective of an omitted noun. The meaning would be "a righteous action."

So what is the righteous deed? The righteous deed is that which meets the conditions of acceptance, which is that it be sincerely for Allah and in accordance with the Law (shari'ah) from Him. That is, it combines two matters: sincerity to Allah, and following His messengers, peace be upon them. This is the righteous deed. So it is what meets the conditions of acceptance, which are sincerity to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and second, following the messengers of Allah, whether Muhammad or others. But it is well known that after the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) it is not valid to follow anyone else.

If sincerity is lacking, the deed is not righteous but is rejected for its doer, because of the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, in the sacred hadith: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in associating others with Me. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his association."[4]

If following is lacking, the deed is not righteous and is rejected, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever does a deed which is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected."[5]

His saying ﴿male or female﴾ is an explanation of ﴿whoever (man)﴾. The "min" here is explanatory (bayaniyyah). How do we say it explains ﴿man﴾? Because ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun is basically vague, so when an explanation follows it, that explanation makes its vagueness clear.

﴿male or female, while being a believer﴾: this is the condition. He must be a believer. If he is not a believer, his righteous deed does not benefit him, even if the deed is one whose benefit extends to others, because of the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah 54]. So the deed of a non-believer does not benefit him. If a disbelieving man repaired the roads, laid water pipes to give water to people, built mosques, printed books, clothed the naked, and fed the hungry, would this benefit him? No. For this reason the deeds of the hypocrites do not benefit them, because they are not believers. And by this we know that faith is the foundation: believe, then act.

He must be a believer. If he is not a believer, his righteous deed does not benefit him, even if the deed's benefit extends to others, because of the saying of Allah: ﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah 54]. So the deed of the non-believer does not benefit him. If a disbelieving man repaired the roads, laid water pipes to give water to people, built mosques, printed books, clothed the naked, and fed the hungry, would this benefit him? No. For this reason the deeds of the hypocrites do not benefit them, because they are not believers. And by this we know that faith is the foundation: believe, then act. As for action without faith, we ask Allah not to strip us and you of faith. Action without faith is dust: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan 23]. Faith must come first; then, when a person believes, he acts; and when he acts, he is sincere and follows.

﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾ [Ghafir 40]: the clause ﴿those﴾ is the answer to the condition, that is, the condition is ﴿and whoever does righteousness﴾ [Ghafir 40].

﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾: here He said ﴿those (ulaika)﴾, the demonstrative used for the distant, indicating the loftiness of their rank, as if you point to them while they are above.

﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾: he said (with the ya' pronounced with a dammah and the kha' with a fathah, "yudkhalun" and the reverse). What is the reverse? "Yadkhulun" is permitted: "yudkhalun" means that Allah causes them to enter; and "yadkhulun" means that they enter by themselves, but by the permission of Allah. It is well known that the people of Paradise do not enter Paradise except after intercession, after the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ) to open Paradise, because they arrive at it while its gate is closed, so they ask someone to intercede for them with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that the gate be opened for them. So the Prophet (ﷺ) alone intercedes that the gate be opened for them, and it is opened.

﴿Being provided therein without account﴾ [Ghafir 40]: ﴿provided (yurzaqun)﴾: provision here means giving, and from it is His saying: ﴿And when relatives, orphans and the needy are present at the division, provide them from it﴾ [al-Nisa' 8], meaning give them. So the meaning of ﴿yurzaqun﴾ is that they are given.

His saying: (﴿without account﴾ means without consequence). It means they will not be held to account for it, and they will not pay a price for it. In this world you do not own provision except for a price; but in the Hereafter you are given provision without price and without consequence, and you will not be held to account for it. Why? Because the price was paid in advance, as a salam (advance sale). Do you know salam? It is paying the price in advance and delaying the delivery of the goods. Here the price was paid in advance: the price was in this world, when they acted in obedience to Allah, and this was the exchange. So these people had entered into this transaction and paid its price in advance. For this reason He said: ﴿being provided therein without account﴾.

* In these three verses there are benefits.
* First: the gentleness (talattuf) of this caller, this believing man who calls to Allah, as shown by his saying ﴿O my people﴾. There is no doubt that this is one of the methods of gentleness.

---

[1] Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3158) and Muslim (2961/6), from the hadith of 'Amr ibn 'Awf al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him), and its wording: "...So rejoice and hope for what pleases you. By Allah, it is not poverty I fear for you, but I fear that the world will be spread out over you as it was spread out over those before you, so you compete for it as they competed for it, and it destroys you as it destroyed them," the hadith.

[2] Related by al-Bukhari (6548) and Muslim, with his wording (2850/43), with their chains from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), that his father told him, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, death will be brought until it is placed between Paradise and the Fire, then it will be slaughtered, then a caller will call: 'O people of Paradise, no death! O people of the Fire, no death!' So the people of Paradise will increase in joy over their joy, and the people of the Fire will increase in grief over their grief." Al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (11255) also related it with his chain from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) with the wording: "...He calls: 'O people of Paradise!' and they stretch their necks and look; and He calls: 'O people of the Fire!' and they stretch their necks and look. It is said: 'Do you know death?' They say: 'Yes.' Death is brought in the form of a white-spotted ram, and it is said: 'This is death,' and it is brought forward and slaughtered. He said: 'O people of Paradise, eternity and no death; and it is said: O people of the Fire, eternity and no death.'" He said: then he recited ﴿And warn them of the Day of regret, when the matter is decided﴾ [Maryam 39].

[3] Related by al-Bukhari (6416) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both).

[4] Related by Muslim (2985/46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).

[5] Agreed upon: al-Bukhari, in a similar wording (2697), and Muslim, with his wording (1718/18), from the hadith of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her).

* One of the benefits of this verse, the first verse, is the steadfastness of this believer, for he was one man saying to this group, "Follow me." This is, as we said in the commentary, an imperative verb.

* Another benefit of this verse is that when a caller invites people to something, he should explain what would encourage the one he invites, so that he becomes active and acts. This is based on His saying: ﴿I will guide you to the path of right guidance﴾ [Ghafir 38].

* Another benefit of this noble verse is the indication of Pharaoh's lie when he said to his people: ﴿I only show you what I see, and I only guide you to the path of right guidance﴾ [Ghafir 29]. So it distinguishes between Pharaoh's statement and the statement of this believer. Pharaoh's statement is a lie, and the statement of this man is undoubtedly true.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that paths differ: there are paths of misguidance, paths of error (ghayy), and paths of right guidance (rashad). The path that leads to Allah is the path of right guidance, and these scattered paths are paths of misguidance. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And that this is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow the [other] paths, for they will separate you from His way. That is what He has instructed you with, that you may become righteous﴾ [al-An'am 153].

* Another benefit of this noble verse is the explanation of the condition of this world: that it is an enjoyment (mata') that a person enjoys, and then it passes away, either by the passing of this enjoyment or by the passing of the one who enjoys it. For this reason, look at the places where worldly people have fallen. Has anyone in it been made eternal? Has anyone in it been granted eternity for what lies before him? None of that has ever happened. So the world is either passing, or it will be taken away from its people. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not grant to any human before you eternity. So if you die, would they be eternal?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 34].

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that the entire world is confined to this small word, "enjoyment." All of the world is enjoyment, and it cannot bear more than that.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is preparation for, and desire for, the Hereafter, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾ [Ghafir 39]. When this is combined with what came before it, it contains two benefits: abstention from the world (zuhd), and desire for the Hereafter.

Then He said: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾ [Ghafir 40], and so on to the end.

* Among its benefits: an evil deed does not increase in sin beyond the measure of the evil itself, based on His saying here: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with the like of it﴾ [Ghafir 40].

* Another benefit of the verse: in a context of warning, one should begin with what indicates warning before beginning with what indicates encouragement, because here He began with the evil deed and then followed it with the righteous. Look at the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, in a context of mentioning the legal rulings, when He said: ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 98].
When Allah, may He be exalted, wanted to speak about Himself and to clarify the perfection of His attributes, He said: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful. And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾ [al-Hijr 49–50]. So for every situation there is a suitable speech. A person should arrange his meanings according to what the situation requires, and not throw out his speech at random. "And the bounty of Allah is given to whom He wills" (Qur'an 57:21). A person may want something and wish to arrange his speech and build it on what the situation requires, but his expression fails him. However, if a person seeks help from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and relies upon Him, Allah makes the matter easy for him.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: a deed is not accepted unless it is righteous, and it does not benefit its doer unless it is righteous.
We have mentioned that the righteous deed is one in which the conditions of acceptance are combined, and they are two: sincerity (ikhlas) and conformity to the Sunnah (mutaba'ah). If sincerity is lacking, the person becomes a polytheist (mushrik); if conformity is lacking, the person becomes an innovator (mubtadi'). For this reason, no deed is accepted except that which is sincere and in accordance with the Shari'ah.
When sincerity is lacking, a person falls into shirk, and when conformity is lacking, a person falls into bid'ah (innovation). Which of them is worse? The first. The second may be worse depending on the degree of opposition, but shirk, as such, is greater than bid'ah. It has been said that bid'ah is more severe and greater, because Allah said: ﴿Say: "My Lord has only forbidden the shameful deeds, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, sin, unjust transgression, associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know"﴾ [al-A'raf 33]. The verse proceeds gradually from the lower to the higher. The people of bid'ah harm themselves and harm others, because such a person becomes a leader calling to opposition to the messengers. What appears is that shirk, as shirk, is greater, but the consequence of bid'ah may be more severe than the consequence of shirk.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: males and females are equal in reward and punishment. This means that Allah does not punish a female more than a male, nor a male more than a female, and likewise He does not reward a male more than a female, nor a female more than a male, based on His saying in this verse: ﴿whether male or female﴾.
A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿So their Lord responded to them: "Indeed, I will not allow to be lost the work of any worker among you, whether male or female"﴾ [Al 'Imran 195].

* Another benefit of this noble verse: a righteous deed does not benefit unless it is built upon faith, based on His saying: ﴿while he is a believer﴾. The clause, as you know, O grammarians (al-mu'ribun, those who study i'rab, grammatical parsing), is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject), meaning: while the state is that he is a believer.
Based on this, we ask: does the deed of a hypocrite benefit him? No, because of the absence of faith; he is not a believer.
Is faith that you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree, both its good and its bad, or is there a faith beyond all that? The second answer is correct. Among the faith upon which righteous deeds must be built is believing in the reward for the deed. For this reason, when a person does a righteous deed while hoping for this reward, there is no doubt that he will increase in desire for the deed and will increase in performing it well, because he knows that the goods are in proportion to the price. If you are working while feeling that you will be fully repaid for this deed, you will do the work well so that the reward and recompense will be good for you. This is an important matter that people often neglect, namely intending by it the reward that Allah has prepared for the one who does this deed.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: the provision of Paradise has no reckoning, meaning that nothing is demanded from the person in exchange, and no liability falls upon him, based on His saying: ﴿They will be provided therein without account﴾ [Ghafir 40].

Then this believing man said: ﴿And O my people, what is [wrong] with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir 41]. This is an interrogative of wonder and denial, as if he is saying: "How strange you are! I invite you to Paradise, and you invite me to the Fire." By Allah, this is truly a matter for wonder: that you invite a man to Paradise while he invites you to the Fire. For example, you come to a man and say: "O so-and-so, leave off drinking wine; drinking wine is forbidden and not permissible. Whoever drinks it in this world will not drink it in the Hereafter. It is the mother of wickedness, the key to every evil." He says to you: "O boy! Pleasure, delight, joy and happiness! Drink, for when you drink you will see yourself as the king of kings." Then he encourages him, and then he also gives him false hopes, saying: "Drink, and when you drink and attain pleasure and delight, then seek forgiveness from Allah; the door is open." Which of them has more right to be answered? The first, of course. This one says: ﴿What [wrong] with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?﴾ This, as I have told you, is an interrogative of wonder and denial, and it is a place for wonder and also a place for denial.

* Student: (...) Is the intention to disobey something for which a person is sinful?
* Shaykh: Intention, may Allah bless you, is of two kinds: an intention accompanied by resolve (hamm), and a mere passing thought (khatir). The second kind does not make a person sinful, neither in Makkah nor elsewhere. The first kind, an intention accompanied by resolve, is one for which a person is sinful.
* Student: In the verse: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation [in it] through injustice – We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj 25]?
* Shaykh: Yes, a painful punishment, because the Sacred Precinct is not like anywhere else. If the resolve to deviate, combined with injustice, brings a painful punishment, then what about the act itself? It will be more severe.
* Student: The saying of Allah in Surah Ibrahim: ﴿To the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy – Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 1–2]. What is the reason for the genitive case (jarr)?
* Shaykh: ﴿To the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy – Allah﴾. This is in the form of an explicative apposition ('atf al-bayan). Who is the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy? Allah. So He clarified it. The word ﴿Allah﴾ in the genitive is an explanation of ﴿the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy﴾.
* Student: Does anything follow from it if we say it is an adjective?
* Shaykh: The custom is that the word of majesty (lafz al-jalalah, "Allah") is the one that is described, because it is the proper name that specifies its referent without any ambiguity. For this reason the grammarians said that it is the most definite of definites, and that it is more definite even than the pronoun. When it is the most definite, it cannot be an adjective; it is a substitute (badal) or an explicative apposition ('atf al-bayan). Concerning explicative apposition, Ibn Malik says:
"And it is seen to be suitable for substitution, except in cases like 'O boy, may he live long' and like 'Bishr, follower of al-Bakri'; and it is not that it is replaced by al-Mardi."
Every explicative apposition is suitable to be a substitute, except in these two matters.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It is not in any case, because by "fighting" here it may be intended a deviation with injustice if he intends a major sin.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, it is the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl). Other separate pronouns, however, originally have a place in the grammatical structure.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. This, may Allah keep you safe, is after the people of Paradise have settled in Paradise, after everything has been finalized. That is, the people of Paradise will not leave it, and the people of the Fire will not leave it, meaning after everything has settled.

**Student:** I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct. O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement. Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account. And O my people, what is with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire? You invite me to disbelieve in Allah and associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I invite you to the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving."﴾ [Ghafir 38–42].

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct."﴾ [Ghafir 38]. At the beginning of these verses Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh said﴾ [Ghafir 28]. Here and in what precedes it, He says: ﴿the one who believed﴾, confirming his faith and that he was truly a believer.

﴿The one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct."﴾ ﴿O my people﴾: its grammatical analysis (i'rab) has already been discussed, and we explained that it is a vocative in the accusative, with the accusative marked on the letter before the omitted first-person ya' (the ya' of the speaker), which was dropped for lightness; the case-ending could not be shown because the final letter is occupied by the vowel of harmony (kasrah).

As for His saying: ﴿O my people, follow me; I will guide you﴾, it is read both with the ya' and without it (ittabi'uni and ittabi'u, and aheedkum). This means that there are two readings: "ittabi'uni" and "ittabi'u". With the ya' the matter is clear, since it is the ya' of the speaker. Without it, it has been dropped for lightness.

His saying ﴿follow me﴾ is an imperative verb, and ﴿I will guide you﴾ is the answer to the imperative. For this reason it is in the jussive mood, with the ya' dropped and the kasrah before it as evidence of it. The original form of ahdikum is ahdeekum (ahdiyukum), but when the present-tense verb comes as an answer to an imperative it is jussive. It is said that it is jussive because of the imperative itself, and it is said that it is jussive because of an implied condition, the meaning being "if you follow me, I will guide you." The same is said of everything that comes in this construction.

﴿I will guide you to the path of right conduct﴾: that is, to its way. The guidance here is guidance of indication (hidayat al-dalalah), because it cannot mean guidance of divine enabling (hidayat al-tawfiq), which lies in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He said to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas 56], meaning you cannot give guidance of enabling. So His saying ﴿I will guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ means: I will show you the path of right conduct. The "path of right conduct" is the opposite of the "path of error" (ghayy). Rushd (right conduct) is good management of one's affairs, and ghayy is committing error deliberately.

﴿O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement.﴾ When he urged them to follow him, he made them renounce the world, because the root of the deviation of the children of Adam is greed for this world, and rivalry is only over it. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, I do not fear poverty for you; rather, I fear that the world will be opened to you so that you compete for it as those before you competed for it, and it destroys you as it destroyed them."[1]

So when he asked them to follow him, he explained to them the state of the world over which they compete, and by which they turned away from the way of Allah. He said: ﴿O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment.﴾ ﴿Only﴾ (innama) is a particle of restriction; ﴿this worldly life﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿a passing enjoyment﴾ is its predicate (khabar). That is, this world is nothing but an enjoyment which a person enjoys for a little while and then it vanishes. For this reason the author says in his commentary: ﴿enjoyment﴾ is a passing enjoyment.

﴿And indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement.﴾ ﴿The Hereafter﴾ is what comes after this world; ﴿is﴾ is a pronoun of separation (dhamir al-fasl), and ﴿the abode of settlement﴾ is the predicate of ﴿indeed (inna)﴾.

Know that the pronoun of separation is a pronoun that has no place in grammatical analysis: it is not parsed as subject, predicate, or anything else. It has no grammatical position.

Know also that it has three benefits:
The first benefit: emphasis.
The second benefit: restriction.
The third benefit: distinguishing the predicate from the adjective.

This appears in the example: if you say "Zayd huwa al-fadil" (Zayd is the excellent one), then "huwa" is a pronoun of separation, from which we derive three benefits.
First, emphasis: we have emphasized that Zayd is the excellent one, or rather, that Zayd is excellent.
Then, restriction: because you said "Zayd huwa," meaning, not someone else: Zayd is the excellent one.
The third benefit: distinguishing between adjective and predicate. If you say "Zayd al-fadil," it could be that "al-fadil" is an adjective of Zayd and the predicate has not yet come. But if you say "huwa al-fadil," it becomes certain that "al-fadil" is the predicate, and thereby the predicate is distinguished from the adjective.

We have mentioned that it has no place in grammatical analysis, and the evidence for this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians if they are the victors﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 40]. Here ﴿the victors﴾ came as the predicate of ﴿kana (were)﴾. If it had a place in grammatical analysis, it would have been "in kanu hum al-ghalibun" (if they were the victors, in the nominative), but it has no place in grammatical analysis.

So what is the abode of settlement? It is the Hereafter, and this has been emphasized by the use of the pronoun of separation.

﴿And indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾: that is, the abode of permanent residence. For this reason: "Death will be brought in the form of a ram, and it will be stopped between Paradise and the Fire, and it will be said: 'O people of the Fire!' And they will stretch their necks and look. Likewise it will be said to the people of Paradise: 'O people of Paradise!' And they will stretch their necks and look. Then it will be said to them: 'Do you recognize this?' They will say: 'Yes, this is death.' It will be slaughtered before them, and it will be said: 'O people of Paradise, there is eternity and no death; O people of the Fire, there is eternity and no death.'"[2]

So this is the settlement. Since there is no movement from this abode, it is the abode of settlement. Now, if it is the abode of settlement and the world is an enjoyment, what should a person work for? The Hereafter, because it is the abode of settlement. As for this world, it is an abode of passing through, an abode of enjoyment. "Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler passing through."[3]

Then he said: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account﴾ [Ghafir 40]. This is an explanation of the state of the Hereafter and how people are recompensed in it. He said: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like.﴾ ﴿Whoever (man)﴾ is conditional; ﴿does﴾ is the conditional verb; and the clause ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ is the answer to the condition.

His saying ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾: ﴿like (mithl)﴾ is the second object of ﴿yujza (is recompensed)﴾, and the first object is the implied subject (naib al-fa'il).

He says: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾. The evil deed (sayyi'ah) is what is bad in its state or in its outcome. What befalls a person of sickness, poverty, affliction or the like is evil in its present state. What befalls a person as punishment for his deeds is evil in its outcome. Sometimes a person is hastened with punishment in this world. So the evil deed is everything that is bad in its present state or in its outcome.

﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾: one evil deed is repaid with one, whatever it is, even if the person is in Makkah, or in Madinah, or in the mosque, or in any place, or at any time. Even if it is in the sacred months in which Allah has forbidden injustice, He said: ﴿Of them four are sacred; that is the correct religion, so do not wrong yourselves therein﴾ [al-Tawbah 36]. For the evil deed is not increased, but know that it may be more severe in its quality, not in its quantity. What is the quality? We see that one blow may be more severe on a person than ten blows because of its intensity and the effect of its impact. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said about the Sacred House in Makkah: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj 25].

By this explanation, which is indicated by the Book and the Sunnah, it becomes clear that what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), that he left Makkah and said: "I will not remain in a city where its evil and good deeds are equal," is not authentic from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him). Ibn 'Abbas was too learned and knowledgeable to be confused about this matter. Moreover, Allah said in Surat al-An'am, which is Makkan: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and they will not be wronged﴾ [al-An'am 160].

He said: ﴿And whoever does righteousness, male or female﴾ [Ghafir 40]. ﴿Whoever (man)﴾ here is conditional. ﴿Righteousness (salihan)﴾ may be parsed as an adjective of an omitted noun, the meaning being "a righteous deed," or it may be taken as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), since the adjective of an omitted verbal noun may be parsed as an absolute object or as an adjective of an omitted noun. The meaning would be "a righteous action."

So what is the righteous deed? The righteous deed is that which meets the conditions of acceptance, which is that it be sincerely for Allah and in accordance with the Law (shari'ah) from Him. That is, it combines two matters: sincerity to Allah, and following His messengers, peace be upon them. This is the righteous deed. So it is what meets the conditions of acceptance, which are sincerity to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and second, following the messengers of Allah, whether Muhammad or others. But it is well known that after the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) it is not valid to follow anyone else.

If sincerity is lacking, the deed is not righteous but is rejected for its doer, because of the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, in the sacred hadith: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in associating others with Me. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his association."[4]

If following is lacking, the deed is not righteous and is rejected, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever does a deed which is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected."[5]

His saying ﴿male or female﴾ is an explanation of ﴿whoever (man)﴾. The "min" here is explanatory (bayaniyyah). How do we say it explains ﴿man﴾? Because ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun is basically vague, so when an explanation follows it, that explanation makes its vagueness clear.

﴿male or female, while being a believer﴾: this is the condition. He must be a believer. If he is not a believer, his righteous deed does not benefit him, even if the deed is one whose benefit extends to others, because of the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah 54]. So the deed of a non-believer does not benefit him. If a disbelieving man repaired the roads, laid water pipes to give water to people, built mosques, printed books, clothed the naked, and fed the hungry, would this benefit him? No. For this reason the deeds of the hypocrites do not benefit them, because they are not believers. And by this we know that faith is the foundation: believe, then act.

He must be a believer. If he is not a believer, his righteous deed does not benefit him, even if the deed's benefit extends to others, because of the saying of Allah: ﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah 54]. So the deed of the non-believer does not benefit him. If a disbelieving man repaired the roads, laid water pipes to give water to people, built mosques, printed books, clothed the naked, and fed the hungry, would this benefit him? No. For this reason the deeds of the hypocrites do not benefit them, because they are not believers. And by this we know that faith is the foundation: believe, then act. As for action without faith, we ask Allah not to strip us and you of faith. Action without faith is dust: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan 23]. Faith must come first; then, when a person believes, he acts; and when he acts, he is sincere and follows.

﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾ [Ghafir 40]: the clause ﴿those﴾ is the answer to the condition, that is, the condition is ﴿and whoever does righteousness﴾ [Ghafir 40].

﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾: here He said ﴿those (ulaika)﴾, the demonstrative used for the distant, indicating the loftiness of their rank, as if you point to them while they are above.

﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾: he said (with the ya' pronounced with a dammah and the kha' with a fathah, "yudkhalun" and the reverse). What is the reverse? "Yadkhulun" is permitted: "yudkhalun" means that Allah causes them to enter; and "yadkhulun" means that they enter by themselves, but by the permission of Allah. It is well known that the people of Paradise do not enter Paradise except after intercession, after the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ) to open Paradise, because they arrive at it while its gate is closed, so they ask someone to intercede for them with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that the gate be opened for them. So the Prophet (ﷺ) alone intercedes that the gate be opened for them, and it is opened.

﴿Being provided therein without account﴾ [Ghafir 40]: ﴿provided (yurzaqun)﴾: provision here means giving, and from it is His saying: ﴿And when relatives, orphans and the needy are present at the division, provide them from it﴾ [al-Nisa' 8], meaning give them. So the meaning of ﴿yurzaqun﴾ is that they are given.

His saying: (﴿without account﴾ means without consequence). It means they will not be held to account for it, and they will not pay a price for it. In this world you do not own provision except for a price; but in the Hereafter you are given provision without price and without consequence, and you will not be held to account for it. Why?
