Because the price was paid in advance, as a salam (advance sale). Do you know salam? It is paying the price in advance and delaying the delivery of the goods. Here the price was paid in advance: the price was in this world, when they acted in obedience to Allah, and this was the exchange. So these people had entered into this transaction and paid its price in advance. For this reason He said: ﴿being provided therein without account﴾.

* In these three verses there are benefits.
* First: the gentleness (talattuf) of this caller, this believing man who calls to Allah, as shown by his saying ﴿O my people﴾. There is no doubt that this is one of the methods of gentleness.

---

[1] Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3158) and Muslim (2961/6), from the hadith of 'Amr ibn 'Awf al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him), and its wording: "...So rejoice and hope for what pleases you. By Allah, it is not poverty I fear for you, but I fear that the world will be spread out over you as it was spread out over those before you, so you compete for it as they competed for it, and it destroys you as it destroyed them," the hadith.

[2] Related by al-Bukhari (6548) and Muslim, with his wording (2850/43), with their chains from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), that his father told him, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, death will be brought until it is placed between Paradise and the Fire, then it will be slaughtered, then a caller will call: 'O people of Paradise, no death! O people of the Fire, no death!' So the people of Paradise will increase in joy over their joy, and the people of the Fire will increase in grief over their grief." Al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (11255) also related it with his chain from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) with the wording: "...He calls: 'O people of Paradise!' and they stretch their necks and look; and He calls: 'O people of the Fire!' and they stretch their necks and look. It is said: 'Do you know death?' They say: 'Yes.' Death is brought in the form of a white-spotted ram, and it is said: 'This is death,' and it is brought forward and slaughtered. He said: 'O people of Paradise, eternity and no death; and it is said: O people of the Fire, eternity and no death.'" He said: then he recited ﴿And warn them of the Day of regret, when the matter is decided﴾ [Maryam 39].

[3] Related by al-Bukhari (6416) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both).

[4] Related by Muslim (2985/46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).

[5] Agreed upon: al-Bukhari, in a similar wording (2697), and Muslim, with his wording (1718/18), from the hadith of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her).

* One of the benefits of this verse, the first verse, is the steadfastness of this believer, for he was one man saying to this group, "Follow me." This is, as we said in the commentary, an imperative verb.

* Another benefit of this verse is that when a caller invites people to something, he should explain what would encourage the one he invites, so that he becomes active and acts. This is based on His saying: ﴿I will guide you to the path of right guidance﴾ [Ghafir 38].

* Another benefit of this noble verse is the indication of Pharaoh's lie when he said to his people: ﴿I only show you what I see, and I only guide you to the path of right guidance﴾ [Ghafir 29]. So it distinguishes between Pharaoh's statement and the statement of this believer. Pharaoh's statement is a lie, and the statement of this man is undoubtedly true.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that paths differ: there are paths of misguidance, paths of error (ghayy), and paths of right guidance (rashad). The path that leads to Allah is the path of right guidance, and these scattered paths are paths of misguidance. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And that this is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow the [other] paths, for they will separate you from His way. That is what He has instructed you with, that you may become righteous﴾ [al-An'am 153].

* Another benefit of this noble verse is the explanation of the condition of this world: that it is an enjoyment (mata') that a person enjoys, and then it passes away, either by the passing of this enjoyment or by the passing of the one who enjoys it. For this reason, look at the places where worldly people have fallen. Has anyone in it been made eternal? Has anyone in it been granted eternity for what lies before him? None of that has ever happened. So the world is either passing, or it will be taken away from its people. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not grant to any human before you eternity. So if you die, would they be eternal?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 34].

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that the entire world is confined to this small word, "enjoyment." All of the world is enjoyment, and it cannot bear more than that.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is preparation for, and desire for, the Hereafter, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾ [Ghafir 39]. When this is combined with what came before it, it contains two benefits: abstention from the world (zuhd), and desire for the Hereafter.

Then He said: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾ [Ghafir 40], and so on to the end.

* Among its benefits: an evil deed does not increase in sin beyond the measure of the evil itself, based on His saying here: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with the like of it﴾ [Ghafir 40].

* Another benefit of the verse: in a context of warning, one should begin with what indicates warning before beginning with what indicates encouragement, because here He began with the evil deed and then followed it with the righteous. Look at the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, in a context of mentioning the legal rulings, when He said: ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 98].
When Allah, may He be exalted, wanted to speak about Himself and to clarify the perfection of His attributes, He said: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful. And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾ [al-Hijr 49–50]. So for every situation there is a suitable speech. A person should arrange his meanings according to what the situation requires, and not throw out his speech at random. "And the bounty of Allah is given to whom He wills" (Qur'an 57:21). A person may want something and wish to arrange his speech and build it on what the situation requires, but his expression fails him. However, if a person seeks help from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and relies upon Him, Allah makes the matter easy for him.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: a deed is not accepted unless it is righteous, and it does not benefit its doer unless it is righteous.
We have mentioned that the righteous deed is one in which the conditions of acceptance are combined, and they are two: sincerity (ikhlas) and conformity to the Sunnah (mutaba'ah). If sincerity is lacking, the person becomes a polytheist (mushrik); if conformity is lacking, the person becomes an innovator (mubtadi'). For this reason, no deed is accepted except that which is sincere and in accordance with the Shari'ah.
When sincerity is lacking, a person falls into shirk, and when conformity is lacking, a person falls into bid'ah (innovation). Which of them is worse? The first. The second may be worse depending on the degree of opposition, but shirk, as such, is greater than bid'ah. It has been said that bid'ah is more severe and greater, because Allah said: ﴿Say: "My Lord has only forbidden the shameful deeds, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, sin, unjust transgression, associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know"﴾ [al-A'raf 33]. The verse proceeds gradually from the lower to the higher. The people of bid'ah harm themselves and harm others, because such a person becomes a leader calling to opposition to the messengers. What appears is that shirk, as shirk, is greater, but the consequence of bid'ah may be more severe than the consequence of shirk.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: males and females are equal in reward and punishment. This means that Allah does not punish a female more than a male, nor a male more than a female, and likewise He does not reward a male more than a female, nor a female more than a male, based on His saying in this verse: ﴿whether male or female﴾.
A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿So their Lord responded to them: "Indeed, I will not allow to be lost the work of any worker among you, whether male or female"﴾ [Al 'Imran 195].

* Another benefit of this noble verse: a righteous deed does not benefit unless it is built upon faith, based on His saying: ﴿while he is a believer﴾. The clause, as you know, O grammarians (al-mu'ribun, those who study i'rab, grammatical parsing), is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject), meaning: while the state is that he is a believer.
Based on this, we ask: does the deed of a hypocrite benefit him? No, because of the absence of faith; he is not a believer.
Is faith that you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree, both its good and its bad, or is there a faith beyond all that? The second answer is correct. Among the faith upon which righteous deeds must be built is believing in the reward for the deed. For this reason, when a person does a righteous deed while hoping for this reward, there is no doubt that he will increase in desire for the deed and will increase in performing it well, because he knows that the goods are in proportion to the price. If you are working while feeling that you will be fully repaid for this deed, you will do the work well so that the reward and recompense will be good for you. This is an important matter that people often neglect, namely intending by it the reward that Allah has prepared for the one who does this deed.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: the provision of Paradise has no reckoning, meaning that nothing is demanded from the person in exchange, and no liability falls upon him, based on His saying: ﴿They will be provided therein without account﴾ [Ghafir 40].

Then this believing man said: ﴿And O my people, what is [wrong] with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir 41]. This is an interrogative of wonder and denial, as if he is saying: "How strange you are! I invite you to Paradise, and you invite me to the Fire." By Allah, this is truly a matter for wonder: that you invite a man to Paradise while he invites you to the Fire. For example, you come to a man and say: "O so-and-so, leave off drinking wine; drinking wine is forbidden and not permissible. Whoever drinks it in this world will not drink it in the Hereafter. It is the mother of wickedness, the key to every evil." He says to you: "O boy! Pleasure, delight, joy and happiness! Drink, for when you drink you will see yourself as the king of kings." Then he encourages him, and then he also gives him false hopes, saying: "Drink, and when you drink and attain pleasure and delight, then seek forgiveness from Allah; the door is open." Which of them has more right to be answered? The first, of course. This one says: ﴿What [wrong] with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?﴾ This, as I have told you, is an interrogative of wonder and denial, and it is a place for wonder and also a place for denial.

* Student: (...) Is the intention to disobey something for which a person is sinful?
* Shaykh: Intention, may Allah bless you, is of two kinds: an intention accompanied by resolve (hamm), and a mere passing thought (khatir). The second kind does not make a person sinful, neither in Makkah nor elsewhere. The first kind, an intention accompanied by resolve, is one for which a person is sinful.
* Student: In the verse: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation [in it] through injustice – We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj 25]?
* Shaykh: Yes, a painful punishment, because the Sacred Precinct is not like anywhere else. If the resolve to deviate, combined with injustice, brings a painful punishment, then what about the act itself? It will be more severe.
* Student: The saying of Allah in Surah Ibrahim: ﴿To the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy – Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 1–2]. What is the reason for the genitive case (jarr)?
* Shaykh: ﴿To the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy – Allah﴾. This is in the form of an explicative apposition ('atf al-bayan). Who is the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy? Allah. So He clarified it. The word ﴿Allah﴾ in the genitive is an explanation of ﴿the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy﴾.
* Student: Does anything follow from it if we say it is an adjective?
* Shaykh: The custom is that the word of majesty (lafz al-jalalah, "Allah") is the one that is described, because it is the proper name that specifies its referent without any ambiguity. For this reason the grammarians said that it is the most definite of definites, and that it is more definite even than the pronoun. When it is the most definite, it cannot be an adjective; it is a substitute (badal) or an explicative apposition ('atf al-bayan). Concerning explicative apposition, Ibn Malik says:
"And it is seen to be suitable for substitution, except in cases like 'O boy, may he live long' and like 'Bishr, follower of al-Bakri'; and it is not that it is replaced by al-Mardi."
Every explicative apposition is suitable to be a substitute, except in these two matters.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It is not in any case, because by "fighting" here it may be intended a deviation with injustice if he intends a major sin.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, it is the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl). Other separate pronouns, however, originally have a place in the grammatical structure.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. This, may Allah keep you safe, is after the people of Paradise have settled in Paradise, after everything has been finalized. That is, the people of Paradise will not leave it, and the people of the Fire will not leave it, meaning after everything has settled.

**Student:** ﴿O my people, what is (the matter with) me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire? (41) You call me to disbelieve in Allah and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving. (42) Undoubtedly, what you call me to has no call (answered) in this world or in the Hereafter, and our return is to Allah, and the transgressors are the companions of the Fire.﴾ [Ghafir 41–43].

* **The Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿O my people, what is (the matter with) me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 41]. We have already discussed this sentence and explained that the interrogative here expresses astonishment and disapproval.

﴿What is (the matter with) me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire﴾. The clause ﴿while you call me to the Fire﴾ is coordinated with the preceding clause. It is neither a resumptive clause (isti'nafiyya) nor a circumstantial clause (haliyya), as some have said. Rather, it is conjoined to what precedes it, because the astonishment arises from the combination of two things: he calls them to salvation, while they call him to the Fire.

His words ﴿to salvation﴾ mean salvation from the Fire. He did not say "to Paradise," even though he said elsewhere ﴿and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾ [Ghafir 39], because they were calling him to destruction, to the Fire. So he matched their call with his own call. It is as if he were saying: "I call you to salvation from the Fire, while you call me to the Fire." Calling to the Fire does not mean that someone says, "Come to the Fire, O people." Rather, it means calling to the deeds of the people of the Fire. It should be known that the Fire is surrounded by desires, and Paradise is surrounded by hardships. The deeds of the people of the Fire are built upon desires or upon doubts (shubuhat). That is, they are either ignorance and error, like the deeds of the Christians, or desires, like the deeds of the Jews. Upon these two the deeds of the people of the Fire revolve: doubts and desires. The remedy for doubts is knowledge, and the remedy for desires is resolve and complete determination to do what Allah loves and is pleased with. ﴿O my people, what is (the matter with) me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 41].

Then, after he had summarized in his words ﴿while you call me to the Fire﴾, he explained the deeds to which they were calling him, saying: ﴿You call me to disbelieve in Allah and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving﴾ [Ghafir 42]. The lam in ﴿You call me to disbelieve﴾ indicates the thing to which one is called (al-mud'a ilayh), that is, "you call me to this." On this basis, ﴿akfura﴾ (that I disbelieve) is in the subjunctive governed by an implied (an) after the lam according to the Basran grammarians, or by the lam itself according to the Kufan grammarians.

﴿To disbelieve in Allah﴾ means to deny Him and reject Him. The intended meaning is the denial of His oneness, as shown by his words ﴿and to associate with Him﴾. It may also be said that the intended meaning is the denial of His existence altogether, or associating partners with Him while affirming Him. Thus they were calling him to two things: either denying the Creator, mighty and majestic, which is derived from ﴿to disbelieve in Allah﴾, meaning "to deny Him," or affirming Him while having a partner with Him, which is derived from ﴿and to associate with Him﴾.

His words ﴿of which I have no knowledge﴾ [Ghafir 42] are a qualifying phrase that describes the reality: everyone who associates partners with Allah does so without knowledge, indeed, with what is known by innate nature (fitra) to be the opposite. However, it is well known that a thing without knowledge has no established reality and no basis. So the relative clause (al-sila) in ﴿of which I have no knowledge﴾ serves to describe the reality. We have already explained that every qualifying phrase that describes reality, or what is usual, or that serves emphasis, has no implicit restrictive meaning (mafhum).

﴿and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving﴾ [Ghafir 42]. He began here with the name "the Mighty" because the context requires it, since these people were Copts from the household of Pharaoh, who thought that might belonged to him. So he said: "I call you to the Mighty," and he did not say "to the Forgiving, the Merciful." Rather, he said ﴿to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving﴾, meaning the Mighty, the Dominant, who will destroy you if you associate partners with Him or disbelieve in Him. ﴿The Much-Forgiving﴾ will forgive you what has passed if you believe in Him. This is part of the perfect understanding of this believing man.

It might be said: the context would require "and I call you to the Forgiving, the Merciful." But the matter is the reverse: the context requires mentioning His name "the Mighty," because these people claimed that they were above the people, and that their lord was Pharaoh, and that he had no conqueror.

His words "the Mighty" are one of the names of Allah, "the Much-Forgiving" is one of the names of Allah, and "the Forgiving" is one of the names of Allah. It should be known that the names of Allah, glorified and exalted, are divided into two categories. The first: what is derived from a transitive attribute. Faith in it is not complete except through three matters: first, affirming it as a name of Allah; second, affirming the attribute it indicates; and third, affirming the ruling that follows from this attribute.

The second category: what is intransitive. Faith in it is not complete except through two matters: affirming it as one of the names of Allah, and affirming the attribute that this name indicates. This is because every name of Allah indicates an attribute. Allah has no name that is inert (jamid), contrary to those who say that the word "Allah" is an inert, non-derived noun. This is not correct. Every name of Allah is derived, because Allah described His names as "the Most Beautiful," and that which does not include an attribute is not beautiful, let alone the most beautiful. Let us give examples of this:

"The Living" (al-Hayy): which of the two categories is it? It is intransitive. You believe in "the Living" as a name of Allah, and in the life that the name indicates. "The Hearing" (al-Samee') is transitive. You believe in "the Hearing" as a name of Allah, in hearing as an attribute of Allah, and that He hears, affirming the ruling, which is the effect that follows from this attribute.

Know further that a name sometimes includes one attribute, sometimes two, and sometimes more, because the types of indication are three: correspondence (mutabaqa), inclusion (tadammun), and concomitance (iltizam). For example, among the names of Allah, the Exalted, is ﴿the Creator﴾ (al-Khallaq): ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Creator﴾ [al-Hijr 86]. You believe in "the Creator" as a name of Allah, and you believe in the attribute of creation that the name "the Creator" includes. Your belief in the name and the attribute together is belief through the indication of correspondence. Your belief in the name alone, or in the attribute alone, is belief through the indication of inclusion. Then your belief that He is All-Knowing and All-Powerful is belief through the indication of concomitance, because there is no creator who is not knowing, and no creator who is not powerful. For if He were ignorant, how could He create? And if He were incapable, how could He create? So the indication of "the Creator" upon knowledge and power is an indication of concomitance.

People differ greatly in this indication, namely the indication of concomitance. Some people Allah grants an understanding by which they perceive the implications that follow from this name, and some people are less than that. You will find some people deriving many benefits through the indication of implication, and another who cannot. And the bounty of Allah He gives to whom He wills.

So, is "the Mighty" (al-'Aziz) not affirmed except through what? Three or two? We first know its meaning: "the Mighty" means the one possessing might: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might﴾ [as-Saffat 180]. They said that might (al-'izza) is of three types:

Might of rank (izzat al-qadr), might of subjugation (izzat al-qahr), and might of inaccessibility (izzat al-imtina'). Might of rank means that He, glorified and exalted, is mighty in rank, such that nothing is comparable to Him. Might of inaccessibility means that He, mighty and majestic, is mighty, that is, evil cannot reach Him. "Mighty" also comes in the sense of inaccessibility, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 20], meaning "not unattainable."

The third: might of subjugation, meaning that He is the Dominant. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They say, "If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it"﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]. "Might" here means domination. If "the Mighty" means "the Dominant," it is a transitive name, since "'azza" means "overpowered," so he is "the dominant" (ghalib), and its opposite is "the overpowered" (maghlub). If "'azza" means "was inaccessible" or "was of great rank," then it is intransitive.

So we say: "the Mighty" is transitive from one perspective, when it means the dominant; and from another perspective it is intransitive, when it means inaccessible or of rank.

A parenthetical remark: Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They say, "If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it." But might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]. Is the answer corresponding to their statement or not? The corresponding answer would be to say: "Allah is more honorable, and the believers too." But this was not said. Rather, He said: ﴿But might belongs to Allah﴾, indicating that the hypocrites have no might at all. Had He said "Allah is more honorable," that would have affirmed some might for the hypocrites, but they have none. He restricted might to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. This is one of the eloquent features of the Qur'an. If you reflect upon the Qur'an, glory be to Allah, matters will become clear to you that dazzle you in its indications, allusions, and hints. Glory be to the One who sent it down, mighty and majestic!

"The Much-Forgiving" (al-Ghaffar) is a name of Allah. Is it transitive? Yes, because Allah said: ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ [Al 'Imran 129]. So we must affirm "the Much-Forgiving" as a name of Allah, and we must affirm the attribute, which is forgiveness: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing﴾ [ar-Ra'd 6]. And we affirm that He forgives, bestowing forgiveness upon whom He wills. He said: ﴿Unquestionably, He is the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving﴾ [az-Zumar 5].

﴿Undoubtedly, what you call me to﴾ [Ghafir 43], namely disbelief in Allah and associating partners with Him, ﴿has no call (answered)﴾, meaning it has no answering of a call, ﴿in this world or in the Hereafter﴾. And also, undoubtedly, ﴿our return is to Allah, and the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾.

The mufassir said: "﴿Undoubtedly﴾ means truly." That is, the meaning of "la jarama" is "truly." On this basis, "la" is superfluous and "jarama" means "truly." This is what the author adopted. The grammarians differ concerning it, and the correct parsing is that "la" is a negation of the genus (la al-nafiya li-l-jins), "jarama" is its noun, and the meaning of "jarama" is "there is no doubt" or "there is no escape." This is correct, the construction is clear, and it is not necessary to assume that "la" is superfluous, or that "jarama" means "cut off," or that the clause becomes a verbal noun (masdar) governed by an implied verb, meaning "I am certainly right that what you call me to..." When we say "there is no doubt that what you call me to..." to the end, "has no call (answered) in this world or in the Hereafter," the difficulty disappears.

On this basis, "jarama" is the noun of "la," and "anna-ma" (that...) with what follows is in the interpretation of a verbal noun, serving as the predicate of "la." The meaning is: there is no doubt and no uncertainty that what you call me to has no call.

His words ﴿anna-ma tad'unani ilayh﴾ are written in my copy as a joined form, i.e., "anna" joined to "ma," but according to the known rules, it should be written separately, because the meaning is "la jarama anna alladhi tad'unani ilayh." When "ma" is relative, it is written separately from "anna." However, the scholars followed the Uthmanic orthography for the mushaf, out of respect for the Qur'an, so that it is not altered. That is why you find "al-salat" written in the mushaf with a waw, "al-zakat" with a waw, "al-riba" with a waw, and ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ [al-A'raf 56] with an open taa. All of this follows the Uthmanic orthography, out of respect for the Book of Allah, so that alteration does not enter it.

The scholars have differed on whether the Qur'an should be written according to the standard rules of spelling, changing with each period, or according to the Uthmanic orthography.

It has been said that it is permissible to write it according to the rules at every time, since the purpose is that the Book of Allah be recited as it was revealed, not as it was written. Was the Qur'an revealed written or revealed recited? Recited. So writing is nothing but conventions that are subject to people's customs.

The second opinion: it is not permissible ever to change it, as a closing of the door and a prevention of alteration, so that no one dares to change the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic. This undoubtedly points to the strength of our reverence for the Noble Qur'an. The first opinion points to the strength of conveying the Qur'an to people in a manner free from difficulty.

The third opinion: if you write it for beginning students, there is no harm in writing it according to the known rules, because beginning students do not know the Uthmanic form. But if you want to write it for reading, then it is written according to the Uthmanic orthography. It appears that this detailed opinion is the most preferred of the three opinions.

﴿Undoubtedly, what you call me to has no call (answered)﴾ [Ghafir 43]. ("Anna") is a particle of emphasis that puts the subject in the accusative and raises the predicate. "Ma" is its noun, and the clause ﴿has no call (answered)﴾ is its predicate.

He says: "(﴿what you call me to﴾) is that I worship (it)." But this explanation is deficient. What did they call him to? To disbelieve in Allah and associate partners with Him. They called him to two matters, and the author restricted it to one matter, which is worshipping other than Allah, and this is association.

(﴿has no call (answered)﴾, meaning it has no answering of a call.) The correct meaning is that it has no call by which it is invoked, and no call that it answers. So the meaning of ﴿has no call (answered)﴾ is that it does not deserve to be invoked, and it also does not respond when it is invoked, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those you invoke besides Him do not possess even a thin membrane of a date pit. If you invoke them, they do not hear your call, and even if they heard, they would not respond to you﴾ [Fatir 13–14]. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will deny your association﴾ [Fatir 14], and ﴿none can inform you like one who is acquainted﴾ [Fatir 14]. This verse is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And who is more astray than one who invokes other than Allah, one who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5]. The one you invoke cannot respond to you until the Day of Resurrection, never.

﴿And they are heedless of their invocation﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5]. The pronoun ﴿they﴾ may refer to those being invoked, and it may refer to those invoking. The pronoun in ﴿their invocation﴾ may refer to this, according to the preceding pronoun.

﴿And when the people are gathered﴾ [al-Ahqaf 6], which is the time when these invokers wish to benefit from those invoked: ﴿And when the people are gathered, they will be enemies to them and will deny their worship﴾ [al-Ahqaf 6]. Because Allah says: ﴿When those who were followed disassociate themselves from those who followed, and they see the punishment, and their ties are cut off﴾ [al-Baqarah 166], that is, the affection and love they used to conceal for them in this world. ﴿And those who followed will say: "If only we had another chance, we would disassociate ourselves from them as they have disassociated from us"﴾ [al-Baqarah 167].

In any case, ﴿has no call (answered)﴾ [Ghafir 43]. The author says: "it has no answered call," meaning it does not respond to the call. The correct meaning is that the expression has two senses: it does not respond, and it does not deserve (to be called). So it does not deserve to be invoked, and even if it is invoked, it does not respond.

﴿has no call in this world or in the Hereafter﴾ [Ghafir 43]. Yes, it cannot do this, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. Idols do not benefit their worshippers, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter.

He says: ﴿And that our return is to Allah﴾ [Ghafir 43]. He reminded them of the reckoning, may Allah have mercy on him and reward him well.

﴿And that our return﴾, meaning our return, ﴿to Allah﴾, mighty and majestic, in this world and the Hereafter, or in the Hereafter only? In this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [an-Nisa' 59]. So the return is to Allah in this world and in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verses 41–43 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And that the extravagant are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 43]. Meaning: "Without doubt, also, the extravagant are the companions of the Fire." These are three matters, each of which he affirmed with certainty:
First: that what you call me to has no supplication (da'wah) in this world or in the Hereafter. Second: that our return is to Allah. Third: that the extravagant are the companions of the Fire.

Al-Musrif (the extravagant) is the active participle of al-israf (extravagance), which means exceeding the limit. It may be disbelief, and it may be less than disbelief. A person who fills his stomach with food and drink is extravagant, but he is not a disbeliever, because Allah said: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant﴾ [al-A'raf 31]. Likewise, extravagance in clothing and other things does not lead to disbelief. But extravagance in worshipping Allah, by directing worship beyond Allah to other than Him, is disbelief, and this is what this believing man meant by ﴿And that the extravagant are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 43].

﴿Hum﴾ (they) is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl). We have previously mentioned that, grammatically, the pronoun of separation has no place in i'rab (grammatical case), so it does not affect what precedes it, nor is it affected by what follows it. We have also mentioned that the pronoun of separation has benefits: emphasis, restriction, and distinguishing the predicate from an adjective. We gave an example of this.

* Among the benefits of these verses: this believing man's denunciation of his people with what sound reason confirms, when he said: ﴿And O my people, how is it that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir 41]. If reason confirms its soundness, then it is a matter of wonder. Every rational person would be astonished that this should be the case: a man calls his people to salvation, and they call him to the Fire!

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: observing the situation in address. Its aspect is that he said ﴿to salvation﴾ even though he was calling them to Paradise. But since their calling him was to destruction, he preferred to say "to salvation."

Question: Does salvation from the Fire necessarily entail entering Paradise? It does necessarily follow. How is the necessity?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The aspect of necessity: if someone said, "One who is saved from the Fire finds a second abode," where did Allah say that? Where is a single verse? This, but this one whom Allah saved from the Fire and left on this earth...
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: But this one was not moved away and admitted. However, one who was moved away from the Fire and whom Allah passed over in silence, there is no evidence for that. The evidence is that in the Hereafter there are only two abodes: either this or that. That is why the people of al-A'raf (the heights), who remain between Paradise and the Fire, ultimately go to Paradise.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever associates others with Allah or denies Him is a disbeliever in Him, and he has no knowledge of that whatsoever. This is derived from: ﴿and to associate with Him what I have no knowledge of﴾ [Ghafir 42].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that associating others with Allah is like denying Allah. From where?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This is also indicated by the saying of Allah the Exalted in the hadith qudsi (sacred hadith): "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in need of a partner. Whoever does an action in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his partner."[[Narrated by Muslim (2985/46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: this believing man's reminding these people of Allah's might and forgiveness, with both encouragement and warning. This is based on his saying: ﴿And I call you to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving﴾ [Ghafir 42]. In which of the two words does the warning lie? In His saying ﴿the Mighty﴾, and the encouragement lies in His saying ﴿the Much-Forgiving﴾. And Allah knows best.

* The student: Regarding what is mentioned in the Qur'an of the speech of specific persons, such as the Queen of Sheba and the believer of Pharaoh's family: is it taken according to its meaning or its wording?
* The Shaykh: This is an important question. He asks: What Allah the Mighty and Majestic relates from earlier nations, is it in meaning or in wording?
The answer: In meaning, without doubt. First, because the language of those people was not Arabic. Second, if it were in wording, the speech of human beings would be inimitable (mu'jiz), because inimitability is achieved with a verse, two verses, or three. How many verses did this believing man speak?
* Student: Perhaps, O Shaykh, it indicates a specific thing, namely that they come as a message (...).
* The Shaykh: Then it is because Allah Himself formulated it, so He relayed it in meaning.

This leads us to something: is the hadith qudsi the speech of Allah in its wording or its meaning?
This, in any case, is a matter of disagreement. Some say: Allah spoke it in wording. Others say: He spoke it in meaning, and the phrasing is from the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Still others say: say "Allah said," and do not say in wording or in meaning. As long as you are in safety, follow the path of safety. But sometimes a person is put in a difficult position, and it is said to him: "Give me the difference between the hadith qudsi and the Qur'an?" If a person can remain safe, then safety is better. But some people will come to you and say: "Tell me the difference between the hadith qudsi and the Qur'an." The difference is this: the hadith qudsi is not the wording of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because if it were the wording of Allah, it would be inimitable, and the rulings of the Qur'an would apply to it: a person in a state of major ritual impurity (junub) may not recite it, it may not be touched except in a state of purity, no one can alter it, and similar matters. All of this is settled.

If someone says: "Does not the Messenger say, 'Allah said'?" We say: Yes. "Does not Allah say, 'Pharaoh said,' 'Moses said,' and similar, when it is in a language other than theirs?" This does not prevent it.

Then, if we said it is the wording of Allah, a great difficulty would arise for us. Either it is through Gabriel, or without an intermediary. If it is without an intermediary, it would have a higher chain of transmission than the Qur'an, because the Qur'an is through whom?
* Students: Gabriel.
* The Shaykh: And if it is without an intermediary, then any person who says it is without an intermediary, we might perhaps choke him or give him a slap on the head. Because if it came through an intermediary, and the Messenger omitted the intermediary, then we would have a problem: what is it? Deception (tadlis). The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is free of this. In any case, as I told you, some say it is the speech of Allah in wording and meaning. The second says it is the speech of Allah in meaning, not wording. The third remains silent: we say "Allah said" and we stay silent. This is the safest if a person is granted safety. But as I told you, sometimes someone says to you: "It is necessary! Give me the difference between the Qur'an and the hadith qudsi." We say: this is the difference: the Qur'an is the speech of Allah in wording and meaning, and the hadith qudsi is the speech of Allah in meaning, not wording.

If someone says: "Then we will demand from you the difference between the prophetic hadith and the qudsi hadith, because the prophetic hadith is the speech of the Messenger." We say: this is easy. The difference between them is that the Messenger does not attribute the prophetic hadith to Allah, while he attributes the hadith qudsi to Allah. The problem in this matter is resolved. Then know that these positions are safer if a person is granted safety. But if a person is tested, he must make distinctions.

Among these matters, and I like to digress because some brothers with us have not grasped what we say in some gatherings, is the term (jism) body. You know that all the Mu'attilah (those who deny Allah's attributes) based their denial on the question of "body." They claimed that if we affirm the face, the hand, or similar, this entails that Allah is a body. Even regarding "istiwa'" (establishment on the Throne), they say: if we affirm that Allah established Himself, then He is a body. We say to them: what is this body that you have made into a spiked club, with which you pierce every fence to affirm the attributes?

If you mean by body a composed, created thing, whose parts can separate from one another, and by the separation of some of it, it decreases and perhaps perishes, then Allah is exalted above this without doubt, and whoever believes this about his Lord is a disbeliever.

But if you mean by body that He has an essence that does whatever He wills, speaks, comes, descends, establishes Himself, and is described by attributes befitting Him, then this is true. However, as to affirming or negating the term "body," this is prohibited. Do not affirm, saying "Allah is a body," nor negate, saying "Allah is not a body," because it has not been reported affirming or negating it.

These are matters that a student of knowledge should understand. For example, if a person argues with you and says: "What do you say about the body?" I say: as to its wording, the obligation is to refrain from it, whether affirming or negating. As to its meaning, we ask for clarification.

* * *

* Student: ﴿So you will remember what I say to you. I entrust my affair to Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of the servants.﴾ (44) ﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted, and there befell the family of Pharaoh the worst of punishment.﴾ (45) ﴿The Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening. And on the Day the Hour is established, [it will be said], "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the severest punishment."﴾ [Ghafir 44–46].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Some benefits remain from what we stopped at previously: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾ [Ghafir 40], then after it ﴿Without doubt, what you call me to has no supplication...﴾ [Ghafir 43] to the end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: every object called upon besides Allah has no entitlement to supplication (da'wah) nor response, based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Without doubt, what you call me to has no supplication in this world or in the Hereafter﴾ [Ghafir 43].

* Among its benefits: these idols do not benefit their worshippers, whether they call upon them with a request (da'wat al-mas'alah) or with worship (da'wat al-'ibadah).

The difference between a supplication of request and a supplication of worship: in the request, a person seeks a particular need. Worship is devotion to Allah. Worship is called supplication because the worshipper, by the language of his state, supplicates that he be rewarded for this worship. This is shown by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord said, "Call upon Me; I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too arrogant to worship Me..."﴾ [Ghafir 60]. He said "Call upon Me," then said "those who are too arrogant to worship Me" [Ghafir 60]. This shows that supplication is worship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming the return to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and that the matters return to Him, in His saying: ﴿And that our return is to Allah﴾ [Ghafir 43]. This verse has parallels, among them: ﴿And to Allah is the return of all matters﴾ [al-Baqarah 210]; and ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return. Then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 25–26]; and ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 6]; and His saying: ﴿And that to your Lord is the finality﴾ [al-Najm 42]. Verses with this meaning are numerous: the return of all creatures is to their Lord, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of extravagance. What is the basis of the indication? From where do we derive the prohibition of extravagance from the verse?
﴿And that the extravagant are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 43].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: extravagance may reach the level of disbelief, from the verse: His saying ﴿they are the companions of the Fire﴾. Whenever you find ﴿the companions of the Fire﴾, they are its people, and they are those who abide in it forever.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strength of this man's faith, when he said: ﴿And that our return is to Allah, and that the extravagant are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 43].

* Among its benefits: the use of allusion (ta'rid).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. How is that?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Well done. Because there is no doubt that the first to enter this statement are these people, but he did not wish to speak of it explicitly.
Can we say: in this verse there is "appearing in place of the pronoun" (izhar fi mawdi' al-idmar)?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What can we say? We could also say: this is a double meaning (tawriyah). In any case, "appearing in place of the pronoun" is one of the styles of the Arabic language, and it is common in the Qur'an. It has benefits, among them:
Intending generality: that the ruling applies generally, to whoever is described by it and to whoever is not.
Among them, stating the cause (ta'lil): because when a description is attached to a ruling, this indicates that the description is the cause.
Among them, a condemnation of those who, by the context, should have been referred to by pronoun, by what this description entails. These are three benefits: intending generality, stating the cause, and passing judgment on these people that they deserve this description.

**Student:** ﴿O my people, what is (the matter with) me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire? (41) You call me to disbelieve in Allah and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving. (42) Undoubtedly, what you call me to has no call (answered) in this world or in the Hereafter, and our return is to Allah, and the transgressors are the companions of the Fire.﴾ [Ghafir 41–43].

* **The Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿O my people, what is (the matter with) me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 41]. We have already discussed this sentence and explained that the interrogative here expresses astonishment and disapproval.

﴿What is (the matter with) me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire﴾. The clause ﴿while you call me to the Fire﴾ is coordinated with the preceding clause. It is neither a resumptive clause (isti'nafiyya) nor a circumstantial clause (haliyya), as some have said. Rather, it is conjoined to what precedes it, because the astonishment arises from the combination of two things: he calls them to salvation, while they call him to the Fire.

His words ﴿to salvation﴾ mean salvation from the Fire. He did not say "to Paradise," even though he said elsewhere ﴿and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾ [Ghafir 39], because they were calling him to destruction, to the Fire. So he matched their call with his own call. It is as if he were saying: "I call you to salvation from the Fire, while you call me to the Fire." Calling to the Fire does not mean that someone says, "Come to the Fire, O people." Rather, it means calling to the deeds of the people of the Fire. It should be known that the Fire is surrounded by desires, and Paradise is surrounded by hardships. The deeds of the people of the Fire are built upon desires or upon doubts (shubuhat). That is, they are either ignorance and error, like the deeds of the Christians, or desires, like the deeds of the Jews. Upon these two the deeds of the people of the Fire revolve: doubts and desires. The remedy for doubts is knowledge, and the remedy for desires is resolve and complete determination to do what Allah loves and is pleased with. ﴿O my people, what is (the matter with) me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 41].

Then, after he had summarized in his words ﴿while you call me to the Fire﴾, he explained the deeds to which they were calling him, saying: ﴿You call me to disbelieve in Allah and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving﴾ [Ghafir 42]. The lam in ﴿You call me to disbelieve﴾ indicates the thing to which one is called (al-mud'a ilayh), that is, "you call me to this." On this basis, ﴿akfura﴾ (that I disbelieve) is in the subjunctive governed by an implied (an) after the lam according to the Basran grammarians, or by the lam itself according to the Kufan grammarians.

﴿To disbelieve in Allah﴾ means to deny Him and reject Him. The intended meaning is the denial of His oneness, as shown by his words ﴿and to associate with Him﴾. It may also be said that the intended meaning is the denial of His existence altogether, or associating partners with Him while affirming Him. Thus they were calling him to two things: either denying the Creator, mighty and majestic, which is derived from ﴿to disbelieve in Allah﴾, meaning "to deny Him," or affirming Him while having a partner with Him, which is derived from ﴿and to associate with Him﴾.

His words ﴿of which I have no knowledge﴾ [Ghafir 42] are a qualifying phrase that describes the reality: everyone who associates partners with Allah does so without knowledge, indeed, with what is known by innate nature (fitra) to be the opposite. However, it is well known that a thing without knowledge has no established reality and no basis. So the relative clause (al-sila) in ﴿of which I have no knowledge﴾ serves to describe the reality. We have already explained that every qualifying phrase that describes reality, or what is usual, or that serves emphasis, has no implicit restrictive meaning (mafhum).

﴿and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving﴾ [Ghafir 42]. He began here with the name "the Mighty" because the context requires it, since these people were Copts from the household of Pharaoh, who thought that might belonged to him. So he said: "I call you to the Mighty," and he did not say "to the Forgiving, the Merciful." Rather, he said ﴿to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving﴾, meaning the Mighty, the Dominant, who will destroy you if you associate partners with Him or disbelieve in Him. ﴿The Much-Forgiving﴾ will forgive you what has passed if you believe in Him. This is part of the perfect understanding of this believing man.

It might be said: the context would require "and I call you to the Forgiving, the Merciful." But the matter is the reverse: the context requires mentioning His name "the Mighty," because these people claimed that they were above the people, and that their lord was Pharaoh, and that he had no conqueror.

His words "the Mighty" are one of the names of Allah, "the Much-Forgiving" is one of the names of Allah, and "the Forgiving" is one of the names of Allah. It should be known that the names of Allah, glorified and exalted, are divided into two categories. The first: what is derived from a transitive attribute. Faith in it is not complete except through three matters: first, affirming it as a name of Allah; second, affirming the attribute it indicates; and third, affirming the ruling that follows from this attribute.

The second category: what is intransitive. Faith in it is not complete except through two matters: affirming it as one of the names of Allah, and affirming the attribute that this name indicates. This is because every name of Allah indicates an attribute. Allah has no name that is inert (jamid), contrary to those who say that the word "Allah" is an inert, non-derived noun. This is not correct. Every name of Allah is derived, because Allah described His names as "the Most Beautiful," and that which does not include an attribute is not beautiful, let alone the most beautiful. Let us give examples of this:

"The Living" (al-Hayy): which of the two categories is it? It is intransitive. You believe in "the Living" as a name of Allah, and in the life that the name indicates. "The Hearing" (al-Samee') is transitive. You believe in "the Hearing" as a name of Allah, in hearing as an attribute of Allah, and that He hears, affirming the ruling, which is the effect that follows from this attribute.

Know further that a name sometimes includes one attribute, sometimes two, and sometimes more, because the types of indication are three: correspondence (mutabaqa), inclusion (tadammun), and concomitance (iltizam). For example, among the names of Allah, the Exalted, is ﴿the Creator﴾ (al-Khallaq): ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Creator﴾ [al-Hijr 86]. You believe in "the Creator" as a name of Allah, and you believe in the attribute of creation that the name "the Creator" includes. Your belief in the name and the attribute together is belief through the indication of correspondence. Your belief in the name alone, or in the attribute alone, is belief through the indication of inclusion. Then your belief that He is All-Knowing and All-Powerful is belief through the indication of concomitance, because there is no creator who is not knowing, and no creator who is not powerful. For if He were ignorant, how could He create? And if He were incapable, how could He create? So the indication of "the Creator" upon knowledge and power is an indication of concomitance.

People differ greatly in this indication, namely the indication of concomitance. Some people Allah grants an understanding by which they perceive the implications that follow from this name, and some people are less than that. You will find some people deriving many benefits through the indication of implication, and another who cannot. And the bounty of Allah He gives to whom He wills.

So, is "the Mighty" (al-'Aziz) not affirmed except through what? Three or two? We first know its meaning: "the Mighty" means the one possessing might: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might﴾ [as-Saffat 180]. They said that might (al-'izza) is of three types:

Might of rank (izzat al-qadr), might of subjugation (izzat al-qahr), and might of inaccessibility (izzat al-imtina'). Might of rank means that He, glorified and exalted, is mighty in rank, such that nothing is comparable to Him. Might of inaccessibility means that He, mighty and majestic, is mighty, that is, evil cannot reach Him. "Mighty" also comes in the sense of inaccessibility, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 20], meaning "not unattainable."

The third: might of subjugation, meaning that He is the Dominant. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They say, "If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it"﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]. "Might" here means domination. If "the Mighty" means "the Dominant," it is a transitive name, since "'azza" means "overpowered," so he is "the dominant" (ghalib), and its opposite is "the overpowered" (maghlub). If "'azza" means "was inaccessible" or "was of great rank," then it is intransitive.

So we say: "the Mighty" is transitive from one perspective, when it means the dominant; and from another perspective it is intransitive, when it means inaccessible or of rank.

A parenthetical remark: Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They say, "If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it." But might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]. Is the answer corresponding to their statement or not? The corresponding answer would be to say: "Allah is more honorable, and the believers too." But this was not said. Rather, He said: ﴿But might belongs to Allah﴾, indicating that the hypocrites have no might at all. Had He said "Allah is more honorable," that would have affirmed some might for the hypocrites, but they have none. He restricted might to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. This is one of the eloquent features of the Qur'an. If you reflect upon the Qur'an, glory be to Allah, matters will become clear to you that dazzle you in its indications, allusions, and hints. Glory be to the One who sent it down, mighty and majestic!

"The Much-Forgiving" (al-Ghaffar) is a name of Allah. Is it transitive? Yes, because Allah said: ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ [Al 'Imran 129]. So we must affirm "the Much-Forgiving" as a name of Allah, and we must affirm the attribute, which is forgiveness: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing﴾ [ar-Ra'd 6]. And we affirm that He forgives, bestowing forgiveness upon whom He wills. He said: ﴿Unquestionably, He is the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving﴾ [az-Zumar 5].

﴿Undoubtedly, what you call me to﴾ [Ghafir 43], namely disbelief in Allah and associating partners with Him, ﴿has no call (answered)﴾, meaning it has no answering of a call, ﴿in this world or in the Hereafter﴾. And also, undoubtedly, ﴿our return is to Allah, and the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾.

The mufassir said: "﴿Undoubtedly﴾ means truly." That is, the meaning of "la jarama" is "truly." On this basis, "la" is superfluous and "jarama" means "truly." This is what the author adopted. The grammarians differ concerning it, and the correct parsing is that "la" is a negation of the genus (la al-nafiya li-l-jins), "jarama" is its noun, and the meaning of "jarama" is "there is no doubt" or "there is no escape." This is correct, the construction is clear, and it is not necessary to assume that "la" is superfluous, or that "jarama" means "cut off," or that the clause becomes a verbal noun (masdar) governed by an implied verb, meaning "I am certainly right that what you call me to..." When we say "there is no doubt that what you call me to..." to the end, "has no call (answered) in this world or in the Hereafter," the difficulty disappears.

On this basis, "jarama" is the noun of "la," and "anna-ma" (that...) with what follows is in the interpretation of a verbal noun, serving as the predicate of "la." The meaning is: there is no doubt and no uncertainty that what you call me to has no call.

His words ﴿anna-ma tad'unani ilayh﴾ are written in my copy as a joined form, i.e., "anna" joined to "ma," but according to the known rules, it should be written separately, because the meaning is "la jarama anna alladhi tad'unani ilayh." When "ma" is relative, it is written separately from "anna." However, the scholars followed the Uthmanic orthography for the mushaf, out of respect for the Qur'an, so that it is not altered. That is why you find "al-salat" written in the mushaf with a waw, "al-zakat" with a waw, "al-riba" with a waw, and ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ [al-A'raf 56] with an open taa. All of this follows the Uthmanic orthography, out of respect for the Book of Allah, so that alteration does not enter it.

The scholars have differed on whether the Qur'an should be written according to the standard rules of spelling, changing with each period, or according to the Uthmanic orthography.

It has been said that it is permissible to write it according to the rules at every time, since the purpose is that the Book of Allah be recited as it was revealed, not as it was written. Was the Qur'an revealed written or revealed recited? Recited. So writing is nothing but conventions that are subject to people's customs.

The second opinion: it is not permissible ever to change it, as a closing of the door and a prevention of alteration, so that no one dares to change the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic. This undoubtedly points to the strength of our reverence for the Noble Qur'an. The first opinion points to the strength of conveying the Qur'an to people in a manner free from difficulty.

The third opinion: if you write it for beginning students, there is no harm in writing it according to the known rules, because beginning students do not know the Uthmanic form. But if you want to write it for reading, then it is written according to the Uthmanic orthography. It appears that this detailed opinion is the most preferred of the three opinions.

﴿Undoubtedly, what you call me to has no call (answered)﴾ [Ghafir 43]. ("Anna") is a particle of emphasis that puts the subject in the accusative and raises the predicate. "Ma" is its noun, and the clause ﴿has no call (answered)﴾ is its predicate.

He says: "(﴿what you call me to﴾) is that I worship (it)." But this explanation is deficient. What did they call him to? To disbelieve in Allah and associate partners with Him. They called him to two matters, and the author restricted it to one matter, which is worshipping other than Allah, and this is association.

(﴿has no call (answered)﴾, meaning it has no answering of a call.) The correct meaning is that it has no call by which it is invoked, and no call that it answers. So the meaning of ﴿has no call (answered)﴾ is that it does not deserve to be invoked, and it also does not respond when it is invoked, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those you invoke besides Him do not possess even a thin membrane of a date pit. If you invoke them, they do not hear your call, and even if they heard, they would not respond to you﴾ [Fatir 13–14]. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will deny your association﴾ [Fatir 14], and ﴿none can inform you like one who is acquainted﴾ [Fatir 14]. This verse is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And who is more astray than one who invokes other than Allah, one who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5]. The one you invoke cannot respond to you until the Day of Resurrection, never.

﴿And they are heedless of their invocation﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5]. The pronoun ﴿they﴾ may refer to those being invoked, and it may refer to those invoking. The pronoun in ﴿their invocation﴾ may refer to this, according to the preceding pronoun.

﴿And when the people are gathered﴾ [al-Ahqaf 6], which is the time when these invokers wish to benefit from those invoked: ﴿And when the people are gathered, they will be enemies to them and will deny their worship﴾ [al-Ahqaf 6]. Because Allah says: ﴿When those who were followed disassociate themselves from those who followed, and they see the punishment, and their ties are cut off﴾ [al-Baqarah 166], that is, the affection and love they used to conceal for them in this world. ﴿And those who followed will say: "If only we had another chance, we would disassociate ourselves from them as they have disassociated from us"﴾ [al-Baqarah 167].

In any case, ﴿has no call (answered)﴾ [Ghafir 43]. The author says: "it has no answered call," meaning it does not respond to the call. The correct meaning is that the expression has two senses: it does not respond, and it does not deserve (to be called). So it does not deserve to be invoked, and even if it is invoked, it does not respond.

﴿has no call in this world or in the Hereafter﴾ [Ghafir 43]. Yes, it cannot do this, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. Idols do not benefit their worshippers, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter.

He says: ﴿And that our return is to Allah﴾ [Ghafir 43]. He reminded them of the reckoning, may Allah have mercy on him and reward him well.

﴿And that our return﴾, meaning our return, ﴿to Allah﴾, mighty and majestic, in this world and the Hereafter, or in the Hereafter only? In this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [an-Nisa' 59]. So the return is to Allah in this world and in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verses 41–43 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And that the extravagant are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 43]. Meaning: "Without doubt, also, the extravagant are the companions of the Fire." These are three matters, each of which he affirmed with certainty:
First: that what you call me to has no supplication (da'wah) in this world or in the Hereafter. Second: that our return is to Allah. Third: that the extravagant are the companions of the Fire.

Al-Musrif (the extravagant) is the active participle of al-israf (extravagance), which means exceeding the limit. It may be disbelief, and it may be less than disbelief. A person who fills his stomach with food and drink is extravagant, but he is not a disbeliever, because Allah said: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant﴾ [al-A'raf 31]. Likewise, extravagance in clothing and other things does not lead to disbelief. But extravagance in worshipping Allah, by directing worship beyond Allah to other than Him, is disbelief, and this is what this believing man meant by ﴿And that the extravagant are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 43].

﴿Hum﴾ (they) is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl). We have previously mentioned that, grammatically, the pronoun of separation has no place in i'rab (grammatical case), so it does not affect what precedes it, nor is it affected by what follows it. We have also mentioned that the pronoun of separation has benefits: emphasis, restriction, and distinguishing the predicate from an adjective. We gave an example of this.

* Among the benefits of these verses: this believing man's denunciation of his people with what sound reason confirms, when he said: ﴿And O my people, how is it that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir 41]. If reason confirms its soundness, then it is a matter of wonder. Every rational person would be astonished that this should be the case: a man calls his people to salvation, and they call him to the Fire!

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: observing the situation in address. Its aspect is that he said ﴿to salvation﴾ even though he was calling them to Paradise. But since their calling him was to destruction, he preferred to say "to salvation."

Question: Does salvation from the Fire necessarily entail entering Paradise? It does necessarily follow. How is the necessity?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The aspect of necessity: if someone said, "One who is saved from the Fire finds a second abode," where did Allah say that? Where is a single verse? This, but this one whom Allah saved from the Fire and left on this earth...
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: But this one was not moved away and admitted. However, one who was moved away from the Fire and whom Allah passed over in silence, there is no evidence for that. The evidence is that in the Hereafter there are only two abodes: either this or that. That is why the people of al-A'raf (the heights), who remain between Paradise and the Fire, ultimately go to Paradise.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever associates others with Allah or denies Him is a disbeliever in Him, and he has no knowledge of that whatsoever. This is derived from: ﴿and to associate with Him what I have no knowledge of﴾ [Ghafir 42].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that associating others with Allah is like denying Allah. From where?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This is also indicated by the saying of Allah the Exalted in the hadith qudsi (sacred hadith): "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in need of a partner. Whoever does an action in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his partner."[[Narrated by Muslim (2985/46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: this believing man's reminding these people of Allah's might and forgiveness, with both encouragement and warning. This is based on his saying: ﴿And I call you to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving﴾ [Ghafir 42]. In which of the two words does the warning lie? In His saying ﴿the Mighty﴾, and the encouragement lies in His saying ﴿the Much-Forgiving﴾. And Allah knows best.

* The student: Regarding what is mentioned in the Qur'an of the speech of specific persons, such as the Queen of Sheba and the believer of Pharaoh's family: is it taken according to its meaning or its wording?
* The Shaykh: This is an important question. He asks: What Allah the Mighty and Majestic relates from earlier nations, is it in meaning or in wording?
The answer: In meaning, without doubt. First, because the language of those people was not Arabic. Second, if it were in wording, the speech of human beings would be inimitable (mu'jiz), because inimitability is achieved with a verse, two verses, or three. How many verses did this believing man speak?
* Student: Perhaps, O Shaykh, it indicates a specific thing, namely that they come as a message (...).
* The Shaykh: Then it is because Allah Himself formulated it, so He relayed it in meaning.

This leads us to something: is the hadith qudsi the speech of Allah in its wording or its meaning?
This, in any case, is a matter of disagreement. Some say: Allah spoke it in wording. Others say: He spoke it in meaning, and the phrasing is from the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Still others say: say "Allah said," and do not say in wording or in meaning. As long as you are in safety, follow the path of safety. But sometimes a person is put in a difficult position, and it is said to him: "Give me the difference between the hadith qudsi and the Qur'an?" If a person can remain safe, then safety is better. But some people will come to you and say: "Tell me the difference between the hadith qudsi and the Qur'an." The difference is this: the hadith qudsi is not the wording of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because if it were the wording of Allah, it would be inimitable, and the rulings of the Qur'an would apply to it: a person in a state of major ritual impurity (junub) may not recite it, it may not be touched except in a state of purity, no one can alter it, and similar matters. All of this is settled.

If someone says: "Does not the Messenger say, 'Allah said'?" We say: Yes. "Does not Allah say, 'Pharaoh said,' 'Moses said,' and similar, when it is in a language other than theirs?" This does not prevent it.

Then, if we said it is the wording of Allah, a great difficulty would arise for us. Either it is through Gabriel, or without an intermediary. If it is without an intermediary, it would have a higher chain of transmission than the Qur'an, because the Qur'an is through whom?
* Students: Gabriel.
* The Shaykh: And if it is without an intermediary, then any person who says it is without an intermediary, we might perhaps choke him or give him a slap on the head. Because if it came through an intermediary, and the Messenger omitted the intermediary, then we would have a problem: what is it? Deception (tadlis). The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is free of this. In any case, as I told you, some say it is the speech of Allah in wording and meaning. The second says it is the speech of Allah in meaning, not wording. The third remains silent: we say "Allah said" and we stay silent. This is the safest if a person is granted safety. But as I told you, sometimes someone says to you: "It is necessary! Give me the difference between the Qur'an and the hadith qudsi." We say: this is the difference: the Qur'an is the speech of Allah in wording and meaning, and the hadith qudsi is the speech of Allah in meaning, not wording.

If someone says: "Then we will demand from you the difference between the prophetic hadith and the qudsi hadith, because the prophetic hadith is the speech of the Messenger." We say: this is easy. The difference between them is that the Messenger does not attribute the prophetic hadith to Allah, while he attributes the hadith qudsi to Allah. The problem in this matter is resolved. Then know that these positions are safer if a person is granted safety. But if a person is tested, he must make distinctions.

Among these matters, and I like to digress because some brothers with us have not grasped what we say in some gatherings, is the term (jism) body. You know that all the Mu'attilah (those who deny Allah's attributes) based their denial on the question of "body." They claimed that if we affirm the face, the hand, or similar, this entails that Allah is a body. Even regarding "istiwa'" (establishment on the Throne), they say: if we affirm that Allah established Himself, then He is a body. We say to them: what is this body that you have made into a spiked club, with which you pierce every fence to affirm the attributes?

If you mean by body a composed, created thing, whose parts can separate from one another, and by the separation of some of it, it decreases and perhaps perishes, then Allah is exalted above this without doubt, and whoever believes this about his Lord is a disbeliever.

But if you mean by body that He has an essence that does whatever He wills, speaks, comes, descends, establishes Himself, and is described by attributes befitting Him, then this is true. However, as to affirming or negating the term "body," this is prohibited. Do not affirm, saying "Allah is a body," nor negate, saying "Allah is not a body," because it has not been reported affirming or negating it.

These are matters that a student of knowledge should understand. For example, if a person argues with you and says: "What do you say about the body?" I say: as to its wording, the obligation is to refrain from it, whether affirming or negating. As to its meaning, we ask for clarification.

* * *

* Student: ﴿So you will remember what I say to you. I entrust my affair to Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of the servants.﴾ (44) ﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted, and there befell the family of Pharaoh the worst of punishment.﴾ (45) ﴿The Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening. And on the Day the Hour is established, [it will be said], "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the severest punishment."﴾ [Ghafir 44–46].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Some benefits remain from what we stopped at previously: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾ [Ghafir 40], then after it ﴿Without doubt, what you call me to has no supplication...﴾ [Ghafir 43] to the end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: every object called upon besides Allah has no entitlement to supplication (da'wah) nor response, based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Without doubt, what you call me to has no supplication in this world or in the Hereafter﴾ [Ghafir 43].

* Among its benefits: these idols do not benefit their worshippers, whether they call upon them with a request (da'wat al-mas'alah) or with worship (da'wat al-'ibadah).

The difference between a supplication of request and a supplication of worship: in the request, a person seeks a particular need. Worship is devotion to Allah. Worship is called supplication because the worshipper, by the language of his state, supplicates that he be rewarded for this worship. This is shown by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord said, "Call upon Me; I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too arrogant to worship Me..."﴾ [Ghafir 60]. He said "Call upon Me," then said "those who are too arrogant to worship Me" [Ghafir 60]. This shows that supplication is worship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming the return to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and that the matters return to Him, in His saying: ﴿And that our return is to Allah﴾ [Ghafir 43]. This verse has parallels, among them: ﴿And to Allah is the return of all matters﴾ [al-Baqarah 210]; and ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return. Then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 25–26]; and ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 6]; and His saying: ﴿And that to your Lord is the finality﴾ [al-Najm 42]. Verses with this meaning are numerous: the return of all creatures is to their Lord, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of extravagance. What is the basis of the indication? From where do we derive the prohibition of extravagance from the verse?
﴿And that the extravagant are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 43].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: extravagance may reach the level of disbelief, from the verse: His saying ﴿they are the companions of the Fire﴾. Whenever you find ﴿the companions of the Fire﴾, they are its people, and they are those who abide in it forever.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strength of this man's faith, when he said: ﴿And that our return is to Allah, and that the extravagant are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 43].

* Among its benefits: the use of allusion (ta'rid).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. How is that?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Well done. Because there is no doubt that the first to enter this statement are these people, but he did not wish to speak of it explicitly.
Can we say: in this verse there is "appearing in place of the pronoun" (izhar fi mawdi' al-idmar)?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What can we say? We could also say: this is a double meaning (tawriyah). In any case, "appearing in place of the pronoun" is one of the styles of the Arabic language, and it is common in the Qur'an. It has benefits, among them:
Intending generality: that the ruling applies generally, to whoever is described by it and to whoever is not.
Among them, stating the cause (ta'lil): because when a description is attached to a ruling, this indicates that the description is the cause.
Among them, a condemnation of those who, by the context, should have been referred to by pronoun, by what this description entails. These are three benefits: intending generality, stating the cause, and passing judgment on these people that they deserve this description.

**Student:** ﴿O my people, what is (the matter with) me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire? (41) You call me to disbelieve in Allah and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving. (42) Undoubtedly, what you call me to has no call (answered) in this world or in the Hereafter, and our return is to Allah, and the transgressors are the companions of the Fire.﴾ [Ghafir 41–43].

* **The Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿O my people, what is (the matter with) me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire﴾ [Ghafir 41]. We have already discussed this sentence and explained that the interrogative here expresses astonishment and disapproval.

﴿What is (the matter with) me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire﴾. The clause ﴿while you call me to the Fire﴾ is coordinated with the preceding clause.
