So when someone says "irtāba" (he had doubt), it is not exactly the same as saying "shakka" (he doubted). Rather, irtiyāb carries unease and agitation, so it is more specific than shakk. Every rayb is a shakk, but not every shakk is a rayb. However, the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, explain a thing by something close to it, as people explain a thing by what approximates it.

As for His saying: ﴿But most of the people do not believe﴾ [Ghafir 59]: do not believe in what? In the coming of the Hour. For this reason, its coming was emphasized to them. And since most people do not believe in it, most people are disbelievers, because belief in the Hour has a great effect on the realization of faith. Whoever does not believe in the Hour does not work for anything. How can someone who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning act? Whoever believes in the Day of Reckoning will be eager to be saved from the consequences of that Day.

﴿But most of the people do not believe (59). And your Lord said, "Call upon Me; I will respond to you"﴾ [Ghafir 59, 60]. When He mentioned the Hour, He mentioned what protects from its consequences, which is calling upon Allah, so He said: ﴿And your Lord said, "Call upon Me"﴾. He expressed the sentence in the third-person form (ghayba) out of glorification of Him, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Your Lord said﴾, and He did not say "I say" or "We said" or anything similar, out of glorification of Allah.

﴿Call upon Me; I will respond to you﴾. ﴿Call upon Me﴾ is an imperative, and ﴿I will respond to you﴾ is its answer (jawab al-talab), the answer to a demand. Here, "calling" (du'a') includes both the supplication of request (du'a' al-mas'alah) and the supplication of worship (du'a' al-'ibadah). The supplication of request is for a person to say, "O my Lord, forgive me." The supplication of worship is for a person to worship Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, by what He has legislated. Worship is called supplication because it includes a person's seeking to be saved from the Fire and to enter Paradise. Isn't that so? If you asked every worshipper, "Why do you worship Allah?" he would say, "I want to be saved from the Fire and to enter the mercy of Allah." Thus worship includes supplication through the language of the state (bi-lisan al-hal).

As for His saying: ﴿I will respond to you﴾, we interpret it, in contrast to the supplication of request, as "I will give you what you ask," and we interpret it with regard to the supplication of worship as "acceptance," meaning: I will accept from you. So Allah's response to the supplication of request is that He gives the petitioner what he asked for, and His response to the supplication of worship is that He accepts from the worshipper. The commentator (al-mufassir) said: "(That is, worship Me, and I will reward you, by the indication of what follows it)." This interpretation, based on what you have heard, would you describe it as what? As deficient. It is considered a deficient interpretation. As for what follows, it is not an indication restricting it to this meaning. Rather, we say: ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me﴾ [Ghafir 60] shows that supplication is worship, because He said: ﴿Call upon Me﴾, and then said: ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me﴾. There is no doubt that whoever is too proud to call upon Allah, and considers himself independent of Allah and not in need of Him, is undoubtedly deserving of this threat: that he will enter Hell in humiliation.

﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me﴾. This is part of what was said. ﴿Will enter﴾ (sayadkhulūn), read with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the kha' (and vice versa). Reverse it to ﴿yudkhalūn﴾ (they will be made to enter). These are two authentic seven canonical recitations.

﴿Jahannam﴾ is the name of the Fire. It is a Arabized (mu'arrab) noun, and its origin, as it has been said, is (Kahannam). It has also been said that it is an Arabic word, and the nūn in it is additional, and its root is from (al-juhmah), meaning darkness. Whatever the case, it is the proper name for the Fire. May Allah protect us and you from it.

As for His saying ﴿humbled﴾ (dākhirīn), it means humiliated, abased. The dākhir is the one who is humiliated.

Let us return to the benefits of the two noble verses. The first: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; there is no doubt about it﴾ [Ghafir 59].

* Among its benefits: the establishment of the Hour's occurrence with emphatic affirmation, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; there is no doubt about it﴾.
* And among its benefits: a warning against neglecting this Hour and not preparing for it, by His saying: ﴿But most of the people do not believe﴾.
* And among its benefits: the obligation to believe in the Resurrection.

And among its benefits: the obligation to believe in the Resurrection, because it is an emphatic report from Allah, and all of Allah's reports are true, and every promise of Allah is true.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the prohibition of doubting this Hour. Because His saying ﴿there is no doubt about it﴾ [al-Kahf 21] may be a plain report for emphasis, and it may be a report with the meaning of a prohibition, that is: do not doubt about it. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿This is the Book about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah 2]. There are two interpretations of it: the first is that it is a pure report, and the second is that it is a report with the meaning of a prohibition, that is: do not doubt about it.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: most people do not believe in this Hour and deny it, saying: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Ya-Sin 78], ﴿There is not but our worldly life; we die and live, and nothing destroys us except time﴾ [al-Jathiyah 24].
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: a refutation of a well-known expression, indeed the nullification of a well-known expression, which is that when a person dies, people say, "He has returned to his final abode." This statement is false, because the grave is not the final abode. The final abode is either Paradise or the Fire. As for the grave, it is a visit and a passage, just as the world is a passage; similarly, the grave is a passage. For this reason, a Bedouin heard a reciter recite Allah's saying: ﴿Competition in worldly gain distracts you until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur 1, 2]. The Bedouin said: "By Allah, the visitor does not remain; there is something beyond the graves." How did he derive it from: ﴿You visit﴾? The visitor stays for a period, then departs.

So if we hear someone say, "He has been buried in his final abode," or something similar, we object to him and say: give up this expression, because its content, if the one who says it believed it, would make him a disbeliever.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And your Lord said, "Call upon Me; I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me"﴾ [Ghafir 60], and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of speech to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Is this speech an inner speech that is not manifested, or is it manifest speech? The second: it is manifest speech, because inner speech, when intended, is specified, as in His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿And they say to themselves, "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?"﴾ [al-Mujadilah 8], and ﴿They conceal within themselves what they do not reveal to you﴾ [Al 'Imran 154]. So when speech is stated without qualification, what is meant is audible speech. This is the view of the early generations (al-salaf) and the leading scholars of later generations: that Allah speaks with an audible voice and with letters, because ﴿Call upon Me; I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir 60] consists of words composed of letters, or not? Therefore, He speaks with letters and with a voice, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for the statement of the one who says that the speech of Allah is the meaning subsisting in the self, and that what is heard is merely an expression of the speech of Allah, created by Allah for people to hear, and otherwise His speech is only what is within Himself, it is false. That is, this is a false statement, because if we interpret "speech" in this way, its meaning becomes knowledge, not speech.

Now we want to compare two statements. One says: "What is in the Mushaf is the speech of Allah, created." And another says: "What is in the Mushaf is an expression of the speech of Allah, created." Which of these is closer to the truth?

* Students: The first.
* The Shaykh: The first. The first is the statement of the Jahmiyyah (Jahmites) and the Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazilites), and the second is the statement of the Ash'ariyyah (Ash'arites). It has now become clear that the statement of the Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah about the speech of Allah is better than the statement of the Ash'arites, even though the Ash'arites claim that they are among the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah). How can this be? So from this verse we establish that speech belongs to Allah, and speech cannot exist except with audible utterance and letters.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of the Lord's greatness and magnificence, from His saying: ﴿And your Lord said﴾ [Ghafir 60], for this form indicates the greatness of the One who speaks, the Mighty and Majestic.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of lordship (rububiyyah) to Allah. It is divided into two types: general and specific.

The general is that which encompasses all creation, which is the nurturing of creation with blessings and sustaining them with blessings. The specific is the nurturing of the believing servants of Allah, whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has raised in what He loves.

Both types came together in His saying, concerning the magicians of the family of Pharaoh: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron"﴾ [al-A'raf 121, 122]. Which is the general? The first, "the Lord of the worlds." "The Lord of Moses and Aaron" is the specific.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: is calling upon Allah obligatory or recommended?
* Students: Calling upon Allah is obligatory.
* The Shaykh: From where do you derive it? From His saying: ﴿Call upon Me; I will respond to you﴾, because it implies: do not call upon other than Me.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah has guaranteed and promised the one who calls upon Him that He will answer him, by His saying: ﴿I will respond to you﴾. If someone says: "We call upon Allah much but see no answer, and we work much but feel no acceptance; what is the answer?"

The answer is that we say: causes do not take effect unless they encounter a receptive locus. Have you seen that when you cut meat with a knife, it is cut, or not? It is cut. When you cut iron with it, it is not cut, even though it is sharp on meat and does nothing to iron. So the cause must have a receptive locus; otherwise it has no effect. In worship, a person worships his Lord and does not feel acceptance because there is something preventing it: either the loss of a condition, a pillar, or an obligation, or the occurrence of something that invalidates it. Isn't that so? Otherwise, if we established the acts of worship as we were commanded, we would find their effect. ﴿And establish prayer. Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut 45]. Which of us, when he prays, feels aversion to immorality and wrongdoing? Prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing, so why do we not feel this? Because we are negligent.

In supplication, we always call upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and see no answer. So we say about it what we said at the beginning: the cause must have a receptive locus. If a person calls upon his Lord but has missed some of the obligatory or recommended etiquettes of supplication, or there is an obstacle preventing the acceptance of the supplication, then the flaw is not in the supplication, but in the one who supplicates and in the locus.

Let us give an example of a person who supplicates without feeling need for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and without feeling the urge to flee to Allah. His supplication is very deficient. If you say, for example, "My Lord, forgive me," you must feel that there are sins that need forgiveness, and that you are in the greatest necessity of the forgiveness of these sins, because if these sins are not forgiven, woe to you! One sin upon another becomes a major sin. For this reason, the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, forbade the belittling of sins and said: "Indeed, the likeness of these is like a people who camped in a land, and each one of them brought a stick, and they gathered a great quantity of firewood and kindled a great fire."[[Ahmad (2679) narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Beware of belittled sins, for they gather upon a man until they destroy him." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave an example of them: like a people who alighted in a barren land, and the food of the people was prepared; a man went and brought a stick, and another man brought a stick, until they gathered a heap, then they kindled a fire and cooked what they threw into it.]] Even though each one of them brought just one stick. So the point is that when you supplicate, you must feel that you are in the utmost need of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Second: among the etiquettes whose absence prevents the answer is that you have doubt about Allah's answering your supplication, such as considering what you ask for to be too great, saying: "This is not going to happen." This is an error, and it is among the things that prevent the answer. For this reason, "the Prophet ﷺ forbade the saying of one who says: 'O Allah, forgive me if You will,' and said: 'Let him resolve in his request and magnify his desire, for Allah is not overwhelmed by anything He gives.'"[[Muslim (3817) with his chain from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When one of you supplicates, let him not say, 'O Allah, forgive me if You will,' but let him resolve in his request and magnify his desire, for Allah is not overwhelmed by anything He gives."]]

Likewise, among the causes of the prevention of the answer is that a person supplicates for something sinful or for severing of kinship ties. He supplicates for sin, such as supplicating against a person who does not deserve to be cursed. This is sin, like supplicating against a ruler who has erred in some matter, saying: "O Allah, do not grant him success," and similar things. This is transgression in supplication. If you see a ruler, whether minor or major, who has erred, his remedy is not for you to say: "O Allah, do not grant him success." His remedy is for you to say: "O Allah, grant him success; let him reform, and let Allah reform through him." This is among the transgressions in supplication that are not accepted. Among the transgressions in supplication is severing of kinship ties: supplicating for the severing of kinship ties is also not accepted. Is the supplication of the oppressor against his victim accepted?
* Student: It is not accepted.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because it is sinful.

Fourth: among the obstacles to acceptance is eating what is forbidden. Eating what is forbidden is among the obstacles to acceptance, because "the Prophet ﷺ mentioned a man who travels far, disheveled and dusty, who raises his hands to the sky, saying: 'O Lord, O Lord'" (all these four aspects are among the causes of the answering of supplication), "while his food is forbidden, his drink is forbidden, his clothing is forbidden, and he has been nourished with what is forbidden. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'How then could it be answered for him?'"[[Narrated by Muslim (1015) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] All these prevent, or come between, a person and the acceptance of his supplication and Allah's answering him.

If there are no obstacles, and the locus is suitable and receptive, then only the matter beyond that remains, which is the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. "Allah may ward off from a person evil greater than what he asked for; He may grant what he asked for; and He may store that for him as a reward on the Day of Resurrection," as came in the hadith.[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3604) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No man supplicates to Allah with a supplication except that it is answered for him: either it is hastened for him in this world, or it is stored up for him in the Hereafter, or an expiation of his sins is made equal to what he supplicated, so long as he does not supplicate for sin, severing of kinship ties, or hastening." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how does one hasten?" He said: "He says: 'I supplicated my Lord, but He did not answer me.'"]] Otherwise, we are most certainly confident of the truth of His saying: ﴿I will respond to you﴾, and that it must come to pass. I think we cannot complete the rest of the benefits, so let us limit ourselves to this. Yes.

* Student: May Allah be good to you. Is what occurs in the heart or in the self called speech, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: No, not unless it is qualified, such as when one says: "He said in himself," as in the hadith: "what its self whispers to it"[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (5269) and Muslim (127/201) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]].
* The Student: The statement of the Ash'arites: "what subsists in the self." Is their statement correct?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not correct. This is a false statement. For this reason, we have now weighed their statement against the statement of the Mu'tazilah, and the statement of the Mu'tazilah became closer to the truth than theirs, because they say: "This that is in the Mushaf is the speech of Allah, created; it is truly the speech of Allah, but it is created." And those (the Ash'arites) say: "It is created and an expression of the speech of Allah."
* Student: May Allah be good to you. The saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I do not bear the concern of being answered, but I bear the concern of supplication." Does he mean (...)?

* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. He means that a person may not have the conditions for acceptance. Now, each of you should take account of himself. When you are in prayer and say, "My Lord, forgive me and have mercy on me" between the two prostrations, do you feel that there are heavy sins from which you are asking God to deliver you? Or is it just a word you say to fulfill the obligation? In fact, when we take account of ourselves, we find great deficiency in us. When a person calls upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, his heart is illuminated simply by calling upon Allah, because supplication is an act of worship. But we ask Allah to help us and you to remember Him, thank Him, and worship Him well.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, this will come, God willing, with the benefits.
* Student: Why do we not say that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic (...)?
* Shaykh: No, because there are controls, as you have heard: eating what is forbidden, if he supplicates for sin or severing of family ties, if the heart is heedless and distracted, if he doubts the matter. There are well-known controls from the Sharia.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Read what follows: ﴿So let them respond to Me and believe in Me, that they may be guided﴾ [al-Baqarah 186].
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. Has he responded to Allah in the etiquette of supplication and in other matters? You must all know that absolute statements in one place must be restricted by what indicates restriction in another place, because the Sharia is one; it came from one niche.
* Student: We said that a person should not undertake supplication until he understands the supplication. For example, a person who knows that this thing is difficult for him..
* Shaykh: Difficult for whom?
* Student: For him.
* Shaykh: For him?! If it were easy for him, he would not need to supplicate; he would just do it.
* Student: He supplicates for it?
* Shaykh: He supplicates, but transgression in supplication is not accepted. If he says: "O Allah, I ask You to make me among the noble messengers," what do we say?
* Students: Transgression.
* Shaykh: This is transgression in supplication. "O Allah, make me not commit a sin," is transgression in supplication. Or he says: "O Allah, I ask You to turn this mosque into gold and emerald; indeed You are over all things capable," (and it becomes) "Be, and it is." But this is contrary to custom, and in most cases there is no benefit in it either.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: This is possible; there is nothing wrong with it. May Allah make you like Sibawayh in grammar and like Ibn Taymiyyah in knowledge, amen. And we, God willing... they say that someone was heard circumambulating the Kaaba, and a person heard him saying: "O Allah, I ask You for grammar like the grammar of Ibn Hisham, and jurisprudence like the jurisprudence of Shaykh al-Islam; indeed You are over all things capable."
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿It is Allah who made the night for you to rest in and the day giving sight. Indeed, Allah is full of bounty to the people, but most of the people do not give thanks. That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things; there is no god but Him, so how are you deluded? Thus are deluded those who used to deny the signs of Allah. It is Allah who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy, and shaped you and perfected your forms, and provided you with good things. That is Allah, your Lord. So blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ghafir 64].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too arrogant to worship Me will enter Hell in humiliation﴾ [Ghafir 60]. We have already discussed this verse, have we not? And we mentioned its benefits.
Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will respond to you.﴾ In this is Allah's promise, glory be to Him, to every supplicant that He will respond to him. But there must be conditions, which I think we have mentioned.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that those who are arrogant toward worshipping Allah will enter Hell in a state of humiliation and abasement, due to His saying: ﴿will enter Hell in humiliation﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed; that is, the punishment corresponds to the offense, because when they were arrogant in this world, they were made to enter the Fire in abasement in the Hereafter: ﴿will enter Hell in humiliation﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the Fire, due to His saying: ﴿Hell﴾.
* Among its benefits: that supplication is an act of worship, due to His saying: ﴿Call upon Me﴾, then He said: ﴿Indeed, those who are too arrogant to worship Me﴾.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said, explaining His favour upon His servants: ﴿It is Allah who made for you the night that you may rest therein﴾ [Ghafir 61]. "Allah" is the subject (mubtada'), and "alladhi" (who) is its predicate (khabar). "Ja'ala" (made) here means ṣayyara (rendered), and it takes two objects: the first is "al-layl" (the night), and the second is "lakum" (for you). The "ja'l" here is a divine decree (ja'l qadari), not a legislative one (ja'l shar'i). Regarding ﴿ja'ala lakum﴾: is the lam here for transitivity, or for transitivity together with causation? The answer is the second.

And His saying ﴿li-taskunū fīh﴾ (that you may rest therein): the lam is for causation (ta'līl). Sukūn (rest) is the opposite of movement and of work, and it encompasses the rest of the limbs, the rest of the heart, and the rest of the soul. For this reason, a person who has become exhausted and then sleeps finds that his vigour is renewed and increased. His saying ﴿wa-al-nahāra mubṣiran﴾ (and the day as something to see by) means: and He made the day something to see by. This is conjoined to "the night," i.e., He made the day mubṣiran. The attribution of seeing (ibṣār) to the day is because it is its place, i.e., the place where people see. For this reason the commentator (al-mufassir) said: "The attribution of seeing to it is metaphorical, because one sees in it." So it is the time of seeing; the day is a place of work and sight.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ [Ghafir 61]. Allah, blessed and exalted, emphasised that He is possessor of bounty toward mankind with "inna" (indeed) and the lam, and "dhū" means "ṣāḥib" (possessor of).

﴿Ladhū faḍlin ʿalā al-nās﴾: "faḍl" means "ifḍāl" (bestowal of bounty). So Allah, glorified and exalted, is the one who bestows bounty upon His servants, and from His bounty—that is, from His bounty—is that He made the night a place of rest and the day something to see by.

His saying ʿalā al-nās (toward mankind) is general, encompassing the believer and the disbeliever, and this is the reality, since the night is a place of rest for believers and disbelievers alike, and the day is something to see by for believers and disbelievers alike.

﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61]: that is, despite Allah being full of bounty toward mankind, most of them do not give thanks—and we seek refuge in Allah—most of them are disbelievers. Similar to this verse are other verses, among them His saying: ﴿And most of mankind, even if you should be eager, are not believers﴾ [Yusuf 103].

The Sunnah has come with the like of this, where the Prophet ﷺ informed: "Allah will call out on the Day of Resurrection: O Adam, bring forth from your offspring a company for the Fire. He will bring forth from every thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine, all of them in the Fire."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4741) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will say on the Day of Resurrection: O Adam! He will say: At Your service, O Lord, and at Your pleasure. He will be called with a voice: Indeed Allah commands you to bring forth from your offspring a company for the Fire. He will say: O Lord, what is the company for the Fire? He will say: From every thousand—I think he said—nine hundred and ninety-nine."]] Of every thousand, one is saved.

Shukr (giving thanks) is the acknowledgement of the bounty-giver for the blessing, with the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. The poet said:

"The blessings have earned you from me three things:
my hand, my tongue, and the hidden inner self (ḍamīr)."

That is: you have taken from me three things because of your blessings upon me: my hand, my tongue, and the concealed inner self.

As for thanking with the heart, it is that you acknowledge in your heart that every blessing upon you is from Allah, as He said: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 53]. The best blessings are the blessings of religion, then reason, then the blessings that follow one another gradually according to need and necessity.

As for the limbs: the hand, the foot, hearing and sight—using these in obedience to Allah is the thanking of the limbs.

The tongue likewise: thanking Allah with the tongue is that you acknowledge with your tongue that whatever blessing you have is from Allah, and that you speak of His blessing upon you—not boastfully or arrogantly, but in need of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and acknowledging His bounty, glorified and exalted is He—because of His saying: ﴿And as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim it﴾ [al-Duha 11]. Then you use this tongue in obedience to the Benefactor. So thanks, in reality, is the whole religion: the heart, the tongue, and the limbs.

﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61]. Furthermore, thanks is divisible: a person may thank his Lord for one blessing and not for others. Allah may bless someone with wealth, and he gives thanks and spends in the way of Allah; and Allah blesses him with knowledge (...), and Allah may bless him with knowledge and he spreads knowledge, but with wealth he is stingy. Thus thanks varies, just as disbelief varies. ﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾.

﴿That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things﴾ [Ghafir 62]. We want to parse this sentence. First, "dhā": there is no doubt it is the subject; the lam indicates distance, the kāf indicates address, and the mīm indicates the plural. "Allāh": do we say it is an apposition (badal) or an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) of the demonstrative, or that it is the predicate? The apparent view is the first. "Rabbukum": the predicate of the subject. "Khāliq kulli shay'": another predicate, since the predicate may be multiple, for the predicate is a description of the thing described; and when it is a description of it, descriptions may be multiple. Allah said: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Owner of the Throne, the Glorious, Doer of what He intends﴾ [al-Buruj 14–16]. How many predicates do we have here? Al-Ghafur, al-Wadud, Dhu al-ʿArsh, al-Majid, Fa''al—five predicates. The predicate may be multiple, because the predicate describes the thing described. So if you say: "Zayd is standing," it means that his description is standing, and descriptions may be multiple for one described thing. So we say: "Khāliq kulli shay'" is a second predicate.

﴿Khāliq kulli shay'﴾ [Ghafir 62]: nothing departs from this sentence at all; it is a general universal. The creator of everything—of entities, attributes, and states: everything—Allah is its creator. The servant is created; the servant's states—sickness, health, reason, madness, and the like—are created; his actions are created; everything is created by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Nothing departs from this sentence at all, even incapacity and shrewdness, which are attributes: incapacity means a person is not decisive, and shrewdness means he is decisive.

﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ [Ghafir 62]: when He explained that He is the Creator of all things, and that there is no creator with Him, based on this general sentence, He explained that there is no deity except Him; that is, there is no one worthy of worship except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Just as He is singular in creation, He must be singled out in worship.

("Ilāh" means "maʾlūh" (one who is worshipped), and fiʿāl often comes in Arabic with the meaning of maf'ūl, as in: ghirās (planted/seedlings), bināʾ (building), firāsh (bedding), kitāb (book), libās (clothing), and ʿudd (counted).)

﴿There is no deity except Him﴾: if someone says: how is this sentence valid alongside His saying ﴿Do not set up with Allah another deity﴾ [al-Isra' 22], and His saying ﴿So their deities did not avail them﴾ [Hud 101], which affirm deities other than Allah?

The answer: this expression is valid if we know the implied predicate: "ḥaqq" (true). "There is no true deity except Allah." Yes. The evidence for this is: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Great﴾ [al-Hajj 62].

﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ [Ghafir 62]: the interrogation here is for wonder and denial. "Anná" means "kayfa" (how). "Tu'fakūn" means you are turned away from faith despite the evidence being established.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus are turned away﴾ [Ghafir 63]. This construction occurs frequently in the Noble Qur'an, and we have previously gone over how to parse it. We said: the kāf is a noun meaning "mithl" (like), and it is an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq) of the verb after it; i.e., like that falsehood, [they] are turned away. "Al-ifk" means "al-ṣarf" (turning away).

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that falsehood, which is associating partners with Allah and not giving thanks for blessings; ﴿is turned away﴾, i.e., like the falsehood of these, the falsehood of ﴿those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir 63] is turned away. As for "alladhīna" (those who), its parsing is that it is a substitute for the subject (nā'ib fā'il).

﴿Those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾: that is, they used to reject the signs of Allah; i.e., they disbelieved. "Jaḥd" here means kufr (disbelief), as evidenced by its being followed by the preposition bā'.

The author's statement: "(﴿the signs of Allah﴾: His miracles)" is without doubt an error. Rather, we say the signs of Allah are His indications which point to His perfection, glorified and exalted, and His worthiness of worship alone. They are signs and not miracles. ﴿The signs of Allah﴾ means the indications that point to His perfection and to His worthiness of being worshipped alone. The signs of Allah, glorified and exalted, are of two kinds: cosmic and legislative. All created things are cosmic signs pointing to His perfection:

"And in everything there is a sign of His
indicating that He is one."

So everything in the universe bears witness to Allah's perfection, His power, His might, His authority, and other attributes. In short, all created beings are cosmic signs pointing to their Creator, and to His wisdom, His mercy, and other attributes of perfection.

Legislative signs are what the messengers brought: just rulings, true reports, and beneficial narratives. These are legislative signs: the obligations, commands, and prohibitions are all just, the reports are all true, nothing in them is false, and the stories are all beneficial: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf 3].

﴿Thus are turned away those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir 63].

* Benefits in these verses: Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is Allah who made for you the night that you may rest therein﴾ [Ghafir 61].

First: the perfection of Allah's power, glorified and exalted, in bringing the night and the day into being, for this is from His immense power. Can mankind, when the sun rises, turn it back so that it sets? And when it sets, drag it back so that it returns? Never. For this reason Allah said: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you light? Will you not then hear?﴾ [71] ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you a night in which you may rest? Will you not then see?﴾ [al-Qasas 71–72]. I say: the night and day which Allah made for the servants cannot be altered by anyone at all. Furthermore, when we look at this night and day, their alternation and the one entering into the other, it is another sign. Sometimes the night lengthens and sometimes the day lengthens. Who can do that except Allah, glorified and exalted?!

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rationale behind Allah's divine decrees is as established in the legislative rulings; that is, the cosmic rulings of Allah cannot but be for some wisdom. From where is this taken? ﴿li-taskunū﴾ (that you may rest), and the lam, I told you, is for causation. So Allah made that so that we may rest.

We have mentioned that Allah's cosmic rulings have reasons, like His legislative rulings. But does it follow that we must know the reason? It does not follow. If Allah opens to us what He opens of this, it is good and a bounty; and if we are deprived of it because of our sins, we are at fault. In any case, there is nothing without wisdom.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's favour, glorified and exalted, through the night and day, in that He made the night a place of rest and the day something to see by: ﴿that you may rest therein, and the day as something to see by﴾ [Ghafir 61]. Were it not for this, people would not rest. For this reason, you find that by nature a person loves rest when the night comes. Were it not that in our present age lights have spread and illumination has become widespread, and night has become like day, you would find a great pleasure in the night—and we experienced that: you find pleasure and love for rest, rest of the heart, rest of the body, rest of the soul. Then when dawn breaks, it is like fresh dates after dried dates; we rejoice in it, and when the day comes, the day comes. Now it is as if there were neither night nor day, and so we do not find the pleasure we used to know before. Perhaps some of you have experienced that. In any case, go out to the desert for a week and stay away from lights, and you will find this. In any event, this is from the favour of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who made for us the night for rest and the day for work.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah is full of bounty toward mankind in general. Do you take that?

* Student: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ [Ghafir 61].

* The Shaykh: ﴿toward mankind﴾, or toward the believers? In another verse: ﴿And Allah is full of bounty toward the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 152]. How do we reconcile generality and specificity? We say: bounty is of two kinds: general and specific. The general is for all people, and the specific is for the believers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that most of Allah's servants do not thank Allah, because of His saying: ﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against measuring the legislative rulings by the actions of people. That is, if we tell a person "this is forbidden," and he says "everyone does it," making the standard the actions of people—this is an error. That everyone does a thing is not a proof: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah﴾ [al-An'am 116]. The proof is in what Allah and His Messenger said: ﴿If you disagree over anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa' 59], whether the other group is more numerous than the one before it or the reverse. Therefore it is not permissible to make people's actions the standard for legislative rulings.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to thank Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and an indication that this thanks should be of the same kind as the bounty. Thanks should be of the same kind as the bounty. So what is the thanks of the person who has wealth?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: His thanks to his Lord—how?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: That he spends it in the way of Allah.
What is the thanks of knowledge?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Correct, and giving it out.
What is the thanks of one whom Allah has given courage and physical strength while jihad is ongoing?

* Student: That he strive in the way of Allah.

* The Shaykh: That he strive in the way of Allah. So thanks is of the same kind as the blessings, because Allah said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61]—the bounty.

* Among the second benefits of this noble verse: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ [Ghafir 62]: the affirmation of Allah's lordship over everything, that He is the Lord of everything, by His saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾.

* Among its benefits: an indication of the obligation to obey Him and worship Him, because of His saying: ﴿your Lord﴾. If He is the Lord, He is the Master; if He is the Lord, He is the one who holds authority; if He is the Lord, He is the one who has the right to be worshipped. Everything that establishes lordship is evidence for the obligation of divinity. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, argues against the polytheists by the fact that they affirm lordship and deny divinity; so whoever affirms lordship is bound to affirm divinity.

So the tawhid of lordship necessitates the tawhid of divinity, and the tawhid of divinity includes the tawhid of lordship, since no one can worship Allah without knowing that He is a Lord worthy of worship.

So if someone asks you: are the two forms of tawhid mutually entailing? Say: as for the tawhid of lordship, it necessitates the tawhid of divinity; and as for the tawhid of divinity, it includes the tawhid of lordship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's creation of everything, by His saying: ﴿the Creator of all things﴾ [Ghafir 62]. If someone says: "Reason excepted itself, so it is not a creator of itself"—is this statement valid?

* Student: No.

* The Shaykh: Why? Because it itself did not enter at all, since there is an agent and an object, and the agent cannot enter the object so as to be excepted from it. We say: the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, did not enter into His saying "all things" at all in this verse, because creation—or if you wish, say: because the created is separate from the Creator—so the Creator cannot enter into the created so that we say "reason is excepted." Exception is the removal of a thing from a thing, and here it did not enter at all.

I say: Allah is the Creator of all things. Is it appropriate to say: "and reason excepted itself, so it is not a creator of itself"?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: This verse: Allah is the Creator of all things. Do we say: except His essence?
We say: no. Why? Because the principle is that He did not enter at all into being the creator of all things; that is, He did not enter the created. He is the agent and others are the object, so He did not enter at all, so that we would say: exclude what reason can exclude in this domain.

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah Ghafir (40), verses 61–63 (Part 2 of 2):

The Jahmiyya and the Mu'tazila argued that the Speech of Allah is created, because the Speech of Allah is "a thing" and so falls under the general scope [of "Allah is the Creator of all things"]. We say: then it necessarily follows that you must also say that Allah is created, since Allah is "a thing." ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "Allah"﴾ [al-An'am 19]. So say also that Allah is created. If they say, "We cannot say that, because the agent (al-fa'il) is not the thing acted upon (al-maf'ul)," we reply: the attributes of the agent are like the agent itself. Attributes follow the essence (yuhdha bi-ha hadhw al-dhat). If the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is a Creator, and other than Him is created, then His attributes are also uncreated. The Qur'an is not created, because it is the Speech of Allah, and the Speech of Allah is among His attributes, and all of Allah's attributes are uncreated.

If someone says: creation is also affirmed for the servant. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿So blessed be Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun 14], thus affirming that there are [other] creators. And the Messenger ﷺ said about the makers of images: «Give life to what you have created»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5951) and Muslim (2108/97) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.]], thus affirming that they are creators.

The answer: the creation affirmed for the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, is not like the creation affirmed for the created. The creation of the created being means transforming a thing from one state to another, not bringing it into existence. When the carpenter makes a piece of wood into a door, does one say that he created the wood? He transformed it from wood into a door; he did not create it. Even if we say that his making is a "creation," it in reality means change and transformation, not bringing into existence. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, also challenged the idols that are worshipped besides Allah and that are claimed to be gods, saying: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gather together for it﴾ [al-Hajj 73].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the foundation of the Tawhid of worship (tawhid al-uluhiyya) being built upon the Tawhid of Lordship (tawhid al-rububiyya); for His statement afterward: ﴿Allah is your Lord, the Creator of all things﴾ ﴿there is no deity except Him﴾ [Ghafir 65], meaning: there is no one worshipped except Him, i.e., do not worship anyone but Him, as shown by His saying: ﴿there is no deity except Him﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the denunciation of amazement at those who have turned away from the truth despite its clarity and manifestness, as shown by His saying: ﴿How are they deluded?﴾ [Ghafir 62].
* Among the benefits of the third verse: that those who deny the signs of Allah produce things that are a cause for wonder, as shown by His saying: ﴿Thus are they deluded, those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir 63].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that sins come between a person and seeing the truth, because these people, when they denied the signs of Allah, were turned away from it. This is a reality: sins come between a person and seeing the truth. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients"﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 13]. Can anyone say that this great Qur'an is "tales of the ancients"? Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿No! Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 14], from evil deeds, until they saw this clear truth and made it into tales.

Therefore, we must treat ourselves if we find that we read the Qur'an as though it were mere letters recited, hoping for its blessing and reward. If it does not affect the heart with softness, humility and returning to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, then that is a sign of a sick heart, and perhaps we would say of a dead heart; we ask Allah for well-being. Likewise, "thus are they deluded, those who used to deny the signs of Allah." We ask Allah to make us and you among those who believe in His signs and follow what pleases Him.

* The student: Shaykh, does the word khalaqa occur in the Arabic language with the meaning of making/transforming?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. From it: ﴿You only worship besides Allah idols, and you invent a lie (takhluqun ifka)﴾ [al-'Ankabut 17], meaning: you say a falsehood.
* The student: Other than this in the Arabic language, so that we may confront them with it...
* The Shaykh: The Qur'an is in Arabic.
* A student: In schools they teach a principle: that matter is neither destroyed nor created from nothing. What is your view?
* The Shaykh: My view is that this is disbelief. Whoever believes the meaning of this is a disbeliever. Everything perishes except the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas 88]. The meaning of "perishing" (halik) is: subject to perishing, though Allah may make it everlasting, like Paradise and Hellfire. But He who brought it into existence is able to annihilate it, and annihilation is easier than bringing into existence. Their saying also, "it is not newly created," means that they have judged it to be eternal and everlasting. No believer says this, and this is in the schools!?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) A student was given in the examination: what is the ruling on cracking the knuckles during prayer? The student said: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "A section: it is disliked in prayer to turn one's head, to raise one's gaze toward the sky, to crack one's fingers, to interlace them, and to sit in iq'a..." until he mentioned the whole section, ten (...), then said: take what you want and leave what you want. You want us to go and read all the chemistry books so we can find that matter is neither created nor destroyed?
* A student: The disbelieving nations exploit the stillness of night and the vision of day more than the Muslim nation...
* The Shaykh: Amazing, how is that?
* The student: They sleep early, at nine o'clock they are asleep, and in the early morning, four or five, they are awake.
* The Shaykh: Subhan Allah, although this is the Shari'a: «The Prophet ﷺ used to dislike sleeping before 'Isha' and talking after it»[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (568) from Abu Barza, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to dislike sleeping before 'Isha' and talking after it.]]; because sleeping before 'Isha' may continue on, and because one rises for the 'Isha' prayer lazily; and because some people, if they sleep an hour or half an hour, sleep leaves them and they do not sleep the whole night. Three reasons. But why do they bring these televisions and keep them on until midnight or later? Or are they fooling us? Allah is the One sought for help.
* A student: They are fooling us.
* The Shaykh: They are fooling us. Allah is the One sought for help.
* The student: But we have heard, Shaykh, that when the sun sets they also close their shops at five or six.
* The Shaykh: Amazing! So after sunset, Allahu Akbar, is it not our time? I mean in America, in England, in France, and you are at two in the night.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: They are disbelievers and have no reward, but they are closer to the truth than us on this matter: early sleep is better.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said, explaining His favour upon His servants: ﴿It is Allah who made for you the night that you may rest therein﴾ [Ghafir 61]. "Allah" is the subject (mubtada'), and "alladhi" (who) is its predicate (khabar). "Ja'ala" (made) here means ṣayyara (rendered), and it takes two objects: the first is "al-layl" (the night), and the second is "lakum" (for you). The "ja'l" here is a divine decree (ja'l qadari), not a legislative one (ja'l shar'i). Regarding ﴿ja'ala lakum﴾: is the lam here for transitivity, or for transitivity together with causation? The answer is the second.

And His saying ﴿li-taskunū fīh﴾ (that you may rest therein): the lam is for causation (ta'līl). Sukūn (rest) is the opposite of movement and of work, and it encompasses the rest of the limbs, the rest of the heart, and the rest of the soul. For this reason, a person who has become exhausted and then sleeps finds that his vigour is renewed and increased. His saying ﴿wa-al-nahāra mubṣiran﴾ (and the day as something to see by) means: and He made the day something to see by. This is conjoined to "the night," i.e., He made the day mubṣiran. The attribution of seeing (ibṣār) to the day is because it is its place, i.e., the place where people see. For this reason the commentator (al-mufassir) said: "The attribution of seeing to it is metaphorical, because one sees in it." So it is the time of seeing; the day is a place of work and sight.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ [Ghafir 61]. Allah, blessed and exalted, emphasised that He is possessor of bounty toward mankind with "inna" (indeed) and the lam, and "dhū" means "ṣāḥib" (possessor of).

﴿Ladhū faḍlin ʿalā al-nās﴾: "faḍl" means "ifḍāl" (bestowal of bounty). So Allah, glorified and exalted, is the one who bestows bounty upon His servants, and from His bounty—that is, from His bounty—is that He made the night a place of rest and the day something to see by.

His saying ʿalā al-nās (toward mankind) is general, encompassing the believer and the disbeliever, and this is the reality, since the night is a place of rest for believers and disbelievers alike, and the day is something to see by for believers and disbelievers alike.

﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61]: that is, despite Allah being full of bounty toward mankind, most of them do not give thanks—and we seek refuge in Allah—most of them are disbelievers. Similar to this verse are other verses, among them His saying: ﴿And most of mankind, even if you should be eager, are not believers﴾ [Yusuf 103].

The Sunnah has come with the like of this, where the Prophet ﷺ informed: "Allah will call out on the Day of Resurrection: O Adam, bring forth from your offspring a company for the Fire. He will bring forth from every thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine, all of them in the Fire."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4741) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will say on the Day of Resurrection: O Adam! He will say: At Your service, O Lord, and at Your pleasure. He will be called with a voice: Indeed Allah commands you to bring forth from your offspring a company for the Fire. He will say: O Lord, what is the company for the Fire? He will say: From every thousand—I think he said—nine hundred and ninety-nine."]] Of every thousand, one is saved.

Shukr (giving thanks) is the acknowledgement of the bounty-giver for the blessing, with the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. The poet said:

"The blessings have earned you from me three things:
my hand, my tongue, and the hidden inner self (ḍamīr)."

That is: you have taken from me three things because of your blessings upon me: my hand, my tongue, and the concealed inner self.

As for thanking with the heart, it is that you acknowledge in your heart that every blessing upon you is from Allah, as He said: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 53]. The best blessings are the blessings of religion, then reason, then the blessings that follow one another gradually according to need and necessity.

As for the limbs: the hand, the foot, hearing and sight—using these in obedience to Allah is the thanking of the limbs.

The tongue likewise: thanking Allah with the tongue is that you acknowledge with your tongue that whatever blessing you have is from Allah, and that you speak of His blessing upon you—not boastfully or arrogantly, but in need of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and acknowledging His bounty, glorified and exalted is He—because of His saying: ﴿And as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim it﴾ [al-Duha 11]. Then you use this tongue in obedience to the Benefactor. So thanks, in reality, is the whole religion: the heart, the tongue, and the limbs.

﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61]. Furthermore, thanks is divisible: a person may thank his Lord for one blessing and not for others. Allah may bless someone with wealth, and he gives thanks and spends in the way of Allah; and Allah blesses him with knowledge (...), and Allah may bless him with knowledge and he spreads knowledge, but with wealth he is stingy. Thus thanks varies, just as disbelief varies. ﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾.

﴿That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things﴾ [Ghafir 62]. We want to parse this sentence. First, "dhā": there is no doubt it is the subject; the lam indicates distance, the kāf indicates address, and the mīm indicates the plural. "Allāh": do we say it is an apposition (badal) or an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) of the demonstrative, or that it is the predicate? The apparent view is the first. "Rabbukum": the predicate of the subject. "Khāliq kulli shay'": another predicate, since the predicate may be multiple, for the predicate is a description of the thing described; and when it is a description of it, descriptions may be multiple. Allah said: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Owner of the Throne, the Glorious, Doer of what He intends﴾ [al-Buruj 14–16]. How many predicates do we have here? Al-Ghafur, al-Wadud, Dhu al-ʿArsh, al-Majid, Fa''al—five predicates. The predicate may be multiple, because the predicate describes the thing described. So if you say: "Zayd is standing," it means that his description is standing, and descriptions may be multiple for one described thing. So we say: "Khāliq kulli shay'" is a second predicate.

﴿Khāliq kulli shay'﴾ [Ghafir 62]: nothing departs from this sentence at all; it is a general universal. The creator of everything—of entities, attributes, and states: everything—Allah is its creator. The servant is created; the servant's states—sickness, health, reason, madness, and the like—are created; his actions are created; everything is created by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Nothing departs from this sentence at all, even incapacity and shrewdness, which are attributes: incapacity means a person is not decisive, and shrewdness means he is decisive.

﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ [Ghafir 62]: when He explained that He is the Creator of all things, and that there is no creator with Him, based on this general sentence, He explained that there is no deity except Him; that is, there is no one worthy of worship except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Just as He is singular in creation, He must be singled out in worship.

("Ilāh" means "maʾlūh" (one who is worshipped), and fiʿāl often comes in Arabic with the meaning of maf'ūl, as in: ghirās (planted/seedlings), bināʾ (building), firāsh (bedding), kitāb (book), libās (clothing), and ʿudd (counted).)

﴿There is no deity except Him﴾: if someone says: how is this sentence valid alongside His saying ﴿Do not set up with Allah another deity﴾ [al-Isra' 22], and His saying ﴿So their deities did not avail them﴾ [Hud 101], which affirm deities other than Allah?

The answer: this expression is valid if we know the implied predicate: "ḥaqq" (true). "There is no true deity except Allah." Yes. The evidence for this is: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Great﴾ [al-Hajj 62].

﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ [Ghafir 62]: the interrogation here is for wonder and denial. "Anná" means "kayfa" (how). "Tu'fakūn" means you are turned away from faith despite the evidence being established.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus are turned away﴾ [Ghafir 63]. This construction occurs frequently in the Noble Qur'an, and we have previously gone over how to parse it. We said: the kāf is a noun meaning "mithl" (like), and it is an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq) of the verb after it; i.e., like that falsehood, [they] are turned away. "Al-ifk" means "al-ṣarf" (turning away).

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that falsehood, which is associating partners with Allah and not giving thanks for blessings; ﴿is turned away﴾, i.e., like the falsehood of these, the falsehood of ﴿those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir 63] is turned away. As for "alladhīna" (those who), its parsing is that it is a substitute for the subject (nā'ib fā'il).

﴿Those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾: that is, they used to reject the signs of Allah; i.e., they disbelieved. "Jaḥd" here means kufr (disbelief), as evidenced by its being followed by the preposition bā'.

The author's statement: "(﴿the signs of Allah﴾: His miracles)" is without doubt an error. Rather, we say the signs of Allah are His indications which point to His perfection, glorified and exalted, and His worthiness of worship alone. They are signs and not miracles. ﴿The signs of Allah﴾ means the indications that point to His perfection and to His worthiness of being worshipped alone. The signs of Allah, glorified and exalted, are of two kinds: cosmic and legislative. All created things are cosmic signs pointing to His perfection:

"And in everything there is a sign of His
indicating that He is one."

So everything in the universe bears witness to Allah's perfection, His power, His might, His authority, and other attributes. In short, all created beings are cosmic signs pointing to their Creator, and to His wisdom, His mercy, and other attributes of perfection.

Legislative signs are what the messengers brought: just rulings, true reports, and beneficial narratives. These are legislative signs: the obligations, commands, and prohibitions are all just, the reports are all true, nothing in them is false, and the stories are all beneficial: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf 3].

﴿Thus are turned away those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir 63].

* Benefits in these verses: Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is Allah who made for you the night that you may rest therein﴾ [Ghafir 61].

First: the perfection of Allah's power, glorified and exalted, in bringing the night and the day into being, for this is from His immense power. Can mankind, when the sun rises, turn it back so that it sets? And when it sets, drag it back so that it returns? Never. For this reason Allah said: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you light? Will you not then hear?﴾ [71] ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you a night in which you may rest? Will you not then see?﴾ [al-Qasas 71–72]. I say: the night and day which Allah made for the servants cannot be altered by anyone at all. Furthermore, when we look at this night and day, their alternation and the one entering into the other, it is another sign. Sometimes the night lengthens and sometimes the day lengthens. Who can do that except Allah, glorified and exalted?!

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rationale behind Allah's divine decrees is as established in the legislative rulings; that is, the cosmic rulings of Allah cannot but be for some wisdom. From where is this taken? ﴿li-taskunū﴾ (that you may rest), and the lam, I told you, is for causation. So Allah made that so that we may rest.

We have mentioned that Allah's cosmic rulings have reasons, like His legislative rulings. But does it follow that we must know the reason? It does not follow. If Allah opens to us what He opens of this, it is good and a bounty; and if we are deprived of it because of our sins, we are at fault. In any case, there is nothing without wisdom.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's favour, glorified and exalted, through the night and day, in that He made the night a place of rest and the day something to see by: ﴿that you may rest therein, and the day as something to see by﴾ [Ghafir 61]. Were it not for this, people would not rest. For this reason, you find that by nature a person loves rest when the night comes. Were it not that in our present age lights have spread and illumination has become widespread, and night has become like day, you would find a great pleasure in the night—and we experienced that: you find pleasure and love for rest, rest of the heart, rest of the body, rest of the soul. Then when dawn breaks, it is like fresh dates after dried dates; we rejoice in it, and when the day comes, the day comes. Now it is as if there were neither night nor day, and so we do not find the pleasure we used to know before. Perhaps some of you have experienced that. In any case, go out to the desert for a week and stay away from lights, and you will find this. In any event, this is from the favour of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who made for us the night for rest and the day for work.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah is full of bounty toward mankind in general. Do you take that?

* Student: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ [Ghafir 61].

* The Shaykh: ﴿toward mankind﴾, or toward the believers? In another verse: ﴿And Allah is full of bounty toward the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 152]. How do we reconcile generality and specificity? We say: bounty is of two kinds: general and specific. The general is for all people, and the specific is for the believers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that most of Allah's servants do not thank Allah, because of His saying: ﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against measuring the legislative rulings by the actions of people. That is, if we tell a person "this is forbidden," and he says "everyone does it," making the standard the actions of people—this is an error. That everyone does a thing is not a proof: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah﴾ [al-An'am 116]. The proof is in what Allah and His Messenger said: ﴿If you disagree over anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa' 59], whether the other group is more numerous than the one before it or the reverse. Therefore it is not permissible to make people's actions the standard for legislative rulings.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to thank Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and an indication that this thanks should be of the same kind as the bounty. Thanks should be of the same kind as the bounty. So what is the thanks of the person who has wealth?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: His thanks to his Lord—how?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: That he spends it in the way of Allah.
What is the thanks of knowledge?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Correct, and giving it out.
What is the thanks of one whom Allah has given courage and physical strength while jihad is ongoing?

* Student: That he strive in the way of Allah.

* The Shaykh: That he strive in the way of Allah. So thanks is of the same kind as the blessings, because Allah said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61]—the bounty.

* Among the second benefits of this noble verse: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ [Ghafir 62]: the affirmation of Allah's lordship over everything, that He is the Lord of everything, by His saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾.

* Among its benefits: an indication of the obligation to obey Him and worship Him, because of His saying: ﴿your Lord﴾. If He is the Lord, He is the Master; if He is the Lord, He is the one who holds authority; if He is the Lord, He is the one who has the right to be worshipped. Everything that establishes lordship is evidence for the obligation of divinity. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, argues against the polytheists by the fact that they affirm lordship and deny divinity; so whoever affirms lordship is bound to affirm divinity.

So the tawhid of lordship necessitates the tawhid of divinity, and the tawhid of divinity includes the tawhid of lordship, since no one can worship Allah without knowing that He is a Lord worthy of worship.

So if someone asks you: are the two forms of tawhid mutually entailing? Say: as for the tawhid of lordship, it necessitates the tawhid of divinity; and as for the tawhid of divinity, it includes the tawhid of lordship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's creation of everything, by His saying: ﴿the Creator of all things﴾ [Ghafir 62]. If someone says: "Reason excepted itself, so it is not a creator of itself"—is this statement valid?

* Student: No.

* The Shaykh: Why? Because it itself did not enter at all, since there is an agent and an object, and the agent cannot enter the object so as to be excepted from it. We say: the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, did not enter into His saying "all things" at all in this verse, because creation—or if you wish, say: because the created is separate from the Creator—so the Creator cannot enter into the created so that we say "reason is excepted." Exception is the removal of a thing from a thing, and here it did not enter at all.

I say: Allah is the Creator of all things. Is it appropriate to say: "and reason excepted itself, so it is not a creator of itself"?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: This verse: Allah is the Creator of all things. Do we say: except His essence?
We say: no. Why? Because the principle is that He did not enter at all into being the creator of all things; that is, He did not enter the created. He is the agent and others are the object, so He did not enter at all, so that we would say: exclude what reason can exclude in this domain.

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah Ghafir (40), verses 61–63 (Part 2 of 2):

The Jahmiyya and the Mu'tazila argued that the Speech of Allah is created, because the Speech of Allah is "a thing" and so falls under the general scope [of "Allah is the Creator of all things"]. We say: then it necessarily follows that you must also say that Allah is created, since Allah is "a thing." ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "Allah"﴾ [al-An'am 19]. So say also that Allah is created. If they say, "We cannot say that, because the agent (al-fa'il) is not the thing acted upon (al-maf'ul)," we reply: the attributes of the agent are like the agent itself. Attributes follow the essence (yuhdha bi-ha hadhw al-dhat). If the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is a Creator, and other than Him is created, then His attributes are also uncreated. The Qur'an is not created, because it is the Speech of Allah, and the Speech of Allah is among His attributes, and all of Allah's attributes are uncreated.

If someone says: creation is also affirmed for the servant. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿So blessed be Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun 14], thus affirming that there are [other] creators. And the Messenger ﷺ said about the makers of images: «Give life to what you have created»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5951) and Muslim (2108/97) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.]], thus affirming that they are creators.

The answer: the creation affirmed for the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, is not like the creation affirmed for the created. The creation of the created being means transforming a thing from one state to another, not bringing it into existence. When the carpenter makes a piece of wood into a door, does one say that he created the wood? He transformed it from wood into a door; he did not create it. Even if we say that his making is a "creation," it in reality means change and transformation, not bringing into existence. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, also challenged the idols that are worshipped besides Allah and that are claimed to be gods, saying: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gather together for it﴾ [al-Hajj 73].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the foundation of the Tawhid of worship (tawhid al-uluhiyya) being built upon the Tawhid of Lordship (tawhid al-rububiyya); for His statement afterward: ﴿Allah is your Lord, the Creator of all things﴾ ﴿there is no deity except Him﴾ [Ghafir 65], meaning: there is no one worshipped except Him, i.e., do not worship anyone but Him, as shown by His saying: ﴿there is no deity except Him﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the denunciation of amazement at those who have turned away from the truth despite its clarity and manifestness, as shown by His saying: ﴿How are they deluded?﴾ [Ghafir 62].
* Among the benefits of the third verse: that those who deny the signs of Allah produce things that are a cause for wonder, as shown by His saying: ﴿Thus are they deluded, those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir 63].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that sins come between a person and seeing the truth, because these people, when they denied the signs of Allah, were turned away from it. This is a reality: sins come between a person and seeing the truth. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients"﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 13]. Can anyone say that this great Qur'an is "tales of the ancients"? Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿No! Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 14], from evil deeds, until they saw this clear truth and made it into tales.

Therefore, we must treat ourselves if we find that we read the Qur'an as though it were mere letters recited, hoping for its blessing and reward. If it does not affect the heart with softness, humility and returning to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, then that is a sign of a sick heart, and perhaps we would say of a dead heart; we ask Allah for well-being. Likewise, "thus are they deluded, those who used to deny the signs of Allah." We ask Allah to make us and you among those who believe in His signs and follow what pleases Him.

* The student: Shaykh, does the word khalaqa occur in the Arabic language with the meaning of making/transforming?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. From it: ﴿You only worship besides Allah idols, and you invent a lie (takhluqun ifka)﴾ [al-'Ankabut 17], meaning: you say a falsehood.
* The student: Other than this in the Arabic language, so that we may confront them with it...
* The Shaykh: The Qur'an is in Arabic.
* A student: In schools they teach a principle: that matter is neither destroyed nor created from nothing. What is your view?
* The Shaykh: My view is that this is disbelief. Whoever believes the meaning of this is a disbeliever. Everything perishes except the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas 88]. The meaning of "perishing" (halik) is: subject to perishing, though Allah may make it everlasting, like Paradise and Hellfire. But He who brought it into existence is able to annihilate it, and annihilation is easier than bringing into existence. Their saying also, "it is not newly created," means that they have judged it to be eternal and everlasting. No believer says this, and this is in the schools!?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) A student was given in the examination: what is the ruling on cracking the knuckles during prayer? The student said: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "A section: it is disliked in prayer to turn one's head, to raise one's gaze toward the sky, to crack one's fingers, to interlace them, and to sit in iq'a..." until he mentioned the whole section, ten (...), then said: take what you want and leave what you want. You want us to go and read all the chemistry books so we can find that matter is neither created nor destroyed?
* A student: The disbelieving nations exploit the stillness of night and the vision of day more than the Muslim nation...
* The Shaykh: Amazing, how is that?
* The student: They sleep early, at nine o'clock they are asleep, and in the early morning, four or five, they are awake.
* The Shaykh: Subhan Allah, although this is the Shari'a: «The Prophet ﷺ used to dislike sleeping before 'Isha' and talking after it»[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (568) from Abu Barza, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to dislike sleeping before 'Isha' and talking after it.]]; because sleeping before 'Isha' may continue on, and because one rises for the 'Isha' prayer lazily; and because some people, if they sleep an hour or half an hour, sleep leaves them and they do not sleep the whole night. Three reasons. But why do they bring these televisions and keep them on until midnight or later? Or are they fooling us? Allah is the One sought for help.
* A student: They are fooling us.
* The Shaykh: They are fooling us. Allah is the One sought for help.
* The student: But we have heard, Shaykh, that when the sun sets they also close their shops at five or six.
* The Shaykh: Amazing! So after sunset, Allahu Akbar, is it not our time? I mean in America, in England, in France, and you are at two in the night.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: They are disbelievers and have no reward, but they are closer to the truth than us on this matter: early sleep is better.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said, explaining His favour upon His servants: ﴿It is Allah who made for you the night that you may rest therein﴾ [Ghafir 61]. "Allah" is the subject (mubtada'), and "alladhi" (who) is its predicate (khabar). "Ja'ala" (made) here means ṣayyara (rendered), and it takes two objects: the first is "al-layl" (the night), and the second is "lakum" (for you). The "ja'l" here is a divine decree (ja'l qadari), not a legislative one (ja'l shar'i). Regarding ﴿ja'ala lakum﴾: is the lam here for transitivity, or for transitivity together with causation? The answer is the second.

And His saying ﴿li-taskunū fīh﴾ (that you may rest therein): the lam is for causation (ta'līl). Sukūn (rest) is the opposite of movement and of work, and it encompasses the rest of the limbs, the rest of the heart, and the rest of the soul. For this reason, a person who has become exhausted and then sleeps finds that his vigour is renewed and increased. His saying ﴿wa-al-nahāra mubṣiran﴾ (and the day as something to see by) means: and He made the day something to see by. This is conjoined to "the night," i.e., He made the day mubṣiran. The attribution of seeing (ibṣār) to the day is because it is its place, i.e., the place where people see. For this reason the commentator (al-mufassir) said: "The attribution of seeing to it is metaphorical, because one sees in it." So it is the time of seeing; the day is a place of work and sight.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ [Ghafir 61]. Allah, blessed and exalted, emphasised that He is possessor of bounty toward mankind with "inna" (indeed) and the lam, and "dhū" means "ṣāḥib" (possessor of).

﴿Ladhū faḍlin ʿalā al-nās﴾: "faḍl" means "ifḍāl" (bestowal of bounty). So Allah, glorified and exalted, is the one who bestows bounty upon His servants, and from His bounty—that is, from His bounty—is that He made the night a place of rest and the day something to see by.

His saying ʿalā al-nās (toward mankind) is general, encompassing the believer and the disbeliever, and this is the reality, since the night is a place of rest for believers and disbelievers alike, and the day is something to see by for believers and disbelievers alike.

﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61]: that is, despite Allah being full of bounty toward mankind, most of them do not give thanks—and we seek refuge in Allah—most of them are disbelievers. Similar to this verse are other verses, among them His saying: ﴿And most of mankind, even if you should be eager, are not believers﴾ [Yusuf 103].

The Sunnah has come with the like of this, where the Prophet ﷺ informed: "Allah will call out on the Day of Resurrection: O Adam, bring forth from your offspring a company for the Fire. He will bring forth from every thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine, all of them in the Fire."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4741) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will say on the Day of Resurrection: O Adam! He will say: At Your service, O Lord, and at Your pleasure. He will be called with a voice: Indeed Allah commands you to bring forth from your offspring a company for the Fire. He will say: O Lord, what is the company for the Fire? He will say: From every thousand—I think he said—nine hundred and ninety-nine."]] Of every thousand, one is saved.

Shukr (giving thanks) is the acknowledgement of the bounty-giver for the blessing, with the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. The poet said:

"The blessings have earned you from me three things:
my hand, my tongue, and the hidden inner self (ḍamīr)."

That is: you have taken from me three things because of your blessings upon me: my hand, my tongue, and the concealed inner self.

As for thanking with the heart, it is that you acknowledge in your heart that every blessing upon you is from Allah, as He said: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 53]. The best blessings are the blessings of religion, then reason, then the blessings that follow one another gradually according to need and necessity.

As for the limbs: the hand, the foot, hearing and sight—using these in obedience to Allah is the thanking of the limbs.

The tongue likewise: thanking Allah with the tongue is that you acknowledge with your tongue that whatever blessing you have is from Allah, and that you speak of His blessing upon you—not boastfully or arrogantly, but in need of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and acknowledging His bounty, glorified and exalted is He—because of His saying: ﴿And as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim it﴾ [al-Duha 11].
