Then you use this tongue in obedience to the Benefactor. So thanks, in reality, is the whole religion: the heart, the tongue, and the limbs.

﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61]. Furthermore, thanks is divisible: a person may thank his Lord for one blessing and not for others. Allah may bless someone with wealth, and he gives thanks and spends in the way of Allah; and Allah blesses him with knowledge (...), and Allah may bless him with knowledge and he spreads knowledge, but with wealth he is stingy. Thus thanks varies, just as disbelief varies. ﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾.

﴿That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things﴾ [Ghafir 62]. We want to parse this sentence. First, "dhā": there is no doubt it is the subject; the lam indicates distance, the kāf indicates address, and the mīm indicates the plural. "Allāh": do we say it is an apposition (badal) or an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) of the demonstrative, or that it is the predicate? The apparent view is the first. "Rabbukum": the predicate of the subject. "Khāliq kulli shay'": another predicate, since the predicate may be multiple, for the predicate is a description of the thing described; and when it is a description of it, descriptions may be multiple. Allah said: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Owner of the Throne, the Glorious, Doer of what He intends﴾ [al-Buruj 14–16]. How many predicates do we have here? Al-Ghafur, al-Wadud, Dhu al-ʿArsh, al-Majid, Fa''al—five predicates. The predicate may be multiple, because the predicate describes the thing described. So if you say: "Zayd is standing," it means that his description is standing, and descriptions may be multiple for one described thing. So we say: "Khāliq kulli shay'" is a second predicate.

﴿Khāliq kulli shay'﴾ [Ghafir 62]: nothing departs from this sentence at all; it is a general universal. The creator of everything—of entities, attributes, and states: everything—Allah is its creator. The servant is created; the servant's states—sickness, health, reason, madness, and the like—are created; his actions are created; everything is created by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Nothing departs from this sentence at all, even incapacity and shrewdness, which are attributes: incapacity means a person is not decisive, and shrewdness means he is decisive.

﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ [Ghafir 62]: when He explained that He is the Creator of all things, and that there is no creator with Him, based on this general sentence, He explained that there is no deity except Him; that is, there is no one worthy of worship except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Just as He is singular in creation, He must be singled out in worship.

("Ilāh" means "maʾlūh" (one who is worshipped), and fiʿāl often comes in Arabic with the meaning of maf'ūl, as in: ghirās (planted/seedlings), bināʾ (building), firāsh (bedding), kitāb (book), libās (clothing), and ʿudd (counted).)

﴿There is no deity except Him﴾: if someone says: how is this sentence valid alongside His saying ﴿Do not set up with Allah another deity﴾ [al-Isra' 22], and His saying ﴿So their deities did not avail them﴾ [Hud 101], which affirm deities other than Allah?

The answer: this expression is valid if we know the implied predicate: "ḥaqq" (true). "There is no true deity except Allah." Yes. The evidence for this is: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Great﴾ [al-Hajj 62].

﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ [Ghafir 62]: the interrogation here is for wonder and denial. "Anná" means "kayfa" (how). "Tu'fakūn" means you are turned away from faith despite the evidence being established.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus are turned away﴾ [Ghafir 63]. This construction occurs frequently in the Noble Qur'an, and we have previously gone over how to parse it. We said: the kāf is a noun meaning "mithl" (like), and it is an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq) of the verb after it; i.e., like that falsehood, [they] are turned away. "Al-ifk" means "al-ṣarf" (turning away).

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that falsehood, which is associating partners with Allah and not giving thanks for blessings; ﴿is turned away﴾, i.e., like the falsehood of these, the falsehood of ﴿those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir 63] is turned away. As for "alladhīna" (those who), its parsing is that it is a substitute for the subject (nā'ib fā'il).

﴿Those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾: that is, they used to reject the signs of Allah; i.e., they disbelieved. "Jaḥd" here means kufr (disbelief), as evidenced by its being followed by the preposition bā'.

The author's statement: "(﴿the signs of Allah﴾: His miracles)" is without doubt an error. Rather, we say the signs of Allah are His indications which point to His perfection, glorified and exalted, and His worthiness of worship alone. They are signs and not miracles. ﴿The signs of Allah﴾ means the indications that point to His perfection and to His worthiness of being worshipped alone. The signs of Allah, glorified and exalted, are of two kinds: cosmic and legislative. All created things are cosmic signs pointing to His perfection:

"And in everything there is a sign of His
indicating that He is one."

So everything in the universe bears witness to Allah's perfection, His power, His might, His authority, and other attributes. In short, all created beings are cosmic signs pointing to their Creator, and to His wisdom, His mercy, and other attributes of perfection.

Legislative signs are what the messengers brought: just rulings, true reports, and beneficial narratives. These are legislative signs: the obligations, commands, and prohibitions are all just, the reports are all true, nothing in them is false, and the stories are all beneficial: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf 3].

﴿Thus are turned away those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir 63].

* Benefits in these verses: Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is Allah who made for you the night that you may rest therein﴾ [Ghafir 61].

First: the perfection of Allah's power, glorified and exalted, in bringing the night and the day into being, for this is from His immense power. Can mankind, when the sun rises, turn it back so that it sets? And when it sets, drag it back so that it returns? Never. For this reason Allah said: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you light? Will you not then hear?﴾ [71] ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you a night in which you may rest? Will you not then see?﴾ [al-Qasas 71–72]. I say: the night and day which Allah made for the servants cannot be altered by anyone at all. Furthermore, when we look at this night and day, their alternation and the one entering into the other, it is another sign. Sometimes the night lengthens and sometimes the day lengthens. Who can do that except Allah, glorified and exalted?!

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rationale behind Allah's divine decrees is as established in the legislative rulings; that is, the cosmic rulings of Allah cannot but be for some wisdom. From where is this taken? ﴿li-taskunū﴾ (that you may rest), and the lam, I told you, is for causation. So Allah made that so that we may rest.

We have mentioned that Allah's cosmic rulings have reasons, like His legislative rulings. But does it follow that we must know the reason? It does not follow. If Allah opens to us what He opens of this, it is good and a bounty; and if we are deprived of it because of our sins, we are at fault. In any case, there is nothing without wisdom.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's favour, glorified and exalted, through the night and day, in that He made the night a place of rest and the day something to see by: ﴿that you may rest therein, and the day as something to see by﴾ [Ghafir 61]. Were it not for this, people would not rest. For this reason, you find that by nature a person loves rest when the night comes. Were it not that in our present age lights have spread and illumination has become widespread, and night has become like day, you would find a great pleasure in the night—and we experienced that: you find pleasure and love for rest, rest of the heart, rest of the body, rest of the soul. Then when dawn breaks, it is like fresh dates after dried dates; we rejoice in it, and when the day comes, the day comes. Now it is as if there were neither night nor day, and so we do not find the pleasure we used to know before. Perhaps some of you have experienced that. In any case, go out to the desert for a week and stay away from lights, and you will find this. In any event, this is from the favour of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who made for us the night for rest and the day for work.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah is full of bounty toward mankind in general. Do you take that?

* Student: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ [Ghafir 61].

* The Shaykh: ﴿toward mankind﴾, or toward the believers? In another verse: ﴿And Allah is full of bounty toward the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 152]. How do we reconcile generality and specificity? We say: bounty is of two kinds: general and specific. The general is for all people, and the specific is for the believers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that most of Allah's servants do not thank Allah, because of His saying: ﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against measuring the legislative rulings by the actions of people. That is, if we tell a person "this is forbidden," and he says "everyone does it," making the standard the actions of people—this is an error. That everyone does a thing is not a proof: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah﴾ [al-An'am 116]. The proof is in what Allah and His Messenger said: ﴿If you disagree over anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa' 59], whether the other group is more numerous than the one before it or the reverse. Therefore it is not permissible to make people's actions the standard for legislative rulings.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to thank Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and an indication that this thanks should be of the same kind as the bounty. Thanks should be of the same kind as the bounty. So what is the thanks of the person who has wealth?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: His thanks to his Lord—how?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: That he spends it in the way of Allah.
What is the thanks of knowledge?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Correct, and giving it out.
What is the thanks of one whom Allah has given courage and physical strength while jihad is ongoing?

* Student: That he strive in the way of Allah.

* The Shaykh: That he strive in the way of Allah. So thanks is of the same kind as the blessings, because Allah said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Ghafir 61]—the bounty.

* Among the second benefits of this noble verse: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ [Ghafir 62]: the affirmation of Allah's lordship over everything, that He is the Lord of everything, by His saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾.

* Among its benefits: an indication of the obligation to obey Him and worship Him, because of His saying: ﴿your Lord﴾. If He is the Lord, He is the Master; if He is the Lord, He is the one who holds authority; if He is the Lord, He is the one who has the right to be worshipped. Everything that establishes lordship is evidence for the obligation of divinity. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, argues against the polytheists by the fact that they affirm lordship and deny divinity; so whoever affirms lordship is bound to affirm divinity.

So the tawhid of lordship necessitates the tawhid of divinity, and the tawhid of divinity includes the tawhid of lordship, since no one can worship Allah without knowing that He is a Lord worthy of worship.

So if someone asks you: are the two forms of tawhid mutually entailing? Say: as for the tawhid of lordship, it necessitates the tawhid of divinity; and as for the tawhid of divinity, it includes the tawhid of lordship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's creation of everything, by His saying: ﴿the Creator of all things﴾ [Ghafir 62]. If someone says: "Reason excepted itself, so it is not a creator of itself"—is this statement valid?

* Student: No.

* The Shaykh: Why? Because it itself did not enter at all, since there is an agent and an object, and the agent cannot enter the object so as to be excepted from it. We say: the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, did not enter into His saying "all things" at all in this verse, because creation—or if you wish, say: because the created is separate from the Creator—so the Creator cannot enter into the created so that we say "reason is excepted." Exception is the removal of a thing from a thing, and here it did not enter at all.

I say: Allah is the Creator of all things. Is it appropriate to say: "and reason excepted itself, so it is not a creator of itself"?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: This verse: Allah is the Creator of all things. Do we say: except His essence?
We say: no. Why? Because the principle is that He did not enter at all into being the creator of all things; that is, He did not enter the created. He is the agent and others are the object, so He did not enter at all, so that we would say: exclude what reason can exclude in this domain.

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah Ghafir (40), verses 61–63 (Part 2 of 2):

The Jahmiyya and the Mu'tazila argued that the Speech of Allah is created, because the Speech of Allah is "a thing" and so falls under the general scope [of "Allah is the Creator of all things"]. We say: then it necessarily follows that you must also say that Allah is created, since Allah is "a thing." ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "Allah"﴾ [al-An'am 19]. So say also that Allah is created. If they say, "We cannot say that, because the agent (al-fa'il) is not the thing acted upon (al-maf'ul)," we reply: the attributes of the agent are like the agent itself. Attributes follow the essence (yuhdha bi-ha hadhw al-dhat). If the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is a Creator, and other than Him is created, then His attributes are also uncreated. The Qur'an is not created, because it is the Speech of Allah, and the Speech of Allah is among His attributes, and all of Allah's attributes are uncreated.

If someone says: creation is also affirmed for the servant. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿So blessed be Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun 14], thus affirming that there are [other] creators. And the Messenger ﷺ said about the makers of images: «Give life to what you have created»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5951) and Muslim (2108/97) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.]], thus affirming that they are creators.

The answer: the creation affirmed for the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, is not like the creation affirmed for the created. The creation of the created being means transforming a thing from one state to another, not bringing it into existence. When the carpenter makes a piece of wood into a door, does one say that he created the wood? He transformed it from wood into a door; he did not create it. Even if we say that his making is a "creation," it in reality means change and transformation, not bringing into existence. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, also challenged the idols that are worshipped besides Allah and that are claimed to be gods, saying: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gather together for it﴾ [al-Hajj 73].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the foundation of the Tawhid of worship (tawhid al-uluhiyya) being built upon the Tawhid of Lordship (tawhid al-rububiyya); for His statement afterward: ﴿Allah is your Lord, the Creator of all things﴾ ﴿there is no deity except Him﴾ [Ghafir 65], meaning: there is no one worshipped except Him, i.e., do not worship anyone but Him, as shown by His saying: ﴿there is no deity except Him﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the denunciation of amazement at those who have turned away from the truth despite its clarity and manifestness, as shown by His saying: ﴿How are they deluded?﴾ [Ghafir 62].
* Among the benefits of the third verse: that those who deny the signs of Allah produce things that are a cause for wonder, as shown by His saying: ﴿Thus are they deluded, those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir 63].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that sins come between a person and seeing the truth, because these people, when they denied the signs of Allah, were turned away from it. This is a reality: sins come between a person and seeing the truth. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients"﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 13]. Can anyone say that this great Qur'an is "tales of the ancients"? Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿No! Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 14], from evil deeds, until they saw this clear truth and made it into tales.

Therefore, we must treat ourselves if we find that we read the Qur'an as though it were mere letters recited, hoping for its blessing and reward. If it does not affect the heart with softness, humility and returning to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, then that is a sign of a sick heart, and perhaps we would say of a dead heart; we ask Allah for well-being. Likewise, "thus are they deluded, those who used to deny the signs of Allah." We ask Allah to make us and you among those who believe in His signs and follow what pleases Him.

* The student: Shaykh, does the word khalaqa occur in the Arabic language with the meaning of making/transforming?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. From it: ﴿You only worship besides Allah idols, and you invent a lie (takhluqun ifka)﴾ [al-'Ankabut 17], meaning: you say a falsehood.
* The student: Other than this in the Arabic language, so that we may confront them with it...
* The Shaykh: The Qur'an is in Arabic.
* A student: In schools they teach a principle: that matter is neither destroyed nor created from nothing. What is your view?
* The Shaykh: My view is that this is disbelief. Whoever believes the meaning of this is a disbeliever. Everything perishes except the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas 88]. The meaning of "perishing" (halik) is: subject to perishing, though Allah may make it everlasting, like Paradise and Hellfire. But He who brought it into existence is able to annihilate it, and annihilation is easier than bringing into existence. Their saying also, "it is not newly created," means that they have judged it to be eternal and everlasting. No believer says this, and this is in the schools!?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) A student was given in the examination: what is the ruling on cracking the knuckles during prayer? The student said: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "A section: it is disliked in prayer to turn one's head, to raise one's gaze toward the sky, to crack one's fingers, to interlace them, and to sit in iq'a..." until he mentioned the whole section, ten (...), then said: take what you want and leave what you want. You want us to go and read all the chemistry books so we can find that matter is neither created nor destroyed?
* A student: The disbelieving nations exploit the stillness of night and the vision of day more than the Muslim nation...
* The Shaykh: Amazing, how is that?
* The student: They sleep early, at nine o'clock they are asleep, and in the early morning, four or five, they are awake.
* The Shaykh: Subhan Allah, although this is the Shari'a: «The Prophet ﷺ used to dislike sleeping before 'Isha' and talking after it»[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (568) from Abu Barza, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to dislike sleeping before 'Isha' and talking after it.]]; because sleeping before 'Isha' may continue on, and because one rises for the 'Isha' prayer lazily; and because some people, if they sleep an hour or half an hour, sleep leaves them and they do not sleep the whole night. Three reasons. But why do they bring these televisions and keep them on until midnight or later? Or are they fooling us? Allah is the One sought for help.
* A student: They are fooling us.
* The Shaykh: They are fooling us. Allah is the One sought for help.
* The student: But we have heard, Shaykh, that when the sun sets they also close their shops at five or six.
* The Shaykh: Amazing! So after sunset, Allahu Akbar, is it not our time? I mean in America, in England, in France, and you are at two in the night.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: They are disbelievers and have no reward, but they are closer to the truth than us on this matter: early sleep is better.

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, says: ﴿Allah is the One who made the earth a resting place for you, and the sky a canopy, and fashioned you and made your forms good, and provided you with good things. That is Allah, your Lord. So blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds.﴾

The grammatical analysis: *(Allah)* is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *(alladhi)* is its predicate. The meaning is: Allah is the One who made the earth a resting place for you and the sky a structure, and so on. *Ja'ala lakum* ("made for you") is one of the verbs of transformation, meaning "He made for you." *(Qararan)* means "having stability," i.e., stable. *(As-sama' bina')* means "above you."

Allah has explained in another verse that the sky is a ceiling. So Allah made the earth a *qarar*, meaning stable.

Does this *qarar* mean that the earth does not move, or that it does not sway with us? It is said: the Qur'an explains itself. Allah says: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and rivers and roads﴾ [An-Nahl 15]. This shows that the meaning of *qarar* is that it does not shake with its inhabitants, i.e., it does not convulse. The meaning is not that it is absolutely immobile, as will come, Allah willing, in the benefits (*fawa'id*) section.

﴿And the sky a structure﴾ [Ghafir 64], meaning a high ceiling. The sky here refers to the heavens with their celestial bodies. This is because the word *sama'* (sky) has two meanings. The first is height, and the second is the ceiling-sky. What determines which meaning is intended is the context (*siyaq*).

Allah's saying: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their measure﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 17]: here *sama'* means height, because rain does not descend from the ceiling-sky itself but from the height. This is supported by His saying: ﴿and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah 164]. Here *sama'* means the ceiling-sky, and rain descends from the clouds. If the clouds are subjected between the sky and the earth, it follows that the rain does not descend from the ceiling-sky but from the sky in the sense of height. In our verse, ﴿and the sky a structure﴾, the intended meaning is the ceiling-sky.

﴿And fashioned you and made your forms good﴾ [Ghafir 64], meaning He gave you a particular form. *Surah* means shape. The shape of the human being is the finest and most excellent shape among created things. ﴿We created man in the best of stature﴾ [At-Tin 4]. There is no form more beautiful than the human form, and no shape better than his. Therefore He said: ﴿and made your forms good﴾.

﴿And provided you with good things﴾ [Ghafir 64]. In this verse Allah has mentioned four things: the earth, which is the place of dwelling; the sky, which is the place of shade; the fashioning, which is the human frame; and the provision for this frame, which is His saying ﴿and provided you with good things﴾. *Razaqakum* means He gave you. *At-tayyibat* here means what is good and pleasant.

Know that *at-tayyib* is sometimes intended to mean lawful, sometimes good, and sometimes pleasant. The context determines which. Allah's saying: ﴿that Allah may distinguish the bad from the good﴾ [Al-Anfal 37]: here *at-tayyib* means the good, and *al-khabith* means the inferior. His saying: ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 57]: here it means the lawful, because of His following saying: ﴿and give thanks to Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah 172]. For if it were said that it means the pleasant, then His saying ﴿and give thanks to Allah﴾ would have no meaning, since thanks can only be rendered when a person consumes something lawful. Here, His saying ﴿of the good things﴾ means what is good and pleasant. We say this because the provision of Allah, in the general sense, includes both lawful and unlawful things. Therefore we say: if a person acquires wealth unlawfully, for example through usury, he is undoubtedly provided for, but it is a provision that carries accountability.

﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ [Ghafir 64]. *Dhalikum Allah*: *dhalika* is a demonstrative pronoun serving as subject, and what follows is either an appositive or an adjective. *Rabb* is the predicate of the subject. The meaning is: the One who gave you these four things is Allah, and no one else. His saying *Rabbukum* means that He, may He be majestic and exalted, is the Lord of His servants, the Creator, the Owner, and the Governor. This is because *rabb* combines three attributes: creation, sovereignty, and management.

﴿So blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ghafir 64]. *Tabaraka*: it is said that its meaning is "exalted and magnified." This meaning is close, but *tabaraka* is more specific than that. Its meaning is that He possesses great and enduring blessing. For this reason it is not applied to anyone other than Allah in this sense, because this attribute befits none but Allah, may He be mighty and majestic. As for what some people say, as will come, Allah willing, in the benefits section, we will discuss it there. His saying *Rabb al-'alamin* ("Lord of the worlds"): *Rabb* here is an appositive or an adjective to the Divine Name (*lafz al-jalala*). *Al-'alamin* means everything other than Allah. All creation is *'alamin*, and they were so named because they are a sign (*'alam*) of their Creator. In all creation there is a sign of Allah, as it is said:

*And in everything there is a sign of His,*
*indicating that He is One.*

The lordship here is the general lordship, because He attributed it to *al-'alamin*, so it is general and comprehensive.

**Benefits of this verse:**

First: Allah, may He be exalted, is the Creator of the earth, by His saying ﴿who made the earth for you﴾ [Ghafir 64].

Another benefit: it is a blessing from Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, upon us that the earth is a place of stability, i.e., firm, not tilting.

Another benefit: the earth does not move, by His saying *qararan*. This is what some scholars have said. However, if we compare this verse with His saying: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you﴾ [An-Nahl 15], it becomes clear that using this verse as evidence that the earth does not move is open to question. So it is said: one benefit of this verse is that it is a blessing from Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, upon us that the earth does not sway or convulse with us. From this we understand the judgment regarding the disagreement among people today, between those who affirm and those who deny, as to whether the earth moves or not. It is well known among astronomers that it moves. For them, this is among the self-evident, certain matters that are not open to dispute. They say: the earth moves and rotates on its axis, a rotation by which night and day alternate, and it revolves around the sun, by which the seasons vary. They have no doubt about this and do not argue about it.

Some scholars have said: No, it does not rotate; rather it is still and stable, and the alternation of night and day occurs because the sun revolves around the earth, not because the earth revolves. What appears to me is that the Noble Qur'an contains nothing explicit stating that the earth rotates or does not rotate. And it is closer to the earth rotating than to it not rotating, because the negation of the more specific, in His saying ﴿lest it shake with you﴾, implies the existence of the more general. Just as we said regarding His saying: ﴿Vision does not grasp Him﴾ [Al-An'am 103]: this verse proves that the vision of Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, is established, because the negation of perceiving (*idrak*) indicates the establishment of the basic fact of vision. Likewise, the negation of shaking indicates the existence of the basic fact of movement.

But the crucial matter, in my view, is: does the sun revolve around the earth at sunrise and sunset, or not? We believe that it is the sun that revolves, and there is no objection to the earth also having a rotation and the sun having a revolution. There is no objection, because the apparent meanings of the Book and the Sunnah all indicate that it is the sun that rises, sets, inclines, declines, and turns aside, and similar expressions. Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And you see the sun when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it sets, passing them on the left﴾ [Al-Kahf 17]. These are four verbs, all attributed to the sun. The principle is that what is attributed to a thing is its action. Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, says in Surah Sad: ﴿I have preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord, until it [the sun] disappeared behind the veil﴾ [Sad 32]. And in Surah al-Kahf: ﴿until, when he reached the setting place of the sun﴾ [Al-Kahf 86], and ﴿when he reached the rising place of the sun﴾ [Al-Kahf 90]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Dharr when the sun had set: "Do you know where it went?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." [Narrated by al-Bukhari (3199), in whose wording this is, and Muslim (159), with their chains, from Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Dharr when the sun had set: "Do you know where it goes?" I said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It goes until it prostrates beneath the Throne, and it asks permission, and permission is granted. It is about to prostrate, and it will not be accepted from it. It asks permission and it is not granted. It is said to it: 'Return from where you came,' and it rises from its west. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾ [Ya-Sin 38]."]

All these actions are attributed to the sun itself. So how can we turn away from the apparent meaning of this wording to another meaning without a definitive proof that would constitute our argument before Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, for opposing the apparent sense of His speech? However, for one to whom the matter has become clear, and who sees it as a definite, certain, self-evident matter, as they say, then it is possible to interpret the verses such that the attribution of rising, setting, and going to the sun is according to what appears to the eye, not according to the reality. But up to now it has not become clear to me that the alternation of night and day occurs by the rotation of the earth; rather it occurs by the rotation of the sun. And Allah is capable of all things.

Another benefit of this noble verse: the sky is a built structure, by His saying: ﴿and the sky a structure﴾ [Ghafir 64]. And so it is. Allah says: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the sky? He built it﴾ [An-Nazi'at 27], and He says: ﴿And the sky We built with might﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 47]. So it is indeed made of celestial bodies, and there is no doubt about this. These bodies are protected, and it is not possible to enter them except with permission. This is evidenced by the fact that the best of human messengers, Muhammad (ﷺ), and the best of angelic messengers, Jibril, both did not enter the lowest heaven and what lies beyond it except after seeking permission. This indicates the perfection of its protection.

Another benefit of this noble verse: the favour of Allah upon us, the human beings, in that He fashioned our forms in this wondrous fashioning, which is the finest of forms. He said: ﴿He fashioned you and made your forms good﴾ [Ghafir 64].

Another benefit of this noble verse: the prohibition of making images (*taswir*). Can the prohibition of image-making be derived from it? How so?

**A student:** (...) attribution to Allah, may He be exalted.

**The Shaykh:** It can be derived from it. We say: whoever makes an image has contended with Allah in what is exclusive to Him, which is creation. For this reason it has come in a hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection it will be said to the image-makers: Give life to what you have created." This is the correct view: that image-making is forbidden, and indeed it is among the major sins, because the Prophet (ﷺ) cursed its doer. But there are three matters here:

The first matter: the sculpted image (*surah timthaliyyah*), meaning that a person creates from clay, wood, or iron something in the shape of a figure. There is no doubt about its prohibition. For this reason, in the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, narrated by Muslim, he said to Abu al-Hayyaj: "Shall I send you on the same mission the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me? Do not leave a raised grave without leveling it, nor a statue without defacing it." [Narrated by Muslim (969/93).] I know of no disagreement among the scholars regarding the prohibition of this.

The second: what is made by drawing (*bi-al-raqm*), meaning drawing by hand. This is a matter on which the earlier and later scholars differed. Some of them said it is not forbidden, based on the authentic hadith narrated by al-Bukhari: "except a drawing on cloth." This is a drawing on cloth, so it is not forbidden. Also, because this is not a three-dimensional object that would correspond to what Allah created; it is merely a shape. The image Allah created is a tangible, touchable physical body seen by the eye, whereas this is merely coloring, so it does not fall within the hadith. But the majority hold that it does fall within the hadith, based on the hadith of the cushion, the hadith of 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to his house and did not enter because of an image on a cushion that she had made for the Prophet (ﷺ). [Narrated by al-Bukhari (5961) and Muslim (2107/96), from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her): she bought a cushion with images on it. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw it, he stood at the door and did not enter. She recognized, or she recognized the displeasure in his face, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I repent to Allah and His Messenger; what have I done wrong?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What is the matter with this cushion?" She said: "I bought it for you, that you might sit on it and recline on it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The makers of these images will be punished, and it will be said to them: Give life to what you have created." Then he said: "The house in which there are images, the angels will not enter it."] This is the correct view: that drawing by hand is forbidden, falls under the curse, and it is not permissible for anyone to do it.

The third: what is made by capturing light, not by hand. This is what is known as photography, in which the person has no action at all. Rather, it is something that appears before a particular light and is imprinted, and the person has no action in it except moving the device that captures the image. This has been greatly disputed among later scholars, since it appeared only recently, so they disagreed about it. What appears to me is that it does not fall within image-making, because this was not created by hand as Allah created. It did not shape the eye, the nose, the mouth, the lip, or anything else. At most, this light was reflected onto the subject and it was imprinted. It is like looking into a mirror and seeing your image in it, except that the difference is that this one is fixed, whereas what is in the mirror disappears when it leaves. For this reason we call the image of one who looks into a mirror an "image," yet by agreement it does not fall within the prohibited image-making.

But there remains the question: why was this person photographed? Now it has been established for me that this image-making is permissible. But why was it made? We say: we apply to this what we apply to all permissible matters, namely that if it serves a legitimate purpose, it is permissible, and if it serves a forbidden purpose, it is forbidden. If a person took a picture of a foreign woman in order to enjoy looking at her whenever the opportunity arose, we would say: this is undoubtedly forbidden. If he wanted to photograph a great man in order to hang it in his house, we would say: this is forbidden. If he wanted to photograph his father, brother, uncle, or friend in order to find consolation in it during calamities, we would say: this is forbidden. So the ruling on this permissible act is the ruling of the purpose for which it was made. This is what appears to me regarding this issue. People are divided over it between the lax and the strict, and what appears to me, and Allah knows best, is this.

Another benefit of this noble verse: the favour of Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, in providing us with good things, by His saying: ﴿and provided you with good things﴾ [Ghafir 64]. We mentioned that the meaning of "good things" here is pleasant things, so that it includes general and specific provision. Know that provision is divided into two kinds: general provision and specific provision. The general: everything from which a person benefits is provision, as al-Saffarini, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Provision is what benefits, whether lawful or its opposite," meaning the unlawful. This is general provision, in which believer and disbeliever, righteous and wicked, one who earns lawfully and one who earns unlawfully, all share. All of this is provision. Accordingly, what is stolen is provision for the thief, but it is provision that will become a burden upon him in the Hereafter, even if he enjoys it in this world.

The second type of provision is the good and lawful provision (al-rizq al-tayyib al-halal). This is the specific provision, which is good and lawful, and it belongs only to the believer. On this basis, the disbeliever has no specific provision at all. Even if he earns it through something lawful, it is not a specific provision but falls under the general category, because of the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision? Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world, purely for them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-A'raf 32]. As for those who did not believe, these things are not theirs. For this reason we say: the disbeliever will be held accountable for every morsel he eats and every sip he drinks, and he will be called to account for it on the Day of Resurrection.

Indeed, it is dangerous for a believer to be held accountable for good things except under the conditions that Allah mentioned: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believed and did righteous deeds for what they ate, when they fear Allah and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good﴾ [al-Ma'idah 93]. These are heavy conditions for the lawfulness of provision even though it is good. We ask Allah to help us fulfil these conditions. So the disbeliever cannot have a specific provision at all; all provision, even if it is good, is general in relation to him, because he is held accountable for it. As for the believer, his provision is divided into specific and general. What he sinned in is of the general kind, and what he did not sin in is of the specific kind.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it shows that the lordship (rububiyyah) of Allah, mighty and majestic, is founded upon mercy. This is shown by His saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾, meaning: the One who gave you these four things. ﴿Allah is your Lord﴾. So the lordship of Allah, mighty and majestic, is founded upon mercy. What indicates this is His saying in Surat al-Fatihah: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Fatihah 2-3]. So His lordship, mighty and majestic, is founded upon mercy and compassion.

If someone says: this is refuted by what occurs in the life of this world of troubles that harm a person and may even injure him? We say: this is mercy. It is mercy for the believer. How so? Because it expiates sins: "No hardship, grief, or harm befalls a Muslim, but that Allah expiates some of his sins because of it, even the thorn that pricks him." [Reported by al-Bukhari (5640) and Muslim (2572), both through their two chains from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No calamity afflicts a Muslim but that Allah expiates some of his sins because of it, even the thorn that pricks him."] So it is mercy, because it expiates misdeeds. And if he seeks reward from Allah, mighty and majestic, it becomes good deeds, because hoping for the reward of Allah and seeking His recompense is a righteous deed for which a person is rewarded. This harm or injury that reaches the servant is a passing matter that goes away. Is that not so? For this reason, if you look back in your thinking, you will find that many harms and many injuries have passed over you and then disappeared as though they had never been. So the reward that was gained and the expiation of misdeeds that was achieved are better than this harm and these injuries, and thus it is mercy, and it does not fall outside the scope of mercy in lordship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it shows the greatness of Allah, mighty and majestic, in His saying: ﴿So blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ghafir 64]. Some scholars have deduced from this that the name of Allah, mighty and majestic, brings blessing, and they cited as evidence His saying (ﷺ): "Every matter of importance that does not begin with the name of Allah is cut off (abtar)." [Narrated by al-Khatib in al-Jami' (1210) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] This is not far-fetched, although there is some weakness in its wording.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of the lordship of Allah, mighty and majestic, by His saying: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾.
It follows from this that a person must strengthen his reliance upon Allah in bringing about benefits and repelling harms, because if He is the Lord of the worlds, mighty and majestic, then He controls all the worlds and has authority over all the worlds.
It also follows from this another matter: seeking refuge with Allah, mighty and majestic, when distress comes from the children of Adam or from other than the children of Adam, because He, glorified be He, is the Lord of the worlds, in whose hand is the affair. He is able to protect a person from a fierce attacking lion, even if a person is not able to do so by his own power alone, for Allah, exalted be He, may turn it away from him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it establishes the general lordship (rububiyyah 'ammah) by His saying: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. There is also a specific lordship and a more specific lordship. Both types were brought together in His saying, exalted be He, about the magicians of the family of Pharaoh: ﴿They said: We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ [al-A'raf 121-122]. So the general lordship of Allah encompasses the believer and the disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked. The specific lordship is for the believers. The lordship that is more specific is for the messengers and prophets, peace be upon them. By this we know that among the attributes of Allah, glorified be He, are some that are general, some that are specific, and some that are more specific.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: all created beings are signs of Allah, by His saying: ﴿the worlds﴾. We have said that they were so named because they are a sign (alam) pointing to their Creator, majestic is He. And Allah knows best.

* Student: O Shaykh, how do we reconcile his ﷺ statement that the sun prostrates every sunset beneath the Throne, then afterwards asks its Lord for permission to rise and is granted it, with what modern science has established, that the sun never sets at all? At every moment it is either rising over some people or setting over others, and in the northern hemisphere the sun does not set for six full months and is absent for six full months?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. We have mentioned the principle that matters of the unseen, which the senses do not perceive, are left upon their apparent meaning, and one does not ask, "How do we reconcile them?" Because this is a matter we do not perceive, so that we could reconcile it. So we say as the Messenger ﷺ said: that when it sets, it prostrates. The Messenger ﷺ did not say that it prostrates whenever it sets in any place. Its prostration may be when it sets from this face of the earth, the face on which the Two Sanctuaries are, as opposed to when it sets over another face. We do not know. So we say as the Messenger, peace be upon him, said, and we restrict the time by what the Messenger ﷺ restricted it to; that is, when it sets over Madinah, this occurs. This is possible and plausible, because the best part of the earth is this face on which the Masjid al-Haram, the Prophet's Mosque, and al-Masjid al-Aqsa are located.

* Student: O Shaykh, sometimes the suitor is unable to see his betrothed. Is it permissible for him to look at a picture of her?

* The Shaykh: It is part of the Sunnah for the suitor to look at his betrothed, under the known conditions that the scholars have set. Can a picture take the place of looking? It does not take the place of looking, and there is no benefit in it. First: because you often see a person's picture in a magazine or newspaper, and then when you see the man himself you find him different. This is something tested and observed. That is one point.

The second point: perhaps this woman, at the time the photograph is taken, is at her most beautiful or has been made up with makeup, kohl, and the like, so she is photographed in this state and given to the suitor. When he looks at her in reality, as they say, he finds otherwise. He finds that she has no eyes and no face, and then harm results. So what we see is that it is forbidden for the two betrothed to exchange pictures.

Furthermore, this picture may remain with the suitor or with the betrothed even after the engagement has been broken off, so he may enjoy looking at it whenever he wishes, and she may likewise enjoy looking at him whenever she wishes.

* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. You mentioned, regarding pictures, the capturing of light, meaning the camera that captures light and produces the picture immediately. Now there is a camera that does capture light in fact, and another process called retouching (al-rutush). In retouching, the photographer, with a pencil, alters parts of the picture as he wishes, meaning if he wants...

* The Shaykh: Beautification, you mean?

* The Student: Yes. What is your opinion, Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: It appears that this falls under the prohibition, because he is doing work on the form of the picture.

* Student: When people (...) it is not forbidden on the basis of blocking the means (sadd al-dhari'ah, closing the avenues that lead to harm). Now people use photography and other things, such as television, ninety-nine percent of the time for what is not permitted. So why not say it is forbidden by blocking the means, and permitted only out of necessity, like identity cards and the like?

* The Shaykh: We are speaking about photography as such, not about the photographer. The photographer and his intention: if his intention is bad, it is forbidden; if it is not bad, it is lawful.

* Student: Shaykh, some young children, who are not legally accountable, draw drawings of people. Do we say that this is forbidden for them just as it is forbidden for adults, according to the consistent rule?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. What is forbidden for adults is forbidden for children, but the child is not held accountable for it. Rather, his guardian is held accountable for it if he did not prevent him from it. Furthermore, there are things a person can amuse himself with other than pictures of living creatures: trees, mountains, stars, sun, rivers, buildings. That is possible. But it is a trial. That is, Satan has made the evil of deeds appealing to people; he commands them to make this doubtful thing, or the thing that is clearly forbidden with no doubt about it, and to turn away from something permissible. Now, among manufactured objects there are things that are beautiful, and a person enjoys looking at them even though they are made: a car, a pen, a watch, and other things. So why do we turn away from the permissible to something that is doubtful, or to something clearly forbidden with no doubt about it?!

Student: ﴿He is the Living; there is no god but He, so call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him. All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ (65) ﴿Say: "Indeed, I have been forbidden to worship those you invoke besides Allah, since clear proofs have come to me from my Lord, and I have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ [Ghafir 65, 66].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿He is the Living; there is no god but He﴾. ﴿He is the Living﴾ is a declarative sentence that conveys restriction (ḥaṣr, exclusive limitation). This restriction is a relative restriction (ḥaṣr idafi), because the intended meaning of "the Living" here is the Living with complete life, whereas mere life is found in Him and in others, as Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk 2]. As for complete life, it belongs to Allah, mighty and majestic.

﴿There is no god but He﴾: (lā) is the negation of the genus (lā al-nāfiyah lil-jins), and (lā al-nāfiyah lil-jins) is explicit in generality. (ilah) means (maʾlūh), i.e., one who is worshipped, because the pattern faʿāl comes in Arabic with the meaning of maf‘ūl, and it has many examples, such as ghirās (something planted), bināʾ (something built), firāsh (something spread), and similar words. Thus (ilah) means (maʾlūh).

What is the meaning of al-maʾlūh? It is that which hearts worship out of love and reverence; that is, one desires it and inclines toward it out of love for it and reverence for it. By love comes the performance of what is commanded, and by reverence comes the avoidance of what is forbidden.

As for His saying ﴿but He﴾: (illā) is a particle of restriction (adāt ḥaṣr), and restriction is the affirmation of a ruling for what is restricted and its negation for everything else. If that is the case, a difficulty remains: when you say "there is no god but He" and you affirm that this is a restriction, there arises in the heart, or is raised against it, the claim that there are other gods besides Allah according to the explicit text of the Qur'an, as Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿So their gods, which they invoked besides Allah, did not avail them﴾ [Hud 101], and Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ [al-Qasas 88].

The answer to this is to say: the predicate of (lā) is omitted, and its estimated form is "ḥaqq" (true); that is, "there is no true god except Allah." If this is the estimate, the difficulty we mentioned does not arise, because all the gods other than Allah are false, as Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Most Great﴾ [al-Hajj 62].

What we have established here, in this word, the word of sincerity (kalimat al-ikhlas), is what the soul is at ease with. Otherwise, the scholars have differed about it, both the scholars of Arabic and the scholars of tawhid, in several opinions reaching about six.

Among what has been mentioned is that the predicate is omitted and its estimate is "mawjūd" (existent): "there is no existent god except Allah." This is undoubtedly false, because if you say "there is no existent god except Allah," it would follow that the objects worshipped besides Allah are Allah, and that their worship is true and their divinity is true.

So the correct view is what the Qur'an indicates: that the predicate is omitted and its estimate is "ḥaqq," based on His saying: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾.

He says: ﴿so call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him, the religion﴾. The commentator said: (﴿call upon Him﴾: worship Him; ﴿sincere in devotion to Him, the religion﴾). This explanation is considered deficient, because the intended meaning of "calling upon" here is both the calling of worship, as the commentator said, and the calling of request (duʿāʾ al-masʾalah). The one who is called upon in the calling of request is Allah, and the one who is called upon in the calling of worship is Allah.

It seems that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, restricted it to worship because of His saying ﴿sincere in devotion to Him, the religion﴾, since (dīn) is action. But it is said: supplication is itself an action, and it necessarily requires sincerity. So the correct view is that His saying ﴿call upon Him﴾ means: worship Him and ask Him. It is thus both the calling of worship and the calling of request.

If someone says: the calling of request is clearly a supplication; you say, "O Lord, forgive me," or "O Lord, ease my affair and the affairs of our Muslim brothers," for example. This is clearly a calling of request. But how is worship a calling?

The answer: the worshipper calls upon Allah through the tongue of his state, because if you asked him, "Why did you worship Allah?" he would say, "I hope for His reward and fear His punishment." So he is one who calls upon Him through the tongue of his state.

﴿So call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him﴾: (mukhlisīn) is an active participle, and its verb is (akhlasa). The meaning of (akhlasa) is: he purified the thing from other than it; (akhlasahu) means he made it pure, without any admixture. So the meaning of (mukhlisīn) is: purifying the worship and the invocation for Him alone.

His saying ﴿the religion is for Him﴾: (dīn) is used in the Noble Qur'an with two meanings. The first meaning: action. The second meaning: recompense. From the first is His saying: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun 6]. From the second is His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Fatihah 4], because the Day of Resurrection has no action in it, so ﴿Master of the Day of Recompense﴾ means the Day of Judgment.

The intended meaning here, in ﴿sincere in devotion to Him, the religion﴾, is: is the meaning action or recompense? It is action: ﴿sincere in devotion to Him, the religion﴾ means: sincere to Him in your action, which is the invocation.

His saying (from polytheism) relates to ﴿sincere﴾; that is, purifying yourselves for Him from polytheism, such that there is no association in your action.

﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾: this is a sentence containing praise of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the generality of His lordship. (ḥamd) is a verbal noun from ḥamida, yaḥmadu, ḥamdan, and it is: describing the praised one with perfection in a manner of love and reverence.

Our saying "describing the praised one with perfection" excludes disparagement (qadḥ), because disparagement is describing the described with deficiency. Our saying "in a manner of love and reverence" excludes mere praise (madḥ), because bare praise may not be from love or reverence; it may be from fear. A man may praise an unjust ruler not out of love or reverence for him, but out of fear of him. As for ḥamd, it issues only from love and reverence.

His saying ﴿for Allah﴾: the lām here is for exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ) and for entitlement (istiḥqāq). It is for exclusivity because absolute praise is valid only for Allah alone, and for entitlement because the one truly entitled to praise is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. A created being may deserve praise, but not truly, because every good that comes to you from a created being, or every perfection in a created being, comes from Allah. So when a creature does good to me, or when I see in him attributes of perfection, I praise him, not because he is independent in that, but because he is the means. So the lām here in ﴿for Allah﴾ is what?

* Students: For entitlement and exclusivity.

* The Shaykh: For entitlement and exclusivity, good.

His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾: al-Rabb is the Creator, the Owner, the Governor. That is, the word "Lord" (rabb), when attributed to Allah or used to describe Him, includes three meanings: creation, ownership, and governance. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is the Creator of everything, the Owner of everything, and the Governor of everything. Even the polytheists acknowledge this: ﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth, or who owns hearing and sight, and who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and who manages the affair?" They will say, "Allah"﴾ [Yunus 31].

His saying ﴿the worlds﴾: the scholars said: "the world" (ʿālam) is everything other than Allah, and they were called ʿālam because they are a sign (ʿalam) pointing to their Creator, glory be to Him, since in each of these creatures there is a sign indicating the greatness, power of the Lord, and other things that the meanings of lordship require.

* In this noble verse there are benefits. Among them: the affirmation of absolute life for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying ﴿He is the Living﴾. The life of Allah, the Exalted, is complete in every respect: it is complete because no non-existence preceded it, complete because no extinction reaches it, complete because it includes all attributes of perfection, and complete because it is free of every attribute of deficiency. So its perfection is from how many aspects?

* Student: Four aspects.

* The Shaykh: Four. Count them.

* The student: From the aspect that it was not preceded by non-existence, from the aspect that extinction does not befall it, and from the aspect that it is complete..

* The Shaykh: Including all attributes of perfection. And the fourth aspect?

* Student: Free of deficiency.

* The Shaykh: Free of every deficiency, as Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿The Living, the Self-Subsisting. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ [al-Baqarah 255]. Notice that ﴿the Self-Subsisting; neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ is an attribute of perfection and a negation of deficiency.

If someone asks: is (al-Hayy) one of the intransitive names or the transitive names? It is one of the intransitive names. The scholars mentioned in the books of tawhid that if the names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are transitive, faith in them is not complete except through three matters: affirming them as a name of Allah, affirming the attributes they indicate, and affirming what follows from this attribute. As for when the name is intransitive, it includes two things: affirming that name for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and second, affirming only the attributes it indicates.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the negation of divinity from all that is other than Allah, by His saying ﴿there is no god but He﴾. You have known the meaning of divinity (ulūhiyyah): the servant's devotion (taʾalluh) to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, out of love and reverence.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of sincerity to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in worship and supplication, by His saying ﴿so call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him, the religion﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the perfection of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in His essence and in His bounty, by His saying ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. Allah praised Himself with this because of the perfection of His attributes.

* Among its benefits: the generality of the lordship of Allah, glory be to Him, over everything, by His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the one entitled to praise is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the one specifically owning absolute praise is Allah, glory be to Him and exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 66 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: Indeed I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides Allah﴾, to the end of the verse.

﴿Say﴾: The address is to the Prophet ﷺ. To whom is he addressed? He was commanded to address the polytheists, saying: ﴿Indeed I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides Allah﴾.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed I have been forbidden﴾, the sentence here is emphasized with *inna* (indeed), and ﴿have been forbidden﴾ (*nuhītu*) is a past verb in the passive voice, with the agent omitted because it is known. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and man was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa 28], where the agent is omitted because it is known, since no one disputes that the Creator is Allah. Here the matter is one of Sharia, a prohibition, and there is no dispute that the One who holds command and prohibition is Allah, just as He is the One who holds creation. Thus the one who forbids is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Prohibition (*nahy*) is the demand to refrain, in the form of superiority. This is the definition of prohibition in *usul al-fiqh* (the principles of jurisprudence). "Demand to refrain" excludes command and permissibility. "In the form of superiority" excludes supplication, such as ﴿Our Lord, do not hold us accountable﴾ [al-Baqarah 286], because we do not supplicate Allah from a position of superiority but from a position of humility, acknowledging our weakness before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. "In the form of the present tense preceded by the prohibitive *lā*" excludes expressions such as "Desist from such-and-such" or "Avoid such-and-such." These are prohibitions in the general sense but not in the technical sense; they are commands to avoid.

So if someone said to you: ﴿Avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj 30], would this be a prohibition against the abomination of the idols or a command to avoid it? We say: the second; it is a command to avoid it. But if you say: "Do not approach the abomination of the idols," it becomes a prohibition.

﴿I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides Allah﴾. ﴿To worship﴾ (*an a'bud*): worship (*ibadah*) is humbling oneself before the one worshipped, out of love and veneration.

As for His saying ﴿those whom you invoke besides Allah﴾, the commentator (al-Mufassir) said: "(those) you worship besides Allah." This also has some deficiency. The correct meaning is that ﴿invoke﴾ means: you worship and you ask, because among the polytheists are those who ask their idols and humble themselves to them through requests. So the verb is more general than what the commentator mentioned, may Allah have mercy on him.

﴿I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides Allah﴾, and His saying ﴿besides Allah﴾ means: other than Allah.

As for His saying ﴿when the clear proofs have come to me from my Lord﴾: ﴿when﴾ (*lammā*) is a temporal adverb meaning "when." In the Arabic language, *lammā* occurs in four ways:

The first: it means "when," as in this verse.

The second: it means "except," as in His saying: ﴿there is not a soul but that over it is a guardian﴾ [at-Tariq 4]. The meaning of ﴿but that over it is a guardian﴾ is: "except that over it is a guardian."

The third: it is a particle of jussive (*jazm*), as in His saying: ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad 8]; that is: "Rather, they have not tasted My punishment, but it is near."

The fourth: it is a particle indicating that one event occurs upon the occurrence of another, as in your saying: "When Zayd came, 'Amr came."

﴿When the clear proofs have come to me from my Lord﴾, that is: "when they came to me." ﴿The clear proofs﴾ (*al-bayyinat*) is an adjective of an omitted noun known from context, and the implied phrase is: "the clear signs." The commentator said: "(the proofs of Tawhid)." But the meaning is more general than what he, may Allah have mercy on him, said. Rather, these are the proofs of Tawhid, the proofs of Allah's power, the proofs of hearing and sight, and other things. The point is that clear proofs came to him from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

You see in the Noble Qur'an that the word *al-bayyinat* is always one whose noun is omitted, because it is known. What is known may be omitted, as Ibn Malik said in the *Alfiyya* (his versified grammar): "The omission of what is known is permissible." This is a general rule in everything, not only in the subject and predicate but in everything.

As for His saying ﴿from my Lord﴾, it is connected to ﴿came﴾; that is: it came to me from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But He mentioned it by the name of Lordship (*rububiyyah*), because this is a special Lordship by which Allah trains His prophets and messengers. ﴿And I have been commanded﴾ corresponds to ﴿I have been forbidden﴾: ﴿I have been forbidden to worship﴾ and ﴿I have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾. Who is the one who commands? Allah. Command (*amr*) is the demand to perform an act in the form of superiority, by the imperative (*if'al*) or by other expressions that indicate command.

As for His saying ﴿to submit﴾ (*an uslima*): *an* is a verbal particle (*masdariyyah*), and ﴿uslima﴾ is a present-tense verb in the subjunctive governed by it. The meaning of ﴿uslima﴾ is: I surrender to the Lord of the worlds. The submission meant here is legislated submission (*al-islam al-shar'i*), because it is what is within our capacity: we can do it or not do it, and it can only come from a believer. As for universal submission (*al-islam al-kawni*), it is not within our capacity, and we cannot repel it; it occurs from both the believer and the disbeliever.

Thus it becomes clear that submission has two meanings: the first is universal, decreed submission; the second is legislated, religious submission.

From the first is His saying: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah, while to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they will be returned?﴾ [Ali 'Imran 83]. Is submission here universal or legislated? It is universal, because He said ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾, and legislated submission cannot be by compulsion, nor is it general to everything. So submission here is universal and decreed.

Here, His saying ﴿to submit﴾ refers to legislated, religious submission; that is: ﴿that I submit﴾, meaning: that I surrender in worship and humility to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for His saying ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾, we say about it what we said about the similar preceding verse. But if someone asks: why did He not say "to submit to Allah"?

We say: so that this would be an indication of the reason for submission; that is, why did I submit? Because Allah is the Lord of the worlds, and the Lord of the worlds is most deserving to be submitted to and to be worshipped by Him, the Mighty and Majestic. So it serves as the evidence for the preceding ruling, which is submission.

* In this noble verse there are benefits:

* First: that the Prophet ﷺ is a servant who is commanded and forbidden, as is taken from ﴿to submit﴾.
* Following from this benefit: the invalidity of the claim of those who say that the Prophet ﷺ holds command and prohibition over the heavens and the earth, because he cannot be so while he is commanded and forbidden.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation of sincerity (*ikhlas*) to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying ﴿I have been forbidden to worship﴾ and ﴿I have been commanded to submit﴾. This is the reality of sincerity.
* Among its benefits: an allusion to the well-known principle that emptying (*takhliyah*) precedes adorning (*tahliyah*). This is not "the adorning of water"; *tahliyah* means decoration. Emptying precedes adorning. It is taken from ﴿I have been forbidden to worship﴾, which is emptying, and ﴿I have been commanded to submit﴾, which is adorning.
The reason emptying precedes adorning is that if adornment is placed upon an unclean place, it becomes deficient and soiled. So you first cleanse the place, then you adorn it second. Likewise the word of sincerity: "There is no god" is negation, and "but Allah" is affirmation. The first is emptying and the second is adorning.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the invalidity of worshipping other than Allah, because prohibition implies invalidity and corruption. Since we are forbidden to worship other than Allah, this indicates that it is invalid.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Prophet ﷺ, like others, needs knowledge, from His saying ﴿when the clear proofs have come to me from my Lord﴾.

But if someone says: there is a great difficulty here. How could the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, not have known the invalidity of these deities until the prohibition came to him, when the invalidity of these deities is embedded in natural disposition (*fitrah*) and intellect?

As for its being embedded in natural disposition, it is due to his saying ﷺ: "No child is born except upon the fitrah" [agreed upon: al-Bukhari (6599) and Muslim (2658/23), from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. The fitrah is the worship of Allah alone. As for intellect, Ibrahim, upon him be prayers and peace, argued for the invalidity of the deities by rational evidence when he said to his father: ﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees nor avails you at all?﴾ [Maryam 42].

We say: the Messenger ﷺ knew the invalidity of these deities, but he attributed this knowledge to the clear signs in order to establish prophethood. Thus prophethood confirms what natural disposition requires and what the intellect indicates.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that what the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, brought consists of clear signs with no obscurity, from His saying ﴿the clear proofs﴾.

It is remarkable that the polytheists used to come secretly to the house of the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, to listen to the Qur'an, because it captured their hearts and minds. Yet they, may Allah protect us, denied it out of arrogance and obstinacy.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against the obscuring of what the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, brought. That is: whoever does not see that what the Messenger brought contains clear signs should know that there is a veil over his heart, because a pure, clean heart must recognize that what the Messenger brought is truth, clear and evident. But sins may accumulate upon hearts so that they no longer recognize the truth. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Legends of the ancients." No! Rather, what they have been earning has rusted over their hearts﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 13-14]. So they came to see this noble Qur'an as legends of the ancients. We ask Allah not to blind our hearts and your hearts. The matter is serious: if you do not find your heart illuminated by this Qur'an, or in more general terms, by what the Messenger brought, then know that there is a disease in the heart. Treat the heart while the sickness is still in its early stage, so that the disease does not spread and destroy the heart, and you are no longer able to repair it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's care for His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, shown in affirming the special Lordship in His saying ﴿from my Lord﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation of submission to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying ﴿and I have been commanded to submit﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that the heart must always be in motion, either toward falsehood or toward truth, from His saying ﴿I have been forbidden﴾. This is emptying, and this emptiness must be filled with something, which is submission. Because whenever something has no replacement, the matter remains empty. So when the place is emptied of falsehood, it must be filled with truth.
Likewise, if you reflect, you will find that every falsehood, if it is not replaced by truth, leaves the matter empty, and a person wavers. When Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do not say "Ra'ina" [an ambiguous term]﴾ [al-Baqarah 104], what did He say? ﴿But say "Unzurna" [look at us]﴾. There must be speech. When falsehood is nullified, truth must replace it.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that other than Allah does not deserve to be submitted to, from His saying ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾. Whoever is the Lord of the worlds is most deserving of submission to Him, and none may be described as Lord of the worlds except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the general Lordship of Allah, from His saying ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: observing the appropriate attribute even if it departs from the more common expression, from His saying ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾, a departure from "to Allah," although "Allah" is the more common name. Yet considering the appropriate attribute is preferable. And Allah knows best.

* Student: We said that a command is not considered a prohibition in the technical sense. Does the rule (...) not apply to it?
* Shaykh: No, because a command to avoid also implies invalidity.

* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. How do we distinguish between intransitive and transitive names?
* Shaykh: Whatever extends to another is transitive, and whatever does not is not. If you say "Allah is the All-Hearing," it means there must be something heard. But "the Living" does not extend to another; He is living by Himself, great by Himself. Yes.
* Student: What about names that are intransitive, other than "the Living" and "the Great"?
* Shaykh: There are many: "the Majestic..."

* Student: May Allah reward you well, Shaykh. We distinguish between supplication of request and supplication of worship. Is not all supplication considered worship?
* Shaykh: Yes, but there is a difference between my standing to pray and my saying: "O Lord, forgive me." The second is an explicit request.
* Student: But both are supplication?
* Shaykh: We said this: why is worship called supplication? Because the worshipper seeks reward and salvation from punishment, so he is a supplicant by the tongue of his state. But explicit supplication is by the tongue of speech: "O Allah, forgive me and have mercy on me," and the like.
* Student: Both are called worship.
* Shaykh: Yes, but supplication is worship, because you worship Allah and humble yourself to Him by asking. Worship is well known, and all of it is also called a request (*masalah*), because the worshipper is a petitioner.

* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. Praise (*hamd*) is describing the praiseworthy with perfection in a manner of veneration and love. We said this is more eloquent than mere commendation (*mad*). In his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: "No one loves praise more than Allah" [agreed upon: al-Bukhari (5220) and Muslim (2760/35), from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him], commendation is not love and veneration as in its linguistic explanation. So how is this objection to be understood?
* Shaykh: The word "praise" here means *hamd*.
* Student: Shaykh, some explained ﴿there is no god but Him﴾, saying the implied meaning is "worthy," and that the word *ilah* in the Arabic language does not come for false deities, and its occurrence in the Qur'an is by way of accommodation to the opponent?
* Shaykh: That is wrong, this is not correct, because these polytheists worship these idols just as believers worship Allah, venerating them in their souls. Did you not hear Abu Sufyan's saying on the day of Uhud: "Exalt Hubal!"
* Student: As a matter of consonance (*mushakalah*)?
* Shaykh: Not at all, and there is no consonance. The original meaning is the literal one.

* Student: Shaykh, some of the early scholars regarded as good saying: "There is no god but Allah, sincere to Him in religion, even if the disbelievers dislike it."
* Shaykh: This is not correct; it is a commendation in the wrong place. The Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, used to say in the remembrances after prayer: "There is no god but Allah, and we worship none but Him, sincere to Him in religion" [Abu Dawud (1506) with his chain from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: The Prophet ﷺ, when he finished the prayer, would say: "There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things capable. There is no god but Allah. Sincere to Him in religion, even if the disbelievers dislike it. The People of blessing, grace and good praise. There is no god but Allah, sincere to Him in religion, even if the disbelievers dislike it."]. Is it "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds," or "even if the disbelievers dislike it"?
* Student: "Even if the disbelievers dislike it..."
* Shaykh: Fine.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, he never says that. We do not say it is legislated.

* Student: In the verse you mentioned that absolute life belongs to Allah and to others, then you cited His saying ﴿He created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk 2]. The citation here...
* Shaykh: The inference.
* Student: But is there not an omitted assumption: "and He created life"?
* Shaykh: Yes, He created life, and created life is the life of whom? The life of a creature. So absolute life belongs both to Allah and to the creature. I wanted to cite this verse instead of His saying ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾ [al-An'am 95], because that one is explicit that life is created, and created life can only be the life of a creature.

* Student: The prohibition (...) is in the present tense form. What about the past tense form?
* Shaykh: The particle *lā* cannot come with the past tense.
* Student: (*nuhītu*)?
* Shaykh: No, this is not the form of prohibition.
* Student: *Nuhītu* (...)?
* Shaykh: The particle *lā* is undoubtedly a prohibition. The general (*ma'nawi*) prohibition is different from the technical (*istilahi*) prohibition. ﴿Avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj 30]: is this a prohibition or not? It is not a prohibition in the technical sense.
* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes indeed. In terminology, *nahy* (prohibition) is a demand to refrain, issued from a position of superiority, in the form of the present tense preceded by the prohibitive *lā*.
* Student: (...).
