His saying: ﴿Aw natawaffayannaka﴾ is conjoined to ﴿nuriyannaka﴾, and it is the counterpart of His saying: ﴿Fa-imma nuriyannaka﴾; meaning: either you see the punishment before your death, or We take you and then punish them after they return to Us. This is more severe, for the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting. For this reason it has come in a hadith that when Allah, glorified and exalted, loves a person, He hastens his punishment in this world; he is punished in this world through his wealth, body, family, or community; otherwise He leaves him until he meets it on the Day of Resurrection. [[Al-Tirmidhi (2396) narrated from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When Allah wants good for His servant, He hastens his punishment in this world; and when Allah wants evil for His servant, He withholds from him for his sin until he meets it on the Day of Resurrection."]] We ask Allah to protect us and you from the punishment of this world and the Hereafter, and to grant us well-being.

﴿Aw natawaffayannaka fa-ilayna yurja'un﴾ (then We punish them with the most severe punishment; the response mentioned applies to the conjoined element only). Where is the conjoined element?
* A student: ﴿Aw natawaffayannaka﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Aw natawaffayannaka﴾ means: if We take you in death, then to Us they will be returned.

* In this noble verse: the obligation of patience, because Allah, the Exalted, commanded it in His saying: ﴿So be patient﴾, and the reason it is obligatory is that the original ruling for an imperative is obligation.

This question has been disputed among the jurists of legal theory (usuliyyun): is the original ruling of an imperative in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ obligation, or is the original ruling recommendation?

If we say the original ruling is obligation, then the commanded act is binding. If we say recommendation, the person has a choice: if he does it, it is good, and if he leaves it, there is nothing upon him. Do you understand, O brothers? This is in fact a matter of difficulty; in application it is a point of difficulty, and upon examination there is also room for consideration. Pay attention, for this is a matter of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that we study, because, as I told you before, we have guests who may not encounter this discussion.

I say: the jurists differed on whether the imperative is for obligation or recommendation, and the intended meaning is the bare imperative free of any indicator. As for what an indicator shows, the imperative in it is clear: if it indicates obligation, it is obligatory; if it indicates preference, it is recommended; if it indicates permissibility, it is permissible; and if it indicates threat, it is for threat: ﴿Do whatever you wish﴾ [Fussilat 40]. Does the meaning mean the person may do whatever he wishes, or is this a threat?
* Students: A threat.
* The Shaykh: Yes. ﴿Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf 29].

But the intended meaning here is the bare imperative free of every indicator: is it for obligation or for recommendation?

Among the scholars are those who said it is for obligation, and they have evidences.
Among them are those who said it is for recommendation, and they have evidences.

Those who say obligation argue with such a saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial strike them or a painful punishment strike them﴾ [al-Nur 63]. They said: this indicates a warning against whoever opposes the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so it indicates that the imperative is for obligation.

They also said: the Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "What I command you, do of it what you are able, and what I forbid you, avoid it." [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7288) and Muslim (1337/130), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him.]] This also indicates obligation, because he said: "Do what you are able," and such an expression is used for what is obligatory; "and what I forbid you, avoid it." Also, it is customarily repugnant for a master to tell his servant: do such-and-such, and then he opposes him. So opposing the command is repugnant, and what is repugnant is forbidden and disliked.

As for those who say the original ruling of an imperative is recommendation, they say: that it is commanded indicates the doing of it, and the default is the clearing of the dhimma (burden), so we do not hold a person sinful for leaving what he was commanded unless there is evidence; because the default is the clearing of the dhimma. Also, we have found many issues and many evidences in which the imperative, the scholars unanimously agreed, is for recommendation, and this weakens the view that the imperative is for obligation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 77 (part 2 of 2):

Some scholars took a middle position and said: if the command concerns worship ('ibadah), it denotes obligation (wujub); if it concerns etiquette (adab), it denotes recommendation (istihbab). This is closer to the truth than the absolute view that it always denotes obligation or the absolute view that it always denotes recommendation. In other words, this distinction is the closest of the views, yet it is not precisely governed by a fixed rule, for there are commands concerning etiquette that are in fact obligatory.

So in any case we say: the closest thing to be said on this question is that the basic principle regarding commands in worship is, what? Obligation, because we were created for worship and were commanded to perform it. And the basic principle regarding commands outside worship, such as etiquette for example, is recommendation. The same applies to prohibitions: whether they denote prohibition (tahrim) or disapproval (karahah).

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that the promise of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, has come to pass and is true, and it must happen; this is based on His words: ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾. This sentence is emphasized by what? The sentence here is emphasized by (inna), which indicates that the promise of Allah must come to pass.

Good. Is His threat likewise?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, even His threat is true and must come to pass, except that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may bestow pardon; otherwise the basic principle is that His threat will be realized. Have you understood now? It should not be said, as some people have said: the threat is not realized and is not true, while the promise is true. We say: all of it is true, but Allah, glorified and exalted is He, may pardon the threat, and pardon is generosity.

* And one of the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the speech of Allah, that Allah speaks. From where is this derived?

* A student: From His words: ﴿the promise of Allah﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿the promise of Allah﴾; because a promise is made by speech, and there is no doubt that Allah, exalted is He, speaks, and that there is no end to His words. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Say: Were the sea ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would surely be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted﴾ [al-Kahf 109]. ﴿The sea﴾ is a generic noun encompassing all seas. The sea would be exhausted before the words of Allah are exhausted. Glory be to Allah! Even if the seas were all ink with which to write, they would be exhausted before the words of Allah were exhausted. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if whatever trees upon the earth were pens and the sea [were ink], replenished thereafter by seven seas﴾, meaning: even if the trees upon the earth were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven more seas after it, meaning: were used as ink with which to write, what would be the result? ﴿The words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman 27]. This indicates the greatness of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, because He is the governor of the universe, and when He wills a matter, He says to it: "Be," and it is. And there is no limit to the will of Allah.

Good. Is the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, audible speech; that is, with a sound or without sound?

* The students: With a sound.

* The Shaykh: With a sound. The speech of Allah is with a sound, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mount and brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam 52], and there is no calling and intimate conversation except with a sound.

The sound is also explicitly mentioned in what is established from the Prophet ﷺ that Allah, exalted is He, says: "O Adam" on the Day of Resurrection, "and he says: Here I am at Your service and good fortune. Then He calls out with a voice: Indeed Allah commands you to bring forth from your progeny a group for the Fire. He says: O Lord, what is the group for the Fire?..."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3348) and Muslim (222 / 379), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him. The wording of al-Bukhari: "Allah says: O Adam. He says: Here I am at Your service and good fortune. Then he is called with a voice: Indeed Allah commands you to bring forth from your progeny a group for the Fire." In one narration: "fayunadi" with a kasra on the dal. See Fath al-Bari by Ibn Hajar (13 / 460).]] to the end. This is explicit that Allah speaks with a voice.

On this matter there are views, and we mention the three well-known ones:

- That He speaks with an audible voice and an uncreated letter, because it is His speech. This is the view of the Salaf and the leading scholars of the later generations: that Allah speaks with an audible voice and, what else? An uncreated letter. So the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is both its wording and its meaning.

- The second view: that Allah, exalted is He, speaks with an audible voice and a created letter, and the speech is His speech. This is the view of the Jahmiyyah, who say that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah but it is created, because all the speech of Allah, in their view, is created.

- The third: those who say that He does not speak with a voice or with a created letter; rather His speech is the meaning subsisting in His essence, but He creates something that expresses what is in His essence, which is heard and is attributed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as an attribution of honor and dignity. This is the view of the Ash'arites, who are the people of kalam (speculative theology), and who claim that they are the ones who defended Islam against the Mu'tazilah and championed Islam. In reality they did not champion Islam, nor did they break the enemies of Islam. Indeed, we may say that their view on speech is worse than the view of the Jahmiyyah. How so? Because they agree that what is heard of Allah's speech is created, and that the Qur'an is created. But the Jahmiyyah say: it is created and it is the speech of Allah. These say: it is created and is not the speech of Allah; rather it is an expression of it. Fine, then where is the speech of Allah? They said: the meaning subsisting in His essence.

In reality, the meaning subsisting in the self is not speech, but rather knowledge; He knew what speech He would create, and so they say: this is His speech. And what is strange is that they cited a verse and a poem; verse:

As for the verse, they said: Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And they say to themselves, "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?"﴾ [al-Mujadilah 8], so He affirmed inner speech.

As for the poem, they said: the poet said:

Indeed, speech lies within the heart, and the tongue was only made a sign upon the heart.

The heart (fu'ad) means the qalb.

We say to them: as for the verse, it provides no evidence for you; rather it is against you, for Allah did not leave speech unqualified, but restricted it, saying: ﴿and they say within themselves﴾. This is like the saying of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my nation what their souls whisper to them"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5269) and Muslim (127 / 201), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. Whispering of the soul cannot be called speech, nor can it be called utterance, except with a qualifier. Therefore, if "within themselves" were removed and it were said: "and they say, why does Allah not punish us," what would be understood? Speech with the tongue. But they, within themselves, make an assumption: one of them says: "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?" So what we say is true, because Allah has not punished us. This is what a person assumes within himself.

As for the poem: "Indeed speech lies within the heart..." it is the saying of al-Akhtal, the Christian poet, said after the tongues had changed. And even supposing it agrees with the view, it must be understood to mean: the speech that is regarded is what is first conceived in the heart and then the tongue utters. Hence, speech that slips out on the tongue is not regarded as speech and is not held to account, whereas real, weighty speech that is regarded is that which first exists in the heart and is then expressed by the tongue. This is the meaning of the line, which admits of no other.

So we will leave some benefits, God willing, for the next lesson.

* * *

* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah bless you, inner resentment of the heart is one of the most severe matters. Some say: this is something beyond my capacity; I hate it, but I find it in myself, and I resist it, yet I keep finding it and finding it.

* The Shaykh: There is a difference between hating what is decreed and hating the decree itself. Hating what is decreed is part of human nature; everyone dislikes being harmed. But hating the decree, this is what is meant: that you hate Allah's decree insofar as it is an act of Allah, and this may lead you to hate Allah, Mighty and Majestic, (we seek refuge in Allah), perhaps you come to hate Allah; you say: what kind of Lord is this?! How does He decree this upon me?! As for hating what is decreed, it is unavoidable; every person who is afflicted with what does not suit his nature will dislike that thing.

* The student: O Shaykh, this aversion occurs in the heart while a person outwardly dislikes it and resists it, yet he finds it in his heart.

* The Shaykh: No, I do not think so. No believing person conceives of hating what Allah has decreed insofar as it is a decree of Allah, never. Why would he hate it? Are you not owned by Allah?! How can you hate this thing?! Are you not slaughtering your camel to eat it? The camel dislikes this thing, but it is your property. So beware of hating Allah's decree insofar as it is a decree; as for insofar as it is something decreed, this is something, as I said, that is unavoidable.

* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, what is the difference between the two phrases when a person is afflicted with something disliked: one says "Qaddara Allah wa ma sha'a fa'al" and another says "Qadaru Allah wa ma sha'a fa'al"?

* The Shaykh: Both are permissible. (Qaddara Allahu) is a past-tense verb, and (Qadaru Allahi) is a predicate of an omitted subject, the meaning being: this is the decree of Allah.

* * *

* A student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And We have already sent messengers before you; among them are those We have related to you and among them are those We have not related to you. And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah. So when the command of Allah comes, it will be concluded in truth, and the falsifiers will lose everything at that time. (78) It is Allah who made for you the livestock that you may ride some of them and eat from them. (79) And for you in them are benefits, and that you may reach by them a need within your breasts; and upon them and upon the ships you are carried﴾ [Ghafir 78-80].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have already sent messengers before you; among them are those We have related to you and among them are those We have not related to you﴾.
﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ [Ghafir 77].

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: that the promise of Allah is true, established, and must come to pass, and it is so; Allah has stated this in His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ [Aal 'Imran 9].

* And one of the benefits of this noble verse: a warning to these deniers of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, with one of two matters: either a punishment in this world before he dies, or a punishment deferred to the Day of Resurrection; based on His words: ﴿So whether We show you part of what We promise them or We cause you to die, to Us they will be returned﴾ [Ghafir 77].

* And one of the benefits of this noble verse: that the return of all matters is to Allah, and they are not by the choice of anyone; He is the one who decrees what He wills, whether in this world or the Hereafter; based on His words: ﴿So whether We show you part of what We promise them or We cause you to die﴾.

* And among them: that the punishment of an enemy soothes the anger of one's enemy; based on His words: ﴿So whether We show you part of what We promise them﴾; for when a person sees Allah's punishment befall his enemy, there is no doubt that it soothes his rage.

* And among its benefits: there is no harm in our rejoicing when Allah afflicts our enemy with a calamity; because the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿So whether We show you part of what We promise them﴾ is so that his eye may be comforted by that. So if our enemies are struck by a landslide, lightning, floods, or the like, and we rejoice at this, there is no blame upon us; for they, our enemies, rejoice at what befalls us, and the recompense is of the same kind as the deed.

* And among them: the affirmation of the return of creation to Allah; based on His words: ﴿to Us they will be returned﴾, and this is general in everything: in all states and times and all things, the return is to Allah alone.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 78 (part 1 of 2):

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And We have certainly sent messengers before you; among them are those whom We have related to you, and among them are those whom We have not related to you.﴾ [Ghafir 78], to the end.

This sentence is emphasized with three emphatics: the lam, qad, and the implied oath. The implied meaning is: "By Allah, We have certainly sent messengers before you."

The messenger (rasul) is a human being to whom revelation of a law (shar') is sent and who is commanded to convey it. This is why he is called rasul, meaning one who is dispatched by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to convey. As for the prophet (nabi), he is a human being to whom revelation of a law is sent, but he is not charged with conveying it. In other words, he renews the law of the one before him if there was a messenger before him, so that he revives the aspirations of people and they follow him. If people do not need a messenger, no one is sent to them. Adam, peace be upon him, was a prophet and not a messenger. He was a prophet who worshipped Allah, the Exalted, by what Allah revealed to him, but he was not sent because people had not yet differed, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Mankind were one community; so Allah sent the prophets as bringers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth to judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah 213]. So the messengers were only sent after the differing. For this reason some scholars said: the implied meaning of the noble verse is: "Mankind were one community, then they differed, so Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings." And they said: there is an ellipsis (ijaz hadhf) in the verse; that is, what the context indicates has been omitted. In any case, who is the messenger? A human being to whom revelation of a law is sent and who is commanded to convey it. This is the messenger.

﴿And We have certainly sent messengers before you﴾. These messengers were sent only to their own peoples, as is established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Jabir: "Every prophet was sent only to his own people, but I have been sent to all people"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (438), and Muslim (521 / 3), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.]], and there is no nation in which a warner has not passed, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: every nation to which Allah sent a messenger, so that the proof might be established.

﴿Among them are those whom We have related to you, and among them are those whom We have not related to you﴾. The word (min) here is partitive: that is, some of them We have related to you and informed you about, and some of them We have not related to you.

The scholars said: Allah related to His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, only those who were from the Arabian Peninsula and its surroundings, because the reports of these people have a remnant among the Arabs; for this reason Allah related them. As for those who were in America, or in East Asia, or other similar distant places, nothing of their news has been related to us.

(﴿Among them are those whom We have related to you, and among them are those whom We have not related to you﴾ It is narrated that Allah sent eight thousand prophets: four thousand from the Children of Israel and four thousand from the rest of mankind.) It would have been fitting for the author, may Allah have mercy on him, to say "it is narrated" in the passive form, because this is not sound. How could there be four thousand from the Children of Israel, who came after many nations, and four thousand from the rest of mankind?! This is far-fetched; rather, Allah sent at every time and every era what establishes the proof.

Is it incumbent upon us to search for the number of these? No. And even if we say it is incumbent, it is not obligatory upon us; that is, if it were said to us that we should investigate for knowledge, it would not be correct to say that it is obligatory upon us to investigate. Rather, we say: we believe in Allah and in His messengers, those of them we know and those we do not know.

He said: (﴿And it was not for any messenger﴾ among them ﴿to bring a sign except by permission of Allah﴾ [Ghafir 78], because they are servants who are nurtured.)

His words ﴿وَمَا كَانَ﴾: ﴿ما﴾ is a negation particle, ﴿كَانَ﴾ is a past defective verb, ﴿لِرَسُولٍ﴾ is its predicate, and ﴿أَنْ يَأْتِيَ بِآيَةٍ﴾ is its subject; that is: "It was not the case that any of them brought a sign except by the permission of Allah."

﴿And it was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah﴾. It means that the messengers, peace be upon them, were given signs by Allah, but do they themselves possess this? No, it is from Allah. Allah, the Exalted, has made clear that there is no messenger except that he was given a sign; ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs﴾ [al-Hadid 25], meaning with clear signs, so that mankind may believe and so that they have no argument before Allah. For if Allah were to send a messenger to people in this manner and he said, "I am the messenger of Allah," without bringing a sign, the people would not accept from him; otherwise it would be possible for every liar to claim prophethood. But there must be clear signs, that is, evident ones, that he is a messenger; and even with this, it is not possible for a messenger to bring a sign except by Allah's permission.

As for His words ﴿except by permission of Allah﴾: this is the cosmic permission (idhn kawni). When Allah permits, cosmically, that the messenger bring a sign, he brings a sign. A messenger may bring a sign on his own initiative, and he may bring a sign at the request of those to whom he was sent; as in the authentic hadith that the Quraysh said to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace: "Show us a sign," so he pointed to the moon and it split into two halves, one on al-Safa and the other on al-Marwa, and the people witnessed it[[Muslim (2800 / 45) related from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The moon split in two during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; the mountain concealed one half, and one half remained above the mountain. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Allah, bear witness."]]. Yet even so: ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say: "Continuous magic"﴾ [al-Qamar 2]. They said: Muhammad has bewitched us, and the moon had not split. But since they did not specify the sign they requested, they were not punished, because when nations specify the sign they asked for and then do not believe, Allah hastens punishment upon them.

﴿And it was not for any messenger to bring a sign﴾ ("sign" — that is, a mark of his truthfulness) ﴿except by permission of Allah﴾. Here he said "sign" (aya) and did not say "miracle" (mu'jizah). Many scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, have commonly named the signs of the prophets "miracles," but this designation is not correct. Rather, it is better that we express it with what?

* The students: "with aya."
* The Shaykh: With aya. We say "the sign of the prophet," and we do not say "miracle."

First: because this is the Qur'anic expression.

Second: because a miracle (mu'jizah) comes from the messenger, and comes from the sorcerer, and comes from the devils; there comes from these what human beings cannot do. So the correct expression is to say "aya."

First: to agree with the Qur'an.

Second: because "miracle" applies to the messenger and to others.

Third: that the word "aya" indicates that what this messenger brought, which overwhelms mankind, is what? A sign, a mark.

So these are three matters that show the preference for expressing it as "aya" over "mu'jizah."

Expressing it as "al-aya" is better than expressing it as "al-mu'jizah" in how many respects? In three respects:

First: the Qur'an came with the expression "aya" and not "mu'jizah."

Second: a miracle may come from someone other than the prophet, from the sorcerer, the charlatan, and the devils.

Third: the intent is not merely inimitability (i'jaz); the intent is that it be a sign of the prophet's truthfulness.

The Mighty and Majestic said: (﴿So when the command of Allah comes﴾ — with the descent of punishment upon the disbelievers — ﴿it will be judged﴾ between the messengers and their deniers ﴿with truth, and there the falsifiers will lose﴾ [Ghafir 78]; that is, the judgment and the loss became manifest to the people, though they were already losers at every time before that.)

﴿When the command of Allah comes﴾: the cosmic command of Allah, because the command of Allah is divided into two types: cosmic and legislative, as we will mention, Allah willing.

﴿So when the command of Allah comes﴾: with what? With the descent of punishment upon the disbelievers, and the descent of victory for the messengers and their followers.

﴿It will be judged with truth﴾. The judge is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the agent is omitted here because it is known; for Allah, the Exalted, is the one who judges with truth, as He said: ﴿And Allah judges with truth, while those they invoke besides Him judge nothing﴾ [Ghafir 20]. The agent is sometimes omitted because it is known, as in His words: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [al-Nisa' 28], and as in this verse. It may be said that the agent is omitted here for generality, so that the judge is Allah; and likewise, those who judge with truth are the messengers and their followers, because they judged with truth by triumphing over their enemy. But the first is preferable: that the agent be one, but omitted because it is known.

﴿It will be judged with truth, and there the falsifiers will lose﴾ [Ghafir 78]. Here ﴿خَسِرَ﴾: loss is the failure of gain. ﴿هُنَا﴾ is a demonstrative noun of place, and what is meant by it is time; for this reason the author said "at every time." The meaning: the falsifiers lost at that time.

If someone says: Do you not say that ﴿هُنَا﴾ indicates place?

We say: Yes, but it may be used metaphorically to indicate time.

The lam in His words ﴿هُنَالِكَ﴾ is for distance, and the kaf is a particle of address.

﴿الْمُبْطِلُونَ﴾: that is, those who fell into falsehood, because judgment with truth requires the removal of falsehood, and when falsehood is removed its people lose.

Falsehood is the opposite of truth, and it is interpreted in every context according to that context. Falsehood in declarative speech is lying; falsehood in judgment is injustice; falsehood in transaction is deceit and the like. The point is that falsehood is interpreted in each context according to it.

The author's words "and they are losers at every time" are a safeguard against the implication in His words ﴿there﴾, lest someone think they are losers only at the time the punishment descends, while in fact they are losers at every time.

It may be said: there is no need for that; that is, there is no need for what the author said, because the intent of ﴿and there they lost﴾ is that their loss became manifest and clear. Before they are given the punishment, someone might say they gained, as Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud: "A day for a day of Badr, and war is a matter of turns"[[Related by al-Bukhari (3039) from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. He thought he had gained on that day.

So it is better to let the verse stand on its apparent meaning, and not to add to the Qur'an, saying: ﴿and there they lost﴾ means: their loss became manifest and clear. As for their loss before the punishment descends, it is not evident; for someone might say they will gain if Allah grants the disbelievers a temporary turn over the Muslims. We may not believe that Allah grants disbelief a lasting turn over Islam; whoever thinks this about Allah has thought an evil thought about Him. Rather, Allah says: ﴿Those are the days We alternate among the people﴾ [Al 'Imran 140].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse:
* First: the affirmation of the earlier messengers, from His words: ﴿And We have certainly sent messengers before you﴾.
* Among its benefits: the justice of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, toward His servants, since He did not punish them except after sending messengers and after these people to whom they were sent denied them.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that there is no messenger after Muhammad, from His words: ﴿And We have certainly sent messengers before you﴾, and He did not say "We will send." This benefit is, in reality, not that strong; that is, its derivation from the verse, were it not for the reality, would not be taken from the verses alone, because Allah speaks only of something past.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that among the messengers are those whom Allah related to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and among them are those He did not relate; from His words: ﴿Among them are those whom We have related to you, and among them are those whom We have not related to you﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, the Exalted, speaks; that is, the affirmation of the speech of Allah, from His words: ﴿among them are those whom We have related﴾. Qass originally means tracing a trail, and in speech it means mentioning the reports of those who passed. This indicates that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, speaks, and this is what the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations indicate.

But does He speak with an audible voice or not?

* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, He speaks with a voice that is heard.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's wisdom in His account of the earlier nations, since He divided those whose news was related to us from those not related; and this is only for a great and perfect wisdom.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the messengers, peace be upon them, were supported by Allah, the Exalted, with signs; from His words: ﴿And it was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah﴾.

* Among its benefits: that messengers do not possess the power to produce signs, however high their rank; they cannot bring even one sign; from His words: ﴿And it was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the consolation of the Messenger, peace be upon him, for the disbelievers ask him for signs, but Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And they say: "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Signs are only with Allah"﴾ [al-'Ankabut 50]. It consoles the Messenger, peace be upon him, that this matter is not up to you; it is up to Allah. If He wills to give you a sign, He gives it to you; otherwise He is the Wise.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's permission (idhn), and permission is of two kinds: legislative permission (idhn shar'i) and cosmic permission (idhn kawni). Cosmic permission relates to created beings and their bringing into existence, annihilation, alteration, and the like; legislative permission relates to what is legislated.

Consider His words: ﴿Say: "Did Allah permit you, or do you fabricate against Allah?"﴾ [Yunus 59]. This is legislative, and it cannot be cosmic, because we know that when they do it, Allah has permitted it.

And His words: ﴿Or do they have partners who have legislated for them in religion what Allah has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shura 21]. This is legislative. We mentioned the legislative in the first example; likewise here: ﴿they have legislated for them in religion what Allah has not permitted﴾, that is, He did not permit it legislatively, and it cannot be cosmic permission, because it occurred; Allah has permitted cosmically what those people legislated.

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 255].

* Students: Cosmic.
* Students: Legislative.
* A student: Cosmic and legislative.
* The Shaykh: How "cosmic and legislative"?
* The student: On the Day of Resurrection.
* The Shaykh: That does not contradict it; it is on the Day of Resurrection, but where is the legislation?! Intercession is sought from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He lighten the punishment for a person or the like, or raise his ranks; and this is undoubtedly cosmic permission.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of Allah's voluntary actions; that is, that Allah, the Exalted, may bring about what He wills by His command; from His words: ﴿So when the command of Allah comes﴾. And here "idha" is a conditional particle for the past, the future, or the present? Answer.

* Students: For the future.

* The Shaykh: For the future. So the command has not yet come. This indicates that Allah, glorified and exalted, is described by voluntary actions, contrary to the Ash'aris and their like who said that Allah, the Exalted, is not described by voluntary actions. How can He be described by voluntary actions?!

If we say He is described by them, they say this entails one of two matters: either that Allah is originated (hadith), or that He is deficient. As for the claim that it entails Allah being originated, it is because originated things subsist only in an originated thing; so if you affirm that originated things subsist in Him, it necessarily follows that Allah is originated, because originated things subsist only in an originated thing. This is one. As for deficiency, we say: if this act He is now doing is a perfection, why did He not have it before? If it is a perfection, why does it come into being after it was not? Why was He not described by it before? And if it is not a perfection, then it is a deficiency from which Allah must be exempted.

Do you understand? This is undoubtedly a deception. As for the first claim, that "events cannot occur except by an event," we say: from where did you get this? Is it from your pockets or from your corrupt opinions? Who said that events cannot occur except by an event?! Events among us now occur before they exist, and we precede them. Likewise, what Allah the Mighty and Majestic brings into being, He brings into being while He precedes it, and His precedence is eternal. So your claim is false, and it needs what? It needs evidence, and there is no evidence; rather, the evidence refutes it.

As for your statement: if it is a perfection, why was He not characterized by it before? And if it is not a perfection, then it is a deficiency, so it must be negated. We say: this too is false, because we say that the act of Allah which He brings into being is a perfection at the time of its bringing into being, and it is not a perfection at the time of its non-existence, because Allah the Exalted is characterized by perfection. In the state of its non-existence it is not a perfection, and in the state of its existence it is the perfection. This is clear. A human's act, and he is a human, is sometimes appropriate and in its place, and sometimes inappropriate, and wisdom requires that he not do it.

By this we know that returning to reason regarding what pertains to Allah is what? It is false and misguided, because reason may slip and may err. So returning, regarding what pertains to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, to the Book and the Sunnah is without a third. Except that it may be said: the consensus of the early generations (ijma' al-salaf, the scholarly consensus of the Companions and their successors) is also referred to, so the sources of acquiring knowledge in belief and in what pertains to the Essence of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, His Names and His Attributes, are three: the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations. But we say: there is no need to say "the consensus of the early generations," because the consensus of the early generations is only based on a Book or a Sunnah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the threat to these polytheists who denied the Messenger (ﷺ); due to His saying: ﴿So when the command of Allah comes, it will be judged in truth﴾. The aspect of the threat is that scholars of rhetoric (balagha) say that ﴿إِذَا (idhā)﴾ indicates the occurrence of the condition in the future, as when I say to you: "When Zayd comes, honour him." You understand from this that Zayd will come, but later. This is unlike (in, إنْ), which is conditional but for what is possible: "If Zayd comes, honour him." Is his coming certain?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: No, but if he comes, honour him; the coming is certain, but it is tied to a future time.
This: ﴿When the command of Allah comes﴾ indicates that the command of Allah must come.
The command of Allah is divided into two types: cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i). So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [An-Nisa' 58] — is it legislative or cosmic?
* The students: Legislative.
* The Shaykh: Why can it not be cosmic?
* A student: Because (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, because if it were cosmic, all people would render trusts to their owners; therefore it is legislative.
﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Aal 'Imran 47]?
* The students: Cosmic.
* The Shaykh: Cosmic. So the command now is cosmic and also legislative.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that what Allah the Exalted decrees of punishment or torment is true; due to His saying: ﴿it will be judged in truth﴾. Accordingly, it is negated that Allah the Exalted is unjust to whomever He punishes.

If someone says: Does not punishment descend upon a nation in which there are righteous people?

The answer: Yes, punishment descends upon a nation in which there are righteous people, but it is a punishment for the wrongdoer, and an elevation of ranks and expiation of sins for whom? For the righteous. For this reason, when one of the Mothers of the Believers said: "Will we be destroyed while there are righteous people among us? He said: 'Yes, when wickedness becomes abundant.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7135) and Muslim (2880/1), from the hadith of Zaynab bint Jahsh (may Allah be pleased with her).]] So when wickedness overcomes goodness, punishment befalls everyone.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the one who is in falsehood is a loser when punishment descends upon him; due to His saying: ﴿There the falsifiers will lose﴾.
And if the falsifier is a loser, then the reformer is a winner. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers﴾ [Hud 117]. So when the people are reformers, Allah does not destroy the nation; but if they are righteous, the nation may still be destroyed when wickedness becomes abundant. This is a point that many students may not notice: the absence of destruction occurs when? When the people are reformers and striving for reform. As for when they are merely righteous, destruction may occur when wickedness becomes abundant. But with reform, even if wickedness is abundant, so long as the nation tries to reform and strives for it, it will not be destroyed. This is a point, as I told you, that many people may not notice. We ask Allah to reform our conditions and your conditions.
* A student: We have said: it is from the justice of Allah the Mighty and Majestic that He will not punish the servants except after sending Messengers to them. In this verse, is there a criterion for excusing ignorance, for those who fall into falsehood while believing it to be correct: will they be excused for their ignorance in these days?
* The Shaykh: They may be excused for their ignorance, because among the common people there are those who know the truth only through specific individuals, and those individuals are deviant, so they are excused. And perhaps there are people in remote forests who hear no broadcasts, read no newspapers, and know nothing.
* A student: Some orientalists raised an objection to Allah's saying: ﴿And there has not been a nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24], claiming that there are intervals between the prophets, intervals (...) in which there is no prophet, the message ceased.
* The Shaykh: No, this is wrong, because when a warner comes, it does not mean that the warner remains a warner only as long as he is alive. His message may remain. Did not the message of Isma'il and Ibrahim (peace be upon them) remain among the Arabs until close to the sending of the Messenger (ﷺ)? The first polytheism entered the Arabs through 'Amr ibn Luhayy, which is a later development.
* The student: (...) Christians before the Messenger (ﷺ), before the sending of the Messenger there was an interval in which revelation nearly ceased, and the message nearly ceased.
* The Shaykh: That interval was for a wisdom, meaning the span between 'Isa and Muhammad (peace be upon them both) was for a wisdom: so that people would know how greatly they needed the message.
* A student: (...) The definition of a prophet is one who is commanded with revelation but not commanded to convey it. How do we reconcile this with the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "There was no prophet whom Allah sent except that it was incumbent upon him to make clear to his nation the good he knows, and to warn them against the evil he knows"?[[Recorded by Muslim (1844/46) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both), with the wording: "Indeed, there was no prophet before me except that it was incumbent upon him to guide his nation to the good he knows for them, and to warn them against the evil he knows for them..." the hadith.]]
* The Shaykh: This... the intended meaning of "prophet" is the Messenger; the intended meaning is the Messenger. For this reason you find in the Noble Qur'an prophets who are messengers, but they are mentioned with the term "prophets": ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Nuh and the prophets after him﴾ [An-Nisa' 163], then He said at the end: ﴿messengers as bearers of good news and warners﴾ [An-Nisa' 165], and ﴿Indeed, he was a truthful man, a prophet﴾ [Maryam 41].
* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah bless you, is it correct to apply the term "signs" (dala'il) to the signs of the prophets?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed; because the evidence (dalil) is what guides to something else. For this reason the man who shows you the way is called a guide (hadi). Thus the signs are undoubtedly evidence and clear proofs.
* A student: Is there a text stating that signs are called dala'il, like the miracles, O Shaykh? We said: they are not called... that we apply it to the signs of the prophets?
* The Shaykh: We say: the sign is evidence, and the language is synonymous; so long as the term is synonymous with the other and does not include a prohibition, there is no barrier to expressing it with it.
* A student: Is there evidence for the number of prophets and messengers?
* The Shaykh: There is the hadith of Abu Dharr that they were twenty-four thousand, of whom three hundred and some odd (fifteen) men were messengers, and the rest were prophets.[[Ahmad (22288) with his chain from Abu Dharr who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, how many were the prophets?" He said: "One hundred thousand and twenty-four thousand; the messengers among them were three hundred and fifteen, a great multitude." And the narration of Ibn Hibban in al-Sahih (361) with the wording: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, how many were the prophets?' He said: 'One hundred thousand and twenty thousand.'"]] But some scholars said that the hadith is not authentic, although Ibn Hibban authenticated it; Allah knows best. There is nothing upon which a person may rely in belief that their number is such and such, neither the prophets nor the messengers.
* A student: Is it, O Shaykh, the statement that every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet is a messenger?
* The Shaykh: Correct.
* A student: The criteria for the miracle (mu'jiza) and the karama (charisma).
* The Shaykh: We have the miracle, the karama, and sorcery (shi'wadha).
The miracle is the signs of the prophets, and as you have heard, we call them "ayah" (sign) and do not call them "mu'jiza."
The karama is every extraordinary matter that Allah the Exalted manifests at the hand of one who follows the Messenger. Not at the hand of the Messenger, but at the hand of a follower of the Messenger.
As for magic and sorcery, it is every extraordinary matter that appears at the hand of one who opposes the Messenger.
The Mu'tazila have denied the karamat and said: If we affirmed the karamat, the prophet would be confused with the saint (wali), and the saint with the sorcerer.
It is said: this is a sophism, because the prophet says that he is a prophet, and the one at whose hand the karama appeared says that he is a saint and not a prophet, and the sorcerer is neither a prophet nor a saint; he is known to be a wrongdoer opposing the Shari'a, so confusion is impossible.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿It is Allah who made the cattle for you, that you may ride some of them and eat some of them (79). And for you in them are benefits, and that you may attain by them a need in your breasts, and upon them and upon the ships you are carried﴾ [Ghafir 79–80].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: (﴿It is Allah who made the cattle for you﴾. It has been said: here it refers specifically to camels, but the apparent meaning is camels, cattle and sheep.)

﴿It is Allah who made the cattle for you﴾: ﴿made﴾ means He rendered them subjugated to you. The "making" here is a cosmic (kawni) making, because the making attributed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may be cosmic (kawn) or legislative (shar'), that is, it may be a cosmic making or a legislative making. In His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Allah did not institute any bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah or ham﴾ [al-Ma'idah 103], this making is legislative. In His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and We made you more numerous in manpower﴾ [al-Isra' 6], this is a cosmic making. In His saying here, ﴿It is Allah who made the cattle for you﴾, it is a cosmic making.

And ﴿al-an'am (the cattle)﴾ is the plural of na'am. The author, the commentator, said: (It has been said: here it refers specifically to camels, but the apparent meaning is camels, cattle and sheep.) Rather, the apparent meaning is broader than that: it is what Allah has bestowed upon us of animals that He subjected to us, of camels, cattle, sheep, elephants and others; everything.

And His saying: ﴿that you may ride some of them and eat some of them﴾. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, divided these cattle into two categories: a category that is ridden and a category that is eaten; that is, not ridden. Accordingly, (min) in both places is partitive (lil-tab'id), and the sign of partitive (min) is that the word (ba'd, some) can take its place. So here, remove (min) and say: (that you may ride some of them and some of them you eat), and the sentence is sound; this is the sign of partitive (min): that the word (ba'd) can take its place.

And His saying: ﴿and some of them you eat﴾: this division does not mean exclusive division; that is, it is possible that among the cattle there are animals that are both eaten and ridden, such as camels, for they are eaten and ridden.

(﴿that you may ride some of them and eat some of them (79). And for you in them are benefits﴾ from milk, offspring, fur and wool) meaning: and hair, and other benefits such as transporting goods and others. For this reason the word (manafi', benefits), the plural of manfa'ah, came in the form of the plural of ultimate plurals (sigha muntaha al-jumu'), and the form of the ultimate plurals is that which is on the pattern (mafa'il) or (mafa'il).

(﴿and that you may attain by them a need in your breasts﴾ is the carrying of loads to lands) ﴿and upon them and upon the ships you are carried﴾.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and that you may attain by them a need in your breasts﴾, the author explained it as carrying loads, but what appears is that it is other than that, and that it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home and when you send them out to pasture (6). And they carry your loads to a land﴾ [al-Nahl 6–7]; that is, what is in a person's heart of love of pride and vanity and other things. Although these needs may be blameworthy, like pride and vanity, there is no doubt that this is a need for every person: that he finds joy and delight when he acquires many livestock, of camels, cattle, sheep, gazelles, rabbits and others; a person finds a sweetness in his soul from this.

It may also be said: among the needs of the soul is trading in them, for some people trade in these cattle; and Allah, Glorified and Exalted, did not mention the type of need, so it includes everything that occurs in the heart of such matters.

﴿and that you may attain by them a need in your breasts, and upon them and upon the ships you are carried﴾ (﴿upon them﴾ on land, ﴿upon the ships﴾ the vessels at sea, ﴿you are carried﴾). Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explained that these cattle are those upon which we are carried, and likewise the ships, as in His saying: ﴿And He made for you of the ships and the cattle that which you ride (12), that you may settle upon their backs and then remember the favor of your Lord when you are settled on them and say, "Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it [by our own capability]. (13) And indeed, to our Lord we are returning"﴾ [al-Zukhruf 12–14].

* Among the benefits of this verse: the demonstration of Allah's favor upon us through these cattle, in that He made them subjugated and tractable for us.

* Among the lessons of this verse: the permissibility of riding them and eating them. It is well known that this is not absolute: whatever is ridden is not ridden in a way that burdens it. If a person wanted to ride an animal that cannot bear more than one person, and he made another ride behind him, we would say: this is not permitted, because of the hardship it causes. Likewise, ﴿of them you eat﴾ is not absolute, for among these cattle are some we do not eat, such as donkeys; they are not eaten, but they are carried upon and ridden.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the原 principle is the permissibility of every form of benefit taken from these cattle; ﴿and for you in them are benefits﴾. On this basis it is permissible to ride an animal that is not ordinarily ridden, provided it does not cause it hardship, because that is a benefit. If a person had a cow and needed to ride upon it, we would say to him: ride, for this is a benefit, and Allah, Exalted, made the benefits absolute so long as they do not burden the animal. If it burdens it, it is forbidden, for harming an animal is prohibited.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the permissibility of the joy and delight that arise in a servant's heart from these cattle, on condition that this does not lead to arrogance and vanity. As long as this joy remains within the scope of what is permissible, a person is not blamed for it; rather, it is among the things Allah has granted him.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's favor in carrying us upon these cattle and upon the ship; that is, Allah subjected to us what we ride on water and what we ride on land.

And here there is a third subjugation that occurred after the revelation of the Qur'an, namely what we are carried upon in the air. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has favored us with aerial, marine and land vehicles.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 81:

The Most High said: ﴿And He shows you His signs, so which of Allah's signs do you deny?﴾ [Ghafir 81]. ﴿He shows you﴾ means He manifests them to you so that you see them. On this basis, يُرِي (yurī) is from the quadriliteral (al-rubaʿi, a verb of four root letters) and not the triliteral (al-thulathi, a verb of three root letters), because it is from: أَرَى يُرِي (araa yuriy), meaning he made the thing appear until a person sees it.

His saying ﴿signs﴾ (āyātihi) is the plural of āyah, and the āyah is the sign of a thing, as the Most High said: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Yasin 41], and He said: ﴿Was it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel knew it?﴾ [al-Shuʿara 197], meaning a sign. So what is the sign?

The āyah is a sign of what is specific to it of attributes. For example, when rain falls and the earth brings forth growth, it is a sign of what? 

* Student: Of the mercy of Allah.

* Shaykh: Of the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. When the earth quakes with its people, or swallows them up, it is a sign of what?

* Student: Of the wrath of Allah.

* Shaykh: Of the wrath of Allah and His punishment, and of His power, since He shakes this great, mighty earth. So this is a sign of what is specific to it. Therefore the signs are signs of the attributes that are specific to them. We do not say that they are all a sign of one thing; rather, some of them are a sign of mercy, some a sign of might, some a sign of wisdom, some a sign of power, and so on.

So ﴿signs﴾ (āyātihi): we say it is the plural of āyah, and it is … what?

* Student: The sign.

* Shaykh: The sign, good. Do all these signs indicate one specific thing among the signs, or does each sign have what is specific to it?

* Student: Each sign has what is specific to it.

* Shaykh: Each sign has what is specific to it, may Allah bless you.

﴿So which of Allah's signs do you deny?﴾ The word ﴿which﴾ (ayya) here is interrogative and in the accusative case, being the fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam) of the verb ﴿you deny﴾ (tunkirūna). I ask you: if it were (tunkirūnahā) or (tunkirūnahu), would we put (ayy) in the accusative or the nominative?

* Student: In the nominative.

* Shaykh: In the nominative, though the accusative is permissible, because this falls under the construction of ishtighal (ishtighal, the construction in which a verb is occupied with a pronoun referring to a preceding noun). I will give you an example from my own speech, so that we do not alter the words of Allah. If you say (Zaydan akramtu, "Zayd I honored"), the accusative is required, as it is a fronted object. If you say (Zaydun akramtuhu, "Zayd, I honored him"), both cases are permissible, and the nominative is preferred because it is the basic form. The accusative here is by way of ishtighal. Accordingly, when a fronted object comes with a verb placed after it that has not fully exercised its governing, that preceding object must take the form required by that verb.

﴿So which of Allah's signs do you deny?﴾ (﴿Allah's signs﴾ indicating His oneness ﴿you deny﴾). That is, it would have been better if the author had said something more general, because (...) are not signs indicating oneness only, but indicate oneness and what is specific to that sign.

(﴿you deny﴾ is an interrogative of reproach and reminder.) (An interrogative of reproach) refers to His saying ﴿So which of Allah's signs do you deny?﴾, and it is also an interrogative of challenge. It combines reproach and challenge; meaning, these are manifest signs that you cannot deny.

He said: (And the masculine form of (ayy) is more common than its feminine), because it is said ayyatu and it is said ayyu. According to the author's statement, the masculine is more common than the feminine even if the referent is feminine. For this reason He said ﴿ayya āyāti Allāh﴾, and āyāt is feminine, and He did not say fa-ayyatu āyāti Allāh. However, outside the Qur'an, if one said fa-ayyatu āyāti Allāh, it would be permissible, though less preferred.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the favour of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, upon His servants by showing them the signs that point to Him. Had Allah willed, He would have hidden that from us and left us to what is in our souls and natural dispositions (fitar). But from His mercy He manifests the signs so that this becomes a help toward the knowledge of Allah's signs, Mighty and Majestic, that is in the natural disposition.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of challenging a person with what he would acknowledge were it not for his denial; from His saying ﴿So which of Allah's signs do you deny?﴾. Do you know of anyone who denied the signs while being certain of them? Who?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: And others.

* Student: Pharaoh.

* Shaykh: Yes, well done. Pharaoh and his people, for they denied the signs of Allah although their own souls were certain of them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 82–85 (part 1 of 3):

Then He said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than them and greater in strength﴾ [Ghafir 82], and so on to the end.

﴿Have they not travelled through the land﴾: this interrogative may be for urging, in which case it carries the sense of a command, i.e., "Travel through the land." What supports this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say: Travel through the land﴾ [al-An'am 11]. It may also be for rebuke, i.e., rebuking these people for not travelling through the land.

Travel here includes travel by foot and travel by the heart. As for travel by the heart, it returns to true reports, such that a person reads about the nations of the past. There is nothing more authentic than the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in speaking about the nations of the past, because of the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them, whom none knows except Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. There is nothing more authentic in reports than what the Noble Book has brought and what the Sunnah has confirmed. This is what we mean by travel of the heart.

Travel by foot is that a person walks to see what Allah the Exalted did to the deniers. An example of this is that a person travels to the dwellings of Thamud to see what Allah did to them. However, as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, it is not permissible to enter them except while weeping, for fear that what befell those deniers may befall him.[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2980 / 38) from Abdullah ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the companions at al-Hijr: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping. If you are not weeping, then do not enter upon them, lest there befall you what befell them."]] As for one who goes there for recreation and sightseeing, that is not permissible, as many people do today: they go there not for the sake of admonition and reflection, nor to enter while weeping, but merely to view the remains of the earlier peoples and for leisure. This is haram and not lawful.

As for His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of﴾, the grammatical analysis of the two clauses is that we say: (لم) is a particle of negation, jazm (apocopation) and qalb (conversion): a particle of negation because it negates, jazm because it jussifies, and qalb because it converts the present tense into the past.

The fa' in His saying ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا﴾ is undoubtedly a conjunctive fa', but is it conjoining to an implied omitted element or conjoining to what precedes it among the sentences? There are two opinions:
The first opinion: it conjoins to an omitted element estimated after the hamza, which is supplied according to what suits the context; on this view its placement after the hamza is natural.
The second: it conjoins to the preceding sentence, and accordingly the fa' here is displaced from its place, since its place would be before the hamza.
Both opinions are known to the scholars of grammar. On the first estimate, that it conjoins to an element estimated after the hamza, the meaning is: "Have they been heedless and so not travelled through the land?"

As for His saying ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾, the fa' conjoins to what?
* Student: To ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾.
* Shaykh: To ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾. On this view the meaning is: "Have they not travelled and so not looked?" It may also be that it is a fa' of causation, governing the subjunctive; i.e., their travel is negated, so they look, as you say: "You did not visit me, so I will honour you," and similar speech.

As for His saying ﴿كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ [Ghafir 82], ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is an interrogative noun, in the position of an accusative as a predicate of ﴿كَانَ﴾ placed first, and ﴿عَاقِبَةُ﴾ is its subject.
﴿عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾: what is the end? The end was mentioned by Allah the Exalted in Surah Muhammad in His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are similar things﴾ [Muhammad 10]. This is the benefit of looking: these deniers were stronger than these in strength, yet Allah the Mighty and Majestic destroyed them.
﴿كَانُوا أَكْثَرَ مِنْهُمْ﴾: i.e., in number. ﴿وَأَشَدَّ قُوَّةً﴾: i.e., in quality, so they were distinguished from them in number and quality. (﴿وَآثَارًا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾: from构 monuments and palaces.) ﴿فَمَا﴾..
On the first estimate, that it conjoins to an element estimated after the hamza, the meaning is: "Have they been heedless and so not travelled through the land?"

As for His saying ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾, the fa' conjoins to ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾, and on this view the meaning is: "Have they not travelled and so not looked?" It may also be a fa' of causation governing the subjunctive, i.e., their travel is negated, so they look, as you say: "You did not visit me, so I will honour you," and similar speech.

As for His saying ﴿كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ كَانُوا مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ [Ghafir 21], ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is an interrogative noun, in the position of an accusative as a predicate of ﴿كَانَ﴾ placed first, and ﴿عَاقِبَةُ﴾ is its subject. ﴿عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ كَانُوا مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾: what is the end? The end was mentioned by Allah the Exalted in Surah Muhammad in His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are similar things﴾ [Muhammad 10]. This is the benefit of looking: these deniers were stronger than these, yet Allah the Mighty and Majestic destroyed them. ﴿كَانُوا أَكْثَرَ مِنْهُمْ﴾: i.e., in number; ﴿وَأَشَدَّ قُوَّةً﴾: i.e., in quality, so they were distinguished from them in number and quality, ﴿وَآثَارًا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ [Ghafir 21]: from monuments and palaces.

﴿فَمَا أَغْنَى عَنْهُمْ مَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ [Ghafir 82]: ﴿مَا﴾ is a negation, ﴿أَغْنَى﴾ is a past-tense verb, and in ﴿مَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾, ﴿مَا﴾ is a relative pronoun serving as the subject, and ﴿كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ is the relative clause. It may also be that ﴿مَا﴾ is interrogative, and the meaning is: "What then availed them what they earned?" The interrogative is more forceful, since it carries negation together with challenge: what thing availed them their earnings when Allah destroyed them? Is that so?
* Student: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: What did you say about ﴿مَا﴾?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: You did not say "yes, yes"?! Fine. This neighbour of yours on the right, what do you say?
* Student: Relative.
* Shaykh: No, we did not say this; this is what you said.
* Student: That it is a negation ﴿مَا﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, well done, may Allah bless you. If it is a negation, the meaning is: "Their earnings did not avail them anything." If it is interrogative, the sense is: "What availed them what they used to earn?" A parallel to this is the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Have you considered, if We let them enjoy for years, then there comes to them what they were promised, what they were enjoying will not avail them﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 205–207], i.e., "What thing availed them?" or the meaning is the negation of availing.
* Student: The one who goes to the dwellings of Thamud for lesson but cannot weep, does he feign weeping?
* Shaykh: I do not know of it in a hadith, except: "If you do not weep, then feign weeping" [[Narrated by Ibn Majah (1337) from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him).]]. He said: "Do not enter them except while you are weeping" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2980/38) from the hadith of Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), and its wording: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the companions at al-Hijr: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping. If you are not weeping, then do not enter upon them, lest there befall you what befell them."]]. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by it, he covered his head, meaning he covered it, lowered it, and hastened.
* Student: So we say: weep or return?
* Shaykh: Yes, we say: either you weep or you return. If you are not weeping and you pass through the town, hasten and cover your head as the Messenger (peace be upon him) did.
* Student: Shaykh, on this basis we say that it is impermissible for one who photographs these sites and shows them to people and publishes them?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. The apparent ruling is that prohibition is closer, because he shows them only to demonstrate the strength of those people, not to demonstrate that Allah destroyed them despite their strength. This is the apparent intent of such photographers.
* Student: Does this include all ancient monuments or only those who were punished?
* Shaykh: We have read a verse that indicates the intended meaning: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are similar things﴾.
* Student: We said: if a person owns a cow, may he ride it? And in the hadith: "We were not created for this" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2324) with his chain from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "While a man was riding a cow, it turned to him and said: I was not created for this, I was created for ploughing..." the hadith.]]...?
* Shaykh: The way to reconcile these is that this cow was burdened with what it could not bear, or it would be hard for it to be ridden, since some animals not accustomed to riding find it difficult even when they are able to carry the rider.
* Student: Some people use these livestock in sorcery (...) and similar things?
* Shaykh: Without doubt, using these animals for what is forbidden, intentionally or in essence, is not permissible. Even if one rides these animals to reach a town where indecencies are committed or gambling is played, this is haram.
* Student: Some earlier peoples whom Allah destroyed outside their homelands, such as the Pharaohs, shall we say: we do not enter their monuments, just as we analogize with the dwellings of Thamud?
* Shaykh: No. On this basis we say: it is permissible for us to enter the place where Pharaoh was drowned, and it is permissible for us to enter Egypt as well, because Pharaoh was not destroyed in Egypt.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than them and greater in strength and in monuments in the land, but what they earned did not avail them. (82) When their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they exulted in what knowledge they had, and there encompassed them what they used to mock. (83) When they saw Our might, they said: We believe in Allah alone and disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him. (84) Their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might; this is the way of Allah which has passed among His servants, and there the disbelievers lost﴾ [Ghafir 82–85].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ We mentioned in this construction ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا﴾ and similar forms, two analyses?
* Student: The first analysis: we say that the hamza here is an interrogative hamza, and after it there is an implied clause, so this is from the category of conjoining clauses to implied clauses, and the estimate is according to the context.
* Shaykh: The omitted element is estimated according to what it implies.
* Student: And here its estimate: "Have they been heedless and so not travelled?"
* Shaykh: The second aspect?
* Student: The second aspect: the fa' is delayed from its place, the original being "fa-a-lam yasiru", and it conjoins to what came before.
* Shaykh: And the clause is conjoined to what came before.
The second is easier, since the first may be difficult or hard to estimate the omitted element; but this one is easy, containing merely the displacement of the fa' from its place.

As for His saying ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾: i.e., upon the earth, since ﴿فِي﴾ denotes enclosure. If we took ﴿فِي﴾ as enclosure in this context, the verse would mean they should enter into the inside of the earth, and this is definitely not intended. So ﴿فِي﴾ here means (على), like His saying: ﴿Are you secure from Him who is in the heaven?﴾ [al-Mulk 16], i.e., upon the heaven, and it is not meant that Allah is inside the heaven, for that is impossible, since His Throne has encompassed the heavens and the earth.

As for His saying ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ it includes travel by foot and travel by the heart. As for travel by foot, it is well known. As for travel by the heart, its meaning is that a person reflects on what passed of the history of nations, and the most authentic reference we return to regarding the histories of nations is the Noble Qur'an.

As for His saying ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾, this is conjoined to (يسيروا); meaning that Allah rebuked them for two matters: not travelling, and not looking. They did not travel and did not look: ﴿so that they might look at how was the end of those before them﴾. The looking here: is it the looking of insight or of sight? If we say that His saying ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾ is travel of foot, then the looking is sight; and if we say ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾ is travel of heart, then the looking is insight.

﴿كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾: we parsed ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ as a predicate placed first of ﴿كَانَ﴾, and here the placing first is necessary, since ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is an interrogative, and the interrogative has precedence; accordingly it is a predicate placed first of ﴿كَانَ﴾, and ﴿عَاقِبَةُ﴾ is its subject: ﴿the end of those before them﴾, i.e., of the nations. What is the end? Allah indicated it in Surah Muhammad in His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are similar things﴾.

Then Allah explained the condition of those earlier peoples, saying: ﴿They were more numerous than them and greater in strength and in monuments in the land﴾ [Ghafir 82]: more numerous than them in number, and abundance of number necessitates strength in quantity; and greater in strength is strength in quality. Then He said: ﴿and monuments in the land﴾, i.e., of buildings, palaces and others, and despite that this multitude did not benefit them, nor this strength. He says: (from monuments and palaces) is an explanation of His saying ﴿وَآثَارًا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾.

﴿فَمَا أَغْنَى عَنْهُمْ مَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾: ﴿مَا أَغْنَى﴾: ﴿ما﴾ may be a negation, i.e., "what they earned did not avail them"; and it may be interrogative, and the meaning is: "What then availed them?" The interrogative here is more forceful, since it is imbued with challenge: what thing availed them? The answer: nothing. ﴿فَمَا أَغْنَى عَنْهُمْ مَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾, i.e., what they used to earn of strength, monuments in the land and other things, because Allah the Exalted destroyed them and destroyed their strength.

﴿فَلَمَّا جَاءَتْهُمْ رُسُلُهُمْ بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ﴾: this which comes after mention of their destruction is in fact a return to explaining what occurred. Allah sent to them messengers with clear proofs, and sent down books; but when their messengers came to them with the clear proofs, the author said: (the manifest miracles). The correct wording would be: the clear signs. He, may Allah have mercy on him, rendered al-bayyinat as meaning al-zahirat (the manifest), which is true, and made (al-bayyinat) an adjective of an omitted noun whose estimate is: the miracles; and this is open to scrutiny. Rather, one should estimate: the signs (āyāt). This is because the word "miracles" (mu'jizat) does not occur in the Book and the Sunnah in place of āyāt at all; furthermore, miracles may come from messengers and from non-messengers, for sorcerers, for example, are brought miracles by the devils. But āyāt, i.e., the signs indicating their truthfulness, are more eloquent; therefore, when you find in books, and you find it often, "the miracles" or "the miracle of the prophets" or similar, then set it aside entirely and say instead "the signs," as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said, "the signs." And āyāt, as I told you, is more precise than the word "miracles," since "miracles" includes what overwhelms humans among what the devils produce together with sorcerers and others.

(﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ أي الكفار ﴿بِمَا عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ أي: الرسل ﴿مِنَ الْعِلْمِ﴾ فرح استهزاء وضحك منكرين له) ﴿فَلَمَّا جَاءَتْهُمْ رُسُلُهُمْ بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ فَرِحُوا﴾ The *wāw* (واو) is the subject (fā'il). Who is the one rejoicing? The author says: "(i.e., the disbelievers)." This is correct: the disbelievers rejoiced at what they had of knowledge. As for His words ﴿بِمَا عِنْدَهُمْ﴾, the pronoun returns to the messengers, according to the author's interpretation: "at what the messengers had of knowledge," meaning what they brought of clear proofs. But is this rejoicing the rejoicing of good tidings (istibshar) or the rejoicing of mockery? The author says it is the rejoicing of mockery, laughter and derision.

However, if you reflect on this interpretation, you will find it to be a *taḥrīf* (distortion) rather than an interpretation, because of its semantic and linguistic problems. As for the linguistic problem, it causes a scattering of pronouns: the *wāw* in ﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ refers to the disbelievers, while the *hā'* in ﴿بِمَا عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refers to the messengers. This is a scattering of pronouns. If we keep the speech in one continuous structure, there is no doubt that the *hā'* refers to the disbelievers, meaning "at what the disbelievers had of knowledge."

As for the semantic problem, rejoicing (*farah*) originally means joy at good tidings. If we turn it away from its apparent meaning to be rejoicing of mockery, this removes the meaning from what the apparent wording indicates. In summary, this interpretation that the author mentioned is very weak, indeed it is a distortion. The correct meaning is: the disbelievers rejoiced at what they had, that is, at what the disbelievers had of knowledge, and they said: "We are more knowledgeable about what benefits us, and what benefits our worldly life and our religion, which we follow. As for you, O messengers, you are sorcerers or madmen," as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Thus, no messenger came to those before them except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman!"﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 52]. If they believed in their hearts, or said with their tongues what they did not believe, that the messengers were sorcerers or madmen, then undoubtedly they would consider what they had of knowledge to be the true knowledge, and so they would rejoice in it.

Based on this, we say: the rejoicing here is the rejoicing of arrogance (*baṭar*) and of assumed good tidings, that they possessed a knowledge superior to the knowledge of the prophets, peace be upon them. ﴿They rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾ [Ghafir 83]. It may amaze a person sometimes what some scholars adopt in explaining verses or hadiths.

Now, if you recited this verse to a common person: ﴿So when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾, upon what does the pronoun in ﴿بِمَا عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refer for this layman? To the disbelievers: they rejoiced in what they had, and a person rejoices in what he has, not in what others have.

﴿And there befell them what they used to mock﴾ [Ghafir 83]. ﴿حَاقَ﴾ (ḥāqa): the author says it means "descended" (nazala). However, it is not exactly like "nazala" in every respect, because "nazala" can be used for good and for evil. ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 193-194]. Is this good or evil? Good. But "ḥāqa" is only used for evil. One does not say "ḥāqa bihi al-Qur'an" or "ḥāqa 'alayhi al-Qur'an" as one says "nazala 'alayhi." So "ḥāqa" here means "nazala," but it is only used for the descent of evil. It is evil for the one upon whom it descends, though it may be good for others.

﴿وَحَاقَ بِهِمْ مَا كَانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ [Ghafir 83]: ﴿مَا﴾ is the subject (fā'il) of ﴿حَاقَ﴾. ﴿كَانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ means: previously. That is, when the might of Allah the Mighty and Majestic came to them and descended upon them, ﴿there befell them what they used to mock﴾ previously, when they used to mock the messengers, what they brought, and the laws, and perhaps even mock Allah the Mighty and Majestic.
