Consider the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Was it Allah and His verses and His messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ [At-Tawbah 65]. This shows that the disbelievers mock Allah, mock His verses, and mock the messengers.

(﴿وَحَاقَ بِهِمْ مَا كَانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ i.e., the punishment) meaning: the punishment they used to mock befell them, when the messengers threatened them with it. They began mocking, saying: "What is the punishment you speak of? Where is it?" They asked in mockery.

﴿فَلَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا﴾ [Ghafir 84] i.e., the severity of Our punishment. ﴿رَأَوْا﴾ means with their eyes, that is, they saw it with the sight of the eye. And *ba's* (بأس) is the most severe punishment.

﴿قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ وَحْدَهُ وَكَفَرْنَا بِمَا كُنَّا بِهِ مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [Ghafir 84]: ﴿قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ وَحْدَهُ﴾ i.e., apart from our associates and apart from what we used to worship. This is the utmost sincerity. Then they affirmed this with their saying: ﴿وَكَفَرْنَا بِمَا كُنَّا بِهِ مُشْرِكِينَ﴾. ﴿بِمَا﴾: the *bā'* (باء) is a preposition governing ﴿كَفَرْنَا﴾. And ﴿بِهِ﴾ may be causal, meaning "because of what we used to associate," or it may be connected to ﴿مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ as the preposition connected to its governing word. The meaning: when they saw the punishment of Allah, they believed. But would this faith benefit them? No.

When Pharaoh drowned and drowning overtook him, what did he say?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: He said: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel have believed﴾.
* Shaykh: Correct. He said: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel have believed﴾ [Yunus 90]. But what was said to him? It was said to him: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾ [Yunus 91]. So his faith did not benefit him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And repentance is not [accepted] from those who continue to do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have now repented"﴾ [An-Nisa' 18]. Repentance does not benefit this person, because he saw and witnessed. He witnessed what was no longer unseen, which he would have disbelieved in. Faith based on witnessing does not benefit, because every person believes in what he sees, even if he is the greatest of disbelievers. What a person is praised for, and what saves him from the punishment of Allah, is that he believes in the unseen, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ [Al-Baqarah 3].

﴿They said, "We have believed in Allah alone and disbelieved in what we used to associate with Him."﴾ [Ghafir 84]. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So their faith was not of benefit to them when they saw Our punishment﴾ [Ghafir 85]. ﴿لَمْ يَكُ﴾: its original form is *lam yakun*, but the *nūn* was deleted for lightness. Deletion and retention have occurred in two verses of the Book of Allah. Allah the Exalted said concerning Abraham: ﴿and he was not among the polytheists﴾, and He said: ﴿and he was not among the polytheists﴾ [An-Nahl 120]. It is one sentence in which the *nūn* was deleted and also retained. This deletion is for lightness, and it has well-known conditions in the books of grammar.

﴿فَلَمْ يَكُ يَنْفَعُهُمْ إِيمَانُهُمْ لَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا﴾ [Ghafir 85] (*īmān*, إيمانُ): do you parse it as the postponed noun of *yakun*, or as the subject of *yanfa'u* with the implied pronoun as its subject? The second. The estimation according to this: "so their faith did not benefit them." According to the first, it would be: "so it did not benefit them, their faith," and then the subject of *yakun* would be an omitted pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n).

And His words ﴿لَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا﴾: ﴿لَمَّا﴾ here is an adverb meaning "when" (ḥīn). Know that *lammā* (لَمَّا) comes in the Arabic language in several ways:

First: that it is a temporal adverb meaning "when," as in this verse. The meaning of ﴿لَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا﴾ is "when they saw Our punishment."

It also comes as a jussive particle (jāzima), like His saying: ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad 8].

It comes as a conditional particle, like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 89].

It comes with the meaning of "except" (illā), as in His saying: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾ [At-Tariq 4], and likewise His saying: ﴿And indeed, all of them will be brought before Us [for judgment]﴾ [Ya-Sin 32].

So these are four meanings of *lammā*. The first meaning: "when," as in this verse: ﴿So their faith was not of benefit to them when they saw Our punishment﴾ [Ghafir 85], meaning when they saw Our punishment. The second: with the meaning of "except." Like?

* Student: ﴿And indeed, all of them will be brought before Us [for judgment]﴾.
* Shaykh: Another verse?
* Student: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾.
* Shaykh: The conditional one, like?
* Student: ﴿So when they saw Our punishment, they said, "We have believed in Allah alone"﴾ [Ghafir 84].
* Shaykh: ﴿So when they saw Our punishment, they said, "We have believed in Allah alone"﴾. Correct. And likewise: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾. It comes as a jussive particle. What is its example? ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾. It is also for negation: jussive and negating. However, the difference between it and *lam* is that *lammā* indicates the nearness of what follows it: ﴿they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾, but they will taste it soon. Unlike *lam*, which comes for absolute negation.

﴿لَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا﴾. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is the way of Allah which has already occurred among His servants﴾ [Ghafir 85]. ﴿سُنَّتَ﴾ (sunnata): the commentator says: "its being in the accusative is as an infinitive (maṣdar) with a verb implied from its own root." *Sunnah* (سُنَّة) means a way or practice: this is the way of Allah.

And ﴿سُنَّتَ﴾ in such a construction may be nominative, meaning "the sunnah of Allah," as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "this is the sunnah of Allah." It may also be accusative. The author says it is accusative by a verb implied from its own root, meaning: Allah established His sunnah with them.

﴿سُنَّتَ اللَّهِ﴾ may also be an infinitive whose governing verb is omitted but implied from the preceding sentence, because this expression has exactly the same meaning as what precedes it, that is, ﴿the sunnah of Allah﴾ means what precedes it, namely the seizing of the deniers with punishment. So it is accusative by the content of the sentence, not by an implied verb. What the author, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned is undoubtedly a valid aspect. The important point is that *sunnah* means "way." So what is the way of Allah? The way of Allah, the Exalted, is the destruction and punishment of the deniers, and that if they believe after the punishment descends, it will not benefit them.

(﴿الَّتِي قَدْ خَلَتْ فِي عِبَادِهِ﴾ [Al-Fath 23]: among the nations, that faith does not benefit them at the time the punishment descends.) This is one point. The second is that He punishes the deniers. So the sunnah we derive from this verse is two things: first, the destruction of the deniers, and second, that their faith does not benefit them when they see the punishment.

He said: ﴿And there the disbelievers will lose﴾ [Ghafir 85]. The author explained ﴿خَسِرَ﴾ to mean: "their loss became evident to everyone, although they were losers at every time before that." ﴿وَخَسِرَ هُنَالِكَ الْكَافِرُونَ﴾. It is known that *hunālika* (هنالك) is an adverb of place or time? Place. This is the original usage: it is a demonstrative pointing to a place. It may be used as a demonstrative for time. You say: *hunāka* meaning "at that time," and this verse is an example. Now, if you say "so-and-so is there (hunāka)," this is a place adverb, and this is the original usage. If you say, for example, "so-and-so's arrival was then (hunāka)," pointing to a time, it has become a demonstrative for time, but this is contrary to the original usage.

It remains to be said: the disbelievers lost at that time. Were the disbelievers not losers at all times? Indeed they were, but their loss became apparent and clear, because before the punishment descended upon them they thought they were winning. This is why they rejoiced in what knowledge they had. But when the punishment befell them, their loss became manifest.

* From the benefits of these verses: encouraging reflection on the conditions of earlier nations. This is derived from: ﴿Have they not traveled through the land and observed how was the end of those before them?﴾ [Ghafir 82]. The point of evidence: Allah rebuked them for not traveling.

* Another benefit: travel through the land with the feet, if not accompanied by contemplation and taking lessons, does not benefit. This is from His saying: ﴿Have they not traveled [in the land] so they might have hearts by which to reason and ears by which to hear?﴾ ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾ (then look).

* Related to this: what many people do today of traveling to the dwellings of Thamud, where they travel with their bodies but not with their hearts, and do not take lessons, but go there to see the glories and the traces of the people that show their strength. This is not permissible. Whoever travels to those dwellings must enter them weeping, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "If you are not weeping, then do not enter them." Feigned weeping does not help, because of his saying: "If you are not weeping, then do not enter them." He did not say: "then weep." So whoever has not prepared himself with this quality, which the Prophet ﷺ permitted for entering the dwellings of Thamud, it is not permissible for him to enter. Most people who go there now go only for sightseeing and recreation, and this is forbidden.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: some nations are stronger and have greater monuments than what Quraysh had, because of His saying: ﴿They were more numerous than them and greater in strength and in traces left upon the earth﴾ [Ghafir 82].

* From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah the Exalted is not overcome by the strength of the enemy nor by the enemy's multitude, for Allah the Exalted destroyed them despite their numbers and strength.

Does Allah the Mighty and Majestic, when He wills to destroy them, make their destruction extend over a period of time until He finishes them? No. Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them one shout, and they became like the dry, broken branches of a fence builder﴾ [Al-Qamar 31]. ﴿الْمُحْتَظِرِ﴾ means one who surrounds his land with a *ḥiẓār* (fence), and the *ḥiẓār*, as you know, is made of light sticks or palm fronds, and the sun and wind quickly consume it.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: a person's strength and the multitude of his numbers do not avail him anything against the punishment of Allah, because of Allah's saying: ﴿So what they used to earn did not avail them﴾ [Al-Hijr 84].

* From the benefits of these verses: Allah, glorified and exalted, sent the messengers with clear signs that demonstrate His truthfulness.

* Two or more benefits follow from this: the mercy of Allah toward His servants, and the wisdom of Allah in His actions.

As for Allah's mercy toward His servants: if Allah had sent them messengers without signs, that would have been a burden beyond their capacity, because a person cannot believe in a messenger without signs that show his truthfulness. Otherwise every liar could claim to be a messenger.

As for the wisdom: it is clear that when Allah, glorified and exalted, sent the messengers, He did not leave them without means, but gave them what humankind could believe in on its like, as our Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and his family, informed: "Allah did not send a messenger except that He gave him what humankind could believe in on its like." What the Messenger, peace be upon him, was given was the revelation, the Qur'an. This is why he said: "So I hope to be the one with the most followers on the Day of Resurrection," because the Qur'an is a sign remaining until the Day of Resurrection, or until Allah permits the corruption of the world. As for the signs of the messengers, most of them end within their own time, but the sign of the Messenger remains.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the signs of the messengers are clear and do not admit doubt, because of His saying: "clear" (*bayyināt*).

* It follows from this: the scholar who spreads the law of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, should, when he spreads it among people, do so in a clear manner with no ambiguity. Why? First: to follow the example of the messengers. Second: so that the listener gains more tranquility, because tranquility has an effect on accepting what is presented and on acting upon it. If the truth is not made clear to a person in a way that brings tranquility, you will find him walking or taking the truth while hesitant. But if tranquility is increased, he benefits from that. Is that not so, brother? What did you say?

* Student: The Prophet must have followers?
* Shaykh: The Prophet? No, I did not say that. Did I say this?
* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: The Messenger said: "And the Prophet, and with him no one."

* The Student: Shaykh, may God bless you. We said that destruction happens once. Isn't this a matter of the nations' differences? With 'Ad, God the Exalted sent upon them a furious wind (rih sarsar) in days of misfortune (ayyam nahsat). Or was the wind sent upon them and it destroyed them, and then it continued upon them?

* The Shaykh: No. With 'Ad, God the Exalted prolonged the punishment for them, because they would say: "Who is stronger than us in power?" So God sent upon them the wind, which was the lightest and gentlest of things, and it destroyed them.

* The Student: Little by little?

* The Shaykh: He says: ﴿He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days, consecutively, so you would see the people in it fallen down as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Haqqah 7]. During this period, some of them may have perished on the first day, some on the second day, according to what shelters they had or did not have.

* The Student: Is this an exception to the punishment?

* The Shaykh: No, because He sent the punishment upon them in this form.

* The Student: But did we notice the benefit, or not?

* The Shaykh: No (...), because this is the basic principle. And it is said: even though this lasted, from the moment the punishment began, whoever was to perish perished.

* The Student: What was reported from the Imam (...) said: (...). Could it be said that they had instruments with which they made these things? Now, with the existence of these instruments, it is not possible for a person..

* The Shaykh: It may imply instruments, or it may imply that, because of their numbers, each one took up a task and performed it, and you know that when a person becomes accustomed to a specific work, even if it is arduous, it becomes easy for him.

* The Student: At the end of the surah He said: ﴿And the disbelievers were lost therein﴾ [Ghafir 85]. Is it permissible to change, meaning (...)?

* The Shaykh: The benefit of this is to clarify that every disbeliever is a falsifier (mubtil), having no truth with him, and every falsifier says nothing but falsehood is a disbeliever; that is, the falsifier in all his states is a disbeliever; meaning he has none of the truth with him, and the disbeliever is a falsifier who likewise has none of the truth with him. So the variation in expression is for increasing the meaning.
Just as it also occurs sometimes in the variant readings (qira'at), such as the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their people﴾ [al-Nur 27]. In another reading: "tasta'dhinu" (you seek permission). ﴿If a deviator comes to you with news, verify it﴾ [al-Hujurat 6]; in one reading: ﴿fa-tathabbatu﴾ (so be steadfast in verifying); so this reading explains the second reading.

* The Student: In the orthography of the Qur'an, ﴿sunnata Allah﴾ [Ghafir 85], the ﴿sunnata﴾ has an open ta'. In Surat al-Dukhan it has the ta' marbuta (ta' of feminine). What is the reason for this?

* The Shaykh: Have you understood his question? He says: the ta' in ﴿sunnata﴾ is open, and the rule is that it is marbuta, because it is for the singular. It is said that the Uthmanic script is not according to the well-known rules now; rather it is tawqifi (fixed by revelation/transmission). The scholars, may God have mercy on them, differed on whether the Qur'an must be written in the Uthmanic script, or not required, or whether one should distinguish between teaching young or older students, in three opinions:
The first opinion: it is not permissible to write the Qur'an except in the Uthmanic script in every case, even if you are teaching children. So in the Uthmanic script you write: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers a decree of specified times﴾ [al-Nisa' 103], you write (al-salwa) with a waw, even if you are teaching a child, following the script. ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾ [al-Baqarah 43]: al-salat with a waw and (al-zakwa) with a waw, because this is the Uthmanic script.
Some said: rather it is not required, because when the Uthmanic script was set in the mushaf, it happened to be in this form; and if the Uthmanic script had been not according to this rule, it would have been written according to the rule that was current at that time. So the matter is not tawqifi, but it happened that the script at that time was in this form, so the Qur'an was written upon it. This is because the Qur'an was not revealed in writing so that we would say it must be as it was written; rather it was revealed to be recited, and the rules of orthography vary from place to place. This opinion has a strong basis, because we know with certainty that if the orthographic rule had been otherwise in that era, it would have been written according to the well-known rule of that era.
The third opinion says: if the Qur'an is written for children to learn, write it according to the rule known among them; and if it is for adults, meaning one writes a mushaf for himself, then he should write it according to the Uthmanic script. This combines the two opinions, because if you write the Qur'an for a child according to the Uthmanic script, you would cause him to distort it, because the rules before him differ from the script, so he distorts it, reading for example: al-zakat - al-zakwa, al-salat - al-salwa, al-riba - al-ribw, and so on, clear.
So I incline to the view that there is no harm in writing according to the prevailing rule for the learner, without doubt; for others there is some allowance, but the view of prohibition is open to question.
* * *
* The Student: I seek refuge with God from the accursed Satan. In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate: ﴿Ha Mim. A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. A Book whose verses have been detailed, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know. Bearing good tidings and warning, yet most of them turn away, so they do not hear﴾ [Fussilat 1-4].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with God from the accursed Satan.
* Among the benefits of this verse, ﴿When their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾: the clarification of the wisdom and mercy of God, the Mighty and Majestic, since He made the signs that the messengers brought clear signs, so that no proof remains.
* Among its benefits: that the disbelievers boast of the knowledge they have, even if it is falsehood; as He says: ﴿They rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾ [Ghafir 83]. What existed previously exists now as well: some of those people to whom God gave worldly knowledge, you find them rejoicing in it, saying: it is better than the knowledge of those who seclude themselves, meaning the scholars of the Shari'ah.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strong warning against rejecting what the messengers brought; as He says: ﴿And there befell them what they used to mock﴾ [Ghafir 83].
Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir 84], to the end.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that those people who denied the messengers, when they see the punishment, say: "We believe." The example of this is Pharaoh, when drowning overtook him, he said: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾ [Yunus 90].
* Among its benefits: that those who believe after the punishment has descended upon them gain nothing from their faith; as He says: ﴿But their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir 85].
Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the sunnah of God, the Mighty and Majestic, regarding His servants is one; He does not show favoritism to anyone for wealth, poverty, or anything else; rather the most honored of creation before God is the most righteous; as He says: ﴿the sunnah of God that has passed among His servants﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the warning against denying the messengers, and that whoever denies the messengers will be overtaken by what overtook them of punishment, that is, what overtook the earlier nations of punishment.
* Among its benefits also: the manifestation of loss for these deniers before they die; as He says: ﴿and the disbelievers were lost therein﴾, that is: when the might came upon them, the loss became clear to them. ﴿And the disbelievers were lost therein﴾.
Then the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, to the end. The basmalah has been discussed at length before, and we explained that it is a verse of God's Book, but it is not a verse belonging to the surah after it or the one before it; rather it is a verse brought at the beginning of surahs, except Surat Bara'ah.
As for its meaning, a person says: I begin with every name of God. We made the meaning "with every name of God" because "ism" (name) is a singular construct (mufrad mudaf), and a singular construct gives generality. Every singular construct added to a definite noun gives generality. Have you not considered the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿And if you were to count the favor of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ [al-Nahl 18]? ﴿Ni'mata Allah﴾: if we looked at its wording we would say it is singular, but it is many and cannot be counted. So this singular that is added becomes general; this is the rule: every singular construct added to a definite noun gives generality; for this reason we said: "with every name of God."
And (al-Rahman al-Rahim) are two attributes of the Name Allah. But the first takes into account the description, and the second takes into account the act, which is the conveying of mercy. As for the object of this prepositional phrase, it is omitted, and it is estimated as a suitable delayed verb for the context. So if you want to read and say: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," estimate "I read" (aqra'). This was chosen, meaning it was chosen that it be a verb, because the original in action is verbs; for this reason the verb acts without condition, while nouns that act like verbs require conditions, as is known in the science of grammar. We chose that it be delayed for two benefits:
The first benefit: seeking blessing by mentioning the name of God.
The second benefit: the intention of restriction (hasr), because when the operator is delayed, that is a restriction. If you say "Zaydan akrim" (Zayd, honor!), the meaning is: do not honor other than him; but if you say "akrim Zaydan" (honor Zayd), it does not prevent honoring others. So we delayed it for two benefits: the first: seeking blessing by mentioning God, the Mighty and Majestic. And the second?
* Student: Restriction.
* The Shaykh: Conveying restriction. We estimated it as suitable because it makes the intended meaning clearer. If someone said: "In the name of God I begin," we would say: correct, but it does not make the intended meaning as clear as "In the name of God I read," because beginning can be for reading or for other than reading; for this reason it was chosen to suit the context. The summary now: the object of the prepositional phrase is omitted, a verb, delayed, suitable to the context.
God the Exalted said: ﴿Ha Mim﴾, and the commentator said: "God knows best what He means by it." This is the etiquette with the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ: that about what you do not know the meaning of, say: God knows best what He means by it; as God the Exalted says: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of those will be questioned﴾ [al-Isra' 36].
But someone may say: we know that these disjointed letters found in many surahs have no meaning; we know this from the Qur'an's indication, for God the Exalted said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart, that you may be of the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 193-195].
The Arabic tongue does not use such letters with meaning in themselves: if you say "alif, ba, jim, ha, kha," they have no meaning. So if they have no meaning according to the Arabic tongue, we say that His saying ﴿Ha Mim﴾, ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾, ﴿Alif Lam Ra﴾ and the like have no meaning in themselves.
It is objected: if they have no meaning, they would be idle, and there is no idle speech in God's words. It is answered: they are not idle; rather the purpose is to establish proof against those polytheists, since they were unable to bring the like of the Qur'an or even one verse. They were unable, even though this Qur'an came with letters they know. Did it come with letters they do not know, so that they could excuse themselves and say: "It came with letters unknown to us"? The answer is no; the Qur'an came with letters they know.
Shaykh al-Islam, may God have mercy on him, said: "For this reason you hardly see a surah beginning with these letters without the mention of the Qur'an after them." Begin from the start of al-Baqarah until you reach the last surahs beginning with these letters, and you will find that after them is mention of the Qur'an, as an indication that this Qur'an which has defeated you, O Arabs, is made of these letters from which you form your speech. This view of Shaykh al-Islam, may God have mercy on him, is very clear. As for the claim that they have no meaning, it was stated by Mujahid ibn Jabr, the most knowledgeable of the Successors in the Book of God, the Mighty and Majestic.
He said: ﴿A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [Fussilat 2-3]. The author, the commentator, may God have mercy on him, said: "(A revelation) is the subject, (a Book) is its predicate." It would be clearer if it were said the reverse: "A Book whose verses have been detailed" as the predicate of "a revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate"; because one predicates the meaning about the essence, and does not predicate the essence about the meaning; this is the principle. So you say: "Zayd is standing," where "standing" is the predicate, and you do not say "Zayd" is the predicate. But what the author went to regarding the grammatical analysis has a basis; that is, it is not false. But if it were said that "a revelation" is the predicate placed first and "a Book" is the delayed subject, it would be clearer and more evident.
"A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate": who is meant by it? It means the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic; that is: a revelation from God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. But He brought these two noble names as an indication that the Qur'an is mercy, because its sending down is by the requirement of God's mercy, the Mighty and Majestic.
Could it not be said: "a revelation from God"? Yes, as came in another verse; but He said: ﴿from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, as an indication that this Qur'an was sent down by the requirement of God's mercy, and that God showed mercy to the servants through it.
"Al-Rahman al-Rahim" are two names of God, among the most noble names of God the Mighty and Majestic. They come together, and they come separately from each other. If they are separate, each one includes the meaning of the other. His saying ﴿The Most Merciful, established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha 5] is separate from "al-Rahim," so it includes the attribute and the act; that is, God the Exalted is described with vast mercy, and He, the Exalted, has mercy through this mercy on whomever He wills of His servants.
And in His saying ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾ also, we say: "al-Rahim" here includes the attribute and the act, because it is separate from al-Rahman. But when "al-Rahman" and "al-Rahim" come together, "al-Rahman" is for the attribute and "al-Rahim" is for the act; for this reason "al-Rahman" is on the pattern (fa'lan), and this pattern in the Arabic language implies fullness..

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 82–85 (part 1 of 3):

Then He said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than them and greater in strength﴾ [Ghafir 82], and so on to the end.

﴿Have they not travelled through the land﴾: this interrogative may be for urging, in which case it carries the sense of a command, i.e., "Travel through the land." What supports this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say: Travel through the land﴾ [al-An'am 11]. It may also be for rebuke, i.e., rebuking these people for not travelling through the land.

Travel here includes travel by foot and travel by the heart. As for travel by the heart, it returns to true reports, such that a person reads about the nations of the past. There is nothing more authentic than the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in speaking about the nations of the past, because of the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them, whom none knows except Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. There is nothing more authentic in reports than what the Noble Book has brought and what the Sunnah has confirmed. This is what we mean by travel of the heart.

Travel by foot is that a person walks to see what Allah the Exalted did to the deniers. An example of this is that a person travels to the dwellings of Thamud to see what Allah did to them. However, as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, it is not permissible to enter them except while weeping, for fear that what befell those deniers may befall him.[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2980 / 38) from Abdullah ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the companions at al-Hijr: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping. If you are not weeping, then do not enter upon them, lest there befall you what befell them."]] As for one who goes there for recreation and sightseeing, that is not permissible, as many people do today: they go there not for the sake of admonition and reflection, nor to enter while weeping, but merely to view the remains of the earlier peoples and for leisure. This is haram and not lawful.

As for His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of﴾, the grammatical analysis of the two clauses is that we say: (لم) is a particle of negation, jazm (apocopation) and qalb (conversion): a particle of negation because it negates, jazm because it jussifies, and qalb because it converts the present tense into the past.

The fa' in His saying ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا﴾ is undoubtedly a conjunctive fa', but is it conjoining to an implied omitted element or conjoining to what precedes it among the sentences? There are two opinions:
The first opinion: it conjoins to an omitted element estimated after the hamza, which is supplied according to what suits the context; on this view its placement after the hamza is natural.
The second: it conjoins to the preceding sentence, and accordingly the fa' here is displaced from its place, since its place would be before the hamza.
Both opinions are known to the scholars of grammar. On the first estimate, that it conjoins to an element estimated after the hamza, the meaning is: "Have they been heedless and so not travelled through the land?"

As for His saying ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾, the fa' conjoins to what?
* Student: To ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾.
* Shaykh: To ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾. On this view the meaning is: "Have they not travelled and so not looked?" It may also be that it is a fa' of causation, governing the subjunctive; i.e., their travel is negated, so they look, as you say: "You did not visit me, so I will honour you," and similar speech.

As for His saying ﴿كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ [Ghafir 82], ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is an interrogative noun, in the position of an accusative as a predicate of ﴿كَانَ﴾ placed first, and ﴿عَاقِبَةُ﴾ is its subject.
﴿عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾: what is the end? The end was mentioned by Allah the Exalted in Surah Muhammad in His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are similar things﴾ [Muhammad 10]. This is the benefit of looking: these deniers were stronger than these in strength, yet Allah the Mighty and Majestic destroyed them.
﴿كَانُوا أَكْثَرَ مِنْهُمْ﴾: i.e., in number. ﴿وَأَشَدَّ قُوَّةً﴾: i.e., in quality, so they were distinguished from them in number and quality. (﴿وَآثَارًا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾: from构 monuments and palaces.) ﴿فَمَا﴾..
On the first estimate, that it conjoins to an element estimated after the hamza, the meaning is: "Have they been heedless and so not travelled through the land?"

As for His saying ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾, the fa' conjoins to ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾, and on this view the meaning is: "Have they not travelled and so not looked?" It may also be a fa' of causation governing the subjunctive, i.e., their travel is negated, so they look, as you say: "You did not visit me, so I will honour you," and similar speech.

As for His saying ﴿كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ كَانُوا مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ [Ghafir 21], ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is an interrogative noun, in the position of an accusative as a predicate of ﴿كَانَ﴾ placed first, and ﴿عَاقِبَةُ﴾ is its subject. ﴿عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ كَانُوا مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾: what is the end? The end was mentioned by Allah the Exalted in Surah Muhammad in His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are similar things﴾ [Muhammad 10]. This is the benefit of looking: these deniers were stronger than these, yet Allah the Mighty and Majestic destroyed them. ﴿كَانُوا أَكْثَرَ مِنْهُمْ﴾: i.e., in number; ﴿وَأَشَدَّ قُوَّةً﴾: i.e., in quality, so they were distinguished from them in number and quality, ﴿وَآثَارًا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ [Ghafir 21]: from monuments and palaces.

﴿فَمَا أَغْنَى عَنْهُمْ مَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ [Ghafir 82]: ﴿مَا﴾ is a negation, ﴿أَغْنَى﴾ is a past-tense verb, and in ﴿مَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾, ﴿مَا﴾ is a relative pronoun serving as the subject, and ﴿كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ is the relative clause. It may also be that ﴿مَا﴾ is interrogative, and the meaning is: "What then availed them what they earned?" The interrogative is more forceful, since it carries negation together with challenge: what thing availed them their earnings when Allah destroyed them? Is that so?
* Student: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: What did you say about ﴿مَا﴾?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: You did not say "yes, yes"?! Fine. This neighbour of yours on the right, what do you say?
* Student: Relative.
* Shaykh: No, we did not say this; this is what you said.
* Student: That it is a negation ﴿مَا﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, well done, may Allah bless you. If it is a negation, the meaning is: "Their earnings did not avail them anything." If it is interrogative, the sense is: "What availed them what they used to earn?" A parallel to this is the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Have you considered, if We let them enjoy for years, then there comes to them what they were promised, what they were enjoying will not avail them﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 205–207], i.e., "What thing availed them?" or the meaning is the negation of availing.
* Student: The one who goes to the dwellings of Thamud for lesson but cannot weep, does he feign weeping?
* Shaykh: I do not know of it in a hadith, except: "If you do not weep, then feign weeping" [[Narrated by Ibn Majah (1337) from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him).]]. He said: "Do not enter them except while you are weeping" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2980/38) from the hadith of Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), and its wording: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the companions at al-Hijr: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping. If you are not weeping, then do not enter upon them, lest there befall you what befell them."]]. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by it, he covered his head, meaning he covered it, lowered it, and hastened.
* Student: So we say: weep or return?
* Shaykh: Yes, we say: either you weep or you return. If you are not weeping and you pass through the town, hasten and cover your head as the Messenger (peace be upon him) did.
* Student: Shaykh, on this basis we say that it is impermissible for one who photographs these sites and shows them to people and publishes them?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. The apparent ruling is that prohibition is closer, because he shows them only to demonstrate the strength of those people, not to demonstrate that Allah destroyed them despite their strength. This is the apparent intent of such photographers.
* Student: Does this include all ancient monuments or only those who were punished?
* Shaykh: We have read a verse that indicates the intended meaning: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are similar things﴾.
* Student: We said: if a person owns a cow, may he ride it? And in the hadith: "We were not created for this" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2324) with his chain from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "While a man was riding a cow, it turned to him and said: I was not created for this, I was created for ploughing..." the hadith.]]...?
* Shaykh: The way to reconcile these is that this cow was burdened with what it could not bear, or it would be hard for it to be ridden, since some animals not accustomed to riding find it difficult even when they are able to carry the rider.
* Student: Some people use these livestock in sorcery (...) and similar things?
* Shaykh: Without doubt, using these animals for what is forbidden, intentionally or in essence, is not permissible. Even if one rides these animals to reach a town where indecencies are committed or gambling is played, this is haram.
* Student: Some earlier peoples whom Allah destroyed outside their homelands, such as the Pharaohs, shall we say: we do not enter their monuments, just as we analogize with the dwellings of Thamud?
* Shaykh: No. On this basis we say: it is permissible for us to enter the place where Pharaoh was drowned, and it is permissible for us to enter Egypt as well, because Pharaoh was not destroyed in Egypt.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than them and greater in strength and in monuments in the land, but what they earned did not avail them. (82) When their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they exulted in what knowledge they had, and there encompassed them what they used to mock. (83) When they saw Our might, they said: We believe in Allah alone and disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him. (84) Their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might; this is the way of Allah which has passed among His servants, and there the disbelievers lost﴾ [Ghafir 82–85].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ We mentioned in this construction ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا﴾ and similar forms, two analyses?
* Student: The first analysis: we say that the hamza here is an interrogative hamza, and after it there is an implied clause, so this is from the category of conjoining clauses to implied clauses, and the estimate is according to the context.
* Shaykh: The omitted element is estimated according to what it implies.
* Student: And here its estimate: "Have they been heedless and so not travelled?"
* Shaykh: The second aspect?
* Student: The second aspect: the fa' is delayed from its place, the original being "fa-a-lam yasiru", and it conjoins to what came before.
* Shaykh: And the clause is conjoined to what came before.
The second is easier, since the first may be difficult or hard to estimate the omitted element; but this one is easy, containing merely the displacement of the fa' from its place.

As for His saying ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾: i.e., upon the earth, since ﴿فِي﴾ denotes enclosure. If we took ﴿فِي﴾ as enclosure in this context, the verse would mean they should enter into the inside of the earth, and this is definitely not intended. So ﴿فِي﴾ here means (على), like His saying: ﴿Are you secure from Him who is in the heaven?﴾ [al-Mulk 16], i.e., upon the heaven, and it is not meant that Allah is inside the heaven, for that is impossible, since His Throne has encompassed the heavens and the earth.

As for His saying ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ it includes travel by foot and travel by the heart. As for travel by foot, it is well known. As for travel by the heart, its meaning is that a person reflects on what passed of the history of nations, and the most authentic reference we return to regarding the histories of nations is the Noble Qur'an.

As for His saying ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾, this is conjoined to (يسيروا); meaning that Allah rebuked them for two matters: not travelling, and not looking. They did not travel and did not look: ﴿so that they might look at how was the end of those before them﴾. The looking here: is it the looking of insight or of sight? If we say that His saying ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾ is travel of foot, then the looking is sight; and if we say ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾ is travel of heart, then the looking is insight.

﴿كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾: we parsed ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ as a predicate placed first of ﴿كَانَ﴾, and here the placing first is necessary, since ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is an interrogative, and the interrogative has precedence; accordingly it is a predicate placed first of ﴿كَانَ﴾, and ﴿عَاقِبَةُ﴾ is its subject: ﴿the end of those before them﴾, i.e., of the nations. What is the end? Allah indicated it in Surah Muhammad in His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are similar things﴾.

Then Allah explained the condition of those earlier peoples, saying: ﴿They were more numerous than them and greater in strength and in monuments in the land﴾ [Ghafir 82]: more numerous than them in number, and abundance of number necessitates strength in quantity; and greater in strength is strength in quality. Then He said: ﴿and monuments in the land﴾, i.e., of buildings, palaces and others, and despite that this multitude did not benefit them, nor this strength. He says: (from monuments and palaces) is an explanation of His saying ﴿وَآثَارًا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾.

﴿فَمَا أَغْنَى عَنْهُمْ مَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾: ﴿مَا أَغْنَى﴾: ﴿ما﴾ may be a negation, i.e., "what they earned did not avail them"; and it may be interrogative, and the meaning is: "What then availed them?" The interrogative here is more forceful, since it is imbued with challenge: what thing availed them? The answer: nothing. ﴿فَمَا أَغْنَى عَنْهُمْ مَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾, i.e., what they used to earn of strength, monuments in the land and other things, because Allah the Exalted destroyed them and destroyed their strength.

﴿فَلَمَّا جَاءَتْهُمْ رُسُلُهُمْ بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ﴾: this which comes after mention of their destruction is in fact a return to explaining what occurred. Allah sent to them messengers with clear proofs, and sent down books; but when their messengers came to them with the clear proofs, the author said: (the manifest miracles). The correct wording would be: the clear signs. He, may Allah have mercy on him, rendered al-bayyinat as meaning al-zahirat (the manifest), which is true, and made (al-bayyinat) an adjective of an omitted noun whose estimate is: the miracles; and this is open to scrutiny. Rather, one should estimate: the signs (āyāt). This is because the word "miracles" (mu'jizat) does not occur in the Book and the Sunnah in place of āyāt at all; furthermore, miracles may come from messengers and from non-messengers, for sorcerers, for example, are brought miracles by the devils. But āyāt, i.e., the signs indicating their truthfulness, are more eloquent; therefore, when you find in books, and you find it often, "the miracles" or "the miracle of the prophets" or similar, then set it aside entirely and say instead "the signs," as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said, "the signs." And āyāt, as I told you, is more precise than the word "miracles," since "miracles" includes what overwhelms humans among what the devils produce together with sorcerers and others.

(﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ أي الكفار ﴿بِمَا عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ أي: الرسل ﴿مِنَ الْعِلْمِ﴾ فرح استهزاء وضحك منكرين له) ﴿فَلَمَّا جَاءَتْهُمْ رُسُلُهُمْ بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ فَرِحُوا﴾ The *wāw* (واو) is the subject (fā'il). Who is the one rejoicing? The author says: "(i.e., the disbelievers)." This is correct: the disbelievers rejoiced at what they had of knowledge. As for His words ﴿بِمَا عِنْدَهُمْ﴾, the pronoun returns to the messengers, according to the author's interpretation: "at what the messengers had of knowledge," meaning what they brought of clear proofs. But is this rejoicing the rejoicing of good tidings (istibshar) or the rejoicing of mockery? The author says it is the rejoicing of mockery, laughter and derision.

However, if you reflect on this interpretation, you will find it to be a *taḥrīf* (distortion) rather than an interpretation, because of its semantic and linguistic problems. As for the linguistic problem, it causes a scattering of pronouns: the *wāw* in ﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ refers to the disbelievers, while the *hā'* in ﴿بِمَا عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refers to the messengers. This is a scattering of pronouns. If we keep the speech in one continuous structure, there is no doubt that the *hā'* refers to the disbelievers, meaning "at what the disbelievers had of knowledge."

As for the semantic problem, rejoicing (*farah*) originally means joy at good tidings. If we turn it away from its apparent meaning to be rejoicing of mockery, this removes the meaning from what the apparent wording indicates. In summary, this interpretation that the author mentioned is very weak, indeed it is a distortion. The correct meaning is: the disbelievers rejoiced at what they had, that is, at what the disbelievers had of knowledge, and they said: "We are more knowledgeable about what benefits us, and what benefits our worldly life and our religion, which we follow. As for you, O messengers, you are sorcerers or madmen," as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Thus, no messenger came to those before them except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman!"﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 52]. If they believed in their hearts, or said with their tongues what they did not believe, that the messengers were sorcerers or madmen, then undoubtedly they would consider what they had of knowledge to be the true knowledge, and so they would rejoice in it.

Based on this, we say: the rejoicing here is the rejoicing of arrogance (*baṭar*) and of assumed good tidings, that they possessed a knowledge superior to the knowledge of the prophets, peace be upon them. ﴿They rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾ [Ghafir 83]. It may amaze a person sometimes what some scholars adopt in explaining verses or hadiths.

Now, if you recited this verse to a common person: ﴿So when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾, upon what does the pronoun in ﴿بِمَا عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refer for this layman? To the disbelievers: they rejoiced in what they had, and a person rejoices in what he has, not in what others have.

﴿And there befell them what they used to mock﴾ [Ghafir 83]. ﴿حَاقَ﴾ (ḥāqa): the author says it means "descended" (nazala). However, it is not exactly like "nazala" in every respect, because "nazala" can be used for good and for evil. ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 193-194]. Is this good or evil? Good. But "ḥāqa" is only used for evil. One does not say "ḥāqa bihi al-Qur'an" or "ḥāqa 'alayhi al-Qur'an" as one says "nazala 'alayhi." So "ḥāqa" here means "nazala," but it is only used for the descent of evil. It is evil for the one upon whom it descends, though it may be good for others.

﴿وَحَاقَ بِهِمْ مَا كَانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ [Ghafir 83]: ﴿مَا﴾ is the subject (fā'il) of ﴿حَاقَ﴾. ﴿كَانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ means: previously. That is, when the might of Allah the Mighty and Majestic came to them and descended upon them, ﴿there befell them what they used to mock﴾ previously, when they used to mock the messengers, what they brought, and the laws, and perhaps even mock Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Consider the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Was it Allah and His verses and His messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ [At-Tawbah 65]. This shows that the disbelievers mock Allah, mock His verses, and mock the messengers.

(﴿وَحَاقَ بِهِمْ مَا كَانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ i.e., the punishment) meaning: the punishment they used to mock befell them, when the messengers threatened them with it. They began mocking, saying: "What is the punishment you speak of? Where is it?" They asked in mockery.

﴿فَلَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا﴾ [Ghafir 84] i.e., the severity of Our punishment. ﴿رَأَوْا﴾ means with their eyes, that is, they saw it with the sight of the eye. And *ba's* (بأس) is the most severe punishment.

﴿قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ وَحْدَهُ وَكَفَرْنَا بِمَا كُنَّا بِهِ مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [Ghafir 84]: ﴿قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ وَحْدَهُ﴾ i.e., apart from our associates and apart from what we used to worship. This is the utmost sincerity. Then they affirmed this with their saying: ﴿وَكَفَرْنَا بِمَا كُنَّا بِهِ مُشْرِكِينَ﴾. ﴿بِمَا﴾: the *bā'* (باء) is a preposition governing ﴿كَفَرْنَا﴾. And ﴿بِهِ﴾ may be causal, meaning "because of what we used to associate," or it may be connected to ﴿مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ as the preposition connected to its governing word. The meaning: when they saw the punishment of Allah, they believed. But would this faith benefit them? No.

When Pharaoh drowned and drowning overtook him, what did he say?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: He said: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel have believed﴾.
* Shaykh: Correct. He said: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel have believed﴾ [Yunus 90]. But what was said to him? It was said to him: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾ [Yunus 91]. So his faith did not benefit him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And repentance is not [accepted] from those who continue to do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have now repented"﴾ [An-Nisa' 18]. Repentance does not benefit this person, because he saw and witnessed. He witnessed what was no longer unseen, which he would have disbelieved in. Faith based on witnessing does not benefit, because every person believes in what he sees, even if he is the greatest of disbelievers. What a person is praised for, and what saves him from the punishment of Allah, is that he believes in the unseen, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ [Al-Baqarah 3].

﴿They said, "We have believed in Allah alone and disbelieved in what we used to associate with Him."﴾ [Ghafir 84]. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So their faith was not of benefit to them when they saw Our punishment﴾ [Ghafir 85]. ﴿لَمْ يَكُ﴾: its original form is *lam yakun*, but the *nūn* was deleted for lightness. Deletion and retention have occurred in two verses of the Book of Allah. Allah the Exalted said concerning Abraham: ﴿and he was not among the polytheists﴾, and He said: ﴿and he was not among the polytheists﴾ [An-Nahl 120]. It is one sentence in which the *nūn* was deleted and also retained. This deletion is for lightness, and it has well-known conditions in the books of grammar.

﴿فَلَمْ يَكُ يَنْفَعُهُمْ إِيمَانُهُمْ لَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا﴾ [Ghafir 85] (*īmān*, إيمانُ): do you parse it as the postponed noun of *yakun*, or as the subject of *yanfa'u* with the implied pronoun as its subject? The second. The estimation according to this: "so their faith did not benefit them." According to the first, it would be: "so it did not benefit them, their faith," and then the subject of *yakun* would be an omitted pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n).

And His words ﴿لَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا﴾: ﴿لَمَّا﴾ here is an adverb meaning "when" (ḥīn). Know that *lammā* (لَمَّا) comes in the Arabic language in several ways:

First: that it is a temporal adverb meaning "when," as in this verse. The meaning of ﴿لَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا﴾ is "when they saw Our punishment."

It also comes as a jussive particle (jāzima), like His saying: ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad 8].

It comes as a conditional particle, like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 89].

It comes with the meaning of "except" (illā), as in His saying: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾ [At-Tariq 4], and likewise His saying: ﴿And indeed, all of them will be brought before Us [for judgment]﴾ [Ya-Sin 32].

So these are four meanings of *lammā*. The first meaning: "when," as in this verse: ﴿So their faith was not of benefit to them when they saw Our punishment﴾ [Ghafir 85], meaning when they saw Our punishment. The second: with the meaning of "except." Like?

* Student: ﴿And indeed, all of them will be brought before Us [for judgment]﴾.
* Shaykh: Another verse?
* Student: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾.
* Shaykh: The conditional one, like?
* Student: ﴿So when they saw Our punishment, they said, "We have believed in Allah alone"﴾ [Ghafir 84].
* Shaykh: ﴿So when they saw Our punishment, they said, "We have believed in Allah alone"﴾. Correct. And likewise: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾. It comes as a jussive particle. What is its example? ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾. It is also for negation: jussive and negating. However, the difference between it and *lam* is that *lammā* indicates the nearness of what follows it: ﴿they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾, but they will taste it soon. Unlike *lam*, which comes for absolute negation.

﴿لَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا﴾. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is the way of Allah which has already occurred among His servants﴾ [Ghafir 85]. ﴿سُنَّتَ﴾ (sunnata): the commentator says: "its being in the accusative is as an infinitive (maṣdar) with a verb implied from its own root." *Sunnah* (سُنَّة) means a way or practice: this is the way of Allah.

And ﴿سُنَّتَ﴾ in such a construction may be nominative, meaning "the sunnah of Allah," as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "this is the sunnah of Allah." It may also be accusative. The author says it is accusative by a verb implied from its own root, meaning: Allah established His sunnah with them.

﴿سُنَّتَ اللَّهِ﴾ may also be an infinitive whose governing verb is omitted but implied from the preceding sentence, because this expression has exactly the same meaning as what precedes it, that is, ﴿the sunnah of Allah﴾ means what precedes it, namely the seizing of the deniers with punishment. So it is accusative by the content of the sentence, not by an implied verb. What the author, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned is undoubtedly a valid aspect. The important point is that *sunnah* means "way." So what is the way of Allah? The way of Allah, the Exalted, is the destruction and punishment of the deniers, and that if they believe after the punishment descends, it will not benefit them.

(﴿الَّتِي قَدْ خَلَتْ فِي عِبَادِهِ﴾ [Al-Fath 23]: among the nations, that faith does not benefit them at the time the punishment descends.) This is one point. The second is that He punishes the deniers. So the sunnah we derive from this verse is two things: first, the destruction of the deniers, and second, that their faith does not benefit them when they see the punishment.

He said: ﴿And there the disbelievers will lose﴾ [Ghafir 85]. The author explained ﴿خَسِرَ﴾ to mean: "their loss became evident to everyone, although they were losers at every time before that." ﴿وَخَسِرَ هُنَالِكَ الْكَافِرُونَ﴾. It is known that *hunālika* (هنالك) is an adverb of place or time? Place. This is the original usage: it is a demonstrative pointing to a place. It may be used as a demonstrative for time. You say: *hunāka* meaning "at that time," and this verse is an example. Now, if you say "so-and-so is there (hunāka)," this is a place adverb, and this is the original usage. If you say, for example, "so-and-so's arrival was then (hunāka)," pointing to a time, it has become a demonstrative for time, but this is contrary to the original usage.

It remains to be said: the disbelievers lost at that time. Were the disbelievers not losers at all times? Indeed they were, but their loss became apparent and clear, because before the punishment descended upon them they thought they were winning. This is why they rejoiced in what knowledge they had. But when the punishment befell them, their loss became manifest.

* From the benefits of these verses: encouraging reflection on the conditions of earlier nations. This is derived from: ﴿Have they not traveled through the land and observed how was the end of those before them?﴾ [Ghafir 82]. The point of evidence: Allah rebuked them for not traveling.

* Another benefit: travel through the land with the feet, if not accompanied by contemplation and taking lessons, does not benefit. This is from His saying: ﴿Have they not traveled [in the land] so they might have hearts by which to reason and ears by which to hear?﴾ ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾ (then look).

* Related to this: what many people do today of traveling to the dwellings of Thamud, where they travel with their bodies but not with their hearts, and do not take lessons, but go there to see the glories and the traces of the people that show their strength. This is not permissible. Whoever travels to those dwellings must enter them weeping, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "If you are not weeping, then do not enter them." Feigned weeping does not help, because of his saying: "If you are not weeping, then do not enter them." He did not say: "then weep." So whoever has not prepared himself with this quality, which the Prophet ﷺ permitted for entering the dwellings of Thamud, it is not permissible for him to enter. Most people who go there now go only for sightseeing and recreation, and this is forbidden.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: some nations are stronger and have greater monuments than what Quraysh had, because of His saying: ﴿They were more numerous than them and greater in strength and in traces left upon the earth﴾ [Ghafir 82].

* From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah the Exalted is not overcome by the strength of the enemy nor by the enemy's multitude, for Allah the Exalted destroyed them despite their numbers and strength.

Does Allah the Mighty and Majestic, when He wills to destroy them, make their destruction extend over a period of time until He finishes them? No. Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them one shout, and they became like the dry, broken branches of a fence builder﴾ [Al-Qamar 31]. ﴿الْمُحْتَظِرِ﴾ means one who surrounds his land with a *ḥiẓār* (fence), and the *ḥiẓār*, as you know, is made of light sticks or palm fronds, and the sun and wind quickly consume it.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: a person's strength and the multitude of his numbers do not avail him anything against the punishment of Allah, because of Allah's saying: ﴿So what they used to earn did not avail them﴾ [Al-Hijr 84].

* From the benefits of these verses: Allah, glorified and exalted, sent the messengers with clear signs that demonstrate His truthfulness.

* Two or more benefits follow from this: the mercy of Allah toward His servants, and the wisdom of Allah in His actions.

As for Allah's mercy toward His servants: if Allah had sent them messengers without signs, that would have been a burden beyond their capacity, because a person cannot believe in a messenger without signs that show his truthfulness. Otherwise every liar could claim to be a messenger.

As for the wisdom: it is clear that when Allah, glorified and exalted, sent the messengers, He did not leave them without means, but gave them what humankind could believe in on its like, as our Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and his family, informed: "Allah did not send a messenger except that He gave him what humankind could believe in on its like." What the Messenger, peace be upon him, was given was the revelation, the Qur'an. This is why he said: "So I hope to be the one with the most followers on the Day of Resurrection," because the Qur'an is a sign remaining until the Day of Resurrection, or until Allah permits the corruption of the world. As for the signs of the messengers, most of them end within their own time, but the sign of the Messenger remains.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the signs of the messengers are clear and do not admit doubt, because of His saying: "clear" (*bayyināt*).

* It follows from this: the scholar who spreads the law of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, should, when he spreads it among people, do so in a clear manner with no ambiguity. Why? First: to follow the example of the messengers. Second: so that the listener gains more tranquility, because tranquility has an effect on accepting what is presented and on acting upon it. If the truth is not made clear to a person in a way that brings tranquility, you will find him walking or taking the truth while hesitant. But if tranquility is increased, he benefits from that. Is that not so, brother? What did you say?

* Student: The Prophet must have followers?
* Shaykh: The Prophet? No, I did not say that. Did I say this?
* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: The Messenger said: "And the Prophet, and with him no one."

* The Student: Shaykh, may God bless you. We said that destruction happens once. Isn't this a matter of the nations' differences? With 'Ad, God the Exalted sent upon them a furious wind (rih sarsar) in days of misfortune (ayyam nahsat). Or was the wind sent upon them and it destroyed them, and then it continued upon them?

* The Shaykh: No. With 'Ad, God the Exalted prolonged the punishment for them, because they would say: "Who is stronger than us in power?" So God sent upon them the wind, which was the lightest and gentlest of things, and it destroyed them.

* The Student: Little by little?

* The Shaykh: He says: ﴿He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days, consecutively, so you would see the people in it fallen down as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Haqqah 7]. During this period, some of them may have perished on the first day, some on the second day, according to what shelters they had or did not have.

* The Student: Is this an exception to the punishment?

* The Shaykh: No, because He sent the punishment upon them in this form.

* The Student: But did we notice the benefit, or not?

* The Shaykh: No (...), because this is the basic principle. And it is said: even though this lasted, from the moment the punishment began, whoever was to perish perished.

* The Student: What was reported from the Imam (...) said: (...). Could it be said that they had instruments with which they made these things? Now, with the existence of these instruments, it is not possible for a person..

* The Shaykh: It may imply instruments, or it may imply that, because of their numbers, each one took up a task and performed it, and you know that when a person becomes accustomed to a specific work, even if it is arduous, it becomes easy for him.

* The Student: At the end of the surah He said: ﴿And the disbelievers were lost therein﴾ [Ghafir 85]. Is it permissible to change, meaning (...)?

* The Shaykh: The benefit of this is to clarify that every disbeliever is a falsifier (mubtil), having no truth with him, and every falsifier says nothing but falsehood is a disbeliever; that is, the falsifier in all his states is a disbeliever; meaning he has none of the truth with him, and the disbeliever is a falsifier who likewise has none of the truth with him. So the variation in expression is for increasing the meaning.
Just as it also occurs sometimes in the variant readings (qira'at), such as the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their people﴾ [al-Nur 27]. In another reading: "tasta'dhinu" (you seek permission). ﴿If a deviator comes to you with news, verify it﴾ [al-Hujurat 6]; in one reading: ﴿fa-tathabbatu﴾ (so be steadfast in verifying); so this reading explains the second reading.

* The Student: In the orthography of the Qur'an, ﴿sunnata Allah﴾ [Ghafir 85], the ﴿sunnata﴾ has an open ta'. In Surat al-Dukhan it has the ta' marbuta (ta' of feminine). What is the reason for this?

* The Shaykh: Have you understood his question? He says: the ta' in ﴿sunnata﴾ is open, and the rule is that it is marbuta, because it is for the singular. It is said that the Uthmanic script is not according to the well-known rules now; rather it is tawqifi (fixed by revelation/transmission). The scholars, may God have mercy on them, differed on whether the Qur'an must be written in the Uthmanic script, or not required, or whether one should distinguish between teaching young or older students, in three opinions:
The first opinion: it is not permissible to write the Qur'an except in the Uthmanic script in every case, even if you are teaching children. So in the Uthmanic script you write: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers a decree of specified times﴾ [al-Nisa' 103], you write (al-salwa) with a waw, even if you are teaching a child, following the script. ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾ [al-Baqarah 43]: al-salat with a waw and (al-zakwa) with a waw, because this is the Uthmanic script.
Some said: rather it is not required, because when the Uthmanic script was set in the mushaf, it happened to be in this form; and if the Uthmanic script had been not according to this rule, it would have been written according to the rule that was current at that time. So the matter is not tawqifi, but it happened that the script at that time was in this form, so the Qur'an was written upon it. This is because the Qur'an was not revealed in writing so that we would say it must be as it was written; rather it was revealed to be recited, and the rules of orthography vary from place to place. This opinion has a strong basis, because we know with certainty that if the orthographic rule had been otherwise in that era, it would have been written according to the well-known rule of that era.
The third opinion says: if the Qur'an is written for children to learn, write it according to the rule known among them; and if it is for adults, meaning one writes a mushaf for himself, then he should write it according to the Uthmanic script. This combines the two opinions, because if you write the Qur'an for a child according to the Uthmanic script, you would cause him to distort it, because the rules before him differ from the script, so he distorts it, reading for example: al-zakat - al-zakwa, al-salat - al-salwa, al-riba - al-ribw, and so on, clear.
So I incline to the view that there is no harm in writing according to the prevailing rule for the learner, without doubt; for others there is some allowance, but the view of prohibition is open to question.
* * *
* The Student: I seek refuge with God from the accursed Satan. In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate: ﴿Ha Mim. A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. A Book whose verses have been detailed, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know. Bearing good tidings and warning, yet most of them turn away, so they do not hear﴾ [Fussilat 1-4].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with God from the accursed Satan.
* Among the benefits of this verse, ﴿When their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾: the clarification of the wisdom and mercy of God, the Mighty and Majestic, since He made the signs that the messengers brought clear signs, so that no proof remains.
* Among its benefits: that the disbelievers boast of the knowledge they have, even if it is falsehood; as He says: ﴿They rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾ [Ghafir 83]. What existed previously exists now as well: some of those people to whom God gave worldly knowledge, you find them rejoicing in it, saying: it is better than the knowledge of those who seclude themselves, meaning the scholars of the Shari'ah.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strong warning against rejecting what the messengers brought; as He says: ﴿And there befell them what they used to mock﴾ [Ghafir 83].
Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir 84], to the end.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that those people who denied the messengers, when they see the punishment, say: "We believe." The example of this is Pharaoh, when drowning overtook him, he said: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾ [Yunus 90].
* Among its benefits: that those who believe after the punishment has descended upon them gain nothing from their faith; as He says: ﴿But their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir 85].
Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the sunnah of God, the Mighty and Majestic, regarding His servants is one; He does not show favoritism to anyone for wealth, poverty, or anything else; rather the most honored of creation before God is the most righteous; as He says: ﴿the sunnah of God that has passed among His servants﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the warning against denying the messengers, and that whoever denies the messengers will be overtaken by what overtook them of punishment, that is, what overtook the earlier nations of punishment.
* Among its benefits also: the manifestation of loss for these deniers before they die; as He says: ﴿and the disbelievers were lost therein﴾, that is: when the might came upon them, the loss became clear to them. ﴿And the disbelievers were lost therein﴾.
Then the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, to the end. The basmalah has been discussed at length before, and we explained that it is a verse of God's Book, but it is not a verse belonging to the surah after it or the one before it; rather it is a verse brought at the beginning of surahs, except Surat Bara'ah.
As for its meaning, a person says: I begin with every name of God. We made the meaning "with every name of God" because "ism" (name) is a singular construct (mufrad mudaf), and a singular construct gives generality. Every singular construct added to a definite noun gives generality. Have you not considered the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿And if you were to count the favor of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ [al-Nahl 18]? ﴿Ni'mata Allah﴾: if we looked at its wording we would say it is singular, but it is many and cannot be counted. So this singular that is added becomes general; this is the rule: every singular construct added to a definite noun gives generality; for this reason we said: "with every name of God."
And (al-Rahman al-Rahim) are two attributes of the Name Allah. But the first takes into account the description, and the second takes into account the act, which is the conveying of mercy. As for the object of this prepositional phrase, it is omitted, and it is estimated as a suitable delayed verb for the context. So if you want to read and say: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," estimate "I read" (aqra'). This was chosen, meaning it was chosen that it be a verb, because the original in action is verbs; for this reason the verb acts without condition, while nouns that act like verbs require conditions, as is known in the science of grammar. We chose that it be delayed for two benefits:
The first benefit: seeking blessing by mentioning the name of God.
The second benefit: the intention of restriction (hasr), because when the operator is delayed, that is a restriction. If you say "Zaydan akrim" (Zayd, honor!), the meaning is: do not honor other than him; but if you say "akrim Zaydan" (honor Zayd), it does not prevent honoring others. So we delayed it for two benefits: the first: seeking blessing by mentioning God, the Mighty and Majestic. And the second?
* Student: Restriction.
* The Shaykh: Conveying restriction. We estimated it as suitable because it makes the intended meaning clearer. If someone said: "In the name of God I begin," we would say: correct, but it does not make the intended meaning as clear as "In the name of God I read," because beginning can be for reading or for other than reading; for this reason it was chosen to suit the context. The summary now: the object of the prepositional phrase is omitted, a verb, delayed, suitable to the context.
God the Exalted said: ﴿Ha Mim﴾, and the commentator said: "God knows best what He means by it." This is the etiquette with the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ: that about what you do not know the meaning of, say: God knows best what He means by it; as God the Exalted says: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of those will be questioned﴾ [al-Isra' 36].
But someone may say: we know that these disjointed letters found in many surahs have no meaning; we know this from the Qur'an's indication, for God the Exalted said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart, that you may be of the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 193-195].
The Arabic tongue does not use such letters with meaning in themselves: if you say "alif, ba, jim, ha, kha," they have no meaning. So if they have no meaning according to the Arabic tongue, we say that His saying ﴿Ha Mim﴾, ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾, ﴿Alif Lam Ra﴾ and the like have no meaning in themselves.
It is objected: if they have no meaning, they would be idle, and there is no idle speech in God's words. It is answered: they are not idle; rather the purpose is to establish proof against those polytheists, since they were unable to bring the like of the Qur'an or even one verse. They were unable, even though this Qur'an came with letters they know. Did it come with letters they do not know, so that they could excuse themselves and say: "It came with letters unknown to us"? The answer is no; the Qur'an came with letters they know.
Shaykh al-Islam, may God have mercy on him, said: "For this reason you hardly see a surah beginning with these letters without the mention of the Qur'an after them." Begin from the start of al-Baqarah until you reach the last surahs beginning with these letters, and you will find that after them is mention of the Qur'an, as an indication that this Qur'an which has defeated you, O Arabs, is made of these letters from which you form your speech. This view of Shaykh al-Islam, may God have mercy on him, is very clear. As for the claim that they have no meaning, it was stated by Mujahid ibn Jabr, the most knowledgeable of the Successors in the Book of God, the Mighty and Majestic.
He said: ﴿A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [Fussilat 2-3]. The author, the commentator, may God have mercy on him, said: "(A revelation) is the subject, (a Book) is its predicate." It would be clearer if it were said the reverse: "A Book whose verses have been detailed" as the predicate of "a revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate"; because one predicates the meaning about the essence, and does not predicate the essence about the meaning; this is the principle. So you say: "Zayd is standing," where "standing" is the predicate, and you do not say "Zayd" is the predicate. But what the author went to regarding the grammatical analysis has a basis; that is, it is not false. But if it were said that "a revelation" is the predicate placed first and "a Book" is the delayed subject, it would be clearer and more evident.
"A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate": who is meant by it? It means the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic; that is: a revelation from God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. But He brought these two noble names as an indication that the Qur'an is mercy, because its sending down is by the requirement of God's mercy, the Mighty and Majestic.
Could it not be said: "a revelation from God"? Yes, as came in another verse; but He said: ﴿from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, as an indication that this Qur'an was sent down by the requirement of God's mercy, and that God showed mercy to the servants through it.
"Al-Rahman al-Rahim" are two names of God, among the most noble names of God the Mighty and Majestic. They come together, and they come separately from each other. If they are separate, each one includes the meaning of the other. His saying ﴿The Most Merciful, established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha 5] is separate from "al-Rahim," so it includes the attribute and the act; that is, God the Exalted is described with vast mercy, and He, the Exalted, has mercy through this mercy on whomever He wills of His servants.
And in His saying ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾ also, we say: "al-Rahim" here includes the attribute and the act, because it is separate from al-Rahman. But when "al-Rahman" and "al-Rahim" come together, "al-Rahman" is for the attribute and "al-Rahim" is for the act; for this reason "al-Rahman" is on the pattern (fa'lan), and this pattern in the Arabic language implies fullness..

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 40, verse 82–85 (part 1 of 3):

Then He said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than them and greater in strength﴾ [Ghafir 82], and so on to the end.

﴿Have they not travelled through the land﴾: this interrogative may be for urging, in which case it carries the sense of a command, i.e., "Travel through the land."
